Instructions

ANSI: 6.3.2, 8.3; rexxref: General Concepts > Clauses and Instructions

An instruction is a clause that does something when the interpreter reaches it. A program is a sequence of clauses, and the interpreter runs them in the order written until an instruction moves control elsewhere or the program ends. This chapter specifies what each kind of instruction does. The lexical chapter already says where a clause ends and how its first tokens decide what kind it is, and the expressions chapter says how the expressions inside an instruction are evaluated, so this chapter takes both as given.

The pages of this chapter are:

  • Assignments: symbol = expression and the extended forms such as +=.
  • Message instructions: a message term used as a clause, and the assignments term~name = expression and term[...] = expression.
  • Commands: an expression sent to the current environment, and the return code that comes back.

The keyword rule below lists the keyword instructions, with a link on each name whose page exists. The lexical chapter calls a keyword instruction simply an instruction, and this chapter says keyword instruction wherever the other three kinds are also in play. The directives, which start with two colons, are not instructions, and their own chapter specifies them.

Kinds of instruction

[instr.index.kinds]

A clause that is not a null clause, a label or a directive is an instruction of one of four kinds: an assignment, a message instruction, a keyword instruction or a command. The lexical rule decides from the first tokens of a clause which of the four it is, so a symbol followed by = is an assignment before any keyword is looked at. This chapter adds the naming and the pages. A message assignment, which the message page specifies, is a message instruction like the lone message term, and what the lexical chapter calls an instruction is the keyword instruction here. Because every clause that is none of the other three is a command, a clause that holds only a function call, a string, or a parenthesized expression is a command, and so is a message term that an operator or another term follows.

address system
o = .box~new
o~tell
say 'keyword'
'exit 2'
say rc
::class box
::method tell
  say 'told'

told
keyword
2
[instr.index.keywords]

The keyword instruction names are ADDRESS, ARG, CALL, DO, DROP, EXIT, EXPOSE, FORWARD, GUARD, IF, INTERPRET, ITERATE, LEAVE, LOOP, NOP, NUMERIC, OPTIONS, PARSE, PROCEDURE, PULL, PUSH, QUEUE, RAISE, REPLY, RETURN, SAY, SELECT, SIGNAL, TRACE and USE. A clause that is not an assignment and whose first token is one of these names is that instruction, whatever the case of the name. A name that is not on the list starts no keyword instruction. A clause that begins with such a name is a command, so that the name is evaluated as an expression like any other symbol. The names of directives and of builtin functions are not keywords: endlocal as a clause is a command, and so are class and method without colons. The words THEN, ELSE, END, WHEN and OTHERWISE are the exception, and the next rule covers them.

address nosuch
call try 'nop'
call try 'NoP'
call try 'trace n'
call try 'push 1'
call try 'endlocal'
call try 'class'
call try 'method'
exit
try:
  signal on failure name sent
  interpret arg(1)
  say arg(1) '=> instruction'
  return
sent: say arg(1) '=> command' condition('d')
  return

nop => instruction
NoP => instruction
trace n => instruction
push 1 => instruction
endlocal => command ENDLOCAL
class => command CLASS
method => command METHOD
[instr.index.parts]

The words THEN, ELSE, WHEN, OTHERWISE and END are not instructions: they are parts of IF, SELECT and DO, and the pages of those instructions say where each may stand. A clause that begins with one of them where its construct does not expect it is not a command either. It raises a SYNTAX error: 8.1 for THEN, 8.2 for ELSE, 9.1 for WHEN, 9.2 for OTHERWISE and 10.1 for END. In a program file the error is found when the program is read, as the expression rules say, and the program writes nothing.

call try 'then'
call try 'else'
call try 'when 1'
call try 'otherwise'
call try 'end'
exit
try:
  signal on syntax name e
  interpret arg(1)
  say arg(1) '=> ok'
  return
e: say arg(1) '=>' condition('o')~code
  return

then => 8.1
else => 8.2
when 1 => 9.1
otherwise => 9.2
end => 10.1

ADDRESS

ADDRESS [name | VALUE expression | (expression)] [command] [WITH redirection]

ANSI: 6.3.2.21, 8.3.1; rexxref: Keyword Instructions > ADDRESS

Deviations: D52

ADDRESS chooses the environment that receives the commands of a program, and it can also send a single command to another environment, and redirect where a command reads its input and writes its output. This page specifies the forms of the instruction and the redirections. The environment that is current, the name that the ADDRESS function answers, the swap of the current and the previous environment and the scope of both across calls are specified with that function, and the page links them. What a command is, how it is evaluated and sent and what its return code is belong to the commands page. The environments that exist, other than the one that runs commands in the host's shell, belong to the environment chapter.

The examples use the name system for that shell and, in a few, names of environments that do not exist, because the result of the instruction shows in the ADDRESS function.

The forms

[instr.address.form.name]

ADDRESS name makes name the current environment, and the environment that was current the previous one, as the swap rule says. The name is one symbol or one string, and the function's name rule says which characters it has. A symbol is not looked up as a variable. The instruction sends no command.

system = 'other'
address system
say address()
address Foo.Bar
say address()

SYSTEM
FOO.BAR
[instr.address.form.value]

ADDRESS VALUE expression takes the value of the expression as the name, as the function's name rule says. The expression is what follows VALUE, up to a WITH that is not inside parentheses, so a variable named with cannot end it and ADDRESS VALUE WITH has no expression. The word VALUE may be left out when the expression starts with a parenthesis, so that ADDRESS (expression) is the same instruction; the expression is then what follows, up to that WITH, and not only the part in parentheses.

x = 'dyn'
address value x 'env'
say '['address()']'
address (x 'foo')
say '['address()']'
address (x) 'bar'
say '['address()']'
call try "address value 'a' with"
call try "address value ('a' with)"
call try "address value 'a' || with"
call try "address value with"
exit
try: procedure
  signal on syntax name e
  interpret arg(1)
  say arg(1) '->' '['address()']'
  return
e: say arg(1) '->' condition('o')~code
  return

[dyn env]
[dyn foo]
[dyn bar]
address value 'a' with -> 20.933
address value ('a' with) -> [a WITH]
address value 'a' || with -> 35.1
address value with -> 35.914
[instr.address.form.bare]

ADDRESS with nothing after it swaps the current and the previous environment, as the swap rule says. It sends no command.

address first
address second
address
say address()
address value 'third' with output normal
say address()
address
say address()

[instr.address.command]

ADDRESS name expression has a symbol or a string for the name, and whatever follows it, up to a WITH that starts a redirection, is an expression. It is evaluated as the expression of a command is, and its value is sent to the named environment as one command. The current environment and the previous one stay as they were, so the function answers the same name after the command. RC is set as the commands page says. An error in the expression raises that error and sends nothing.

address first
address system 'exit 2'
say rc address()
address "system" 'exit' 1 + 2
say rc address()
signal on syntax name e
address system 'exit' + 1
e: say condition('o')~code address()

2 FIRST
3 FIRST
41.1 FIRST

Redirection

[instr.address.with.syntax]

A clause of the forms above may end with WITH and one to three redirections, in any order, each introduced by INPUT, OUTPUT or ERROR and each used at most once. The redirection is then one of NORMAL; STEM followed by a stem symbol, which ends in a period; or STREAM or USING followed by an expression in parentheses, a string, a constant symbol or an environment symbol, where STREAM names a stream. A plain variable symbol after STREAM or USING is not one of these. OUTPUT and ERROR may put APPEND or REPLACE before STEM, STREAM or USING, and replace is meant when neither is written. The keywords may be in any case. The word WITH directly after ADDRESS is the name of an environment and not the keyword, so ADDRESS WITH OUTPUT NORMAL sends the command OUTPUT NORMAL to the environment WITH.

address first
i.0 = 1
i.1 = 'z'
address system 'cat' with Error stem e. OUTPUT append stem o. input stem i.
say o.0 o.1
address with output normal
say rc address()

1 z
30 FIRST
[instr.address.with.normal]

NORMAL is no redirection: the command reads and writes the program's own standard input, output and error, as a command does with no redirection at all.

address system with output stem o.
address system 'echo kept' with output normal
say symbol('o.1')

kept
LIT
[instr.address.with.stem]

STEM name. reads or writes the lines of a stem. For input, the stem's 0 tail holds the number of lines and the tails 1 to that number hold them. For output and error, a replace clears every tail of the stem, keeps the default value of the stem, and then sets the tails 1 and up and the tail 0, which holds the number of lines. An append keeps the stem and numbers the lines after the number that its 0 tail holds. A line is the text up to a line end, without it; a carriage return directly before a line feed is not part of the line, text after the last line end is a line, and an empty line is kept. An input line that holds a line feed is sent as it is, and the command reads it as two lines.

address system 'echo a; echo; echo c d' with output stem b.
say b.0 '['b.1']' '['b.2']' b.3
o.0 = 3
o.3 = 'old'
address system 'echo m' with output stem o.
say o.0 o.1 symbol('o.3')
address system 'echo x; echo y >&2' with output stem a. error stem e.
say a.0 a.1 e.0 e.1
i.0 = 2
i.1 = 'l1'
i.2 = 'l2'
address system 'cat' with input stem i. output stem o.
say o.0 o.1 o.2
o.0 = 5
address system 'echo n' with output append stem o.
say o.0 o.6
address system 'printf "p\r\nq"' with output stem c.
say c.0 c2x(c.1) c2x(c.2)
j.0 = 1
j.1 = 'u' || '0a'x || 'v'
address system 'cat' with input stem j. output stem c.
say c.0 c.1 c.2

6 n

[instr.address.with.stem.count]

The 0 tail of an input stem is the number of lines, a whole number of zero or more, in any form that the whole-number form allows and whose value is whole: 1.0, 1e0, +1 and ' 1 ' are 1. A 0 tail that was not assigned raises SYNTAX 98.998, and the default value of the stem does not count as an assignment. One that is not a whole number of zero or more raises SYNTAX 26.904; so does a count too large to be a number of lines, such as one of twenty digits. The NUMERIC DIGITS setting plays no part, and the error is not the SYNTAX 40.12 of the digits rule. A count of 0 sends nothing, and a tail from 1 to the count that is not set sends the stem's own default value, which for a stem that was never assigned is the stem's name with its period. For an append, a 0 tail that was not assigned, or that holds only the default value of the stem, counts as 0; any other 0 tail is checked as for input, and SYNTAX 26.904 is raised for a bad one.

cat = "address system 'cat' with input stem j."
o. = 'def'
o.5 = 'five'
address system 'echo a' with output stem o.
say o.0 o.1 o.5 symbol('o.5') o.9
i.0 = 2
i.1 = 'x'
address system 'cat' with input stem i.
call try 'unset', "address system 'cat' with input stem j."
call try 'abc', "j.0 = 'abc'; address system 'cat' with input stem j."
call try 'minus', "j.0 = -1; address system 'cat' with input stem j."
call try 'frac', "j.0 = 2.5; address system 'cat' with input stem j."
call try 'default', "d. = 2; address system 'cat' with input stem d."
call try 'huge', "j.0 = 99999999999999999999;" cat
call try 'wide', "numeric digits 2; j.0 = 123;" cat "output stem w.;" ,
  "say w.0"
call try 'zero', "j.0 = 0; address system 'cat' with input stem j."
t = "address system 'echo z' with output append stem m."
call try 'bad append', "m.0 = 'xyz';" t
call try 'blanks', "m.0 = ' 2 ';" t "; say m.3"
call try 'unset append', t "; say m.0 m.1"
exit
try: procedure
  signal on syntax name e
  interpret arg(2)
  say arg(1) 'ok'
  return
e: say arg(1) condition('o')~code
  return

[instr.address.with.stream]

STREAM names a stream by the name that the stream functions take. An output or error stream is written with the lines of the command, and a replace empties it first. A command with an input stream reads the lines of the stream.

f = 'spec-address-with.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
address system 'echo one' with output stream (f)
address system 'echo two' with output append stream (f)
say linein(f) linein(f) lines(f)
call stream f, 'c', 'close'
address system 'echo three' with output replace stream (f)
say linein(f) lines(f)
call stream f, 'c', 'close'
address system 'cat' with input stream (f)
call stream f, 'c', 'close'
call sysfiledelete f

[instr.address.with.using]

For output and error, USING names the object that receives the lines. An ordered collection, an Array, a List, a Queue or a subclass of one, gets each line by the message APPEND, after it is emptied, by the message EMPTY, when the redirection is a replace. A RexxQueue object gets each line by the message QUEUE. A Stem object, an object of the Stem class itself and not of a subclass, is written as STEM writes a stem: a replace clears it and sets the tails 1 and up and 0, and an append numbers the lines after its 0 tail. A stream object, an object of an OutputStream or InputOutputStream class (a .Stream among them), gets each line by LINEOUT; it takes neither REPLACE nor APPEND, and either raises SYNTAX 98.997. Any other object, a string, .nil, a Set, a Directory, a Bag, a MutableBuffer, an object of a subclass of Stem, an object of an InputStream class that is not also an OutputStream, and an object of a class of the program that has an APPEND method of its own, raises SYNTAX 98.996 when the command is about to be sent, whether or not the command would have written anything.

a = .array~new
address system 'echo a1; echo a2' with output using (a)
address system 'echo b1' with output append using (a)
say a~items a[1] a[2] a[3]
address system 'echo c1' with output using (a)
say a~items a[1]

address system 'echo l1' with output using (l)
q = .queue~new

address system 'echo s' with output append using (st)
rq = .rexxqueue~new
address system 'echo r1; echo r2' with output using (rq)
say l~items q~items st[0] st[1] st[3] rq~queued rq~pull rq~pull

[instr.address.with.using.input]

For input, USING names the source of the lines. A string is one line, and so is a MutableBuffer, by its string value. A Stem object, of the Stem class itself, is read as STEM reads a stem. A stream object, an object of an InputStream or InputOutputStream class (a .Stream among them), is read line by line until its end. Any other object that has a MAKEARRAY method, among them a List, a Queue, a Set, a Directory, a Bag, a RexxQueue and an object of a class of the program with such a method, gives one line for each item of the array that the method answers; the lines of a RexxQueue are taken from it. An item that is not a string is replaced by a string as the string argument rule says. A MAKEARRAY that answers no array, any other object, and .nil, raise SYNTAX 98.924 when the command is about to be sent.

[instr.address.with.once]

A redirection written on a clause with a command applies to that command and to no other. The streams the clause does not name keep what they had, which is the setting of the earlier clauses.

address system with output stem s.

[instr.address.with.set]

A clause with a redirection and no command sets the redirection of the environment that it names, and makes that environment current as ADDRESS name does. The commands sent to that environment from then on use the setting, until another such clause names the same environment. It sets all three streams at once: a stream the clause does not name goes back to NORMAL. A name without WITH makes an environment current with the setting it last had, or with none when it never had one, and the swap of the current and the previous environment brings an environment back with its setting. The environment is the same whatever the case of its name. The setting of one environment does not touch the commands that another receives. The stem, the stream expression or the USING expression is kept as it was written and is evaluated again when each command is sent, in the variables of the code that sends it.

[instr.address.with.error]

Syntax that does not fit the forms is found when the program is read, so a program file with one writes nothing and ends with the return code of the error. The subcodes show in INTERPRET text. SYNTAX 35.914 is VALUE with no expression. SYNTAX 20.933 is WITH with nothing after it, and SYNTAX 20.932 is STEM with no stem symbol. SYNTAX 25.933 is a word that is not a type where the type is due, among them APPEND or REPLACE before NORMAL or before an input type, and the end of the clause; SYNTAX 25.930, SYNTAX 25.931 and SYNTAX 25.932 are INPUT, OUTPUT and ERROR named twice, and SYNTAX 25.934 is a word where INPUT, OUTPUT or ERROR is due. SYNTAX 35.935 is STREAM or USING with no expression, and SYNTAX 35.1 is a plain variable symbol after either.

Scope

[instr.address.scope]

The redirections of the setting rule have the scope that the current environment has, and the scope rules of the function say it. An internal routine starts with the caller's redirections, a stem it names is the one in its own variables, and the caller has its own redirections back when the routine returns. A routine with PROCEDURE and no EXPOSE therefore fills a stem of its own and leaves the caller's stem as it was. A method, and a ::ROUTINE, starts with none, so its commands read and write the program's own streams. Code run by INTERPRET shares them.

address system with output stem o.
call plain
say 'A' o.0 o.1
call inherit
say 'B' o.0 o.1
say .o~new~m
say 'C' o.0 o.1
interpret "'echo int'"
say 'D' o.0 o.1
call plain2
'echo back'
say 'E' o.0 o.1
call hid
say 'F' o.0 o.1
exit
plain:
  'echo plain'
  address system with output normal
  'echo plainnormal'
  return
inherit: procedure expose o.
  'echo inherit'
  return
hid: procedure
  'echo h'
  say 'hid' o.0 o.1
  return
plain2:
  address system with output stem p.
  'echo plain2'
  return
::class o
::method m
  'echo meth'
  return 'm'

Deviations

[instr.address.deviation.52]

When a write of a command's output or error raises a condition, as the message APPEND to a collection or LINEOUT to a stream object may, the condition is raised whatever return code the command answered. ooRexx raises it only when the command answered 0, and ends the clause with the return code otherwise. The example shows the interrexx output; ooRexx shows ok 1.

signal on syntax name e
address system 'echo x; exit 1' with output using (.bad~new)
say 'ok' rc
exit

ARG

ARG [template_list]

ANSI: 6.3.2.36, 8.3.2; rexxref: Keyword Instructions > ARG

ARG parses the arguments of the running routine, method or program, after it has made them upper case. It is a short form of PARSE: the clause ARG template_list does what PARSE UPPER ARG template_list does, and this page says what follows from that. The builtin of the same name, ARG, is a function and is not related to the instruction except through the arguments it reports.

[instr.arg.short]

ARG followed by a template list is the instruction PARSE UPPER ARG followed by the same list. Each argument, in order, is the source of the template that stands in the same place after the commas, as the comma rule says, and every one of them is made upper case before it is parsed, as the case conversion defines. An argument that is missing is the null string, by the same rule.

call show 'Mixed  Case', 'two words'
call show 'only'
call show
exit
show:
  arg a b, c d
  say '[' || a || '][' || b || '][' || c || '][' || d || ']'
  parse upper arg x y, z
  say (x == a) (y == b) (z == strip(c d))
  return

1 1 1
[][][][]

[instr.arg.template]

Everything after the keyword is the template list, and ARG has no keywords of its own. A word that PARSE would read as an option, such as upper or caseless, is a variable of the template, and so is a source keyword. The case of the arguments is changed and nothing else about them is, so the template patterns are written in upper case to match, and the arguments the caller passed are not changed. The errors of the template are the template errors. An ARG with no template assigns nothing.

call show 'key=Value', 'extra'
exit
show:
  arg upper caseless
  say '[' || upper || '][' || caseless || ']'
  arg k '=' v
  say k v
  arg k '=' v, e
  say k v e
  arg
  say arg(1) arg(2)
  return

[KEY=VALUE][]
KEY VALUE
KEY VALUE EXTRA
key=Value extra

Assignments

ANSI: 6.3.2.8, 8.3.3; rexxref: General Concepts > Clauses and Instructions > Assignments; General Concepts > Assignments and Symbols; General Concepts > Assignments and Symbols > Extended Assignments

An assignment gives a variable a new value. Its form is a symbol, an equal sign and an expression, and the symbol decides which variable changes: a simple symbol names one variable, a stem symbol names a stem, and a compound symbol names the variable that its tail works out to. This page specifies what the assignment does with the value, the order in which its parts are evaluated, what it does to a stem, the extended forms that combine an operator with the assignment, and the errors it raises. How a clause is recognized as an assignment is the business of the lexical rules, and the variables themselves are specified in the expressions chapter.

The value

[instr.assignment.value]

An assignment evaluates its expression and makes the result the value of the variable. The expression is everything after the first =, so a further = in it is a comparison. The variable holds the object that the expression answered and not a copy: two variables assigned from one object hold the same object. A symbol with no value that stands alone as the expression has its name in upper case as value, as the variable rule says, and the assignment gives that to the variable.

a = 3; b = a = 3; c = (a = 4)
say b c
o = .array~new; p = o; p~append('x')
say o~items (o == p)
y = unknown_name
say y

1 0
1 1
UNKNOWN_NAME
[instr.assignment.order]

The expression is evaluated before the variable is chosen. For a compound symbol this matters when evaluating the expression changes a variable that its tail uses: the tail is read after the expression has run, so the assignment goes to the variable that the changed value names. The terms of the expression itself are evaluated as the expression rules say.

i = 1
a.i = f()
say a.1 a.2
i = 1
b.i.i = f()
say symbol('b.1.1') symbol('b.2.2')
exit
f: i = 2; say 'f called'; return 'v'

f called
A.1 v
f called
LIT VAR
[instr.assignment.error]

An error raised while the expression is evaluated ends the clause, and the variable keeps the value it had: nothing is assigned, and the stem or the compound variable that the target names is left as it was. The error is the one the expression raises.

x = 'old'; x.1 = 'keep'
call try 'x = 1 / 0'
call try 'x.1 = 1 / 0'
call try 'x. = 1 / 0'
call try 'x = .nosuch~foo'
say x x.1
exit

  signal on syntax name e
  interpret arg(1)
e: say arg(1) '=>' condition('o')~code
  return

x.1 = 1 / 0 => 42.3
x. = 1 / 0 => 42.3
x = .nosuch~foo => 97.1

Stems and compound variables

[instr.assignment.stem]

An assignment to a stem symbol gives the stem a new default value, and every compound variable of the stem that had its own value loses it, as the stem rule says. The expression is evaluated first, so it can still read the compound variables that the assignment is about to discard. The simple variable that has the stem's name does not change, as the separation rule says.

s.1 = 'x'; s.2 = 'y'; s = 'simple'
s. = s.1 s.2
say s. s.1 s.2 s.3 s

x y x y x y x y simple
[instr.assignment.compound]

An assignment to a compound symbol sets the one variable that its derived name names. It leaves the default of the stem and every other compound variable as they were, so the default rule still gives the other tails the default.

k = 'TWO'
f. = 'dflt'
f.1 = 'one'
f.k = 'second'
say f.1 f.2 f.two f.k f.three

one dflt second second dflt

Special names

[instr.assignment.special]

The names that the interpreter sets itself, RC, RESULT and SIGL, are ordinary variable symbols, and an assignment to one of them is an assignment like any other. So are TRUE and NIL, which differ from the environment symbols .TRUE and .NIL in the period. The interpreter assigns the three special variables again when the event that sets them happens, as a command sets RC.

rc = 'mine'; result = 'mine'; sigl = 'mine'
say rc result sigl
true = 4
say true .true

mine mine mine
4 1
[instr.assignment.constant]

An assignment whose symbol is a constant symbol that starts with a digit raises SYNTAX 31.2, and one whose symbol is an environment symbol, or a constant symbol that starts with a period, raises SYNTAX 31.3, as the symbol rules say. In a program file the fault is found when the program is read, so that no clause runs, even one before the assignment, and the exit code is 225, which is 256 minus 31. In the text of INTERPRET the error is raised when the clause runs.

say 'before'
exit
2b = 4

say 'before'
.widget = 4

call try '2b = 4'
call try '.widget = 4'
call try '1.5 = 4'
call try '.widget.name = 4'
exit

  signal on syntax name e
  interpret arg(1)
e: say arg(1) '=>' condition('o')~code
  return

.widget.name = 4 => 31.3
[instr.assignment.empty]

An assignment with no expression after the = raises SYNTAX 35.918, as the clause rule says. In a program file this is found when the program is read, so the program writes nothing and exits with 221. An expression that cannot be read raises the error that the expression rules give, such as 35.1, in the same way.

say 'before'
x =

call try 'x ='
call try 'x +='
call try 'x = 1 +'
exit
try:
  signal on syntax name e
  interpret arg(1)
e: say arg(1) '=>' condition('o')~code
  return

x = => 35.918
x += => 35.918
x = 1 + => 35.1

Extended assignments

[instr.assignment.extended]

In an extended assignment target op= expression, the clause is the plain assignment target = target op (expression), as the clause rule says, and the left operand is read before the expression is evaluated. For a compound symbol the variable that is read and the variable that is assigned are worked out separately: the first uses the tail as it is before the expression runs, and the second uses it as the expression left it.

i = 1
a.1 = 10; a.2 = 20
a.i += f()
say a.1 a.2 i
exit
f: i = 2; return 1

10 11 2
[instr.assignment.extended.error]

An extended assignment raises what the operator raises for its operands, and leaves the variable as it was. A variable that has no value contributes its name, so u += 1 on an unset variable raises SYNTAX 41.1, a zero divisor raises 42.3 and a logical operator on a value that is not 0 or 1 raises 34.901. An empty expression raises 35.918, as for a plain assignment.

x = 5
call try 'u += 1'
call try 'x /= 0'
call try 'x %= 0'
call try 'x &= 2'
call try 'x ||= '
call try 'x -= "a"'
say x
exit
try:
  signal on syntax name e
  interpret arg(1)
e: say arg(1) '=>' condition('o')~code
  return

u += 1 => 41.1
x /= 0 => 42.3
x %= 0 => 42.3
x &= 2 => 34.901
x ||=  => 35.918
x -= "a" => 41.1
5
[instr.assignment.extended.stem]

When the target of an extended assignment is a stem symbol, the value of the symbol is the left operand, and the result is assigned to the stem as any assignment to a stem symbol does. The value is a Stem object, which passes an operator message that it does not define on to its default value, so the operator is in effect applied to that value and runs as that value's own method when it has one. A stem that has no default has its name as the value the operator meets, which no arithmetic operator accepts. A default that does not understand the operator raises 97.1.

s. = 5
s.1 = 7
s. += 1
say s. s.1 s.2
signal on syntax name e
t. += 1
e: say condition('o')~code

6 6 6
41.1

s. = .t~new
s.1 = 'one'
s. += 1
say s. s.1
w. = .array~of(1)
signal on syntax name e
w. += 1
e: say condition('o')~code
::class t
::method '+'
  say 'plus called with' arg(1)
  return 'summed'
::method string
  return 'tstring'

plus called with 1
summed summed
97.1

CALL

CALL {name | (expression)} [argument] [, [argument]]... | CALL ON condition [NAME label] | CALL OFF condition

ANSI: 6.3.2.37, 8.3.4; rexxref: Keyword Instructions > CALL

CALL runs a routine as a subroutine and goes on with the clause after it when the routine returns. The routine is an internal one, which is a label of the same program, a built-in function, or an external routine, and the name of the CALL decides where the search for it looks. The routine may return a value, which the CALL leaves in the variable RESULT. The ON and OFF forms do not call anything: they switch the trap of a condition. This page specifies the arguments, the search order as far as it separates internal routines from built-in ones, RESULT and SIGL, and the errors. How a routine is found outside the program belongs to the environment chapter, and what a trap does when its condition occurs to the chapter on conditions.

Running a routine

[instr.call.run]

CALL name evaluates the arguments from left to right and runs the routine with them. When the routine returns, control continues with the clause after the CALL, whether the routine is an internal one, a built-in function or an external routine. The routine reads its arguments with the ARG built-in function, the ARG and PARSE ARG instructions or USE ARG. A symbol that is the name is a constant, so a variable of the same name has no part in the call.

hello = 'a variable'
call hello 'x', 1 + 1
call length 'abc'
say 'length gave' result
exit
hello: say 'hello' arg() arg(1) arg(2); return

hello 2 x 2
length gave 3
[instr.call.args]

The arguments are expressions separated by commas, and a position that has no expression is an omitted argument, which the routine sees as absent. An omitted argument in front of a given one counts as a position, so call f ,, 3 passes three arguments of which the first two are absent. An omitted argument after the last given one is dropped and does not count, so call f 1,; passes one argument. A comma at the end of a line is not a separator but a continuation, as the continuation rule says. A parenthesis that follows the name directly or after a blank begins the first argument as a parenthesized expression, and the CALL does not read the name as a function call, so call f(1) and call f (1) both pass one argument, the value 1.

call show
call show 1,;
call show ,, 3
call show , 2
call show(1)
call show (1)
call show 1 2, 3
call show a,
  b
exit
show: say arg() '['arg(1)']' '['arg(2)']' 'present' arg(1, 'e') arg(2, 'e')
return

0 [] [] present 0 0
1 [1] [] present 1 0
3 [] [] present 0 0
2 [] [2] present 0 1
1 [1] [] present 1 0
1 [1] [] present 1 0
2 [1 2] [3] present 1 1
1 [A B] [] present 1 0

Which routine

[instr.call.search]

A name written as a symbol is read in upper case and searched in this order: a label of the code that holds the CALL, then a built-in function, then an external routine. That code is the main program, or the body of the one routine or method that the CALL is in, so the labels of the other parts of the file are not searched. A label wins over a built-in function of the same name, so a program can replace a built-in one. A name written as a string is used as it is written and is not searched among the labels at all, so the search starts with the built-in functions, whose names are in capitals, and goes on to the external routines. A string that is not in capitals therefore never reaches a built-in function, and a label of the same text is not found by it either: with the labels 'myLab': and mylab:, the string 'myLab' finds neither. The labels of a method are the ones that a CALL in it finds, as the second example shows. How external routines are found is the subject of the environment chapter. A name that nothing answers to raises SYNTAX 43.1 when the CALL runs.

call length 'abc'
say 'symbol:' result
call 'LENGTH' 'abc'
say 'string:' result
call ('LENGTH') 'abc'
say 'expression:' result
call try '"length"'
call try '("length")'
call try 'nosuch'
call try '"myLab"'
call try '"MYLAB"'
call try '(labname)'
call try 'mylab'
labname = 'myLab'
call try '(labname)'
exit
length: return 'label'
'myLab': return 'string label'
mylab: return 'symbol label'
try:
  signal on syntax name e
  interpret 'call' arg(1) '"abc"'
  say arg(1) '=> ok' result
  return
e: say arg(1) '=>' condition('o')~code
  return

symbol: label
string: 3
expression: label
"length" => 43.1
("length") => 43.1
nosuch => 43.1
"myLab" => 43.1
"MYLAB" => 43.1
(labname) => 43.1
mylab => ok symbol label
(labname) => ok string label

.c~new~m
exit
mainlab: say 'main label'
::class c
::method m
  call inner 'x'
  say 'method' sigl result
  signal on syntax name e
  call mainlab
e: say 'method' condition('o')~code
  return
inner: return 'inner' arg(1)

method 6 inner x
method 43.1
[instr.call.expr]

CALL (expression) evaluates the expression first, and the arguments after it, and uses the string the value converts to as the name, by the conversion rule. The name is compared as it is, so GREET matches a label in the example, SUBSTR the built-in function, and a lower-case value matches neither. Unlike a name written as a string, the value is searched among the labels first, so the order of the search rule holds for it.

n = 'GREET'
call (n) 'world'
call ('SUBSTR') 'abcdef', 3, 2
say result
call try '"greet"'
call try 'n || "x"'
call (.z~new)
call (.y~new)
exit
greet: say 'hello' arg(1); return
cms: say 'makestring'; return
cst: say 'string'; return
try:
  signal on syntax name e
  interpret 'call (' || arg(1) || ') 1'
  say arg(1) '=> ok'
  return
e: say arg(1) '=>' condition('o')~code
  return
::class z
::method makestring
  return 'CMS'
::method string
  return 'CST'
::class y
::method string
  return 'CST'

hello world
cd
"greet" => 43.1
n || "x" => 43.1
makestring
string

What the call leaves

[instr.call.result]

When the routine returns a value, RESULT is set to it, and when the routine returns no value, RESULT is dropped and is unset afterwards. This holds for every kind of routine, so a built-in function that answers a value sets RESULT like any other, and a routine that returns nothing drops the value that an earlier call left. A function call in an expression does not set it. Where a message instruction sets the variable, the message rule says.

call giver 2
say 'giver:' result
call quiet
say 'quiet:' symbol('result')
result = 'old'
call abs -4
say 'abs:' result
result = 'old'
call quiet
say 'quiet:' symbol('result') result
result = 'kept'
x = giver(1)
say 'function:' result
exit
giver: return arg(1) * 21
quiet: return

giver: 42
quiet: LIT
abs: 4
quiet: LIT RESULT
function: kept
[instr.call.restore]

The settings of an internal routine are its own. When NUMERIC settings, the trace setting or the default environment of ADDRESS are changed inside the routine, the caller has the ones it had before the CALL when the routine returns, whether or not the routine starts with PROCEDURE. For NUMERIC, the scope rule says it, and for the trace setting the TRACE rule does. The same holds for the address environment, which the ADDRESS page specifies, and the traps of conditions that the conditions chapter specifies. The routine of the example traces, and that trace output goes to standard error, so the output block shows only the standard output.

numeric digits 5
trace o
address foo
call s
say digits() 1/3 address()
exit
s: numeric digits 3; trace r; address bar
  return

5 0.33333 FOO
[instr.call.sigl]

A CALL of an internal routine sets SIGL, in the variable scope of the caller, to the line number of the CALL clause, which is the line where the clause starts when it runs over several lines. A routine that starts with PROCEDURE has its own scope and sees SIGL only if it exposes it. A CALL of a built-in function or of an external routine does not set it, and an external routine has a scope of its own that holds no SIGL. The SIGNAL rule says what SIGNAL sets.

say 'start' sigl
call abs 1
say 'builtin' sigl
call ext
say 'external' sigl
call sub
say 'sub' sigl
call psub
call esub
call sub 1,
  2
say 'two lines' sigl
exit
sub: say 'in sub' sigl; return
psub: procedure
  say 'in psub' symbol('sigl')
  return
esub: procedure expose sigl
  say 'in esub' sigl
  return
::routine ext
  say 'in ext' symbol('sigl')

start SIGL
builtin SIGL
in ext LIT
external SIGL
in sub 6
sub 6
in psub LIT
in esub 9
in sub 10
two lines 10

Errors

[instr.call.error]

A CALL with no name raises SYNTAX 19.2, and a name written as a symbol with a colon after it raises 20.922, because the colon form is the call of a routine of a namespace, which this chapter does not specify. Both are found when the program is read, so none of its clauses run. A routine that is not found raises 43.1 when the CALL runs, as the search rule says, and an error that a built-in function or a routine raises is raised at the CALL. A parenthesized name that is not closed raises 36.901.

say 'before'
call

call try 'call'
call try 'call hello:'
call try 'call abs'
call try 'call (n'
call try 'call nosuch 1'
exit
try:
  signal on syntax name e
  interpret arg(1)
  say arg(1) '=> ok'
  return
e: say arg(1) '=>' condition('o')~code
  return

call => 19.2
call hello: => 20.922
call abs => 40.3
call (n => 36.901
call nosuch 1 => 43.1

ON and OFF

[instr.call.on]

CALL ON condition enables the trap of a condition and CALL OFF condition disables it, and neither calls a routine. The condition is ERROR, FAILURE, HALT or NOTREADY, or ANY, or USER followed by the name of a user condition, a symbol read as a constant in upper case, not a string. ON may be followed by NAME and a routine name, a symbol or a string, and the default name is the name of the condition. The routine is not looked for when the trap is enabled, so a CALL ON for a name that is not a routine is not an error then. What a trap does when its condition occurs belongs to the chapter on conditions. The conditions that only SIGNAL can trap are not accepted: NOVALUE, SYNTAX, LOSTDIGITS, NOMETHOD and NOSTRING raise SYNTAX 25.1 after ON and 25.2 after OFF.

do c over .array~of('error', 'failure', 'halt', 'notready', 'any')
  interpret 'call on' c
  interpret 'call off' c
  say c 'on and off'
end
call on user foo name lbl
call off user foo
call on error name nolabel
call off error
say 'done'
exit
lbl: return

error on and off
failure on and off
halt on and off
notready on and off
any on and off
done
[instr.call.on.error]

The errors of the ON and OFF forms are found when the program is read. A CALL ON with no condition raises SYNTAX 20.911 and an OFF 20.912, and a USER with no name, or with a string for the name, 20.915. A word that is not a condition raises 25.1 after ON and 25.2 after OFF. A NAME with no routine name raises 19.3, data after the name raises 21.903 on an ON, and any NAME on an OFF raises 21.904. A word after the condition that is not NAME raises 25.914.

call try 'call on'
call try 'call off'
call try 'call on user'
call try 'call on user "foo"'
call try 'call off user "foo"'
call try 'call on syntax'
call try 'call off novalue'
call try 'call on foo'
call try 'call on error name'
call try 'call on error name lbl extra'
call try 'call off error name lbl'
call try 'call on error lbl'
exit
try:
  signal on syntax name e
  interpret arg(1)
  say arg(1) '=> ok'
  return
e: say arg(1) '=>' condition('o')~code
  return

call on => 20.911
call off => 20.912
call on user => 20.915
call on user "foo" => 20.915
call off user "foo" => 20.915
call on syntax => 25.1
call off novalue => 25.2
call on foo => 25.1
call on error name => 19.3
call on error name lbl extra => 21.903
call off error name lbl => 21.904
call on error lbl => 25.914

Commands

ANSI: 6.3.2.10, 8.3.5; rexxref: General Concepts > Clauses and Instructions > Commands; General Concepts > Commands to External Environments > Commands

Deviations: D40

A command hands work to something outside the program. The clause is a bare expression, and the interpreter works out its value as a string and sends that string to an environment, which runs it and answers with a return code. This page specifies what is sent, where the return code goes and what else a command leaves behind. Which clauses are commands is decided by the lexical rules. Which environment is current, how the ADDRESS instruction changes it and what the environments are belong to the ADDRESS instruction and to the environment chapter, so the examples here use the environment named system, which runs its commands in the host's shell, and the name that the ADDRESS function reports is the one the ADDRESS instruction set. What a command does is the business of the environment, and the examples need of it only that exit n for a small n answers the return code n and that echo writes its arguments.

What is sent

[instr.command.send]

The expression of a command is evaluated like any other, and its string value is sent to the current environment. Symbols in it are replaced by their values, and a symbol that has none contributes its own name in upper case, so a word that is meant as it is must be a string. The whole value is one command string: the blanks between its parts are the single blanks that the expression joined them with. The string may be null, and a null string is sent like any other.

address system
verb = 'echo'
verb 'one' 1 + 1
'echo' 'two'
signal on failure name f
address nosuch
echo three
f: say condition('d')

one 2
two
ECHO THREE

address system
''
say 'A' rc .rs
address nosuch
signal on failure name f
''
f: say 'B' condition('c') rc .rs

A 0 0
B FAILURE 30 -1
[instr.command.string]

A value that is not a string is turned into one before it is sent, as the conversion rule says. A number is sent in the form that the operation gave it, so 'exit' 2 + 3 sends exit 5.

address system
'exit' 2 + 3
say rc
cmd = .cmd~new
cmd
say rc
::class cmd
::method makestring
  return 'exit 6'

5
6
[instr.command.error]

An error raised while the expression is evaluated ends the clause before anything is sent. The error is the one the expression raises, and the environment does not see a command.

address system
say 'before'
'echo sent' + 1

before

The return code

[instr.command.rc]

When the environment has run a command, the variable RC is assigned the return code it answered, also when that is 0, and the new value replaces whatever RC held, an assignment of the program included. Until the first command or the first trapped condition that sets it, RC has no value. No instruction other than a command assigns RC on its own account. A trapped SYNTAX, ERROR or FAILURE condition sets it as the error rule and the conditions chapter say, so a trapped SYNTAX error sets it to the error number.

address system
say symbol('rc') rc
'exit 3'
say rc
'exit 0'
say rc
rc = 'mine'
x = 1
say rc
'exit 2'
say rc
.array~new~items
say rc
signal on syntax name s
x = 1 / 0
s: say rc

LIT RC
3
0
mine
2
2
42
[instr.command.scope]

RC is a variable like any other, so the command sets it in the variables of the code that runs it. A routine that the program calls by its label, with no PROCEDURE instruction, shares its variables with the caller, so the caller sees the RC that the routine's commands set. A routine with PROCEDURE and a method have variables of their own, so they leave the RC of their caller as it was, and an INTERPRET instruction shares the variables of the code that ran it.

address system
'exit 1'
call plain
say 'A' rc
call hidden
say 'B' rc
interpret "'exit 4'"
say 'C' rc
say 'D' .o~new~go rc
exit
plain: 'exit 2'; return
hidden: procedure; 'exit 3'; say 'in hidden' rc; return
::class o
::method go
  'exit 5'
  return rc

A 2
in hidden 3
B 2
C 4
D 5 4
[instr.command.status]

The environment symbol .RS holds the status of the last command: 0 when the command raised neither ERROR nor FAILURE, 1 when it raised ERROR and -1 when it raised FAILURE. It holds a value only after a command has run, and before that it is an environment symbol that finds no object, so its value is its own characters. Which return codes and which environments raise the two conditions is part of the conditions chapter and of the environment chapter. For the environment system, exit 3 is an error and a command that is not sent to an existing environment is a failure.

say .rs
address system
'exit 0'
say rc .rs
'exit 3'
say rc .rs
'exit 0'
say rc .rs
address nosuch
'exit 0'
say .rs

.RS
0 0
3 1
0 0
-1
[instr.command.status.scope]

.RS follows a different rule from RC. A routine that the program calls by its label starts with the .RS of its caller, with or without PROCEDURE, and the commands it runs change only its own .RS, so the caller's value is the same on return, where a routine without PROCEDURE shares RC. A method, and a routine of a ::routine directive, starts with no .RS and sets its own. An INTERPRET instruction shares the .RS of the code that ran it.

address system
'exit 3'
say 'A' .rs rc
call hidden
say 'B' .rs rc
interpret "say 'I' .rs; 'exit 0'; say 'I' .rs"
say 'C' .rs rc
say 'D' .o~new~go
call plain
say 'E' .rs rc
exit
hidden: procedure
  say 'hidden' .rs rc
  'exit 5'
  say 'hidden' .rs rc
  return
plain:
  say 'plain' .rs rc
  address nosuch
  'exit 0'
  say 'plain' .rs rc
  return
::class o
::method go
  say 'method' .rs
  'exit 4'
  return .rs

hidden 1 RC
hidden 1 5
B 1 3
I 1
I 0
C 0 0
method .RS
D 1

plain -1 30

Conditions

[instr.command.conditions]

A command can raise the conditions ERROR and FAILURE, which a program traps with SIGNAL ON or CALL ON as the traps rule specifies. When neither is trapped, the clause ends and the program goes on with the next clause, whatever the return code was.

address system
'exit 3'
say 'went on' rc
signal on error name caught
'exit 4'
say 'not reached'
caught: say 'trapped' rc condition('c')

went on 3
trapped 4 ERROR

Deviations

[instr.command.deviation.40]

The examples of this page write with say between commands and show their output in program order. That holds because a standard output that is a pipe or a file is handed over before a command is sent, as Deviation 40 says. A program that relies on the order of its own output and a command's output in one stream gets it from the hand-over and not from each line being written at once.

address system
say 'one'
'echo two'
say 'three'

one
two
three

DO

DO [LABEL name] [COUNTER name] [repetitor] [conditional]; instructions; END [name]

ANSI: 6.3.2.12, 8.3.6; rexxref: Keyword Instructions > DO

Deviations: D1, D25, D26, D38, D47, D118

DO opens a block of instructions that ends at a matching END. Without anything after the keyword it groups the clauses so that they stand where the language expects one instruction. With a repetitor, a condition, or both, it runs the block again and again: a number of times, for ever, with a variable that steps through a range, or once for each item of a collection. This page specifies each form, the order in which the parts of the clause are evaluated, the tests that end a loop, the value that the control variable has afterwards, and the errors. LOOP is the same instruction under another keyword, and LEAVE and ITERATE steer a loop from inside.

The clause has one of these shapes, where each part in brackets is optional. The LABEL and COUNTER phrases come first, in either order. Then comes at most one repetitor, which is a count, FOREVER, name = expression with TO, BY and FOR phrases, name OVER expression, or WITH with an INDEX and an ITEM phrase and OVER expression. Then comes at most one WHILE or UNTIL phrase. The block follows, and END closes it.

Groups

[instr.do.group]

A DO with nothing after the keyword, or with only a LABEL phrase, is a simple group. The interpreter runs the clauses between the DO and its END once, in order, and no variable changes because of the DO. A group lets several clauses stand in the place of one, as the branch of an IF does. It is not a loop, so a LEAVE or an ITERATE with no name does not see it, as the LEAVE rule says, while a LEAVE that names its label does leave it.

x = 1
if x = 1 then do
  say 'one'
  say 'still the first branch'
end
else say 'two'
do; say 'bare'; end
do label blk
  say 'labelled'
  leave blk
  say 'skipped'
end blk
say 'done'

one
still the first branch
bare
labelled
done

Counts and endless loops

[instr.do.count]

DO expression runs the block a fixed number of times. The expression is evaluated once, when the DO is reached, and its value is the number of passes, so a later assignment to a variable of the expression changes nothing. The value must be a whole number that is not negative. It may be written with a decimal point or an exponent when that is its value, and it must be below 10 to the power of NUMERIC DIGITS however it is written: at DIGITS 5, 9.9999e4 is a count and 1e5 is not. No count may reach 10 to the power of 18, whatever DIGITS is. Any other value raises SYNTAX 26.2. A count of zero runs no pass and does not raise an error. When LOSTDIGITS is trapped, a count written with more than DIGITS digits raises that condition before the error, if any, as the lost-digits rule describes for an operand.

n = 3
do n
  n = 1
  say 'pass'
end
do 0
  say 'never'
end
k = 0
do 1e1; k = k + 1; end
say k n
call try 'do 1.5; end'
call try 'do -1; end'
call try 'do "x"; end'
call try 'do ""; end'
call try 'numeric digits 5; do 12345; leave; end'
call try 'numeric digits 5; do 123456; leave; end'
call try 'numeric digits 5; do 9.9999e4; leave; end'
call try 'numeric digits 5; do 1e5; leave; end'
call try 'numeric digits 20; do 999999999999999999; leave; end'
call try 'numeric digits 20; do 1000000000000000000; leave; end'
signal on lostdigits name wide
numeric digits 5
do 123456
  say 'never'
end
wide: say condition('c') condition('d')
exit
try:
  signal on syntax name e
  interpret arg(1)
  say arg(1) '=> ok'
  return
e: say arg(1) '=>' condition('o')~code
  return

pass
pass
pass
10 1
do 1.5; end => 26.2
do -1; end => 26.2
do "x"; end => 26.2
do ""; end => 26.2
numeric digits 5; do 12345; leave; end => ok
numeric digits 5; do 123456; leave; end => 26.2
numeric digits 5; do 9.9999e4; leave; end => ok
numeric digits 5; do 1e5; leave; end => 26.2
numeric digits 20; do 999999999999999999; leave; end => ok
numeric digits 20; do 1000000000000000000; leave; end => 26.2
LOSTDIGITS 123456
[instr.do.forever]

DO FOREVER has no end test of its own, so the block runs until a LEAVE, an EXIT, a RETURN, a SIGNAL or an error ends it. It may be followed by a WHILE or an UNTIL phrase, which the condition rules cover. Anything else after FOREVER raises SYNTAX 27.901, because the clause is read before it runs. LOOP with nothing after it is the same endless loop.

n = 0
do forever
  n = n + 1
  if n = 4 then leave
end
say n

Controlled loops

[instr.do.control]

DO name = initial [TO limit] [BY step] [FOR count] is a controlled loop. The three phrases come in any order after the initial expression, each at most once, and a repeated phrase raises SYNTAX 27.902. The interpreter evaluates the initial expression and then the phrases in the order written, each exactly once, and only after all of them does it assign the initial value to the control variable. A phrase therefore sees the variables as they were before the loop, even name itself, and nothing the block does to a variable of a phrase affects the loop. A missing STEP is 1. A missing LIMIT means that no limit ends the loop, and a missing COUNT means that no count does. A control variable written as a string is not specified.

do i = f('init', 1) to f('to', 3) by f('by', 1) for f('for', 5)
  say 'body' i
end
say '--'
do i = f('init', 1) for f('for', 2) to f('to', 9) by f('by', 1)
  say 'body' i
end
say '--'
i = 3
do i = 1 to i + 2 by i - 1
  say 'i' i
end
say '--'
t = 3
do j = 1 to t
  t = 10
  say 'j' j 't' t
end
call try 'do i = 1 to 3 by 1 to 5; end'
call try 'do i = 1 for 2 for 3; end'
exit

  say arg(1) '=> ok'
  return

  return

[instr.do.control.check]

The interpreter checks each value when it has evaluated that expression, and before it evaluates the next, so the first fault in the written order is the one that is reported. The initial value, the LIMIT and the STEP must be numbers, and the first that is not raises SYNTAX 41.1. The COUNT must be a value that the count rule accepts, and raises SYNTAX 26.3 when it is not. The initial value is taken as the prefix + would answer it, so it is rounded and written like the result of an operation: blanks go, an exponent is written out as a result would show it, and the digits are cut to NUMERIC DIGITS, but a trailing zero after the point stays.

call try 'do i = "a" to "b"; end'
call try 'do i = 1 to "b" by 1/0; end'
call try 'do i = 1 by 1/0 to "b"; end'
call try 'do i = 1 to 2 by "c"; end'
call try 'do i = 1 for 1.5; end'
call try 'do i = 1 for -1 to "b"; end'
call try 'do i = 1 for "d" by "c"; end'

do i = 1.00 to 1; say i; end
do i = '1e1' to 10; say i; end

exit

[instr.do.control.step]

After each pass the interpreter adds STEP to the control variable, with the rules of addition at the current NUMERIC settings, and then decides whether to run another pass. No pass runs when FOR has counted out. No pass runs either when the control variable has passed LIMIT, which for a STEP that is zero or positive means that it is greater, and for a negative STEP that it is smaller. The comparison is a numeric one, so NUMERIC FUZZ applies to it. A STEP of zero is treated as a positive one, so it never moves the variable and ends the loop only through FOR, a condition, a LEAVE, or an initial value beyond LIMIT. The test happens before the first pass too, so a loop can run no pass at all.

do i = 1 to 2 by 0.5; say i; end
do i = 5 to 1 by -2; say i; end
do i = 3 to 1; say 'never' i; end
do i = 1 to 3 by -1; say 'never' i; end
do i = 3 to 1 by 0; say 'never' i; end
do i = 1 to 1 by 0 for 3; say 'zero step' i; end
do i = 1 to 3 for 2; say 'for' i; end
numeric digits 3
do i = 998 for 4; say 'digits' i; end
numeric digits 4
numeric fuzz 1
do i = 3 to 2.999; say 'fuzz' i; end

[instr.do.control.after]

When the loop ends, the control variable holds the value that it last had. If a pass ran to its end and the step and the tests ended the loop, that is the value after the last step, which is one step beyond the last value that the block saw. If a LEAVE ended the loop, it is the value the block saw. If the tests ended the loop before the first pass, it is the initial value. A WHILE that fails ends the loop with the stepped value, and an UNTIL that holds ends it before the step, so it keeps the value of the last pass.

do i = 1 to 3; leave; end; say i

do i = 1 for 2; end; say i
do i = 1 to 3 while i < 2; end; say i
do i = 1 to 3 until i = 2; end; say i
do i = 1 to 3 until 1; end; say i

[instr.do.control.body]

The control variable is an ordinary variable that the block can read and assign. The step adds to the value that the variable has then, so an assignment in the block moves the loop, and a value that is not a number, or a variable that was dropped, raises SYNTAX 41.1 at the step. When the control variable is a compound symbol, its tail is worked out again each time that the loop uses the variable, from the values of the tail variables at that moment, so the block can change which variable the loop steps.

do i = 1 to 5
  say i
  if i = 2 then i = 4
end
say 'end' i

  if k = 1 then do; s.2 = 10; k = 2; end
end

  i = 'abc'

signal on syntax name e2

  drop i
end
e2: say condition('o')~code symbol('i')

Collections

[instr.do.over]

DO name OVER expression runs the block once for each item that a collection yields, and assigns the item to name before the pass. The expression is evaluated once, before name is assigned, and the loop sends it the message MAKEARRAY, whatever the class of the object is: an instance of a subclass of List is sent it as any other collection is (Deviation 118). The items are those of the Array that comes back, in its order, and they are taken when the loop starts, so a change to the collection during the loop does not add, remove or alter an item that the loop visits. An Array yields its items in index order and skips an index that holds none, and a List and a Queue yield theirs from first to last. A String yields its lines, so a null string yields none. A Stem, a Directory and a Table yield their indexes, which for a Stem are the tails of the existing compound variables, and a Set yields its members. The order of those four is not specified, as Deviation 1 says for a Stem and Deviation 33 for the others. A collection that yields nothing leaves name as it was, and otherwise name holds the last item after the loop.

a = .array~of('x', 'y', 'z')
do e over a
  say e
end
say 'e' e
do e over .list~of(1, 2)
  say 'list' e
end
do e over .queue~of('p', 'q')
  say 'queue' e
end
do e over .array~of('a', , 'c')
  say 'item' e
end
do e over 'l1' || '0a'x || 'l2'
  say '['e']'
end
do e over ''
  say 'never'
end
say 'e' e
b = .array~of(1, 2, 3)
do e over b
  say 'visit' e
  if e = 1 then b~append(4)
end
say b~items

say seen~sort~makeString('l', ' ')
seen = .array~new

  seen~append(e)

[instr.do.with]

DO WITH INDEX name ITEM name OVER expression runs the block once for each entry of a collection, and assigns the index and the item of the entry. The two phrases come in either order, and one or both may be left out. With neither, the loop is an OVER loop that assigns nothing: it behaves as the OVER rules say, and the sentences below about SUPPLIER do not apply to it. With INDEX or ITEM, the loop sends the value of the expression the message SUPPLIER and walks the Supplier that comes back, assigning the index first and the item after it, so that a variable named by both ends up holding the item. The entries are taken when the loop starts. A FOR phrase limits the number of entries as it does in an OVER loop. A phrase repeated raises SYNTAX 27.902. WITH starts this form only when INDEX, ITEM or OVER follows it, and such a clause with no OVER raises SYNTAX 27.904. An object that does not answer SUPPLIER raises SYNTAX 97.1, and an answer that is not a Supplier raises SYNTAX 98.994.

  say ix it

  say ix it
end

  say 'index' ix
end

  say 'same' i
end

end

Conditions

[instr.do.while]

A WHILE phrase ends the loop when its expression is false. It is tested before every pass, after the step and the LIMIT and FOR tests of a controlled loop and after the item of an OVER or WITH loop was assigned, so the expression sees the control variable of the pass that it guards. A WHILE that is false the first time runs no pass. The expression must be a logical value, and a value that is not 0 or 1 raises SYNTAX 34.3. The list form WHILE a, b follows the list rule of IF: the expressions are evaluated from left to right up to the first that is false, and an expression that is evaluated and is not 0 or 1 raises SYNTAX 34.6. WHILE and UNTIL cannot both appear in one clause, and the attempt raises SYNTAX 27.1.

n = 0
do while n < 3
  n = n + 1
  say 'w' n
end
do while 0
  say 'never'
end
do i = 1 to 5 while i < 3
  say 'wi' i
end
say 'i' i
do e over .array~of(1, 2, 3) while e < 3
  say 'w' e
end
say 'e' e
do 2 while 1, 1
  say 'list'
end
do while 0, 2
  say 'never'
end
call try 'do while 2; end'
call try 'do while "a"; end'
call try 'do while 1, 2; end'
call try 'do while 1 until 1; end'
exit

[instr.do.until]

An UNTIL phrase ends the loop when its expression is true. It is tested after every pass, so the block runs at least once, and it is tested before the control variable steps. An ITERATE counts as the end of a pass, so it does reach the test. The expression follows the same rules as for WHILE, and a value that is not 0 or 1 raises SYNTAX 34.4, or 34.6 for an expression of the list form.

Counting passes

[instr.do.counter]

A COUNTER phrase names a variable that holds the number of the current pass. The variable is set to zero before the expressions of the repetitor are evaluated, so they can read it, and then to 1, 2, and so on at the start of each pass, once the tests have decided that the pass runs. A test of WHILE therefore sees the number of the previous pass. An assignment to the variable in the block does not disturb the count, which the loop keeps itself, so the next pass sets the variable again. After the loop the variable holds the value that the last pass left in it: the number of that pass unless the block assigned the variable. The phrase belongs to a loop and not to a simple group, and a COUNTER on a DO with nothing else raises SYNTAX 27.905. The name may be a compound symbol, and it comes before any repetitor.

do counter c i = 5 to 7
  say c i
end
do counter c while t(c) < 3
  say 'body' c
end
say 'c' c

end
say 'c' c

  c = 100
  say c
end

  if i = 3 then c = 100
end

end
call try 'do counter c; end'
exit

Labels and the end of a block

[instr.do.label]

A LABEL phrase gives the block a name that LEAVE, ITERATE and END can use. The name is the label when the block has a LABEL phrase, and otherwise the control variable of a controlled loop or of an OVER loop. A block with neither has no name. The interpreter compares a name to the names in those clauses without regard to case, and a compound symbol matches by its text, without working out the tail. Once a block has a LABEL, the name of its control variable no longer names it, so LEAVE, ITERATE and END have to use the label. When two active blocks have the same name, the name means the innermost. The phrase works on every form, a simple group included. It comes before any repetitor, and in either order with COUNTER. A LABEL phrase does not create a label for CALL or SIGNAL. A LABEL with no symbol after it, or with a string there, raises SYNTAX 20.918.

do label outer i = 1 to 2
  loop label inner j = 1 to 3
    if j = 2 then iterate outer
    say i j
  end inner
end OUTER
do label x 2
  do label x 2
    say 'inner'
    leave x
  end x
  say 'outer reached'
end x

call try 'do label; end'

[instr.do.end]

END closes the nearest DO or LOOP that is still open. It may be followed by one symbol, which has to be the name of the block, so s.k closes only s.k and not s.j. A symbol after the END of a block that has no name, which includes a count, FOREVER, a bare condition, a WITH loop and a loop that has only COUNTER, raises SYNTAX 10.3. A symbol that does not match raises SYNTAX 10.2, and an END with no open block is a part out of place. A token after END that is not a symbol raises SYNTAX 20.909, and a second token after the symbol 21.909. A DO with no END raises SYNTAX 14.1 as a simple group and 14.5 as a loop. Errors

[instr.do.syntax]

Errors in the shape of the clause are found when the program is read, so a program with one runs no clause at all, as the read-first rule says. The text of an INTERPRET is read in the same way, as the INTERPRET rule says. A TO, BY, FOR, INDEX or ITEM phrase given twice raises SYNTAX 27.902, an unwanted word after FOREVER 27.901, a WHILE and an UNTIL together 27.1, an INDEX or ITEM phrase with no OVER 27.904, and a COUNTER on a simple group 27.905. A missing expression raises SYNTAX 35.904 after the =, 35.905 after BY, 35.906 after TO and 35.907 after FOR, 35.911 after OVER, and 35.929 after WHILE or UNTIL. A LABEL with no symbol, or with a string there, raises SYNTAX 20.918, a COUNTER with no symbol or with a string 20.934, and an INDEX or ITEM with no symbol 20.929. A control, COUNTER, INDEX or ITEM name that starts with a digit raises 31.2, and one that starts with a period 31.3. Anything that follows a COUNTER or LABEL phrase out of its place is part of the expression before it, so that the errors of that expression are raised instead. The errors of a value, 26.2, 26.3 and 41.1, are raised when the clause runs.

say 'before'
do i = 1 to 3 by 1 to 5; end

say 'before'
do while 1 until 1; end

call try 'do i = 1 to by; end'
call try 'do i = 1 to 2 by; end'
call try 'do i = 1 for; end'

call try 'do counter; end'
call try 'do 2 label a; end'
call try 'do i = 1 to 2 counter c; end'
call try 'do 2 counter c; end'

[instr.do.deviation.1]

The order in which a DO OVER over a Stem visits its tails is not specified. ooRexx visits them in an order that its storage fixes, which is neither the order of assignment nor a sorted order, and interrexx may visit them in another. Which tails the loop visits is specified, as the OVER rule says.

[instr.do.deviation.25]

When the TO test or the direction test of a controlled loop sends a comparison message to an object, the loop reads the answer as it reads a WHILE. The answer 1 ends the loop, 0 lets it go on, and any other answer raises SYNTAX 34.901. ooRexx ends the loop only when the answer is the .true object itself, and goes on for every other answer, a computed 1 included, so a loop that ends here can run for ever there. The direction test is the message < that the loop sends to the step, and a computed 1 there marks a negative step for interrexx and a positive one for ooRexx. The first example shows the TO test, the second the answer x, and the third the direction test, where interrexx ends the loop before the first pass and ooRexx runs four passes.

do i = .num~new(1) to 3
  say 'pass' i~v
end
say 'finished'

DROP

DROP name | (name) [name | (name)]...

ANSI: 6.3.2.59, 8.3.7; rexxref: Keyword Instructions > DROP

Deviations: D70

DROP returns variables to the state they had before any assignment: they have no value, and a reference to one yields the name of the variable in upper case. Its operands are variable symbols, written as the names themselves or, in parentheses, as a variable whose value is a list of names. This page specifies what each kind of name drops, the order in which the names are processed, the list form, how DROP treats a variable that a routine or a method has exposed, and the errors. How a variable gets a value is the business of the assignment page.

What is dropped

[instr.drop.simple]

A simple symbol names one variable, and DROP leaves that variable unset. It is not an error to drop a variable that has no value, or a name that no earlier clause has used, and a name that appears more than once is dropped once. The special variables RC, RESULT and SIGL are ordinary variables here and can be dropped. The SYMBOL function then reports LIT for a dropped name, and the interpreter sets RC, RESULT and SIGL again when the event happens that sets them.

a = 1; b = 2; rc = 5; result = 6; sigl = 7
say symbol('a') symbol('b') a
drop a b nosuch a
say symbol('a') symbol('b') a b symbol('nosuch')
drop rc result sigl
say rc result sigl symbol('rc')

VAR VAR 1
LIT LIT A B LIT
RC RESULT SIGL LIT
[instr.drop.compound]

A compound symbol names the variable that its derived name names, and DROP works the name out when it reaches the symbol, from the values that the tail variables have at that moment. It drops that variable only: the other variables of the stem keep their values. A dropped compound variable has its derived name as value, even when its stem has a default.

t.1 = 'a'; t.2 = 'b'; t.3 = 'c'
f. = 'dflt'; f.1 = 'one'; f.2 = 'two'

say t.1 t.2 t.3
say f.1 f.2 f.3

drop t.k
say t.1 t.2 t.3

[instr.drop.stem]

A stem symbol names the stem. DROP makes the symbol refer to a new stem that has no default and no values, so that each variable of the stem has its derived name as value, until the stem or the variable is assigned again. The former stem object is not changed: any other reference to it, such as a variable that holds the stem as a value, still sees its default and its values. The simple variable that has the stem's name is another variable and does not change, as the separation rule says.

s. = 'dflt'; s.1 = 'one'; s.x = 'ex'
drop s.
say s. s.1 s.x s.zzz symbol('s.1')
say s

say s.1 s.2 s.3

Order

[instr.drop.order]

DROP processes its names from left to right, and a name sees what the names before it did: when an earlier name drops a variable that the tail of a later compound symbol uses, the later symbol is worked out from that variable's name and not from its former value. The same holds for a name that is dropped twice, which the second mention leaves as it was.

i = 1; a.1 = 'x'; a.2 = 'y'
drop i a.i
say symbol('i') symbol('a.1') symbol('a.2') symbol('a.i')
i = 1; a.1 = 'x'; a.2 = 'y'
drop a.i i
say symbol('i') symbol('a.1') symbol('a.2')

LIT VAR VAR LIT
LIT LIT VAR

The list form

[instr.drop.list]

A name in parentheses is not dropped. Its value is converted to a string, as the conversion rule says for an object, and the string is a list of names separated by whitespace. DROP drops each name of the list as if it had been written in the clause, in upper case, from left to right, and a name may be a simple symbol, a stem symbol or a compound symbol. The list may be empty or hold only whitespace, and then nothing is dropped. The parentheses hold one name and no list holds parentheses itself. Blanks may stand inside the parentheses, and a name may precede them without a blank. A list that names the variable which holds it drops that variable with the others.

say symbol('alpha') symbol('beta') symbol('gamma') symbol('set')
say s.1 t.1 t.2

say 'nothing dropped' symbol('empty') symbol('blank')

say symbol('m') symbol('n')

say symbol('ref') symbol('r2')

drop ( w ) (w2)
say symbol('o') symbol('o2')
p3 = 'o3'; o3 = 1
drop o(p3)
say symbol('o3')

Exposed variables

[instr.drop.exposed]

A variable that a PROCEDURE EXPOSE or an EXPOSE has made visible is dropped in the scope that owns it: DROP of the name unsets the variable of the exposing scope, so the caller of the routine or the other methods of the object find it unset. A name that is not exposed names a variable of the routine or the method, and DROP leaves any variable of the caller with that name as it was. The same holds for the names in a list.

[instr.drop.syntax]

A DROP that has no operand, an operand that is not a variable symbol or a name in parentheses, or a malformed parenthesis, raises a SYNTAX error that a program file raises when it is read. [instr.drop.deviation.70]

When a clause holds both parenthesised lists and other names, DROP processes every name and every list from left to right, so a later name sees what an earlier list dropped and an earlier name is dropped before a later list is read. ooRexx processes the parenthesised lists first, in reverse order, and then the other names, so a list is read before the names that precede it.

EXIT

EXIT [expression [, expression]...]

ANSI: 6.3.2.61, 8.3.8; rexxref: Keyword Instructions > EXIT

EXIT ends the program at once, however many routines, loops and INTERPRET texts it is in, and the value of its expression is the program's value. In a method or in a routine of a ::ROUTINE directive it ends only that unit, as RETURN would. This page specifies where EXIT stops, the end of the program as an implied EXIT, what the expression is, and how the value of the main program becomes the exit code of the process.

Where it stops

[instr.exit.program]

EXIT in the main program, or in an internal routine of it that a CALL or a function call started, ends the program. No clause after the EXIT runs, the routines that were being called are abandoned without returning, and a function call that is still waiting for its value does not raise SYNTAX 44.1. An EXIT in the text of an INTERPRET that such code runs ends the program too, and in a method or a ::ROUTINE it ends that unit, as the rule on leaving the text says.

say 'start'
call outer
say 'not reached'
exit 1
outer: procedure
  do i = 1 to 3
    say 'outer' i
    if i = 2 then call inner
  end
  return
inner:
  say 'inner'
  exit 9

start
outer 1
outer 2
inner

say 'start'
x = quit()
say 'not reached'
quit: exit

start
[instr.exit.unit]

EXIT in a method or in a routine that a ::ROUTINE directive defines ends that unit, including the internal routines it called, and hands the value to the sender of the message or to the caller of the routine in the way that RETURN does. The program goes on, so the main program is not ended by it.

say 'start'
r = .box~new~go
say 'main goes on' r
call early
say 'and on' result
exit 3

::method go
  call helper
  say 'not reached'

  exit 'from method'
::routine early
  exit 'from routine'

and on from routine
[instr.exit.end]

When the program runs past its last clause, it ends as if there were an EXIT without an expression, so the program has no value and the exit code is 0. This holds when the last clause is in the body of a routine that a CALL started, because the routine does not return from the end of the program; the caller does not continue.

say 'a'
call f
say 'not reached'
f: say 'in f'

a
in f
[instr.exit.end.unit]

A method or a routine of a ::ROUTINE directive that runs past its last clause is different: it returns to its sender without a value, as a RETURN without an expression does, and the program goes on.

The expression

[instr.exit.value]

The expression is evaluated when the EXIT runs, with the variables and the settings of the code that holds it. An error in it is raised before the program ends, and a trap for the condition handles it as it would anywhere else. EXIT without an expression has no value. Several expressions separated by commas give an Array, as for RETURN does, so that a method which exits with two of them answers an Array, and the main program has an Array for its value.

signal on syntax name e
x = 5
exit x * 'a'
e: say condition('o')~code x

The exit code

[instr.exit.code]

The value of the main program, which is that of its EXIT or of a RETURN that ends it, becomes the exit code of the process in this way. A value that is not a string is first replaced by a string as the conversion rule says; where that rule refuses the conversion, as for an object whose REQUEST is private, or whose MAKESTRING or STRING method is private and would be sent, the exit code is 0 and no error is raised. A string that has the form of a whole-number argument, and that is a whole number from -2147483648 to 2147483647, is handed to the host as that integer. Blanks around the number, an exponent, and a decimal part of zeros do not matter. An integer from 0 to 255 is the exit status itself. What a host makes of an integer outside 0 to 255 is not specified. Any other value gives the exit code 0 and raises no error: no value, a fraction, a string that is no number, a whole number outside the 32-bit range, and an object whose string is none of these. A string of more than 18 digits, zeros included, is not specified.

Note. Unix-like hosts keep the low eight bits of the integer, so that 257 and -1 give 1 and 255; another host may report the integer as it is. An expression such as -2147483647 is not a string but a negation, whose result is rounded at the NUMERIC DIGITS setting, so exit -2147483647 gives 0 and exit -1073741823 gives 4, while the strings '-2147483647' and '-1073741823' give 1.

EXPOSE

EXPOSE [name | (name)]...

rexxref: Keyword Instructions > EXPOSE

Deviations: D70

EXPOSE lets a method use the variables that belong to its object. A method starts with no variables but its own, and the variables it sets are gone when it returns. The names that EXPOSE lists are the object's: they keep their values from one method call to the next, and every method of the object that exposes the same name sees the same variable. This page specifies which variables a name shares, the forms of the names, the one place where EXPOSE may stand, and the errors. The stems and compound names are those of the variables chapter, and the forms of the names are those of PROCEDURE, which does the same for the routine of a caller.

Object variables

[instr.expose.object]

A name that EXPOSE lists is a variable of the object that received the message, not of the method call. The method reads its value, an assignment changes it, and DROP unsets it, all for the object, so the effect outlasts the call and other methods and later calls see it. A name that is not listed is a variable of the call: it starts unset, and it is gone when the method returns. Two objects of one class have separate object variables. A name that no method has set is unset in the object, and a method that exposes it finds it unset.

c = .counter~new
c~inc; c~inc
say c~get c~peek
d = .counter~new
say d~get
::class counter
::method init
  expose n
  n = 0
::method inc
  expose n
  n += 1
  scratch = 'gone'
::method get
  expose n
  return n
::method peek
  return symbol('n') symbol('scratch')

[instr.expose.scope]

The object variables of one object are divided by the class that defines the method. Methods of one class that expose a name share a variable, and a method of a subclass that exposes the same name has a variable of its own, for the same object. A method inherited from a class works on the variables of that class.

o = .sub~new
say o~setBase('base') o~setSub('sub')
say o~getBase o~getSub

The variables of a method are visible to what the method runs in its own code. The text of an INTERPRET sees the exposed names, and so does an internal routine that a CALL starts without PROCEDURE. A routine that begins with PROCEDURE sees none of them unless it exposes them with PROCEDURE EXPOSE.

say o~run
say o~after

::method run
  expose a
  a = 'A0'
  interpret 'a = a || "+i"'
  call bump
  call hid
  call hid2
  return a
bump:
  a = a'+b'
  return
hid: procedure
  say symbol('a')
  return
hid2: procedure expose a
  say symbol('a')
  a = a'+h'
  return
::method after
  expose a
  return a
