Exposing names

[instr.procedure.expose]

PROCEDURE EXPOSE lists names that stay shared with the caller. An exposed variable is the caller's variable: the routine reads its value, and an assignment in the routine changes the caller's variable. A name the caller has not set stays unset in the routine, and setting it in the routine sets it in the caller. A name that is not listed is the routine's own. The names are variable symbols separated by whitespace, and they are taken in upper case. A name may be listed twice.

a = 1; b = 2; c = 3
call r1
say a b c symbol('d') symbol('e')
exit
r1: procedure expose a d
  say symbol('a') symbol('b') symbol('c') symbol('d')
  a = a + 10
  d = 'new d'
  b = 'local b'
  e = 'local e'
  return

VAR LIT LIT LIT
11 2 3 VAR LIT
[instr.procedure.stem]

A stem symbol in the list, which is a name ending in a period, exposes the whole stem: every compound variable of it, those the caller has set and those that either side sets later, and the stem's default value.

a.1 = 'one'; a.0 = 'zero'
call s2
say a.1 a.0 a.3 a.9
exit
s2: procedure expose a.
  say 'in' a.1 a.3
  a.3 = 'three'
  a. = 'reset'
  return

in one A.3
reset reset reset reset
[instr.procedure.compound]

A compound symbol in the list exposes the one variable that it names. Its tail is replaced by the value that the variable has in the caller when PROCEDURE runs, and a variable in the tail is not exposed by that. A later change of the tail variable in the routine does not move the exposed name, and a compound name that now has another tail is the routine's own variable.

i = 1; a.1 = 'one'; a.2 = 'two'
call s1
say i a.1 a.2
exit
s1: procedure expose a.i i
  say 'in' a.i
  i = 2
  say a.i
  a.i = 'local'
  return

in one
A.2
2 one two
[instr.procedure.chain]

A routine that exposes a name of its caller shares the variable with the caller's caller as well, if the caller shared it, so a chain of routines that each expose the name reaches the original variable. A name that the caller did not expose is the caller's own variable, and a change of it does not reach the routine above.

x = 'main x'; y = 'main y'
call outer
say x y symbol('z')
exit
outer: procedure expose x
  y = 'outer y'
  z = 'outer z'
  call inner
  say 'outer' x y z
  return
inner: procedure expose x y
  x = x'+'
  y = y'+'
  return

outer main x+ outer y+ outer z
main x+ main y LIT

The list form

[instr.procedure.list]

A name in parentheses is exposed as a name outside them is, and its value in the routine after that is a list of further names. The name may be a simple, a stem or a compound symbol. The value is converted to a string as the DROP list rule describes, split at whitespace, and each word is exposed as if it had been written in the clause, as a simple, stem or compound symbol. A list that is empty or all whitespace exposes nothing. The routine sees the variable that holds the list, and an assignment to it reaches the caller. A compound name in parentheses exposes the caller's variable, with the tail resolved in the caller as the compound rule says. The list is then read from the routine's own variable of that name, with the tail resolved in the routine, where the tail variable is unset unless an earlier name of the clause exposed it. So (a.i) with i set in the caller exposes the caller's a.1, reads the list from the routine's A.I, which is unset and yields its name, and so exposes A.I and nothing more, as the second example shows. When the caller's i is unset too, the exposed variable is A.I itself and its value is the list, as the third example shows. Whether an earlier name of the clause can change that is the matter of the deviation rule. Blanks may stand inside the parentheses, and one list may follow another without a blank.

x = 'X'; y = 'Y'; s.1 = 's1'; i = 1
names = 'x s.'
empty = ''
arr = .array~of('y')
call p1
say x y s.2 names
call p2
say names
exit
p1: procedure expose (names) (empty)(arr)
  say symbol('x') symbol('y') symbol('names') symbol('i') s.1
  x = 'x set'
  s.2 = 's2 set'
  names = 'new list'
  return
p2: procedure expose ( names )
  say names
  return

new list

f: procedure expose (a.i)
  say symbol('x') symbol('a.1') symbol('a.i') a.i

a.i = 'x y'; x = 'X'; y = 'Y'

  say symbol('x') symbol('y') symbol('a.i') a.i
  return

[instr.procedure.list.error]

A word in a list that is not a variable symbol raises the error that the DROP list gives, when the PROCEDURE runs. The routine has no variable exposed then. In the example the handler runs in the routine, as the rule on a jump out of a routine says, so its RETURN leaves the routine and the loop goes on.

signal on syntax name e
do l over .array~of('c 3', 'c .x', 'c (d)', 'c "d"', 'c d+e', ' ', 'c')
  call charout , l '=> '
  call p
end
exit
e: say condition('o')~code
  signal on syntax name e
  return
p: procedure expose (l)
  say 'ok'
  return

Errors

[instr.procedure.syntax]

A fault in the form of the clause is raised when the program is read, so no clause runs: 20.902 for an EXPOSE with no name and for text where a name should be, such as a string, a comma or an =; 25.17 for a word after PROCEDURE that is not EXPOSE; 20.906 for an empty or doubled parenthesis; 46.1 for two names in one parenthesis; 46.901 for a parenthesis that is not closed; and 31.2 or 31.3 for a name that starts with a digit or a period. The text of an INTERPRET raises the same errors when the INTERPRET runs, before the PROCEDURE can be found misplaced.

say 'before'
procedure expose

say 'before'
procedure foo

call try 'procedure expose'
call try 'procedure expose "a"'
call try 'procedure expose a, b'
call try 'procedure expose a = 1'
call try 'procedure foo'
call try 'procedure 1'
call try 'procedure expose ()'
call try 'procedure expose (a b)'
call try 'procedure expose (a'
call try 'procedure expose 3a'
call try 'procedure expose .a'
call try 'procedure expose a.3'
exit
try:
  signal on syntax name e
  interpret arg(1)
  say arg(1) '=> ok'
  return
e: say arg(1) '=>' condition('o')~code
  return

procedure 1 => 25.17
procedure expose () => 20.906
procedure expose (a b) => 46.1
procedure expose (a => 46.901
procedure expose 3a => 31.2
procedure expose .a => 31.3
procedure expose a.3 => 17.1

Deviations

[instr.procedure.deviation.70]

When a clause holds both parenthesised lists and other names, PROCEDURE EXPOSE processes every name and every list from left to right, so a variable that an earlier name has exposed is already the caller's when a later list's own variable is read. ooRexx processes the parenthesised lists first, in reverse order, and then the other names, so the variable of a list is read before any name of the clause is exposed. In the example, ooRexx reads a.i while i is still the routine's own unset variable, and so exposes another name than x.

i = 1; a.1 = 'x'; x = 'X'
call f
exit
f: procedure expose i (a.i)
  say symbol('x')
  return

PULL

PULL [template_list]

ANSI: 6.3.2.77, 8.3.19; rexxref: Keyword Instructions > PULL

PULL takes a line from the external data queue, makes it upper case and parses it. It is a short form of PARSE: PULL template_list does what PARSE UPPER PULL template_list does. Lines get into the queue with PUSH and QUEUE, and the builtins QUEUED and RXQUEUE count the lines and choose the queue.

Note. The examples create a queue of their own, make it the current queue, and delete it when they are done, so they do not depend on the SESSION queue. The standard input of the examples is empty.

[instr.pull.short]

PULL followed by a template list is the instruction PARSE UPPER PULL followed by the same list. The line is made upper case before the template sees it, as the case conversion defines, so the patterns of the template are written in upper case, and the case of the line that was in the queue is not kept. A PULL with no template still takes the line out of the queue and assigns nothing.

q = rxqueue('Create', 'spec_instr_pull_short')
call rxqueue 'Set', q
queue 'Mixed Case=Value'
queue 'another line'
queue 'third'
pull a '=' b
say a '|' b queued()
pull
say queued()
parse upper pull c
say c queued()
call rxqueue 'Set', 'SESSION'
call rxqueue 'Delete', q

[instr.pull.source]

PULL takes the line at the head of the current queue and removes it, so lines come out in the order in which PUSH and QUEUE arranged them. Only when the queue holds no line does PULL read the next line of the default input stream, as PARSE LINEIN does, and the end of that input ends the same way. A line that is the null string is a line: a PULL that takes it does not read the input.

q = rxqueue('Create', 'spec_instr_pull_source')
call rxqueue 'Set', q
call on notready name nr
queue ''
queue 'x'
pull a
say '[' || a || ']' queued()
pull a
say '[' || a || ']' queued()
pull a
say '[' || a || ']' queued()
call rxqueue 'Set', 'SESSION'
call rxqueue 'Delete', q
exit
nr: say 'notready' condition('d')
    return

[instr.pull.current]

The queue is the current queue, the one that RXQUEUE last chose, or SESSION if none was chosen. A current queue that does not exist counts as one with no line: PULL raises no error, and reads the default input stream. The lines of another queue stay where they are.

a = rxqueue('Create', 'spec_instr_pull_a')
b = rxqueue('Create', 'spec_instr_pull_b')
call rxqueue 'Set', a
queue 'in a'
call rxqueue 'Set', b
queue 'in b'
pull x
say x queued()
call rxqueue 'Set', a
pull x
say x queued()
call rxqueue 'Delete', a
say queued()
pull x
say '[' || x || ']'
call rxqueue 'Set', 'SESSION'
call rxqueue 'Delete', b

PUSH

PUSH [expression]

ANSI: 6.3.2.78, 8.3.20; rexxref: Keyword Instructions > PUSH

PUSH puts one line on the external data queue, at the head. The next PULL or PARSE PULL takes the line that was pushed last, so the queue works as a stack. QUEUE is the instruction that puts a line at the other end. The queue is the current one, which the builtin RXQUEUE chooses and QUEUED counts.

Note. The examples create a queue of their own, make it the current queue, and delete it when they are done, so they do not depend on the SESSION queue.

[instr.push.lifo]

PUSH adds a line at the head of the current queue, in front of every line that is there. Lines pushed one after another come out in the opposite order, last in and first out, and they come out before any line that QUEUE put at the tail. A line that is the null string is a line like any other.

q = rxqueue('Create', 'spec_instr_push_lifo')
call rxqueue 'Set', q
queue 'tail'
push 'one'
push 'two'
push ''
say queued()
do while queued() > 0
  parse pull line
  say '[' || line || ']'
end
call rxqueue 'Set', 'SESSION'
call rxqueue 'Delete', q

[instr.push.value]

The expression is everything after the keyword. PUSH evaluates it once and puts the string value of the result, made as the conversion rule says, on the queue as one line, and nothing is converted or trimmed, so a line keeps its blanks and its case. Without an expression the line is the null string. A string that holds a line feed or other control characters is still one line, and it comes back whole. If the evaluation raises a condition, nothing is pushed. PUSH sets no variable, and leaves RC and RESULT as they were.

parse pull a
say a

say 'not reached'
nv: say condition('c') queued()
call rxqueue 'Set', 'SESSION'
call rxqueue 'Delete', q

QUEUE

QUEUE [expression]

ANSI: 6.3.2.79, 8.3.21; rexxref: Keyword Instructions > QUEUE

QUEUE puts one line on the external data queue, at the tail. The next PULL or PARSE PULL takes the line that has waited longest, so the queue works as a line of waiting lines. PUSH is the instruction that puts a line at the other end. The queue is the current one, which the builtin RXQUEUE chooses and QUEUED counts.

Note. The examples create a queue of their own, make it the current queue, and delete it when they are done, so they do not depend on the SESSION queue.

[instr.queue.fifo]

QUEUE adds a line at the tail of the current queue, behind every line that is there. Lines queued one after another come out in the same order, first in and first out. A line that a PUSH put at the head comes out before them, and a line that is the null string is a line like any other.

q = rxqueue('Create', 'spec_instr_queue_fifo')
call rxqueue 'Set', q
queue 'one'
queue 'two'
queue ''
push 'head'
queue 'three'
say queued()
do while queued() > 0
  parse pull line
  say '[' || line || ']'
end
call rxqueue 'Set', 'SESSION'
call rxqueue 'Delete', q

[instr.queue.value]

The expression is everything after the keyword. QUEUE evaluates it once and puts the string value of the result on the queue as one line, without any conversion or trimming. Without an expression the line is the null string. A string with a line feed is one line. If the evaluation raises a condition, nothing is queued. QUEUE sets no variable, and leaves RC and RESULT as they were. PUSH says the same of the head of the queue.

RAISE

RAISE condition [DESCRIPTION expr] [ADDITIONAL expr | ARRAY (expr, ...)] [RETURN [expr] | EXIT [expr]]

rexxref: Keyword Instructions > RAISE

Deviations: D65

RAISE raises a condition on purpose, and it also ends the code that runs it. The condition is raised in the code that called the code that ended, so the instruction is how a routine or a method reports an event to its caller, whose traps answer it as they answer any condition. SYNTAX and the main program are the exceptions, and so is the text of an INTERPRET with RETURN; this page specifies them. The instruction names the condition, carries the values that the condition object holds, and chooses whether the code ends as RETURN or as EXIT does, which also decides who is the caller.

This page specifies the form of the clause, what each option sets, where the condition is raised for each kind of code, what happens when no trap answers, and the PROPAGATE form that raises a trapped condition again. What a trap does, and what a program reads from a condition, belong to the conditions chapter, and the rules here link the ones they use.

The clause

[instr.raise.form]

RAISE is followed by a condition word: ERROR, FAILURE, HALT, LOSTDIGITS, NOMETHOD, NOSTRING, NOTREADY, NOVALUE, PROPAGATE, SYNTAX or USER, in any case. ERROR and FAILURE then take a code, SYNTAX takes a number and USER takes a name, and the other words take nothing. The options come after that, in any order, each at most once: DESCRIPTION and an expression, ADDITIONAL and an expression or ARRAY and a parenthesized list of expressions (the two are one option, so a clause has at most one of them), and RETURN or EXIT with an optional expression (again one option). The code, the number and the expression of an option are each one term: a literal string, a constant symbol, an environment symbol or an expression in parentheses. A variable symbol is not a term here, so its value is written in parentheses. A RETURN or EXIT that has no expression ends the clause: any option after it is read as its expression. ANY is not a condition word, because the names rule says that nothing raises it.

call on user alpha name h
call on user beta name h
call on error name h
call on notready name h
signal on syntax name s
do i = 1 to 5
  call ('R'i)
end
exit
h: say 'h' condition('c') '['condition('d')']',
     condition('o')~hasindex('ADDITIONAL')
  return
s: say 'syntax' condition('o')~code
  exit
::routine r1
  RAISE USER Alpha
::routine r2
  raise user beta additional ('x') description 'two words'
::routine r3
  raise error 5 description ('a' || 'b') additional (.nil)
::routine r4
  raise notready description 'late' array (1, 2) return
::routine r5
  raise user alpha return 'v' description 'rv'

h USER ALPHA [] 0
h USER BETA [two words] 1
h ERROR [ab] 1
h NOTREADY [late] 1
h USER ALPHA [rv] 0
[instr.raise.errors]

A RAISE clause that breaks the form is an error found while the program is read. Nothing is raised: the clause is not part of a program that runs, as the reading rule says, and the same error is an ordinary SYNTAX condition in the text of an INTERPRET. The error is 20.914 when nothing follows RAISE, 25.906 when the word after it is not a condition word, 20.915 when USER has no symbol after it, and 35.1 when a code or number is missing or is not a term, or when a RETURN or EXIT without an expression is followed by another option, which it then reads as its expression. A missing expression after DESCRIPTION or ADDITIONAL is 35.922 or 35.923, and an ARRAY without its opening parenthesis is 35.924. An ARRAY list whose parenthesis is not closed is 36.901. The options that appear twice are 25.908 for DESCRIPTION, 25.909 for ADDITIONAL or ARRAY together, whichever two they are, and 25.911 for RETURN or EXIT together. Any other word after the options is 25.907.

say 'before'
raise user quux return description

clause.1 = 'raise'
clause.2 = 'raise nosuchkeyword'
clause.3 = 'raise any'
clause.4 = 'raise user'
clause.5 = "raise user 'quoted'"
clause.6 = 'raise error'

clause.8 = 'raise error somevar'
clause.9 = 'raise user q description'
clause.10 = 'raise user q additional'
clause.11 = 'raise user q array 1, 2'
clause.12 = 'raise user q array (1, 2'
clause.13 = "raise user q description 'a' description 'b'"
clause.14 = 'raise user q additional (1) array (2)'
clause.15 = 'raise user q return 1 exit 2'
clause.16 = "raise user q return description 'x'"
clause.17 = 'raise user q 5'
clause.18 = 'raise user q return 1 2'
do i = 1 to 18
  call try clause.i
end
exit

  signal on syntax name e
  interpret arg(1)
  say 'no error:' arg(1)
  return
e: say right(condition('o')~code, 6) '<-' arg(1)
  return

What each condition takes

[instr.raise.condition]

Each condition word raises the condition of that name, and the clause sets what the condition word takes. ERROR and FAILURE take a code, which is any string: the text of the literal, of the constant symbol in upper case, or of the value of the parenthesized expression, with no check that it is a number. The code is the value that RC has in the code that answers the condition, as the rule for RC says. The RC entry of the condition object holds the code itself: when the parenthesized expression is an object that is not a string, the entry holds that object, and so does the variable RC in the code of the trap. The user conditions take a name, which the name rule specifies. HALT, LOSTDIGITS, NOMETHOD, NOSTRING, NOTREADY and NOVALUE take nothing, and the condition has the entries that the entries rule lists for a condition that an instruction raised.

names = 'HALT LOSTDIGITS NOMETHOD NOSTRING NOTREADY NOVALUE'
do w over names~makearray(' ')
  call go w
end
call go 'ERROR 12'
call go 'FAILURE 13'
call go 'USER plain'
exit
go: procedure
  signal on any name a
  parse arg kind code
  call (kind) code
  say kind 'ignored'
  return
a: o = condition('o')
  say arg(1) '=>' condition('c') '['condition('d')']' o~hasindex('RC')
  return
::routine halt; raise halt
::routine lostdigits; raise lostdigits
::routine nomethod; raise nomethod additional (.nil) description 'msg'
::routine nostring; raise nostring

[instr.raise.number]

The number of RAISE SYNTAX is a major error number from 1 to 99, which may be followed by a point and a subcode from 0 to 999. It is read from the text of the value, and the digits after the point are one whole number, so 40.3, 40.003 and 040.03 are the error 40.3, and 40.030 is the subcode 30. A number without a point is the error of that number with the subcode 0. The CODE entry of the condition holds the number as m.n, and the RC entry holds the major number. A number of digits, or of digits, a point and digits, that no error has raises SYNTAX 98.941. The null string, a minus sign, a letter that is not the exponent of a number, a second point, a point with no digit on one side of it, a major number outside 1 to 99 and a subcode above 999 raise SYNTAX 33.904. The text of any other form, such as a number with a plus sign, with blanks in it or with an exponent, is not specified. The error 33.904 is a fault of the clause itself, so it is raised in the code that holds the RAISE, as an error found at that clause would be, whichever option ends the clause. The error 98.941 is a SYNTAX condition that the clause raises, like the condition that the clause names: it goes where the RETURN rule puts it, and with EXIT where the EXIT rule puts it.

end

  return

[instr.raise.syntax]

A SYNTAX condition that RAISE raised holds, besides CODE and RC, the description that DESCRIPTION gave, which is the null string without it. Its ADDITIONAL entry is always an array, whatever the clause gave: the array is empty when the clause has neither ADDITIONAL nor ARRAY, it is the array of ARRAY's values, and it is the value of ADDITIONAL made an array, where an array stays as it is, a string becomes an array of one item and a list becomes an array of its items. The null object .nil and an instance of the class Object cannot be made an array, and an ADDITIONAL with such a value raises SYNTAX 98.939 in the raising code, as the SYNTAX rule says; whether an object of any other class is converted is not specified. The values of the array are what the message of the error names, and the text of the message is not specified. Every other condition has the entry only when the clause gave one, as the rule for the options says.

do i = 1 to 5
  call go 'R'i
end
exit
go: procedure
  signal on syntax name s
  call (arg(1))
s: o = condition('o')
  a = o~additional
  say arg(1) o~code o~rc '['o~description']' a~class a~items
  if a~items > 0 then say '   first' a~at(1)
  return
::routine r1; raise syntax 40.3
::routine r2; raise syntax 40.3 description 'why' additional ('one')
::routine r3; raise syntax 40.3 additional (.array~of('p', 'q'))
::routine r4; raise syntax 40.3 array ('p', 'q', 'r')
::routine r5; raise syntax 40.3 additional (.list~of('l', 'm'))

The options

[instr.raise.description]

DESCRIPTION gives the description of the condition. The DESCRIPTION entry of the condition object holds the value of the expression as it is, whatever object that is, and CONDITION('D') answers that same object, which SAY and concatenation show as its string value. Without DESCRIPTION the description is the null string.

call on user foo name h
x = 'value of x'
do i = 1 to 5
  call ('R'i)
end
exit
h: o = condition('o')
  say 'description [' || condition('d') || ']' o~hasindex('ADDITIONAL')
  return
::routine r1; raise user foo
::routine r2; raise user foo description 'plain text'
::routine r3; x = 'local x'; raise user foo description (x '!')
::routine r4; raise user foo description .nil
::routine r5; raise user foo description 17 return

call r1
call r2

  say 'entry' o~description~class '/ string [' || condition('d') || ']'
  return

::routine r2; raise user foo description (.object~new) return

entry The Object class / string [an Object]
[instr.raise.additional]

ADDITIONAL gives the object of the ADDITIONAL entry, any object, and ARRAY gives an array of the values of its list, whose items may be omitted, and which may be empty. A condition that neither option accompanies has no ADDITIONAL entry, except SYNTAX, which always has one. The entry is what CONDITION('A') answers. An ADDITIONAL that holds the null object .nil is still present. An ADDITIONAL belongs to the clause that gave it: a RAISE that no trap answers leaves nothing for the condition that is raised next.

call on user foo name h
do i = 1 to 7
  call ('R'i)
end
exit
h: o = condition('o')
  if \o~hasindex('ADDITIONAL') then do
    say 'no ADDITIONAL'
    return
  end
  a = o~additional
  if a~isA(.array) then say 'array of' a~items
  else say 'value' a
  return
::routine r1; raise user foo
::routine r2; raise user foo additional 'a literal'
::routine r3; raise user foo additional (3 + 4)
::routine r4; raise user foo additional .nil
::routine r5; raise user foo additional (.array~of('p', 'q'))
::routine r6; raise user foo array ('p', 'q', 'r')
::routine r7; raise user foo array ()

  return

[instr.raise.order]

The expressions of the clause are evaluated before anything is raised, in the code that holds the RAISE and with its variables, in a fixed order that does not depend on the order of the options: the code or the number first, then the DESCRIPTION expression, then the ADDITIONAL expression or the ARRAY list from left to right, and last the RETURN or EXIT expression. A name of a user condition is not evaluated. When the number of a RAISE SYNTAX is not valid, the number is checked as soon as it is evaluated, and the error 33.904 of the number rule is raised before the DESCRIPTION, ADDITIONAL, ARRAY, RETURN and EXIT expressions are evaluated.

call on error name h
call on user foo name h
call one
call two
exit
h: say 'handler' condition('c'); return
::routine one
  raise error (t('code')) return (t('value')) additional (t('extra')),
        description (t('text'))
::routine two
  raise user foo array (t('first'), t('second')) exit (t('value'))
::routine t
  say 'evaluate' arg(1)
  return arg(1)

evaluate code
evaluate text
evaluate extra
evaluate value
handler ERROR
evaluate first
evaluate second
evaluate value
handler USER FOO

raise syntax (t('abc')) description (t('text')) additional (t('extra')),
      return (t('value'))
s: say condition('c') condition('o')~code
exit
t: say 'evaluate' arg(1)
  return arg(1)

evaluate abc
SYNTAX 33.904

Where the condition is raised

[instr.raise.leave]

RAISE ends the code that holds it, and the option says how: RETURN ends it as RETURN does and EXIT ends it as EXIT does, and EXIT is what a clause without either option does. A method and a routine of a ::ROUTINE directive end alone, either way, as RETURN and EXIT say. The value of the option is handed back as that instruction hands it back: it is RESULT after a CALL, the value of a function call, and the value of a message. A clause without a value hands back none, so a function call raises SYNTAX 44.1, as RETURN does, and a message used as a term raises SYNTAX 91.999, as the rule for a unit says. The condition is raised after the value is computed, and a CALL trap runs its handler once the clause of the caller has finished, as the CALL trap rule says.

call on user foo name h
say 'A'
call ru
say 'B' result
call rx
say 'C' result
x = ru()
say 'D' x
x = rx()
say 'E' x
o = .box~new
say 'F' o~m
o~m
say 'G' result
exit
h: say 'h' condition('c') sigl; return
::routine ru
  say 'in ru'
  raise user foo return 'from ru'
  say 'not reached'
::routine rx
  raise user foo exit 'from rx'
::class box
::method m
  raise user foo return 'from m'

[instr.raise.caller]

A condition other than SYNTAX that a RAISE with RETURN raises is raised in the code that called the code that holds the RAISE, at the clause that made the call, which is a CALL, a function call or a message, whether the code called is a routine, an internal routine or a method. A RAISE with EXIT ends more than the code that holds it, and the exit rule says who the caller is then. The traps of that caller answer it, as the choice rule says, so a SIGNAL trap abandons the clause, and an assignment in it is not made. The raising code's own traps take no part in the answer, even when they are on, and a caller that has no trap for the condition does not hand it to its own caller: only a SYNTAX condition travels up. SIGL in the code that answers is the line of the clause in the caller, and the POSITION entry is the line of the RAISE clause.

call on user foo name main_h
say 'start'
call tt
say 'after tt'
call il
say 'after il'
exit
il:
  say 'in il'
  raise user foo return
  say 'not reached'
main_h: say 'main' condition('c') 'sigl' sigl,
    'position' condition('o')~position
  return
::routine tt
  call on user foo name mine
  raise user foo
mine: say 'mine'
  return

start
main USER FOO sigl 3 position 17
after tt
in il
main USER FOO sigl 5 position 10
after il

x = 'old'
x = f()
say 'not reached'
exit
h: say 'h' x
::routine f
  raise user foo return 'new'

h old

call on user foo name h
.box~new~outer
say 'after outer'
exit
h: say 'h at' sigl; return
::class box
::method outer
  call inner
  say 'outer goes on'
  return
inner: raise user foo return

outer goes on
after outer
[instr.raise.exit]

A RAISE with EXIT, which is what a clause with neither option does, ends the whole unit that holds it, as EXIT does: a RAISE in an internal routine ends the ::ROUTINE, the method or the main program that the internal routine belongs to, and so does a RAISE in the text of an INTERPRET in any of these. A condition other than SYNTAX is raised in the caller of that unit, at the clause that called the unit, and the traps of the unit and of its internal routines play no part in the answer. The main program has no caller, and the rule for the main program says what happens there. A SYNTAX condition is raised in the unit itself, at the clause that runs at the level of the unit. That clause is the RAISE when it is in the code of the unit or in INTERPRET text there, and it is the call of the internal routine when the RAISE is in an internal routine. The traps that the unit has at that level answer the condition, and a SYNTAX that they do not answer goes up to the caller of the unit as the propagation rule says. A HALT or a NOMETHOD is answered by a trap of the caller, its own or the ANY trap, as the choice rule says, so a CALL trap for ANY answers a HALT and not a NOMETHOD. When no trap of the caller answers it, the condition becomes the SYNTAX that the untrapped rule says, and that SYNTAX is raised in the unit as any SYNTAX of a RAISE with EXIT is. RAISE PROPAGATE with EXIT is not specified.

call on user foo name hm
say 'A' plain()
say 'B' .box~new~m
say 'C' viaint()
say 'D' viatext()
say 'E' outer()
exit
hm: say '   main' condition('c') sigl; return
::routine plain
  call on user foo name t
  raise user foo exit 'plain'
t: say '   plain trap' sigl; return
::class box
::method m
  call on user foo name t
  raise user foo exit 'm'
t: say '   m trap' sigl; return
::routine viaint
  call on user foo name t
  v = il()
  say '   viaint goes on'
  return 'viaint' v
il: raise user foo exit 'il'
t: say '   viaint trap' sigl; return
::routine viatext
  call on user foo name t
  interpret "raise user foo exit 'vt'"
t: say '   viatext trap' sigl; return
::routine outer
  call on user foo name t
  v = plain()
  say '   outer goes on'
  return 'outer' v
t: say '   outer trap' sigl; return

[instr.raise.here]

A SYNTAX condition that a RAISE with RETURN raises is raised at the RAISE clause itself, as an error found there would be. The trap of the raising code for SYNTAX or ANY answers it when that trap is ON, so a routine that switched the trap on, and an internal routine that has it on from its caller, handle their own RAISE SYNTAX. When that trap is OFF, the condition goes up to the caller as the propagation rule says, and the caller sees POSITION as the line of the RAISE, SIGL as the line of its own clause and PROPAGATED as 1, as the propagated rule says. The SYNTAX that an unanswered HALT or NOMETHOD becomes is raised in the same way. With EXIT the SYNTAX is raised in the unit that holds the RAISE, as the exit rule says.

call go 'plain'
call go 'own'
call go 'mid'
call internal
signal on syntax name m
call inh
say 'after inh'
exit

  signal on syntax name s
  call (arg(1))
  say arg(1) 'returned'
  return
s: say arg(1) 'caught by go' sigl condition('o')~code,
      condition('o')~position condition('o')~propagated
  return

  signal on syntax name is
  raise syntax 40.3 return
is: say 'internal caught' sigl condition('o')~code
  return
m: say 'inherited' sigl condition('o')~code
  return
inh: procedure
  raise syntax 40.3 return

::routine own
  signal on syntax name mine
  raise syntax 40.3 return
mine: say 'own caught' sigl condition('o')~code
  return

  call plain
  say 'not reached'

[instr.raise.interpret]

In the text of an INTERPRET instruction, a RAISE with RETURN raises the condition in the code that holds the INTERPRET, at the INTERPRET clause, and not in the caller of that code. That code then ends as the rule for leaving the text says: RETURN returns from the routine, method or internal routine that holds the INTERPRET. A routine whose own trap is on therefore answers the condition that its INTERPRET raised, and a routine with no trap ignores it, without the trap of its caller seeing it. A RAISE with EXIT in INTERPRET text ends the unit, and the condition is raised as the exit rule says, in the caller of the unit. In the main program, the INTERPRET clause is where a RAISE with RETURN in INTERPRET text raises the condition, and the traps of the main program answer it there. A RAISE with EXIT there ends the program, and the rule for the main program says that nothing answers it.

call on user foo name h
say 'A' with()
say 'B' without()
say 'C' leaving()
exit
h: say 'h' condition('c') sigl; return
::routine with
  call on user foo name inner
  interpret "raise user foo return 'with value'"
  say 'not reached'
inner: say 'inner' condition('c') sigl; return
::routine without
  interpret "raise user foo return 'without value'"
  say 'not reached'
::routine leaving
  call on user foo name inner
  interpret "raise user foo exit 'leaving value'"
inner: say 'inner' condition('c') sigl; return

say 'not reached'
exit
h: say 'h' condition('c') sigl; return

[instr.raise.main]

The main program has no caller. A RAISE in it ends the program, as RETURN or EXIT would, with the value of the option as the exit code, as RETURN specifies, and the condition is raised in the main program itself, at the RAISE clause. No trap answers a condition other than SYNTAX there, ANY included, so it is ignored, except for an unanswered HALT or NOMETHOD, which becomes a SYNTAX condition as the untrapped rule says. The same holds for a RAISE with EXIT in an internal routine of the main program and in INTERPRET text of the main program: the program ends, and as the exit rule says, a condition other than SYNTAX has no caller to be raised in, so no trap sees it. A SYNTAX is raised in the main program at the clause that runs at the level of the program, which is the call of the internal routine or the INTERPRET clause, and the traps of the main program answer it. A RAISE with RETURN in an internal routine of the main program is the case of the caller rule: the main program is the caller.

signal on any name sa

say 'start'
raise user foo return 'x'
say 'not reached'
exit
ca: say 'call trap' condition('c'); return
sa: say 'signal trap' condition('c'); exit
sy: say 'sy' condition('c'); exit

When no trap answers

[instr.raise.untrapped]

A condition that RAISE raises and that no trap answers is handled as the untrapped rule says, and the HALT rule says that a HALT becomes SYNTAX 4.1 whatever description the clause gave. RAISE adds two cases. An untrapped NOMETHOD becomes SYNTAX 97.1 when the clause gave ADDITIONAL or ARRAY, and SYNTAX 97.5 when it gave neither, whatever its description. A FAILURE that RAISE raised is not answered as an ERROR when its own trap is off, unlike the FAILURE of a command, which falls back to the ERROR trap. A SYNTAX condition with no answering trap ends the program, as the SYNTAX rule says.

do w over 'R1 R2 R3 R4 R5 R6 R7'~makearray(' ')
  call go w
end
exit
go: procedure
  signal on syntax name s
  call (arg(1))
  say arg(1) 'ignored'
  return
s: say arg(1) 'SYNTAX' condition('o')~code
  return
::routine r1; raise halt return
::routine r2; raise halt description 'stop'
::routine r3; raise nomethod
::routine r4; raise nomethod description 'bark'
::routine r5; raise nomethod additional ('obj') description 'bark'
::routine r6; raise nomethod array ('o', 'p')
::routine r7
  signal on syntax name mine
  raise halt return
mine: say 'r7 itself' condition('o')~code sigl
  return

R1 SYNTAX 4.1
R2 SYNTAX 4.1
R3 SYNTAX 97.5
R4 SYNTAX 97.5
R5 SYNTAX 97.1
R6 SYNTAX 97.1
r7 itself 4.1 20
R7 ignored

call on error name e
call r1
call r2
exit
e: say 'e' condition('c') rc; return
::routine r1; raise failure 7 return
::routine r2; raise error 8 return

e ERROR 8

say 'before'
call r
say 'not reached'

before

Raising a condition again

[instr.raise.propagate]

RAISE PROPAGATE raises again the condition that the code holding the clause has recorded, as the record rule and the scope rule of CONDITION describe. The condition is raised in the caller of that code, as for any other condition, and it keeps its name and the entries that it held, so a user condition is still the same user condition, a SYNTAX keeps its CODE and RC, and the ADDITIONAL entry stays, unless the clause replaces it as the replacement rule says. In the new condition object PROPAGATED is 1, as the propagated rule specifies, so for a SYNTAX the value does not tell a PROPAGATE from a condition that travelled on its own. The POSITION entry of a propagated user condition is still the line of the original RAISE, and that of a propagated SYNTAX is the line of the clause in the caller, which is also SIGL. A RETURN or EXIT value on the clause is the value that the code hands back, as the rule for leaving says, and the Deviation on values says what the condition holds of it.

signal on syntax name top
call r
say 'not reached'
exit
top: o = condition('o')
  say 'top' o~code o~rc o~propagated o~position sigl
::routine r
  signal on syntax name lbl
  x = 1 + 'a'
lbl: say 'r' condition('c') condition('o')~propagated
  raise propagate

r SYNTAX 0
top 41.1 41 1 2 2

signal on user foo name top
call r
say 'not reached'
exit
top: o = condition('o')
  say 'top' o~condition o~propagated '['o~description']' o~position sigl,
      o~additional
::routine r
  signal on user foo name lbl
  call s
  say 'not reached'
lbl: o = condition('o')
  say 'r' o~condition o~propagated '['o~description']' o~position sigl,
      o~additional
  raise propagate
::routine s
  raise user foo description 'first' additional ('first')

r USER FOO 0 [first] 17 10 first
top USER FOO 1 [first] 17 2 first

call on user foo name top
x = r()
say 'x is' x
exit
top: say 'top' condition('o')~propagated; return
::routine r
  signal on user foo name lbl
  call s
lbl: raise propagate return 'handed back'
::routine s
  raise user foo return

top 1
x is handed back

signal on syntax name h
say 'start'
x = 1 + 'a'
h: say 'h' condition('c')
raise propagate

start
h SYNTAX
[instr.raise.propagate.replace]

DESCRIPTION, ADDITIONAL and ARRAY on a RAISE PROPAGATE replace the values that the condition passed on holds: the description becomes the value of the DESCRIPTION expression, and the ADDITIONAL entry becomes the value of the ADDITIONAL expression or the array that ARRAY gives. An entry that the clause does not name keeps the value that the condition had.

call on user foo name top
do i = 1 to 4
  call ('MID'i)
end
exit
top: o = condition('o')
  a = o~additional
  if a~isA(.array) then a = 'array' a~toString('l', ',')
  say i '['o~description']' a
  return
::routine mid1
  signal on user foo name lbl
  call src
lbl: raise propagate
::routine mid2
  signal on user foo name lbl
  call src
lbl: raise propagate description 'new'
::routine mid3
  signal on user foo name lbl
  call src
lbl: raise propagate additional ('new add')
::routine mid4
  signal on user foo name lbl
  call src
lbl: raise propagate array ('p', 'q') description 'd4'
::routine src
  raise user foo description 'orig' additional ('orig add')

1 [orig] orig add
2 [new] orig add
3 [orig] new add
4 [d4] array p,q
[instr.raise.propagate.none]

When the code that holds RAISE PROPAGATE has no recorded condition, the clause raises SYNTAX 98.918, in the way a SYNTAX is raised.

signal on syntax name s
v = 'before'
call r
say 'not reached'
exit
s: say 'syntax' condition('o')~code
::routine r
  raise propagate

syntax 98.918

Deviations

[instr.raise.deviation.65]

A value on RAISE's RETURN or EXIT option is the condition object's RESULT for every condition, and a RAISE PROPAGATE keeps it. ooRexx sets RESULT only for SYNTAX.

call on user foo name h
call on error name h
call r1
call r2
call r3
call r4
call keeper
signal on syntax name s
call r5
exit
h: o = condition('o')
  if o~hasindex('RESULT') then say condition('c') 'RESULT' o~result
  else say condition('c') 'no RESULT entry'
  return
s: o = condition('o')
  say condition('c') o~code 'RESULT' o~result
::routine r1; raise user foo return 'one'
::routine r2; raise user foo exit 'two'
::routine r3; raise error 3 return 'three'
::routine r4; raise user foo
::routine r5; raise syntax 40.3 return 'five'
::routine keeper
  signal on user foo name again
  call source
  say 'not reached'
again: raise propagate
::routine source
  raise user foo return 'kept'

USER FOO RESULT one
USER FOO RESULT two
ERROR RESULT three
USER FOO no RESULT entry
USER FOO RESULT kept
SYNTAX 40.3 RESULT five

REPLY

REPLY [expression]

rexxref: Keyword Instructions > REPLY

REPLY ends a method call early. The caller gets the answer at once and goes on, and the method goes on with the clauses after the REPLY, on an activity of its own. It is how a method hands out a result and then does the slow part of its work while the caller carries on. This page specifies what the caller and the continuation each see, what the continuation may and may not do, the places where REPLY may stand, and the errors.

The order in which the caller's later clauses and the continuation's clauses run is not specified, unless a wait, a guard or the instruction itself puts them in order. Every example below puts them in order, so that its output does not depend on it.

The early answer

[instr.reply.early]

REPLY evaluates its expression and hands the value to whoever sent the message, as RETURN does, and the caller continues with it. A REPLY with no expression hands over no value, and the caller sees what it sees after a RETURN with none, as the message rule says. The method does not end. The clause after the REPLY runs next, on a new activity, with the variables of the method as they were, its arguments, and its object variables. For a message sent with ~start, the value of the REPLY is the ~result of the message object. The method call that sent the message is over for the caller, so the method's later RETURN or EXIT has no value to hand over.

log = .array~new
o = .rep~new(log)
m = o~start('work', 'a1', 'a2')
log~append('caller got' m~result)
o~go
o~wait
say log~makeString('l', '|')
o~noval
say symbol('result')
exit
::class rep
::method init
  expose log go done
  use arg log
  go = .false; done = .false
::method go unguarded
  expose go
  go = .true
::method wait unguarded
  expose done
  guard on when done
::method work
  expose log go done
  use arg a, b
  loc = 'local'
  reply 'early'
  guard on when go
  log~append('cont' a b loc arg() self~class~id)
  done = .true
::method noval
  reply

caller got early|cont a1 a2 local 2 REP
LIT
[instr.reply.guard]

A method that holds its object's guard when it replies keeps it on the new activity, when its call is the only one on its activity that holds the guard of the object. The continuation then has exclusive use of the object variables, and a guarded method that another activity sends to the object waits until the continuation has ended, as the exclusion rule of GUARD says. When a guarded method of the same object has called the replying method on that activity, it still holds the guard after the reply, and the continuation takes the guard again before its first clause runs, which waits until that method has given it up.

log = .array~new
o = .vault~new(log)
say o~holder
p = o~start('probe')
o~release
p~result
say log~makeString('l', ' ')
::class vault
::method init
  expose log go
  use arg log
  go = .false
::method holder
  expose log go
  reply 'replied'
  do until go; end
  log~append('continued')
::method probe
  expose log
  log~append('probe')
  return 'p'
::method release unguarded
  expose go
  go = .true

replied
continued probe

log = .array~new
o = .outer~new(log)
m = o~start('a')
do until o~inB; end
o~release
m~result
o~waitDone
do l over log; say l; end
::class outer
::method init
  expose log go inb done
  use arg log
  go = .false; inb = .false; done = .false
::method a
  expose log go
  x = self~b
  log~append('A after b got' x)
  do until go; end
  log~append('A end')
::method b
  expose log inb done
  inb = .true
  reply 'r'
  log~append('B cont')
  done = .true
::method release unguarded
  expose go
  go = .true
::method inB unguarded
  expose inb
  return inb
::method waitDone unguarded
  expose done
  guard on when done

A after b got r
A end
B cont

After the REPLY

[instr.reply.once]

One REPLY is allowed in a call; a second raises SYNTAX 98.935. A RETURN with an expression after a REPLY raises SYNTAX 98.936, and an EXIT with an expression SYNTAX 98.937, because the value has nowhere to go. A RETURN or an EXIT without an expression ends the continuation, and the method is over. These errors arise in the continuation, so a trap in the method sees them. An error that no trap handles ends the continuation only, with its message on standard error: the caller has the answer already, and the program goes on.

log = .array~new
o = .rep~new(log)
do m over .array~of('twice', 'retval', 'exitval', 'plain', 'plainexit')
  log~append(m 'got' o~send(m))
  o~go
  o~wait
end
do l over log; say l; end
say o~lost
say 'main continues'
exit
::class rep
::method init
  expose log go done
  use arg log
  go = .false; done = .false
::method go unguarded
  expose go
  go = .true
::method wait unguarded
  expose done
  guard on when done
  done = .false
::method twice
  expose log go done
  signal on syntax name oops
  reply 'one'
  guard on when go
  go = .false
  reply 'two'
oops: log~append('twice' condition('o')~code)
  done = .true
::method retval
  expose log go done
  signal on syntax name oops
  reply 'one'
  guard on when go
  go = .false
  return 5
oops: log~append('retval' condition('o')~code)
  done = .true
::method exitval
  expose log go done
  signal on syntax name oops
  reply 'one'
  guard on when go
  go = .false
  exit 5
oops: log~append('exitval' condition('o')~code)
  done = .true
::method plain
  expose log go done
  reply 'one'
  guard on when go
  go = .false
  log~append('plain continued')
  done = .true
  return
::method plainexit
  expose log go done
  reply 'one'
  guard on when go
  go = .false
  log~append('plainexit continued')
  done = .true
  exit
::method lost
  reply 'lost answer'
  x = 1 / 0

twice 98.935
retval got one
retval 98.936
exitval got one
exitval 98.937
plain got one
plain continued

plainexit continued
lost answer
main continues
[instr.reply.value]

An error in the expression of the REPLY is raised before the method is split: the caller gets the error, as it would for a RETURN, and no continuation runs.

o = .rep~new
signal on syntax name e
say o~bad
say 'not reached'
e: say 'caller trapped' condition('o')~code
::class rep
::method bad
  reply 1/0
  say 'the continuation must not run'

caller trapped 42.3

Where REPLY may appear

[instr.reply.method]

REPLY works in the code of a method, anywhere among its own clauses, in a DO, an IF or a SELECT as well. In the main program, in a routine of a ::ROUTINE directive and in an internal routine, including one that a method calls, it raises SYNTAX 99.919 when it runs. The handler of a CALL ON is an internal routine, so a REPLY there raises SYNTAX 99.919 too; the handler of a SIGNAL ON is not, and a REPLY there is plain. The text of an INTERPRET raises SYNTAX 99.924 when the INTERPRET runs, so no clause of the text runs.

o = .box~new
say 'inside =>' o~inside
call try 'main'
call try 'internal'
call try 'routine'
say o~nested
exit
try:
  what = arg(1)
  signal on syntax name e
  if what = 'main' then reply 1
  if what = 'internal' then do; call lab; return; end
  if what = 'routine' then call r
  say what '=> ok'
  return
e: say what '=>' condition('o')~code
  return
lab:
  reply 1
::routine r
  reply 1
::class box
::method inside
  signal on syntax name h
  interpret 'reply 1'
  return 'no'
h: return condition('o')~code
::method nested
  do i = 1 to 2
    if i = 2 then reply 'second round'
  end
  return

main => 99.919
internal => 99.919
routine => 99.919
second round

o = .box~new
say 'result:' o~callon
say o~signalon
::class box
::method callon
  signal on syntax name s
  call on notready name h
  x = linein('/nonexistent/dir/file')
  return 'method continued'
h:
  say 'in call on handler'
  reply 'from call on handler'
  say 'not reached'
  return
s: say 'trapped' condition('o')~code
  return 'trapped answer'
::method signalon
  signal on notready name h
  x = linein('/nonexistent/dir/file')
  return 'not reached'
h:
  reply 'from signal on handler'
  return
