trapped 99.919
result: method continued
from signal on handler

REPLY in a labelled group

[instr.reply.group]

A REPLY inside a DO group that has a label and no repetition (DO LABEL blk) runs as the rules above describe, at any depth within the group: the caller receives the value, and the method goes on to the end of the group and past it. A group, a loop, a SELECT or an IF nested in it is inside it as well, and the group may itself stand in any other DO, loop, SELECT or IF.

o = .rep~new
say 'before'
say o~m
::class rep
::method m
  do label blk
    reply 'from block'
  end
  return

before
from block

RETURN

RETURN [expression [, expression]...]

ANSI: 6.3.2.80, 8.3.22; rexxref: Keyword Instructions > RETURN

RETURN ends the routine, method or program that is running and hands an optional value back to whoever started it. What the starter does with the value depends on how the code was started: a CALL stores it in RESULT, a function call uses it as the value of the call, a message answers it, and for the main program it becomes the program's exit code. This page specifies RETURN in each of these places, the list form with several expressions, and the errors of the clause. EXIT is the instruction that ends the whole program from any depth, and the page of the exit code is that one.

Returning from a routine

[instr.return.routine]

RETURN in an internal routine, which is the code from a label that a CALL or a function call started, ends the routine and continues with the caller, even when the RETURN is nested inside DO, IF or SELECT constructs, which it abandons. A RETURN with an expression hands its value to the caller, and a CALL stores it in RESULT as the CALL rule says. A RETURN without an expression hands over no value, so a CALL drops RESULT, and a function call that has no value raises SYNTAX 44.1, as the rule for a call in an expression says. The caller's settings come back as the CALL rule says.

call find 6
say 'found' result
call find 99
say 'found' result
say 'direct' find(4) 'then' find(5)
result = 'old'
call quiet
say symbol('result')
signal on syntax name e
say quiet()
e: say condition('o')~code
exit
find: procedure
  arg target
  do i = 1 to 3
    do j = 1 to 3
      if i * j = target then return i'x'j
    end
  end
  return 'none'
quiet: return

found 2x3
found none
direct 2x2 then none
LIT
44.1
[instr.return.value]

The expression is evaluated before the routine is left, with the variables and the settings that the routine has. When the routine started with PROCEDURE, its variables are dropped only after the expression has been evaluated, so the value may use them, and the caller's variable of the same name is untouched.

total = 'caller total'
say sum(3, 4) total
exit
sum: procedure
  total = arg(1) + arg(2)
  return total * 2

14 caller total

Returning from a program, a method or a routine directive

[instr.return.program]

A RETURN in the code of the main program, outside any internal routine, method or routine directive, ends the program, as EXIT does, and its value is the program's value, whose use as the exit code is specified with EXIT. This holds for a RETURN inside a DO, IF or SELECT, and for a RETURN after a label that the program reached by running into it, since no CALL started that code. A RETURN without an expression gives no value and the exit code 0.

say 'main'
helper:
say 'at helper'
return 7
say 'not reached'

main
at helper
[instr.return.unit]

RETURN in a method or in a routine that a ::ROUTINE directive defines ends that method or routine and hands the value to whoever sent the message or made the call, whatever the program as a whole is doing. A message instruction stores the value in RESULT as the message rule says, and a message that has no value and is used as a term raises SYNTAX 91.999, as the cascade rule says. A CALL of the routine stores the value as for an internal routine.

o = .box~new
o~note
say 'A' result
o~quiet
say 'B' symbol('result')
call twice 4
say 'C' result
say 'D' twice(5)
exit 2
::class box
::method note
  return 'noted'
::method quiet
  return
::routine twice
  return arg(1) * 2

A noted
B LIT
C 8
D 10
[instr.return.interpret]

A RETURN in the text of an INTERPRET returns from the routine, method or program that holds the INTERPRET, as the rule on leaving the text says. The rest of the text and the clauses after the INTERPRET do not run.

say pick(1) pick(2)
exit
pick:
  interpret 'if arg(1) = 1 then return "one"'
  return 'other'

one other

Several expressions

[instr.return.list]

RETURN may have several expressions separated by commas, and the value it hands over is then a new Array that holds the values in order. An expression that is left out leaves its position empty, so the Array counts it in its size but not in its items. A comma at the end of a line is not a separator but a continuation, as the continuation rule says. For the main program the value is an Array, which is not a number, so the exit code is 0.

call pair 'x', 'y'
say result~class~id result~items result[1] result[2]
call gap
say result~items result~size
exit
pair: return arg(1), arg(2)
gap: return 1,,3

Array 2 x y
2 3

Errors

[instr.return.syntax]

A malformed expression in a RETURN raises the SYNTAX error of the expression, 35.1 for an operator with nothing after it. Like any fault of the clause, it is found when the program is read, so no clause runs and the exit code is 221, and the text of an INTERPRET raises it when the INTERPRET runs.

say 'before'
return 1 +

signal on syntax name e
interpret 'say "first"; return 1 +'
e: say condition('o')~code

35.1

SAY

SAY [expression]

ANSI: 6.3.2.81, 8.3.23; rexxref: Keyword Instructions > SAY

Deviations: D40, D98

SAY writes one line of text to the standard output. It evaluates its expression, converts the result to a string and writes that string followed by a line end. Without an expression it writes an empty line. The instruction does nothing else: it sets no variable, and it leaves the special variables RC and RESULT as they were. The output goes to the same stream that the builtins with no stream name write to, so SAY mixes with them in the order the program ran them.

What is written

[instr.say.write]

The expression is everything after the keyword. SAY evaluates it, takes the string value of the result and writes the string, then a line end. The expression is an ordinary expression, so the operators join, add and compare as they do anywhere else, and a number is written in the form that the operation that made it gave it.

numeric digits 4
x = 'abc'
say x 'def'
say 1 + 1 2 * 3
say 1 / 3
say (1 = 1) (1 = 2)
say 'a' || 'b' x

abc def
2 6
0.3333
1 0
ab abc
[instr.say.null]

A SAY with no expression writes a line end and nothing before it. So does a SAY whose expression is the null string, and one whose value is a string of blanks writes the blanks.

say 'one'
say
say ''
say '  '
say 'two'

one


  
two
[instr.say.bytes]

SAY writes the characters of the string as they are. It does not change control characters or other unprintable ones, it adds no padding and it does not stop at a character that other contexts treat as an end of text, such as '00'x or '1A'x. A line feed in the string is written as it is, so it breaks the line where it stands, and the line end that SAY adds follows the string. Which bytes make up the line end that SAY adds is not specified.

say 'a' || '00'x || 'b' || '0D'x || '1A'x || '7F'x
say 'x' || '0A'x || 'y'

a\x00b\x0D\x1A\x7F
x
y
[instr.say.object]

A result that is an object and not a string is turned into a string first, as the conversion rule says. The conversion happens before anything is written.

say .viamake~new
say .viastring~new
say .both~new 'tail'
say .viamake~new||'!'
::class viastring
::method string
return 'viastring'
::class viamake
::method makestring
return 'made'
::class both
::method string
return 'plain'
::method makestring
return 'preferred'

made
viastring
preferred tail
made!

The output stream

[instr.say.stream]

SAY writes to the standard output, the stream that a builtin names with a null name or none when it writes. The line end is the only thing SAY adds, so text that a CHAROUT call left unfinished on the current line is followed by the SAY text on that same line, and a SAY is followed by CHAROUT text on the next line. The text a program writes this way appears in the order the program wrote it. The standard output is also what .OUTPUT denotes by default, and what SAY does when a program has redirected .OUTPUT is not specified here.

call charout , 'p'
say 'c'
call charout , 'q'
call charout , 'r'
say 'd'
call lineout , 'e'
say 'f'

pc
qrd
e
f
[instr.say.result]

SAY does not set RESULT and does not drop it, and it does not change RC. A routine that says something and then returns a value gives its caller that value in RESULT, and the SAY has no part in it.

result = 'keep'; rc = 'mine'
call giver
say 'got' result
say result rc
exit
giver: say 'in giver'
return 'given'

in giver
got given
given mine

Syntax

[instr.say.keyword]

The word SAY starts the instruction in any case, and it may be followed directly by a parenthesis, a quote or a sign, as the keyword rule says. A clause that begins with say = is an assignment to a variable of that name and not a SAY, as the kind rule says, and so is a clause that begins with say.x =, because a symbol with a period is not a keyword.

Say(1+2)
SAY"q"
say-4
say = 'var'
say say
say.x = 'stem'
say say.x

3
q
-4
var
stem
[instr.say.error]

An error in the expression ends the SAY before anything is written, and the clause writes no part of the line. The error is the one the expression raises, for example 42.3 for a zero divisor, 41.1 for a name that is not a number in arithmetic and 97.1 for a message that nothing answers. An expression that cannot be read raises its SYNTAX 35.1 or 37.2 when the program is read, so a program with such a SAY runs nothing, as the expression rule says.

call try 'say 1 / 0'
call try 'say "n" + u'
call try 'say .nosuch~foo'
call try 'say "partial" 1 / 0'
call try 'say 1 2 )'
call try 'say 1 +'
say 'done'
exit
try:
  signal on syntax name e
  interpret arg(1)
  say 'ok' arg(1)
  return
e: say condition('o')~code '<=' arg(1)
  return

42.3 <= say 1 / 0
41.1 <= say "n" + u
97.1 <= say .nosuch~foo
42.3 <= say "partial" 1 / 0
37.2 <= say 1 2 )
35.1 <= say 1 +
done

say 'before'
say 1 +

Deviations

[instr.say.deviation.40]

SAY and the builtins that write to the standard output share one stream, and the text of all of them appears in the order the program wrote it. A standard output that is a pipe or a file is buffered, and it is handed over at the points that Deviation 40 names. ooRexx writes each line at once, so text still buffered when the process is killed or crashes is lost here and is not lost there.

say 'one'
call charout , 'two'
call lineout , ' three'
say 'four'

one
two three
four
[instr.say.deviation.98]

After a close of the standard output (see the stream lifetime rule), SAY writes its line as usual, and the output is opened again. In ooRexx the line does not appear at once, and what is written after the last close, flush or open is lost. SAY raises no NOTREADY condition in either, whatever the state of the standard output, so the trap in the example does not run.

say 'one'
call stream 'stdout', 'c', 'close'
signal on notready name nr
say 'two'
say 'three'
exit
nr: say 'notready'

one
two
three

SELECT

SELECT [LABEL name] [CASE expression]; WHEN expression [, expression]... [;] THEN [;] instruction ... [OTHERWISE [instructions]] END [name]

ANSI: 6.3.2.17, 8.3.24; rexxref: Keyword Instructions > SELECT

Deviations: D39

SELECT chooses one of several alternatives. The block holds a sequence of WHEN clauses, each with a test and one instruction, and an optional OTHERWISE part. The tests run in order and the instruction of the first true one runs, after which control leaves the block at its END. In the second form, SELECT CASE, the tests compare a value that SELECT computes once. This page specifies the order of evaluation, what a test must be, the CASE comparison, the label of the block and the errors. The two-way choice is IF.

What it does

[instr.select.run]

SELECT evaluates the expressions of its WHEN clauses from the first to the last, and it stops at the first one that is true. The instruction after the THEN of that clause runs, and control then passes to the clause after the END of the SELECT, so the WHEN clauses after it are not evaluated and the OTHERWISE part does not run. THEN may begin a later clause than the expression of its WHEN, as the rule for THEN says, and the instruction after each THEN follows the rules of IF for null clauses and for the implied semicolons after THEN.

n = 7
select
  when n < 5 then say 'small'
  when n < 10 then say 'medium'
  when f(n) then say 'never evaluated'
  otherwise say 'large'
end
say 'after'
exit
f: say 'f called'; return 1

medium
after
[instr.select.then]

A WHEN accepts null clauses between its expression and its THEN, and after the THEN, just as an IF does: a line end, a semicolon, blank lines and comments there neither end the WHEN nor take the place of its instruction. The first SELECT below has a THEN on a later line than its WHEN, and a semicolon and a comment before it. The second has a null clause after the THEN.

select
  when 0
  then say 'no'
  when 1; /* c */

  then say 'yes'
  when 1;; then say 'not reached'
  otherwise say 'other'
end
select
  when 1 then
    ;
    say 'branch'
end

yes
branch

The test of a WHEN

[instr.select.when]

In a SELECT without CASE, the expression of a WHEN must have the value 0 or 1, as the value of an IF must, and any other value raises SYNTAX 34.2. A WHEN can hold a list of expressions separated by commas, and the list is true and is evaluated as the list of an IF is. An expression of the list that is evaluated and is not 0 or 1 raises SYNTAX 34.6. The error is raised when the WHEN is reached, so a WHEN that comes after a true one is never evaluated and cannot raise it.

call try 'select; when 2 then nop; end'
call try 'select; when 1, 5 then nop; end'
call try 'select; when 0, 5 then nop; otherwise say "short"; end'
call try 'select; when 1, f(1), f(1) then say "all"; end'
call try 'select; when 1 then say "first"; when 2 then nop; end'
call try 'select; when 0 then nop; when "a" then nop; end'
exit
f: say 'f('arg(1)')'; return arg(1)
try:
  signal on syntax name e
  interpret arg(1)
  say arg(1) '=> ok'
  return
e: say arg(1) '=>' condition('o')~code
  return

select; when 2 then nop; end => 34.2
select; when 1, 5 then nop; end => 34.6
short
select; when 0, 5 then nop; otherwise say "short"; end => ok
f(1)
f(1)
all
select; when 1, f(1), f(1) then say "all"; end => ok
first
select; when 1 then say "first"; when 2 then nop; end => ok
select; when 0 then nop; when "a" then nop; end => 34.2

OTHERWISE

[instr.select.otherwise]

The OTHERWISE part runs when no WHEN was true. It holds any number of instructions up to the END, and it may hold none, in which case a SELECT with no true WHEN does nothing. A SELECT that has no OTHERWISE part and no true WHEN raises SYNTAX 7.3 when the END is reached, which is when the program runs and not when it is read, so the clauses before it have run. OTHERWISE is the last part of the block, and a WHEN after it raises SYNTAX 9.1, and a second OTHERWISE raises 9.2, when the program is read.

select
  when 0 then say 'no'
  otherwise
    say 'o1'
    say 'o2'
end
select
  when 0 then say 'no'
  otherwise
end
say 'empty otherwise is fine'
call try 'select; when 0 then say "no"; end'
call try 'select; when 1 then nop; otherwise nop; when 1 then nop; end'
call try 'select; when 0 then nop; otherwise nop; otherwise nop; end'
exit
try:
  signal on syntax name e
  interpret arg(1)
  say arg(1) '=> ok'
  return
e: say arg(1) '=>' condition('o')~code
  return

o1
o2
empty otherwise is fine
select; when 0 then say "no"; end => 7.3
select; when 1 then nop; otherwise nop; when 1 then nop; end => 9.1
select; when 0 then nop; otherwise nop; otherwise nop; end => 9.2

SELECT CASE

[instr.select.case]

SELECT CASE evaluates its expression once, before the first WHEN, and each WHEN then holds one expression or a comma-separated list of them. The WHEN is true when the strict comparison == of the case value with one of its expressions is true, where the case value is the receiver and the expression the argument, and the list is evaluated from left to right and stops at the first true comparison. The comparison is the strict one, so 1 does not equal 1.0, a blank counts, and the case of letters counts. The expressions need not be 0 or 1, and no value of a WHEN raises SYNTAX 34.2, so a case that matches no WHEN raises SYNTAX 7.3 as above. When the case value is an object, the == message goes to it, and its answer must be 0 or 1: any other answer, such as the text banana or the number 2, raises SYNTAX 34.905.

x = 'b'
select case x
  when 'a' then say 'is a'
  when 'c', 'b' then say 'is b or c'
  otherwise say 'other'
end
select case 1
  when 1.0 then say 'numeric equal'
  when 1 then say 'strict equal'
end
select case 'a '
  when 'a' then say 'blank ignored'
  when 'A', 'a ' then say 'blank counts, case counts'
end
select case f(2)
  when f(1), f(2), f(3) then say 'hit'
  otherwise nop
end
select case .probe~new('A')
  when .probe~new('B') then say 'matched B'
  when .probe~new('A') then say 'matched A'
end
call try 'select case 3; when 1, 2 then nop; end'
call try 'select case .bad~new; when 1 then nop; end'
call try 'select case .num~new; when 1 then nop; end'
exit
f: say 'f('arg(1)')'; return arg(1)
try:
  signal on syntax name e
  interpret arg(1)
e: say arg(1) '=>' condition('o')~code
  return
::class probe
::method init
  expose n
  use arg n
::attribute n get
::method '=='
  expose n
  use arg other
  say 'receiver' n 'argument' other~n
  return n = other~n
::class bad
::method '=='
  return 'banana'
::class num
::method '=='
  return 2

is b or c
strict equal
blank counts, case counts
f(2)
f(1)
f(2)
hit
receiver A argument B
receiver A argument A
matched A
select case 3; when 1, 2 then nop; end => 7.3
select case .bad~new; when 1 then nop; end => 34.905
select case .num~new; when 1 then nop; end => 34.905
[instr.select.case.syntax]

The expression after CASE is required, and so is the expression of every WHEN in a SELECT CASE, including each one that follows a comma. A missing case expression raises SYNTAX 35.933, and a missing expression in a WHEN 35.934. Both are found when the program is read. A SELECT with a token after it that is not LABEL or CASE raises 25.923. The word LABEL has to come before CASE: after the CASE expression, the word is part of that expression.

call try 'select case ; when 1 then nop; end'
call try 'select case 1; when then nop; end'
call try 'select case 1; when 1, then nop; end'
call try 'select case 1; when , 1 then nop; end'
call try 'select 1; when 1 then nop; end'
call try 'select label a case 1; when 1 then say "ok"; end'
call try 'select case 1 label a; when 1 then say "ok"; end'
exit
try:
  signal on syntax name e
  interpret arg(1)
  say arg(1) '=> ok'
  return
e: say arg(1) '=>' condition('o')~code
  return

select case ; when 1 then nop; end => 35.933
select case 1; when then nop; end => 35.934
select case 1; when 1, then nop; end => 35.934
select case 1; when , 1 then nop; end => 35.934
select 1; when 1 then nop; end => 25.923
ok
select label a case 1; when 1 then say "ok"; end => ok
select case 1 label a; when 1 then say "ok"; end => 7.3

The label of a block

[instr.select.label]

A LABEL phrase gives the block a name that LEAVE can use, whether or not the SELECT has a CASE. LEAVE name ends the block from any depth inside it. An END after the block may repeat the name, which is compared without regard to case, and a different name raises SYNTAX 10.4 and any name on the END of a SELECT that has no LABEL raises 10.7. Both are found when the program is read. An unnamed LEAVE or ITERATE does not select a SELECT, because it is not a loop, as the LEAVE rule says.

select label pick
  when 1 then do
    say 'in'
    leave PICK
    say 'skipped'
  end
  otherwise say 'not run'
end pick
say 'after'
call try 'select label a; when 1 then nop; end A'
call try 'select label a; when 1 then nop; end b'
call try 'select; when 1 then nop; end b'
call try 'select; when 1 then nop; end 5'
exit
try:
  signal on syntax name e
  interpret arg(1)
  say arg(1) '=> ok'
  return
e: say arg(1) '=>' condition('o')~code
  return

in
after
select label a; when 1 then nop; end A => ok
select label a; when 1 then nop; end b => 10.4
select; when 1 then nop; end b => 10.7
select; when 1 then nop; end 5 => 10.7

What the block holds

[instr.select.body]

Between the SELECT and its OTHERWISE or END, the only clauses are WHEN clauses with their instruction, and null clauses. A label there raises SYNTAX 47.4 when the program is read, as the label rule says. The instruction after a THEN is one instruction, which may be a DO group, an IF or another SELECT, so a second instruction raises SYNTAX 7.2 when the program is read. In an IF in the instruction, an ELSE that follows pairs with that IF, as the ELSE rule says, and in a nested SELECT the OTHERWISE and the END belong to the nearest SELECT that is still open.

select
  when 1 then if 0 then say 'a'
  else say 'if else'
  otherwise say 'outer otherwise'
end
select
  when 1 then
    select
      when 0 then say 'inner'
      otherwise say 'inner otherwise'
    end
  otherwise say 'outer otherwise'
end
select
  when 1 then do
    say 'g1'
    say 'g2'
  end
end

if else
inner otherwise
g1
g2

Errors

[instr.select.syntax]

Errors in the shape of a SELECT are found when the program is read, so a program that has one runs none of its clauses. A SELECT with no WHEN before its OTHERWISE or END raises SYNTAX 7.1, and another clause where a WHEN is required raises 7.2. A WHEN or an OTHERWISE outside a SELECT raises the codes of a part out of place. A WHEN with no THEN raises 18.2, and an END where the instruction of a THEN should be is a part out of place, as is a stray END. A SELECT with no END raises 14.2 and one whose OTHERWISE part has no END 14.901.

say 'before'
select
  when 1 then say 'a'
  say 'second instruction'
end

call try 'select; end'
call try 'select; otherwise say 1; end'
call try 'select; say 1; end'
call try 'select; when 1 then say "a"; say "b"; end'
call try 'do; when 1 then say "a"; end'
call try 'otherwise say 1'
call try 'select; when 1 say "a"; end'
call try 'select; when 1 then end'
call try 'select; when 1 then say 1'
call try 'select; when 1 then say 1; otherwise say 2'
call try 'select; when 1 then say 1; end; end'
call try 'select; when 1 then say 1; else say 2; end'
exit
try:
  signal on syntax name e
  interpret arg(1)
  say arg(1) '=> ok'
  return
e: say arg(1) '=>' condition('o')~code
  return

select; end => 7.1
select; otherwise say 1; end => 7.1
select; say 1; end => 7.2
select; when 1 then say "a"; say "b"; end => 7.2
do; when 1 then say "a"; end => 9.1
otherwise say 1 => 9.2
select; when 1 say "a"; end => 18.2
select; when 1 then end => 10.1
select; when 1 then say 1 => 14.2
select; when 1 then say 1; otherwise say 2 => 14.901
select; when 1 then say 1; end; end => 10.1
select; when 1 then say 1; else say 2; end => 8.2

Deviations

[instr.select.deviation.39]

A label spelled THEN that stands as a clause of its own after the expression of a WHEN raises SYNTAX 18.2, because the WHEN is still waiting for its THEN. ooRexx raises 35.1 at the colon. When the then: follows the expression in the same clause, both raise 35.1.

call try 'select; when 1 then: say 1; end'
call try 'select; when 1; then: say 1; end'
exit
try:
  signal on syntax name e
  interpret arg(1)
  say arg(1) '=> ok'
  return
e: say arg(1) '=>' condition('o')~code
  return

select; when 1 then: say 1; end => 35.1
select; when 1; then: say 1; end => 18.2

SIGNAL

SIGNAL {label | [VALUE] expression | ON condition [NAME label] | OFF condition}

ANSI: 6.3.2.82, 8.3.25; rexxref: Keyword Instructions > SIGNAL

SIGNAL moves control to a label, and it also switches the trap of a condition on or off. The jump goes to a label by name, anywhere in the program, and it abandons the blocks that are open in the routine, so it is the instruction for leaving a deeply nested construct and for a handler that does not come back. The other form, with ON or OFF, does not move control. This page specifies how the label is found, what the jump ends, what it sets, and the shape of the ON and OFF forms. What a trap does when its condition occurs belongs to the chapter on conditions, which also specifies SIGNAL's role there.

The label

[instr.signal.label]

SIGNAL name continues at the first label that has the text of the name, among the labels of the code that holds the SIGNAL: the main program, or the body of the one routine or method that the SIGNAL is in. A name written as a symbol is read in upper case, and a name written as a string is used as it is written. The label rule says which labels these find and which of several of one name is the first. A symbol is a constant here: its value as a variable plays no part. When no label has the name, the instruction raises SYNTAX 16.1. The error is raised when the SIGNAL runs, so the clauses before it have run. A label of the main program is therefore not one that a method or a routine can reach, and the labels of a method are not those of the main program.

signal Go
say 'skipped'
go: say 'at go'
signal 'GO2'
say 'skipped'
go2: say 'at go2'
signal "Mixed"
say 'skipped'
"Mixed": say 'at Mixed'
signal 5
say 'skipped'
5: say 'at five'
call try 'mixed'
call try '"mixed"'
call try 'nosuch'
exit
try:
  signal on syntax name e
  interpret 'signal' arg(1)
e: say arg(1) '=>' condition('o')~code
  return

at go
at go2
at Mixed
at five
mixed => 16.1
"mixed" => 16.1
nosuch => 16.1

.c~new~m
exit
mainlab: say 'main label'
::class c
::method m
  signal on syntax name e
  signal mainlab
e: say 'method' condition('o')~code
  signal here
  say 'skipped'
here: say 'method label'

method 16.1
method label
[instr.signal.value]

SIGNAL VALUE expression evaluates the expression and uses the string it converts to as the name, by the conversion rule. The value is compared with the labels as it is, so a lower-case value finds no symbol label, which is written in capitals. A token after SIGNAL that is neither a symbol nor a string, such as a parenthesis, starts an expression, so VALUE is needed only when the expression itself starts with a symbol or a string, which would otherwise be the name. A value that matches no label raises SYNTAX 16.1, and so does one that is not a name at all, such as -1.

signal value .name~new
say 'skipped'
ms: say 'at ms'
st: say 'at st'
name = 'DEST'
signal value name
say 'skipped'
dest: say 'at dest'
signal value 'DE' || 'ST2'
say 'skipped'
dest2: say 'at dest2'
signal ('DE' || 'ST3')
say 'skipped'
dest3: say 'at dest3'
call try 'value "dest"'
call try 'value 1 2'
call try '-1'
call try 'value "DEST" || "x"'
exit
try:
  signal on syntax name e
  interpret 'signal' arg(1)
e: say arg(1) '=>' condition('o')~code
  return
::class name
::method makestring
  return 'MS'
::method string
  return 'ST'

at ms
at st
at dest
at dest2
at dest3
value "dest" => 16.1
value 1 2 => 16.1
-1 => 16.1
value "DEST" || "x" => 16.1
[instr.signal.syntax]

A SIGNAL with a name takes nothing after it: data after a symbol or a string raises SYNTAX 21.905, so signal 'a' || 'b' is an error, since the string is already a complete name. A SIGNAL with nothing after it raises 19.4, and a VALUE with no expression raises 35.915. These are found when the program is read, so none of its clauses run.

say 'before'
signal a b

call try 'signal a b'
call try 'signal "a" || "b"'
call try 'signal'
call try 'signal value'
exit
try:
  signal on syntax name e
  interpret arg(1)
e: say arg(1) '=>' condition('o')~code
  return

signal a b => 21.905
signal "a" || "b" => 21.905
signal => 19.4
signal value => 35.915

What it ends

[instr.signal.ends]

A jump ends every DO, LOOP, SELECT and IF that is open in the routine that holds the SIGNAL, without running their tests and without stepping a control variable, which keeps its value. A loop that was ended is not resumed, and a jump to a label before a loop runs the loop afresh. A label cannot stand inside a loop, as the label rule says, so a SIGNAL cannot enter one. The blocks of the callers of the routine are not ended: a routine that jumps inside itself returns to a caller that is still in its loop. A SIGNAL in the text of an INTERPRET also leaves the text, as the INTERPRET rule says.

do i = 1 to 2
  call sub
  say 'caller loop' i
end
say 'end' i
do j = 1 to 3
  select
    when j = 2 then signal out
    otherwise nop
  end
end
out: say 'out' j
n = 0
top:
do k = 1 to 3
  n = n + 1
  if n = 2 then signal top
  say n k
end
say 'again' n k
exit
sub:
  do 2
    signal done
  end
done: say 'done' i
  return

done 1
caller loop 1
done 2
caller loop 2
end 3
out 2
1 1
3 1
4 2
5 3
again 5 4

What it sets

[instr.signal.sigl]

When control reaches the label, the variable SIGL holds the number of the line of the SIGNAL clause, which is the line where the clause starts when it runs over several lines. SIGL is an ordinary variable that the interpreter sets, so an assignment to it is replaced by the next SIGNAL or CALL, and before the first of them it is unset. SIGNAL sets nothing else: RESULT and RC are unchanged.

say 'start' sigl
signal first
nop
first: say 'first' sigl
signal second /* the comment
                 spans two lines */
second: say 'second' sigl
sigl = 'mine'
rc = 'r'; result = 'v'
signal third
third: say 'third' sigl rc result

start SIGL
first 2
second 5
third 10 r v
[instr.signal.routine]

A SIGNAL that jumps to a label outside the routine that holds it does not leave the routine. The routine keeps its variables, its arguments and its PROCEDURE scope, so the code at the label sees them and not the caller's, and SIGL is set in that scope. A RETURN that the code at the label then reaches returns from the routine to the clause after its CALL, with the value of the RETURN as RESULT.

z = 'main'
call sub 'p', 'q'
say 'caller continues' result
exit
back: say 'at back' arg() symbol('z') y sigl
  return 'ret'
sub: procedure
  y = 'sub y'
  signal back

at back 2 LIT sub y 9
caller continues ret

ON and OFF

[instr.signal.on]

SIGNAL ON condition enables the trap of a condition, and SIGNAL OFF condition disables it. The condition is ERROR, FAILURE, HALT, LOSTDIGITS, NOMETHOD, NOSTRING, NOTREADY, NOVALUE, SYNTAX or ANY, or USER followed by the name of a user condition, which is a symbol read as a constant in upper case, so user foo names the condition USER FOO, and not a string. ON may be followed by NAME and a label, a symbol or a string, that the trap goes to, and the default label is the name of the condition. The label is not looked for when the trap is enabled, so an ON for a label that does not exist is not an error then. What a trap does when its condition occurs, and the role of the label, are the subject of the conditions chapter. OFF takes no NAME.

do c over .array~of('error', 'failure', 'halt', 'lostdigits',,
    'nomethod', 'nostring', 'notready', 'novalue', 'syntax', 'any')
  interpret 'signal on' c
  interpret 'signal off' c
  say c 'on and off'
end
signal on user foo name lbl
signal off user foo
signal on error name nolabel
signal on novalue name 'Mixed Case'
signal off error
signal off novalue
say 'done'
lbl: nop

error on and off
failure on and off
halt on and off
lostdigits on and off
nomethod on and off
nostring on and off
notready on and off
novalue on and off
syntax on and off
any on and off
done

signal on user foo name h
call raiser
h: say condition('c')
exit
::routine raiser
  raise user foo

USER FOO
[instr.signal.on.error]

The errors of the ON and OFF forms are found when the program is read. A SIGNAL ON with no condition raises SYNTAX 20.911 and an OFF 20.912, and a USER with no name, or with a string for the name, 20.915. A word that is not a condition raises 25.3 after ON and 25.4 after OFF. A NAME with no label raises 19.3. Data after the label raises 21.903 on an ON and any NAME on an OFF raises 21.904. A word after the condition that is not NAME raises 25.915.

call try 'signal on'
call try 'signal off'
call try 'signal on user'
call try 'signal on user "foo"'
call try 'signal off user "foo"'
call try 'signal on foo'
call try 'signal off foo'
call try 'signal on error name'
call try 'signal on error name lbl extra'
call try 'signal off error name lbl'
call try 'signal on error lbl'
exit
try:
  signal on syntax name e
  interpret arg(1)
  say arg(1) '=> ok'
  return
e: say arg(1) '=>' condition('o')~code
  return

signal on => 20.911
signal off => 20.912
signal on user => 20.915
signal on user "foo" => 20.915
signal off user "foo" => 20.915
signal on foo => 25.3
signal off foo => 25.4
signal on error name => 19.3
signal on error name lbl extra => 21.903
signal off error name lbl => 21.904
signal on error lbl => 25.915

TRACE

TRACE [setting | VALUE expression | (expression)]

ANSI: 6.3.2.85, 8.3.26; rexxref: Keyword Instructions > TRACE; Keyword Instructions > TRACE > The Format of Trace Output

Deviations: D0, D7, D50

TRACE chooses how much of a running program the interpreter reports, and the report is a stream of lines in a fixed format. This page specifies the forms of the instruction, when a new setting takes effect, where the lines go and what each kind of line looks like. The nine settings, what the TRACE function answers and how a setting is scoped across calls belong to the TRACE function, and this page links them instead of repeating them.

The examples that show trace lines first send them to standard output with .traceoutput~destination(.output), because the lines go to the error stream otherwise, and the examples are checked on standard output only.

The forms

[instr.trace.form.name]

TRACE followed by one symbol or one string takes it as the setting. A symbol is never looked up: whatever the variable of that name holds, its own characters, in either case, are the setting. A setting is chosen by its first letter after the prefix, as the letter rule says, so a whole word such as Results does as well as R, and the string 'a' does as well as A.

r = 'I'
trace r
say trace()
trace 'a'
say trace()
trace Results
say trace()
trace "Normal"
say trace()
trace off
say trace()

R
A
R
N
O
[instr.trace.form.value]

TRACE VALUE expression evaluates the expression and takes its value as the setting, with the same choice by first letter. A value that is not a string is converted as a string argument says, and .nil is not a setting. VALUE may be left out when the expression starts with a parenthesis, or with an operator character other than +, -, = and ~, so TRACE (expression) is the same instruction; the expression is then the rest of the clause, as it is after VALUE. TRACE = expression is an assignment to the variable TRACE, and TRACE~name a message instruction, as the kinds rule says; neither sets a trace setting. A null value is the setting N. The expression ends the clause, so TRACE VALUE 'l' 'x' takes the value l x, which is the setting L.

r = 'I'
trace value r
say trace()
trace value 'a' || 'c'
say trace()
trace (r)
say trace()
trace ('E')
say trace()
trace value ''
say trace()
trace value 'l' 'x'
say trace()

N

call try "trace value .array~new"
call try "trace value .nil"
exit

  signal on syntax name e
  interpret arg(1)
  say arg(1) 'set' trace()

e: say arg(1) condition('o')~code

trace (r) || 'x' set R
trace ('r') 'x' set R

trace value .nil 24.1
[instr.trace.form.bare]

TRACE with nothing after it sets N, and so does the null string in any form of the instruction. Where interactive tracing is on, a setting is ignored, as the instruction rule of the function says; a number still raises the error of the number rule.

trace r
say trace()
trace
say trace()

R
N
[instr.trace.form.interactive]

A question mark before the setting, or alone, turns interactive tracing on or off in the way of the prefix rule: TRACE ? alone flips it and leaves the letter. The instruction cannot turn interactive tracing off, which the function can. What an interactive session accepts as input and what it writes is not specified; a program run with no input at all goes on after each pause. An example that waits for input is never written here.

trace ?r
say trace()
call trace '?'
say trace()
trace ?
say trace()

?R
R
?R
[instr.trace.number]

A setting that is a whole number, written as a symbol, as a string or as the value of an expression, with a sign and blanks around it as a number may have, raises SYNTAX 24.901. A number only has a meaning in interactive tracing, which this book does not specify. A value that is not a whole number is not numeric here and is judged by the letter rule as any other, so 1.5 raises SYNTAX 24.1, as does .5. A sign directly after TRACE, followed by one symbol or string, makes a signed number of it: a whole number raises SYNTAX 24.901, and any other operand raises SYNTAX 26.7. A parenthesis after the sign raises SYNTAX 35.1, and data after the number raises SYNTAX 21.906. A sign alone is no number: TRACE - is the bare form, and TRACE + and a second sign after the first raise SYNTAX 35.1.

call try '5'
call try '-3'
call try '007'
call try ' 5 '
call try '1.0'
call try '1e1'
call try '1.5'
call try '.5'
exit
try: procedure
  signal on syntax name e
  trace value arg(1)
  say arg(1) 'set'
  return
e: say arg(1) condition('o')~code
  return

-3 24.901

1.0 24.901
1e1 24.901
1.5 24.1
.5 24.1

[instr.trace.invalid]

A setting that is neither a number nor valid raises SYNTAX 24.1. A letter that is valid but is followed by anything else is no error, so a5 is A.

call try 'x'

call try 'a5'
call try 'resultsx'

e: say arg(1) condition('o')~code

[instr.trace.syntax]

Data after the setting, other than the expression of VALUE or the rest of a clause that starts as the value rule says, raises SYNTAX 21.906. VALUE with no expression raises SYNTAX 35.916. Both are found when the program is read, so a program file that has one writes nothing and ends with the return code of the error, and the subcode shows only in INTERPRET text.

say 'not run'
trace results extra

say 'not run'
trace value

call try 'trace results extra'
call try 'trace value'
call try 'trace'
exit

  signal on syntax name e
  interpret arg(1)
  say arg(1) 'ok'
  return
e: say arg(1) condition('o')~code
  return

trace results extra 21.906
trace value 35.916
trace ok

When it takes effect

[instr.trace.effect]

A clause is traced with the setting that was in force when it began. The TRACE clause itself is therefore traced under the old setting and not the new one: TRACE R after N shows nothing, and TRACE N after R is the last line shown. The setting is in force from the next clause on.

.traceoutput~destination(.output)
trace r
x = 1
trace n
x = 2

     3 *-* x = 1
       >>>   "1"
     4 *-* trace n
[instr.trace.scope]

The instruction changes the setting that the TRACE function reports and changes, and the setting has the same scope: an internal routine starts with the caller's setting and the caller has its own back when the routine returns, wherever the routine changed it.

trace r
call sub
say 'caller' trace()
exit
sub:
  say 'sub' trace()
  trace i
  say 'sub' trace()
  return

sub R
sub I
caller R

Where the lines go

[instr.trace.destination]

Every trace line is written by sending the message LINEOUT to the object that the environment symbol .TRACEOUTPUT holds, with one argument, an object whose string value is the line without a line end. The .TRACEOUTPUT object is a monitor, and by default it writes to the error stream, so a program that traces shows nothing on its standard output. A program sets another destination with the message DESTINATION to .TRACEOUTPUT: any object that understands LINEOUT will do, and .OUTPUT sends the lines to standard output.

trace r
x = 1
say 'done'

done

.traceoutput~destination(.sink~new)
trace r
x = 1
trace n
exit
::class sink
::method lineout
  use arg line
  .output~lineout('got <'line'>')
  return 0

got <     3 *-* x = 1>
got <       >>>   "1">
got <     4 *-* trace n>

The format of a line

[instr.trace.line]

A line that shows a clause has the line number right-aligned in six columns, a blank, the flag *-*, a blank, the indentation and the text of the clause. The line number is the program line on which the clause starts, and clauses that share a line share its number. A clause run by INTERPRET carries the line number of the INTERPRET clause, and its text is the text of the string.

.traceoutput~destination(.output)
trace r
x  =  3
y = x + 4 ; z = 'a'  'b'
-- 5
-- 6
-- 7
-- 8
-- 9
w = 10

     3 *-* x  =  3
       >>>   "3"
     4 *-* y = x + 4 ;
       >>>   "7"
     4 *-* z = 'a'  'b'
       >>>   "a b"
    10 *-* w = 10
       >>>   "10"

.traceoutput~destination(.output)
trace r
interpret 'x = 1; y = 2'

     3 *-* interpret 'x = 1; y = 2'
       >>>   "x = 1; y = 2"
     3 *-* x = 1;
       >>>   "1"
     3 *-* y = 2
       >>>   "2"
[instr.trace.text]

The text of a clause is shown as it was written, from its first token on: the blanks between tokens are kept, a comment between tokens is kept, a comment before the first token and a line end are not, and a clause that ends with a semicolon shows the semicolon. A comment before that semicolon is shown, and one after it is not. A comment after the last token on its line, with no semicolon after it, is kept. A clause that ran over several lines, by a continuation or by a comment, is shown on one line with the line ends removed, the comma of a continuation and the blanks that begin the next line kept, and carries the number of its first line. The text of an IF or WHEN clause ends before THEN, so it keeps the blanks that stood before THEN.

.traceoutput~destination(.output)
trace r
/* lead */ a  =  1 /* mid */ + 2 ;
b = 3 +,
    4
c = 5   /* tail */

     3 *-* a  =  1 /* mid */ + 2 ;
       >>>   "3"
     4 *-* b = 3 +,    4
       >>>   "7"
     6 *-* c = 5   /* tail */
       >>>   "5"

.traceoutput~destination(.output)
trace r
n = 1
if n=1 then nop
if (n=1)then nop
g = 7 ; -- after the semicolon
c = 3 /* before */ ;
f = 6 /* two
  lines */ + 1

     3 *-* n = 1
       >>>   "1"
     4 *-* if n=1 
       >>>   "1"
     4 *-*   then
     4 *-*     nop
     5 *-* if (n=1)
       >>>   "1"
     5 *-*   then
     5 *-*     nop
     6 *-* g = 7 ;
       >>>   "7"
     7 *-* c = 3 /* before */ ;
       >>>   "3"
     8 *-* f = 6 /* two  lines */ + 1
       >>>   "7"
[instr.trace.result]

A line that shows a value is written below the line of its clause, with seven blanks, a three-character flag, a blank, the indentation of the clause, two more blanks and the value in double quotation marks. Blanks inside the quotes are the value's own. The tab '09'x, the line feed '0A'x and the carriage return '0D'x are shown as themselves, every other byte below '20'x is shown as ?, and the bytes from '20'x up, '7F'x and 'FF'x among them, are shown as themselves. A value that is not a string is shown as its string value.

.traceoutput~destination(.output)
trace r
x = ' two  blanks '
y = .array~new
z = 1.50 + 1

     3 *-* x = ' two  blanks '
       >>>   " two  blanks "
     4 *-* y = .array~new
       >>>   "an Array"
     5 *-* z = 1.50 + 1
       >>>   "2.50"

.traceoutput~destination(.sink~new)
trace r
x = 'a' || '01'x || 'b' || '09'x || '1b'x || 'c' || '7f'x || 'ff'x
trace n
exit
::class sink
::method lineout
  use arg line
  line = '' || line
  if line~pos('>>>') > 0 then say line~right(10)~c2x
  return 0

22613F62093F637FFF22

What a setting lists

[instr.trace.setting.clauses]

Under A every clause is shown, before it runs, and nothing else about it. R shows the same clauses and below each of them the final value of its expression, with the flag >>>. I shows in addition every step of the evaluation, with the flags that the tag rule lists. O shows nothing. The TRACE clause that ends a setting is shown under the setting it ends, as the effect rule says.

.traceoutput~destination(.output)
call work 'A'
say '--'
call work 'R'
say '--'
call work 'I'
say '--'
call work 'O'
exit
work: procedure
  trace value arg(1)
  n = 2
  x = n + 1
  trace off
  return

    12 *-*   n = 2
    13 *-*   x = n + 1
    14 *-*   trace off
--
    12 *-*   n = 2
       >>>     "2"
    13 *-*   x = n + 1
       >>>     "3"
    14 *-*   trace off
--
    12 *-*   n = 2
       >L>     "2"
       >>>     "2"
       >=>     N <= "2"
    13 *-*   x = n + 1
       >V>     N => "2"
       >L>     "1"
       >O>     "+" => "3"
       >>>     "3"
       >=>     X <= "3"
    14 *-*   trace off
--
[instr.trace.setting.commands]

A command is shown by A, R and I with the rest of the clauses, and three more settings show commands and nothing else. C shows each command before it runs. E shows a command that raised ERROR or FAILURE, F shows one that raised FAILURE, and N shows what F shows. A shown command is followed by a line with the flag >>> that holds the command string that was sent, and by a line with the flag +++ that holds RC(n) and the return code, when the command raised one of the two conditions; the return code is 30 when the environment does not exist. Which commands raise the conditions is specified with the commands page.

.traceoutput~destination(.output)
call cmds 'C'
say '--'
call cmds 'E'
say '--'
call cmds 'F'
say '--'
call cmds 'N'
exit
cmds: procedure
  trace value arg(1)
  address system
  'exit 0'
  'exit 3'
  address nosuch
  'exit 0'
  trace off
  return

    13 *-*   'exit 0'
       >>>     "exit 0"
    14 *-*   'exit 3'
       >>>     "exit 3"
       +++     "RC(3)"
    16 *-*   'exit 0'
       >>>     "exit 0"
       +++     "RC(30)"
--
    14 *-*   'exit 3'
       >>>     "exit 3"
       +++     "RC(3)"
    16 *-*   'exit 0'
       >>>     "exit 0"
       +++     "RC(30)"
--
    16 *-*   'exit 0'
       >>>     "exit 0"
       +++     "RC(30)"
--
    16 *-*   'exit 0'
       >>>     "exit 0"
       +++     "RC(30)"
[instr.trace.setting.labels]

L shows a label clause when control reaches it: by running into it, by a CALL of the routine it names, or by a SIGNAL to it. It shows no other clause.

.traceoutput~destination(.output)
trace l
x = 1
fall:
y = 2
call sub
signal there
z = 3
there:
exit
sub:
  return

     4 *-* fall:
    11 *-*   sub:
     9 *-* there:

Note. A method or routine that traces from its first clause also writes a line with the flag >I> when it is entered and <I< when it returns, and the text of those lines names the package. The book does not specify them.

The tags

[instr.trace.tags]

The flag of a value line says what produced the value. Under R the value lines carry >>>, the final value of an expression, a value that a PARSE, ARG, PULL or USE instruction took from its source, and the value that a routine returns to its caller; a message instruction and a message assignment write no value line. The flag >K> marks, under R and I, the value of a keyword's expression in DO, NUMERIC, PARSE, RAISE, FORWARD, GUARD, SIGNAL VALUE and TRACE with a value, and a redirection of an ADDRESS command; it is shown as the keyword and its value. ADDRESS VALUE and OPTIONS write only >>>. >R> is a variable reference that USE ARG took, shown as "V" => "W", and is written under R and I. The +++ line of a command is the other kind of line of this setting. The other flags belong to I alone. >L> is a literal and >V> the value of a variable, shown as NAME => "value". >C> is a compound variable whose tail was substituted, shown as the substituted name, as in S.K => "S.1", >E> an environment symbol, and >N> a symbol qualified by a namespace, shown as NS:C => "The C class". >O> is the result of a binary operator and >P> that of a prefix operator, each shown as the operator and its result, >F> the result of a function call and >M> that of a message, shown as the name and the result, and >A> an argument of a call or of a message. >=> is an assignment, shown as NAME <= "value", and >.> a value that a placeholder period of a template took. Names are shown in upper case.

.traceoutput~destination(.output)
trace i
s.1 = 5
k = 1
y = s.k + -abs(-2)
a = .array~new
b = a~items
parse value 'p q' with . w
numeric digits 12

     3 *-* s.1 = 5
       >L>   "5"
       >>>   "5"
       >C>   S.1 => "S.1"
       >=>   S.1 <= "5"
     4 *-* k = 1
       >L>   "1"
       >>>   "1"
       >=>   K <= "1"
     5 *-* y = s.k + -abs(-2)
       >C>   S.K => "S.1"
       >V>   S.K => "5"
       >L>   "2"
       >P>   "-" => "-2"
       >A>   "-2"
       >F>   ABS => "2"
       >P>   "-" => "-2"
       >O>   "+" => "3"
       >>>   "3"
       >=>   Y <= "3"
     6 *-* a = .array~new
       >E>   .ARRAY => "The Array class"
       >M>   "NEW" => "an Array"
       >>>   "an Array"
       >=>   A <= "an Array"
     7 *-* b = a~items
       >V>   A => "an Array"
       >M>   "ITEMS" => "0"
       >>>   "0"
       >=>   B <= "0"
     8 *-* parse value 'p q' with . w
       >L>   "p q"
       >K>   "VALUE" => "p q"
       >>>   "p q"
       >.>   "p"
       >=>   W <= "q"
     9 *-* numeric digits 12
       >L>   "12"
       >K>   "DIGITS" => "12"

.traceoutput~destination(.output)
trace r
parse value 'a b c' with p . r
call sub 1, 2
exit
sub: use arg a, b
  return a + b

     3 *-* parse value 'a b c' with p . r
       >K>   "VALUE" => "a b c"
       >>>   "a b c"
       >>>   "a"
       >>>   "c"
     4 *-* call sub 1, 2
     6 *-*   sub:
     6 *-*   use arg a, b
       >>>     "1"
       >>>     "2"
     7 *-*   return a + b
       >>>     "3"
       >>>   "3"
     5 *-* exit

.traceoutput~destination(.output)
x = .array~new
v = 4
trace r
x~append(1)
x[1] = 2
call sub >v
signal on syntax name e
raise syntax 93.900 description 'd' additional 'ad'
e: exit
sub: use arg >w
  return

     5 *-* x~append(1)
     6 *-* x[1] = 2
     7 *-* call sub >v
    11 *-*   sub:
    11 *-*   use arg >w
       >R>     "V" => "W"
    12 *-*   return
     8 *-* signal on syntax name e
     9 *-* raise syntax 93.900 description 'd' additional 'ad'
       >K>   "SYNTAX" => "93.900"
       >K>   "DESCRIPTION" => "d"
       >K>   "ADDITIONAL" => "ad"
    10 *-* e:
    10 *-* exit

.traceoutput~destination(.output)
trace i
v = 1
call sub >v
trace n
exit
sub: use arg >w
  return

     3 *-* v = 1
       >L>   "1"
       >>>   "1"
       >=>   V <= "1"
     4 *-* call sub >v
       >O>   ">" => "V"
       >A>   "1"
     7 *-*   sub:
     7 *-*   use arg >w
       >R>     "V" => "W"

trace value 'r'

Indentation

[instr.trace.indent]

The text of a clause is indented by two blanks for each level of nesting. A level is added inside a DO group or loop, after THEN or ELSE, after WHEN or OTHERWISE, and for each active internal call. THEN, ELSE, WHEN and OTHERWISE are shown on a line of their own, one level in from the IF or SELECT, and the clause after them one level further. DO, SELECT and the IF clause stand at the level of their surroundings, and the END that closes a DO or a SELECT stands there too. The lines of values are indented by the level of their clause and two blanks more. The label of an internal routine and the clauses of its body are shown one level deeper than the CALL that started it.

.traceoutput~destination(.output)
trace r
n = 2
do
  if n = 2 then do
    select
      when n = 1 then nop
      otherwise
        m = n
    end
  end
  call f
end
exit
f:
  i = 1
  return

     3 *-* n = 2
       >>>   "2"
     4 *-* do
     5 *-*   if n = 2 
       >>>     "1"
     5 *-*     then
     5 *-*       do
     6 *-*         select
     7 *-*           when n = 1 
       >>>             "0"
     8 *-*           otherwise
     9 *-*             m = n
       >>>               "2"
    10 *-*         end
    11 *-*       end
    12 *-*   call f
    15 *-*     f:
    16 *-*     i = 1
       >>>       "1"
    17 *-*     return
    13 *-* end
    14 *-* exit
[instr.trace.indent.signal]

A SIGNAL sets the level to zero, so the clauses after it are shown from the left margin, also when the SIGNAL stood in a DO group or in a called routine. A condition that SIGNAL ON traps does the same.

.traceoutput~destination(.output)
trace r
call f
c = 3
exit
f:
  do
    d = 4
    signal g
  end
g:
  e = 5
  return

     3 *-* call f
     6 *-*   f:
     7 *-*   do
     8 *-*     d = 4
       >>>       "4"
     9 *-*     signal g
    11 *-* g:
    12 *-* e = 5
       >>>   "5"
    13 *-* return
     4 *-* c = 3
       >>>   "3"
     5 *-* exit

.traceoutput~destination(.output)
trace r
signal on syntax name trap
call f
exit
f:
  do
    x = 1 / 0
  end
trap:
  z = 1

     3 *-* signal on syntax name trap
     4 *-* call f
     6 *-*   f:
     7 *-*   do
     8 *-*     x = 1 / 0
    10 *-* trap:
    11 *-* z = 1
       >>>   "1"

Concurrent activities

[instr.trace.concurrent]

Each activity traces with its own setting and its own indentation, and the lines of one activity reach the destination in the order that activity wrote them. How the lines of two activities that trace at the same time are interleaved is not specified, as Deviation 7 says.

sink = .sink~new
.traceoutput~destination(sink)
m = .worker~new~start('run')
trace r
a1 = 1
a2 = 2
trace n
m~result
.traceoutput~destination(.output)
say 'main:'
do l over sink~lines
  if pos('*-* a', l) > 0 then say word(l, 1) word(l, 3)
end
say 'worker:'
do l over sink~lines
  if pos('*-* b', l) > 0 then say word(l, 1) word(l, 3)
end
::class sink
::method init
  expose lines
  lines = .array~new
::method lines
  expose lines
  return lines
::method lineout
  expose lines
  use arg l
  lines~append('' || l)
  return 0
::class worker
::method run
  trace r
  b1 = 1
  b2 = 2
  trace n
  return 1

main:
5 a1
6 a2
worker:
33 b1
34 b2

Deviations

[instr.trace.deviation.0]

interrexx indents by the block structure alone, as the indentation rule says. ooRexx drops one level too many when a loop ends because its test failed, and the lines after the loop stand one level short until a construct around it restores the level. The example shows the interrexx output; ooRexx shows the clause x = 1 at the left margin.

.traceoutput~destination(.output)
trace r
do
  do i = 1 to 2
    nop
  end
  x = 1
end
y = 2

     3 *-* do
     4 *-*   do i = 1 to 2
       >K>     "TO" => "2"
     5 *-*     nop
     6 *-*   end
     4 *-*   do i = 1 to 2
       >>>       "1"
       >>>       "2"
     5 *-*     nop
     6 *-*   end
     4 *-*   do i = 1 to 2
       >>>       "2"
       >>>       "3"
     7 *-*   x = 1
       >>>     "1"
     8 *-* end
     9 *-* y = 2
       >>>   "2"
[instr.trace.deviation.7]

The order in which the lines of two activities that trace at once reach the destination is not specified; interrexx gives one of the orders ooRexx can give. The rule above is what a program may rely on, together with the count of the lines, which does not depend on the order.

sink = .sink~new
.traceoutput~destination(sink)
m = .worker~new~start('run')
trace r
a1 = 1
trace n
m~result
.traceoutput~destination(.output)
n = 0
do l over sink~lines
  if pos('*-*', l) > 0 then n = n + 1
end
say n 'clause lines'
::class sink
::method init
  expose lines
  lines = .array~new
::method lines
  expose lines
  return lines
::method lineout
  expose lines

USE

USE [STRICT] ARG [target [= default]] [, ...] | USE LOCAL [name]...

rexxref: Keyword Instructions > USE

Deviations: D71

USE has two unrelated forms. USE ARG takes the arguments of the running program, routine or method and stores the argument objects themselves in variables, where ARG and PARSE ARG make strings of them and cut them up with a template. USE STRICT ARG is the same with a check of the number of arguments. USE LOCAL is for methods only and decides which of the method's variables are its own. This page specifies the targets and defaults of USE ARG, the strict form and the errors of both forms. How the arguments are counted and read is the matter of the ARG builtin.

USE ARG

[instr.use.arg]

The targets of USE ARG are filled from left to right. The target in position n receives argument n, as an object, without any change: it is not converted to a string, its case stays, and a collection is the same collection that the caller passed. A target for which no argument was passed, because the caller passed fewer arguments or left that position empty, is dropped, so a variable it had before is unset. An argument beyond the last target is ignored. The clause may run again, and it reads the arguments the call was made with, not the current values of the variables. A target can be a simple symbol, a compound symbol or a stem symbol, or it can be left empty, which skips its argument and sets nothing.

call show 1, 2, 3
call show 'a'
call show
call show , 'b'
call show 1, , 3, 4
call take .array~of('x', 'y'), 'Mixed Case', 12
exit
show:
  use arg x, y, z
  say 'x=' || x 'y=' || y 'z=' || z symbol('x') symbol('y') symbol('z') arg()
  return
take:
  use arg a, b, c
  a = 'changed'
  use arg again
  say again~class~id again~items b c + 1
  return

[instr.use.compound]

The tail of a compound target is resolved when that target is filled, with the values its variables have at that moment, as for an assignment to the symbol. A target to the left that set a variable of the tail therefore counts. The argument is stored under the resulting name.

k = 5
call fill 'v1', 'v2'
say c.1 c.5
call chain 7, 'second'
say d.7
exit
fill:
  use arg c.1, c.k
  return
chain:
  use arg t, d.t
  return

v1 v2
second
[instr.use.stem]

A stem symbol as a target receives the argument as the stem. When the caller passed a stem, as in call s st., the target is that stem, not a copy, so the routine's assignments to it are the caller's. When the argument is not a stem, the target is a new stem that has the argument as its default value, as assigning a value to a stem does.

st.1 = 'one'
call change st.
say st.1 st.2
exit
change: procedure
  use arg sub.
  say sub.1
  sub.2 = 'two'
  return

  say s.1 s.xyz s.~class~id
  return

[instr.use.message]

A target can be a message term, such as obj~name or arr[1], whose object is a variable that has a value, one that an earlier target of the clause set included. The argument is then sent as the assignment of that term, as the message assignment rule describes, so it sets the attribute or the item. The message terms are evaluated in order, and a message term whose argument is missing is skipped: it sends nothing and changes nothing.

o = .thing~new
arr = .array~new
arr[2] = 'keep'
call fill o, arr, 'v1', 'v2'
say o~name arr[1] arr[2]

say o~name arr[1] arr[2]
call fill o, arr, 'w1'
say o~name arr[1] arr[2]
exit
fill:
  use arg obj, ar, obj~name, ar[1]
  return

[instr.use.reference]

A target written with a < before its name is an alias of a variable of the caller. The caller passes the variable as a reference, with a < before it in the call, and the target is then the same variable: a value read through it is the caller's, and an assignment changes the caller's variable. The target needs a reference as its argument, and a plain value raises SYNTAX 88.928. The argument must not be omitted, which raises SYNTAX 88.931. The alias name must not be a variable of the routine that has a value, or the clause raises SYNTAX 98.995. A default after a reference target raises SYNTAX 99.950 when the program is read. This book does not specify a reference term anywhere else, nor the form with >.

call try
call taken <v
exit

[instr.use.default]

A target can be followed by = and a default. When the argument for that position was not passed, the target takes the value of the default, which is evaluated at that moment and only then, after the targets to its left have been filled. An argument of the null string is passed, so it replaces the default. The default is a literal string, a constant symbol such as a number, an environment symbol such as .nil, or an expression in parentheses. Any other text after the = raises SYNTAX 35.1 for a variable symbol and 35.930 for something that is not a single term or has no term at all.

USE STRICT ARG

[instr.use.strict]

USE STRICT ARG fills the targets as USE ARG does, after it has checked the number of arguments. A target with no default is required, and a target with a default is optional, so the number of arguments passed must not be smaller than the number of required targets, and must not be greater than the number of targets. A position that is left empty counts, but trailing positions left empty do not, in the sense of the ARG builtin. A required position that is left empty is a third fault. In a program, an internal routine or an external routine the three faults raise SYNTAX 40.3, 40.4 and 40.5; in a method they raise SYNTAX 93.901, 93.902 and 93.903. A required target may follow an optional one: the count must still reach it. Without a target the clause demands no argument at all.

call s 1, 2
call s 1, 2, 3
call s , 2

  say arg() 'ok' a b c

[instr.use.ellipsis]

Three periods after the last target of a USE STRICT ARG mean that more arguments may follow, so the upper limit of the count is lifted and the lower limit stays. The arguments beyond the targets are not stored, and the routine reads them with the ARG builtin. The three periods are accepted after USE ARG without strict too, where they change nothing. They must be the last item of the clause: a target after them raises SYNTAX 99.930.

USE LOCAL

[instr.use.local]

USE LOCAL reverses the division of a method's variables. With it every variable of the method is an object variable, as if it were exposed, except the names the clause lists, which are the method's own. A listed name can be a simple or a stem symbol; a stem lists every compound variable of it. The special variables RC, RESULT, SIGL, SELF and SUPER are never object variables, whatever USE LOCAL lists. A USE LOCAL with no name leaves only these local. The EXPOSE rule says what an object variable is.

o = .box~new
say o~a
say o~b
say o~c
::class box
::method a
  use local keep st.
  keep = 'local'
  st.1 = 'local too'
  shared = 'object'
  call sub
  return symbol('result') symbol('sigl') symbol('keep') symbol('st.1')
sub:
  return 'r'
::method b
  use local
  return symbol('shared') symbol('keep') symbol('st.1') symbol('result'),
    symbol('sigl')
::method c
  use local
  return symbol('shared') shared

[instr.use.local.place]

USE LOCAL must be the first instruction of a method, with only comments and null clauses before it. Any other instruction before it, a label, a USE ARG, an EXPOSE or a second USE LOCAL included, and a position inside a DO or an IF, raise SYNTAX 99.910 when the program is read. An EXPOSE after it raises 99.907, since it is not the first instruction. USE ARG may follow it. In the main program or a routine, USE LOCAL as the first instruction raises SYNTAX 98.993 when it runs, and the text of an INTERPRET raises 99.915 when the INTERPRET runs. A name that is a compound symbol raises 99.948, one that starts with a digit 31.2, and a comma, a string, a parenthesis or an = where a name should be 20.927.

Errors of the clause

[instr.use.syntax]

A fault in the form of the clause is raised when the program is read. USE with no word after it, and USE with a word that is not ARG, STRICT or LOCAL, raise SYNTAX 25.905. STRICT that is not followed by ARG raises 25.929. Two targets that follow each other with no comma raise 46.902.
