Parsing

ANSI: 6.3.2.71, 8.3.17; rexxref: Parsing

Parsing takes a string, the source, and a template, and assigns parts of the source to variables. The template says where to cut the source and which variable receives each part. It is the one mechanism behind PARSE, ARG and PULL: those instructions differ only in where the source comes from and in whether they change its case, and the instructions chapter specifies them. This chapter specifies what a template does with a source once there is one.

A template is a list of targets and triggers. A target is a place that receives a value, usually a variable. A trigger is a pattern that finds a place in the source, or a position that names one. The pages of this chapter are:

  • Templates: templates made of targets alone, which cut the source into words, and the period that takes a word and discards it.
  • Patterns: the triggers: strings, positions, relative positions and patterns that come from a variable or an expression.
  • Several strings: the comma that moves on to the next template and the next source string, and the options that change the case of the source or of the comparison.

PARSE VALUE and PARSE VAR are the sources the examples use, because each takes a single string. The ARG source is the only one that provides several strings, and its template list is on the last page.

What a template is made of

[parse.index.elements]

A template holds these elements, in any order and number. A target is a variable symbol of any of the three forms, a message term that can stand on the left of an assignment, or a period. A trigger is a string literal, a hex or binary literal included, an expression in parentheses, or a position: a whole number, or one of the characters +, -, =, > and < followed by a whole number or by an expression in parentheses. A comma ends the template and begins the next one. Any other token is a syntax error, and the pattern page describes it.

data = 'tag:12:east'
parse var data kind ':' count ':' side
say kind count side
parse var data . 4 text 7 .
say text

tag 12 east
:12
[parse.index.pieces]

The triggers of a template divide the source into pieces. Each piece lies between two triggers, or between the start or end of the source and a trigger, and the targets that stand between those two triggers share it. A template with no trigger has one piece, the whole source. The targets of a piece take its words as the templates page says, and a piece with no target is skipped. Where each trigger lies, and so where a piece begins and ends, is the subject of the patterns page.

parse value 'alpha beta;gamma delta' with u v ';' w y
say u'|'v'|'w'|'y
parse value 'alpha beta;gamma delta' with u v w y
say u'|'v'|'w'|'y

alpha|beta|gamma|delta
alpha|beta;gamma|delta|

Order of work

[parse.index.order]

The interpreter evaluates the source before it assigns anything, so a target that is also the variable of the source does not change what is parsed. It then works through the template one piece at a time, from left to right. For each piece it first finds the trigger that ends it, evaluating the expression of that trigger if it is a parenthesized one, and only then assigns the targets of the piece, left to right. An expression in a trigger therefore sees the values that the targets of the earlier pieces have received, but the old values of the targets of the piece that the trigger itself ends. The tail of a compound symbol that is a target is evaluated when that target is assigned, so it sees the targets before it in its own piece too. When the same variable appears as a target twice, the later assignment is the one that remains.

u = 'ef'
parse value 'ab,cd,ab,ef' with u ',' v ',' (u) w
say u v w
n = 2
parse value '5 abcdef' with n =(n) v
say n'|'v
n = 2
parse value '5 abcdef' with n ' ' =(n) v
say n'|'v
text = 'one two three'
parse var text first text
say first'|'text
i = 1
parse value 'p,2,r' with a.i ',' i ',' a.i
say a.1 i a.2
parse value '3 x' with i b.i
say b.3
parse value 'm n' with k k
say '['k']'

ab cd ,ef
5| abcdef
5|cdef
one|two three
p 2 r
x
[n]
[parse.index.nothing]

A parse changes only its targets. No other variable changes, the special variables RC and RESULT are not set, and a template with no target changes nothing at all, even when it contains triggers that find nothing. The source expression of PARSE VALUE is still evaluated.

rc = 'keep'; result = 'also'
parse value 'abc' with
parse value 'abc' with 'b' "z"
say rc result
parse value tell() with
say 'done'
exit
tell: say 'evaluated'; return 'abc'

keep also
evaluated
done

Templates

ANSI: 8.3.17; rexxref: Parsing > Simple Templates for Parsing into Words, Parsing > The Period as a Placeholder, Parsing > Message Term Assignments

A template with no trigger cuts the source into words. This page specifies that case, and every other template reduces to it: the pieces rule hands each piece of a source to the targets that stand next to it, and what those targets do with a piece is what this page says. The examples use parse var and parse value … with.

Words

[parse.templates.words]

Each target of a piece, except the last, receives one word of it. To find the word, the parse skips the whitespace at the start of what remains of the piece, takes the characters up to the next whitespace character or the end, and then removes one whitespace character after the word, if there is one. A word is what the builtins call one, and whitespace is as the conventions define it, so a line feed can be part of a word.

s = '  alpha   beta'||'09'x||'gamma delta  '
parse var s u v w
say u'|'v'|'w'|'
parse value 'ab'||'0a'x||'cd ef' with u v
say c2x(u) v

alpha|beta|gamma delta  |
61620A6364 ef
[parse.templates.last]

The last target of a piece receives all that remains of the piece after the words of the targets before it, and nothing is removed from it: its leading whitespace beyond the one character that ended the previous word, its interior whitespace and its trailing whitespace all stay. A piece with a single target therefore gives that target the whole piece, with the whitespace at both ends. Words beyond the number of targets are therefore in the last target, unless that is a period, which discards them.

s = '  alpha   beta  gamma delta  '
parse var s u
say '['u']'
parse var s u v
say '['u']['v']'
parse var s . v
say '['v']'
parse value 'one  ' with u v
say '['u']['v']'

[  alpha   beta  gamma delta  ]
[alpha][  beta  gamma delta  ]
[  beta  gamma delta  ]
[one][ ]
[parse.templates.fewer]

When the words of a piece run out, each target that remains receives the null string, except that the last target of the piece receives what is left, as the previous rule says, and that is the null string only when nothing is left. So a null source, and a source of whitespace only, give two targets the null string, while a single target receives the whitespace itself. Every target is assigned: a variable that held a value before the parse does not keep it.

u = 'old'; v = 'old'; w = 'old'
parse value 'one' with u v w
say '['u']['v']['w']'
u = 'old'; v = 'old'
parse value '' with u v
say '['u']['v']'
u = 'old'; v = 'old'
parse value '   ' with u v
say '['u']['v']'
parse value '   ' with u
say '['u']'

[one][][]
[][]
[][]
[   ]

The period

[parse.templates.period]

A period stands where a variable could and discards what that variable would receive. It takes its place in the sequence of targets as a variable would, so it consumes the next word, or the rest of the piece when it is the last, and assigns nothing. A period at the end of a template is the usual way to ignore the surplus of the source.

parse value 'red green blue amber' with . second . fourth
say second fourth
parse value 'red green blue amber' with first .
say first
parse value 'red green blue amber' with . . third
say third

green amber
red
blue amber

Targets

[parse.templates.targets]

A target that is a simple symbol or a compound symbol is assigned like the left side of an assignment, and the tail of a compound symbol is evaluated when the assignment is made, as the order rule says. A stem symbol is a target too, and assigning to it gives the stem that value as its default, so that every compound variable of the stem has the value at once. A message term, such as slots[2] or obj~attr, receives its value as a message assignment does, by sending the assignment message with the value as its argument. The answer of that message is discarded, and unlike the instruction a parse does not set RESULT. The receiver and the arguments of the message are evaluated when the target is assigned, and so see the targets assigned before it.

parse value 'p q r' with s. t
say s.1 s.any t
slots = .array~new
k = 1
parse value '2 red blue' with k slots[k * 2] slots[k - 1]
say k slots[4] slots[1]
result = 'untouched'
reg = .directory~new
box = .cell~new
parse value 'n:7 s:9' with 'n:' reg['north'] ' s:' box~amount
say reg['north'] box~amount result
exit
::class cell
::method 'amount='
  expose amount
  use arg amount
  return 'answered'
::method amount
  expose amount
  return amount

p p q r
2 red blue
7 9 untouched
[parse.templates.empty]

A template that has no tokens, whether it is missing after the keywords of the instruction or stands between two commas, assigns nothing. It raises no error, however much the source holds.

parse value 'abc def' with
parse var undefined_name with
say 'no assignment, no error'

no assignment, no error

Patterns

ANSI: 8.3.17; rexxref: Parsing > Templates Containing String Patterns, Parsing > Templates Containing Positional (Numeric) Patterns, Parsing > Parsing with Variable Patterns, Parsing > Advanced Topics in Parsing > Combining String and Positional Patterns

A pattern is a trigger: it makes a break in the source, and the targets on either side of it share the pieces that the break separates. This page says where each kind of trigger puts its break and which characters the pieces hold. What a target does with its piece is the business of the templates page.

A break has a start and an end. For a string it is the span of the match, and for a position it is a single point, so its start and its end are the same. Unless a rule below says otherwise, a piece begins where the previous break ends, or at the first character of the source before any break, and it ends where the next break begins, or at the end of the source after the last break. Positions count as the convention says, from 1, and the point at a position lies just before the character there.

Strings

[parse.patterns.string]

A string literal, or a hex or binary literal, finds the first place, at or after the point where the piece begins, where its characters occur in the source, comparing each character exactly as it is, so case matters. The break is the span of that occurrence: the piece ends just before it and the next piece begins just after it, and the matched characters belong to no piece. An occurrence at the very beginning of the piece leaves an empty piece before it, and an empty piece gives its targets the null string.

parse value 'id=42;tag=blue' with key '=' val
say key'|'val
parse value 'id=42;tag=blue' with key '=' val ';' rest
say key'|'val'|'rest
parse value 'id=42;tag=blue' with 'id=' num
say num
parse value 'id=42;tag=blue' with before 'id' after
say '['before']['after']'
parse value 'id=42;Tag=blue' with before 'tag' after
say '['before']['after']'

id|42;tag=blue
id|42|tag=blue
42;tag=blue
[][=42;tag=blue]
[id=42;Tag=blue][]
[parse.patterns.string.missing]

When the string does not occur, and when it is the null string, which never matches, the break lies at the end of the source. The piece before it runs to the end, and the next piece begins there, so each target after the pattern receives the null string, as for a null source does each target. A later string cannot match either.

parse value 'alpha beta' with u ',' v
say '['u']['v']'
parse value 'alpha beta' with u 'a' v "" w
say '['u']['v']['w']'
parse value 'alpha beta' with u '' v
say '['u']['v']'
parse value '' with u ',' v 3 w
say '['u']['v']['w']'

[alpha beta][]
[][lpha beta][]
[alpha beta][]
[][][]
[parse.patterns.string.sequence]

When strings follow each other with no target between them, the second searches from the end of the first match, not from the beginning of the source. The characters between the two matches belong to no piece.

parse value ',,tail' with ',' ',' rest
say rest
parse value 'a<b>c' with '<' '>' rest
say rest
parse value ',x' with u ',' v ',' w
say '['u']['v']['w']'

tail
c
[][x][]

Variable patterns

[parse.patterns.variable]

An expression in parentheses is evaluated when the template reaches the end of the piece that it ends, which is after the targets of the earlier pieces are assigned and before the targets of that piece are. Its value is a string trigger as the string rule describes. A value that is an object and not a string is replaced by its string, as the conventions say. The value is used as the string that it is, so a value that looks like a number is still the characters to find, and a value that is the null string is the null string, which never matches. The expression may be as long as any expression, with operators and function calls.

sep = ','; n = 4; none = ''
parse value 'ab,cd,ef' with u (sep) v
say u'|'v
parse value 'abc4efg' with u (n) v
say u'|'v
parse value 'abcdefg' with u (n) v
say '['u']['v']'
parse value 'ab,cd,ef' with u (none) v
say '['u']['v']'
parse value 'ab,cd,ef' with u (left(sep, 1) || 'c') v
say u'|'v
sep = '-'
parse value ',ab,cd' with sep (sep) rest  /* still the old '-' */
say '['sep']['rest']'
sep = '-'
parse value ',ab,cd' with sep 2 (sep) rest  /* now the comma */
say '['sep']['rest']'

ab|cd,ef
abc|efg
[abcdefg][]
[ab,cd,ef][]
ab|d,ef
[,ab,cd][]
[,][cd]

mark = .dash~new
parse value 'ab--cd' with u (mark) v
say u'|'v
exit
::class dash
::method makestring
  return '--'

ab|cd

Note. The ANSI draft (6.3.2.71) allows only a variable symbol in the parentheses of a variable pattern, and nothing else. ooRexx, and this book, take any expression.

Positions

[parse.patterns.absolute]

A whole number written as a trigger, or = followed by a whole number, puts a point at that position: the piece before it ends there and the next piece begins there. The characters before position n are the characters numbered below n, so u 4 v gives u the first three. A position beyond the end of the source puts the point at the end, and position 0 is the same as position 1, so a source of L characters has the points 1 to L+1. The = form says the same as the bare number. Only the = form can take the position from a variable or an expression, written in parentheses, as the bare parentheses are a string trigger.

parse value 'abcdefghij' with u 4 v
say u'|'v
parse value 'abcdefghij' with u 4 v =8 w =(2 + 1) y
say u'|'v'|'w'|'y
parse value 'abcdefghij' with u 11 v
say '['u']['v']'
parse value 'abcdefghij' with u 99 v
say '['u']['v']'
parse value 'abcdefghij' with 0 u
say u
n = 6
parse value 'abcdefghij' with u =(n) v
say u'|'v
parse value 'abcdefghij' with u (n) v
say '['u']['v']'

abc|defghij
abc|defg|hij|cdefghij
[abcdefghij][]
[abcdefghij][]
abcdefghij
abcde|fghij
[abcdefghij][]
[parse.patterns.backward]

A position that lies at the beginning of the current piece or before it makes the piece run to the end of the source, not end empty or before its start. The next piece begins at the position, so the text from there on is shared out again. This is the way a template reads part of the source twice.

parse value 'abcdefghij' with u 8 v 3 w
say u'|'v'|'w
parse value 'abcdefghij' with u 1 v
say u'|'v
parse value 'abcdefghij' with u 5 v 5 w
say u'|'v'|'w
parse value 'abcdefghij' with 6 u 2 v
say u'|'v

abcdefg|hij|cdefghij
abcdefghij|abcdefghij
abcd|efghij|efghij
fghij|bcdefghij
[parse.patterns.relative]

A plus or minus sign followed by a whole number puts a point that many characters after, or before, the start of the previous break. That start is the start of the matched characters for a string, the position itself for a position, the beginning of the source before any break, and the end of the source after a break that found nothing. The point is limited to the positions from 1 to the end of the source. A relative position does not begin the piece that precedes it where the previous break ended, as other triggers do, but where that break began, so the characters of a matched string are part of that piece. A point that is not after the start of that piece makes it run to the end of the source, as for any position. +0 and -0 put the point at the start of the previous break.

parse value 'abcdefghij' with u +3 v +3 w +3 y
say u'|'v'|'w'|'y
parse value 'abcdefghij' with 5 u -2 v
say u'|'v
parse value 'abcdefghij' with u 'g' w +1 y
say u'|'w'|'y
parse value 'abcdefghij' with u 'g' +1 y
say u'|'y
parse value 'abcdefghij' with u 'z' -2 v
say u'|'v
parse value 'abcdefghij' with u 20 -2 v
say u'|'v
parse value 'abcdefghij' with u 3 -9 v
say u'|'v
parse value 'abcdefghij' with u +0 v
say u'|'v

abc|def|ghi|j
efghij|cdefghij
abcdef|g|hij
abcdef|hij
abcdefghij|ij
abcdefghij|ij
ab|abcdefghij
abcdefghij|abcdefghij
[parse.patterns.length]

A > or < followed by a whole number, or by an expression in parentheses, puts a point relative to the start of the previous break, which is the same start that a sign uses. The number is checked as for any position. >n and <n are the two length patterns, and the next two rules describe them.

n = 2
parse value 'abcdefghij' with u > 3 v < (n) w
say u'|'v'|'w

abc|bc|bcdefghij
[parse.patterns.length.after]

>n puts the point n characters after the start of the previous break, limited to the end of the source, and it is the same as +n for every n above 0. At 0 they differ: the piece before >0 ends at once, where the previous break starts, so it is empty, and the next piece begins there, while +0 makes the preceding piece run to the end of the source.

parse value 'abcdefghij' with u >3 v >3 w
say u'|'v'|'w
parse value 'abcdefghij' with u 'c' v >0 w
say '['u']['v']['w']'
parse value 'abcdefghij' with u 'c' v +0 w
say '['u']['v']['w']'
parse value 'abcdefghij' with u >20 v
say '['u']['v']'
n = 2
parse value 'abcdefghij' with u 'f' near <(n) rest >(n) last
say u'|'near'|'rest'|'last

abc|def|ghij
[ab][][cdefghij]
[ab][cdefghij][cdefghij]
[abcdefghij][]
abcde|de|de|fghij
[parse.patterns.length.before]

<n puts the point n characters before the start of the previous break, limited to position 1, and it does not leave the targets between the previous break and <n the piece that the earlier triggers gave them. Those targets receive the n characters that lie just before the start of the previous break, or the characters from position 1 when fewer lie there, and the next piece begins at the point. So <n reads again the text before the break that precedes it. It is not the same as -n, which leaves the preceding piece to run to the end of the source. When no break precedes it, the start is position 1 and the targets before <n receive the null string.

parse value 'abcdefghij' with u 'f' near <3 rest
say u'|'near'|'rest
parse value 'abcdefghij' with u 5 near <9 rest
say u'|'near'|'rest
parse value 'abcdefghij' with u 5 near <0 rest
say u'|'near'|'rest
parse value 'abcdefghij' with u <2 v
say '['u']['v']'
parse value 'abcdefghij' with u 5 near -3 rest
say u'|'near'|'rest

abcde|cde|cdefghij
abcd|abcd|abcdefghij
abcd||efghij
[][abcdefghij]
abcd|efghij|bcdefghij

Note. The ANSI draft has no > or < pattern: they are an addition of ooRexx, which this book follows.

[parse.patterns.number]

The number of a position is a constant written in the template, or the value of an expression in parentheses after a sign, =, > or <. Blanks may separate the sign, =, > or < from the number or the parenthesis. The number, whether constant or expression, must be whole: a constant may be written in any form whose value is whole, such as 03, 4.0 or 1e1, and 3.5 is not. It must have no more digits than the current NUMERIC DIGITS allows, so 1e9 is accepted only when that setting is at least 10, counted on its value (0999 passes under 3 and 0.1e4 does not), and it must not be negative. A number that fails any of these checks raises SYNTAX 26.4 when the clause runs. A fraction, text, the null string and a negative value of an expression all raise it; the direction of a relative position is the sign in the template. A constant that is a symbol is checked the same way when the clause runs, so 3.5 and 3a raise SYNTAX 26.4 then and not when the program is read. A value of an expression that is an object and not a string is replaced by its string, as the conventions say, and that string is then checked; this holds after =, +, -, > and <.

parse value 'abcdefghij' with u 03 v 4.0 w 1e1 y
say u'|'v'|'w'|'y
n = ' 3 '
parse value 'abcdefghij' with u =(n) v
say u'|'v
parse value 'abcdefghij' with u + 3 v - (n) w
say u'|'v'|'w
call try 3.5, 'abcdefghij'
call try 'ab', 'abcdefghij'
call try '', 'abcdefghij'
call try -2, 'abcdefghij'
numeric digits 3
call try 999, 'abcdefghij'
call try 1000, 'abcdefghij'
call lit 'u 999 v'
call lit 'u 1000 v'
call lit 'u 0999 v'
call lit 'u 0.1e4 v'
call lit 'u +3a v'
call lit 'u 1e3 v'
call lit 'u +3.5 v'
call lit 'u >1000 v'
numeric digits 12
call lit 'u 1e9 v'
exit
try:
  signal on syntax name e
  p = arg(1)
  parse value arg(2) with u =(p) v
  say p 'ok' u'|'v
  return
e: say p condition('o')~code
  return
lit:
  signal on syntax name e2
  interpret 'parse value "abcdefghij" with' arg(1)
  say arg(1) 'ok'
  return
e2: say arg(1) condition('o')~code
  return

ab|c|defghi|j
ab|cdefghij
abc|defghij|abcdefghij
3.5 26.4
ab 26.4
 26.4
-2 26.4
999 ok abcdefghij|
1000 26.4
u 999 v ok
u 1000 v 26.4
u 0999 v ok
u 0.1e4 v 26.4
u +3a v 26.4
u 1e3 v 26.4
u +3.5 v 26.4
u >1000 v 26.4
u 1e9 v ok

arr = .array~of(2)
parse value 'abcdefghij' with u +(arr) v
say u'|'v
parse value 'abcdefghij' with u >(arr) v
say u'|'v
parse value 'abcdefghij' with u =(arr) v
say u'|'v

ab|cdefghij
ab|cdefghij
a|bcdefghij

Errors in the template

[parse.patterns.syntax]

A template is checked when the program is read. A token that cannot be part of a template, such as *, ||, >> or >=, raises SYNTAX 38.1. A sign, =, > or < followed by any token other than a number or an opening parenthesis, a comma or a symbol that does not start with a digit or a period among them, raises SYNTAX 38.2, and one that is the last token of the clause raises SYNTAX 38.901. (A - that ends a line is a continuation and not a template token.) A program file that holds any of these does not run at all, and its exit code is 218. The text of INTERPRET raises the same error when it is read.

say 'never shown'
parse value 'abc' with u =n v

say 'never shown'
parse value 'abc' with u * v

say 'never shown'
parse value 'abc' with u >

call try 'u * v'
call try 'u || v'
call try 'u >> v'
call try 'u =n v'
call try 'u + v'
call try 'u > v'
call try 'u < , v'
call try 'u 3 = v'
call try 'u + (1) v'
call try 'u >(1) v'
call try 'u +'
call try 'u 3 ='
call try 'u <'
exit
try:
  signal on syntax name e
  interpret 'parse value "abc" with' arg(1)
  say 'ok' arg(1)
  return
e: say condition('o')~code '<=' arg(1)
  return

38.1 <= u * v
38.1 <= u || v
38.1 <= u >> v
38.2 <= u =n v
38.2 <= u + v
38.2 <= u > v
38.2 <= u < , v
38.2 <= u 3 = v
ok u + (1) v
ok u >(1) v
38.901 <= u +
38.901 <= u 3 =
38.901 <= u <

Several strings and case

ANSI: 8.3.17; rexxref: Parsing > Advanced Topics in Parsing > Parsing Several Strings, Parsing > Using UPPER, LOWER, and CASELESS

This page covers the two features that act on a whole parse and not on one template: the comma that moves to the next template and the next source string, and the options UPPER, LOWER and CASELESS that decide how the source is read. The instructions chapter specifies the keywords of PARSE, ARG and PULL that give a source and select an option. This page specifies what the options do to a parse.

Several templates

[parse.multiple.comma]

A comma ends the template before it and begins the next one, and the next template parses the next source string. Each template starts afresh on its own string: its first piece begins at the first character, and a relative position before any trigger counts from there. The instructions that take their source from the arguments of a call, ARG and PARSE ARG, have one string for each argument, in order. An argument that was omitted is the null string.

call show 'ab cd', 'ef=gh', 'ij kl mn'
call show 'ab cd', , 'ij kl mn'
exit
show: parse arg u v, w '=' y, z +2 q
  say u'|'v'|'w'|'y'|'z'|'q
  return

ab|cd|ef|gh|ij| kl mn
ab|cd|||ij| kl mn
[parse.multiple.single]

A source of any other kind, such as a VALUE or a VAR, is one string. Its first template parses it. A template with no string left to parse, whether it follows such a source or the last argument, parses the null string, so each target of it receives the null string and a pattern in it finds nothing.

parse value 'ab cd ef' with u v, w y, z
say '['u']['v']['w']['y']['z']'
data = 'one two'
parse var data first, second
say first'|'second'|'

[ab][cd ef][][][]
one two||
[parse.multiple.counts]

A source string with no template after the last comma is not parsed, and no variable sees it. A template that is missing, for example the one before a leading comma, assigns nothing and still uses up its string.

call one 'ab', 'cd', 'ef'
call two 'ab'
call three 'ab', 'cd'
exit
one: parse arg u
  say u
  return
two: parse arg u, v, w
  say '['u']['v']['w']'
  return
three: parse arg , v
  say v
  return

ab
[ab][][]
cd
[parse.multiple.shared]

The templates of one list are parsed from left to right, each after the one before it, so the variables assigned by an earlier template are in place for the later ones. The order rule applies across the commas as well.

call mark 'a-b', 'x-a-z'
exit
mark: parse arg first '-' second, third (first) fourth
  say first second third fourth
  return

a b x- -z

Case

[parse.multiple.convert]

The options UPPER and LOWER change the source before any matching: UPPER makes each of the ASCII letters a to z upper case, and LOWER makes each of A to Z lower case, and no other character changes. Every source string is changed, so a parse with several strings changes them all. The values assigned are pieces of the changed string. The patterns of the template are not changed, so a literal pattern must be written in the case that the option produces, or it will not match.

s = 'Alpha-BETA-gamma'
parse upper var s u '-' v '-' w
say u v w
parse lower var s u '-' v '-' w
say u v w
parse upper var s u 'beta' v
say '['u']['v']'
parse upper var s u 'BETA' v
say '['u']['v']'
parse lower value 'ABC É' with u v
say u v
call two 'Ab-Cd', 'eF-gH'
exit
two: parse upper arg p '-' q, r '-' s
  say p q r s
  return

ALPHA BETA GAMMA
alpha beta gamma
[ALPHA-BETA-GAMMA][]
[ALPHA-][-GAMMA]
abc É
AB CD EF GH
[parse.multiple.caseless]

The option CASELESS makes the matching of string triggers ignore the case of the ASCII letters: a and A count as the same character, and so on for each letter. It applies to string patterns, and to the value of a variable pattern in the same way. The source is not changed, so the values assigned keep their case, and positions, words and the whitespace rules are as they are without it. Without CASELESS, matching is exact. A conversion and CASELESS may be given together, and then the conversion changes the source and the match ignores the case of what is left.

s = 'Alpha-BETA-gamma'
parse caseless var s u 'beta' v
say u'|'v
parse var s u 'beta' v
say u'|'v
pat = 'bEtA'
parse caseless var s u (pat) v
say u'|'v
parse caseless var s u 'GAMMA'
say u
parse caseless value 'xyz' with u 'Y' v
say u v
parse upper caseless value 'Ab-cD' with u 'cd' v
say u'|'v

Alpha-|-gamma
Alpha-BETA-gamma|
Alpha-|-gamma
Alpha-BETA-
x z
AB-|

Note. The ANSI draft (8.3.17) has the option UPPER and no other: it has neither LOWER nor CASELESS, which ooRexx adds and this book follows.

Directives

rexxref: Directives

A directive is a clause that starts with two colons. It does not run: it declares a piece of the program, such as a class, a method or a routine, and the interpreter acts on it before the program's own instructions run. A program is a package: a set of declared pieces, and the instructions that come before the first directive. This chapter specifies how a program is split by its directives, and the pages that follow specify each directive.

The directives are ANNOTATE, ATTRIBUTE, CLASS, CONSTANT, METHOD, OPTIONS, REQUIRES, RESOURCE and ROUTINE. The pages of this chapter are:

  • ::CLASS: a class, its superclass, metaclass and inheritance, and the order in which the classes of a package come into being.
  • ::METHOD: a method of a class, the options that set its access and its kind, and a method that belongs to no class.
  • ::ATTRIBUTE: the methods that read and write an attribute.
  • ::CONSTANT: a constant of a class or of the package.
  • ::ROUTINE: a routine of the package and whether other packages see it.
  • ::REQUIRES: the program or library that a package needs.
  • ::OPTIONS: the settings that the code of a package starts with.
  • ::RESOURCE: a block of text that the package holds as data.
  • ::ANNOTATE: the annotations on the package, a class, a method, an attribute, a constant or a routine.

The classes that the directives create are objects too, and what their own methods do is specified in the classes chapter. This chapter says only what a directive makes and what the options on it mean.

A note on the examples. A directive cannot be run by INTERPRET, and a fault in one of them ends a program file before it writes anything. Where an example shows which condition a directive raises, it builds the text of a package with the Package class and catches the condition that building it raises. That class has its own page in the classes chapter, so the examples use it for one thing only: .package~new(name, lines) translates the lines as a package, installs it as the installation rule says and runs its instructions before the next clause of the caller.

What a directive is

[dir.index.directive]

A clause is a directive when its first token is ::, which may be followed by blanks or comments before the keyword. The keyword is not case sensitive. A directive begins its clause at the start of a line or after a semicolon; after a label on the same line the :: is read as part of an expression and raises SYNTAX 35.1. A keyword that names no directive raises SYNTAX 99.916, and :: followed by nothing that is a symbol raises SYNTAX 20.916. The error is found when the program is read, so that a program file with such a clause writes nothing and exits with 256 minus the error number, 157 for 99.916, as the reading rule describes for any fault of the text. A directive cannot be part of the text of INTERPRET, which refuses it.

call try '::class k1'
call try ':: /* a comment */ Class k2'
call try '::CLASS k3'
call try '::frob k4'
call try '::'
call try '::"class" k5'
call try 'lab: ::class k6'
exit
try:
  signal on syntax name e
  p = .package~new('spec-dir-index-kw', .array~of(arg(1)))
  say arg(1) '=> ok'
  return
e: say arg(1) '=>' condition('o')~code
  return

::class k1 => ok
:: /* a comment */ Class k2 => ok
::CLASS k3 => ok
::frob k4 => 99.916
:: => 20.916
::"class" k5 => 20.916
lab: ::class k6 => 35.1

say 'before'
::frob k
[dir.index.end]

A directive ends where a clause ends: at the end of the line or at a semicolon, and a comma at the end of a line continues it on the next line, as the clause rules say for any clause. A comment after the directive is part of the clause's white space. What follows the semicolon is the next clause, so a directive and the first clause of its body can share a line.

src = .array~of('::class k', '::method one; return 1; ::method two; return 2')
p = .package~new('spec-dir-index-end', src)
src = .array~of('say .box~new~m', '::class box,', '  public -- a comment', -
  '::method m', '  return 3')
p = .package~new('spec-dir-index-end2', src)

3

The prolog and the sections

[dir.index.prolog]

The clauses before the first directive are the prolog, the main code of the package. It runs once the package is installed, and its end is the end of the program: the interpreter never goes on into the code that follows the first directive, which is reached only through the routine or method that it declares. A file without directives is all prolog, and a file whose first clause is a directive has no prolog. An exit or return in the prolog ends the program there, and the directives have been installed all the same.

say 'start'
say .box~new~m
say 'end of the prolog'
::class box
::method m
  say 'running m'
  return 'result of m'
say 'this clause is part of m'

start
running m
result of m
end of the prolog

say 'start'
exit
::class box
::method activate class
  say 'activated'

activated
start
[dir.index.section]

The clauses after a directive, up to the next directive or the end of the program, are that directive's section. The section is the body of the method or routine that the directive declares, and the directive clause itself is not part of it. A directive that declares no code, such as ::CLASS, allows only comments and empty lines between it and the next directive. Any other clause there raises a SYNTAX error found when the program is read: 99.916 after ::class. The pages of the directives that take a body or are refused one say which subcode their own case raises.

call try '::class k', '-- a comment', '', '/* another */', '::method m'
call try '::class k', 'say 1', '::method m'
call try '::class k', 'x = 2'
call try '::class k', '::method m', 'say 1', 'x = 2'
exit
try:
  signal on syntax name e
  src = .array~new
  do i = 1 to arg()
    src~append(arg(i))
  end
  p = .package~new('spec-dir-index-sec', src)
  say src~makestring('l', ' / ') '=> ok'
  return
e: say src~makestring('l', ' / ') '=>' condition('o')~code
  return

::class k / -- a comment /  / /* another */ / ::method m => ok
::class k / say 1 / ::method m => 99.916
::class k / x = 2 => 99.916
::class k / ::method m / say 1 / x = 2 => ok
[dir.index.unit]

Each section, and the prolog, is a code unit of its own. Its labels are known only inside it, its variables are not shared with another unit, and a construct that it opens must end inside it: a DO, IF or SELECT that is still open at the next directive raises SYNTAX 14.1, 14.3 or 14.2, and an ELSE that has no instruction by then raises SYNTAX 14.4, all found when the program is read. A routine or method that needs a value of another unit receives it as an argument or through an object variable.

x = 'prolog variable'
say r1()
call try 'do', '::class k'
call try 'if 1 then', '::class k'
call try 'select', '::class k'
exit
try:
  signal on syntax name e
  src = .array~new
  do i = 1 to arg()
    src~append(arg(i))
  end
  p = .package~new('spec-dir-index-unit', src)
  say 'ok'
  return

Installation

[dir.index.install]

The interpreter installs a package before it runs the prolog, in four steps. First the ::REQUIRES directives are processed in text order wherever they stand, except that the library rule processes the LIBRARY ones before the others, and each required package is installed and runs its own prolog before the next step. Then the package's routines become known and every class is created, in the order that the class rule gives, and each new class object is sent an INIT message. When all classes exist, each is sent an ACTIVATE message in the order of creation. Only then does the prolog run, so a class method that ACTIVATE runs sees every class and routine of the package, and the prolog sees every class already activated. A class is reachable by its name, as the environment symbol that is a period followed by the name, once its INIT message has returned. During the INIT of a class the classes created before it are reachable, and the class itself and the classes created later are not, so that their symbols have the symbol's own text as value. The routines of the package are known from the start. Every class is reachable by the time the first ACTIVATE message is sent.

f = 'spec-dir-index-lib.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
call lineout f, 'say "lib prolog"'
call lineout f, '::class libc public'
call lineout f, '::method activate class'
call lineout f, '  say "lib activate"'
call lineout f
src = .array~of('say "prolog"', -
  '::class one', -
  '::method init class', -
  '  say "init one"', -
  '::method activate class', -
  '  say "activate one, routine says" r()', -
  '::requires "'f'"', -
  '::class two', -
  '::method init class', -
  '  say "init two"', -
  '::method activate class', -
  '  say "activate two"', -
  '::routine r', -
  '  return "r"')
p = .package~new('spec-dir-index-main', src)
call sysfiledelete f

lib activate
lib prolog
init one
init two
activate one, routine says r
activate two
prolog

  return

[dir.index.failure]

A fault found while the package is read stops everything: nothing is installed and no prolog runs. A fault raised while the package is installed, such as a class that cannot be found or a required file that does not exist, stops installation at that step, so that no class activates after it and the prolog does not run. The condition is SYNTAX in both cases, and a program file ends with 256 minus the error number as its exit status, 158 for 98.909, as the SYNTAX rule says. The classes created before such a fault have received their INIT message, as the next example shows, and have received no ACTIVATE message. A class that names itself, directly or through the classes it names, is an exception: the order rule finds it before any class is created, so no INIT message has been sent.

call try '::class k public private'
call try '::class k', '::class l subclass nosuchsuperclass'
call try '::requires "spec-dir-index-nosuchfile-xyz.rex"'
exit
try:
  signal on syntax name e
  src = .array~of('say "prolog"')
  do i = 1 to arg()
    src~append(arg(i))
  end
  p = .package~new('spec-dir-index-fail', src)
  say 'ok'
  return
e: say 'caught' condition('o')~code
  return

caught 25.901
caught 98.909
caught 43.901

::class k
::method init class
  say 'init k'
::method activate class
  say 'activate k'

Names

[dir.index.names]

A name that a directive takes is a symbol or a string. A symbol names the element in upper case, and a string names it as written, so ::class Box creates the class BOX and ::class "Box" creates the class Box. A lookup of a class or a method by name ignores case, whatever the spelling in the directive, and two directives that name one class, or one method of a class, in different cases declare it twice. The pages of the directives say what each does with a duplicate.

say .Widget~id .WIDGET~id .gadget~id .Gadget~id
::class Widget
::class "Gadget"

WIDGET WIDGET Gadget Gadget

::CLASS

::CLASS name [METACLASS m] [SUBCLASS s | MIXINCLASS s] [PUBLIC | PRIVATE] [ABSTRACT] [INHERIT i ...]

rexxref: Directives > ::CLASS

Deviations: D32, D114

::CLASS declares a class. The class comes into being when the package is installed, before the prolog runs, and the methods that the ::METHOD directives after it declare belong to it until the next ::CLASS. This page specifies the name of the class, the options that place it in a hierarchy and make it visible to other packages, and the order in which the classes of a package are made. What a class object does once it exists, the methods of Class such as new, id and superclass among them, is specified in the classes chapter; the examples here use those methods only to show what the directive made.

The class and its name

[dir.class.create]

::CLASS creates one class, named by a symbol or a string, and the class is reachable from every code of the package as the environment symbol that is a period followed by its name, from the point that the installation rule gives. The class's id is the name that the name rule gives, and .shown and .SHOWN are one class. A class declared with no SUBCLASS or MIXINCLASS option is a subclass of Object, and a class is a mixin class only when MIXINCLASS says so. A program may declare a class named like a built-in one, and its own then hides the built-in one in every code of the package.

say .plain~superclass~id .plain~new~class~id
say .Shown~id .ALSO~id .also~id
say .array~new~hi .array~new~class~id
::class plain
::class Shown
::class "Also"
::class array
::method hi
  return 'my array'

Object PLAIN
SHOWN Also Also
my array ARRAY
[dir.class.duplicate]

A package may declare a class name once. A second ::CLASS that names it again raises SYNTAX 99.901, whatever the case of either spelling, whether the directive is a symbol or a string and whether the first one was PUBLIC. The error is found when the program is read, as the directive rule says for the other faults of the text.

call try '::class Foo', '::class FOO'
call try '::class Foo', '::class "Foo"'
call try '::class Foo public', '::class foo private'
call try '::class Foo', '::class Bar'
exit

  signal on syntax name e

    src~append(arg(i))
  end
  p = .package~new('spec-dir-class-dup', src)
  say src~makestring('l', ' / ') '=> ok'
  return
e: say src~makestring('l', ' / ') '=>' condition('o')~code
  return

Options

[dir.class.options]

The keywords after the name are METACLASS, SUBCLASS, MIXINCLASS, PUBLIC, PRIVATE, ABSTRACT and INHERIT, in any case. They may stand in any order, except that INHERIT takes every word that follows it as the name of a class, so it comes last. Each of the four groups METACLASS, SUBCLASS or MIXINCLASS, PUBLIC or PRIVATE and ABSTRACT may appear once. A word that is none of the keywords, a keyword repeated, and a keyword that excludes one already given, such as PRIVATE after PUBLIC or SUBCLASS after MIXINCLASS, raise SYNTAX 25.901. METACLASS, SUBCLASS, MIXINCLASS and INHERIT without a name after them raise 19.906, 19.907, 19.913 and 19.908, and a ::CLASS with no name raises 19.901. Every one of these is found when the program is read.

call try '::class a public private'
call try '::class a public public'
call try '::class a mixinclass object subclass object'
call try '::class a abstract abstract'
call try '::class a frob'
call try '::class a inherit m public'
call try '::class A SubClass Object Public Abstract'
call try '::class a public abstract subclass object metaclass class'
call try '::class'
call try '::class a metaclass'
call try '::class a subclass'
call try '::class a mixinclass'
call try '::class a inherit'
exit

  signal on syntax name e
  p = .package~new('spec-dir-class-opt', .array~of(arg(1), -
    '::class m mixinclass object'))
  say arg(1) '=> ok'
  return
e: say arg(1) '=>' condition('o')~code
  return

Note. The inherit m public case reads public as the name of a second mixin class, and the package fails to find it, 98.909, when it is installed.

[dir.class.visibility]

A class is private unless PUBLIC says otherwise. A private class is known only to the package that declares it. A public class is also known to every package that requires the package, directly or through a chain of ::REQUIRES, and a class name is looked up first among the classes that the package declares, then among the public classes of the packages it requires, taking the first of those in the order of the ::REQUIRES directives. The order is depth first: a required package contributes its own public classes, then those it makes visible by its own ::REQUIRES, and all of these come before the classes of the next ::REQUIRES directive of the requiring package. A private class of a required package does not hide a public class of the same name that the package makes visible. When none of these has the name, the lookup goes on as the environment rule says, which finds the built-in classes and any class object that the program has stored in .environment under the name. This book does not specify which other directories that lookup searches. The same lookup finds the class that SUBCLASS, MIXINCLASS, METACLASS and INHERIT name. A name that no step finds is the environment symbol's own text, and the options that need a class raise the error that their rule gives.

The hierarchy

[dir.class.subclass]

SUBCLASS names the class's superclass, by a symbol or a string that the lookup of the visibility rule resolves. The new class inherits the instance methods and the class methods of the superclass, and the class that the program names may be a built-in one. A name written with a leading period is looked up as written: subclass .object looks for a class named .OBJECT, which no ::CLASS declares unless it spells its own name that way, so the built-in Object is not found. A name that is found nowhere raises SYNTAX 98.909 when the package is installed, and a class that is its own superclass, directly or through the classes it names, raises 98.911.

call try '::class a subclass array'
call try '::class a subclass "String"'
call try '::class a subclass .object'
call try '::class a subclass nosuchsuperclass'
call try '::class a subclass a'
call try '::class a subclass b', '::class b subclass a'
exit

  signal on syntax name e
  src = .array~new
  do i = 1 to arg()
    src~append(arg(i))
  end
  p = .package~new('spec-dir-class-sub', src)
  say src~makestring('l', ' / ') '=> ok'
  return
e: say src~makestring('l', ' / ') '=>' condition('o')~code
  return

[dir.class.mixin]

MIXINCLASS makes the class a mixin class and names its superclass as SUBCLASS does, so that the name is required. Only a mixin class may be inherited by INHERIT, which takes a list of class names, and the classes of the list are inherited in the order written. INHERIT of a class that is not a mixin class raises SYNTAX 98.942. A class that appears twice in the list, or is both the superclass and in the list, raises 98.944. A class that would become its own ancestor through INHERIT, itself included, raises 98.911. The class that MIXINCLASS names for a mixin class that is inherited must be the superclass of the inheriting class or one of the superclass's ancestors, or INHERIT raises SYNTAX 98.943 when the package is installed. When that class is itself a mixin class, the test applies to the class its own MIXINCLASS names, and so on down to the first class that is not a mixin class. A mixin class can itself be a subclass and inherit other mixin classes.

call try '::class c inherit plain'
call try '::class c inherit m1 m1'
call try '::class c subclass m1 inherit m1'
call try '::class c inherit c'
call try '::class m3 mixinclass m1 inherit m2'
exit

  say arg(1) '=> ok'
  return
e: say arg(1) '=>' condition('o')~code
  return

[dir.class.search]

A message sent to an instance finds its method by looking first at the methods the class itself declares and then at those of the classes it descends from through SUBCLASS and INHERIT, in the order that the order rule of the method search gives; the first method found runs. When the superclass and its ancestors inherit no mixin classes and each class that INHERIT names is a mixin class whose MIXINCLASS option names Object and that inherits none itself, as in the example, that order is the class, its superclass and the superclass's ancestors other than Object, the mixin classes in the order written, and Object last. A superclass then hides a method of a mixin class that the subclass inherits, and an earlier mixin class hides a later one. A mixin class with another base class, and a class that more than one listed class reaches, stand where the base rule and the shared-class rule say.

[dir.class.metaclass]

METACLASS names a class that is a subclass of Class, and the instance methods of that class become class methods of the new class, so that they answer messages sent to the class itself. A class method that the new class declares with the CLASS option hides a metaclass method of the same name, and both hide a class method that the new class inherits. A subclass has its superclass's metaclass unless it names its own. A metaclass name that is found nowhere raises SYNTAX 98.908, where SUBCLASS, MIXINCLASS and INHERIT raise 98.909. A name that is found and is not a subclass of Class raises SYNTAX 99.927 when the package is installed, after the classes created before it have received INIT as the failure rule says, and a metaclass that is the class itself raises 98.911. A new of the METACLASS that answers an object that is not a class raises SYNTAX 98.900 when the package is installed (Deviation 114).

[dir.class.abstract]

ABSTRACT marks the class as one that has no instances of its own: the NEW method that Class supplies raises SYNTAX 98.989 for it, before any INIT runs, and a class method NEW that the abstract class declares itself runs instead. Order of creation

[dir.class.forward]

A class may name a class that the package declares further on, in SUBCLASS, MIXINCLASS, METACLASS or INHERIT. The classes are created in text order, except that a class waits until every class it names has been created, and is then created at once, before the next class in the text. The order of creation is the order in which the classes receive their INIT and ACTIVATE messages, as the installation rule says. A class that names itself, directly or through the classes it names, raises SYNTAX 98.911 before any class of the package is created, so that no INIT has run, not even for the classes that come before it in the text and take no part in the cycle.

Deviations

[dir.class.deviation.32]

When the new of the METACLASS answers a class that Class did not build, interrexx ends the program with exit code 120 while the directive is read, so that the program writes nothing, as the chapter rule states for subclass, mixinclass and the directive; ooRexx rewires the existing class in place and runs the program. See Deviation 32.

say 'before'
::class meta subclass class
::method new class
  return .array
::class k metaclass meta
[dir.class.deviation.114]

When the new of the METACLASS answers an object that is not a class, the package is not installed: SYNTAX 98.900 is raised while the directive is read, so the program writes nothing, as the chapter rule states for subclass and mixinclass. ooRexx crashes.

say 'before'
::class meta subclass class
::method new class
  return .nil
::class k metaclass meta

::METHOD

::METHOD name [CLASS] [PUBLIC | PRIVATE | PACKAGE] [GUARDED | UNGUARDED] [PROTECTED | UNPROTECTED] [ATTRIBUTE | ABSTRACT | EXTERNAL spec | DELEGATE var]

rexxref: Directives > ::METHOD

Deviations: D105

::METHOD declares a method. Its section, the clauses up to the next directive, is the method's code, and the method belongs to the class of the most recent ::CLASS directive. A ::METHOD before any ::CLASS belongs to no class. This page specifies the name of a method, the options that set who may send it and how it is guarded, the forms that have no code of their own, and the method that belongs to no class. What a method object does once it exists, and the methods of Class that add one to a class, belong to the classes chapter.

The method and its name

[dir.method.create]

The section of a ::METHOD is the code of an instance method of the class that the most recent ::CLASS declared, and the directive clause itself is not part of it. The method runs with SELF as the object it was sent to, and it reads and writes the object's variables through EXPOSE. The most recent ::CLASS is the one that counts even when other directives, such as a ::ROUTINE, come between. A method with no clause in its section returns no value, so a message whose result is used raises SYNTAX 91.999. The code is a unit of its own: a label or variable of another section is not known in it.

o = .counter~new
say o~add(2) o~add(3)
say o~total
o~empty
signal on syntax name e
x = o~empty
e: say condition('o')~code

::routine helper
  return 'a routine between'
::method add
  expose n
  use arg step
  if \datatype(n, 'W') then n = 0
  n += step
  return n
::method total
  expose n
  return n
::method empty

[dir.method.name]

The name of a method is a symbol or a string, and the name rule gives the name, so ::method "Mixed" is found by mixed and by MIXED. A string may hold any characters, so it can name an operator method such as "+"; a symbol cannot, and a ::method followed by something that is not a symbol or a string raises SYNTAX 19.902. A class declares one method of a name: a second ::METHOD of the same name, in any case, raises SYNTAX 99.902. An instance method and a class method of the same name are two methods.

Options

[dir.method.options]

The keywords after the name are CLASS, PUBLIC, PRIVATE, PACKAGE, GUARDED, UNGUARDED, PROTECTED, UNPROTECTED, ATTRIBUTE, ABSTRACT, EXTERNAL and DELEGATE, in any case and in any order. A method names at most one keyword of each of these groups: access (PUBLIC, PRIVATE, PACKAGE), guarding (GUARDED, UNGUARDED), protection (PROTECTED, UNPROTECTED) and the kind of code (ABSTRACT, EXTERNAL, DELEGATE), and CLASS and ATTRIBUTE at most once each. ATTRIBUTE goes with any one keyword of the kind group. A word that is none of the keywords, a keyword repeated or a second keyword of one group raises SYNTAX 25.902. EXTERNAL and DELEGATE take an operand, and the other keywords do not. The errors of the directive are found when the program is read. A clause after an ATTRIBUTE method raises the error that the attribute rule gives, except with DELEGATE, where it raises the error of the delegate rule.

[dir.method.class]

CLASS makes the method a class method: the section is code that answers messages sent to the class object itself, with SELF the class, and not messages sent to its instances. The subclasses of the class inherit it as they inherit any class method, and an instance does not see it. CLASS requires a ::CLASS directive before the ::METHOD, and without one the directive raises SYNTAX 99.905, found when the program is read.

[dir.method.access]

PUBLIC is the default, and a public method accepts a message from any sender. A PRIVATE method, an instance method or a class method, accepts a message only from a method whose SELF, the sender, is the class that declares it or a subclass of it, or is an instance of one of those; a class that inherits a mixin class counts as a subclass of it. The sender may be another object, so objects of one class can send each other private messages, and a class method of the class can send a private instance method. A message from the prolog, from a routine, or from a method of an unrelated class raises SYNTAX 97.2. The test is on SELF, not on the class whose method runs, so a method of a superclass that runs with an instance of the superclass as SELF cannot send a private method of a subclass, and the same method running with an instance of the subclass as SELF can. A PACKAGE method accepts a message from any code of the package that declares it and from no other package, which raises SYNTAX 97.3. A message sent with START is checked as a Deviation states.

[dir.method.guard]

A method is guarded unless UNGUARDED says otherwise, and the instruction page of GUARD says what that means: a guarded method starts with the exclusive use of its object's variables, and an unguarded one does not. An unguarded method can therefore run while another method holds the guard. GUARDED may be written, and it is the same as writing no option.

log = .array~new
o = .box~new(log)
h = o~start('hold')
do until o~inside; end
g = o~start('probe')
u = o~start('quick')
u~result
o~release
h~result; g~result
say log~makestring('l', ' ')
exit
::class box
::method init
  expose log inside go
  use arg log
  inside = .false
  go = .false
::method hold
  expose log inside go
  inside = .true
  do until go; end
  log~append('hold-end')
::method probe guarded
  expose log
  log~append('probe')
::method quick unguarded
  expose log
  log~append('quick')
::method inside unguarded
  expose inside
  return inside
::method release unguarded
  expose go
  go = .true

quick hold-end probe
[dir.method.protected]

PROTECTED marks the method so that a security manager, when the program has one, decides whether the call may run. UNPROTECTED is the default. A program with no security manager runs a protected method like any other, and the security manager is not specified here.

o = .box~new
say o~locked o~open
::class box
::method locked protected
  return 'ran'
::method open unprotected
  return 'ran too'

ran ran too

Methods without code of their own

[dir.method.attribute]

ATTRIBUTE declares two methods at once and takes no code: a method of the given name that returns the value of the object variable of that name, and a method name= that assigns its one argument to the variable and returns no value, so that a message whose result is used raises SYNTAX 91.999. The object variable is named as the directive spells the name: a symbol gives it in upper case, and a string as written, so an attribute that a lower-case string declares is not the variable that an EXPOSE of the symbol names. The access, guarding and protection options apply to both methods, and so does CLASS, which makes them class methods. An unset variable returns its own name as spelled. The first method takes no argument, and the second takes exactly one: SYNTAX 93.902 for an extra argument and 93.903 for a missing one. A clause after the directive that is not a null clause raises SYNTAX 99.934, found when the program is read, because the directive has no section; that holds for ATTRIBUTE with ABSTRACT too, which declares both methods abstract, and for ATTRIBUTE with EXTERNAL, which looks for its library as the external rule says. ATTRIBUTE with DELEGATE raises 99.946 instead, as the delegate rule says.

[dir.method.abstract]

ABSTRACT declares a method that has no code, a method a subclass declares in full. A message that reaches an abstract method raises SYNTAX 93.965, and a subclass that declares a method of the same name answers the message instead. The class that declares an abstract method is not itself abstract. A clause after the directive that is not a null clause raises SYNTAX 99.933, found when the program is read.

[dir.method.external]

EXTERNAL names a method that a native library supplies, and takes no code. Its operand is a string whose first word is LIBRARY, in any case, followed by the name of the library and optionally one more word, the entry in it. A missing operand, or one that is not a string, raises SYNTAX 19.905. A string that does not have that form, whose first word is another word, or that has no library name or more than two words after LIBRARY, raises 99.917; both are found when the program is read. A clause after the directive that is not a null clause raises 99.936. A library that cannot be loaded raises SYNTAX 98.903 when the directive's section ends, which is before the next directive is read. It therefore comes before every fault raised when the package is installed and before a fault found when a later directive is read, while a fault found when an earlier directive is read comes first, and a clause in the section raises 99.936 and not 98.903. With ATTRIBUTE the library is looked for in the same way, and a clause after the directive raises 99.934, as the attribute rule says. How a library is searched for, and which routine of it the method runs, are not specified here.

[dir.method.delegate]

DELEGATE takes the name of an object variable as a symbol and no code. A message sent to the method is forwarded, with its arguments, to the object that the variable holds, as if the section were expose var followed by forward to(var). The operand must be a symbol, and a missing operand or a string raises SYNTAX 20.926; a symbol that cannot name a variable raises 99.925. A clause after the directive that is not a null clause raises 99.946. All three are found when the program is read.

Methods of no class

[dir.method.floating]

A ::METHOD that comes before every ::CLASS belongs to no class, and the package keeps it as a method object of its own. The environment symbol .METHODS holds a table of the package's floating methods, whose indexes are the method names in upper case, and a lookup in it is by exact index, so .methods['greet'] is the .nil object. The symbol exists only in a package that has a floating method; for any other package it is the symbol's own text. Each package has its own table. A floating method may not use CLASS, which raises SYNTAX 99.905, and a name declared twice raises 99.902, as the methods of a class do.

say .methods~allindexes~sort~makearray~makestring('l', ' ')
.box~define('GREET', .methods['GREET'])
say .box~new~greet('world')
say .methods['greet'] .methods['GREET']~class~id

exit

Deviations

[dir.method.deviation.105]

A message sent with START is checked for PRIVATE and PACKAGE access as the same message sent directly by the code that starts it. A method of a class may start a private method of its own class, code of a package may start a PACKAGE method of that package, and a PACKAGE method started from another package raises SYNTAX 97.3. ooRexx raises 97.2 for every started private message and 97.1 for every started PACKAGE message, whichever code starts it.

::class vault
::method open unguarded
  m = self~start('code')
  return m~result
::method code private
  return 'private answer'

::ATTRIBUTE

::ATTRIBUTE name [GET | SET] [CLASS] [PUBLIC | PRIVATE | PACKAGE] [GUARDED | UNGUARDED] [PROTECTED | UNPROTECTED] [ABSTRACT | EXTERNAL spec | DELEGATE var]

rexxref: Directives > ::ATTRIBUTE

::ATTRIBUTE declares the accessor methods of an object variable: a getter that returns the variable and a setter that assigns it, or only one of the two. A directive with no code of its own generates both methods, and a directive with GET or SET takes the code of that one method from its section. The options that set who may send the messages and how they are guarded are the ones of ::METHOD, and this page names them without restating them. What a method object does once it exists, and the methods of Class that add one to a class, belong to the classes chapter.

The generated methods

[dir.attribute.create]

::ATTRIBUTE with no GET and no SET declares two methods of the class that the most recent ::CLASS declared: a method of the attribute's name and a method of that name followed by an equals sign. The first takes no argument and returns the value of the object variable of that name, which is the variable's own name, spelled as the name rule gives it, while it is unset. The second takes exactly one argument and assigns it to the variable; it is what a message assignment obj~name = value sends, and it returns no value, so a message whose result is used raises SYNTAX 91.999. An extra argument raises SYNTAX 93.902 and a missing one 93.903. A clause after the directive is refused as the section rule says. The form of ::METHOD with the keyword ATTRIBUTE declares the same two methods.

o~size = 4
say o~size
say o~peek

call try 'o~"SIZE="(1, 2)'
call try 'say o~"SIZE="(1)'

e: say condition('o')~code

[dir.attribute.name]

The name is a symbol or a string. As the names rule says, a symbol names the variable in upper case and a string names it exactly as written, so the variable of ::attribute "Mixed" is not the one that the symbol mixed names in an EXPOSE, and while it is unset the getter answers Mixed. The messages mixed and mixed= still reach the methods, because the lookup of a method by name ignores case. A name that cannot be the name of a variable, such as a string with a blank or a number, raises SYNTAX 99.925, and a directive whose name is missing or is neither a symbol nor a string raises 19.914. Both are found when the program is read.

o = .box~new
o~"Mixed" = 5
o~lower = 6
say o~mixed o~lower
say o~peek

say o2~mixed

call try '::attribute 1'
call try '::attribute'

GET and SET

[dir.attribute.getset]

GET declares only the getter and SET only the setter, so that the two can have different options. GET and SET together raise SYNTAX 25.925. A GET or SET directive without a keyword of the kind group (ABSTRACT, EXTERNAL, DELEGATE) that has a section takes the section as the code of its method, with the directive clause left out, and without a section it declares the generated method. In the code of a setter the argument is the value that name = value assigned, and the variable is reached through EXPOSE as in any method.

o = .box~new
o~size = 3
say o~size o~peek
o~tag = 'abc'
say o~tag
o~note = 7
say o~note
signal on syntax name e
o~count = 1
e: say condition('o')~code

  size = value * 10
::attribute tag get

  return 'tag:' tag

::attribute note set
::attribute count get
::method peek

  return size

[dir.attribute.options]

The keywords after the name are GET, SET, CLASS, PUBLIC, PRIVATE, PACKAGE, GUARDED, UNGUARDED, PROTECTED, UNPROTECTED, ABSTRACT, EXTERNAL and DELEGATE, in any case and in any order. The groups and the rules about them are those of ::METHOD, except that ATTRIBUTE is not a keyword and GET and SET make a group of their own: a word that is none of the keywords, a keyword repeated or a second keyword of one group raises SYNTAX 25.925. The access, guarding and protection options apply to every method that the directive declares, as access, guarding and protection say for a method. A GET and a SET directive for one name may therefore differ: a public getter and a private setter make an attribute that others read and only the object itself writes.

Class attributes

[dir.attribute.class]

CLASS makes the declared methods class methods, as it does for ::METHOD, and the variable that they reach is an object variable of the class object. An instance does not see the methods, and an attribute of the same name without CLASS reaches a different variable, so a class and its instances can hold a value each under one name. CLASS requires a ::CLASS directive before it, and without one the directive raises SYNTAX 99.905.

say o~count

Names that are taken

[dir.attribute.duplicate]

A class declares one method of a name, and a second declaration of one of the attribute's method names in the same class raises a SYNTAX error when the program is read. The names are the getter's name and the setter's name with the equals sign, so a GET directive and a SET directive of one name do not collide, while two of the same half, or a plain directive and a GET or SET one, do. The code is that of the later directive: 99.931 for an attribute, 99.902 for a ::METHOD and 99.932 for a ::CONSTANT. An attribute with CLASS and one without it are two methods of different kinds, so they do not collide.

exit

[dir.attribute.delegate]

DELEGATE takes the name of an object variable as a symbol, as it does for ::METHOD, and forwards the message of each method that the directive declares to the object that the variable holds. The getter forwards name and the setter forwards name= with its argument, so assigning to the attribute assigns to the attribute of the same name of the delegate. A missing operand or a string raises SYNTAX 20.926 and a symbol that cannot name a variable raises 99.925.

[dir.attribute.external]

EXTERNAL takes the operand that ::METHOD describes and declares the method or methods from a native library. A missing operand, or one that is not a string, raises SYNTAX 19.905, and a string that does not start with the word LIBRARY or has too many words raises 99.917. A library that cannot be loaded raises 98.903, and a library that loads but has no method entry of the given name raises 90.998. Both are raised when the section of the directive ends, so a clause in the section is refused first, as the section rule below says. How they are ordered against the faults of other directives is the subject of the rule for external methods.

The section

[dir.attribute.section]

A directive that declares the generated methods takes no code, and any clause after it that is not a null clause raises a SYNTAX error when the program is read. The code is 99.937 after a directive with neither GET nor SET, whatever its kind keyword. After GET or SET it is 99.940 with ABSTRACT, 99.935 with EXTERNAL and 99.947 with DELEGATE. GET or SET with no kind keyword is the form whose section is code, so no clause is refused there. Comments and blank lines between the directive and the next one are null clauses.

exit

Attributes of no class

[dir.attribute.floating]

An ::ATTRIBUTE before every ::CLASS declares methods of no class, which the package keeps as method objects of its own, as floating methods are kept. The methods are in the table that .METHODS names, under the names of the getter and of the setter in upper case, and a GET or SET directive adds only its own. Duplicate names raise SYNTAX 99.931 as they do in a class, and CLASS raises 99.905.

::CONSTANT

::CONSTANT name [value | (expression)]

rexxref: Directives > ::CONSTANT

Deviations: D69

::CONSTANT declares a name that answers one value for the class and for each of its instances. The value is a literal, a symbol taken as text or an expression in parentheses that is evaluated once, when the package is installed. The directive has no code section and no setter. This page specifies what the directive declares, the forms of the value, when an expression runs and what it can see, and the names that a constant takes. What a method object does once it exists belongs to the classes chapter.

What a constant is

[dir.constant.create]

::CONSTANT declares one method of the class that the most recent ::CLASS declared, and the method is both an instance method and a class method, so the class and every instance of it, subclasses included, answer the name with the value. A subclass that declares a method of the name answers it instead. The method takes no argument, and an argument raises SYNTAX 93.902. There is no method that assigns, so a message assignment raises SYNTAX 97.1. A value left out makes the constant answer its own name, in upper case for a symbol and as written for a string. A constant needs no class before it, as the rule for constants of no class says.

say .shape~sides .shape~new~sides
say .shape~kind .shape~new~kind
say .shape~"Quiet" .shape~new~quiet
say .square~sides .square~new~sides
say .triangle~sides
call try 'say .shape~sides(1)'
call try '.shape~new~sides = 4'
call try '.shape~sides = 4'
exit
try:
  signal on syntax name e
  interpret arg(1)
  return
e: say arg(1) '=>' condition('o')~code
  return

[dir.constant.name]

The name of a constant is a symbol or a string, with the rules that ::METHOD gives for the name of a method, and the names rule gives for its spelling. A missing name raises SYNTAX 19.915. A class declares one method of a name, and the constant is both an instance and a class method, so a second declaration of its name in the same class raises a SYNTAX error when the program is read, also when the other one is a ::METHOD of the class kind or an ::ATTRIBUTE. The code is that of the later directive: 99.932 for a constant, 99.902 for a ::METHOD and 99.931 for an ::ATTRIBUTE. Two classes may each have a constant of one name.

The value

[dir.constant.value]

A value that is not in parentheses is one token. A string is the value as written, with the quotes removed. A symbol is the value in upper case and it is never looked up: .nil is the text .NIL and Hello.World is HELLO.WORLD, whatever variable or environment symbol the name could be. A number is not normalized, so 007 stays 007 and 1e3 is 1E3 as the symbol it is. A sign, + or -, may come before a number, with blanks between or not, and the value is the sign and the number joined, so - 7 is -7 and +5 is +5. A sign followed by anything other than a number, or by nothing before a semicolon, raises SYNTAX 19.916, and a second token raises 21.913. These errors are found when the program is read. A sign that is the last token on its line is a continuation and not a sign.

say .k~lit .k~sym .k~nil .k~dotted
say .k~num .k~exp .k~neg .k~plus .k~spaced

call try '::constant a 1 2'
call try '::constant a "x" "y"'
call try '::constant a (1) (2)'
exit

Expressions

[dir.constant.expression]

A value in parentheses is an expression, which the interpreter evaluates once and keeps, so each message answers the same value that the evaluation produced. The evaluation is part of installation: it runs after every class of the package has been created and has received its INIT message, and before any class receives ACTIVATE, so before the prolog too. It runs the constants of the classes in the order in which the classes were created, and in text order within a class. In the expression SELF is the class object, whichever of the class and its instances later receives the message, and the code is that of a method named ::CONSTANT whose line is the directive's. An error in the expression raises its own condition, and the installation stops at that constant as the failure rule says, so that no class activates and the prolog does not run. A syntax error in the expression is found when the program is read.

say 'prolog'
say .k~a .k~b
say .k~who
say .k~name .k~line
call try 'say "prolog"', '::class k', '::constant a (1/0)'
call try 'say "prolog"', '::class k', '::constant a (undefined_xyz())'
call try '::class k', '::constant a (1 +)'
call try '::class k', '::constant a (1))'
exit

  src = .array~new
  do i = 1 to arg()

  end
  p = .package~new('spec-dir-constant-expr', src)
  say 'ok'
  return
e: say src~makestring('l', ' / ') '=>' condition('o')~code
  return

[dir.constant.order]

An expression that reads another constant sees its value only when that constant is already evaluated. A constant whose value is a literal, a symbol or a number is there from the start, so an expression may read it wherever it is declared, in its own class or another. An expression constant is evaluated in the order of the expression rule, so an expression that reads one that comes after it, itself included, raises SYNTAX 97.4 during installation. The classes are created in the order that the class rule gives, which a forward reference to a superclass changes from the text order.

call try '::class k', '::constant a (.l~x)', '::class l', '::constant x (5)'
call try '::class k', '::constant a (1)', '::constant b (self~a + 1)'
exit

Deviations

[dir.constant.deviation.69]

The code of an expression constant is a method of its own, and the source that it reports, through .context~executable~source, is the text of its own directive. In ooRexx the expression constants of a class are joined into one method, so the source of the one that is running is not its own directive.

say .k~a
say .k~b
::class k
::constant a (.context~executable~source~makestring('l', '|'))
::constant b (.context~executable~source~makestring('l', '|'))

::constant a (.context~executable~source~makestring('l', '|'))
::constant b (.context~executable~source~makestring('l', '|'))

::ROUTINE

::ROUTINE name [PUBLIC | PRIVATE] [EXTERNAL spec]

rexxref: Directives > ::ROUTINE

::ROUTINE declares a routine that the code of its package calls by name, as a function or with CALL. A routine is private to its package unless PUBLIC makes it visible to the packages that require it. This page specifies the routine and its name, the options, the place of a routine in the search for a called name, what a required package makes visible, and the routines that a native library supplies. What a routine object does once it exists belongs to the classes chapter.

The routine

[dir.routine.create]

The section of a ::ROUTINE, the clauses up to the next directive, is the body of a routine, and the directive clause itself is not part of it. A call runs the body as a unit of its own, as the unit rule says: its variables and labels are its own, and the arguments are read with ARG and USE ARG. A routine returns a value with RETURN. A routine whose body is empty returns none, so a function call of it raises SYNTAX 44.1, and a CALL of it leaves RESULT dropped. The routine is installed before the prolog runs, as the installation rule says, so the prolog and the ACTIVATE method of a class can call it.

say r1(2, 3)
call R1 4, 5
say result
say 'Mixed'(1) mixed(7)
x = 'prolog'
say sees()
call nothing
say symbol('result')
signal on syntax name e
say nothing()
e: say condition('o')~code
exit
::routine r1
  use arg a, b
  return a * b
::routine "Mixed"
  return 'm' arg(1)
::routine sees
  return symbol('x') x
::routine nothing

20

[dir.routine.name]

The name of a routine is a symbol or a string. The names rule gives its spelling, and the lookup of a routine by name ignores case, so ::routine "Mixed" is called by mixed and by MIXED. A package declares one routine of a name: a second ::ROUTINE of the name, in any case, raises SYNTAX 99.903 when the program is read. A directive whose name is missing, or is neither a symbol nor a string, raises 19.903. A routine and a method of the same name are unrelated.

call try '::routine r', '::routine R'
call try '::routine r', '::routine "r"'
call try '::routine r', '::routine "Rr"'
call try '::routine "a b"'
call try '::routine'
call try '::routine +'
call try '::class k', '::routine r', '::class l', '::routine r'
call try '::class k', '::method r', '::routine r'
exit
try:
  signal on syntax name e
  src = .array~new
  do i = 1 to arg()
    src~append(arg(i))
  end
  p = .package~new('spec-dir-routine-name', src)
  say src~makestring('l', ' / ') '=> ok'
  return
e: say src~makestring('l', ' / ') '=>' condition('o')~code
  return

::routine r / ::routine R => 99.903
::routine r / ::routine "r" => 99.903
::routine r / ::routine "Rr" => ok
::routine "a b" => ok
::routine => 19.903
::routine + => 19.903
::class k / ::routine r / ::class l / ::routine r => 99.903
::class k / ::method r / ::routine r => ok

Options

[dir.routine.options]

The keywords after the name are PUBLIC, PRIVATE and EXTERNAL, in any case. PRIVATE is the default, and writing it is the same as writing no access keyword. A routine names at most one of PUBLIC and PRIVATE, and a keyword written twice, a word that is not one of the three, and so a keyword of ::METHOD such as PACKAGE or GUARDED, raise SYNTAX 25.903. EXTERNAL takes an operand and the others do not, as the rule for external routines says. The errors of the directive are found when the program is read.

call try '::routine r public'
call try '::routine r Private'
call try '::routine r PUBLIC private'
call try '::routine r public public'
call try '::routine r private private'
call try '::routine r package'
call try '::routine r guarded'
call try '::routine r class'
call try '::routine r frob'
exit
try:
  signal on syntax name e
  p = .package~new('spec-dir-routine-opt', .array~of(arg(1)))
  say arg(1) '=> ok'
  return
e: say arg(1) '=>' condition('o')~code
  return

::routine r public => ok
::routine r Private => ok
::routine r PUBLIC private => 25.903
::routine r public public => 25.903
::routine r private private => 25.903
::routine r package => 25.903
::routine r guarded => 25.903
