  o~description = 'changed'
  say condition('d') condition('o')~description
  o~extra = 'x'
  say condition('o')~extra
  c = condition('o')
  c~description = 'copy changed'
  say condition('d') o~description
  o~condition = 'USER BAR'
  o~instruction = 'SIGNAL'
  say condition('c') condition('i')
  return
::routine r
  raise user foo description 'raised'

The condition object

[cond.information.object]

The condition object is a directory with these entries, whose names are in capital letters. CONDITION, DESCRIPTION, INSTRUCTION and ADDITIONAL are the entries that the object rule of CONDITION names. PACKAGE is the package that holds the code that raised the condition, and PROGRAM its name. POSITION is the number of the line on which the clause that raised the condition starts, in that code, and a NOTREADY that the interpreter raised has none. PROPAGATED is 1 when the condition left the level that raised it and 0 otherwise, as the propagated rule specifies. STACKFRAMES and TRACEBACK are lists with one item for each active level of code at that time, the main program's included, and the text of a traceback line is not specified. ADDITIONAL is present for a SYNTAX, NOMETHOD, NOSTRING or NOTREADY that the interpreter raised. A condition that a RAISE instruction raised has POSITION, and has ADDITIONAL exactly when the instruction gave one, whatever the name of the condition, as the options rule of RAISE says. The exception is a SYNTAX, which always has an ADDITIONAL array, empty when the instruction gave none, as the SYNTAX rule of RAISE says. SYNTAX adds CODE, the error number with its subcode as 41.1, RC, its major number, ERRORTEXT, the text of the error that the ERRORTEXT builtin answers for RC, and MESSAGE, the text with the details of this occurrence. ERROR and FAILURE have RC, the return code of the command. The texts of the messages are not specified, and the entry RESULT is not specified here.

address system
call on error name h
call on failure name h
call on notready name h
call on halt name h
call on user foo name h
call on user bar name h
signal on novalue name n1
'exit 3'
address nosuch
'exit 3'
y = linein()
call rh
call rf
call rb
x = undefinedvar
n1: call show condition('o')
signal on syntax name n2
x = 1 + 'a'
n2: call show condition('o')
signal on nostring name n3
z = 'a' || .nostr~new
n3: call show condition('o')
signal on nomethod name n4
.nil~foo
n4: call show condition('o')
numeric digits 3
signal on lostdigits name n5
z = 12345 + 1
n5: call show condition('o')
exit
h: call show arg(1)
  return
rh: raise halt return
rf: raise user foo return
rb: raise user bar additional ('x') return
show: procedure
  o = arg(1)
  all = 1
  do k over .array~of('CONDITION', 'DESCRIPTION', 'INSTRUCTION',,
      'PACKAGE', 'PROGRAM', 'PROPAGATED', 'STACKFRAMES', 'TRACEBACK')
    if \o~hasIndex(k) then all = 0
  end
  line = left(o~condition, 10) 'common='all
  do k over .array~of('ADDITIONAL', 'CODE', 'ERRORTEXT', 'MESSAGE',,
      'POSITION', 'RC')
    if o~hasIndex(k) then line = line k
  end
  say line
  return
::class nostr
::method makestring
  return .nil

NOVALUE    common=1 POSITION
SYNTAX     common=1 ADDITIONAL CODE ERRORTEXT MESSAGE POSITION RC
NOSTRING   common=1 ADDITIONAL POSITION
NOMETHOD   common=1 ADDITIONAL POSITION
LOSTDIGITS common=1 POSITION

  return

  return

[cond.information.object.values]

For a SYNTAX condition, CODE is the string m.n of the error number and subcode, RC is m, ERRORTEXT equals what the ERRORTEXT builtin answers for RC, PACKAGE is the package that .CONTEXT~PACKAGE answers in the code that raised it, PROGRAM is the name of that package, and POSITION is the line of the clause, and PROPAGATED is 0 when the code that raised it answers it, as the propagated rule says for the other case. ADDITIONAL is an array of the values that the error message names, a for the nonnumeric value 'a' of error 41.1. The description of a SYNTAX condition is the null string.

signal on syntax name s
x = 1 + 'a'
s: o = condition('o')
say o~code o~rc o~position o~propagated '['o~description']'
say (o~errortext == errortext(o~rc)) (o~program == .context~package~name),
    (o~package == .context~package)
say o~additional~class o~additional~items o~additional~at(1)
say o~stackframes~class o~traceback~class

[cond.information.context]

In a trapped condition's code, .CONTEXT~CONDITION answers a new directory that holds the same entries as CONDITION('O'), and .nil when the code holds no record. Every call answers a new directory, so two answers are not identical and a change to one is seen by neither the other nor the builtin. The method reads the record that the scope rule of CONDITION describes, so the option R of CONDITION clears what the method reads.

say '[' || .context~condition || ']' (.context~condition == .nil)
signal on syntax name h
x = 1 + 'a'
h: c = .context~condition
say c~class c~condition c~code (c == condition('o')),
    (c~code == condition('o')~code)
say (c == .context~condition) (c~condition == .context~condition~condition)
c~condition = 'changed'
say condition('c') condition('o')~condition .context~condition~condition
say '['condition('r')']' (.context~condition == .nil) sub()
return
sub: return (.context~condition == .nil)

The variables RC and SIGL

[cond.information.rc]

Before control reaches the code of a trap, the trap sets RC for some conditions. After a SYNTAX condition it is the major number of the error, so 35 for 35.1, and it equals the RC entry of the object. After ERROR and FAILURE it is the return code of the command, which the command rule already sets. Every other condition leaves RC as it was.

rc = 'before'
signal on novalue name h1
x = undefinedvar
h1: say 'novalue' rc
signal on syntax name h2
x = 1 + 'a'
h2: say 'syntax' rc condition('o')~code condition('o')~rc
rc = 'again'
signal on syntax name h3
interpret 'say 1 +'
h3: say 'syntax' rc condition('o')~code
rc = 'u'
call on user foo name u
call r
say 'after user' rc
address system
signal on error name h4
'exit 7'
h4: say 'error' rc condition('o')~rc
exit
r: raise user foo return
u: say 'user' rc
  return

novalue before
syntax 41 41.1 41
syntax 35 35.1
user u
after user u
error 7 7
[cond.information.sigl]

When a trap answers a condition, SIGL is the number of the line on which starts the clause that was running in the code of the trap, in the level that the trap belongs to. A level is the main program or a running routine, method or internal routine. When the condition is raised in the level whose trap answers, the clause is the one that raised it, and when it is raised deeper, in a level that has no trap of its own, the clause is the one that called that level. A clause that spans several lines counts at its first, and the clause of an INTERPRET is the INTERPRET instruction, not a clause of its text. The POSITION entry is the line of the clause that raised the condition, in the code that raised it, so it differs from SIGL when the condition was raised in a deeper level that has no trap. The SIGL of a CALL trap is set as the CALL trap rule says.

signal on syntax name h
say 'a',
    'b' + 'c',
    'd'
h: say 'multi-line' sigl condition('o')~position
signal on syntax name h2
call inner
h2: say 'inner trap' sigl condition('o')~position
signal on syntax name h3
call outer
h3: say 'outer' sigl condition('o')~position
signal on syntax name h4
say .o~new~go
h4: say 'method' sigl condition('o')~position
signal on syntax name h5
interpret 'say 1;',
  'x = 1 + "a"'
h5: say 'interpret' sigl condition('o')~position
exit
inner:
  x = 1 + 'a'
outer: procedure
  signal off syntax
  x = 1 + 'a'
::class o
::method go
  return 1 + 'x'

inner trap 21 21
outer 10 24
method 13 27

interpret 16 16

From the code that raised it to its caller

[cond.information.propagate]

A SYNTAX condition that is raised in a level where no trap answers it, as the choice rule decides, ends the clause that raised it, and then the clause of the level that called this one, so that no clause of the first level runs on, and is raised again at the clause that made the call, in the level above: a CALL, a function call, a message term or a message instruction. A level above whose trap answers ends the chain there, and the code of the trap runs in that level, with the record and the object of the original condition: POSITION names the line where the error was found, and STACKFRAMES lists the active levels as they were then. A level that does not answer passes the condition on, up to the main program, where an untrapped condition ends the program as the SYNTAX rule says. A level that starts with every trap OFF, a ::ROUTINE or a method, passes it on until it switches a trap on, and an internal routine does when its copy of the trap states has no trap that answers.

signal on syntax name top
say 'start'
say a()
say 'not reached'
exit
top: say 'top' condition('o')~code sigl rc condition('o')~position
say 'frames' condition('o')~stackFrames~items
::routine a
  say 'in a'
  return .o~new~m + 1
::class o
::method m
  say 'in m'
  signal on novalue name nope
  x = 1 + 'a'
  say 'not reached'
nope: nop

start
in a
in m
top 41.1 3 41 15
frames 3

signal on syntax name top
say 'start'
say a()
say 'caller goes on'
exit
top: say 'top'
::routine a
  say 'in a'
  signal on syntax name mine
  return .o~new~m + 1
mine: say 'a handles' condition('o')~code sigl
  return 'a done'
::class o
::method m
  say 'in m'
  x = 1 + 'a'
  say 'not reached'

start
in a
in m
a handles 41.1 10
a done
caller goes on
[cond.information.propagated]

The PROPAGATED entry of the object that the trap sees is 1 when the condition left the level that raised it, which is the case for a SYNTAX that reached a caller from a ::ROUTINE, from a method or from an internal routine, and after a RAISE with PROPAGATE. It is 0 for a condition that the level which raised it answers, a SYNTAX or a user condition alike.

signal on syntax name t
call r
t: say 'routine' condition('o')~propagated
signal on syntax name v
say .o~new~m
v: say 'method' condition('o')~propagated
signal on syntax name w
x = 1 % 0
w: say 'same level' condition('o')~propagated
exit
::routine r
  x = 1 % 0
::class o
::method m
  x = 1 % 0

routine 1
method 1
same level 0
[cond.information.propagated.internal]

An internal routine that switched the trap off passes the condition on in the same way, and the object that its caller sees has 1.

signal on syntax name v
call iq
v: say 'caller' condition('o')~propagated condition('o')~code
exit
iq: procedure
  signal off syntax
  x = 1 % 0

caller 1 42.3
[cond.information.propagate.only]

Only a SYNTAX condition is passed on. Any other condition is answered or ignored in the level that raised it, by the trap states that level has, so a trap that the level above set for itself does not see it. An internal routine has a copy of the trap states of its caller, as the scope rule says, so a trap that its caller switched on does answer a condition raised in the routine, and it does so in the routine, not in the caller. A HALT or NOMETHOD that nothing answers becomes a SYNTAX condition first, as the untrapped rule says, and that one is passed on.

signal on novalue name nv
address system
call on error name er
say 'main' r()
exit
nv: say 'nv in main' sigl
er: say 'er in main'; return
::routine r
  x = unsetvar
  'exit 3'
  return 'r done'

main r done

signal on novalue name nv
address system
call on error name er
say 'main' r()
say 'after'
exit
nv: say 'nv' sigl; return 'from nv'
er: say 'er' sigl rc; return
r:
  'exit 3'
  say 'back in r'
  x = unsetvar
  say 'not reached'
  return 'r done'

back in r

main from nv

SYNTAX

ANSI: 8.4.1, 8.4.2, 9.2.4; rexxref: Conditions and Condition Traps; Conditions and Condition Traps > Condition Information > Descriptive Strings; Conditions and Condition Traps > Condition Information > Condition Object; Conditions and Condition Traps > Condition Information > The Special Variable RC

SYNTAX is the condition of an error in the program as it runs. It is raised by a clause that cannot be carried out: arithmetic on a value that is no number, a call with a wrong argument, a routine that does not exist, and the other faults that the error numbers describe. It is also the condition that HALT and NOMETHOD become when nothing answers them, and it is never ignored: a trap answers it, or the program ends. This page specifies what raises SYNTAX, what identifies the error, which traps can answer it and what a program sees after one has. The numbers of the errors are listed on the pages of the clauses that raise them and in the error numbers chapter, and the traps page and the information page specify what any trap does and what it records.

What raises it

[cond.syntax.raise]

An error that is found while a clause runs raises SYNTAX at that clause. The clause ends at the point of the error, so that an assignment it would have made is not made, a command it would have sent is not sent, and output that it would have written after the point is not written, while the effects it had before the point, such as the output of a function that the expression called, stay. The error can come from an expression, from a builtin function or a method, from a call that finds no routine, from the text of an INTERPRET instruction, from a trap that has no label, and from a RAISE instruction that names SYNTAX, as the last two examples show. A fault in the text of an INTERPRET is found when that text is read as a whole, as the whole-text rule says, so none of its clauses has run then. An error found while the program itself is read is not a condition, as the reading rule says.

total = 10
signal on syntax name s
say 'before'
total = noisy() + 'x'
say 'not reached'
s: say 'total' total condition('c') condition('o')~code
::routine noisy
  say 'noisy ran'
  return 5

before
noisy ran
total 10 SYNTAX 41.1

say 'start'
call try "total = total + 'x'"
call try "total = 9 // 0"
call try "total = nosuchroutinexyz(1)"
call try "total = abs()"
call try "total = substr('abc', 0)"
call try "total = 3 +"
call try "say 'seen'; total = 4 * 'y'; say 'late'"
call try "say 'fine'"
exit
::routine try
  use arg text
  signal on syntax name e
  interpret text
  say 'no error:' text
  return
e: o = condition('o')
  say left(text, 28) o~code o~rc

start
total = total + 'x'          41.1 41
total = 9 // 0               42.3 42
total = nosuchroutinexyz(1)  43.1 43
total = abs()                40.3 40
total = substr('abc', 0)     93.924 93
total = 3 +                  35.1 35
seen
say 'seen'; total = 4 * 'y'; 41.1 41
fine
no error: say 'fine'

address system
signal on syntax name s
'echo sent' 1 + 'a'
say 'not reached'
s: say 'syntax' condition('o')~code

syntax 41.1

address system
signal on syntax name s
signal on error name nolabel
'exit 3'
say 'not reached'
s: say 'syntax' condition('o')~code sigl

syntax 16.1 4

signal on syntax name s
raise syntax 93.900 additional ('boom')
say 'not reached'
s: o = condition('o')
say o~code o~rc

What identifies the error

[cond.syntax.code]

An error has a number and a subcode. The number names the kind of error and the subcode the particular fault, so errors of one kind share an RC and differ in CODE, as the values rule says of the entries, and as the RC rule says of RC in the code of a trap. A program tells the errors apart with CODE, never with the text of the message, which is not specified.

call try "x = abs()"
call try "x = abs(1, 2)"
call try "x = left('abc', -2)"
call try "x = copies('ab', -2)"
exit
::routine try
  use arg text
  signal on syntax name e
  interpret text
e: o = condition('o')
  say left(text, 22) o~code o~rc,
      (o~rc == word(translate(o~code, ' ', '.'), 1)),
      (o~errortext == errortext(o~rc))

x = abs()              40.3 40 1 1
x = abs(1, 2)          40.4 40 1 1
x = left('abc', -2)    93.923 93 1 1
x = copies('ab', -2)   93.906 93 1 1

Which traps answer it

[cond.syntax.trap]

SYNTAX is answered by SIGNAL ON SYNTAX and by SIGNAL ON ANY, and by no CALL trap: CALL ON SYNTAX is itself an error, as the CALL ON rule says, and a CALL ON ANY trap does not see a SYNTAX condition, as the choice rule says for the conditions that CALL cannot trap. A SYNTAX that no SIGNAL trap answers ends the program as the untrapped rule says, whatever other traps were on, and the exit code is the one of that rule.

call on any name h
call on error name h
x = 1 + 'a'
say 'not reached'
h: say 'not called'

signal on any name a
x = 1 + 'a'
a: say 'ANY' condition('c') condition('o')~code

ANY SYNTAX 41.1

call on syntax name h
h: say 'not reached'

After the error

[cond.syntax.handler]

The SIGNAL trap that answers a SYNTAX condition is OFF in the code that it reaches, as the SIGNAL trap rule says, so an error that code makes before it enables the trap again is not answered by it. Unless another trap is on, that second error is untrapped and ends the program with the exit code of the second error. A handler that enables the trap again at its start can catch the errors that follow.

signal on syntax name s
say 'one'
x = 1 + 'a'
s: say 'caught' condition('o')~code condition('s')
y = 1 % 0
say 'not reached'

one
caught 41.1 OFF

signal on syntax name s
say 'one'
x = 1 + 'a'
s: say 'caught' condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name t
y = 2 // 0
say 'not reached'
t: say 'caught again' condition('o')~code

one
caught 41.1
caught again 42.3

ERROR and FAILURE

ANSI: 8.4.1; rexxref: Conditions and Condition Traps; Conditions and Condition Traps > Condition Information > Descriptive Strings; Conditions and Condition Traps > Action Taken when a Condition Is Trapped; Conditions and Condition Traps > Action Taken when a Condition Is Not Trapped

ERROR and FAILURE are the two conditions of a command. After an environment has run a command, or has failed to, the interpreter looks at the return code and raises one of them. ERROR means that the command ran and answered with a return code that is not zero, and FAILURE means that the command could not be run at all. A program that wants to react to a failing command traps one or both. This page specifies when each is raised, what the condition records, and the way a FAILURE that nothing answers reaches an ERROR trap. How a command is sent, and how it sets RC, is on the command page.

ERROR

[cond.error.raise]

A command that the environment has run, and whose return code is not zero, raises ERROR at the end of the clause that sent it, so that the command has run and RC holds its return code before the trap answers. A return code of zero raises nothing. The record of the condition has the command string as its description, and the RC entry of the condition object holds the return code, which is also the value of RC in the code of the trap. The POSITION entry and SIGL are the line of the command clause. A SIGNAL trap goes to its label after the command has run, and a CALL trap calls its routine and then goes on with the clause after the command. The status .RS of the command is 1 for a command that raised ERROR, as the status rule says.

address system
call on error name h
'exit 0'
say 'zero' rc .rs
'exit 3'
say 'after' rc .rs
cmd = 'exit' 2 + 5
cmd
signal on error name s
'echo ran; exit 4'
say 'not reached'
s: say 'signal' rc condition('c') condition('s') condition('i')
exit
h: o = arg(1)
  say 'handler' rc '['condition('d')']' o~rc o~condition sigl o~position
  return

zero 0 0
handler 3 [exit 3] 3 ERROR 5 5
after 3 1
handler 7 [exit 7] 7 ERROR 8 8
ran
signal 4 ERROR OFF SIGNAL
[cond.error.untrapped]

An ERROR that no trap answers is ignored, as the untrapped rule says, unless the package's ::OPTIONS makes it a SYNTAX condition: the clause is over, RC holds the return code, .RS is 1, and the program goes on. The traps that answer it are the ones of the code that sent the command, which for an internal routine are its copy of the traps of its caller, as the scope rule says. The condition is not passed on to the next level, as the propagation rule says, so a routine that has its trap off ignores the ERROR although its caller has the trap on.

address system
'exit 3'
say 'went on' rc .rs
call on error name caught
call fresh
say 'back' rc
call copy
say 'back again' rc
call quiet
say 'and again' rc
exit
caught: say 'caught' condition('c') rc sigl; return
copy:
  'exit 6'
  return
quiet:
  call off error
  'exit 7'
  say 'quiet went on' rc
  return
::routine fresh
  'exit 5'
  say 'fresh went on' rc

went on 3 1
fresh went on 5
back 3
caught ERROR 6 14
back again 6
quiet went on 7
and again 7

FAILURE

[cond.error.failure]

A command raises FAILURE, and not ERROR, when it could not be run. That is the case when the current environment does not exist, as the status rule says, whatever the command is. On a POSIX host it is also the case when the return code is 127, in the command environments system, command, sh, bash and path, whether the command was not found or exited with that code. Whether other environments of a host do the same is not specified. No other return code is a failure: 126 raises ERROR, and so does a negative one, which is not the failure of classic Rexx here. FAILURE, like ERROR, waits for the clause to end, and its record has the return code in RC, the command string as its description, and .RS is -1. A trap for ERROR does not answer a FAILURE as such, so it needs the fallback of the next rule, and a trap for FAILURE does not answer an ERROR.

address system
call on failure name f
signal on error name e
'exit 127'
say 'after' rc .rs
address nosuch
'exit 0'
say 'after env' rc .rs
address system
'exit 126'
say 'not reached'
f: say 'F' rc '['condition('d')']' condition('o')~rc sigl,
     condition('c')
  return
e: say 'E' rc .rs condition('c')

F 127 [exit 127] 127 4 FAILURE
after 127 -1
F 30 [exit 0] 30 7 FAILURE
after env 30 -1
E 126 1 ERROR

address bash
call on failure name f
call on error name e
'exit 127'
address sh 'exit 127'
address command 'exit 127'
address path 'nosuchprogram_interrexx_spec'
'kill -9 $$'
exit
f: say 'F' rc .rs; return
e: say 'E' rc .rs; return

F 127 -1
F 127 -1
F 127 -1
F 127 -1
E -9 1
[cond.error.fallback]

The FAILURE of a command that its own trap and the ANY trap do not answer is answered as an ERROR by the ERROR trap, when that is on, as the untrapped rule and the choice rule also say. The condition is then ERROR for everything that reads it: CONDITION('C') answers ERROR, and the record holds the same return code and command string. .RS stays -1, because the command failed. A FAILURE trap that was switched off explicitly does not prevent this. An ANY trap that is on answers the FAILURE under its own name, so the ERROR trap is reached only when neither of the two is on. When no trap of the three is on, the FAILURE is ignored and nothing else is raised. A FAILURE that the RAISE instruction raised does not fall back: when its own trap and the ANY trap do not answer it, it is ignored, and the ERROR trap does not see it, as the untrapped rule of RAISE says. The second example shows both.

address system
call on error name h
'exit 127'
call off failure
'exit 127'
call on failure name f
'exit 127'
say 'a' rc
call off error
call off failure
'exit 127'
say 'ignored' rc .rs
signal on any name any
signal on error name er
'exit 127'
any: say 'ANY' condition('c') rc
exit
er: say 'not reached'
h: say 'ERROR trap' condition('c') condition('i') condition('s') rc .rs
  return
f: say 'FAILURE trap' condition('c') rc; return

ERROR trap ERROR CALL DELAY 127 -1
ERROR trap ERROR CALL DELAY 127 -1
FAILURE trap FAILURE 127
a 127

HALT

ANSI: 8.4.1; rexxref: Conditions and Condition Traps; Conditions and Condition Traps > Condition Information > Descriptive Strings; Conditions and Condition Traps > Action Taken when a Condition Is Trapped; Conditions and Condition Traps > Action Taken when a Condition Is Not Trapped

HALT is the condition of a request to stop the program from outside its own flow of clauses. A user of a terminal asks for it with an interrupt key, and a host program asks for it through an interface, and the interpreter raises it between two clauses. A program that traps HALT can tidy up and end on its own terms. This page specifies what a program sees of HALT, the effect of each kind of trap and what happens when none is on. The interrupt keys, the signals and the interfaces are of the host and not specified, so every example on this page raises HALT with a RAISE instruction, which has its own page in the instructions chapter.

Raising it

[cond.halt.raise]

HALT is raised by a request that the host makes, and by a RAISE instruction that names it. Which host requests exist, and at which clause boundary one is noticed, is not specified. The condition has no description unless the RAISE instruction gave one with DESCRIPTION, so CONDITION('D') answers the null string otherwise. Its condition object has the entries that every condition has and POSITION, and neither RC, CODE nor ADDITIONAL, as the entries rule lists them. A HALT that the host raises is not passed on to the caller of the code that was running, as the propagation rule says for every condition but SYNTAX. Which level a RAISE instruction raises HALT in, the one that runs it or the caller of that one, is specified with that instruction. The examples whose trap answers HALT raise it with RETURN, which raises it in the caller.

call on halt name h
call plain
call with
exit
h: o = arg(1)
  say 'HALT' condition('c') '['condition('d')']' condition('i'),
      condition('s'),
      o~hasindex('POSITION') o~hasindex('RC') o~hasindex('CODE'),
      o~hasindex('ADDITIONAL')
  return
plain: raise halt return
with: raise halt description 'asked to stop' return

HALT HALT [] CALL DELAY 1 0 0 0
HALT HALT [asked to stop] CALL DELAY 1 0 0 0

The traps

[cond.halt.signal]

A SIGNAL trap for HALT ends the clause that was running and goes to the label, ending the open DO and SELECT constructs as the SIGNAL trap rule says. A program uses it to leave a loop that has no other end. The trap is OFF at the label, and a second HALT is untrapped unless the program enables the trap again.

signal on halt
n = 0
do forever
  n = n + 1
  call check n
end
halt: say 'stopped at' n '['condition('d')']' condition('c') condition('s')
::routine check
  use arg n
  if n = 3 then raise halt description 'enough' return

stopped at 3 [enough] HALT OFF

n = 0
signal on halt name h
call stop
say 'not reached'
h: n = n + 1
say 'halt' n
if n = 1 then signal on halt name h
call stop
say 'not reached either'
::routine stop
  raise halt return

halt 1
halt 2
[cond.halt.call]

A CALL trap for HALT lets the clause that was running finish, calls its routine, and goes on with the next clause when the routine returns. The state of the trap is DELAY in the routine, as the delay rule says. A program that wants to stop in the routine ends it with EXIT.

call on halt name h
say 'one'
call stop 'first'
say 'two'
call stop 'second'
say 'three'
exit
h: say 'handler' condition('d') condition('s')
  if condition('d') = 'second' then exit
  return
stop: d = arg(1)
  raise halt description (d) return

one
handler first DELAY
two
handler second DELAY

When nothing traps it

[cond.halt.untrapped]

A HALT that neither its own trap nor the ANY trap answers is not ignored. As the untrapped rule says, it becomes the SYNTAX condition 4.1 at the same clause, which a SYNTAX trap sees under the name SYNTAX, and the SYNTAX rule says what follows when none answers. That condition has CODE 4.1, RC 4 and no description, whatever description the RAISE instruction gave.

say 'before'
raise halt
say 'not reached'

before

signal on syntax name s
raise halt description 'ignored text'
s: o = condition('o')
say condition('c') o~code o~rc '['condition('d')']'

SYNTAX 4.1 4 []

NOVALUE

ANSI: 8.4.1; rexxref: Conditions and Condition Traps; Conditions and Condition Traps > Condition Information > Descriptive Strings; Conditions and Condition Traps > Action Taken when a Condition Is Trapped

NOVALUE is the condition of reading a variable that has no value. A variable that was never assigned, or that was dropped, is not an error in Rexx: its symbol then stands for its own name, as the variable rule says. A program that wants to find such reads traps the condition, which turns a misspelled variable into a stop with the name in hand. This page specifies which uses of a variable raise NOVALUE, which do not, what the description holds, and which traps can answer it. The ::OPTIONS directive can make an untrapped NOVALUE into an error, and its rule specifies that.

When it is raised

[cond.novalue.raise]

NOVALUE is raised when the value of a simple or compound variable symbol is needed and the variable has no value. That is so for a term of an expression wherever an expression is evaluated, among them the right side of an assignment, the condition of an IF or a WHEN, the bounds of a DO, an argument of a call and the value of a NUMERIC setting; for the variable that PARSE VAR reads; for a pattern in parentheses in a template; for a variable that names the override class of a message term; and for a variable that names a list in parentheses in DROP, in EXPOSE or in PROCEDURE EXPOSE. The clause ends at that point, so an assignment it would have made is not made. The stem symbol alone, as in st., is never without a value, as the stem rule says, so reading it raises nothing. A variable that is only assigned, dropped or named in an EXPOSE list, with no parentheses, is not read. EXPOSE must be the first instruction of a method, so no trap can precede it, and the ::OPTIONS example below makes the read visible with NOVALUE SYNTAX, which turns the untrapped condition into an error. An environment symbol such as .foo that finds no object is not a variable, so it raises nothing and stands for its own name in upper case. A symbol in the tail of a compound symbol raises nothing, and stays as its own name in the derived name. SYMBOL and VALUE do not raise it, as the function rules say.

do k = 1 to 16
  call probe k
end
exit
::routine probe
  use arg k
  signal on novalue name raised
  select
    when k = 1 then x = 1 + unset1
    when k = 2 then if unset2 = 3 then nop
    when k = 3 then do i = unset3 to 2; end
    when k = 4 then call length unset4
    when k = 5 then numeric digits unset5
    when k = 6 then parse value 'a b' with (unset6) w1 w2
    when k = 7 then parse var unset7 w1 w2
    when k = 8 then say .probe~new~go
    when k = 9 then say st.
    when k = 10 then say symbol('unset10') value('unset10')
    when k = 11 then drop unset11
    when k = 12 then unset12 = 5
    when k = 13 then say st.1
    when k = 14 then call hasexpose
    when k = 15 then drop (unset15)
    when k = 16 then say .unsetenv
  end
  say k 'no NOVALUE'
  return
raised: say k 'NOVALUE' condition('d')
  return
hasexpose: procedure expose unset15
  return
::class probe
::method go
  signal on novalue name q
  return 'abc'~length:unset16()
  q: return 'method' condition('d')

1 NOVALUE UNSET1
2 NOVALUE UNSET2
3 NOVALUE UNSET3
4 NOVALUE UNSET4
5 NOVALUE UNSET5
6 NOVALUE UNSET6
7 NOVALUE UNSET7
method UNSET16
8 no NOVALUE
ST.
9 no NOVALUE
LIT UNSET10
10 no NOVALUE
11 no NOVALUE
12 no NOVALUE
13 NOVALUE ST.1
14 no NOVALUE
15 NOVALUE UNSET15
.UNSETENV
16 no NOVALUE

signal on novalue name n
call keep
say 'went on'
exit
n: say 'novalue' condition('d')
  exit
keep: procedure expose (names)
  return

novalue NAMES

say .store~new~fill
::options novalue syntax
::class store
::method fill
  expose (names)
  return 'filled'
[cond.novalue.description]

The description of a NOVALUE condition is the name of the variable that was read, in upper case. For a compound symbol it is the derived name, in which a tail symbol that has a value is replaced by it and one that has none stays as its own name, as the tail rule says. CONDITION('D') and the DESCRIPTION entry answer it, and the condition has no ADDITIONAL and no RC. A tail symbol that has no value is not a NOVALUE condition of its own, so the one condition names the compound variable.

signal on novalue name n
i = 3
x = abc
n: say condition('c') '['condition('d')']' sigl
signal on novalue name n2
x = st.i
n2: say '['condition('d')']'
signal on novalue name n3
x = st.i.j
n3: say '['condition('d')']'
signal on novalue name n4
key = 'a b'
x = stem.key
n4: say '['condition('d')']'
o = condition('o')
say o~hasindex('ADDITIONAL') o~hasindex('RC') o~description

NOVALUE [ABC] 3
[ST.3]
[ST.3.J]
[STEM.a b]
0 0 STEM.a b

Which traps answer it

[cond.novalue.trap]

NOVALUE is answered by SIGNAL ON NOVALUE and by SIGNAL ON ANY, and by no CALL trap: CALL ON NOVALUE is an error, as the CALL ON rule says, and a CALL ON ANY trap does not see it, as the choice rule says. With the trap OFF, and no ANY trap on, the symbol has its own name as value and the clause goes on, as the untrapped rule says. A SIGNAL trap ends the clause, so the value that the clause would have computed is not used. NOVALUE is not passed on, as the propagation rule says. The traps that answer it are the ones of the code that read the variable, which for an internal routine are its copy of the traps of its caller, as the scope rule says. A ::ROUTINE starts with every trap OFF, and an internal routine that switches the trap off is not answered either.

x = 'before'
call on any name h
y = abc
say 'ignored' y
signal on novalue name n
x = abc
say 'not reached'
n: say 'trapped' x condition('c')
signal on any name a
x = abd
a: say 'ANY' condition('c') condition('d')
call r
say 'back'
exit
h: say 'not called'
  return
::routine r
  say 'in r' abe

ignored ABC
trapped before NOVALUE
ANY NOVALUE ABD
in r ABE
back

signal on novalue name h
call copy
say 'back'
call quiet
say 'back again'
exit
h: say 'trap' condition('d') sigl
  return
copy:
  x = abe
  return
quiet:
  signal off novalue
  x = abf
  say 'quiet went on' x
  return

trap ABE 10
back
quiet went on ABF
back again

call on novalue name h

NOSTRING

rexxref: Conditions and Condition Traps; Conditions and Condition Traps > Condition Information > Descriptive Strings; Conditions and Condition Traps > Condition Information > Additional Object Information; Conditions and Condition Traps > Action Taken when a Condition Is Trapped

Deviations: D30, D77

NOSTRING is the condition of needing the string value of an object that does not provide one. Most values a program handles are strings or answer as strings, and the interpreter converts them without notice. An object of a class that has no way to give a string is different: Rexx can still print it or join it to text, but it first tells the program, so that a program that trusts its values to be text can stop at the point where one is not. This page specifies which uses of an object raise NOSTRING, what the condition holds, which traps answer it and what a clause does when nothing does.

When it is raised

[cond.nostring.raise]

NOSTRING is raised when a clause needs the string value of an object that is not a string, and request with the argument STRING, sent to the object, answers no string: an object with no MAKESTRING method does so, and so does one whose MAKESTRING or own request answers .nil or another object that is not a string, whatever its STRING method answers. An object whose request is private, or whose MAKESTRING or STRING method is private and would be sent, raises no NOSTRING at the uses listed below: the message is refused, as the conventions say for builtin arguments, and the clause raises SYNTAX 97.2. A string, a number and an instance of a subclass of String never raise it, and neither does an object whose request answers a string, as Object does with the answer of MAKESTRING. The uses that raise it include the three concatenation operators (the explicit ||, the abuttal and the blank), the operand of SAY, the source of PARSE VALUE, the text that INTERPRET runs, an operand of an arithmetic or comparison operator whose left operand is a string, the tail of a compound variable, and an argument of a builtin function that is to be a string, except for the builtins that link the native call rule, which raise SYNTAX 88.909 for it. Sending the message STRING to the object raises nothing, because the object is then not converted. Which other positions convert, such as the arguments of method calls, is not specified. What a builtin does with such an argument when no trap answers is the object rule of the conventions. The table below has one row for each object and one column for each of six uses, N where NOSTRING is raised and - where it is not.

objs = .array~of(.object~new, .made~new, .string.sub~new('xy'), 42)
say 'cols: || abuttal blank ~string parse upper'
do k = 1 to 4
  line = k
  do j = 1 to 6
    line = line probe(j, objs[k])
  end
  say line
end
exit
::routine probe
  use arg j, o
  signal on nostring name n
  select
    when j = 1 then x = 'a' || o
    when j = 2 then x = 'a'o
    when j = 3 then x = 'a' o
    when j = 4 then x = o~string~length
    when j = 5 then parse value o with x .
    when j = 6 then x = upper(o)
  end
  return '-'
n: return 'N'
::class made
::method makestring
  return 'made'
::class string.sub subclass string

cols: || abuttal blank ~string parse upper
1 N N N - N N
2 - - - - - -
3 - - - - - -
4 - - - - - -

The next program tries the other positions and the private methods. A comparison or an arithmetic operator with the object on its left is a message to the object, so the operands here stand to the right of a string.

do j = 1 to 8
  say probe(j)
end
exit
::routine probe
  use arg j
  signal on syntax name s
  signal on nostring name n
  select
    when j = 1 then x = 1 + .object~new
    when j = 2 then x = ('a' = .object~new)
    when j = 3 then do; t = .object~new; a.t = 5; end
    when j = 4 then x = 'a' || .ps~new
    when j = 5 then x = 'a' || .pm~new
    when j = 6 then x = filespec('n', .object~new)
    when j = 7 then parse value .ps~new with x .
    when j = 8 then do; t = .pm~new; a.t = 5; end
  end
  return j 'nothing'
n: return j 'NOSTRING'
s: return j 'SYNTAX' condition('o')~code
::class ps
::method string private
  return 'x'
::class pm
::method makestring private
  return 'x'

The last program gives objects their own request: one that answers .nil, one that answers a string and one that answers another object. The columns are ||, the length of ~string, and upper; N and the description show a raised NOSTRING.

objs = .array~of(.rn~new, .rs~new, .ro~new)
do k = 1 to 3
  line = k
  do j = 1 to 3
    line = line probe(j, objs[k])
  end
  say line
end
exit
::routine probe
  use arg j, o
  signal on nostring name n
  select
    when j = 1 then x = 'a' || o
    when j = 2 then x = o~string~length
    when j = 3 then x = upper(o)
  end
  return '-'

[cond.nostring.information]

The description of a NOSTRING condition is the text that the STRING method of the object answers when that is a string, and its ADDITIONAL entry is the object. When the answer is an object that is not a string but has a string value, such as an array, the description is that value. When the answer has no string value, Deviation 30 applies. The condition object has the entries that every condition has, ADDITIONAL and POSITION, and neither RC nor CODE, as the entries rule lists them. The text is the one that the object would have as its string value when no trap answers, as the untrapped rule says.

signal on nostring name n
say 'start'
say .object~new
say 'not reached'
n: say 'say:' condition('c') '['condition('d')']' sigl
signal on nostring name n2
interpret .object~new
n2: say 'interpret:' condition('c') '['condition('d')']'
o = condition('o')
say o~hasindex('ADDITIONAL') o~hasindex('POSITION') o~hasindex('CODE'),
    o~hasindex('RC') o~additional~class
signal on nostring name n3
x = 'a' || .plain~new
n3: say 'plain:' '['condition('d')']'
signal on nostring name n4
x = 'a' || .told~new
n4: say 'told:' '['condition('d')']' condition('o')~additional~class
signal on nostring name n5
x = 'a' || .badmake~new
n5: say 'badmake:' '['condition('d')']' condition('o')~additional~class
signal on nostring name n6
x = 'a' || .arr~new
n6: say 'arr:' '['condition('d')']' condition('o')~additional~class
::class plain
::class told
::method string
  return 'told text'
::class badmake
::method makestring
  return .nil
::method string
  return 'bad text'
::class arr
::method string
  return .array~of('arr text')

Which traps answer it

[cond.nostring.trap]

NOSTRING is answered by SIGNAL ON NOSTRING and by SIGNAL ON ANY, and by no CALL trap: CALL ON NOSTRING is SYNTAX 25.1, as the CALL rule says, and a CALL ON ANY trap does not see it, as the choice rule says. A SIGNAL trap ends the clause that needed the string, so the clause makes none of its changes, and sets SIGL to the line of that clause. The condition is raised in the code that needed the string and goes no further, so the trap of a caller does not answer a NOSTRING that a routine raised, as the propagation rule says.

signal on syntax name s
interpret 'call on nostring name h'
s: say condition('c') condition('o')~code
call on any name h
x = 'kept'
signal on nostring name n
x = 'a' || .object~new
say 'not reached'
n: say 'trapped' x condition('c') sigl
signal on any name a
y = 'a' || .object~new
a: say 'ANY' condition('c') '['y']'
signal on nostring name main
call r
say 'back from r'
exit
main: say 'main trap'
h: say 'not called'
  return
::routine r
  z = 'a' || .object~new
  say 'in r' z

trapped kept NOSTRING 7
ANY NOSTRING [Y]
in r aan Object
back from r

When nothing traps it

[cond.nostring.untrapped]

A NOSTRING that neither its own trap nor the ANY trap answers is ignored, as the untrapped rule says: the clause goes on and uses as the string value of the object the text that its STRING method answers when that is a string, and the string value of that answer when it is another object that has one, such as an array. Deviation 30 applies when the answer has none. The ::OPTIONS directive can turn an untrapped NOSTRING into a SYNTAX condition, and its rule specifies that.

say 'a' || .plain~new
say 'b' || .told~new
say .badmake~new
say length(.told~new) 'c' .told~new
say 'd' || .arr~new

::class told
::method string
  return 'told text'
::class badmake
::method makestring
  return .nil
::method string
  return 'bad text'

  return .array~of('arr text')

Deviations

[cond.nostring.deviation.77]

The string value of a stem is its default value's, and NOSTRING is raised, with the default's description, only when the default has no string value. A stem that has no default is a string, its own name, and one with a string default is that string. ooRexx raises NOSTRING for every stem in a position that needs a string, with the name of the stem as description. Parsing states the same for a stem that is the source of PARSE.

signal on nostring name n
t.1 = 'element'
say 'a' || t.
u. = 'dflt'
say 'b' || u.
v. = .plain~new
say 'c' || v.
say 'not reached'
n: say 'NOSTRING' '['condition('d')']' condition('o')~additional~class
::class plain

aT.
bdflt
NOSTRING [a PLAIN] The Stem class
[cond.nostring.deviation.30]

When the STRING method of an object answers an object with no string value, interrexx gives ooRexx's answer wherever that is defined, and elsewhere ends the program with exit code 120 after raising NOSTRING if it is trapped. For a NOSTRING raised for such an object, the description is not specified. ooRexx reads .nil as a string there, with garbage results or a crash. The conventions state it for builtin arguments.

signal on nostring name n
say 'x' .weird~new
n: say 'trapped' condition('c') condition('o')~additional~class
x = 'a' || .weird~new
say 'not reached'
::class weird
::method string
  return .directory~new

trapped NOSTRING The WEIRD class

NOMETHOD

rexxref: Conditions and Condition Traps; Conditions and Condition Traps > Condition Information > Descriptive Strings; Conditions and Condition Traps > Condition Information > Additional Object Information; Conditions and Condition Traps > Action Taken when a Condition Is Trapped

NOMETHOD is the condition of a message that reaches an object with nothing to run for it. Sending a message is the way Rexx objects are used, and a message whose name is misspelled or meant for another class has no method to find. A program traps NOMETHOD to learn which message was lost and to which object it went. This page specifies when the condition is raised, what it holds, which traps answer it and what becomes of it when none does.

When it is raised

[cond.nomethod.raise]

NOMETHOD is raised when a message is sent to an object, the object has no method of that name that the sender may run, and the object has no UNKNOWN method that takes the message instead. A private method sent from code that may not run it, such as a routine or a method of an unrelated class, counts as missing: the message goes to UNKNOWN when the object has one and otherwise raises NOMETHOD with the name of the method. The access rule says which senders may run a private method, among them methods of the class, of its subclasses and of their instances, and class methods. The message may be written with ~, with ~~, or with a scope override such as ~name:super, as the information rule shows, and it may be sent by the SEND method of an object. The arguments of the message are evaluated before the lookup, so the clause has evaluated them when the condition is raised. The condition is raised in the code that sent the message, and the clause ends there when a SIGNAL trap answers. The exception is a message that FORWARD sends without CONTINUE, which the FORWARD rule raises in the caller of the forwarding method. A class with an UNKNOWN method raises nothing, because that method receives the message. The UNKNOWN method and the way a class defines methods belong to the classes chapter.

do k = 1 to 5
  call probe k
end
exit
::routine probe
  use arg k
  signal on nomethod name n
  select
    when k = 1 then x = .a~new~foo
    when k = 2 then x = .a~new~nothere(arg1())
    when k = 3 then x = 'abc'~~nothere
    when k = 4 then x = .a~new~send('Not Here')
    when k = 5 then x = .b~new~nothere
  end
  say k 'no condition'
  return
n: say k 'NOMETHOD' condition('d')
  return
::routine arg1
  say 'argument evaluated'
  return 1
::class a
::method foo
  return 1
::class b
::method unknown
  return 'unknown took it'

1 no condition
argument evaluated
2 NOMETHOD NOTHERE
3 NOMETHOD NOTHERE
4 NOMETHOD NOT HERE
5 no condition
[cond.nomethod.information]

The description of a NOMETHOD condition is the name of the message in upper case, and its ADDITIONAL entry is the object that received the message. The condition object has the entries that every condition has, ADDITIONAL and POSITION, and neither RC nor CODE, as the entries rule lists them. For a message with a scope override the receiver is the object that the message was sent to, not its class.

signal on nomethod name n
x = 'abc'~lost(1, 2)
n: o = condition('o')
say condition('c') '['condition('d')']' condition('i') sigl condition('s')
say o~hasindex('ADDITIONAL') o~hasindex('POSITION') o~hasindex('CODE'),
    o~hasindex('RC') '['o~additional']'
say .a~new~go
signal on nomethod name n3
x = .a~new~'Mixed case'
n3: say '['condition('d')']' condition('o')~additional~class
::class a
::method go
  signal on nomethod name inner
  x = self~missing:super
  inner: say 'in go' '['condition('d')']' condition('o')~additional~class
  return 1

[MIXED CASE] The A class

Which traps answer it

[cond.nomethod.trap]

NOMETHOD is answered by SIGNAL ON NOMETHOD and by SIGNAL ON ANY, and by no CALL trap: CALL ON NOMETHOD is SYNTAX 25.1, as the CALL rule says, and a CALL ON ANY trap does not see it, as the choice rule says. The trap is OFF at its label, as the SIGNAL trap rule says, so a second lost message is untrapped until the program enables the trap again.

signal on syntax name s
interpret 'call on nomethod name h'
s: say condition('c') condition('o')~code
signal on any name a
x = .nil~nothere
a: say 'ANY' condition('c') condition('d') condition('s')
signal on nomethod name n
x = .nil~first
n: say 'first' condition('d') condition('s')
signal on syntax name s2
x = .nil~second
s2: say 'second' condition('c') condition('o')~code
exit
h: say 'not called'
  return

SYNTAX 25.1
ANY NOMETHOD NOTHERE OFF
first FIRST OFF
second SYNTAX 97.1

When nothing traps it

[cond.nomethod.untrapped]

A NOMETHOD that neither its own trap nor the ANY trap answers is not ignored. It becomes the condition SYNTAX 97.1 raised at the same clause, as the untrapped rule says, and a SYNTAX trap answers it under the name SYNTAX. A message to a private method that the sender may not run becomes SYNTAX 97.2 instead. Because that is a SYNTAX condition, it leaves the code that sent the message and goes on to its caller, as the propagation rule says. So a NOMETHOD trap in the caller of a method does not answer a message that the method lost, and a SYNTAX trap in the caller does. Without a trap the program ends as the SYNTAX rule says.

signal on nomethod name nm
signal on syntax name sy
.a~new~go
say 'not reached'
nm: say 'NOMETHOD in main' condition('d')
exit
sy: o = condition('o')
say 'SYNTAX in main' o~code o~rc '['condition('d')']'
::class a
::method go
  x = self~nothere
  say 'not reached'

SYNTAX in main 97.1 97 []

signal on syntax name s
x = .a~new~hidden
say 'not reached'
s: say condition('c') condition('o')~code
say 'before'
x = .a~new~hidden
say 'not reached'
::class a
::method hidden private
  return 'ran'

SYNTAX 97.2
before

say 'before'
x = 'abc'~nothere
say 'not reached'

before

NOTREADY

ANSI: 8.4.1; rexxref: Conditions and Condition Traps; Conditions and Condition Traps > Condition Information > Descriptive Strings; Conditions and Condition Traps > Condition Information > Additional Object Information; Conditions and Condition Traps > Action Taken when a Condition Is Trapped

NOTREADY is the condition of a stream operation that could not do what it was asked to. A read that reaches the end of the data, a name that cannot be opened and a write that fails all leave the program with an answer that is shorter than it expected, and the condition is how a program finds out without testing every call. Unlike an error it does not stop anything: a stream call answers as its page says whether or not a trap exists. The builtin pages and the NOTREADY rule of the builtins say which calls raise it and when, and this page specifies what the condition holds, which traps answer it and how far it reaches.

What it holds

[cond.notready.information]

The description of a NOTREADY condition is the name of the stream, spelled as the stream rule says, and its ADDITIONAL entry is the stream object, whose string value is that name. The condition object has the entries that every condition has and ADDITIONAL, and no POSITION, RC or CODE, as the entries rule lists them. The whole clause that held the call has finished by the time a CALL trap runs, as the CALL trap rule says.

f = 'spec-notready-info.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
call lineout f, 'one'
call lineout f
say linein(f)
call on notready name h
x = linein(f)
say 'x is [' || x || ']'
call sysfiledelete f
exit
h: o = condition('o')
  say condition('c') '[' || condition('d') || ']' condition('i') sigl,
      condition('s')
  say o~hasindex('ADDITIONAL') o~hasindex('POSITION') o~hasindex('CODE'),
      o~hasindex('RC') '[' || o~additional || ']'
  return

one
NOTREADY [spec-notready-info.tmp] CALL 7 DELAY
1 0 0 0 [spec-notready-info.tmp]
x is []

Which traps answer it

[cond.notready.call]

NOTREADY is answered by CALL ON NOTREADY, by SIGNAL ON NOTREADY and by the ANY traps of both kinds. A CALL trap lets the stream call finish, and the clause that held the call finishes too. The routine is called before the next clause, with the state DELAY in the routine and SIGL the line of that clause, as the CALL trap rule says. The clause has then finished, so the routine sees its assignment already made, and the clause is not resumed after the routine.

f = 'spec-notready-call.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
call lineout f, 'only line'
call lineout f
call on notready name h
a = linein(f)
b = 'old'
b = linein(f) || mark('second operand')
say 'a=' || a 'b=' || b
call off notready
call on any name h2
c = linein(f)
say 'c=' || c
call sysfiledelete f
exit
mark: say 'evaluating' arg(1)
  return '+'
h: say 'h' sigl condition('c') condition('s') 'b=[' || b || ']'
  return
h2: say 'h2' sigl condition('c')
  return

evaluating second operand
h 8 NOTREADY DELAY b=[+]
a=only line b=+
h2 12 NOTREADY
c=
[cond.notready.signal]

A SIGNAL trap for NOTREADY ends the clause that made the stream call and goes to the label, ending the open DO and SELECT constructs as the SIGNAL trap rule says, so the clause makes none of its assignments. SIGL is the line of that clause and the trap is OFF at the label. A SIGNAL trap for ANY answers it too, and the name stays NOTREADY.

f = 'spec-notready-sig.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
call lineout f, 'only line'
call lineout f
x = 'kept'
signal on notready name n
x = linein(f)
x = linein(f)
say 'not reached'
n: say 'trapped' x condition('c') sigl condition('s')
signal on any name a
x = linein(f)
a: say 'ANY' condition('c') sigl
call sysfiledelete f

trapped only line NOTREADY 8 OFF
ANY NOTREADY 12

How far it reaches

[cond.notready.scope]

NOTREADY is raised in the code that made the stream call, and goes no further. A trap in the caller of a routine does not answer a NOTREADY that a stream call in the routine raised, as the propagation rule says, and the routine's own traps do.

f = 'spec-notready-scope.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
call lineout f, 'only line'
call lineout f
call on notready name h
call rd
say 'back from rd'
x = linein(f)
say 'main read done'
call sysfiledelete f
exit
h: say 'main handler' sigl '[' || condition('d') || ']'
  return
::routine rd
  call on notready name inner
  x = linein('spec-notready-scope.tmp')
  y = linein('spec-notready-scope.tmp')
  say 'rd done'
  return
inner: say 'rd handler' sigl
  return

rd handler 17
rd done
back from rd
main handler 8 [spec-notready-scope.tmp]
main read done

When nothing traps it

[cond.notready.untrapped]

A NOTREADY that neither its own trap nor the ANY trap answers is ignored, as the untrapped rule says, and the stream call answers as its page says. The ::OPTIONS directive can turn an untrapped NOTREADY into a SYNTAX condition, and its rule specifies that.

f = 'spec-notready-none.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
call lineout f, 'only line'
call lineout f
say linein(f) '[' || linein(f) || ']' '[' || linein(f) || ']'
say lines(f)
call sysfiledelete f

only line [] []
0

LOSTDIGITS

ANSI: 8.4.1; rexxref: Conditions and Condition Traps; Conditions and Condition Traps > Condition Information > Descriptive Strings; Conditions and Condition Traps > Condition Information > Additional Object Information; Conditions and Condition Traps > Action Taken when a Condition Is Trapped

LOSTDIGITS is the condition of a number that has more digits than the arithmetic can keep. NUMERIC DIGITS sets how many digits an operation works with, and an operand written with more of them is cut before the operation starts, so the program's result is not the one its text suggests. Nothing is wrong enough to stop the program, and the condition is how a program that cares about exact input finds out. The rules for which operands raise it, and how the cut is made, belong to the chapter on numbers: the arithmetic rule and the comparison rule. This page specifies what the condition holds, which traps answer it and how far it reaches.

What it holds

[cond.lostdigits.information]

The description of a LOSTDIGITS condition is the operand that has too many digits, and the condition is raised in the clause that holds the operation. The condition object has the entries that every condition has and POSITION, and none of ADDITIONAL, RC and CODE, as the entries rule lists them. The form in which the operand is written in the description is the numbers chapter's to specify, in the arithmetic deviation and in the comparison rule.

numeric digits 4
signal on lostdigits name n
y = 98765 * 2
say 'not reached'
n: o = condition('o')
say condition('c') '['condition('d')']' condition('i') sigl condition('s')
say o~hasindex('POSITION') o~hasindex('ADDITIONAL') o~hasindex('CODE'),
    o~hasindex('RC')
signal on lostdigits name n2
say 1234 < 98765
n2: say 'comparison' '['condition('d')']'

LOSTDIGITS [98765] SIGNAL 3 OFF
1 0 0 0
comparison [98765]

Which traps answer it

[cond.lostdigits.trap]

LOSTDIGITS is answered by SIGNAL ON LOSTDIGITS and by SIGNAL ON ANY, and by no CALL trap: CALL ON LOSTDIGITS is SYNTAX 25.1, as the CALL rule says, and a CALL ON ANY trap does not see it, as the choice rule says. A SIGNAL trap ends the clause that held the operation, so the clause assigns nothing. Whether a LOSTDIGITS that a trap is to answer comes before the SYNTAX error that the same operation would raise is the arithmetic chapter's to specify.

numeric digits 4
call on any name h
x = 123456 + 1
say 'call any did not answer:' x
signal on lostdigits name n
y = 98765 * 2
say 'not reached'
n: say condition('c') '['y']'
numeric digits 5
signal on any name a
z = 12345678 - 1
a: say 'ANY' condition('c') condition('d')
signal on syntax name s
interpret 'call on lostdigits name h'
s: say condition('c') condition('o')~code
exit
h: say 'not called'
  return

call any did not answer: 1.235E+5
LOSTDIGITS [Y]
ANY LOSTDIGITS 12345678
SYNTAX 25.1

How far it reaches

[cond.lostdigits.scope]

LOSTDIGITS is raised in the code that holds the operation, which counts the digits against its own NUMERIC DIGITS, and goes no further. A trap in the caller does not answer a LOSTDIGITS that a routine raised, as the propagation rule says, and the routine's own traps do. When no trap answers, the operation goes on with the digits it has, as the arithmetic rule says, unless the package's ::OPTIONS makes it a SYNTAX condition.

signal on lostdigits name main
call r
say 'back from r'
exit
main: say 'main trap' condition('d')
::routine r
  numeric digits 3
  say 'r' 1234 + 0
  signal on lostdigits name mine
  say 'not reached' 5678 + 0
  mine: say 'r trap' condition('d')
  return

r 1.23E+3
r trap 5678
back from r

USER conditions

rexxref: Conditions and Condition Traps; Conditions and Condition Traps > Condition Information > Descriptive Strings; Conditions and Condition Traps > Condition Information > Additional Object Information; Conditions and Condition Traps > Action Taken when a Condition Is Trapped

A user condition is a condition that only the program raises. The interpreter never raises one, so a program can use it for its own events, such as a missing record or a parse that found nothing, and give the code that deals with it the same trap machinery that the built-in conditions have. Every user condition has a name that the program chooses, and the name makes the condition. This page specifies the names, the traps that answer a user condition and what it holds. A user condition is raised with the RAISE instruction, whose page is RAISE, and the examples here raise them with raise user name.

The name

[cond.user.name]

A user condition is raised by RAISE USER and a name, and by nothing else. The name is a symbol that is read as a constant in upper case, whatever it holds as a variable and whatever the spelling of its tail: foo.bar is the name FOO.BAR and does not take the value of bar. The condition is called USER and the name, joined by one blank, and CONDITION('C') answers that. Names are compared as text after the change to upper case, so Foo and FOO are one condition, and the numbers 1.5 and 1.50 are two. A user condition is a condition of its own, so it is not the built-in condition that has the same name, as the names rule says.

bar = 'x'
call on user foo.bar name h
call on user 1.50 name h
call on user Mixed name h
call on any name other
call r1
call r2
call r3
call r4
exit
r1: raise user Foo.Bar return
r2: raise user 1.50 return
r3: raise user 1.5 return
r4: raise user MIXED return
h: say 'h' condition('c') condition('s'); return
other: say 'other' condition('c'); return

h USER FOO.BAR DELAY
h USER 1.50 DELAY
other USER 1.5
h USER MIXED DELAY

Which traps answer it

[cond.user.trap]

A user condition is answered by the trap of its own name, which CALL ON USER and SIGNAL ON USER set, and otherwise by the ANY trap, as the choice rule says. Both kinds of instruction accept it, and the default routine or label of the trap is the name alone, FOO for user foo. A trap for one name does not answer another name, and a trap for ERROR does not answer USER ERROR, as the names rule says. The effects of the trap are those of CALL traps and SIGNAL traps.

call on user alpha
call on user beta name b
signal on error name e
signal on user gamma
call r1
call r2
call r3
call r4
exit
r1: raise user alpha return
r2: raise user beta return
r3: raise user error return
r4: raise user gamma return
alpha: say 'alpha' condition('c') condition('s'); return
b: say 'b' condition('c'); return
e: say 'error trap'
gamma: say 'gamma' condition('c') condition('s')

alpha USER ALPHA DELAY
b USER BETA
gamma USER GAMMA OFF

What it holds

[cond.user.information]

The description of a user condition is the text of the DESCRIPTION option of the RAISE instruction that raised it, or the null string when the instruction gave none. Its ADDITIONAL entry is the value of the ADDITIONAL option, or the array of the ARRAY option, and is present exactly when the instruction gave one of them. The condition object has the entries that every condition has and POSITION, and neither RC nor CODE, as the entries rule lists them.

call on user foo name h
call r1
call r2
call r3
call r4
exit
r1: raise user foo return
r2: raise user foo description 'why' return
r3: raise user foo description 'why' additional ('more') return
r4: raise user foo array ('x', 'y') return
h: o = condition('o')
  say '[' || condition('d') || ']' o~hasindex('ADDITIONAL'),
      o~hasindex('POSITION') o~hasindex('RC') o~hasindex('CODE'),
      o~hasindex('DESCRIPTION') o~description~class
  if o~hasindex('ADDITIONAL') then say '  ' o~additional~class
  return

[] 0 1 0 0 1 The String class
[why] 0 1 0 0 1 The String class
[why] 1 1 0 0 1 The String class
   The String class
[] 1 1 0 0 1 The String class
   The Array class

When nothing traps it

[cond.user.untrapped]

A user condition that neither its own trap nor the ANY trap answers is ignored, as the untrapped rule says, and the program goes on as the RAISE instruction specifies. It never becomes a SYNTAX condition.

say 'start'
call r
say 'back'
signal on syntax name s
call r
say 'still going'
exit
r: raise user lost description 'nobody listens' return
s: say 'not reached'

start
back
still going

Error numbers

ANSI: 8.2.1, 8.4, 8.4.1; rexxref: Conditions and Condition Traps > Condition Information > The Special Variable RC; Error Numbers and Messages

Every fault that raises the SYNTAX condition has an error number. The number says what kind of fault it is, so that a program can answer a kind of error without reading a message. This page specifies how a number is built, what a program sees of it, and what each of the numbers means. It does not list the subcodes: the pages that raise an error name its subcode, and the texts of the messages are not specified, as the error rule of the conventions says. The numbers run from 3 to 99, and the numbers in that range that name no kind of fault are the ones that ERRORTEXT answers with the null string, as its rule lists them.

How a number is built

[cond.errors.scheme]

An error number has two parts, a major number and a subcode written after a point without leading zeros: 40.3, 93.924. How a trap reads the two parts, and why a program tells faults apart by the whole code, is the business of the code rule; this page owns what the major numbers mean. SIGL is set as the SIGL rule says. An error that no SIGNAL trap answers ends the program with the exit code 256 minus the major number, as the untrapped rule says, and the subcode does not enter it. The error of a fault in the text that is read before the program runs is no condition at all, as the reading rule says.

rc = 'unset'
signal on syntax name e
say 'one'
x = 1 + 'a'
e: say condition('o')~code rc sigl
say word(translate(condition('o')~code, ' ', '.'), 1) == rc

one
41.1 41 4
1
[cond.errors.subcodes]

The subcodes of an error number are named on the pages of the clauses and functions that raise it, in the rule that names the fault. This page names a subcode only to show a kind of error.

call try 'x = left("abc", -2)'
call try 'x = copies("ab", -2)'
call try 'x = d2c(-1)'
call try 'x = "abc"~substr(0)'
exit
try:
  signal on syntax name e
  interpret arg(1)
e: o = condition('o')
  say left(arg(1), 26) o~code o~rc
  return

x = left("abc", -2)        93.923 93
x = copies("ab", -2)       93.906 93
x = d2c(-1)                93.927 93
x = "abc"~substr(0)        93.924 93

The numbers

Each entry gives the major number, a short label, constructs that raise it with the full code, and a rule of this book that raises it where one is written. The grouping is by the usual kind of fault, and a number may have subcodes of another kind. The examples run the listed constructs and print the code that the trap reads.

Faults in the form of the text

These faults are usually found in the text of a clause, and a clause that is a directive or part of a block can raise them too. A fault in the text of a program is found when the program is read, and in the text of an INTERPRET when it runs, as the reading rule says.

[cond.errors.form]

The numbers below usually name a fault in the form of the text, and some of them also have subcodes that are raised by values when the clause runs, such as 7.3 and 31.2.

  • 6, unfinished literal or comment: say 'a 6.2, /* open 6.1; rule.
  • 7, SELECT with no usable branch: select; say 1; end 7.2, select; end 7.1, select; when 0 then nop; end 7.3; rule, rule.
  • 8, THEN or ELSE with no partner: then say 1 8.1, else say 1 8.2; rule.
  • 9, WHEN or OTHERWISE outside SELECT: when 1 then nop 9.1, otherwise nop 9.2; rule.
  • 10, END out of place: end 10.1, do; end x 10.3; rule.
  • 13, foreign character: say 1 # 13.1, x = 1 ^ 2 13.1; rule.
  • 14, block left open: do; say 1 14.1, if 1 then do; say 2 14.1, do 1 to 2 to 3 14.5; rule.
  • 15, malformed hex or binary literal: say 'zz'x 15.3, say '12'b 15.4, say '1 2'x 15.5; rule.
  • 18, IF with no THEN: if 1 say 'a' 18.1, if 1; say 2 18.1; rule.
  • 19, missing operand: call 19.2, signal 19.4; rule.
  • 20, wrong token in an operand: drop a b 'c' 20.901, procedure expose 'a' 20.902, parse var 'x' 20.904, numeric 20.905, drop () 20.906; rule.
  • 21, tokens left over: nop 1 21.901, call on error name lbl extra 21.903; rule.
  • 25, keyword not offered: signal on foo 25.3, numeric form foo 25.11, parse foo x 25.12, numeric 1 25.15; rule.
  • 27, clashing DO parts: do forever x 27.901, do i=1 to 2 until 1 while 1 27.1; rule.
  • 30, over-long symbol: x = 1 where x is a symbol of 251 characters 30.1; rule.
  • 31, constant used as a variable: 1x = 2 31.2, drop 1a 31.2, parse value 'x' with .a 31.3, x = '1a'; drop (x) 31.2; rule.
  • 35, expression that does not parse: x = 1 + 35.1, x = * 2 35.1, say () 35.1; rule.
  • 36, bracket left open: x = (1 36.901, x = a[1 36.902; rule.
  • 37, closer with no opener: x = ] 37.901, x = (1] 37.901, x = 1) 37.2; rule.
  • 38, malformed template: parse var x a 3 3 b b ) c 38.1, parse var x 'a' + 38.901; rule.
  • 46, malformed name in parentheses: drop (x y 46.1; rule.
  • 47, label in a text that cannot hold one: x: say 1 47.1; rule.

The numbers 22 and 23 would apply where a string holds a byte that the character set cannot hold. Every string of this book may hold any of the 256 character codes, as the character rule says, so this book names no clause that raises them.

call try "say 'a"
call try "/* open"
call try "select; say 1; end"
call try "select; end"
call try "select; when 0 then nop; end"
call try "then say 1"
call try "else say 1"
call try "when 1 then nop"
call try "otherwise nop"
call try "end"
call try "do; end x"
call try "say 1 #"
call try "x = 1 ^ 2"
call try "do; say 1"
call try "if 1 then do; say 2"
call try "do 1 to 2 to 3"
call try "say 'zz'x"
call try "say '12'b"
call try "say '1 2'x"
call try "if 1 say 'a'"
call try "if 1; say 2"
call try "call"
call try "signal"
call try "drop a b 'c'"
call try "procedure expose 'a'"
call try "parse var 'x'"
call try "numeric"
call try "drop ()"
call try "nop 1"
call try "call on error name lbl extra"
call try "signal on foo"
call try "numeric form foo"
call try "parse foo x"
call try "numeric 1"
call try "do forever x"
call try "do i=1 to 2 until 1 while 1"
call try copies('a', 251) '= 1', '(251 a) = 1'
call try "1x = 2"
call try "drop 1a"
call try "parse value 'x' with .a"
call try "x = '1a'; drop (x)"
call try "x = 1 +"
call try "x = * 2"
call try "say ()"
call try "x = (1"
call try "x = a[1"
call try "x = ]"
call try "x = (1]"
call try "x = 1)"
call try "parse var x a 3 3 b b ) c"
call try "parse var x 'a' +"
call try "drop (x y"
call try "x: say 1"
exit
try:
  signal on syntax name e
  interpret arg(1)
  say left(arg(1), 44) '=> none'
  return
e: label = arg(1)
  if arg(2, 'E') then label = arg(2)
  say left(label, 44) condition('o')~code
  return

say 'a                                       6.2
/* open                                      6.1
select; say 1; end                           7.2
select; end                                  7.1
select; when 0 then nop; end                 7.3

say '12'b                                    15.4

if 1 say 'a'                                 18.1
if 1; say 2                                  18.1
call                                         19.2
signal                                       19.4
drop a b 'c'                                 20.901
procedure expose 'a'                         20.902
parse var 'x'                                20.904
numeric                                      20.905
drop ()                                      20.906
nop 1                                        21.901
call on error name lbl extra                 21.903
signal on foo                                25.3
numeric form foo                             25.11
parse foo x                                  25.12

do i=1 to 2 until 1 while 1                  27.1

drop 1a                                      31.2

x = '1a'; drop (x)                           31.2

Faults in the values and the flow

These faults are found while a clause runs, because a value or the state of the program does not fit the clause.

[cond.errors.run]

The numbers below usually name a fault that the values or the flow of control cause, at the clause that meets it.

  • 16, jump to a missing label: signal nolabelhere 16.1, signal value 'zz' 16.1; rule.
  • 17, misplaced PROCEDURE: procedure 17.1; rule.
  • 24, unknown TRACE setting: trace x1 24.1; rule.
  • 26, value that is no whole number: numeric digits 'a' 26.5, numeric digits 0 26.5, numeric fuzz -1 26.6, x = 2 ** 1.5 26.8; rule.
  • 28, LEAVE or ITERATE with no target: leave 28.1, iterate 28.2, leave nosuchzz 28.3, iterate nosuchzz 28.4; rule.
  • 29, over-long ADDRESS name: address value copies('E', 1000) 29.1.
  • 33, FUZZ not below DIGITS: numeric digits 5; numeric fuzz 5 33.1; rule.
  • 34, operand that is no truth value: if 'a' then say 1 34.1, x = 1 & 'a' 34.901, x = \'a' 34.901; rule.
  • 40, argument count or value refused: x = abs() 40.3, x = abs(1, 2) 40.4, x = left('abc', 'q') 40.12, x = random(5, 1) 40.33; rule, rule.
  • 41, arithmetic on a non-number: x = 1 + 'a' 41.1, x = -'a' 41.1, x = 'a' % 2 41.1; rule.
  • 42, arithmetic with no result: x = 9 // 0 42.3, x = 1e999999999 * 10 42.901, x = 1e-999999999 / 10 42.902, x = 0 ** -1 42.903; rule.
  • 43, call to an unknown routine: x = nosuchroutine_spec_errors() 43.1, call nosuchroutine_spec_errors 43.1, ::requires 'nonexistent_spec_errors_zz.rex' 43.901; rule.
  • 44, call that gives no value: x = nothing() 44.1, say nothing() 44.1; rule.

The number 29 has no rule, and the length at which it is raised is not specified. The number 45 has no construct here: a call made for a value that reaches a RETURN without one raises 44, in an internal routine, a ::ROUTINE or a program file, as the call rule says.

call try "signal nolabelhere"
call try "signal value 'zz'"
call try "procedure"
call try "trace x1"
call try "numeric digits 'a'"
call try "numeric digits 0"
call try "numeric fuzz -1"
call try "x = 2 ** 1.5"
call try "leave"

Faults of the interpreter and its services

[cond.errors.system]

The numbers below usually name a fault that is neither in the text nor in a value of the program: the interpreter that cannot start the program or go on, a program that is stopped, and a request to the system that fails.

  • 3, a program file that does not exist: 3.901, with the exit status 253.
  • 4, a HALT that no trap answers: raise halt 4.1; rule.
  • 11, parentheses or calls nested beyond the limit; rule.
  • 48, a request to the system that fails: call rxqueue 'Set', 'nosuchq' followed by queue 'x' 48.1; rule.

The number 3 comes before any clause runs, so no trap sees it. The numbers 5, 39 and 49 name states that this book does not tie to a clause: how much a program can ask for before 5 is raised, how complex an expression can be before 39, and what 49 reports are not specified. A RAISE HALT is a deterministic way to reach 4.

call try "call gone; queue 'x'"
exit
try:
  signal on syntax name e
  interpret arg(1)
  say arg(1) '=> none'
  return
e: say left(arg(1), 40) condition('o')~code
  return
gone: call rxqueue 'Set', 'spec_errors_no_such_queue'
  return

call gone; queue 'x'                     48.1

signal on syntax name e
raise halt
say 'not reached'
e: say condition('o')~code rc

4.1 4

Faults of messages, objects and directives

[cond.errors.objects]

The numbers from 88 up usually name faults of messages, of objects and of directives.

  • 88, argument value refused: x = filespec('N') 88.901, x = .directory~new~put(1) 88.901, x = charin(, 0, -1) 88.907; rule.
  • 89, USE target of the wrong kind: use arg a, 'b' 89.1, use arg (a) 89.1; rule.
  • 90, EXTERNAL entry that is not there: ::routine r external 'registered nonezz' 90.999; rule.
  • 91, message term with no result: say 'a' .m~new~bar 'b' 91.999; rule.
  • 93, argument value refused: x = left('abc', -2) 93.923, x = copies('ab', -2) 93.906, x = 'abc'~substr(0) 93.924, x = d2c(-1) 93.927, x = .array~new('x') 93.906, x = stream('nofile_zz', 'c', 'bogus') 93.914; rule.
  • 97, message that is not answered: x = 'a'~foo 97.1, x = .nil~foo 97.1, .m~new~p 97.2; rule, rule.
  • 98, fault of a running clause or directive: raise propagate 98.918, ::class a subclass nosuchzzclass 98.909, ::routine r external 'library nonezz' 98.903; rule, rule.
  • 99, fault in a directive or its place: ::routine zz 99.914, expose x 99.908, forward to (.nil) 99.923, use local a 99.915, ::class a (twice) 99.901; rule.

The numbers 40, 88 and 93 all refuse arguments, and which of them a builtin or a method raises is named on its own page. The number 92 belongs to a platform interface that this book does not specify, so no rule or example raises it. The numbers 98 and 99 differ in when the fault is found: 99 is a fault of form found when the text is read, and 98 is a fault found when the clause or directive takes effect. A directive in the text of an INTERPRET is no directive, so it raises 99 there.
