Classes

rexxref: Builtin Classes; Objects and Classes > Mixin Classes; Objects and Classes > Overview of Classes Provided by Rexx; Builtin Classes > Fundamental Classes > Object Class > defaultName; Builtin Classes > Fundamental Classes > Object Class > objectName; Builtin Classes > Fundamental Classes > Object Class > objectName=; Builtin Classes > Fundamental Classes > Object Class > string

Deviations: D30, D32, D36, D109, D114

This chapter specifies the classes that every program can use without declaring them: the classes of the class library. It has a page for each class, or for a few classes that belong together, and a page, the method search, for how a message finds the method that runs it. The chapter index holds what is true of all of them: how a class page is laid out, how the classes are related, what a method does with a wrong argument, what new does, and what the string value of an object is.

Where this chapter says that a program declares a class, the declaring is done by the ::CLASS directive, and the methods of that class by ::METHOD. The chapter does not repeat what those pages say about the options of the directives. It specifies the methods of Class that make and change classes while a program runs.

How a class page is laid out

A class page opens with its front matter, then a title and an overview paragraph, and then the sections below, in this order. A page leaves out a section it has nothing for.

  • The class: rules about the class as a whole: how an instance is made, its string value, how two instances compare, what it inherits.
  • Class methods: the methods of the class object itself, the class side, such as new and of. Each is a rule group.
  • Methods: the methods of an instance, the instance side, grouped by what they do. Each method is a rule group, and a group may cover several methods that share a rule.
  • Deviations: the rules that state a Deviation, as every page does.

A method that the class inherits from a superclass or a mixin class is specified on the page of that class. The page of a class links to it and states only what the class adds or changes. A method whose behavior is shared by the classes of a family, such as the collection classes, is specified once on the page of the class it belongs to, and the pages of the other classes link to it.

The front matter names the element (the class, by its id), kind: class, the sections of the reference manual that describe it, the ANSI section when the ANSI draft has the class, and the Deviations that touch the page.

How rules are named

A rule on a class page is named class. followed by the page, which is the class name in lower case, and then the following words. On a page that holds several classes, the class name in lower case follows the page, as in class.comparators.numeric.compare.

  • class.<page>.<method> is the main rule of a method, with the method name in lower case: class.array.append.
  • class.<page>.<method>.<aspect> is a further rule of the same method, such as an error or a default.
  • class.<page>.<topic> is a rule about the class as a whole, such as creation or comparison. A topic never takes the name of a method of the class: when the class has a method of that name, the main rule of the method is the rule about it, so for a class with a string method the rule about its string value is class.<page>.string.
  • class.<page>.<method>.sends is the rule that states the messages the method sends, as the sends rule says.
  • A class method and an instance method of one class never share an identifier. When a name exists on both sides, the instance method has the plain name, and the class method has the aspect class-side; a further aspect of the class method follows it, as in class.properties.load.class-side.error.
  • The prefix form of - and +, which is the same method sent with no argument, takes the aspect prefix: class.<page>.minus.prefix.
  • A method that is written as a symbol takes a word in place of the symbol: eq for =, seq for ==, ne for \=, sne for \==, ltgt for <>, gtlt for ><, gt, lt, ge and le for >, <, >= and <=, ngt and nlt for \> and \<, sgt, slt, sge and sle for >>, <<, >>= and <<=, nsgt and nslt for \>> and \<<, plus, minus, times, divide, intdiv, remainder and power for +, -, *, /, %, // and **, concat, blank and abuttal for ||, the blank and the abuttal, and, or, xor and not for &, |, && and \, brackets for [], and iif for ?.
  • A method whose name ends in =, an attribute that is assigned, takes the name without it and -set: objectname-set for objectName=, and brackets-set for []=.

Every method that a class defines has a rule on its page, and the identifiers never change once they are in the book. A method that the class only inherits has no rule on its page: the page links to the rule on the page that defines it, in a sentence that is not itself a rule and has no identifier.

A method that the class defines but whose behavior another page owns, such as a String method that a builtin function runs, a Stream method that a stream builtin uses, or an operator method, is covered by one grouped rule per page and group. The identifier of a grouped rule is class.<page>.builtins for the methods that builtin functions run or use, as class.string.builtins and class.stream.builtins, and class.<page>.operators for the operator methods, as class.string.operators; it is a topic in the sense of the list above. The grouped rule lists each such method with a link to the rule that owns its behavior, and has one example that sends several of them as messages. It covers the inventory rows of those methods. Such a method has a rule of its own, in addition, only where something differs when it is sent as a message.

The two sides of a class

[class.index.sides]

A class is an object, and so has methods of its own beside those of its instances. The methods an instance understands are the instance side, and the methods the class object itself understands, such as new and of, are the class side. A message to the class finds a class-side method and never an instance-side one; a message to an instance finds an instance-side method and never a class-side one. hasMethod shows which side a name is on.

say .array~hasMethod('OF') .array~new~hasMethod('OF')
say .array~hasMethod('APPEND') .array~new~hasMethod('APPEND')
say .array~of(4, 5)~items
signal on syntax name e
say .array~append(1)
e: say condition('o')~code

1 0
0 1
2
97.1

The class hierarchy

[class.index.root]

Every class is an instance of Class. Object is the root of the hierarchy: it has no superclass, and every other class has Object among its ancestors. A class has one superclass and may inherit any number of mixin classes. A mixin class is a class that exists to be inherited. Nothing stops a program from sending new to a mixin class: it makes an instance like any other class.

say .object~superclass~isNil .object~class~id .array~class~id
say .circularqueue~isSubclassOf(.object) .circularqueue~isSubclassOf(.array)
say .comparable~isSubclassOf(.object) .comparable~new~class~id

1 Class Class
1 0
1 Comparable
[class.index.hierarchy]

The superClasses method of a class answers an array that holds its superclass first, then its mixin classes in the order of its inherit list, into which the inherit method of Class can insert more (see the page of Class). The four listings below show the library classes related by it, each line giving the superclasses of the class before the colon. The first listing also shows the class of each class, which is Class for every one of them, Singleton included. Every ancestor of its superclass and of its mixin classes is an ancestor of the class too, so CircularQueue has OrderedCollection among its ancestors through Queue, though only Queue is among its superclasses. Apart from ArgUtil, which a rule of its own covers, a class that is not in a listing is described on its own page. RexxInfo, whose class is reached only as .rexxinfo~class, and RegularExpression, which a program gets with ::REQUIRES, are among those.

say .object~superclasses~items .object~class~id
call show 'Class String Method Routine Package Message',

    c = .environment~at(n~upper)
    s = ''
    do x over c~superclasses
      s = s x~id
    end
    say n':' s~strip c~class~id
  end

[class.index.mixins]

The library classes that are mixin classes are the ones for which queryMixinClass answers 1: the two notification classes, the four collection mixins Collection, MapCollection, OrderedCollection and SetCollection, Comparable, Orderable, Comparator and every class below it, CommandHandler, Singleton, and the stream classes InputStream, OutputStream, InputOutputStream and Stream. Every other class listed in the hierarchy is not a mixin class.

mix = ''
other = ''
names = 'MessageNotification AlarmNotification Collection Array',
  'Comparator NumericComparator Singleton CommandHandler Stream String',
  'Message Directory'

  if .environment~at(n~upper)~queryMixinClass then mix = mix n
  else other = other n
end

say 'more:' mix~subword(4)
say 'other:' other~strip

Arguments and the errors of methods

[class.index.errors]

A message to an object of a library class can fail in three ways: no method of that name is found and the class has no UNKNOWN method (Directory, StringTable, Stem, Monitor and their subclasses have one, and their pages say what it does), the arguments do not fit the method, or an argument has a value the method refuses. The first raises NOMETHOD, which untrapped ends as SYNTAX 97.1, and its private and package forms are those of the access rule. The other two raise SYNTAX at the clause that sent the message, as the SYNTAX rule says, with the error number and subcode that the method gives. A rule of this chapter that says a method "raises SYNTAX m.n" means what that convention means: the message returns no value, a trap sees m.n as the code and m as RC, and the text of the error message is not specified.

call try '.array~new~nosuchzz'
call try '.array~new~items(1)'
call try '.array~new~at'
call try '.array~new~section("x")'
call try '.directory~new~nosuchzz'
exit
try:
  signal on syntax name bad
  interpret 'r =' arg(1)
  say arg(1) '=> no error'
  return
bad: say arg(1) '=>' condition('c') condition('o')~code rc
  return

.array~new~nosuchzz => SYNTAX 97.1 97
.array~new~items(1) => SYNTAX 93.902 93
.array~new~at => SYNTAX 93.901 93
.array~new~section("x") => SYNTAX 93.907 93
.directory~new~nosuchzz => no error
[class.index.args.count]

The argument count of a message is the position of the last argument that is not omitted, as it is for a built-in function, so omitted places at the end add nothing. A message with more arguments than the method accepts raises a SYNTAX error whatever the values of the arguments are, and an omitted place before the last argument still counts. The subcode is 93.902 unless the page of the method gives another; some stream methods, such as state and lines, raise 88.922.

A message that leaves out an argument the method requires raises a SYNTAX error. The subcode belongs to the method, and its page gives it. Among those that occur are 93.903, an argument at a given position is missing, as for append, hasMethod, left and the at of List; 93.901, fewer arguments than the method needs, as for the at and put of Array; and 88.901, as for isA and the at and put of Table and Directory.

Making an object with new

[class.index.new]

The new that Class supplies makes an object of the class that received it and sends the new object the message init with the arguments of new, in order. A library class may have a class-side new of its own, which uses the arguments itself and sends init with other arguments or none: .array~new(5) sends init with no argument. The page of each such class states what its new sends to init. The result of new is the new object, whatever init answers. A class that inherits new from a superclass still makes an object of the class that received the message, so a subclass of a class with an init runs that init on its own instances. A class that neither declares nor inherits an init other than that of Object has the init of Object, which accepts no argument: new with an argument raises SYNTAX 93.902 for such a class. A class that is abstract makes no object with the new that Class supplies: it raises SYNTAX 98.989.

p = .point~new(3, 4)
say p~class~id p~x p~y
q = .point3~new(1, 2)
say q~class~id q~x q~y q~z
say .ret~new~class~id
a = .xa~new(5)
say a~class~id a~size
call try '.plain~new(1)'
call try '.plain~new'
call try '.abs~new'
exit
try:
  signal on syntax name bad
  interpret 'r =' arg(1)

[class.index.new.init-again]

The message init is an ordinary message. A program may send it to an object again at any time, by ~, by send or with a scope, and it runs the method it finds, with nothing to mark that the object was already initialized. [class.index.defaultname]

The default name of an object is built from the id of its class. For an ordinary object it is a or an, a blank and the id, with an when the first letter of the id is A, E, I, O or U in either case and a otherwise, and the id keeps its own case: a XYLO, an apple. The default name of a class is The, a blank, the id and class, as in The XYLO class. The defaultName method answers it, and takes no argument.

[class.index.objectname]

The objectName method of an object answers its name: the name set for it, and when none was set, the object's defaultName. The objectName= method sets the name. Its argument must be a string or an object whose request with the argument STRING answers one, which is then the name; an instance of a subclass of String is a string here. The name is kept from then on, even when it is the null string. Any other argument, .nil and an object that has only a string method included, raises SYNTAX 88.909. The object .nil has the name The NIL object. The name belongs to the object alone: it changes no other object, not the objects of its class, and not the class's id. objectName= sent to a String of no subclass and no enhancement, a number included, is refused, as Deviation 36 states; an instance of a subclass of String, or one made by enhanced, takes a name like any other object. objectName takes no argument and objectName= takes one.

[class.index.string]

The string value of an object that is not a string is found as the conversion rule says: the answer of the request message sent to it with the argument STRING when that is a string, and otherwise the answer of its string method. The request of Object sends makeString when the object has one, so an object with a makeString method shows its answer. say and the joining operators use the string value, as the SAY rule and the concatenation rule say. The string method of Object answers the object's objectName, so an object with no makeString method shows the name that was set, and otherwise its default name. A class whose instances should show differently declares string. It declares makeString as well when its instances should be accepted where a method takes a string argument, such as the pad of left, the needle of pos or the argument of objectName=, because such a method sends request with the argument STRING and takes the answer when it is a string, and has no fallback to string: an object whose request answers .nil or another object that is not a string, as Object does for an object with no makeString method, .nil itself among them, raises SYNTAX 88.909. An argument that a method reads as a number, a whole number or a logical value has the fallback: it is read as the conversion rule reads such an argument of a builtin, so "abc"~left(o) uses the answer of string of an object that has only that method. A class that declares request itself decides both the string value and what a method reads from a string argument. An operator method sent as a message, such as "x"~"||"(b), takes the string value of its argument as the operator does. An instance of a subclass of String is a string, and its string value is its own characters, whatever makeString, request and string it declares: no message is sent to it for that (Deviation 109). A string method that answers an object that is not a string is covered by Deviation 30.

call try '"x"~"||"(.shown~new)'
call try '"abc"~left(.count~new)'

Messages a method sends

[class.index.sends]

A method of a library class that sends a message a program can override, to its receiver, to the receiver's class, to an argument, to an item it holds or to an object it makes, has a rule class.<page>.<method>.sends. That rule names the messages, their receivers, their arguments and their order, and says whether the number of times each is sent is specified, with an example in which an override shows each message. A method with no such rule sends no message that a program can override, other than what the string-value rule sends to its string arguments. The methods named here are stated in this rule instead: the new that Class supplies sends init, as the new rule says; the string method of Object sends objectName to the object, and objectName sends defaultName when no name was set; appendAll sends allItems to its argument and appends what it answers; and putAll sends supplier to its argument and puts what it answers.

say .alpha~new~string '|' .beta~new~string
x = .many~of(1, 2)
t = .array~new
t~appendAll(x)
say t~items t~makeString('L', ',')
r = .relation~new
r~putAll(x)
say r~items r~allIndexes~items

Deviations

[class.index.deviation.30]

When the string method of an object answers an object that is not a string, interrexx gives ooRexx's answer wherever that is defined, and elsewhere, as for say, a joining operator or a builtin argument, ends the program with exit code 120 after raising NOSTRING if it is trapped. ooRexx reads .nil as a string there, with garbage results or a crash. The conventions and the NOSTRING rule state it for builtin arguments and for the condition.

say 'before'
say 'x' .weird~new
::class weird
::method string
  return .directory~new

before
[class.index.deviation.32]

When a class-side new reached through enhanced answers an object it did not build, interrexx answers that object unchanged; ooRexx marks it enhanced, which changes every object of its class. When a metaclass new answers a class that subclass, mixinclass or a ::CLASS directive has already completed, or a class of the library such as Array, while a class with that metaclass is made, by subclass, by mixinclass or by a ::CLASS directive with METACLASS, interrexx ends the program with exit code 120; ooRexx rewires the existing class in place, so that y~id in the first example answers Array. A directive is read before the program runs, so the program of the third example writes nothing. In the last example, interrexx answers String for both strings, where ooRexx marks every string as enhanced and answers ODD. See Deviation 32.

say 'before'
y = .k~subclass('Y')
say 'after' y~id

[class.index.deviation.114]

When subclass or mixinclass sends new to a metaclass and the answer is not a class, SYNTAX 98.900 is raised by the message, in the program that sent it, where it can be trapped. The string value of an instance of a subclass of String is its own characters, and the methods that read it as a string, a number or a logical value send it no REQUEST, no MAKESTRING and no STRING, as the rule on the string value says and the String page rule states in full; ooRexx sends the instance request with STRING or MAKESTRING as an argument and as the receiver of some methods, so an override of either can change what is read. Method search

rexxref: Objects and Classes > Default Search Order for Method Selection; Objects and Classes > Changing the Search Order for Methods; Objects and Classes > Defining an UNKNOWN Method; Objects and Classes > Mixin Classes; Objects and Classes > Metaclasses; Objects and Classes > Defining Instance Methods with SETMETHOD or ENHANCED; Objects and Classes > Public, Package-Scope, and Private Methods; Special Variables > SUPER; Builtin Classes > Fundamental Classes > Object Class > setMethod; Builtin Classes > Fundamental Classes > Object Class > unsetMethod; Builtin Classes > Fundamental Classes > Class Class (Metaclass) > define; Builtin Classes > Fundamental Classes > Class Class (Metaclass) > defineMethods; Builtin Classes > Fundamental Classes > Class Class (Metaclass) > delete; Builtin Classes > Fundamental Classes > Class Class (Metaclass) > enhanced; Builtin Classes > Fundamental Classes > Class Class (Metaclass) > inherit; Builtin Classes > Fundamental Classes > Class Class (Metaclass) > uninherit

Deviations: D32, D105, D110, D117

Every message goes to an object, and the object's class decides which method answers it. This page specifies the whole search: which methods an object has of its own, in which order its class and the classes it descends from are looked at, how a message can start the search part of the way down, what UNKNOWN receives when nothing is found, how a class object finds the class methods it answers, and what a change to a class does to objects that already exist. The pages of the classes Object and Class specify the arguments of the methods that make these changes; this page specifies what the changes do to the search. The classes chapter lists which class inherits which. The directives that create classes and methods are in ::CLASS and ::METHOD, and the search rule of the first gives the simple cases.

Two words are used throughout. The method table of a class is the list of names the class itself holds: the methods that its ::METHOD directives declare and that define and defineMethods add. An entry of a table is either a method or a mark that hides the name (see hidden names). The order of a class is the list of classes whose tables a message to one of its instances is looked up in.

The order of a class

[class.methods.order]

The order of Object holds only Object. The order of any other class C starts with C itself and goes on with the orders of the classes in the list of superclasses that C holds, the list its superClasses method reports, one after the other, in the order of that list: the superclass and then the mixin classes in the order they were inherited, except that a mixin class that inherit placed in front of another class of the list, the superclass included, stands there (the change rule). A class that this makes occur more than once keeps only its last place. The order therefore ends with Object, and a class stands after every class that has it as a superclass or inherits it. The list is read from what the class holds, and no message is sent to a class for it: the search, isA, isInstanceOf, inherit and uninherit send none of superClasses, isSubclassOf, queryMixinClass or baseClass, so a metaclass that overrides them changes what a program that sends them gets and nothing else. In the second example the metaclass META announces each of those messages and answers falsely; the only announcement is the one for the superClasses that the program sends itself.

Note. The first example prints the order of two classes. Each who method names its own class and sends who on to the class that follows it, using the special variable SUPER, which the SUPER rule specifies, so that the line shows the classes of the order in turn, Object left out. LEAF2 lists the same mixin classes as LEAF the other way round.

call show .leaf, .leaf2
exit
show:
  do c over arg(1, 'A')
    say c~id':' c~new~who
  end
  return

  use arg id, obj, scope
  signal on nomethod name last
  return id obj~who:scope
last: return id

[class.methods.order.base]

A mixin class has a base class: the class that its MIXINCLASS option names, or, when that is a mixin class too, the base class of that one, and so on until a class that is not a mixin class is reached; the INHERIT list of the mixin class does not enter into it. The base class comes behind the mixin class in its own order. By the order rule a mixin class that a class lists, and that no class listed after it reaches, therefore stands in front of every class of its own order, its base class among them, and of every class of the order of each class listed after it, and behind the other classes of the superclass's order; its methods hide those of the first and lose to those of the second. A mixin class based on an ancestor of the superclass thus hides the methods of that ancestor and of the classes above it, and loses to the classes of the chain below that ancestor unless the order of a class listed after it holds them; a mixin class based on Object loses in the same way to every class of the superclass's chain but Object. The search rule of the directive describes the case in which each listed class is a mixin class whose MIXINCLASS option names Object and that inherits none. In the example, LEAF lists the Object-based mixin class OM first, so it stands in front of BASE, and LEAF2 lists it last, so it stays behind. MO is based on BASE through MX and inherits OM, so in LEAF4 it stands in front of MX and BASE, and OM stands behind them. In the second example MT is based on TOP and listed in front of MM, which is based on the lower class MID; MT stands in front of TOP, and also in front of MID, because a class listed after it reaches MID, but behind LOW.

call show .leaf, .leaf2, .leaf3, .leaf4
exit

  end
  return

[class.methods.order.shared]

A class that can be reached by more than one path stands in the order once, behind every class that reaches it. Two mixin classes that inherit the same mixin class, and a subclass that inherits a mixin class whose own mixin class its superclass already has, are the usual cases. A class cannot be inherited twice by naming it twice or by inheriting it when it is already an ancestor: the mixin rule gives SYNTAX 98.944 for a class that is listed twice or is the superclass, and the same code is raised when the class named is an ancestor of the receiving class at its turn in the list. Listing a mixin class after one that inherits it is therefore the error (INHERIT left shared in the second example), and listing it in front of that one is not (INHERIT shared left).

call show .both, .kid, .late
exit

  do c over arg(1, 'A')
    say c~id':' c~new~who
  end
  return

[class.methods.order.change]

The order of a class is worked out again whenever its list of superclasses changes, and so is the order of every class below it. The inherit method of Class adds a mixin class at the end of the list, or immediately in front of the class that its second argument names, which may be the superclass; the uninherit method takes one out. A mixin class put in front of the superclass then comes first in superClasses, superClass answers it, and its methods hide the superclass's. An uninherit of a mixin class that another class of the order still inherits takes it out of the list of superclasses and leaves it in the order; the first class of the list stays, and the uninherit rule gives the errors for a class that cannot be taken out. The first example prints the order of C and of its subclass SUB and the list of superclasses after each change; its last line shows that the step inherit ma before mx has put the mixin class MA, which is based on Object, in front of P1, so that superClass answers MA, and that MA, standing first, can no longer be taken out. The second example sends uninherit twice for a mixin class that C has by two paths, and once for Object, which is not a mixin class.

.c~inherit(.mb)
call show 'inherit mb'
.c~inherit(.mx, .p1)
call show 'inherit mx before p1'
.c~uninherit(.ma)
call show 'uninherit ma'
.c~inherit(.ma, .mx)
call show 'inherit ma before mx'
.c~uninherit(.mb)
call show 'uninherit mb'
say 'superclass:' .c~superclass~id
signal on syntax name e
.c~uninherit(.ma)
e: say 'uninherit ma:' condition('o')~code
exit

The search for a message

[class.methods.search]

A message to an object is looked up in this sequence. First come the object's own methods, those that setMethod gave it and those that enhanced made it with. Then come the tables of the classes of the order of the object's class, one after another. The name of the message is compared in upper case. The first table that has an entry for the name decides: when the entry is a method that the sender may run, that method runs; when the entry hides the name, or the method is one the sender may not run, the name counts as not found and the search for the name ends, without going on to the classes behind. A name that counts as not found goes to UNKNOWN, as the unknown rule says. The same sequence serves send and the other methods that send a message, and the operators, which are messages. The first example shows each step: a table that is reached first wins, a superclass before a mixin class, and an object's own method before all of them. The message name is written in several cases. The second example sends operators, which find their methods in the same sequence, also when the message is written with a scope or an object has set the operator itself; an operator that finds no method goes to UNKNOWN like any message, with an array of one item for the infix form and an empty one for the prefix form (the operator messages).

o = .sub~new
say o~one '|' o~TWO '|' o~Three '|' o~four
o~put('one', 'return "object one"')
o~put('four', 'return "object four"')
say o~one '|' o~two '|' o~three '|' o~four
say .sub~new~one '|' .sub~new~four

[class.methods.search.access]

A method that the sender may not run, because it is PRIVATE or PACKAGE as the access rule says, does not let the search go on: the name counts as not found, even when a class behind has a public method of that name. The message goes to UNKNOWN when there is one, and otherwise raises the error that the access rule gives, 97.2 for the private method of the example. The sender that may run the method still finds it, and a scoped send from the method reaches a method behind it. A message that START sends is checked as Deviation 105 states.

[class.methods.hidden]

A name can be hidden instead of given a method: the search stops at it, and the name counts as not found. define with no method, an item .nil in the collection that defineMethods or enhanced receives, and, for the object's own methods, setMethod with no method leave a mark in the table. define with .nil as the method hides the name as well, but the table then holds no entry that method could answer, as the define rule says. The delete method of Class removes the mark or the method that the table of the class it is sent to holds for a name, the mark that define with .nil left included, and the name is then looked up in the classes behind at once (Deviation 117). A name the table does not hold is left as it is; delete does not remove a method that only a class behind holds. The example hides a method that the superclass holds, shows that UNKNOWN receives the hidden name, and brings the method back with delete. A second example hides an inherited name with .nil as the method of define.

The object's own methods

[class.methods.object]

setMethod gives the receiving object a method of its own, found before any class. Its first argument is the name, which is used in upper case, and its second is the method: a method object, a string that is the source of the method, or an array of strings, one for each line, from which a method is made. A second setMethod of the same name replaces the method; the call with no second argument hides the name for the object, so that the search stops there and the message goes to UNKNOWN. unsetMethod takes the name off the object again: the name is looked up in the classes as if setMethod had never been sent, and unsetMethod of a name the object has not set is not an error. setMethod and unsetMethod are private methods with a further restriction, which the next rule gives. A define of the same name that is sent to the class afterwards is not seen while the object's own method of that name stands, and is seen after unsetMethod, as the rule on changes says; the second example shows the object's own method and the class's method of the same name. Deviation 110 has the example for the define that is seen after unsetMethod.

o = .k~new
o~put('m', 'return "from a string"')
o~put('a', .array~of('parse arg x', 'return x * 2'))
o~put('n', .method~new('n', 'return "from a method object"'))
say o~m '|' o~a(21) '|' o~n '|' o~old
o~put('m', 'return "replaced"')
say o~m '|' o~old
o~put('old')
say t(o, 'old')
o~unset('old')
o~unset('m')
o~unset('never_set')
say o~old '|' t(o, 'm')
exit

[class.methods.object.scope]

The scope argument of setMethod decides which class a scoped send from the method starts behind. A method set with the scope FLOAT, the default, belongs to no class of the order, and SUPER in it is the object's own class, so that self~m:super runs the class's m. A method set with OBJECT takes the place of a method of the object's class, and SUPER in it is the class that follows the object's class in the order. It takes the place also for a search that starts at the object's class: a scoped message, send with a scope, or FORWARD CLASS naming that class finds it ahead of the class's own entry, while a search that starts at another class does not. A hiding setMethod with OBJECT is not seen there, and a FLOAT method is found by none of these searches. The second example shows both. A method that enhanced adds behaves as one with FLOAT. The scoped send is specified by the scoped send rule.

o~put('m', 'return "float m >" self~m:super', 'FLOAT')
o~put('n', 'return "object n >" self~n:super', 'OBJECT')

o~put('s2', 'return super', 'OBJECT')
say o~m '|' o~n
say o~s1~id o~s2~id
m = .directory~new~~put('return "enhanced m >" self~m:super', 'M')
e = .k~enhanced(m)
say e~m

[class.methods.enhanced]

enhanced answers a new object of the receiving class that has, in addition to the class's methods, the methods of the collection it receives, whose indexes are the names and whose items are method objects, strings or arrays, or .nil to hide a name. It sends the message new to the receiving class with the arguments that follow the collection, so a class method new of the class runs and init receives those arguments, and it gives the object that new answers the added methods. Its class is the receiving class. The added methods are the object's own methods, so they are found before the class's, and unsetMethod leaves them: after a setMethod has replaced one, unsetMethod brings the added method back. The object follows the later changes to the class, to its superclasses and to its mixin classes, and inherit and uninherit, as every instance does.

Changes after objects exist

[class.methods.late]

An object follows every change made to the methods that its class finds, at any time. A define, defineMethods or delete sent to a class C, an inherit or uninherit sent to C, and a change to the table of a superclass of C or of a mixin class in the order of C, all change what the instances of C answer: the instances made before the change as well as those made after it, however many changes came before, and also an object that has methods of its own from setMethod or enhanced. The own methods stay first in the search (the object rule). Deviation 110 gives the examples of the changes to the table of C itself.

Note. In the example, A is an instance of K and S is an instance of a subclass. Both are made first, and each line gives, for each name, what A and S answer after a change to the superclass or to a mixin class, or after inherit or uninherit, with - where the name is not found.

.k~uninherit(.mx)

.base~define('two', 'return "T"')

Starting the search at a class

[class.methods.scoped]

A message written object~name:scope starts the search at a class. The scope is a variable symbol, simple or compound, or an environment symbol such as .base, and its value is evaluated like that of any term; a string, a number or a parenthesized expression there makes the program unreadable with SYNTAX 20.917. The value must be a class that stands in the order of the object's class, that is the class itself, a superclass, an inherited mixin class or Object. Another value raises SYNTAX 88.914 when it is not a class, and 93.957 when it is a class that does not stand in the order. The object's own methods are not looked at, except a method that setMethod gave it with the scope OBJECT, which counts as an entry of the table of the object's class and is found ahead of that table's own entry when the search starts at that class, as the scope rule says. The search begins with the table of the named class and goes on through the classes that follow it in the order of the object's class, whichever class the sending method belongs to. It ends as the search rule says, and a name that is not found goes to UNKNOWN through the plain search for that name, and without one raises NOMETHOD, SYNTAX 97.1 when untrapped. A scoped message can be sent from any code, and the object need not be SELF.

Note. In the first example o has a method of its own, and the scoped messages skip it. ONLYMX is held by a mixin class that stands behind BASE, so a search that starts at BASE reaches it, and ONLYBASE is held by a class in front of MX, so a search that starts at MX does not.

say o~hello '|' o~hello:.leaf '|' o~hello:.mid '|' o~hello:.base
say o~hello:.mx '|' o~onlymx:.base '|' o~onlymx:.mx
call try 'say o~onlybase:.mx'
call try 'say o~onlybase:.base'
exit

[class.methods.super]

SUPER is a variable that every method starts with. Its value is the class that follows, in the order of the receiver's class, the class whose table the running method came from; that is Object for the last class. It is the usual scope of a message that runs the method an override replaces. The value belongs to the activation and depends on the receiver: one mixin class method sees a different class behind it for receivers of different orders. A method that was set with setMethod and the scope FLOAT, and a method that enhanced added, has the receiver's own class as SUPER, and one set with OBJECT has the class that follows the receiver's class, as the scope rule says. SUPER can be assigned like any variable, and the new value counts for the rest of the activation. In the prolog and in a routine SUPER is not set, so that it holds its own name, and a message with the scope super there raises SYNTAX 88.914, because that value is not a class.

Forwarding to a class

[class.methods.forward]

The CLASS option of FORWARD names the class that starts the search, and it starts it as the scope of a scoped message does: the object's own methods are skipped as for a scoped message, the table of the named class comes first, and the classes behind it in the order of the receiver's class follow. forward class (super) therefore runs the method that the running one overrides. The class must be one the receiver is an instance of, or the instruction raises 93.957 as the FORWARD page says. In the example, GO3 of the first mixin class forwards to the class behind it in the order of LEAF, which is the second mixin class, and GO4 of LEAF forwards to the second mixin class by name.

When nothing is found

[class.methods.unknown]

When the search for a name ends without a method, because no table holds it, a mark hides it, or the sender may not run the method that was found, the search is made again for the name UNKNOWN, over the object's own methods and then the order of its class, whatever scope the first message had. The search for UNKNOWN makes no access check: a PRIVATE or PACKAGE UNKNOWN runs for any sender, and a mark that hides UNKNOWN ends the search as if there were none. The first UNKNOWN found runs, with two arguments: the name of the message in upper case, and a new array that holds the arguments of the message at their positions. The array has as many places as the position of the last argument that was not omitted, and a place of an omitted argument holds nothing; for a message with no arguments the array is empty and has dimension 1. The answer of UNKNOWN is the answer of the message, and a message to an UNKNOWN that answers nothing answers nothing, so that using it as a value, as SAY does, raises SYNTAX 91.999. A class in front of another in the order wins also here, so an UNKNOWN of a superclass hides the one of a mixin class and the object's own UNKNOWN hides both. When no UNKNOWN is found, NOMETHOD is raised. A message to a class object is looked up in the class-side order the same way. The second example sends to objects whose UNKNOWN is PRIVATE, is PACKAGE and is hidden, once from the code of another package; the third gives the dimension of the array.

Messages to a class

[class.methods.class-side]

A message to a class object is looked up the same way as one to an instance, with a class-side order in place of the order. The class-side order of a class C starts with C, standing for the class methods that C declares with CLASS. It goes on with the order of the metaclass of C, each class of it standing for its instance methods, which are class methods of C; then the class-side orders of the superclass of C and of its inherited mixin classes, in the order of superClasses. A class that occurs more than once keeps its last place. The metaclass of C is the one METACLASS names, otherwise that of its superclass, otherwise Class, and the order of a metaclass is an ordinary order that ends with Class and Object. When a subclass has the metaclass of its superclass, the class methods of the subclass come first, those of the superclass next, then the methods of the metaclass, and last those of the inherited mixin classes. Naming another metaclass for the subclass puts that metaclass in front of the class methods of the superclass and keeps the metaclass of the superclass behind them. In the example, SUB inherits MIX and has the metaclass of BASE, SUB2 names a metaclass of its own, and SUB3 declares nothing, so it answers with the class method of BASE and then the method of the metaclass.

call show .sub, .sub2, .sub3
exit

  end
  return

[class.methods.class-side.change]

The class methods a class has follow the same changes as its order does. A class that inherits a mixin class at run time gets the class methods of the mixin class, and loses them with uninherit; the class methods of its subclasses change with it. The instance methods of a metaclass can be changed with define like those of any class, and a class object follows every change made to its metaclass or to a class of its order, as any other object follows the changes to its class; a class made afterwards gets them too. Deviation 110 has the example of the changes to a metaclass.

[class.methods.deviation.32]

When the new that enhanced sends answers an object the class did not build, interrexx answers that object unchanged, as the Deviation 32 rule states; ooRexx marks the object enhanced, which changes every object of its class. No method is added to the object, and the search for the messages to it is the search of its own class.

[class.methods.deviation.105]

The access check of the access rule for a message that START sends is made as for the same message sent by the code that starts it, as the Deviation 105 rule states; ooRexx raises 97.2 for every started private message and 97.1 for every started PACKAGE message.

[class.methods.deviation.110]

This Deviation is provisional. An object sees every change made, at any time, to the methods of its class, of that class's superclasses and of their mixin classes, by define, defineMethods, delete, inherit and uninherit (the rule on changes): also when the object has methods of its own from setMethod or enhanced, and when the class has been changed before. A class object follows its metaclass in the same way. ooRexx copies the method table into existing instances. A define, defineMethods or delete sent to a class, even one that changes nothing, does not reach the instances that exist already, and no later change reaches them after it: not to the class, not to its superclasses or their mixin classes, and not inherit or uninherit. An object given a method by setMethod sees no later change to its class or to the classes behind it. A class object sees no change to its metaclass or to the classes behind it that is made after the class itself (Deviation 110). The first example is the one of the rule on changes, with a define sent to K itself and an instance B that is made after it: A, B and S answer alike after every change. The second example gives an object an own method with setMethod and another with enhanced, and changes the class afterwards. The third follows a class object over changes to its metaclass.

.base~define('two', 'return "T"')

Object is the root of the class hierarchy: every class has it among its ancestors, so every object understands the methods of this page, and every class but those that Class~new makes understands its class method new. The page specifies each of them: what it accepts, in which order it checks, what it answers, and which messages it sends to its receiver or to its arguments, so that a class which overrides a method that another one sends can predict what happens.

The names that a program gives an object, its string value and its default name belong to the chapter index; the rules below link to them. How a message finds a method, and what setMethod and unsetMethod do to that search, belong to the method search. The examples that show an error use a small routine try that sends the message in its argument and prints either the answer or the error code, as the builtin pages do.

Class methods

[class.object.new]

The class method new makes an object of the class that received the message and sends it init with the arguments of new, as the new rule says. The arguments keep their places: an argument that is omitted in the middle of the list is omitted in the message to init, and omitted places at the end add nothing to the argument count, as the count rule says. The answer of new is the new object, whatever init answers. Every class that a directive, subclass or mixinClass made has this method, mixin classes and abstract classes included, and an abstract class refuses it as the abstract rule says. The class that Class~new makes is the one exception, and its page rule says what it answers.

o = .dd~new(1, , 3)
o = .dd~new(1, )
o = .dd~new(, )
o = .dd~new(, 2)

call try '.abs~new'
exit

  say arg(1) '=>' r~class~id
  return
bad: say arg(1) '=>' condition('o')~code
  return

Making and copying

[class.object.init]

The init method of Object accepts no argument and answers no value; it changes nothing. A class that declares its own init replaces it, and reaches it with a scoped send to super. new sends init as the new rule says, and a program may send it again at any time, as the init rule says. With any argument the method raises SYNTAX 93.902.

call try '.object~new~init'
call try '.object~new~init(1)'
call try '.object~new~init(, )'
call try 'r = .object~new~init'
say .keep~new(5)~kept
exit

  interpret arg(1)
  say arg(1) '=> no error'
  return
bad: say arg(1) '=>' condition('o')~code
  return

::attribute kept
::method init
  expose kept
  use arg kept
  self~init:super

[class.object.copy]

copy answers a new object of the same class. The copy has the object variables of the receiver, each holding the same object that the receiver's variable holds, so the copy is shallow, and it has the same methods, the receiver's own methods included, and the same name. The copy has its own table of the object's own methods, holding the same method objects, and the variables of those methods are copied as the others are, so a change to one object's own methods or to those variables does not reach the other. It does not send init, and takes no argument: with one it raises SYNTAX 93.902. hashCode answers a string, the hash code of the receiver, and takes no argument. It answers the same string every time for one object. [class.object.hasmethod]

hasMethod answers 1 when a message with the given name finds a method of the receiver, and 0 when it does not. The name is compared in upper case. A class receiver is searched in its class-side order, so hasMethod shows which side a name is on. The argument is a string, or an object whose request with the argument STRING answers one; any other object, .nil included, raises SYNTAX 88.909, and no argument raises 93.903. [class.object.instancemethods]

instanceMethods answers a supplier whose indexes are method names in upper case and whose items are method objects. It lists names that exist when it is sent, and a later change to a class or to the receiver does not reach the supplier. The order of its entries is not specified (Deviation 33). Without an argument it lists every method of the receiver's own methods and of every class of its order, so a name that more than one of them holds is listed once for each. With a class that is in the order of the receiver as its argument, it lists the methods of that class's table, and with .nil the receiver's own methods. With any other argument, a number or a string or a class outside the order included, the supplier has no entries. A table entry that hides a name is not listed; the name is still listed from every other table of the order that holds a method for it, so the listing does not show what the search finds. The argument may be given once: a second raises SYNTAX 93.902. For a class receiver the order is the class-side one.

Conversion

[class.object.request]

request answers the receiver converted to the kind of object that its argument names, or .nil. The argument is a string, taken in upper case. The method first asks whether the receiver has a method named MAKE followed by that name; if it has, request sends that message to the receiver with no argument and answers what it answers, whatever that is, and the answer is not checked: a method may answer .nil or an object of another class. The message is checked for access as if the code that sent request had sent it, as for send: a PRIVATE method runs when request is sent by code that the access rule lets send it, a method of a subclass included, and raises SYNTAX 97.2 otherwise, and a PACKAGE method raises 97.3 when request is sent from another package. When there is no such method, UNKNOWN plays no part, the method compares the name with the id of the receiver's class, without regard to case: when they are equal it answers the receiver itself, and otherwise .nil. The id is that of the class of the receiver only, not of its superclasses. The argument is checked as for hasMethod: none raises 93.903, .nil and objects without a string value 88.909, and a second argument 93.902.

o = .doc~new
say o~request('string') '|' o~request('Array')~class~id '|',
  o~request('doc')~class~id
say o~request('nosuchzz') '|' o~request('') '|' o~request('object')
say .sub~new~request('doc') '|' .sub~new~request('sub')~class~id
say .doc~new~request('plain') '|' .doc~new~request('lazy')
say .doc~new~request('wild')~class~id
say .catchall~new~request('anything')
say 'abc'~request('string') '|' 12~request('integer') '|',
  'x'~request('string')~class~id
call try 'o~request'
call try 'o~request(.nil)'
call try 'o~request(.object~new)'
call try 'o~request("string", 1)'
call try 'o~request("secret")'
exit
try:
  signal on syntax name bad
  interpret 'r =' arg(1)
  say arg(1) '=>' r
  return
bad: say arg(1) '=>' condition('o')~code
  return

  return .nil
::method makewild
  return .object~new

  return 1

  return 'unknown was run'

[class.object.request.access]

The access check of request is that of the code that sent it. In the example, a class in a package of its own has a method that sends request and reaches the PRIVATE and PACKAGE methods, and the program of another package does not.

f = 'spec-class-object-request-zq.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
call lineout f, '::class doc public'
call lineout f, '::method makepk package'
call lineout f, '  return "pk ran"'
call lineout f, '::method makesecret private'
call lineout f, '  return "secret ran"'
call lineout f, '::method inner'
call lineout f, '  signal on syntax name b'
call lineout f, '  return self~request(arg(1))'
call lineout f, 'b: return condition("o")~code'
call lineout f

  'say o~inner("pk") o~inner("secret")', -
  'signal on syntax name b', -
  'say o~request("pk")', -
  'b: say condition("o")~code', -
  'signal on syntax name c', -
  'say o~request("secret")', -
  'c: say condition("o")~code', -
  '::requires "'f'"')
p = .package~new('spec-class-object-request-main', src)
call sysfiledelete f

[class.object.request.sends]

request sends one message to its receiver: MAKE followed by the upper case name of its argument, with no argument, when the receiver has a method of that name (see hasMethod). It sends nothing else to the receiver: it does not send class, so a class that declares class does not change which id is compared, and it sends no UNKNOWN. request sends nothing to the argument other than what the string conversion sends.

o = .watch~new
r = o~request('watch')
say (r == o)
r = o~request('abc')
say r
r = o~request('other')
say r
l = .liar~new
r = l~request('liar')
say (r == l)
r = l~request('box')
say r
::class watch
::method makeabc package
  say 'makeabc sent' arg()
  return 'ABC'
::method class
  say 'class sent'
  return .watch
::method unknown
  say 'unknown sent' arg(1)
  return 'u'
::class liar
::method class
  return .box
::class box

Sending messages

[class.object.send]

send sends the message that its first argument names to the receiver, with the remaining arguments as the arguments of that message, in order, and answers what the message answers. An omitted argument stays omitted in the message, and omitted places at the end add nothing to the argument count. The message is an ordinary one: it is found by the search rule and so also goes to UNKNOWN when nothing is found, raises NOMETHOD (SYNTAX 97.1 when untrapped) when there is no UNKNOWN, and is checked for access as if the code that called send had sent it, so send('secret') from outside the class raises 97.2 for a private method that no UNKNOWN takes. The name is taken in upper case, and a number literal such as 12 names the message 12, as the same characters in quotes do (Deviation 107). The first argument is a string, or an array of two items, the name and a class, which starts the search at that class as the scoped send rule says. An object that is not a string is sent request with the argument ARRAY, and the answer is used as the two-item form, whatever the class of the first argument is (the sends rule; an instance of a subclass of String is read as Deviation 109 states). .nil, and an object that answers .nil, raise SYNTAX 93.972, an answer that is no array and an array of another size 93.946, an array whose first item is missing 88.901 and one whose first item has no string value 88.909, and no argument 88.901. The null string is a name like any other: it names the abuttal method (the joining rule), so send('', 'x') joins and send('') raises that method's 93.903. An array whose second item is not a class raises 88.914. A message that answers nothing makes send answer nothing.

o = .w~new
say o~send('hello', 'W', 'F')
say o~send('HeLLo', 'W', 'F')
say o~send('count') '|' o~send('count', 1, , 3) '|' o~send('count', 1, )
say o~send(.array~of('hello', .w), 'A', 'B')
u = .watcher~new
say u~send('nosuchzz', 1, 2)
say o~send('inside', 'secret') o~send('pack')
call try 'o~send'
call try 'o~send(.nil)'
call try 'o~send("", "x")'
call try 'o~send("")'
call try 'o~send("nosuchzz")'
call try 'o~send(.array~of("count"))'
call try 'o~send(.array~of("count", .w, 3))'
call try 'o~send(.array~of(.nil, .w))'
call try 'o~send(.array~of(.object~new, .w))'
call try 'o~send(.array~new(2)~~put(.w, 2))'
call try 'o~send("secret")'
call try 'o~send("nothing")'
call try 'o~send(.array~of("count", 1))'
exit

[class.object.send.sends]

send sends a first argument that is not a string the message request with the argument ARRAY; the same holds for sendWith, startWith and start, at the call, and for the message name of Message~new, at new. The answer of request is read as the previous rule says. The order differs by method. send and start send request first. sendWith checks the number of its arguments, then sends request to the name, then sends request to the second argument. startWith checks the number of its arguments and that the second is there, sends request to the second argument, and then to the name, so an error in the array leaves the name unasked. Message~new sends request to the name after checking the target, before the option and its arguments are read. A first argument that is a string is sent nothing. The example shows the messages for an instance of an Array subclass and for an object that is no array but answers one.

o = .w~new
call try 'o~sendWith(.duck~new, .logged~new)'
call try 'o~startWith(.duck~new, .logged~new)~result'
call try 'o~sendWith(.duck~new, .logged~new, 3)'
call try 'o~send(.larr~of("count", .w), 9)'
call try 'o~send(.wrong~new, 6)'
call try 'o~send(.none~new, 6)'
call try 'o~send(.larr~of("count"), 6)'
exit

[class.object.sendwith]

sendWith is send with the arguments of the message in an array. The first argument names the message as for send, and is checked first. The second argument is an array, or an object that answers an array to the message request with the argument ARRAY, which is what sendWith sends it; an object that answers anything but an array, including .nil, and an array of more than one dimension, raise SYNTAX 88.913. The items of the array are the arguments in order; a place of a sparse array that holds nothing is an omitted argument, and the argument count is the position of the last item that is present. Both arguments are required (88.901, one missing) and a third raises 93.902.

say o~sendWith('count', .array~new(3))
say o~sendWith('count', .list~of(1, 2))
say o~sendWith('count', .holder~new)
say o~sendWith('count', 'abc')

call try 'o~sendWith("count", .array~new, 3)'
call try 'o~sendWith(.nil, .nil)'
call try 'o~sendWith("nosuchzz", .nil)'
exit

[class.object.start]

start makes a message object for the message that its first argument names, with the remaining arguments, and starts it so that it is run by another activity, while the sender goes on. It answers the message object at once and does not wait for the message to run. The name and the arguments are checked by start as send does, with the same errors raised at the call to start, except that the null string is a name like any other, so start('') answers a message object; an error in the message itself, such as a name with no method or the abuttal method's missing argument, is not raised by start: the message object keeps it, and it is raised when the result is asked for. The access check is that of Deviation 105. How the message is scheduled and what the message object offers is specified in the environment chapter and with the Message class; the examples show only results that no scheduling changes.

say m~result~isNil

call try 'o~start'
call try 'o~start(.nil)'
call try 'o~start(.array~of("count"))'
call try 'o~start(.array~of("count", 1))'

The receiver's own methods

[class.object.setmethod]

setMethod gives the receiver a method of its own, as the object method rule says, and answers no value. It is private, with the restriction that the access rule gives. The first argument is the name and is required (SYNTAX 88.901); an object that is no string and whose request with the argument STRING answers no string raises 88.909. The second is the method: a method object, a string that holds the source of a method, or an array, whose items are read as the source rule reads them, so an item that gives no string raises SYNTAX 93.952. These are instances of Method, String and Array themselves; an instance of a subclass of one of them, Method included, is converted as any other object is. Any other object is sent request with the argument ARRAY, and the array it answers is used; when it answers no array, it is sent request with the argument STRING, and a string answer is used as the source (the sends rule). .nil, and an object whose request with STRING answers .nil, raise SYNTAX 93.974, so a subclass of Method that declares neither MAKEARRAY nor MAKESTRING is refused. When that request answers an object that is not a string, the result is not specified. The method that the receiver gets runs the code of a method object that is given, with the scope that the scope rule says. It is not specified whether the method object that the receiver holds is the argument itself or a copy of it, and what scope the argument object answers afterwards is not specified either. The checks run in this order: the number of arguments, the name, the method, the scope. With no second argument the name is hidden for the receiver. The third argument is the scope, FLOAT or OBJECT as the scope rule says; another value raises 88.916, and .nil raises 88.909. A fourth argument raises 93.902. A source that does not translate raises the translation error from setMethod. The code of a method made from a source runs with the scope FLOAT, whose object variables are separate from those of any class: the methods that the receiver got by setMethod with FLOAT, by run and by enhanced share one set, which is kept for the receiver.

[class.object.unsetmethod]

unsetMethod takes the name off the receiver again, as the object method rule says, and answers no value. It is private with the restriction of the access rule. The argument is the name, required (SYNTAX 88.901), and a value that is no string raises 88.909. A second argument raises 93.902, and the number of arguments is checked first, so a second argument raises it even when the name is missing. The name is taken in upper case. A name for which the receiver has no method of its own is not an error and changes nothing, and so does a name that only a class holds: the class's method stays. A name that setMethod replaced twice is taken off with one unsetMethod. A method that enhanced added to the receiver is not taken off by it, and the receiver keeps it.

o~sm('A1', 'return "second"')

say o~hasMethod('a1')

call try 'x = o~umv'
call try 'o~um("nosuchzz")'
call try 'o~um("base")'

say o~base
o~um('BASE')
say o~base

say e~extra e~hasMethod('extra')
call try 'o~um'
call try 'o~um(.nil)'
call try 'o~um("a1", 2)'
call try 'o~um(, 2)'
call try 'o~unsetMethod("outside")'
exit

[class.object.run]

run runs a method on the receiver once and answers what that method answers. It is private, with the restriction of the access rule. The first argument is the method: a method object, a string that holds the source of a method, or an array of strings, one for each line, which run turns into a method as setMethod does (the argument rule), with the same conversions and the same errors for a value that is no method or fails to translate, and SYNTAX 88.901 when the argument is missing. The method is not kept. The second argument is an option, whose first letter counts and the rest is ignored: I passes the remaining arguments to the method one for each, in order, with omitted ones omitted, and A passes the items of the third argument, converted as sendWith converts its array: a missing array raises SYNTAX 88.901, and one that converts to no array, or to an array of more than one dimension, raises 88.913. A sparse array's empty places are omitted arguments. Without an option the method gets no arguments, and arguments after an omitted option raise 88.901. Any other option, the null string included, raises SYNTAX 93.915; .nil raises 88.909. The checks run in this order: the method, the option, the array. The code runs with the scope FLOAT: its object variables are those of setMethod's floating methods, not those of any class. When the method answers nothing, run answers nothing.

o = .w~new
say o~go('return "plain" arg()')
say o~go('return arg() "|" arg(1) arg(2)', 'I', 'a', 'b')
say o~go('return arg() "|" arg(1) arg(2)', 'individual', 'a', 'b')
say o~go('return arg() "|" arg(1) arg(2)', 'Array', .array~of('a', 'b'))
say o~go('return arg() "|" arg(1, "e") arg(2, "e") arg(3, "e")', 'a', -
  .array~of(1, , 3))
say o~go('return arg() "|" arg(1, "e") arg(2, "e")', 'i', 1, )
say o~go('return arg()', 'A', .array~new)
say o~go('return arg()', 'A', .list~of(1, 2, 3))
say o~go(.array~of('x = 5', 'return x * 2'))
say o~go(.method~new('', 'return "method object"'))
say o~go('expose v; v = 7; return v')
say o~go('expose v; return v + 1')
say o~v
say o~go('return self~class~id')
call try 'o~run("return 1")'
call try 'o~go'

[class.object.run.sends]

run sends the message request with the argument ARRAY, once, to a method argument that is not an instance of Method, String or Array itself, and uses the array it answers; when that answers no array, it sends request with the argument STRING, once, and uses a string answer as the source, as setMethod does. [class.object.deviation.4]

Whether two equal strings or numbers that were built separately are one object is not specified, and shows only through identityHash and the identity collections (Deviation 4). The hashCode of equal strings is equal, and so is any value comparison; ooRexx often answers a new object where interrexx answers the existing one.

a = 'ab' || 'c'
b = 'a' || 'bc'
say (a == b) (a~hashCode == b~hashCode)
say (a~hashCode == 'abc'~hashCode) (a~copy == a)
n = 10 + 2
say (n == 12) (n~hashCode == 12~hashCode)

1 1
1 1
1 1
[class.object.deviation.28]

A method of a built-in class that setMethod gives to an object of an unrelated class, or run or enhanced runs on one, is refused: the program ends with exit code 120. ooRexx reads the object with the layout of the other class and answers garbage or crashes. The check happens when the method is run, so setMethod itself still answers no value.

say 'after'

Deviations: D32, D33, D63, D108, D109, D110, D114

Class is the class of the class objects: every class is an instance of it, or of a subclass of it, which is a metaclass. Its instance methods are therefore what every class object understands: the methods that make and change classes (subclass, mixinClass, define, inherit and the others), that answer questions about a class (id, superClasses, method) and that make objects (enhanced). Class is a subclass of Object, so a class also understands the methods of Object. Its class method new makes a new class.

The chapter index lists how the library classes are related and what new and defaultName do. The method search specifies what define, inherit and the other methods that change a class do to the order in which methods are looked up; this page specifies their arguments, their checks and their errors. A class of the class library accepts none of the methods that change it, as the library rule says. The examples that show an error use a small routine try, as the builtin pages do.

Class methods

[class.class.new]

The class method new of Class makes a class. It is a class method of Class and so of every metaclass, a subclass of Class, and it is not the new that makes the instances of an ordinary class (the Object rule specifies that one). Its first argument is the id of the new class: a string, or an object whose request with the argument STRING answers one, and the null string and a number are allowed. The new class has Object as its superclass, is not a mixin class and not abstract, and is an instance of the class that received new, which is also its metaclass; its package is the package of that class, so .class~new gives a class whose package is the one of the library and a user's metaclass gives one whose package is the package that declares the metaclass. new sends the new class the message init with the arguments that follow the id, in order, and answers the class. The class answers no new of its own: a message new to it raises SYNTAX 97.1, but a subclass of it, made with subclass, has the new of every class. The id is required (SYNTAX 93.901, none), .nil and an object with no string value raise 88.909, and the arguments after the id are those of init, so Class itself, whose init takes none, raises 93.902 for one.

f = .class~new('Foo')
say f~id f~class~id f~superclass~id f~queryMixinClass f~isAbstract
call try 'f~new'
g = f~subclass('Bar')
say g~new~class~id g~superclass~id

say m~id m~class~id m~extra m~metaclass~id
m = .meta~new('Quux')
say m~extra '|' .class~new('')~id '|' .class~new(12)~id '|',
  .class~new(.mk~new)~id
say (.class~new('P')~package == .array~package),
  (.meta~new('P')~package == .context~package)
call try '.class~new'
call try '.class~new(.nil)'
call try '.class~new(.object~new)'
call try '.class~new("Foo", 1)'
exit

[class.class.id]

id answers the id of the class as a string: the name of the class in the case that the ::CLASS directive wrote it, which is upper case for a name written as a symbol, or the string that subclass, mixinClass or new got. [class.class.package]

package answers the package that the class belongs to: for a class that a ::CLASS directive made, the package of the program that declares it, and for a class of the class library the package that holds the library, whose name is REXX. A class made by subclass or mixinClass belongs to no package, and package answers .nil; a class made by the new of a metaclass has the package of that metaclass (the new rule). The supplier lists the names that exist when it is made, and a later change does not reach it. The order of its entries is not specified (Deviation 33). Changing the class

[class.class.define]

define gives the class an instance method, or hides a name, for every instance of the class, those that exist already included, as the rule on changes and the hidden-name rule say, and the search finds it as the search rule says, and answers no value. The first argument is the name, taken in upper case, and may be any string, a number included. The second is the method, in the forms that setMethod takes: a method object, a string that is the source of a method, or an array of strings, one for each line, converted as the setMethod rule says and with the messages of the sends rule. The method that the class holds runs the code of the method object that is given, with the class as its scope. It is not specified whether the method object that the class holds is the argument itself or a copy of it, and what scope the argument object answers afterwards is not specified either. A method replaces what the table held for the name. With no second argument the name is hidden; with .nil as the second argument the name is hidden from the search as well, but the table no longer holds an entry for it that method could answer. An object whose request with STRING answers .nil, as an instance of a subclass of Method that declares neither MAKEARRAY nor MAKESTRING does, raises SYNTAX 93.974, and a source that does not translate raises its translation error from define. A name is required (88.901), a name that is no string and has no string value raises 88.909, and a third argument raises 93.902. The number of arguments is checked first, then the class, then the name, then the method. The classes of the class library accept no define (the library rule), which raises 98.985 before any argument is checked. The examples use objects made after the change.

When that answers no array, it sends request with the argument STRING, once, and uses a string answer as the source; one whose answer is .nil raises SYNTAX 93.974. It sends nothing to the class.

[class.class.definemethods]

defineMethods gives the class every method of a collection, as define gives one. The argument is a collection whose indexes are the method names and whose items are method objects, strings or arrays of strings, as define takes them, or .nil to hide the name, converted as define converts its method, with the same errors for an item that is no method (SYNTAX 93.974). A method object item is installed as define installs a method object: the class holds a method that runs the code of the item with the class as its scope, and it is not specified whether that is the item itself or a copy, or what scope the item answers afterwards. Every item is made into a method before any is defined, so an error leaves the class unchanged. The names are taken in upper case. A name that the class holds is replaced. The method sends the argument the message supplier, with no argument, once, and takes the pairs of what the supplier answers one after the other, so any object that answers a supplier will do, and the indexes of an array are the names 1, 2 and so on. An object that has no supplier method raises SYNTAX 97.1, as .nil does. The object that supplier answers need not be a Supplier (Deviation 108). The argument is required (88.901) and a second raises 93.902. The number of arguments is checked first, then the class, then the argument. The method answers no value, and the classes of the class library accept it as little as define: they raise 98.985 before the argument is checked.

[class.class.delete]

delete removes the entry that the class's own table holds for a name, taken in upper case, whether the entry is a method or a mark that hides the name, and answers no value. A name that define hid with .nil as the method is hidden by such a mark too, and delete ends the hiding at once (Deviation 117). The name is then looked up in the classes behind, as the hidden-name rule says. A name that the table does not hold is not an error and changes nothing, and delete does not remove a method that only a class behind holds. The name is required (SYNTAX 88.901), .nil raises 88.909, and a second argument raises 93.902. The number of arguments is checked first, then the class, then the name. The classes of the class library accept no delete (the library rule); they raise 98.985 before the name is checked.

[class.class.inherit]

inherit makes the class inherit a mixin class, as the INHERIT option of the directive does, and answers no value. The first argument is the mixin class. The second, if given, is a class in the class's list of superclasses, and the mixin class is put immediately in front of it; without it the mixin class is put at the end of the list. How that changes the order of the class, and so the search, is specified by the change rule. An argument that is no mixin class, .nil and a string among them, raises SYNTAX 98.942, and so does a class that is not a mixin class. A mixin class that is already inherited, or that is an ancestor of the class or has the class among its ancestors, raises 98.944. A mixin class whose base class is not the superclass of the class or one of its ancestors raises 98.943. A second argument that is not in the list of superclasses, .nil included, raises 98.945. The first argument is required (88.901) and a third raises 93.902. The checks run in this order: the number of arguments, the class, then 98.942, 98.944, 98.943 and 98.945. A class of the class library accepts no inherit (the library rule); it raises 98.985 before the arguments are checked.

Making classes and objects

[class.class.subclass]

subclass makes a new class that has the receiver as its superclass and answers it. The first argument is the id of the class, which id answers, a string or an object whose request with the argument STRING answers one: none raises SYNTAX 88.901, and .nil and an object with no string value raise 88.909. The null string and a number are allowed, the id need not be unique, and the class is not entered in .environment. The second argument is the metaclass, a class that is Class or a subclass of it; the new class is an instance of it. When the argument is omitted, the metaclass is the one of the receiver, as metaClass says. Any other value, .nil and a class that is no metaclass included, raises SYNTAX 99.927. The third argument is a collection of class methods, given as defineMethods takes its argument, and the new class gets them as class methods of its own, which its subclasses inherit as they inherit any class method. The new class is not a mixin class and not abstract, whatever the receiver is, and it has no package. A fourth argument raises 93.902. The arguments are checked in the order: their number (93.902), the metaclass, the id, then the collection. When an error is raised, the receiver has no new subclass. The method does not check whether the receiver may have subclasses, so a subclass of a library class is made like any other.

[class.class.subclass.sends]

subclass sends the message new to the metaclass, which is the receiver's metaclass when there is no metaclass argument, with the id as its only argument, and the class that new builds for it is the new class: a class method new of the metaclass runs (the new rule specifies the one that Class supplies). The class that new answers receives init, from that new, while it is still a plain class: its superclass is Object and it has only the methods of its metaclass. subclass then sends the third argument supplier, once, with no argument, as defineMethods does. It then makes the receiver the superclass, adds the class methods, sets the package to .nil, and sends the class init a second time, with no argument. A class method init that the receiver declares is therefore run only by the second init. activate is not sent. A new of the metaclass that answers a class that subclass, mixinclass or a ::CLASS directive has already completed, or a class of the library, is treated as Deviation 32 states. A new of the metaclass that answers an object that is not a class raises SYNTAX 98.900 from subclass or mixinclass, in the program that sent it, where it can be trapped (Deviation 114).

say 'plain done'
y = .k~subclass('S2', .meta)
say 'meta done'
z = .k~subclass('S3', , .sp~new)
say z~cm

[class.class.mixinclass]

mixinClass makes a new mixin class that has the receiver as its base class and answers it. Its arguments, their order, their checks and their errors are those of subclass, and so are the messages it sends, in the same order (the sends rule). The new class becomes a mixin class, with its base class, only after the second init: at both inits, queryMixinClass answers 0 and baseClass answers the class itself. Afterwards it is a mixin class, which queryMixinClass shows, its superclass is the receiver, and its baseClass is the receiver or, when the receiver is a mixin class, the receiver's base class. Only a mixin class can be inherited: the new class can be named in inherit of a class whose superclass is the receiver or a descendant of it.
