[class.class.enhanced]

enhanced answers a new object of the receiver whose own methods are those of a collection, added to the methods of the class. The first argument is the collection: its indexes are the names and its items are method objects, strings or arrays of strings, or .nil to hide a name, as defineMethods takes them, with the same errors, except for method object items: the new object holds a method that runs the code of the item, with .nil as its scope. It is not specified whether that method object is the item itself or a copy, or what scope the item answers afterwards. The items are made into methods before new is sent, so an error in one sends no new; the arguments after it are the arguments of the new object. The method sends the collection the message supplier, with no argument, and then sends the receiver the message new with the remaining arguments, so that the class method new that the class declares runs and init gets those arguments. The answer of supplier is read as the defineMethods sends rule says: a Supplier directly, any other object through four messages (Deviation 108). The object that new answers gets the methods and is the answer. Its class is the receiver; the object follows the rules of the enhanced rule for the search, and its default name is that of the default name rule. The abstract property of the receiver is not checked, and the receiver need not accept the arguments after the collection: that is the business of its new and init. The collection is required (SYNTAX 93.901), and an object with no supplier method, .nil included, raises 97.1.

[class.class.deviation.32]

When the new of a metaclass answers a class that subclass, mixinclass or a ::CLASS directive has already completed, or a class of the library such as Array, while subclass or mixinclass makes a class with that metaclass, interrexx ends the program with exit code 120; ooRexx rewires the existing class in place, so that y~id in the examples answers Array. A ::CLASS directive with METACLASS is treated alike, as the chapter rule says. String is the class of every string of characters: a literal, a number, and the result of any operation that makes text. A program never needs to make one with new, but it can, and it can subclass String to give strings more behavior. String is a subclass of Object and inherits Comparable, so a string also understands the methods of Object.

Most methods of String are the methods that a built-in function runs, such as left and pos. The behavior of each belongs to the page of its function, and one rule lists them, with what changes when one is sent as a message. The operator methods, such as + and ||, belong to the expressions chapter, and one rule lists them too. The class methods that name sets of characters and make strings, and the methods that only the class has, such as caselessEquals, makeArray and [], are specified in full below. Examples that show an error use a small routine try, as the builtin pages do.

The class

[class.string.value]

Every string is an instance of String, whether it is a literal, a number, the result of a calculation or of a comparison, or the answer of a method: class answers String for all of them, and there is no separate class for numbers. A string is its own string value, so string and makeString answer a string with the same characters.

say ('a' || 'b')~class~id 'a'~c2x~class~id .string~new('x')~class~id

[class.string.subclass]

A program makes a subclass of String with the directive or with the subclass method of Class. An instance is made with new, takes the characters given there, and has the class of the receiver of new. It is a string wherever a string is wanted, and the class-side methods of String are understood by the subclass. A String method sent to the instance works on the characters of the instance and answers a new string of class String, not an instance of the subclass, and copy, which Object supplies, answers another instance of the subclass. Wherever a string, a number, a logical value or a whole number is read from the instance, as the receiver or as an argument, its own characters are read and none of REQUEST, MAKESTRING and STRING is sent to it (Deviation 109). The instance may have attributes and methods of its own, and an object name (Deviation 36).

[class.string.new]

new makes a string. Its first argument is required, and gives the characters: the string value of the argument, which is the argument itself for a string, a number and an instance of a subclass of String included, and its the string that its request with the argument STRING answers for another object. For another object new has no fallback to string, as the methods that take a string argument have none (the string-value rule). Without an argument new raises SYNTAX 93.903, and with an argument that gives no string, .nil and an object with only a string method included, SYNTAX 88.909. The object that new makes has the class of the receiver, and the characters are in place before init runs, so an init of a subclass can use them. init is sent the arguments after the first, as the new rule says, so a second argument raises SYNTAX 93.902 for a class whose init is that of Object.

[class.string.constants]

The class-side methods alnum, alpha, blank, cntrl, cr, digit, graph, lower, nl, null, print, punct, space, tab, upper and xdigit each answer a string of characters, a character class. None takes an argument (SYNTAX 93.902), and an instance of String does not understand them (SYNTAX 97.1), though a subclass of String understands them as the class does. Only ASCII characters are in any class, and they are written here by code, in ascending order unless the list says otherwise. alnum is the digits 0 to 9, then A to Z, then a to z; alpha is A to Z, then a to z; blank is the tab '09'x and the blank '20'x; cntrl is '00'x to '1F'x and '7F'x; cr is '0D'x, nl is '0A'x, null is '00'x and tab is '09'x; digit is 0 to 9, and xdigit is 0 to 9, A to F, then a to f; graph is '21'x to '7E'x and print is '20'x to '7E'x; lower is a to z and upper is A to Z; punct is the characters of graph that are not in alnum; and space is '09'x to '0D'x and '20'x. The instance methods lower and upper are different methods that a builtin runs.

[class.string.makearray]

makeArray answers a new array of strings, the parts of the receiver, and takes at most one argument, the separator, whose string value is taken like that of an argument of new (SYNTAX 88.909 for an object with none). Without a separator, or when it is omitted, the parts are the lines: the text is cut at each line feed, '0A'x, and a carriage return '0D'x right before a line feed is not part of the line. A carriage return alone is part of its line. With a separator the text is cut at each occurrence of the whole separator, found from the left and without overlap, and the case of letters matters; the null string as the separator makes each character a part. The text before the first cut is the first part, so a text that starts with a separator has an empty first part, and a text that ends with one has no empty part after it. A receiver that is the null string answers an array with no part. A subclass instance and a plain string answer the same.

[class.string.brackets]

The method [], which the subscript syntax string[n] and string[n, len] send (the subscript rule), answers part of the receiver. With one argument n it answers the character at position n, and with two it answers the len characters from position n. The part is cut at the end of the receiver and is not padded, so a position past the end answers the null string. n must be a positive whole number (SYNTAX 93.924) and len a non-negative whole number (93.923); a value that is not a number at all raises the same error as one out of range, and the arguments are checked from left to right. An omitted n raises 93.903, an omitted len is as no len, and a third argument raises 93.902.

Equality and order

[class.string.equals]

equals answers 1 when the argument has exactly the characters of the receiver, and 0 otherwise. It is a strict comparison of text: case matters, a trailing blank matters, and numbers are not compared as numbers, so 1 and 1.0 are not equal. The argument is required (SYNTAX 93.903) and a second raises 93.902. The argument's string value is found as the joining operators find it, so an object whose request answers no string is compared by its string text and .nil as the text The NIL object; no argument is refused.

call try "'abc'~equals('a', 'b')"

[class.string.compareto]

compareTo compares the receiver with its first argument and answers 0 when they are equal, 1 when the receiver is the greater and -1 when it is the lesser. The comparison is of characters by their codes, unsigned, so case matters and 'FF'x is greater than '00'x, and a string that is a leading part of another is the lesser, whatever follows; numbers are not compared as numbers. The second argument start is the position, 1 by default, from which both strings are compared, and the third length is the number of characters compared of each, by default all that are left. A part that runs past the end of a string is cut there. The arguments are checked from left to right: the first, other, is required (SYNTAX 93.903) and has a string value as the conversion rule says (88.909, as for .nil; only the answer of request with the argument STRING is used, and then only for an object that is no string); start must be a positive whole number (93.924) and length a non-negative whole number (93.923); a fourth argument raises 93.902.

[class.string.contains]

contains answers 1 when its first argument, the needle, occurs in the receiver, and 0 otherwise; a needle that is the null string is never found. The search covers the whole receiver unless start, a position, and length, a number of characters from it, limit it, and then the needle must lie within that part. A start or a length that reaches past the end is cut there. The needle is required (SYNTAX 93.903) and is a string or else uses the string it gives (88.909 for .nil), start must be a positive whole number (93.924) and length a non-negative whole number (93.923); the arguments are checked from left to right, and a fourth argument raises 93.902. [class.string.match]

match tests whether a part of its second argument occurs at a given place in the receiver. The arguments are start, the position in the receiver, other, the string, n, the position in other where the part begins (1 by default), and length, the number of characters in the part (by default all that are left from n). [class.string.ceiling]

ceiling answers the smallest whole number that is not less than the receiver, which must be a number (SYNTAX 93.943). [class.string.modulo]

modulo answers the remainder of the receiver divided by its argument n. The answer is never negative and is less than n, so for a negative receiver (-7)~modulo(4) is 1. The receiver must be a number (SYNTAX 93.943) and a whole number (93.940): a number written with no period and no exponent is a whole number whatever its length, and any other number must be exactly whole, without rounding, and its value must have at most NUMERIC DIGITS digits. The argument is required (93.903) and must be a positive whole number (93.907) in the same sense, checked after the receiver; a second argument raises 93.902. An argument that is not a string is converted to a number as the conversion rule says, as the other numeric arguments are. The remainder is found as the // operator finds it, and written as that operator writes it, so a quotient wider than NUMERIC DIGITS raises SYNTAX 26.12, for a negative receiver too.

Methods that a builtin function runs

[class.string.builtins]

A built-in function that runs as a String method is also a method of String with the name of the function, and the behavior of the method is stated on the page of the function: what it accepts, its defaults, its results and the checks it makes. The pages say it as a function call and show the method form beside it. The methods are abbrev, abs, b2x, bitAnd, bitOr, bitXor, c2d, c2x, center, centre, changeStr, compare, copies, countStr, d2c, d2x, dataType, delStr, delWord, format, insert, lastPos, left, length, lower, max, min, overlay, pos, reverse, right, sign, space, strip, subWord, substr, translate, trunc, upper, verify, word, wordIndex, wordLength, wordPos, words, x2b, x2c and x2d, each with the rule that opens its page. A method of this kind needs no rule of its own here, but the rules that follow state what is the same for all of them when they are sent as messages: their errors (the message rule) and their receiver (the receiver rule). Functions that a program calls but a string does not understand as a message, such as arg and xrange, are not among them: their pages say so.

say 'Hello'~left(3) 'Hello'~pos('l') 'Hello'~reverse 'a b c'~words
say 'abc'~centre(7, '.') '255'~d2x 'ff'~x2d 'abc'~substr(2, 1) 'ABC'~lower
say '3.14159'~format(2, 2) '-4.7'~trunc '4'~max(9, 2) '-4'~sign 'abc'~length
say 'a-b'~translate('+', '-') 'hello world'~wordIndex(2) 'ab'~copies(3)

[class.string.builtins.errors]

A method of the list is checked as the method itself checks it, argument by argument and from left to right, without the earlier check that a function call makes. The function form first checks the form of its arguments, as the order rule says, and raises the codes of the whole-number, pad and argument count rules. In the message form an argument that fails its form raises the code of its range check. The message form raises these errors: for a position that is not a positive whole number, SYNTAX 93.924 whatever the value is, abc or 0 or 1.5; for a length that is not a non-negative whole number, 93.923; for a pad that is not a single character, 93.922; for a missing argument, or an omitted one that is followed by another, 93.903; and for too many arguments, 93.902, as the argument rules say. A count or a number of copies that is not a non-negative whole number raises 93.906, and the other arguments raise the code that the page of the builtin gives. Because the message form checks one argument at a time, a bad position before a length that is not a number is the error raised, where the function form raises 40.12 for the length first.

call try "'abc'~substr('x')"
call try "substr('abc', 'x')"
call try "'abc'~substr(0, 'x')"
call try "substr('abc', 0, 'x')"
call try "'abc'~left('x')"
call try "left('abc', 'x')"
call try "'abc'~left(1, '**')"
call try "left('abc', 1, '**')"
call try "'abc'~left"
call try "left('abc')"
call try "'abc'~left(, 2)"
call try "left('abc', , 2)"
call try "'abc'~left(1, 'x', 3)"
call try "left('abc', 1, 'x', 3)"
call try "'abc'~copies('x')"
call try "'abc'~word(1.5)"
exit

[class.string.builtins.receiver]

When the receiver or an argument of such a method is an instance of a subclass of String, the method works on the characters of the instance itself, and answers a new string of class String. This holds for the message form and for the function form, and for the methods that read a number, such as abs and max, and dataType as well. The characters it reads are never the answer of the instance's MAKESTRING or STRING method, even when the subclass declares one, and neither is sent to the instance (Deviation 109 has the example for the arguments and the function form).

say x~left(3) x~length x~pos('l') x~c2x~left(4) x~reverse x~left(3)~class~id

The operators

[class.string.operators]

Each operator is also a method of String with the name of the operator, as the operator rule says, and what it does belongs to the page of its operator: the arithmetic operators +, -, *, /, %, // and ** (infix, prefix and exponent); the comparisons =, \=, <>, ><, <, >, <=, >=, \< and \> (the normal comparisons) and ==, \==, <<, >>, <<=, >>=, \<< and \>> (the strict ones); the logical operators &, |, && and \ (the logical rules); and the three joining methods ||, the blank and the null string, which is the abuttal (the concatenation rules). How many arguments each takes when it is sent as a message, and the errors for too few or too many, are the message rule. An argument that is not a string is converted as the conversion rule says.

say '3'~"+"(4) '3'~"-" '3'~"*"(4) '3'~"/"(4)
say '3'~"%"(2) '3'~"//"(2) '3'~"**"(2)
say '3'~"="(3.0) '3'~"=="(3.0) 'abc'~"<"('abd') 'abc'~">>"('ab') 'a'~"\="('a')
say '1'~"&"('1') '1'~"|"('0') '1'~"&&"('1') '1'~"\"
say 'ab'~"||"('c') 'ab'~" "('c') 'ab'~""('c')

call try "'3'~'*'"
call try "'3'~'**'(.5)"
call try "'3'~'/'(0)"
call try "'x'~'+'(1)"
call try "'2'~'&'('1')"
exit

  say arg(1) '=>' r

Deviations

[class.string.deviation.4]

Whether two strings with the same characters that were built separately are one object, whether a method that leaves its receiver as it was, such as makeString, strip of a string with nothing to strip, or copy, answers the receiver or a new string, and whether a number and a string with its digits are one object, are not specified, and show only through identityHash and the identity collections (Deviation 4). The characters and the value comparisons are specified, and the hash codes of equal strings are equal. ooRexx answers a new object in many cases where interrexx answers the existing one.

a = 'ab' || 'c'
b = 'a' || 'bc'
say (a == b) (a~hashCode == b~hashCode) (a~makeString == a) (a~copy == a)
say (12~makeString == '12') (12~hashCode == '12'~hashCode)
say ('abc'~strip == 'abc') ('abc'~substr(1) == 'abc')

1 1 1 1
1 1
1 1
[class.string.deviation.36]

objectName= sent to a string that is no instance of a subclass and not enhanced is refused, and the program ends with exit code 120, as the chapter rule says: a number is such a string, and so is a string that new made. An instance of a subclass takes a name, and so does a string that enhanced made. ooRexx gives the name to the string, and an equal string elsewhere can show it.

s = .sub~new('abc')
s~objectName = 'named'
say s~objectName s
say 'before'
t = .string~new('abc')
t~objectName = 'named'
say 'after'

[class.string.deviation.109]

An instance of a subclass of String is read by its own characters wherever a string, a number, a logical value or a whole number is needed, as the receiver and as an argument, in the message form, in the function form and in the operators; REQUEST, MAKESTRING and STRING are not sent to it for that (Deviation 109). In the example the subclass declares MAKESTRING and STRING and counts the sends: the instance n is the number 2, b is the logical value 1 and s is the string ab, and no send is made. ooRexx sends such an instance request with STRING or MAKESTRING in many of these places, as an argument of a method, an operator or a builtin function, as the receiver of the numeric and logical methods and operators, dataType and ?, as the operand of SAY, and in new, so an override of either method can change what is read; elsewhere it reads the instance's own characters, so one instance can answer differently to = and to ==.

Deviations: D41, D109, D115, D118

A Method object is the code of one method together with the facts that decide who may send it and how it runs: whether it is private, package-scope, protected or guarded, which class it belongs to, and the package whose classes and routines its code can name. A class holds its methods as Method objects, ::METHOD makes one for each directive, and a program makes one of its own from source text with new, from a file with newFile, or from a native library with loadExternalMethod.

The page specifies those three class methods, with the checks they make, the messages they send and what the new method may see, and the methods that ask or change what a method object is. The directive that makes a method object is ::METHOD, the annotations come from ::ANNOTATE, how a message finds a method is the method search, and the methods of Class that install a method object, define and setMethod, are on the pages of Object and Class. The messages every object understands are those of Object. The search for a file or a library that newFile and loadExternalMethod start is specified in the environment chapter; the examples here name a file that they create themselves, or a library that every installation has.

The examples that show an error use a routine try that sends the message in its argument and prints the answer, or the error code when the message raises one, as the pages of the other classes do.

The class

[class.method.creation]

A method object made by new or newFile is public, guarded and not protected, belongs to no class (its scope is .nil), has no annotations, and holds the source it was made from. It has no code that runs by itself: it runs when it is installed in a class or an object, and a message that finds it there runs its code. A Method object is an ordinary object otherwise, so it understands the methods of Object and has the default name a Method. The class Method has the superclass Object and no mixin class.

say m~source~items m~annotations~items m~annotation('x')~isNil
say m~defaultName m .method~superclass~id .method~superclasses~items
.holder~define('GREET', m)
say .holder~new~greet('world')

Class methods

new

[class.method.new]

new makes a method object from a name, a source and a context. The name is required (SYNTAX 88.901), and is a string, or the string that its argument gives: an object that gives no string, .nil among them, raises 88.909, and a number is a name like any other string. The name becomes the name of the method's package, which package shows. The source is required too (88.901) and is read as the source rule says. The context is PROGRAMSCOPE in any case, or omitted, or a Method, a Routine or a Package object, and decides what the code can see, as the context rule says; another value raises 40.904. The checks run in this order: the name, the source, the context, and then the source is translated, so a source of .nil raises 93.961 whatever the context is, and a source that does not translate raises its translation error (35.1 for an invalid expression, 13.1 for an invalid character) after the context has been accepted, and new runs none of the code. The arguments from the fourth on are passed to init as the sends rule says. The answer is the new method object.

say m~class~id m~package~name m~source[1]

[class.method.new.source]

The source is one string, or an array of strings. A string is a single line of code, and the method's source is an array of that one line; a string is not split at line ends, and a line end character in a line, '0A'x, '0D'x or '1A'x, makes the translation raise SYNTAX 13.1, while a tab is an ordinary character. An empty string is a source of no lines. An array holds the lines in the order of its indexes. Each item is sent request with the argument STRING and the answer is the line: a string is its own line, a number is a line like any string, a MutableBuffer is the line of its text, and so is an instance of a subclass of String; an item that gives no string, .nil among them, or a hole that is followed by an item, raises SYNTAX 93.952. The answer is a line like any other, so an item whose answer has a line end, such as an array (its makeString joins its items with line ends), raises 13.1. An empty array is a source of no lines. A source that is neither a string nor an array is converted as the sends rule says; .nil raises 93.961. An instance of a subclass of String is such a source: it is not used as the one line that a string is, but is converted by its makeArray, so it is split at its line ends, and a null one is a source of no lines.

[class.method.new.sends]

new sends messages to its source and to the object it makes. A source that is not a string and not an array, and an instance of a subclass of String or Array, is sent request with the argument ARRAY; when that answers an array its items are the lines, read as the source rule reads an array. When it answers an object that is neither an array nor .nil, new raises SYNTAX 88.913 and sends no request with STRING (Deviation 115). An instance of a subclass of List is sent request as well (Deviation 118). When it answers .nil the source is sent request with the argument STRING: an answer that is a string is the one-line source, and for any other answer its objectName is the line, with no MAKESTRING or string message sent to it; .nil from both raises SYNTAX 93.961. A string that is an instance of String itself and an array that is an instance of Array itself are used directly, without a message. The request of Object sends makeArray for the argument ARRAY and makeString for STRING, as its rule says, so an object that declares makeArray or makeString is a source. When the method is made, new sends the new object the message init with the arguments of new from the fourth on, so that a subclass of Method that declares init receives them; the init of Object accepts none, and a fourth argument raises SYNTAX 93.902 after the source has been translated. The class that received new decides the class of the answer: a subclass of Method makes instances of itself.

call try '.method~new("n", .src~new(.nil, "return 2"))~source[1]'
call try '.method~new("n", .src~new(.nil, .nil))'
call try '.method~new("n", .arrsub~of("return 3"))~source[1]'

call try '.method~new("n", .src~new(.nil, .named~new))~source[1]'
call try '.method~new("n", .src~new(.nil, 12))~source[1]'
say .mine~new('n', 'return 5', 'PROGRAMSCOPE', 'a', 'b')~class~id
say .mine~new('n', 'return 5')~source[1]
exit

[class.method.new.context]

The context decides which classes and routines the code of the method can name, as the classes and routines of a package do. The method has a package of its own, a new package named by the name argument, whose source is the source of the method. That package has no classes or routines of its own, and a name that it does not hold is looked up in the package of the context, among the classes and routines that package finds: its own, public or not, and the public ones of the packages it imports. With PROGRAMSCOPE, or with the argument omitted, that is the package of the code that sent new: the method sees the classes and routines of the program that made it. With a Package object it is that package, with a Routine or a Method object it is the package of that object, and the classes and routines of the program that sent new are no longer visible: a class name that is not found is the string of that name, and a routine that is not found raises SYNTAX 43.1. The package of the context is not the package of the new method: package answers another object. A Method or Routine context whose package is .nil, one that loadExternalMethod or loadExternalRoutine made, gives a package whose lookup through the context is not specified.

src = .array~of('return 1', '::class there', '::routine thereproc')
src~append('  return "there routine"')
p = .package~new('other', src)
rout = .routine~new('rr', 'return 1', p)
default = .method~new('m1', 'return .here~class~id here()')
inpkg = .method~new('m2', 'return .there~class~id thereproc()', p)
inrout = .method~new('m3', 'return .there~class~id', rout)
inmeth = .method~new('m4', 'return .there~class~id', inpkg)
lost = .method~new('m5', 'return .here~class~id', p)
nohere = .method~new('m6', 'return here()', p)
say run(default)
say run(inpkg)
say run(inrout) run(inmeth)
say run(lost)
say run(nohere)
say (default~package == .context~package) (inpkg~package == p)
say default~package~name inpkg~package~name
exit

  return .runner~new~go

newFile

[class.method.newfile]

newFile makes a method object from the lines of a file. The file name is required (SYNTAX 88.901) and is a string, or an object that gives one (.nil and others that give none raise 88.909), and the context is the second argument, with the same values and the same error 40.904 as for new. newFile takes no other argument: a third raises SYNTAX 93.902 before the file is looked for. The checks run in this order: the number of arguments, the name, the context, and then the file is found and read; a file that cannot be read raises SYNTAX 3.1, and a file that does not translate raises its translation error. The method's package is named by the file name as it was given, and its source is the lines of the file that come before its first directive, except that a first line that begins with #! is not part of the source. A directive in the file still makes the classes and routines of the method's package, which the package answers to classes and routines, and the code of the method sees them. The context is used as for new. How the file is searched for is specified in the environment chapter. newFile sends init with no argument to the new object, and a subclass of Method makes instances of itself.

[class.method.newfile.sends]

newFile sends the new object the message init with no argument, after the file has been read and translated, so that a subclass of Method that declares init runs it once for each newFile. A file name that is an object is sent request with the argument STRING, once, before init, and the request of Object sends MAKESTRING in turn; no other message is sent. The arguments of newFile are only the name and the context, so no argument reaches init.

loadExternalMethod

[class.method.loadexternalmethod]

loadExternalMethod makes a method object whose code is a routine of a native library, the same kind of method that ::METHOD EXTERNAL declares. It takes a name and a descriptor and no other argument (a third raises SYNTAX 93.902). Both are required (88.901), and each is a string or an object that gives one (88.909 for .nil and for an object that gives none). The descriptor has the form that the directive's operand has: the word LIBRARY in any case, the name of the library, and optionally the name of the entry in it, which is the method name when it is left out; a descriptor of another form raises SYNTAX 99.917. When the library cannot be loaded, or has no entry of that name, the answer is .nil and nothing is raised. Otherwise the answer is a method object that is public and guarded, whose source is an empty array and whose package is .nil. Where the library is searched for, and whether its name is case sensitive, is specified in the environment chapter. The result is an instance of Method also when a subclass received the message, and no init is sent.

m = .method~loadExternalMethod('m', 'LIBRARY rxregexp RegExp_Pos')
say m~class~id m~source~items m~package~isNil m~isGuarded m~isPrivate
m = .method~loadExternalMethod('m', 'library rxregexp regexp_pos')
say m~class~id
say .method~loadExternalMethod('m', 'LIBRARY rxregexp')~isNil
say .method~loadExternalMethod('m', 'LIBRARY rxregexp nosuchentry')~isNil
say .method~loadExternalMethod('m', 'LIBRARY nosuchlibraryzq nosuch')~isNil
say .mine~loadExternalMethod('m', 'LIBRARY rxregexp RegExp_Pos')~class~id

call try '.method~loadExternalMethod("m", "LIBRARY rxregexp RegExp_Pos", 1)'
exit

Methods

What the method is

[class.method.source]

source answers a new array that holds the lines of the method's source, one string for each line, so changing the array changes nothing in the method. A method made by new has the lines of its source argument, one made by newFile the lines of its file before the first directive, without a first line that begins with #!, and one that a ::METHOD directive makes has the lines of its section. Text that follows the ; of the directive on its line is the first line of the section, blank included, and the last line of a section is left out when it is empty; a line of blanks is kept. A method that has no Rexx code of its own, such as an attribute method, a constant method, an abstract method, a method of a library class and one that loadExternalMethod loaded, answers an array of no items. The method takes no argument (SYNTAX 93.902).

m = .method~new('n', .array~of('say 1', 'return 2'))
a = m~source
say a~class~id a~items (a == m~source)
a~put('changed', 1)
say m~source[1]
say .k~method('plain')~source~items .k~method('plain')~source[1]~strip
say .k~method('at')~source~items .k~method('abs')~source~items
say .k~method('cc')~source~items .array~method('append')~source~items
call try 'm~source(1)'
exit

  interpret 'zres =' arg(1)
  say arg(1) '=>' zres
  return
bad: say arg(1) '=>' condition('o')~code
  return

::method abs abstract

[class.method.package]

package answers the package that holds the method's code, which decides which classes and routines the code names. For a method that a ::METHOD directive makes it is the package of the program that holds the directive. For a method made by new or newFile it is the package that new made, as the context rule says, which is named by the name argument or the file name and is the same object every time. For a method of a library class it is the package named REXX, and for one that loadExternalMethod made it is .nil. The method takes no argument.

me = .context~package
m = .k~method('plain')
say (m~package == me) (m~package == m~package)
n = .method~new('named', 'nop')
say n~package~class~id n~package~name (n~package == n~package)
say .array~method('append')~package~name
ext = .method~loadExternalMethod('m', 'LIBRARY rxregexp RegExp_Pos')
say ext~package~isNil
call try 'n~package(1)'
exit

[class.method.scope]

scope answers the class that the method belongs to, which is the class whose ::METHOD directive or define gave it to the class, and .nil for a method that belongs to no class, such as one made by new or newFile. A method that a class inherits from a superclass or a mixin class keeps the scope of the class that defined it, so instanceMethod of an instance of a subclass shows the superclass. The method that define installs runs the code of the method object that is given, with the class as its scope, so method of the class answers a method with that scope. The method that setMethod installs runs the code with the scope that the scope rule says, which is none for FLOAT. Whether the installed method is the argument or a copy of it, and what scope the argument answers afterwards, is not specified. The method takes no argument.

Changing the method

[class.method.setguarded]

setGuarded makes the method guarded and answers no value, so using its answer as a term raises SYNTAX 91.999. It has no effect on a method that is guarded already. It takes no argument (SYNTAX 93.902). The method object that method of a class answers is the one the class holds, so the example sees the change through the class.

say m~isGuarded

setProtected makes the method protected and answers no value, so using its answer raises SYNTAX 91.999. It takes no argument (SYNTAX 93.902). [class.method.setsecuritymanager]

setSecurityManager gives the method a security manager, or with no argument removes the one it has, and answers 1. It is a protected method. The manager is any object, .nil as well, and it is not checked when it is set: .nil is an object like any other, which is sent the checkpoints and does not understand them (SYNTAX 97.1), so only a call with no argument removes the manager. A second argument raises SYNTAX 93.902. While the code of the method runs, and in the internal routines of that code, the actions that the checkpoint rules name are offered to the manager first; the code of other packages that the method calls is not under the manager. A manager that was set before define installed the method stays with the installed method, as the example shows.

m = .method~new('n', 'address system "echo not run"; return "ran"')
say m~setSecurityManager(.guard~new)
.k~define('GO', m)
say .k~new~go
say m~setSecurityManager
say .method~new('x', 'nop')~setSecurityManager(.nil)
call try 'm~setSecurityManager(1, 2)'
exit

Deviations

[class.method.deviation.41]

A source that is an encoded program image, which has the line #!/usr/bin/env rexx, the marker line /**/@REXX@ and then encoded text, and whose decoded bytes lack the tag of an image, raises SYNTAX 3.903 from new, as the deviation says for a program. ooRexx translates the partly decoded bytes as source, with results that are not predictable: it raises 13.1 for the source of the example.

img = .array~of('#!/usr/bin/env rexx', '/**/@REXX@', 'c2F5ICdkZWNvZGVkJw==')
signal on syntax name bad
m = .method~new('n', img)
say 'made'
exit
bad: say condition('o')~code

3.903
[class.method.deviation.109]

An instance of a subclass of String that is the name or the source of new is read by its own characters, and REQUEST, MAKESTRING and STRING are not sent to it (Deviation 109). ooRexx sends the name request with STRING or MAKESTRING, so an override of either can change what is read; the source is read as the instance's own characters on both. In the example MAKESTRING answers another name.

m = .method~new(.name~new('Foo'), .name~new('say "src"'))
say m~package~name m~source[1]
::class name subclass string
::method makestring
  return 'other'

Foo say "src"
[class.method.deviation.115]

A source that answers request with ARRAY by an object that is neither an array nor .nil makes new raise SYNTAX 88.913, whatever the object is: a string, a list or any other object, and no request with STRING is sent after it. ooRexx crashes. The Routine page rule has the examples for Routine~new; the examples here have request answer a string and a directory.

call try '.method~new("n", .src~new("return 1"))'
call try '.method~new("n", .src~new(.directory~new))'
call try '.method~new("n", .src~new(.array~of("return 1")))~source[1]'
call try '.method~new("n", .src~new(.nil))~source[1]'
exit

A source that is an instance of a subclass of List is sent request with the argument ARRAY, as the sends rule states for any other object that is not a string and not an array, and the lines are the items of the array that it answers (Deviation 118). ooRexx sends the instance no request and takes the items it holds as the lines, so the example writes held on ooRexx.

l = .ll~new
l~append('held')
m = .method~new('m', l)

Routine

rexxref: Builtin Classes > Fundamental Classes > Routine Class; Builtin Classes > Fundamental Classes > Routine Class > new (Class Method); Builtin Classes > Fundamental Classes > Routine Class > newFile (Class Method); Builtin Classes > Fundamental Classes > Routine Class > loadExternalRoutine (Class method); Builtin Classes > Fundamental Classes > Routine Class > []; Builtin Classes > Fundamental Classes > Routine Class > annotation; Builtin Classes > Fundamental Classes > Routine Class > annotations; Builtin Classes > Fundamental Classes > Routine Class > call; Builtin Classes > Fundamental Classes > Routine Class > callWith; Builtin Classes > Fundamental Classes > Routine Class > package; Builtin Classes > Fundamental Classes > Routine Class > setSecurityManager; Builtin Classes > Fundamental Classes > Routine Class > source; The Security Manager

Deviations: D41, D109, D111, D115, D118

A Routine object is a piece of code that is called with arguments and answers a value, as a routine of a program is. A ::ROUTINE directive makes one for each directive, and a program makes one of its own from source text with new, from a file with newFile, or from a native library with loadExternalRoutine. A routine object is called by the messages call, callWith and [], and every call is a call of an external routine: the code runs in a variable pool of its own, sees nothing of its caller's variables, and finds classes and routines through its package.

The page specifies the class methods that make a routine, the messages that call it and ask about it, and the security manager that a routine can be put under. The routine that a directive makes is specified by ::ROUTINE, the annotations by ::ANNOTATE, and the instruction that calls a routine by name by CALL. A routine is made from source in the way a method is, so the rules of the Method page for the source and the context apply to new and newFile here, and this page states what is its own. The search for a file or a library that newFile and loadExternalRoutine start is specified in the environment chapter; the examples here name a file that they create themselves, or a library that every installation has.

The examples that show an error use a routine try that sends the message in its argument and prints the answer, or the error code when the message raises one.

The class

[class.routine.creation]

A routine object made by new or newFile is called by sending it call, and holds the source it was made from. It has no annotations and belongs to a package of its own, as the context rule says for a method. A Routine object is an ordinary object otherwise, so it understands the methods of Object and has the default name a Routine. The class Routine has the superclass Object and no mixin class.

r = .routine~new('adder', 'use arg a, b; return a + b')
say r~class~id r~defaultName r~call(2, 3)
say r~source~items r~annotations~items r~package~class~id r~package~name
say .routine~superclass~id .routine~superclasses~items

Routine a Routine 5
1 0 Package adder
Object 1

Class methods

new

[class.routine.new]

new makes a routine from a name, a source and a context, with the same arguments, the same checks, in the same order, and the same errors as the new of Method: the name and the source are required (SYNTAX 88.901), a name that gives no string, .nil among them, raises 88.909, a context that is not PROGRAMSCOPE, a Method, a Routine or a Package raises 40.904, and a source that does not translate raises its translation error, and the code does not run. The source is read as the source rule says, with the messages of the sends rule, and the context decides what the routine finds as the context rule says. The arguments from the fourth on are passed to init of the new object, and the class that received new is the class of the answer, as for a method. The name is the name of the routine's package.

r = .routine~new('who', 'return "I am" .context~executable~class~id')
say r~call r~package~name
d = .routine~new('d', 'return helper() .here~class~id')
say d~call
call try '.routine~new()'
call try '.routine~new("n")'
call try '.routine~new(.nil, "nop")'
call try '.routine~new("n", .nil)'
call try '.routine~new("n", "nop", "other")'
call try '.routine~new("n", "say (")'
call try '.routine~new("n", "nop", "PROGRAMSCOPE", 1)'
call try '.routine~new("n", .array~of("return 7"))~call'
call try '.routine~new("n", "return" || "0A"x)'
say .mine~new('n', 'nop', , 'a', 'b')~class~id

newFile

[class.routine.newfile]

newFile makes a routine from the lines of a file, with the arguments, the checks, their order and the errors of the newFile of Method: the file name and an optional context, no third argument (SYNTAX 93.902), .nil or an object that gives no string as the name raises 88.909, a context that does not fit raises 40.904 before the file is looked for, and a file that cannot be read raises SYNTAX 3.1. The routine's package is named by the file name as it was given. Its source is the lines of the file before the first directive, except that a first line that begins with #! is not part of it, and the directives of the file still make the classes and routines of its package, which its code can name. call runs the lines before the first directive. How the file is searched for is specified in the environment chapter. newFile sends init with no argument to the new object, and a subclass of Routine makes instances of itself.

loadExternalRoutine

[class.routine.loadexternalroutine]

loadExternalRoutine makes a routine object whose code is a routine of a native library, the same kind of routine that ::ROUTINE EXTERNAL declares. It takes a name and a descriptor, with the checks, the descriptor form and the errors of loadExternalMethod: the word LIBRARY in any case, the library, and optionally the entry in it, which is the name of the routine when it is left out. A third argument raises SYNTAX 93.902, a missing argument 88.901, a .nil argument or one that gives no string 88.909 and a descriptor of another form 99.917. When the library cannot be loaded or has no entry of that name, the answer is .nil. The answer is an instance of Routine also when a subclass received the message, and no init is sent. The routine can be called, with the arguments that the library routine takes, and its source is an empty array and its package is .nil. Where the library is searched for, and whether its name is case sensitive, is specified in the environment chapter.

say p~source~items p~package~isNil

Methods

Calling the routine

[class.routine.call]

call runs the routine with its arguments and answers what it returns. The arguments are the arguments of the message, and the argument count is the position of the last one that is not omitted: an omitted place before it stays omitted for ARG and use arg, and omitted places at the end add nothing. The code runs as the code of an external routine does: it has variables of its own and cannot see those of the program that called it, the classes and routines it names are those of its package, and exit ends the routine and answers the value it gives. A routine that returns no value answers no value, so using the answer of its call as a term raises SYNTAX 91.999. A condition that the routine raises and does not trap reaches the sender of call as it would reach the caller of an external routine; the example shows 42.3 from a division by zero. A routine that was made by loadExternalRoutine calls the library routine with the arguments.

r = .routine~new('n', 'return arg() "<"arg(1)"><"arg(2)"><"arg(3)">"')
call try 'r~call'
call try 'r~call(1)'
call try 'r~call(, 2)'
call try 'r~call(1, , 3)'
call try 'r~call(1, )'
call try 'r~call(, )'
call try '.routine~new("n", "return arg() arg(1, ""e"")")~call(, "x")'
x = 'caller variable'
call try '.routine~new("n", "return symbol(""X"") var(""X"")")~call'
call try '.routine~new("n", "x = 5; return x")~call'
say x
call try '.routine~new("n", "exit 6")~call'
call try '.routine~new("n", "return 1/0")~call'
call try '.routine~new("n", "nop")~call'
call try '.routine~new("n", "return")~call'
exit

[class.routine.callwith]

callWith runs the routine as call does with the arguments that its one argument holds. The argument is required (SYNTAX 93.903) and a second raises 93.902. An instance of Array is used as it is. Any other object, an instance of a subclass of Array included, is sent request with the argument ARRAY, and the array that answers is used; an object for which that answers .nil, and .nil itself, and an array of more than one dimension raise SYNTAX 98.913. A string is converted by its makeArray, one argument for each line, so a string with no line end is one argument and the null string has none; the empty StringTable and Directory have no items. The arguments are the items of the array by position: a hole is an omitted argument, and the argument count is the highest index that holds an item, as the count of a message is for call, so an array with no items gives a routine with no arguments, however large it was made.

r = .routine~new('n', 'return arg() "<"arg(1)"><"arg(2)"><"arg(3)">"')

call try 'r~callWith(.array~of(1, 2)~~put("z", 5))'
call try 'r~callWith("a b")'
call try 'r~callWith("a" || "0A"x || "b")'
call try 'r~callWith("")'

call try 'r~callWith(.holder~new)'
call try 'r~callWith(.arrsub~of(1, 2))'
call try 'r~callWith'
call try 'r~callWith(.nil)'
call try 'r~callWith(.object~new)'
call try 'r~callWith(.array~new(1, 1))'
call try 'r~callWith(.array~of(1), 2)'
exit

What the routine is

[class.routine.source]

source answers a new array that holds the lines of the routine's source, one string for each line, so changing the array changes nothing in the routine. A routine made by new has the lines of its source argument (an empty string and an empty array are a source of no lines), one made by newFile the lines of its file before the first directive, without a first line that begins with #!, and one that a ::ROUTINE directive makes has the lines of its section, which the rule of Method reads as it does for a method: the text after the ; of the directive is the first line, and an empty last line is left out, so a directive with nothing after its ; and no lines has an empty source. A routine that loadExternalRoutine loaded, and an external routine, answer an array of no items. The method takes no argument (SYNTAX 93.902).

r = .routine~new('n', .array~of('say 1', 'return 2'))
a = r~source
say a~class~id a~items (a == r~source)
a~put('changed', 1)
say r~source[1]
say .routine~new('n', '')~source~items,
  .routine~new('n', .array~new)~source~items
say .context~package~findRoutine('PLAIN')~source[1]~strip
say .context~package~findRoutine('PLAIN')~source~items
call try 'r~source(1)'
exit

[class.routine.package]

package answers the package that holds the routine's code, which decides which classes and routines the code names. For a routine that a ::ROUTINE directive makes it is the package of the program that holds the directive. For a routine made by new or newFile it is the package that new made, as the context rule says, which is named by the name argument or the file name, and is the same object every time. For loadExternalRoutine it is .nil. The method takes no argument.

The security manager

[class.routine.setsecuritymanager]

setSecurityManager gives the routine a security manager, or with no argument removes the one it has, and answers 1. It is a protected method. The manager can be any object, .nil as well, and it is not checked when it is set; .nil is an object like any other and is sent the checkpoints, which it does not understand (SYNTAX 97.1), so only a call with no argument removes the manager. A second argument raises SYNTAX 93.902. While the code of the routine runs, and in the internal routines of that code, the actions that the checkpoint rules name are offered to the manager first. The code of other packages, those of the classes and routines that the routine calls, and the packages that it makes, are not under the manager. A manager that is removed no longer sees the actions.

src = 'address system "echo hidden"; return "done"'
r = .routine~new('agent', src)
say r~setSecurityManager(.guard~new)
say r~call
say r~setSecurityManager
say r~call
say r~setSecurityManager(.nil)
call try 'r~call'
call try 'r~setSecurityManager(.guard~new, 1)'
exit
try:
  signal on syntax name bad
  interpret 'zres =' arg(1)
  say arg(1) '=>' zres
  return
bad: say arg(1) '=>' condition('o')~code
  return
::class guard
::method command
  use arg info
  say 'manager saw' info~command
  info~rc = 0
  return 1

done

[class.routine.setsecuritymanager.checkpoints]

The actions that are offered to the manager are the checkpoints: an external routine call (CALL), a command (COMMAND), a loadPackage (REQUIRES), a name looked up in .local (LOCAL) or in .environment (ENVIRONMENT), a stream name of a stream function (STREAM) and a message to a protected method (METHOD). The rules for each name the entries of its information directory. The interpreter sends the manager the message of the checkpoint's name with one argument, a Directory that holds the entries; the manager answers 1 to say it handled the action, and the entries that the checkpoint reads from the directory are used, or 0 to let the action go on as it would. An answer that is neither 0 nor 1 raises SYNTAX 34.903, and an answer of no value raises SYNTAX 91.999. A manager that has no method of the checkpoint's name is sent UNKNOWN as any object is, with the name and an array that holds the directory; when it has none either, the message raises SYNTAX 97.1 at the clause that caused the action. A manager may raise a condition instead of answering: the usual one is SYNTAX 98.948, and it reaches the code of the routine as any error of its clause does.

src = 'signal on syntax; address system "true"; return "ran"; '
src = src || 'syntax: return "error" condition("o")~code'
mgrs = .array~of(.none~new, .zero~new, .one~new, .five~new, .nothing~new)
mgrs~append(.raiser~new)
mgrs~append(.generic~new)
do mgr over mgrs
  r = .routine~new('agent', src)
  r~setSecurityManager(mgr)
  say mgr~class~id '=>' r~call
end
exit
::class none
::class zero
::method command
  return 0
::class one
::method command
  return 1
::class five
::method command
  return 5
::class nothing
::method command
  nop
::class raiser
::method command
  raise syntax 98.948 array('no way')
::class generic

[class.routine.setsecuritymanager.call]

The CALL checkpoint is offered for the call of an external routine: one that is not a label in the code, not a built-in function and not a routine that the routine's package or its context package finds, its own and those it imports; a function of a native library is offered. The directory holds NAME, the upper case name of the routine, and ARGUMENTS, an array of the arguments. A manager that answers 1 takes the call over: the entry RESULT, when the manager set one, is the value of the call, and with no RESULT the call answers no value, which raises SYNTAX 44.1 where the value is used. A manager that answers 0 lets the call go on, which raises SYNTAX 43.1 for a routine that does not exist. A routine that the package or its context finds is not offered, as the call of known in the example shows, and neither is one that they import, as the second example shows.

src = 'say left("abc", 2) lab(1) known(); say zqprovided(4, 5); '
src = src || 'say zqtwice(); say "end"; exit; lab: return "lab" arg(1)'
r = .routine~new('agent', src)
r~setSecurityManager(.mgr~new)
call try 'r~call'
r = .routine~new('agent', 'return zqmissing()')
r~setSecurityManager(.mgr~new)
call try 'r~call'
exit
try:
  signal on syntax name bad
  interpret 'zres =' arg(1)
  say arg(1) '=>' zres
  return
bad: say arg(1) '=>' condition('o')~code
  return
::routine known
  return 'known'
::class mgr
::method call
  use arg info
  say 'call' info~name info~arguments~items
  if info~name == 'ZQPROVIDED' then do
    info~result = 'replaced' info~arguments[2]
    return 1
  end
  if info~name == 'ZQTWICE' then return 1
  return 0

ab lab 1 known
call ZQPROVIDED 2
replaced 5
call ZQTWICE 0
r~call => 44.1
call ZQMISSING 0
r~call => 43.1

src = .array~of('nop', '::routine zqpub public', '  return "pub"')
lib = .package~new('zqlib', src)
ctx = .package~new('zqctx', 'nop')
ctx~addPackage(lib)
src = 'say zqpub(); say sysfileexists("zq_nofile_zz")'
r = .routine~new('agent', src, ctx)
r~setSecurityManager(.mgr~new)
r~call
exit
::class mgr
::method call
  use arg info
  say 'call' info~name
  return 0

pub
call SYSFILEEXISTS

[class.routine.setsecuritymanager.command]

The COMMAND checkpoint is offered for a command that goes to an ADDRESS environment. The directory holds COMMAND, the command string, and ADDRESS, the name of the environment in upper case. A manager that answers 1 has run the command itself: the entry RC, when it is set, is the return code, and 0 is used when it is not. The entry FAILURE, when it is set alone, raises the FAILURE condition for the command, and the entry ERROR, when it is set alone, raises ERROR; when both are set, FAILURE is raised and ERROR is not. The manager answers 0 to let the interpreter run the command. The default environment that a command goes to when the code names no ADDRESS is that of the host and is not specified.

src = 'address system "echo one"; say "rc" rc; signal on failure name fail; '
src = src || 'address system "echo two"; say "not here"; '
src = src || 'fail: say "failure" rc; signal on error name err; '
src = src || 'address system "echo three"; say "not here"; '
src = src || 'err: say "error" rc; signal on failure name fail2; '
src = src || 'signal on error name err2; address system "echo four"; '
src = src || 'say "not here"; fail2: say "both failure" rc; exit; '
src = src || 'err2: say "both error" rc'
r = .routine~new('agent', src)
r~setSecurityManager(.mgr~new)
r~call
exit
::class mgr
::method command
  use arg info
  say 'command' info~address '>'info~command'<'
  say '  entries' info~allIndexes~sort~makearray~makestring('l', ',')
  select
    when info~command = 'echo one' then info~rc = 11
    when info~command = 'echo two' then do
      info~rc = 12
      info~failure = 1
    end
    when info~command = 'echo three' then do
      info~rc = 13
      info~error = 1
    end
    when info~command = 'echo four' then do
      info~rc = 14
      info~failure = 1
      info~error = 1
    end
  end
  return 1

command SYSTEM >echo one<
  entries ADDRESS,COMMAND
rc 11
command SYSTEM >echo two<
  entries ADDRESS,COMMAND
failure 12
command SYSTEM >echo three<
  entries ADDRESS,COMMAND
error 13
command SYSTEM >echo four<
  entries ADDRESS,COMMAND
both failure 14
[class.routine.setsecuritymanager.local]

The LOCAL checkpoint is offered when the code names an object of .local, with the entry NAME, the upper case name, before .local is searched. It is offered for a name that findClass takes from .local or .environment or does not find, except .nil, .true and .false, which are never offered, not for a name that a class of the package, of its context, of the packages it imports or of the library gives, and not for a name in the local directory of the package, which is searched first. A manager that answers 1 with an entry RESULT provides the object; one that answers 1 with no RESULT is read as the name not being found, and the lookup goes on with the ENVIRONMENT checkpoint. The code of the routine is the code that is under the manager; the program that called it is not.

.local~zqvalue = 'in local'
r = .routine~new('agent', 'return .zqvalue "|" .zqother "|" .zqnone')
r~setSecurityManager(.mgr~new)
say r~call
exit
::class mgr
::method local
  use arg info
  say 'local' info~name
  if info~name = 'ZQOTHER' then do
    info~result = 'provided'
    return 1
  end
  if info~name = 'ZQNONE' then return 1
  return 0
::method environment
  use arg info
  say 'environment' info~name
  return 0

local ZQVALUE
local ZQOTHER
local ZQNONE
environment ZQNONE
in local | provided | .ZQNONE

src = src || 'x = .local'
r = .routine~new('agent', src, ctx)

[class.routine.setsecuritymanager.environment]

The ENVIRONMENT checkpoint is offered, after the LOCAL one answered 0 or did not provide the name, for a name that is looked up in .environment: the entry NAME is the upper case name, RESULT and the answer have the same meaning as for LOCAL. A name that LOCAL provided is not offered to ENVIRONMENT, and neither is a name that .local holds, such as .stdout, when LOCAL answered 0.

.environment~zqenvvalue = 'in environment'
r = .routine~new('agent', 'return .zqenvvalue "|" .zqprov "|" .zqloc')

exit

  say 'local' info~name
  if info~name = 'ZQLOC' then do
    info~result = 'from local'
    return 1
  end
  return 0
::method environment
  use arg info
  say 'environment' info~name
  if info~name = 'ZQPROV' then do
    info~result = 'from environment'
    return 1
  end
  return 0

local ZQPROV

local ZQLOC
in environment | from environment | from local

A manager that answers 0 lets the function open the name itself.

[class.routine.setsecuritymanager.requires]

The REQUIRES checkpoint is offered when the code of the routine loads a package from a file, with loadPackage or with the new of Package and a file name. The directory holds NAME, the name of the file. The checkpoint is offered twice for a file that is found, first with the name as it was given and then with its absolute name, and once, with the name as it was given, for a file that is not found, before the load raises SYNTAX 43.901. A package that was loaded before is not loaded again and is not offered, and neither is a loadPackage that has a source, and a ::REQUIRES of a package that the code makes from a source is not offered either. A manager that answers 0 lets the load go on, and so does one that answers 1 and leaves NAME as it is. A manager that replaces NAME in the information of the first message and answers 1 chooses the file: the file of the new name is the one that is loaded, and no second message is sent, so the manager is never asked to approve its own replacement (Deviation 111). A NAME replaced in the second message chooses the file as well, as the second example shows.

f = 'class_routine_requires_zq.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
call lineout f, 'say "loaded body"'
call lineout f

call lineout g, 'say "new body"'
call lineout g

call lineout m, 'say "m body"'
call lineout m

call lineout h, 'say "required body"'
call lineout h

src = src || '"nop")~class~id; '
src = src || 'say .package~new("class_routine_requires_n_zq.tmp")~class~id; '
src = src || 'x = .package~new("x", .array~of("nop", '
src = src || '"::requires ""class_routine_requires_b_zq.tmp"""));'
src = src || 'say p~loadPackage("class_routine_requires_gone_zq.tmp"); '
src = src || 'bad: say condition("o")~code'

[class.routine.setsecuritymanager.method]

The METHOD checkpoint is offered when the code of the routine sends a message to a protected method, before the method runs. The directory holds OBJECT, the receiver, NAME, the upper case name of the method, and ARGUMENTS, an array of the arguments. A manager that answers 1 has run the message itself: the entry RESULT, when it is set, is what the message answers, and with no RESULT the message answers no value, so that using the answer raises SYNTAX 91.999. A manager that answers 0 lets the method run. A message to a protected method from code that is not under a manager runs the method, and so does a message to a method that is not protected.

r = .routine~new('agent', 'o = .box~new; return o~locked(1, 2) o~open')
r~setSecurityManager(.mgr~new)
say r~call
say .box~new~locked(1, 2)
exit

::method locked protected
  return 'locked ran'
::method open
  return 'open ran'
::class mgr
::method method

  say 'method' info~name info~object~class~id info~arguments~items
  info~result = 'replaced'
  return 1

[class.routine.deviation.41]

A source that is an encoded program image whose decoded bytes lack the tag of an image raises SYNTAX 3.903 from new, as the rule of Method says; ooRexx translates the partly decoded bytes as source.

img = .array~of('#!/usr/bin/env rexx', '/**/@REXX@', 'c2F5ICdkZWNvZGVkJw==')
signal on syntax name bad
r = .routine~new('n', img)
say 'made'
exit
bad: say condition('o')~code

3.903
[class.routine.deviation.109]

An instance of a subclass of String that is the name or the source of new is read by its own characters, and REQUEST, MAKESTRING and STRING are not sent to it (Deviation 109). ooRexx sends the name request with STRING or MAKESTRING, so an override of either can change what is read; the source is read as the instance's own characters on both. In the example MAKESTRING answers another name.

r = .routine~new(.name~new('Foo'), .name~new('say "src"'))
say r~package~name r~source[1]
::class name subclass string
::method makestring
  return 'other'

Foo say "src"
[class.routine.deviation.115]

A new whose source answers request with ARRAY by an object that is neither an array nor .nil raises SYNTAX 88.913, as the rule of Method states, and no request with STRING is sent. ooRexx crashes. The examples have request answer a string, a list and an object that is none of them.

call try '.routine~new("n", .src~new("return 1"))'
call try '.routine~new("n", .src~new(.list~of("return 1")))'
call try '.routine~new("n", .src~new(.object~new))'
call try '.routine~new("n", .src~new(.array~of("return 1")))~call'
call try '.routine~new("n", .src~new(.nil))~call'
exit

  say arg(1) '=>' zres
  return

A source that is an instance of a subclass of List is sent request with the argument ARRAY, as the sends rule states, and the lines are the items of the array that it answers (Deviation 118). ooRexx sends the instance no request and takes the items it holds as the lines, so the example writes held on ooRexx.

[class.routine.deviation.111]

A name that the manager replaces in the information of the first requires message chooses the file that is loaded, and the manager is sent no second message for it (Deviation 111). ooRexx uses the new name only to look for a package that is already loaded under it. Otherwise it sends the second message with the full name of the file that the load asked for, and loads that file: the example, whose manager replaces the name at the first message, is sent two messages on ooRexx and loads a. No replacement, and a replacement at the second message, give the same result on both (the checkpoint rule).

A Package object is a unit of code that the interpreter loads: the program that a user runs, a file that ::REQUIRES loads, a source that new is given. It holds the source text, the classes, routines and unattached methods that its directives declare, the resources and annotations, the packages it imports and the namespaces it names them by, the initial settings of the numeric and condition options and of tracing, and the code that comes before its first directive, which is called its prolog. The classes and routines that its code can name are found through the package.

The page specifies the class methods that make a package and set the default options of the packages that are made afterwards, and the methods that ask a package what it holds, find a class, a routine or a namespace in it, add to it, and read or change its options. The directives that fill a package are specified by ::CLASS, ::ROUTINE, ::METHOD, ::REQUIRES, ::OPTIONS, ::RESOURCE and ::ANNOTATE, and the page links them instead of repeating them. A package's source is the source of a method or routine made in the way the Method page describes, and its rules for the source apply here where this page says so. The search for a file or a library that new, loadPackage, loadLibrary and findProgram start is specified in the environment chapter; the examples here name files that they create themselves, or a library that every installation has. The message a package sends to a security manager is specified on the Routine page, which also specifies the checkpoints.

The examples that show an error use a routine try that sends the message in its argument and prints the answer, or the error code when the message raises one. A message that answers .nil prints The NIL object.

The class

[class.package.creation]

A package is made by new, by the interpreter for the program that runs, by ::REQUIRES and by loadPackage, and the library classes belong to a package named REXX. A package made by new is an ordinary object otherwise: it has the default name a Package, and the class Package has the superclass Object and no mixin class. The package of the library, which .object~package answers, holds the classes of the library, is named REXX, has no source, and is found by findNamespace under that name from any package.

p = .package~new('first', 'return 5')
say p~class~id p~defaultName p~name p~source[1]
say .package~superclass~id .package~superclasses~items
rp = .object~package
say rp~name .array~package~name (rp == .string~package)
say rp~source~items rp~sourceSize rp~publicClasses~hasIndex('STRING')
say (p~findNamespace('REXX') == rp) (p~findNamespace('rexx') == rp)

Package a Package first return 5
Object 1
REXX REXX 1
0 0 1
1 1

Class methods

new

[class.package.new]

new makes a package from a name and, optionally, a source and a context. The name is required (SYNTAX 88.901), and is a string or the string that its argument gives: an object that gives no string, .nil among them, raises 88.909. With a source, the name is only the name of the package, and the package is always a new object. With no source, the name is the name of a file, which new looks for and reads, as the file rule says, and there is no context: the arguments from the third on go to init. The context is the third argument. It is a Method, a Routine or a Package object, or omitted; any other value, .nil and PROGRAMSCOPE included, raises SYNTAX 93.953. The checks run in this order: the name, the context, the source (a source that is .nil raises 93.961), and then the source is translated, so that a source that does not translate raises its translation error, and new then installs the package as the install rule says. The arguments from the fourth on are passed to init of the new package, and so are the arguments from the third on when the source is omitted; the init of Object accepts none, and one argument raises SYNTAX 93.902 after the package is installed. A subclass of Package makes instances of itself. The answer is the new package.

p = .package~new('named', 'return 1')
say p~class~id p~name
call try '.package~new()'
call try '.package~new(.nil, "nop")'
call try '.package~new(.list~new, "nop")'

[class.package.new.sends]

new sends the messages that the sends rule of Method states for a source that is not a string and not an array, request with ARRAY and then with STRING (the line is a string answer itself, and any other answer's objectName), and then sends the new package init, after the package has been installed, with the arguments from the fourth on, or from the third on when the source is omitted. An answer to request with ARRAY that is neither an array nor .nil raises SYNTAX 88.913, and no request with STRING follows it (Deviation 115). An instance of a subclass of List is sent request as well (Deviation 118). A name that is an object is sent request with the argument STRING, once, first, before the messages to the source and init.

[class.package.new.source]

The source is a string or an array of strings, read as the source rule of Method says: a string is one line and is not split at line ends, an array holds one line for each item, sent request with the argument STRING, a line end character ('0A'x, '0D'x or '1A'x) in a line raises SYNTAX 13.1, an item that gives no string, .nil among them, or a hole before an item, raises 93.952, and any other object, an instance of a subclass of String included, is converted by the sends rule: request with ARRAY, then with STRING. What differs is that the lines of a package are the whole text, directives included, so source answers the same lines, and that an empty string is one empty line where an empty array is none. A line that the package does not translate raises its error from new.

[class.package.new.context]

The context decides which classes and routines the code of the package can name besides its own and those of the library. A package made with no context sees nothing of the package of the code that made it: a class name that it does not hold is the string of that name, and a routine that it does not hold raises SYNTAX 43.1. With a Package object as the context the package finds, after its own, the classes and routines that the context package finds, its own, those it imports and what its own context finds, and with a Routine or a Method it finds those of the package of that object. A context that is a Method or a Routine whose package is .nil, one that loadExternalMethod or loadExternalRoutine made, gives a package whose lookup through the context is not specified. The context package is not one of the importedPackages of the new package, and its classes and routines are not among the classes and routines of the new package.

src = .array~of('return 1', '::class there', '::routine thereproc')
src~append('  return "there routine"')
p = .package~new('other', src)
r = .routine~new('r', 'return 1', p)
none = .package~new('a', 'say .here~class~id')
via = .package~new('b', 'say .there~class~id thereproc()', p)
viar = .package~new('c', 'say .there~class~id thereproc()', r)
call try '.package~new("d", "say here()")'
call try '.package~new("d", "say here()", p)'
c = .package~new('e', 'return 1', p)
say c~classes~items c~routines~items c~importedPackages~items
say c~findClass('THERE')~id (c~findClass('HERE') == .nil)
say c~findRoutine('THEREPROC')~class~id
src = .array~of('nop', '::class c2cls', '::routine c2r', '  return "c2"')
c2 = .package~new('c2', src)
c1 = .package~new('c1', 'nop', c2)
pc = .package~new('pc', 'nop', c1)
say pc~findClass('C2CLS')~isNil pc~findRoutine('C2R')~isNil
src = .array~of('return 1', '::class libpub public')
src~append('::routine libproc public')
src~append('  return "lib routine"')
p~addPackage(.package~new('lib', src))
imp = .package~new('f', 'say .libpub~class~id libproc()', p)
exit

[class.package.new.file]

With no source, the name is the name of a file, which new looks for as the search rule of ::REQUIRES does, reads and installs. A file that cannot be found raises SYNTAX 43.901. The name of the package is the name of the file as the search resolved it, an absolute name, and not the name that was given. A file that was loaded before, by new, by loadPackage or by a ::REQUIRES, is not read or run again: new answers the same package, which is also the answer when the file is given by another name that resolves to the same file. A package that new made from a source is never found that way, even when it has the name of a file; a package that loadPackage installed from a source is found by its name, as the rule of loadPackage says. How a file is searched for is specified in the environment chapter.

say (p == q) (p == .package~new('./' || f))
say (p == p~loadPackage(f)) (p == .package~new(f, 'say "from source"'))
call sysfiledelete f
call try '.package~new("class_package_file_none.tmp")'
exit

[class.package.new.install]

When new has read the source it installs the package as the program is installed when it runs. The packages of its ::REQUIRES directives are loaded first, each as this rule says, then the classes of its ::CLASS directives are made, and then, unless ::OPTIONS NOPROLOG was given, the prolog runs, which is the code before the first directive. An error in any of these is raised from new, and a package whose prolog ended with EXIT or RETURN is made as it is; the value is dropped. A package that was made has been installed, so a class of the package has had its class init run before the prolog starts. The installation of the directives is specified by the directive pages.

f = 'class_package_order_zq.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
call lineout f, 'say "required prolog"'
call lineout f, '::class reqclass public'
call lineout f, '::method init class'
call lineout f, '  say "required class init"'
call lineout f

src~append('::class own')
src~append('::method init class')
src~append('  say "own class init"')
p = .package~new('order', src)
say 'made' p~classes~items
q = .package~new('quiet', .array~of('say "never"', '::options noprolog'))
say 'quiet made' q~prolog~class~id
call try '.package~new("e1", "say 1; say 1/0")'
src = .array~of('say 2', '::requires "class_package_none.cls"')
call try '.package~new("e2", src)'
call try '.package~new("e3", "exit 5")~class~id'
call try '.package~new("e4", "return 5")~class~id'
call sysfiledelete f
exit

defaultOptions

[class.package.defaultoptions]

defaultOptions reads and sets the options that a package gets when it is made without the corresponding ::OPTIONS. It takes an option name and optionally a value, and no further argument (SYNTAX 93.902). The name is required (88.901), an object that gives no string, .nil among them, raises 88.909, and only its first letter counts: D names DefineDefaultOptions and C names CountOverrides, in any case; another name raises SYNTAX 93.914. With no value the call answers the current value, and with a value it sets it and answers the previous one. DefineDefaultOptions is a string in the form of an ::OPTIONS directive, which is the same form that options answers; a string that is not one ::OPTIONS directive, in any case and after optional blanks, raises 93.900, as a string of two directives does, a string whose options the directive refuses raises the error of the directive (25.924 for an unknown option), and a directive with no options leaves every option at its initial value. The initial value names DIGITS 9, FORM SCIENTIFIC, FUZZ 0, NUMERIC NOINHERIT, each of the six condition options with CONDITION, PROLOG and TRACE NORMAL, as options lists them. CountOverrides is a whole number whose initial value is 0; a value that is not a whole number raises 93.905. While it is positive, every package that is made, by new and by the new and newFile of Method and of Routine, which make a package of their own, gets the default options in place of the initial ones and reduces the count by one; a package that gives an option in a directive keeps its own value for that option. A count that is 0 leaves the packages that are made with the initial options, and a negative count applies the defaults to every package that is made, and is reduced by one for each, so that it stays negative.

say .package~defaultOptions('CountOverrides')
say .package~defaultOptions('DefineDefaultOptions')~subword(1, 3)
old = .package~defaultOptions('DefineDefaultOptions', '::OPTIONS DIGITS 20')
say old~subword(1, 3)
say .package~defaultOptions('D')~subword(1, 3)
say .package~defaultOptions('CountOverrides', 3)
p = .package~new('first', 'nop')
q = .package~new('second', .array~of('nop', '::options digits 11'))
r = .routine~new('third', 'return digits()')
say p~digits q~digits r~call r~package~digits
say .package~defaultOptions('CountOverrides')
s = .package~new('fourth', 'nop')
say s~digits .package~defaultOptions('CountOverrides')

call sysfiledelete f
call lineout f, 'return 1'
call lineout f
.package~defaultOptions('CountOverrides', 2)
say .routine~newFile(f)~package~digits .method~newFile(f)~package~digits
say .package~defaultOptions('CountOverrides')
call sysfiledelete f

t = .package~new('fifth', 'nop')
u = .package~new('sixth', 'nop')
say t~digits u~digits .package~defaultOptions('CountOverrides')
.package~defaultOptions('CountOverrides', 0)

say .package~defaultOptions('DefineDefaultOptions')~subword(1, 3)

[class.package.prolog]

prolog answers a Routine that holds the code of the package that comes before its first directive: its source is those lines, and its package is the package. It is the same object every time. Sending call to it runs the prolog again, as call of a routine does, with the answer of the code. The routine exists also for a package with no code before its first directive, whose source is empty, and for a package with NOPROLOG, whose prolog did not run when the package was made. A first line that begins with #! is not part of the prolog's source, though it stays in the package's own source. The library package, and the package of a method or routine that new or newFile of Method or Routine made, have no prolog: prolog answers .nil. The method takes no argument (SYNTAX 93.902).

say .object~package~prolog
say .method~new('mm', 'return 2')~package~prolog~isNil
say .routine~new('rr', 'return 7')~package~prolog~isNil
call try 'p~prolog(1)'
exit

What the package holds

[class.package.classes]

classes answers a new StringTable of the classes that the package's ::CLASS directives made, public or not, indexed by the upper case class name, together with the classes that addClass and addPublicClass added. The classes that the package imports are not among them. Changing the table does not change the package. The method takes no argument (SYNTAX 93.902).

src = .array~of('return 1', '::class pub public', '::class priv')
p = .package~new('n', src)
t = p~classes
say t~class~id t~items t['PUB']~id t['PRIV']~id
