[class.package.findclass]

findClass looks a name up as the environment symbol of the same name is looked up in the package's code, and answers what it finds, or .nil. The name is taken in upper case. The places that are searched, in this order, are the classes of the package, public or not; the classes that the package of its context finds, which are its own, public or not, the public ones of the packages it imports, and what its own context finds; the public classes of the packages it imports, the one imported first winning among equal names; the public classes of the library; the package's local directory; and then .local and .environment, so the answer may be an object that is not a class, such as .nil, .true or .local, and a name that nothing holds answers .nil. The first place that holds the name decides. The name is required (SYNTAX 88.901), an object that gives no string, .nil among them, raises 88.909, and a second argument raises 93.902. Any string is a name: a name with a blank or a period is found when addClass, addPublicClass or a directory holds it under that name. A name that has a colon is not looked up through a namespace: tg:shown and rexx:string answer .nil, even when a package that holds a public class SHOWN was added under the namespace TG.

src = .array~of('return 1', '::class own public', '::class priv')
p = .package~new('n', src)
say p~findClass('OWN')~id p~findClass('own')~id p~findClass('PRIV')~id
say p~findClass('String')~id p~findClass('RexxInfo')~class~id
say p~findClass('TRUE') p~findClass('nil')~isNil
say p~findClass('LOCAL')~class~id p~findClass('ENVIRONMENT')~class~id
p~addClass('a.b', .array)
say p~findClass('nothere')~isNil p~findClass('a.b')~id
.local~zqfind = 'from local'
say p~findClass('ZQFIND')
o = .package~new('o', .array~of('nop', '::class shown public'))
p~addPackage(o, 'tg')
say p~findClass('SHOWN')~id p~findClass('tg:shown')~isNil
say p~findClass('rexx:string')~isNil p~findClass('rexx:')~isNil
call try 'p~findClass'
call try 'p~findClass(.nil)'
call try 'p~findClass("x", 1)'
exit

  say arg(1) '=>' zres

[class.package.findroutine]

findRoutine answers the routine that has the name it is given, or .nil. The name is taken in upper case. The routines it looks through, in this order, are those of the package, public or not, those that were added to it, the routines that the package of its context finds, which are its own, public or not, the public ones of the packages it imports, and what its own context finds, and the public routines of the packages it imports, the one imported first winning among equal names; the first that holds the name decides. src~append('::routine privr')
src~append('  return "q"')

say p~findRoutine('nothere')~isNil p~findRoutine('')~isNil

q~addPackage(p)
say q~findRoutine('PUBR')~call q~findRoutine('PRIVR')~isNil

call try 'p~findRoutine(.nil)'
call try 'p~findRoutine("x", 1)'

[class.package.addclass]

addClass adds a class to the package under a name, as a class that is not public, and answers the package. The name is required (SYNTAX 88.901), an object that gives no string, .nil among them, raises 88.909, and the class is required too (88.901) and must be a class (SYNTAX 88.914; .nil, a number and an instance that is not a class do not qualify); a third argument raises 93.902. The checks run in that order. The name is taken in upper case, any string is a name, and a class that is added under a name that the package holds replaces the class that was there. The class is in classes, findClass finds it, and the code of the package names it with .name; it is not in publicClasses.

[class.package.addpackage]

addPackage adds a package to the packages that the receiver imports, as a ::REQUIRES of it would, and answers the receiver. The public classes and routines of the added package are then found by the receiver, and appear in importedClasses, importedRoutines and importedPackages. The package is required (SYNTAX 88.901) and must be a Package (SYNTAX 88.914; .nil and other objects do not qualify). The second argument is a namespace name, a string or an object that gives one (88.909 for .nil and for an object that gives none), which names the package in namespaces and for findNamespace; a third argument raises SYNTAX 93.902. A package that was already added is not added again, so it is in importedPackages once, and a package may be added to itself. The namespace is taken in upper case. The namespace may be REXX or the null string: addPackage accepts both and namespaces lists them, but findNamespace with REXX still answers the package of the library classes. A ::REQUIRES that gives the namespace REXX raises 99.944, as the namespace rule says.

[class.package.loadpackage]

loadPackage loads a package by name as a ::REQUIRES of the receiver would, adds it to the packages that the receiver imports, as addPackage does, and answers the loaded package. The name is required (SYNTAX 93.903); an object that gives no string, .nil among them, raises 88.909. With no second argument the name is the name of a file, which is found, read and installed as the file rule of new says, so a file that was loaded before is not read or run again: the answer is the same package. A file that cannot be found raises SYNTAX 43.901. The second argument is a source, which is installed under the name in place of the file. A source that is not an instance of Array itself, a string included, is sent request with the argument ARRAY, once, and an Array is used as it is, with no message. A string is therefore split at its line ends by its makeArray, and the null string is a source of no lines, where for new a string is one line. The items of an array are the lines, and an item is read as the source rule of new reads one: a string is its own line, and any other item is sent request with the argument STRING, so that an item that gives no string, .nil among them, or a hole before an item, raises SYNTAX 93.952 and an answer that has a line end raises 13.1 (Deviation 112). An object for which request answers .nil, .nil itself among them, raises SYNTAX 88.913, and request is not sent with STRING. A source that does not translate raises its translation error. A package that is installed from a source is found afterwards by its name: a loadPackage of that name with no source, the new of Package with that name and a ::REQUIRES of it answer that package and run nothing. A loadPackage with a source for a name that was already loaded, from a file or from a source, answers the package that was loaded first: the new source is not read, translated or run, and no class or routine of it is added. A third argument raises 93.902. How the file is searched for is specified in the environment chapter. The checkpoint that a security manager sees is that of the REQUIRES rule.

call sysfiledelete f
call lineout f, 'say "loaded file"'

say (.package~new(f) == l)

say s~name s~sourceSize p~importedPackages~items
a = p~loadPackage('class_package_arr_zq.cls', .array~of('say "array source"'))
say a~name a~source~items
call sysfiledelete f
call try 'p~loadPackage'
call try 'p~loadPackage(.nil)'
call try 'p~loadPackage("class_package_load_none.tmp")'
call try 'p~loadPackage("class_package_x1.cls", .nil)'
call try 'p~loadPackage("class_package_x2.cls", .object~new)'

[class.package.loadpackage.sends]

loadPackage sends a source that is not an instance of Array itself the message request with the argument ARRAY, once, and uses the array that is answered; an Array is sent nothing, and the array answered is sent nothing either. An instance of a subclass of Array is sent request, and what that sends in turn is stated by the request rule. The message is sent after the name has been read and before the source is translated. The example uses an instance of an Array subclass, an object that answers an array of its own, one that answers an instance of an Array subclass, and an Array.

[class.package.options]

options reads and changes the settings of the package that the ::OPTIONS directive gives, while the program runs. With no argument it answers the current settings as a string in the form of an ::OPTIONS directive. The string starts with ::OPTIONS DIGITS 9 FORM SCIENTIFIC FUZZ 0 NUMERIC NOINHERIT for a package that has the initial settings, goes on with the six condition options ERROR, FAILURE, LOSTDIGITS, NOSTRING, NOTREADY and NOVALUE, each followed by CONDITION or SYNTAX, and ends with PROLOG or NOPROLOG and TRACE and its setting, so the initial string ends with PROLOG TRACE NORMAL. With one argument, the option, it answers the current setting of that option, and with a second argument it sets the option to that value and answers the previous setting. More than two arguments raise SYNTAX 93.902. The option name is a string, an object that gives no string, .nil among them, raises 88.909, and a name that is not an option raises SYNTAX 93.914. The names rule says which strings name which option, and the settings rule says what the settings are. A change takes effect for the code of the package that starts afterwards: a routine or a method of the package that runs next runs under the new settings.

src = .array~of('return 1', '::routine rd')
src~append('  return digits() form() fuzz() trace()')
p = .package~new('n', src)
say p~options~subword(1, 7)
rd = p~findRoutine('RD')
say rd~call
say p~options('Digits', 20) p~options('Digits')
say rd~call
say p~options('Form', 'Engineering') p~options('Form')
say rd~call
say p~options('Trace', 'Results') p~options('Trace')
call try 'p~options("Zzz")'
call try 'p~options(.nil)'
call try 'p~options("Digits", 5, 6)'
exit

[class.package.options.names]

The option name is matched by its first letters, in any case, and the letters after them are ignored. The names are Digits (D), Form (FO), Fuzz (FU), Trace (T), Numeric (NU), Error (E), Failure (FA), Lostdigits (L), NOString (NOS), NOTready (NOT), NOValue (NOV), Prolog (P), and the names that are not settings, All (A), InitialPackageSettings (I), Reset (R), SetPackageSettings (S) and X (X). A name that stops after F or N, or after NO, is not enough to choose, and raises SYNTAX 93.914, as the other strings that are not a name do. A name that has more letters than the ones that choose is taken by the choosing ones: Digitz names Digits.

names = 'D d DI Digitz FO FU T Tr NU Num E Err FA Fail L Lo NOS NOT NOV P'

call try 'p~options("N")'
call try 'p~options("NO")'
call try 'p~options("")'

[class.package.options.settings]

The settings that options reads and sets are these, each with the values that the second argument may take, matched by their first letters and in any case: Digits, a positive whole number, and Fuzz, a whole number that is not negative and is less than Digits; Form, Scientific or Engineering; Numeric, Inherit or Noinherit; Error, Failure, Lostdigits, NOString, NOTready and NOValue, each Condition or Syntax, which is what the directive ::OPTIONS gives; Prolog, Prolog or Noprolog; and Trace, one of the settings of the trace rule. The answer for an option is the string of its setting in upper case, INHERIT, NOINHERIT, CONDITION, SYNTAX, PROLOG or NOPROLOG, and the full name of a trace setting; a number is a decimal string. The second argument raises an error when it is not an acceptable value: SYNTAX 93.900 for the null string, 88.909 for .nil, 93.905 for a Digits value that is not a whole number, 93.907 when it is a whole number that is less than 1, 93.906 for a Fuzz value that is not a whole number that is not negative, 26.900 when a Fuzz value would not be less than Digits, and 33.1 when a Digits value would not be greater than Fuzz (the numeric setting that would be invalid is refused), 93.914 for another value of an option that takes words, and 24.1 for a trace setting that the directive refuses, a number included. The All setting sets the six condition options at once, to Condition or Syntax, and answers the previous six as a string of six names and values, such as ERROR CONDITION FAILURE CONDITION and so on; All cannot be read (SYNTAX 93.903).

[class.package.options.special]

Four names of options take a string of the directive form and not a setting. X takes no second argument and answers the options that the package gave explicitly by an ::OPTIONS directive, as their names separated by blanks, in the order DIGITS, FORM, FUZZ, NUMERIC, ERROR, FAILURE, LOSTDIGITS, NOSTRING, NOTREADY, NOVALUE, PROLOG or NOPROLOG, and TRACE, and answers the null string when it gave none; a setting that options or defaultOptions gave is not explicit. InitialPackageSettings takes no second argument and answers the settings the package had after it was made, in the form of the directive. Reset takes no second argument, answers the current settings in that form, and sets every option back to what InitialPackageSettings answers. SetPackageSettings takes the directive text as its argument, which is required (SYNTAX 93.901) and must begin with ::OPTIONS (SYNTAX 93.900 otherwise); it sets the options that the text gives, resets every other option to its initial value (DIGITS 9, FORM SCIENTIFIC, FUZZ 0 and so on to TRACE NORMAL, as the initial string of options lists them), and answers the previous settings. A second argument on the three raises 93.902.

p = .package~new('n', .array~of('return 1', '::options digits 15 trace r'))
say p~options('X')
p~options('Digits', 20)
say p~options('Digits') '|' p~options('X')
say p~options('InitialPackageSettings')~subword(1, 3)
say p~options('Reset')~subword(1, 3)
say p~options('Digits') p~options('Trace')
say .package~new('m', 'return 1')~options('X')'|'
say p~options('SetPackageSettings', '::OPTIONS DIGITS 7 FUZZ 2')~subword(1, 3)
say p~options~subword(1, 7) p~options('Trace')
say p~options('SetPackageSettings', '::OPTIONS')~subword(1, 3)
say p~options~subword(1, 7)
call try 'p~options("SetPackageSettings")'
call try 'p~options("SetPackageSettings", "DIGITS 7")'
call try 'p~options("SetPackageSettings", "")'
call try 'p~options("X", 1)'
call try 'p~options("Reset", 1)'
call try 'p~options("InitialPackageSettings", 1)'
exit

[class.package.setsecuritymanager]

setSecurityManager gives the package a security manager, or with no argument removes the one it has, and answers 1. It is a protected method. The manager is any object, .nil as well, which is an object like another and is sent the checkpoints, as the Routine rule says; it is not checked when it is set. A second argument raises SYNTAX 93.902. The checkpoints that the checkpoint rules name are offered to the manager for the code of the package that runs after the manager was set, the routines and methods of the package included, and not for the code of other packages.

src~append('  return "done"')

say p~setSecurityManager(.guard~new)
say p~findRoutine('AGENT')~call
say p~setSecurityManager
say p~findRoutine('AGENT')~call
say p~setSecurityManager(.nil) p~setSecurityManager
call try 'p~setSecurityManager(.guard~new, 1)'
exit

rexxref: Builtin Classes > Fundamental Classes > Message Class; Builtin Classes > Fundamental Classes > Message Class > new (Class Method); Builtin Classes > Fundamental Classes > Message Class > arguments; Builtin Classes > Fundamental Classes > Message Class > completed; Builtin Classes > Fundamental Classes > Message Class > errorCondition; Builtin Classes > Fundamental Classes > Message Class > halt; Builtin Classes > Fundamental Classes > Message Class > hasError; Builtin Classes > Fundamental Classes > Message Class > hasResult; Builtin Classes > Fundamental Classes > Message Class > messageComplete; Builtin Classes > Fundamental Classes > Message Class > messageName; Builtin Classes > Fundamental Classes > Message Class > notify; Builtin Classes > Fundamental Classes > Message Class > reply; Builtin Classes > Fundamental Classes > Message Class > replyWith; Builtin Classes > Fundamental Classes > Message Class > result; Builtin Classes > Fundamental Classes > Message Class > send; Builtin Classes > Fundamental Classes > Message Class > sendWith; Builtin Classes > Fundamental Classes > Message Class > start; Builtin Classes > Fundamental Classes > Message Class > startWith; Builtin Classes > Fundamental Classes > Message Class > target; Builtin Classes > Fundamental Classes > Message Class > triggered; Builtin Classes > Fundamental Classes > Message Class > wait; Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > AlarmNotification Class > cancel

Deviations: D105, D107, D109, D113, D116, D118

A Message object is a message that has been written down as an object: a target, the name of a message and its arguments. A program makes one with new, or gets one from the start and startWith methods of Object, and then decides when the message is sent. It can send the message and wait for the answer, start it so that another activity runs it while the sender goes on, or start a copy of it. Afterwards the object keeps what the message answered, or the error that ended it, and a program can ask for them, wait for them, or be told when they are there.

The page specifies the class method that makes a message object, the methods that read what it holds, the methods that run it, the methods that wait for it, stop it or ask for a notification when it is done, and the three methods the class has because it implements the notification interfaces of MessageNotification and AlarmNotification. How an activity is scheduled, when a started message begins to run, and how it interleaves with the activity that started it is specified in the environment chapter. The examples on this page therefore show only results that no scheduling can change: they wait for a message with result or wait, or park the activity of the message on a guard that the example opens, before they print anything that depends on it. The methods that an example waits for, or that the waiting activity calls meanwhile, are UNGUARDED, so that the waiting activity and the activity of the message can both use the object (the guard rule).

The examples that show an error use a routine try that interprets the clause in its argument and prints the clause with the error code, or with the class of the answer when no error is raised.

The class

[class.message.creation]

Message is a class whose superclass is Object and which inherits the mixin classes MessageNotification and AlarmNotification; it is not itself a mixin class. An instance made by new has the default name a Message, and so has its string value (the string rule). A message object that has not been run holds its target, its name and its arguments, has not completed, has no result and has no error.

m = .message~new(.object~new, 'string')
say m~class~id '|' m~string '|' m~defaultName
say .message~superclass~id .message~superclasses~items,
  .message~queryMixinClass
say m~isInstanceOf(.messagenotification) m~isInstanceOf(.alarmnotification)
say m~completed m~hasResult m~hasError m~errorCondition~isNil
say .object~new~start('string')~class~id

[class.message.started]

A message object that has been given start or startWith is a started message. Every later send, sendWith, start, startWith, reply, replyWith, messageComplete or triggered to it raises SYNTAX 98.915, whether or not the first run has ended. No other method refuses it. A message object that has only been sent, that has only received reply or replyWith (its copy was started, and not it), or that has only been run by messageComplete or triggered, is not a started message, and these methods do not refuse it. The copy that reply and replyWith answer is a started message.

t = .t~new
a = .message~new(t, 'hello')
a~start
a~wait
call try 'a~send'
call try 'a~sendWith(, .array~new)'
call try 'a~start'
call try 'a~startWith(, .array~new)'
call try 'a~reply'
call try 'a~replyWith(, .array~new)'
call try 'a~messageComplete(1)'
call try 'a~triggered(1)'
say a~completed a~hasResult a~result a~target~class~id
b = .message~new(t, 'hello')
b~send
b~start
b~wait
say b~result
call try 'b~send'
c = .message~new(t, 'hello')
r = c~reply
call try 'r~send'
call try 'r~start'
call try 'r~reply'
call try 'r~messageComplete(1)'
c~send
c~reply
d = .message~new(t, 'hello')
d~messageComplete
say d~result
d~send
say 'unmarked'
exit

Class methods

new

[class.message.new]

new(target, name, option, ...) makes a message object that has not been run. It needs at least two arguments: fewer raise SYNTAX 93.901, and an omitted target raises 88.901. The target is any object, .nil included. The name is checked next, after the target, as the send rule checks it: a string, or an array of two items, the name and a class that starts the search (the scoped send rule). A name that is not a string is read as the send rule reads it, through request with ARRAY; .nil and an object that answers .nil raise 93.972, an array of another size 93.946, an array whose first item is missing 88.901, an array with a first item that has no string value 88.909 and one with a second item that is not a class 88.914. The null string is a name. The option that follows is the third argument, which says how the remaining arguments are read, as the next rule states. With no option, the message has no arguments. The answer is the new object, and what the object holds is shown by messageName, target and arguments.

t = .t~new
call try '.message~new(t, "hello")'
call try '.message~new(.nil, "hello")'
call try '.message~new(t, "")'
call try '.message~new(t, .array~of("hello", .t))'
call try '.message~new'
call try '.message~new(t)'
call try '.message~new(, "hello")'
call try '.message~new(t, .nil)'
call try '.message~new(t, .array~of("hello"))'
call try '.message~new(t, .array~of(.nil, .t))'
call try '.message~new(t, .array~of("hello", 3))'
call try '.message~new(t, .nil, "Z")'
exit

[class.message.new.options]

The option is a string whose first letter, in either case, is I (individual) or A (array); the other letters are not looked at, so Individual and array are options. Any other string, the null string, and a number raise SYNTAX 93.915, and an option that has no string value raises 88.909; the option is checked after the name. An omitted option with an argument after it raises 88.901. With I, every argument after the option is an argument of the message, in order, and an omitted place stays omitted; omitted places at the end add nothing to the count, as the count rule says, and an argument may be any object, .nil included. With A, the fourth argument is required (SYNTAX 93.901) and is the only argument that may follow: a fifth raises 93.902, also when the fourth is omitted. It holds the arguments of the message: it is an array, or an object that answers an array to the message request with the argument ARRAY, and the items of the array are the arguments in order. The message keeps a copy of the array, made when new runs, so that a change that the caller makes to the array afterwards does not reach the message, and the number of arguments is the position of the last item present, as the count rule says (Deviation 113). An object that answers no array, .nil and an array of more than one dimension among them, raises SYNTAX 88.913.

t = .t~new
say .message~new(t, 'show')~send
say .message~new(t, 'show', 'I', 1, , 3)~send
say .message~new(t, 'show', 'individual', 1, )~send
say .message~new(t, 'show', 'I', , )~send
say .message~new(t, 'show', 'I', 'x', .nil)~send
say .message~new(t, 'show', 'Array', .array~of(4, 5, 6))~send
say .message~new(t, 'show', 'a', .list~of(7, 8))~send
say .message~new(t, 'show', 'A', 'xyz')~send

call try '.message~new(t, "show", "")'

call try '.message~new(t, "show", .nil)'

call try '.message~new(t, "show", , 1)'
call try '.message~new(t, "show", "A")'
call try '.message~new(t, "show", "A", .nil)'
call try '.message~new(t, "show", "A", .array~new(2, 2))'
call try '.message~new(t, "show", "A", .array~of(1), 2)'
exit

[class.message.new.sends]

new sends the message request with the argument ARRAY to the fourth argument of the option A, once, before it sends init, and uses the array that request answers. It sends no message to the target or to the arguments of I, and to the name only the request that the Object sends rule states, before the option is read. It then sends the new object the message init with no argument, whatever arguments new had, so a subclass of Message that declares init sees none of them; the object that init runs on already holds its target, its name and its arguments. The answer of init is not used, and new answers the new object, as the new rule says for every class. new makes an instance of the class that received it, so a subclass of Message makes instances of itself. A name that is no string is sent request once, at new; the message then holds the name the answer gives, and running it sends nothing more. The second example shows it.

t = .t~new
m = .mine~new(t, 'show', 'A', .logged~new)
say 'new answered' m~class~id
m = .mine~new(t, 'show', 'I', 'q', 'r')
say m~send
m = .mine~new(.logged~new, 'show', 'I', .logged~new)
say 'no message to the target or the argument'

  return .array~of(1, 2)

  forward class (super) continue

[class.message.target]

target answers the object that the message is sent to, the object that new was given as the target. A message that has a scoped name sends to this object too, and its target is not the class of the scope. [class.message.arguments]

arguments answers an array that holds the arguments of the message, in order, with the places of omitted arguments empty; it is empty when the message has no arguments. The array is a new one each time the method is sent, so changing it changes nothing in the message. The methods that run the message replace the arguments when they are given some, and the array answers the new ones afterwards. arguments takes no argument.

hasResult answers 1 when the message has been run, has ended without an error and answered a value, and 0 when it has not ended, ended with an error, or answered nothing. The value .nil and the null string are values. It takes no argument. The answer is that of the latest run.

[class.message.haserror]

hasError answers 1 when the latest run ended with an error condition and 0 when the message has not been run, has not ended, or ended without one. The error is a SYNTAX condition that the code of the message raised and nothing trapped there, including the 97.1 of a message that no method of the target understands, and a HALT that nothing trapped, which is the error 4.1 (halt). Any other condition that nothing traps ends the method as the RAISE rule says and is not an error: the message has completed, with no result and no error. The error of an argument that sendWith or the other methods refuse is raised to their caller and is not an error of the message, which is then not run. It takes no argument. The answer, like those of completed, hasResult and errorCondition, is that of the latest run: a message that is sent again starts from the state of one that has not been run.

m = .message~new(t, 'ok')
say m~hasError

say m~hasError

call attempt m
say m~hasError

call attempt m
say m~hasError

say m~hasError

call attempt m
say m~completed m~hasError m~hasResult

end

say g~completed g~hasError
exit

errorCondition answers the condition object of the error that ended the latest run, and .nil when there is none: when the message has not been run, has not ended, or ended without an error. Running the message

[class.message.send]

send(target, argument, ...) sends the message in the activity of the sender and does not answer until the message has ended. It answers what the message answers, and nothing when the message answers nothing, so that a use of the answer as a value then raises SYNTAX 91.999. An error that the message raises is raised at the clause that sent send, as the error of an ordinary message would be, and is also kept: hasError answers 1 and result raises it again. The first argument, when it is not omitted, replaces the target of the message for this and every later run, and it may be .nil. When the call has more than one argument, as the count rule counts them, the arguments after the first replace the arguments of the message likewise; with only a target, or none, the message keeps its arguments. The message is found by the search rule in the target, goes to UNKNOWN when nothing is found, raises NOMETHOD (SYNTAX 97.1 when untrapped) when there is none, and is checked for PRIVATE and PACKAGE access as if the code that called send had sent it. A scoped name starts the search at its class, and raises 93.957 when the target is not an instance of that class; that error is raised to the caller of send, start or the other run methods before the message runs, and is not an error of the message. Each send is a new run: the message can be sent again, and the result, the error and the completion are those of the latest run.

call try 'x = .message~new(t, .array~of("show", .u))~send'
say .message~new(.v~new, 'nosuchzz', 'I', 1, 2)~send
exit

[class.message.sendwith]

sendWith(target, array) is send with the arguments of the message in an array, and it replaces the arguments always. The array is required (SYNTAX 88.901 when it is missing), a third argument raises 93.902, and the first argument is the target, which is replaced as send does when it is not omitted. The second argument is an array, or an object that answers an array to the message request with the argument ARRAY; an object that answers anything else, .nil included, and an array of more than one dimension raise SYNTAX 88.913. The items are the arguments in order. The message keeps a copy of the array, so a later change to it does not reach the message, and the number of arguments is the position of the last item present, as the count rule says (Deviation 113). The target is replaced before the array is checked, so a call that is refused leaves its target in the message; the arguments and what the latest run left are unchanged. Apart from the arguments, sendWith runs the message as send does, answers as it does, and a run replaces the state of the message in the same way.

say m~target~class~id

call try 'm~sendWith(t, .nil)'
call try 'm~sendWith(t, .array~new(2, 2))'
call try 'm~sendWith(t, .array~new, 1)'
r = .message~new(t, 'show')
call try 'r~sendWith(.u~new, .nil)'
say r~target~class~id
exit

[class.message.start]

start(target, argument, ...) starts the message so that another activity runs it, and answers nothing; it does not wait for the message to run. The target and the arguments are taken as send takes them, and a message that has been started is a started message (the started rule). Until the message ends, completed and hasResult answer 0, and hasError answers 0 and errorCondition .nil. When it ends, the message object holds its answer or its error as send leaves them, but an error of the message is not raised to the caller of start: it is kept, and raised to the caller of result. The notifications that notify asked for are sent when the message has ended. The access check is that of Deviation 105.

Note. The error of a started message that nobody asks for is reported on the error stream when the message ends, and the line that the report names is the case of Deviation 67: ooRexx's report often names the line of the activity that waits for the message, and the report of interrexx names the line that raised the error.

[class.message.startwith]

These errors are raised by startWith itself, at the call, and the message is not started when one is raised, though a target given to the call has replaced the message's target. The answer is nothing, and the rest is as for start.

[class.message.reply]

reply(target, argument, ...) makes a copy of the message, starts the copy as start does, and answers the copy at once, so that the sender goes on. The target and arguments are taken as send takes them, and when they are given they replace those of the message and of the copy alike. The copy has the same name and notifications as the message, is a started message (the started rule), and is the object that holds the answer or the error of the run: the message that received reply is not run, and does not complete. It can therefore be given reply again, which starts another copy, and it is send or start that run the message object itself. A program that waits for the answer asks the copy.

Waiting for the message

[class.message.result]

result answers what the message answered, and waits first when the message has been started and has not ended. When the message answered nothing it answers .nil, so that hasResult is the way to tell the two apart. When the latest run ended with an error, result raises that error again, in the activity of its caller, with the code of the error that the message raised: the trap there sees a new condition object each time, with the CODE, RC, CONDITION, DESCRIPTION, ADDITIONAL, ERRORTEXT and MESSAGE of the object that errorCondition answers, which is the same object each time, so that the SYNTAX 42.3 of a division by zero in the message is 42.3 at the clause that asked for result, and asking again raises it again. result takes no argument. What result does for a message that nothing will run, such as one that has never been sent or the original of a reply, is the case of Deviation 20.

[class.message.halt]

halt(description) asks for the HALT condition to be raised in the activity that is running the message, and answers 1 when a run of the message is in progress, started or sent (a sent message runs in the sender's activity, which then gets the HALT), and 0 when the message has not been run. The description is optional and is a string, which the condition has as CONDITION('D'); without one that is the null string. .nil as the description raises SYNTAX 88.909, and a second argument 93.902. Code of the message that traps HALT, as the HALT page describes, handles it as for any HALT. A HALT nothing traps ends the message with the error 4.1, which hasError, errorCondition and result then show as for any other error of a message. For a message that has ended, halt answers 1: a message that send ran gets the HALT raised in the activity that sent it, with the description, and that activity ends with error 4.1 when nothing traps it, and for a message that was started nothing happens, so that hasError, hasResult and result stay as they were. Being told when the message has ended

[class.message.notify]

notify(target) asks for a notification when the message ends: the object target is sent the message messageComplete with the message object as its only argument. The target must be an instance of MessageNotification, a class that inherits it or a subclass of one; any other object, .nil included, raises SYNTAX 88.914, no target 88.901 and a second argument 93.902. notify answers nothing and can be sent any number of times: the targets are kept in the order of the calls, and each is sent messageComplete each time the message ends, in that order. A run of send or sendWith sends them before it returns, in the activity of the sender, and an error that a messageComplete raises is raised there, so that it ends the send clause; the targets after the one that raised it are not sent messageComplete, and when the message itself ended with an error, the sender sees the error of the messageComplete, while errorCondition keeps that of the message. The error does not become an error of a sent message, which has ended without one. When a message that has ended is given a target, the target is sent messageComplete at once, in the activity that called notify. For a started message the targets are sent it in the activity that ran the message; when that happens relative to the activity that waits for the message is a matter of scheduling. For a started message, an error that a messageComplete raises becomes the error of the message: hasError answers 1, errorCondition answers the condition of that error and result raises it, while hasResult keeps the 1 of the run. The targets after the one that raised it are not sent messageComplete, and the target that raised it is sent it that once (Deviation 116). hasError answers 1 once the error has been recorded, which may be after wait has returned. A copy made by reply has the targets of the message, and so has the one that copy makes. The message the target is sent is the completed message object, so completed answers 1 in it.

[class.message.messagecomplete]

messageComplete(source) is the method of the notification interface that a message has itself: a message that is the target of a notify is sent messageComplete when the message it waited for has ended, and starts. It runs the message that received it, as start would, in another activity, and answers nothing at once. The argument, the completed message, is not used and may be omitted; two arguments raise SYNTAX 93.902. The message that receives it is not made a started message, so send can run it afterwards, and one that has been given start or startWith raises 98.915, as the started rule says.

[class.message.triggered]

triggered(source) is the method of the alarm notification interface that a message has itself: an Alarm or Ticker whose target is the message calls it when the alarm goes off. Sends

[class.message.sends]

No method of Message sends a message to the message object itself, so a subclass that overrides send, start, startWith, reply, replyWith, notify or any other method sees it called only by a program: messageComplete and triggered start the message without sending start, reply starts a copy without sending send or start, and the notification of a message sent with notify sends messageComplete to the target, which is where an override of that method in the target shows. The messages that methods of the class send to other objects are stated by the rules of new, sendWith, startWith, replyWith and notify.

say '--'

c~wait
say '--'

s~wait
say '--'

c = r~replyWith(, .array~of(1))
c~wait
say '--'

q~wait

Deviations

[class.message.deviation.105]

A message that start, startWith, reply or replyWith runs is checked for PRIVATE and PACKAGE access as the same message sent by send from the code that called it, as the access rule states for a started message: the code of a class can start a private message to its own objects, and a PACKAGE message to an object of the same package. ooRexx raises 97.2 for every private message and 97.1 for every PACKAGE message that is started (Deviation 105).

o = .w~new
say o~viaStart('secret')
say o~viaStart('pack')
say o~viaReply('secret')
say .message~new(o, 'pack')~~start~result
::class w
::method viaStart unguarded
  m = .message~new(self, arg(1))
  m~start
  return m~result
::method viaReply unguarded
  return .message~new(self, arg(1))~reply~result
::method secret private
  return 'secret ran'
::method pack package
  return 'pack ran'

[class.message.deviation.113]

new with the option A keeps a copy of the array of arguments, so that a change to the caller's array after new does not reach the message, and the number of arguments of the message is the position of the last item present. MessageNotification

rexxref: Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > MessageNotification Class; Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > MessageNotification Class > messageComplete (Abstract Method)

MessageNotification is an interface class: a class that a program's class inherits to say that its instances can be told when a message has ended. An object that was given to the notify method of a Message as the target of a notification has to be an instance of it, and the library then sends that object the one message the interface names, messageComplete, each time the message ends. The class itself implements nothing: its one method is abstract, and an implementation is a class that declares messageComplete.

The page specifies what the class is, what an implementation has to answer to, and when and how the library sends to it. How the activities that run a message and its notifications are scheduled is specified in the environment chapter.

The class

[class.messagenotification.creation]

MessageNotification is a mixin class whose superclass is Object, and queryMixinClass answers 1 for it (the mixin rule). A class implements the interface by inheriting it with the INHERIT option of ::CLASS, or by being a subclass of such a class; an object is an implementation when it is an instance of one of these, which is what isInstanceOf tests, and nothing else counts: an object whose class has a method messageComplete and does not inherit the interface is not accepted by notify, which raises SYNTAX 88.914 for it. new is not refused, and makes an object of the class that received it. Message is itself an implementation, so a message object can be the target of a notification.

say .messagenotification~queryMixinClass .messagenotification~superclass~id
say .messagenotification~new~class~id .messagenotification~new~string
say .impl~new~isInstanceOf(.messagenotification),
  .sub~new~isInstanceOf(.messagenotification),
  .plain~new~isInstanceOf(.messagenotification),
  .message~new(.object~new, 'string')~isInstanceOf(.messagenotification)
m = .message~new(.plain~new, 'messageComplete')
call try 'm~notify(.plain~new)'
call try 'm~notify(.sub~new)'
exit

  signal on syntax name bad
  interpret arg(1)
  say arg(1) '=> ok'
  return
bad: say arg(1) '=>' condition('o')~code
  return

messageComplete

[class.messagenotification.messagecomplete]

messageComplete(source) is abstract. Sent to an object whose class has no messageComplete of its own, whatever arguments it has, it raises SYNTAX 93.965, as the abstract rule says of any abstract method. An implementation declares the method and takes one argument, the message object that has ended, as source: the library sends it after the run has ended, so completed answers 1 for it, and the answer of the message is there for result to give, or its error for errorCondition. What an implementation answers is not used. The library sends the message in the circumstances that the notify rule lists: once for each notify to the target, at each end of the message and in the order of the calls; at once when the message had already ended; and in the activity that ran the message for a message that was started. What an error that a messageComplete raises does to the message depends on how the message was run, as the notify rule states.

g~start

say log~lines~strip

call try '.noimpl~new~messageComplete'
call try '.messagenotification~new~messageComplete(1, 2, 3)'
exit

AlarmNotification

rexxref: Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > AlarmNotification Class; Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > AlarmNotification Class > cancel; Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > AlarmNotification Class > triggered (Abstract method)

Deviations: D119

AlarmNotification is an interface class: a class that a program's class inherits to say that its instances can be told when an alarm goes off or is cancelled. An object that is given to an Alarm or a Ticker as the target of its notification has to be an instance of it, and the library sends that object triggered when the time comes and cancel when the alarm is cancelled. Message is an implementation, so a message object can be the target of an alarm. The interface has two methods: triggered is abstract and an implementation declares it, and cancel does nothing, so that an implementation declares it only when it wants to hear of cancellations.

The page specifies what the class is, what an implementation has to answer to, and when the library sends to it. The classes Alarm and Ticker are specified apart from this page, and the times at which an alarm goes off and how its activity is scheduled are specified in the environment chapter; the examples here wait on a guard that the notification opens before they print what it recorded.

The class

[class.alarmnotification.creation]

AlarmNotification is a mixin class whose superclass is Object, and queryMixinClass answers 1 for it (the mixin rule). A class implements the interface by inheriting it with the INHERIT option of ::CLASS, or by being a subclass of such a class; an object is an implementation when it is an instance of one of these, as isInstanceOf tests. Nothing else counts: an Alarm or a Ticker made with a target that is not an implementation, .nil and an object whose class has a method triggered but does not inherit the interface among them, raises SYNTAX 88.914, and one made with no target raises 93.901. new is not refused for AlarmNotification itself, and makes an object of the class that received it. A Message is an implementation.

say .alarmnotification~new~class~id .alarmnotification~new~string
say .impl~new~isInstanceOf(.alarmnotification),
  .sub~new~isInstanceOf(.alarmnotification),
  .plain~new~isInstanceOf(.alarmnotification),
  .message~new(.object~new, 'string')~isInstanceOf(.alarmnotification)
call try '.alarm~new(60, .plain~new)'
call try '.alarm~new(60, .nil)'
call try '.alarm~new(60)'
call try '.alarm~new(60, .sub~new)~cancel'
call try '.ticker~new(60, .plain~new)'
call try '.ticker~new(60)'
exit

  say arg(1) '=> ok'
  return

  return

[class.alarmnotification.triggered]

triggered(source) is abstract. Sent to an object whose class has no triggered of its own, whatever arguments it has, it raises SYNTAX 93.965, as the abstract rule says of any abstract method. An implementation declares the method and takes one argument, the Alarm or Ticker that went off, as source: the library sends it at the time of the alarm, once for an Alarm, and once at each time for a Ticker until that is cancelled. [class.alarmnotification.cancel]

cancel(source) does nothing and answers nothing, whatever arguments it is sent, none included; an implementation that wants to hear of cancellations declares it. Collection

rexxref: Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Collection Class; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Collection Class > [] (Abstract Method); Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Collection Class > []= (Abstract Method); Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Collection Class > allIndexes (Abstract Method); Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Collection Class > allItems (Abstract Method); Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Collection Class > at (Abstract Method); Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Collection Class > difference; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Collection Class > disjoint; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Collection Class > equivalent; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Collection Class > hasIndex; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Collection Class > hasItem; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Collection Class > index (Abstract Method); Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Collection Class > intersection; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Collection Class > items; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Collection Class > makeArray; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Collection Class > put (Abstract Method); Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Collection Class > subset; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Collection Class > supplier; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Collection Class > union; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Collection Class > xor

Deviations: D78, D109, D118

Collection is the mixin class that all the collection classes have in common. It defines nineteen methods. Seven of them are abstract: they name what a collection has to be able to do, reading and writing an entry by its index and listing its indexes and items, and a class that inherits Collection declares them. The other twelve are written in terms of those seven and of the messages a collection answers for itself. They are the questions about an index, an item, the count and a supplier, and the set operations that combine two collections. A class that inherits only Collection gets all twelve working as the rules below say; a concrete class of the library may declare a method of the same name instead, and its page says what that method does.

The page specifies the methods in that order. Where a method sends a message that a program can override, its .sends rule gives the message, the receiver and the order, as the sends rule asks. The argument of a set operation is read by a rule of its own, shared by the seven operations. OrderedCollection declares its own versions of five of the set operations, and MapCollection its own makeArray; the pages of the concrete collections link to this page for what they do not declare.

The examples use the class box, a collection of strings in which the item and the index of an entry are the same string. It keeps its entries in a directory, answers the indexes and the items in sorted order, and declares put, remove and copy for the set operations; the rest it gets from Collection.

The class

[class.collection.creation]

Collection is a mixin class whose superclass is Object, and queryMixinClass answers 1 for it (the mixin rule). new is not refused: it makes an object of the class that received it, as the new rule says, and that object understands the nineteen methods of the class and no others beyond those of Object. A class that inherits Collection, or a subclass of such a class, understands them all and gets each from this page unless it or a class between it and Collection declares a method of the same name.

c = .collection~new
say c~class~id .collection~queryMixinClass .collection~superclass~id
names = 'allIndexes allItems at difference disjoint equivalent hasIndex',
    'hasItem index intersection items makeArray put subset supplier union',
    'xor [] []='
n = 0
do m over names~makearray(' ')
  if c~hasMethod(m) then n += 1
end
say n c~hasMethod('OF') c~hasMethod('APPEND') c~hasMethod('PUTALL')
say .box~new~hasMethod('UNION') .box~new~hasMethod('FIRST')
::class box inherit collection

The abstract methods

[class.collection.abstract]

The methods [], []=, at, put, allIndexes, allItems and index are abstract. Sent to an object whose class has none of its own, each raises SYNTAX 93.965 whatever arguments the message has, none or too many included, and the raising comes before any check of the arguments, so that at with no argument raises 93.965 and not a missing-argument error (the abstract rule). The assignment c[i] = v is the message []=. A class that declares one of them answers the message itself. The methods that this page defines build on these: allIndexes and allItems are what hasIndex, hasItem, items, makeArray and supplier use, and put is what the set operations use to store.

call try 'c~at(1, 2, 3)'
call try 'c~put(1, 2)'
call try 'c~allIndexes'
call try 'c~allItems(7)'
call try 'c~index("x")'
call try 'c[1]'
call try 'c[1] = "x"'
say .part~new~at(5)
exit

[class.collection.supplier]

supplier answers a Supplier whose items are the objects that allItems answered and whose indexes are the objects that allIndexes answered, the entry at the same position of the two being a pair. It takes its arguments as items does, that is, ignores them. The two answers are taken once, when supplier is sent: the supplier is not a view on the collection. The Supplier class has its own page.

[class.collection.operand]

The argument of union, difference, intersection, xor, subset, disjoint and equivalent is read as a list of entries, and what is sent to it depends on what it is, which the object itself decides by its answers to isA (the isA rule). An ordered argument, one for which isA says it is an OrderedCollection, is sent allItems. Any other object for which isA says it is a MapCollection is sent supplier by union, intersection, xor and disjoint, and allIndexes by difference and subset. Every other object is sent makeArray. An object that is both counts as ordered. An element of an ordered or plain list is an index and an item at once; an entry of a map is its own index with its own item. disjoint reads its argument through intersection, and equivalent through subset. What is done with the answer is the subject of the list rule, the map rule and the answer rule.

do k over .array~of(.ordered~new, .mapped~new, .plain~new, .both~new)
  say '==' k~class~id
  r = a~union(k)
  r = a~difference(k)
  r = a~subset(k)
end

[class.collection.operand.isa]

Each of the seven operations asks the argument what it is by sending isA with the class OrderedCollection and, when the answer is not 1, isA with the class MapCollection. An answer of 1 to the first question ends the questions. The answers are used as logical values, so what an object answers to isA is what decides, not the classes it inherits: an object that inherits no mixin and answers 1 is read as an ordered argument, and an instance of a class that inherits OrderedCollection and answers 0 to both is read as a plain one. An answer that is neither 0 nor 1 raises SYNTAX 34.1, and so does .nil. equivalent asks after its two items messages, as part of the subset it sends, and subset asks once more, with the class Set, as its rule says.

[class.collection.operand.list]

The answer of allItems or makeArray is read as two arrays, the items and the indexes, and the operation takes the entries from position 1 of the items up to its size, an entry being the item at the position and the index at the same position, .nil when there is none. An answer that is an Array of that class itself is both arrays: it is read position by position, so an element is its own index, and a position that holds nothing is an entry whose item and index are .nil. Any other answer, an instance of a subclass of Array included, is sent makeArray twice, and the first answer is the items and the second the indexes; for a List, a Queue, a Set or a string the two are the same. An instance of a subclass of List is such an answer, and is sent makeArray like the instance of any other class that is not Array itself (Deviation 118). Messages that the operation sends to the entries are those of its own rule.

A map argument of union, intersection, xor and disjoint is read from the answer of supplier, and the operation does not need that to be a Supplier: it sends available, and while the answer is true sends index, then the operation's own message to the receiver or the copy with the index, then item only when the operation has an item to store, then next, and asks available again. [class.collection.operand.answer]

The object that makeArray, allItems or allIndexes answered is not required to be a collection, only to understand the messages the operation sends it, and what it lacks is found out when the message is due. The four operations that read a list send makeArray to an answer that is not an Array of that class itself, and one that has no makeArray method raises SYNTAX 98.913; an UNKNOWN method does not count as one. difference sends [] to the answer and subset sends hasItem, and an answer that does not understand one raises SYNTAX 93.948, an UNKNOWN method that answers the message counting as understanding it. difference and subset also send items to the argument itself, after copy, and what that answers is how many positions difference takes: an answer that is not a number raises SYNTAX 41.1, and .nil raises SYNTAX 93.948, and a position beyond the end of the answer reads .nil.

call try 'union', .mp~new(.noindex~new), 'no index'
call try 'difference', .pk~new(.object~new), 'plain object'
call try 'difference', .pk~new(.unk~new), 'UNKNOWN only'
call try 'subset', .pk~new(.object~new), 'plain object'
call try 'subset', .pk~new(.unk~new), 'UNKNOWN only'
call try 'difference', .counted~new('abc'), 'items abc'
call try 'difference', .counted~new(.nil), 'items .nil'
call try 'difference', .counted~new(3), 'items 3'
exit

union, intersection and xor use what hasIndex answers as a logical value. union refuses an answer that is not a string, .nil included, with SYNTAX 93.948 whatever its string value, and a string that is neither 0 nor 1 with SYNTAX 34.901. intersection and xor read an answer that is not a string by its string value, and an answer whose value is neither 0 nor 1, .nil included, raises SYNTAX 34.1 there, and so from disjoint, which reads its argument through intersection. [class.collection.operand.error]

Each of the seven operations takes exactly one argument: none raises SYNTAX 93.901 and a second raises SYNTAX 93.902. An argument that isA does not report as ordered or as a map and that has no makeArray method, .nil and an object of a class with no such method included, raises SYNTAX 93.948 from union, difference, intersection, xor, subset and disjoint. equivalent sends items to the argument first, and raises SYNTAX 97.1 for the same objects. A string is read by its makeArray, so union, intersection, xor and disjoint read a string without line ends as a list of one element. A string has no items method, which difference and subset need after they have read the argument and equivalent needs first: a string raises SYNTAX 93.948 from the first two and SYNTAX 97.1 from equivalent.

[class.collection.union]

union(other) answers a new collection: the object that the receiver's copy answers, with the entries of the argument added whose index it lacks. An argument that is read as a list (the operand rule) adds each element as an item stored at an index equal to it; an argument that is a map adds each of its entries, with its own item, at its own index. An entry whose index the copy has is not added, and the receiver is not changed.

[class.collection.union.sends]

[class.collection.difference.sends]

difference first reads the argument: it sends isA with OrderedCollection and, when that does not answer 1, isA with MapCollection, then allItems, allIndexes or makeArray as the operand rule says. It then sends copy to the receiver and items to the argument, with no argument. It then does the following for each of the positions from 1 up to the number that items answered: it sends [] with the position to the answer that the first step gave, and remove to the copy with what [] answered. A position beyond the end of the answer reads .nil, and the answer of remove is not used. [class.collection.subset]

subset(other) answers 1 when each item that the receiver's makeArray answers is equal to an element that the argument supplies, and 0 otherwise. The argument is read as the operand rule says, so for a plain or ordered argument the elements are its items, and a receiver with no items is a subset of every collection. An item and an element are equal as == compares strings: 1 and 1.0 differ, and so do a and A. For an argument that is read through allIndexes, the elements are its indexes, and an item of the receiver that is one of them must also have a matching entry: the receiver's entry at that index is sent \= with the argument's entry at that index, and an answer of 1 makes the result 0, so a receiver whose entries do not override \= compares them as = does, where 1 and 1.0 are equal and a and A are not. When isA says that the argument is a Set, its entries are not compared, because an index and its item are the same there. The answer of that isA is used as a logical value: a string that is neither 0 nor 1 raises SYNTAX 34.901, and an answer that is not a string, .nil included, raises SYNTAX 93.948 whatever its string value. The answer of \= is used as a logical value: what is neither 0 nor 1 raises SYNTAX 34.6.

[class.collection.subset.sends]

subset first reads the argument: it sends isA with OrderedCollection and, when that does not answer 1, isA with MapCollection, then allItems, allIndexes or makeArray as the operand rule says. For a map it then sends isA with Set. Then it sends copy to the receiver, items to the argument and makeArray to the receiver, each with no argument, and uses none of the first two answers. A copy that answers anything and an items that answers anything do not matter, but an argument that does not understand items raises SYNTAX 93.948. The answer of the receiver's makeArray has to be an Array of that class itself: an instance of a subclass of Array raises SYNTAX 98.913, and nothing is sent to it. subset reads its positions from 1 up to its last, a position that holds nothing giving the item .nil, and for each item, in order, subset sends hasItem with the item to the answer of the first step, and answers 0 at the first item for which that answers 0, sending nothing more. For a map that is not a Set, when hasItem answers 1 it sends [] with the item to the receiver and then [] with the item to the argument itself, and then \= to the receiver's entry with the argument's entry as the argument. An answer of 1 ends the operation with 0. When every item has passed the answer is 1.

say a~subset(.lmap~new('arg', 'k', .e~new('one'), 'm', .e~new('2')))

MapCollection

rexxref: Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > MapCollection Class; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > MapCollection Class > of (Class Method); Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > MapCollection Class > makeArray; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > MapCollection Class > putAll

Deviations: D33

MapCollection is the mixin class of the collections that map an index to an item: the directories, the tables, the relations, the sets and the other classes that the class hierarchy lists as inheriting it. It inherits Collection, and so has every method of that page, and it adds three: the class method of, which builds a collection from index and item pairs, and the instance methods makeArray, which answers the indexes where Collection answers the items, and putAll, which copies every entry of another collection in. The mixin also decides how a map is read when it is the argument of a set operation, which the operand rule states.

A class that inherits only MapCollection has to declare put and allIndexes, which are abstract in Collection; the examples use the class store, which keeps its entries in a directory and declares those two, allItems and a string method that lists its entries in index order.

The class

[class.mapcollection.creation]

MapCollection is a mixin class whose superclass is Collection, and queryMixinClass answers 1 for it (the mixin rule). new is not refused and makes an object of the class that received it, as the new rule says. The instance methods that the class declares are makeArray and putAll, and of is declared on the class side: the class and every class that inherits it understand of, and no instance does, so hasMethod('OF') answers 1 for the class and 0 for an instance. Everything else an instance understands it gets from Collection.

c = .mapcollection~new
say c~class~id .mapcollection~queryMixinClass .mapcollection~superclass~id
say .mapcollection~hasMethod('OF') c~hasMethod('OF')
say c~hasMethod('MAKEARRAY') c~hasMethod('PUTALL') c~hasMethod('UNION')
say .store~hasMethod('OF') .store~new~hasMethod('OF')
::class store inherit mapcollection

Class methods

of

[class.mapcollection.of]

of(pair, ...) answers a new object of the class that received it, made by new and holding one entry for each argument: an argument is an array of exactly two items, the index first and then the item, and the entry is the second item stored at the first. The arguments are taken from left to right, so a later pair with the same index replaces the item of an earlier one when the class's put replaces. With no argument the result is an empty collection. A trailing omitted argument counts for nothing. A class that declares no put of its own gets the abstract put of Collection, so .mapcollection~of with a pair raises SYNTAX 93.965.

[class.mapcollection.of.sends]

of sends new to the class that received it, with no argument, before it looks at any argument. For each argument in order it then asks the argument what it is and how big, by sending it isA with the class Array; when that answers 1, dimension; when that answers 1, items and then last, whatever items answered; and when both answered a number equal to 2, [] with 2 and then [] with 1, and then put to the new object with the item and then the index. dimension, items and last have no argument. An answer of 0 to isA or to dimension ends the checks of that argument with the error rule's error. What new answers is the result, and init is not sent again. The argument need not be an Array: an object that answers those messages as one does is accepted.

[class.mapcollection.of.error]

Each argument is checked when it is reached, after the pairs before it have been stored. The answers to isA and to dimension are used as logical values, and the argument is accepted when both are 1. An argument for which isA answers 0, .nil and a string included, raises SYNTAX 88.923, and so does one whose dimension answers 0; an answer that is neither 0 nor 1 raises SYNTAX 34.901, which is what a multi-dimensional array answers to dimension, and .nil raises SYNTAX 97.1. An argument that is accepted has to answer a number equal to 2 at NUMERIC DIGITS 9, whatever the caller's setting, to both items and last, or it raises SYNTAX 88.924: an array with a hole, such as one with items at positions 1 and 3, has two items but its last is 3. An argument that is omitted and is followed by another raises SYNTAX 93.903.

putAll

[class.mapcollection.putall]

putAll(source) stores every entry of source into the receiver and answers the receiver. The entries are those of the supplier that source answers to supplier, in the order the supplier gives them, each stored by put with the supplier's item and then its index; an entry of the source whose index the receiver has is stored over by put in the way that put of the receiver decides. source need not be a collection: any object that understands supplier is accepted. The method takes exactly one argument: none raises SYNTAX 93.901 and a second raises SYNTAX 93.902.

call try 's~putAll(1, 2)'

OrderedCollection

rexxref: Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > OrderedCollection Class; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > OrderedCollection Class > append (Abstract Method); Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > OrderedCollection Class > appendAll; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > OrderedCollection Class > delete (Abstract Method); Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > OrderedCollection Class > difference; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > OrderedCollection Class > first (Abstract Method); Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > OrderedCollection Class > firstItem (Abstract Method); Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > OrderedCollection Class > insert (Abstract Method); Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > OrderedCollection Class > intersection; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > OrderedCollection Class > last (Abstract Method); Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > OrderedCollection Class > lastItem (Abstract Method); Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > OrderedCollection Class > next (Abstract Method); Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > OrderedCollection Class > previous (Abstract Method); Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > OrderedCollection Class > section (Abstract Method); Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > OrderedCollection Class > sort; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > OrderedCollection Class > sortWith; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > OrderedCollection Class > stableSort; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > OrderedCollection Class > stableSortWith; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > OrderedCollection Class > subset; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > OrderedCollection Class > union; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > OrderedCollection Class > xor

Deviations: D109, D118

OrderedCollection is the mixin class of the collections whose entries have an order of their own: the arrays, the lists, the queues and the circular queues. It inherits Collection and declares twenty methods of its own. The ones that walk and change a sequence, first, firstItem, last, lastItem, next, previous, append, insert, delete and section, are abstract, and the four sorts are written in terms of other messages. The rest are appendAll and the set operations union, difference, intersection, xor and subset, which replace the versions of Collection for a class that inherits this mixin. disjoint and equivalent are not replaced: they are the methods of that page, and they use the set operations of this one through the messages they send.

The set operations here treat the collection as a sequence that may repeat an item: a repeated item counts as many times as it occurs. They are built on messages that the receiver has to understand: removeItem, which no mixin defines, append, which this mixin declares abstract, and hasItem, which Collection defines. The examples use the class seq, which keeps its items in an array and declares init, string, append, removeItem, allItems, items, isEmpty and copy; hasItem it gets from Collection.

The class

[class.orderedcollection.creation]

OrderedCollection is a mixin class whose superclass is Collection, and queryMixinClass answers 1 for it (the mixin rule). new is not refused and makes an object of the class that received it, as the new rule says. The instance methods that the class declares are append, appendAll, delete, difference, first, firstItem, insert, intersection, last, lastItem, next, previous, section, sort, sortWith, stableSort, stableSortWith, subset, union and xor; there is no class method. A class that inherits the mixin gets these before the methods of Collection of the same name, and gets disjoint, equivalent and the rest from Collection.

c = .orderedcollection~new
say c~class~id c~class~queryMixinClass c~class~superclass~id
names = 'append appendAll delete difference first firstItem insert',
  'intersection last lastItem next previous section sort sortWith',
  'stableSort stableSortWith subset union xor'
n = 0
do m over names~makearray(' ')
  if c~hasMethod(m) then n += 1
end
say n c~hasMethod('DISJOINT') c~hasMethod('HASINDEX') c~hasMethod('OF')

The abstract methods

[class.orderedcollection.abstract]

The methods append, delete, first, firstItem, insert, last, lastItem, next, previous and section are abstract. Sent to an object whose class has none of its own, each raises SYNTAX 93.965 whatever arguments the message has, none or too many included (the abstract rule). A class that declares one answers the message itself.

Sorting

[class.orderedcollection.sort]

The methods sort, stableSort, sortWith and stableSortWith sort any receiver through other messages; a class that inherits the mixin and has no sorts of its own, such as List, uses them. They check the number of their arguments first: sort and stableSort take none, and an argument raises SYNTAX 93.902; sortWith and stableSortWith take exactly one, none raises SYNTAX 93.901 and a second SYNTAX 93.902, and the argument is not checked to be a comparator. sort sends stableSort to the receiver, and sortWith sends stableSortWith with its argument. stableSort sends makeArray to the receiver and sort to the answer; stableSortWith sends that answer sortWith with the comparator. Then the receiver is sent first, the sorted array size, and for each place from 1 to that size the array is sent [] with the place, the receiver []= with that item and the current index, and then next with that index, which gives the index for the next item. The receiver answers itself. A receiver whose makeArray reaches an abstract method, an instance of the mixin itself among them, raises SYNTAX 93.965.

c = .orderedcollection~new
call try 'c~sort'
call try 'c~sort(1)'
call try 'c~stableSort'
call try 'c~stableSort(1)'
call try 'c~sortWith'
call try 'c~sortWith(.numericComparator~new)'
call try 'c~sortWith(.nil)'
call try 'c~sortWith(1, 2)'
call try 'c~stableSortWith'
call try 'c~stableSortWith("not a comparator")'
call try 'c~stableSortWith(1, 2)'
exit

[class.orderedcollection.appendall]

appendAll(source) adds every item of source to the end of the receiver, in the order the source gives them, and answers the receiver. The items are those that the source answers to allItems, an array or any collection. The source need not be a collection: any object that understands allItems is accepted, and an answer that is a string counts as one item. The answer of allItems is taken before the first append, so a collection can append its own items. The method takes exactly one argument: none raises SYNTAX 93.901 and a second raises SYNTAX 93.902. A source that does not understand allItems raises SYNTAX 93.948, and an answer of .nil raises SYNTAX 98.913; both are raised before anything is appended.

call try 's~appendAll(1, 2)'
call try 's~appendAll("text")'
call try 's~appendAll(.nil)'
call try 's~appendAll(.nothing~new)'
exit

Set operations

[class.orderedcollection.operand]

The argument of union, difference, intersection, xor and subset is read as a list of items, and so is that of disjoint and equivalent through the methods that they send. The argument is asked isA with the class Collection (the isA rule). When that answers 1, whichever of the mixins the object has, it is sent allItems, with no argument. Any other object is sent makeArray, and what that answers is sent allItems: an object that does not understand makeArray, .nil included, raises SYNTAX 93.948, and so does an answer of makeArray that does not understand allItems, a string included. What allItems answers is read by the answer rule. Each of the five operations takes exactly one argument: none raises SYNTAX 93.901 and a second raises SYNTAX 93.902. A string is read by its makeArray, which answers an array of its lines, so a string without line ends is a list of one item.

say a~union('one two')

call try 'a~union(.nil)'
call try 'a~union(.object~new)'
call try 'a~union(.badmake~new)'
call try 'a~union'
call try 'a~xor(1, 2)'
exit

[class.orderedcollection.operand.isa]

Each of the five operations asks the argument what it is by sending isA with the class Collection, and nothing else: an answer of 1 makes the argument a list that is sent allItems, and an answer of 0 makes it an object that is sent makeArray. The answer decides, not the classes the object inherits: an object that inherits no mixin and answers 1 is read through allItems, and an instance of a class that inherits Collection and answers 0 is read through makeArray. The answer is used as a logical value: a string that is neither 0 nor 1 raises SYNTAX 34.901, and an answer that is not a string, .nil included, raises SYNTAX 93.948 whatever its string value. appendAll does not send isA.

[class.orderedcollection.operand.answer]

The answer of allItems is read as DO OVER reads a collection: makeArray is sent to it once and the items present in the array that comes back are the items of the list, in order, a position that holds nothing being skipped. [class.orderedcollection.union]

union(other) answers a new collection: the object that the receiver's copy answers, with every item of the argument appended to it, in the order the argument gives them. An item that the receiver already has is appended again, so the result has as many copies of an item as the receiver and the argument have together. The receiver is not changed. After the items have been appended, at once when the argument has none, the copy is sent isA with the class Array; its answer is read by its string value as a logical value, and one that is neither 0 nor 1, .nil included, raises SYNTAX 34.1. On 1 the answer is what the copy answers to makeArray, sent with no argument, and on 0 it is the copy.

[class.orderedcollection.xor]

xor(other) answers a new collection: the object that the receiver's copy answers, in which each item of the argument, in order, cancels one occurrence of itself when a working copy of the receiver still has one, and is appended otherwise. Occurrences therefore cancel one against one: an item that the argument has more often than the receiver has it is appended once for each occurrence left over. The receiver is not changed. After the items have been appended or removed, at once when the argument has none, the result is sent isA with the class Array; its answer is read by its string value as a logical value, and one that is neither 0 nor 1, .nil included, raises SYNTAX 34.1. On 1 the answer is what the result answers to makeArray, sent with no argument, and on 0 it is the result.

a = .seq~new('a b b c')
say a~xor(.seq~new('b c c d'))
say a~xor(.array~of('b', 'b', 'b'))
say '['a~xor(a)']' a

[class.orderedcollection.xor.sends]

xor sends copy to the receiver twice: the first answer is the result and the second is a working copy. It then reads the argument as the operand rule says, and sends makeArray once to the answer of allItems, as DO OVER does. For each item present in the array that came back, in order, it sends hasItem to the working copy; when that answers 1 it sends removeItem with the item to the result and then to the working copy, and otherwise it sends append with the item to the result. Then it sends isA with Array to the result, and makeArray to it when that answered 1; nothing else is sent.

a = .lseq~new('a b')
r = a~xor(.tr~new)
say r

[class.orderedcollection.subset]

subset(other) answers 1 when the receiver has no item that the argument lacks, and 0 otherwise, counting repeats: a copy of the receiver has one occurrence of each item of the argument removed, and the answer is 1 when what is left has no items, that is, when items of the copy answers a number equal to 0. The number 0 is compared with the answer by =, so 0.0 and 0 are equal to it, and an answer that is an object is compared as the number 0 sees it, not by its own =, \=, == or \==. An empty receiver is a subset of every collection, and a receiver is a subset of itself.

[class.orderedcollection.subset.sends]

subset sends isA with the class Collection to the argument and, when that does not answer 1, makeArray to it. It then sends copy to the receiver, then allItems to the argument, or to what its makeArray answered, and makeArray once to the answer of allItems, as DO OVER does. It sends removeItem to the copy with each item present in the array that came back, in order, whether or not the copy has it. Last it sends items to the copy and compares 0 with the answer by =, so the = of the answer itself is never sent, and the result is 1 when the two are equal as numbers. The order is that of a plain argument; for an ordered one there is no makeArray before the copy.

say a~subset(.tr~new)
say a~subset(.oa~new)

[class.orderedcollection.deviation.109]

An instance of a subclass of String that subset compares is read by its own characters, and REQUEST and MAKESTRING are not sent to it (Deviation 109). That reaches the answer of items of the copy, which 0 is compared with. ooRexx sends such an instance request with STRING or MAKESTRING, so an override of either can change what is read. In the example MAKESTRING answers other characters.
