SetCollection

rexxref: Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > SetCollection Class

SetCollection is the mixin class that marks a collection as a set: one in which the index of an entry and its item are the same object. It declares no method. A class inherits it to say what kind of collection it is, and the classes of the library that do are Set and Bag, each of which also inherits MapCollection. The page says what the mixin is and what it changes for the programs that combine collections; the behavior of a set or a bag is on the pages of those classes.

The class

[class.setcollection.creation]

SetCollection is a mixin class whose superclass is Collection, and queryMixinClass answers 1 for it (the mixin rule). new is not refused and makes an object of the class that received it, as the new rule says. The class declares no method, on either side: methods with .nil lists no entry, and an instance understands the methods of Collection and nothing more, so the abstract put, allIndexes and allItems of that page are what an instance of a class that inherits only this mixin has for them, and its constraint that index and item are the same is a promise of the class that inherits, not something the mixin enforces.

c = .setcollection~new
say c~class~id .setcollection~queryMixinClass .setcollection~superclass~id
n = 0
s = .setcollection~methods(.nil)
do while s~available
  n += 1
  s~next
end
say n 'own methods'
say c~hasMethod('UNION') c~hasMethod('PUT')
say c~hasMethod('OF') c~hasMethod('APPENDALL')
signal on syntax name bad
c~put(1, 1)
bad: say condition('o')~code

[class.setcollection.operand]

Inheriting SetCollection does not change how an instance is read when it is the argument of a set operation. The operations ask isA about OrderedCollection and MapCollection, and subset about Set as well, and inheriting SetCollection does not make an object an instance of Set (the isA rule), so an instance of a class that inherits SetCollection and not MapCollection is read like any other collection that is not ordered, through makeArray, and an instance of a class that inherits both is read as a map, through supplier or allIndexes.

  r = a~union(k)
  r = a~difference(k)

Deviations: D78, D107, D109

An Array is an ordered collection whose entries are addressed by positive whole numbers. Its indexes may have gaps, so an array can hold items at 1 and 5 and nothing between, and it may have more than one dimension, in which case an entry is addressed by one whole number for each dimension. The class inherits OrderedCollection, and through it Collection, and declares most of their methods itself; the hierarchy rule lists what it inherits.

The page follows the order of the rexxref entry: the class, the way indexes are read, the methods that read and write entries, the questions about the contents, the methods that make other collections, and the ones that sort or print. Examples that show an error use a small routine try, as the builtin pages do. No method that the class declares sends another message to its receiver; the sends rule lists the messages that methods do send, and to whom.

The class

[class.array.creation]

Array declares thirty-six instance methods and two class methods, new and of. The instance methods are [], []=, allIndexes, allItems, append, at, delete, dimension, dimensions, empty, fill, first, firstItem, hasIndex, hasItem, index, insert, isEmpty, items, last, lastItem, makeArray, makeString, next, previous, put, remove, removeItem, section, size, sort, sortWith, stableSort, stableSortWith, supplier and toString, and a copy that this page specifies (the copy rule). The set operations union, difference, intersection, xor, subset, disjoint and equivalent and the method appendAll are those of the mixins, and one rule lists them. A program subclasses Array as it does any class; the rules below say what each method answers for an instance of a subclass.

a = .array~new
own = 'AT PUT APPEND INSERT SECTION SORT TOSTRING SUPPLIER DIMENSIONS'
n = 0
do m over own~makearray(' ')
  if a~hasMethod(m) then n += 1
end
say a~class~id n .array~hasMethod('OF') a~hasMethod('OF')
say a~hasMethod('UNION') a~hasMethod('APPENDALL') a~hasMethod('SIZE')

Making an array

[class.array.new]

new makes an empty array. The arguments say how large the dimensions are expected to be, and they are hints only: the array grows as entries are put into it. With no argument the array has no dimension yet; its dimension is 0 and its size is 0, and the first put gives it as many dimensions as the put has indexes. With one or more arguments, each a whole number that is not negative, the array has one dimension for each argument, of that size, and its size is the product of them, though it holds no item (items is 0). One argument that is an Array of such numbers gives the same dimensions as arguments would; an instance of a subclass is not such an array. An argument that is not a whole number that is not negative raises SYNTAX 93.906, and so does an array of sizes that holds one, or an instance of a subclass; an omitted argument followed by a given one raises SYNTAX 93.903, while omitted arguments at the end count for nothing. A size of 0 is allowed and makes a dimension with no room: new(0) has dimension 1 and size 0. A size is read as the index rule reads an index.

a = .array~new
say a~dimension a~size a~items
b = .array~new(3)
say b~dimension b~size b~items
c = .array~new(2, 3)
say c~dimension c~size c~items c~dimensions~makeString('L', 'x')
d = .array~new(.array~of(2, 3, 4))
say d~dimension d~size
say .array~new(0)~dimension .array~new(0)~size .array~new(2, )~dimension
call try '.array~new(-1)'
call try '.array~new("x")'
call try '.array~new(1.5)'
call try '.array~new(.nil)'
call try '.array~new(.array~of(2, "x"))'
call try '.array~new(, 2)'
call try '.array~new(.pair~of(2, 3))'
exit

[class.array.new.sends]

new sends init to the new object with no argument, whatever arguments the new message had: the sizes are read by new itself and init never sees them. A subclass that overrides the class method new is sent it with the arguments as given, as for any class (the new rule). of is a class method that does not send new; it sends init with no argument and then places the items itself, so that put and append of a subclass are not sent for them.

b = .watch~of(1, 2)
say b~items

[class.array.of]

of makes a one-dimensional array that holds its arguments, the first at index 1, the second at index 2 and so on. An argument left out leaves its index without an item, and arguments left out at the end count for nothing, so of(1, , 3, ) has three indexes. of with no argument makes an empty array that has one dimension, unlike new. An argument that is .nil is an item like any other. The result is an instance of the class that received the message.

say a~size a~items a~dimension a~hasIndex(2)

say b~size b~dimension
c = .array~of(.nil, .nil)
say c~items (c~at(1) == .nil)
say .array~of(, 'b')~first .array~of(, 'b')~size

Indexes

[class.array.indexes]

A method that takes an index takes it as one argument for each dimension, or as one Array that holds them all; at(2, 3) and at(.array~of(2, 3)) name the same entry. Only an instance of Array itself is such a list: an instance of a subclass is one argument like any other object. Each index is a whole number of at least 1, read from the string value of the argument (the conversion rule) as a whole-number argument of a builtin is (the form rule, the digits rule), so "2", ' + 2 ' and 2.0 are as good as 2 and NUMERIC DIGITS plays no part; an argument those rules refuse raises the error this rule names, not SYNTAX 40.12. The number of indexes must be the number of dimensions of the array: too few raise SYNTAX 93.925 and too many SYNTAX 93.926. An index that is not a whole number of at least 1 raises SYNTAX 93.907 when the array has one dimension, and SYNTAX 93.924 when it has more. No index at all, or an empty array of indexes, raises SYNTAX 93.901. An array that has no dimension yet (one made by new without arguments and not yet put into) has no entries, and a message that reads, with two or more indexes, answers as for an index that has no entry without checking them; with one index it is checked as for a one-dimensional array. The sections below say where a method checks fewer or more than this.

a = .array~new(2, 2)
a[2, 1] = 'x'
say a[2, 1] a[.array~of(2, 1)] a~at('2', 1.0)
call try 'a~at(1)'
call try 'a~at(1, 1, 1)'
call try 'a~at(0, 1)'
call try 'a~at(1, "q")'
call try '.array~of(7)~at(0)'
call try '.array~of(7)~at(.nil)'
call try '.array~of(7)~at(1, 1)'
call try '.array~of(7)~at'
call try '.array~of(7)~at(.array~of)'
call try '.array~of(7)~at(1000000000000000000)'
say .array~new~at(0, 0) .array~new~at(5, 5, 5)
call try 'a~at(.pair~of(2, 1))'
exit

Reading and writing entries

[class.array.at]

at(index) answers the item at the index, and .nil when the index has no item, whether the slot lies beyond the array or inside it. The indexes are read as the index rule says. [] is the same method under another name: a[i] is the message [] with the indexes as arguments, and a~"[]"(i) the same message written out. A subclass that overrides at is not asked when [] is sent, nor the other way round.

[class.array.put]

put(item, index) makes the item the entry at the index, replacing any item there, and answers no value. a[i] = v is the message []= with the item first and the indexes after, and it is put under another name. The method needs at least the item and one index: fewer arguments raise SYNTAX 93.901, and an omitted item raises SYNTAX 93.903; both come before any check of the indexes. The indexes are read as the index rule says. A put beyond the present size of a dimension makes the dimension as large as the index, and the array grows. The first put into an array that has no dimension yet gives it as many dimensions as it has indexes, each as large as its index. .nil is an item like any other. A subclass's own put is not asked for []=, nor the other way round.

a = .array~new
a~put('x', 3)
say a~dimension a~size a~items
b = .array~new
b[2, 3] = 'y'
say b~dimension b~dimensions~makeString('L', 'x') b~items b[2, 3]
b~put('z', 4, 1)
say b~dimensions~makeString('L', 'x') b~items
c = .array~of(1, 2)
c~put(.nil, 1)
say c~items (c[1] == .nil)
c~put(9, 2)
say c[2]
call try 'c~put'
call try 'c~put(1)'
call try 'c~put(, 1)'
call try 'c~put(, 0)'
call try 'c~put(1, 0)'
call try 'c~put(1, 1, 1)'
exit

  say arg(1) '=> no error'
  return
bad: say arg(1) '=>' condition('o')~code
  return

Adding and removing items

[class.array.append]

append(item) puts the item at the index after the highest index that holds an item, and answers that index. In an array with no item the index is 1, and an array that has no dimension yet becomes one-dimensional. The size grows when the index is beyond it. The method takes exactly one argument: none, or an omitted one, raises SYNTAX 93.903 and a second argument raises SYNTAX 93.902; an array of more than one dimension raises SYNTAX 93.954, after the argument count has been checked. .nil is an item like any other.

say a~append('d') a~allItems~makeString('L', ',')

say b~append('x') b~size b~dimension

say c~append(.nil) c~dimension c~items

[class.array.insert]

insert(item, index) puts the item at the index after index: it takes the place after the entry at index, every entry after that moves up by one index, and the method answers the index of the new item. An index of .nil puts the item first, at index 1, and an omitted index puts it after the highest index that holds an item. An index beyond the highest index of the array is allowed: the item goes to the index after it. The size of the array becomes the larger of what it was and the highest index the insert uses, the new one's or that of an entry it moved, so it grows only when an entry is pushed past its last place. An omitted item, or no argument at all, makes the new slot empty, and the answer, the size and the moving of the entries after it are as for an item (the omitted item rule). The index is read as the index rule says, so an array of one index is accepted. The method takes one or two arguments: a third raises SYNTAX 93.902; an array of more than one dimension raises SYNTAX 93.954 whatever the index is, after the argument count has been checked. An index that is not a whole number of at least 1 and is not .nil raises SYNTAX 93.907.

a = .array~of('a', 'b', 'c')
say a~insert('x', 1) a~allItems~makeString('L', ',')
say a~insert('y', .nil) a~allItems~makeString('L', ',')
say a~insert('z') a~allItems~makeString('L', ',')
say a~insert('w', 9) a~size a~allIndexes~makeString('L', ',')

b[1] = 'p'
b[2] = 'q'
say b~insert('r', 1) b~size b~allItems~makeString('L', ',')
c = .array~new
say c~insert('s', 1) c~size c~dimension
call try '.array~of(1)~insert(1, 0)'
call try '.array~of(1)~insert(1, "x")'
call try '.array~of(1)~insert(1, 1, 1)'
call try '.array~new(2, 2)~insert(1, 0)'
call try '.array~new(2, 2)~insert(1, 1, 1)'
exit

[class.array.delete]

delete(index) takes the entry at the index out of the array and answers its item; every entry after it moves down by one index and the size drops by one. When the slot at the index is empty the answer is .nil and the slot is still taken out. An index above the size answers .nil and changes nothing. The method takes one argument, which may be an array of one index: none, or an omitted one, raises SYNTAX 93.903 and a second raises SYNTAX 93.902. An array of more than one dimension raises SYNTAX 93.954 whatever the index is, after the argument count has been checked; otherwise the index is read as the index rule says, with SYNTAX 93.907 for an index that is not a whole number of at least 1 and SYNTAX 93.926 for an array of two.

[class.array.remove]

remove(index) takes the item at the index out of its slot and answers it, and leaves the slot empty: no other index changes and the size does not. When the index has no item, because the slot is empty or lies beyond the array, the answer is .nil and nothing changes. It works on arrays of any number of dimensions, so the indexes are read as the index rule says, and it checks no argument count of its own: no argument raises SYNTAX 93.901, and two on a one-dimensional array raise SYNTAX 93.926.

[class.array.removeitem]

removeItem(item) takes out the first item that is equal to the argument, in index order, leaves its slot empty as remove does, and answers the item that was stored, which is .nil when there is none. The method takes one argument: none, or an omitted one, raises SYNTAX 93.903 and a second raises SYNTAX 93.902; it works on arrays of any number of dimensions.

removeItem sends == to the argument, once for each item in index order, with that item as the argument, until one answers true, and sends nothing else. hasItem and index make the same search, and their rules say so. For the very object that is stored, see the deviation rule.

Walking the array

[class.array.order]

The entries of an array of more than one dimension have one order: the order of their slots with the first dimension changing fastest, so that in a 2 by 2 array (1,1) comes first, then (2,1), (1,2) and (2,2). Every method that walks the entries follows it, for the indexes as for the items: allItems, makeArray and allIndexes, supplier, first, last, firstItem and lastItem, next and previous, the search of hasItem, index and removeItem, makeString and the sorts.

a = .array~new(2, 2)
a[1, 2] = 'r'; a[2, 1] = 'q'
say a~allItems~makeString('L', ',')
do i over a~allIndexes
  say i~makeString('L', ',') a[i]
end
s = a~supplier
say s~index~makeString('L', ',') s~item
say a~first~makeString('L', ',') a~last~makeString('L', ',')
say a~next(2, 1)~makeString('L', ',') a~previous(1, 2)~makeString('L', ',')
b = .array~new(2, 2)
b[2, 1] = 7; b[1, 2] = 7
say b~index(7)~makeString('L', ',')
b~removeItem(7)
say b~first~makeString('L', ',')

[class.array.first]

first answers the lowest index that holds an item and last the highest, and firstItem and lastItem answer the items there; all four answer .nil for an array without an item. [class.array.next]

next(index) answers the index of the first item after the index, passing over empty slots, and .nil when there is none; previous(index) answers the index of the last item before it. The index need not hold an item, or exist: next of an index beyond the array answers .nil, and previous of one beyond the array answers as the rule for an index beyond the array says. The index is read as the index rule says, with SYNTAX 93.901 for no index and SYNTAX 93.907 for an index that is not a whole number of at least 1; so index 0 is an error, and previous(1) is .nil.

[class.array.next.beyond]

previous of an index that has a component beyond its dimension answers the index of the last item that lies before a position, or .nil when there is none. In an array of one dimension the position is the index, so an index beyond the array answers the last item. In an array of more than one dimension the slots are numbered with the first dimension running fastest: the slot at i, j is number i + (j - 1) * n, where n is the size of the first dimension, and likewise for more dimensions. The position is the value of the first component, in the order of the dimensions, that is beyond its dimension; the other components do not matter.

a = .array~new(3, 3)
do i = 1 to 3; do j = 1 to 3; a[i, j] = i||j; end; end
say a~previous(4, 1)~makeString('L', ',') a~previous(4, 7)~makeString('L', ',')
say a~previous(1, 5)~makeString('L', ',') a~previous(10, 1)~makeString('L', ',')
b = .array~new(2, 2)
b[2, 2] = 'x'
say (b~previous(3, 1) == .nil) b~previous(5, 1)~makeString('L', ',')
say .array~of('x', 'y')~previous(9)

Size, dimensions and filling

[class.array.items]

items answers the number of items the array holds, size the number of places it has, and isEmpty answers 1 when it holds no item and 0 when it does. The size of an array only grows when an entry is put beyond it, or an item inserted or appended past it, and falls only by one for each delete; remove and empty leave it as it is. The size of a multi-dimensional array is the product of its dimensions. The three methods take no argument: any argument raises SYNTAX 93.902.

a = .array~of('a', , 'c')
say a~items a~size a~isEmpty
a~remove(3)
say a~items a~size a~isEmpty
b = .array~new(4)
say b~items b~size b~isEmpty
b[6] = 'x'
say b~items b~size b~isEmpty
say .array~new(2, 3)~size .array~new~size
call try 'a~items(1)'
call try 'a~size(1)'
call try 'a~isEmpty(1)'
exit

Taking part of an array

[class.array.section]

section(start, count) answers a new array that holds the entries from the index start on: count of them, or all of them up to the end of the array when count is omitted or runs past the end. The first entry of the section is at index 1, and an empty slot of the receiver stays an empty slot. The items are the receiver's own objects, and the receiver is not changed. A start beyond the size of the receiver, or a count of 0, gives an array with no entries and no dimension. The index is read as the index rule says, so an array of one index is accepted, and SYNTAX 93.907 is raised for a start that is not a whole number of at least

  1. The count is read as the index rule reads an index and must be a whole number of 0 or more, or SYNTAX 93.923 is raised. No start, or an omitted one, raises SYNTAX 93.903, and a third argument SYNTAX 93.902; for an array of more than one dimension SYNTAX 93.954 is raised after the count of arguments has been checked, whatever they are. The answer is an instance of the class of the receiver.

The items, the indexes and a supplier

[class.array.makearray]

makeArray and allItems answer a new Array that holds the items of the receiver in the order of its indexes, without the empty slots; the first is at index 1. In an array of more than one dimension that order is the one the order rule gives. allIndexes answers a new Array of the indexes that hold an item, in the same order: whole numbers, or arrays of indexes in a multi-dimensional array. The three answer an Array whatever the class of the receiver is, never the receiver, and do not follow later changes to it. They take no argument: any argument raises SYNTAX 93.902.

The Supplier class has its own page; the supplier of a multi-dimensional array answers an array of indexes as the allIndexes of the array does.

The items as text

[class.array.makestring]

makeString(mode, separator) answers a string made from the items of the array in the order of the slots, with the first dimension changing fastest, and toString is the same method under another name. The first letter of mode, in either case, chooses the form and nothing after it counts: L puts the separator between one item and the next, and is the form when mode is omitted, and C joins the items directly. The separator is read from its string value and is the line end '0A'x when it is omitted; it may be the null string. A mode that does not begin with L or C raises SYNTAX 93.915; a separator with C, even a null one, raises SYNTAX 93.902, as a third argument does; a mode or a separator that has no string value raises SYNTAX 88.909. The mode is checked first, its string value and then its letter, and the separator after it. An item that is a string is used as it is, and any other object, .nil included, gives the answer of its objectName message (a whole-number answer is written as its digits, Deviation 107). An empty slot gives nothing, and no separator is added for it, but an item that is the null string still takes its separator. An array with no item answers the null string.

Sorting

[class.array.sort]

sort and stableSort put the items of the array in ascending order, in place, and answer the receiver; sortWith(comparator) and stableSortWith(comparator) do the same by the order the comparator gives. Items are compared by compareTo, which for strings is the string rule: 10 sorts before 9, and upper case before lower case. The comparator is any object that understands compare, and when it answers a negative number for two items the first sorts before the second, when it answers 0 they are equal, and when it answers a positive number the first sorts after. stableSort and stableSortWith keep items that are equal in their order; whether sort and sortWith do is not specified. The sorted items fill the slots from index 1 on in the order of the slots (in a multi-dimensional array the first dimension changing fastest), so an array whose items are not in the first slots, with an empty slot before an item, raises SYNTAX 98.975 before any comparison and stays as it was; empty slots after the items stay empty, and the size does not change. An array of fewer than two items is not compared; sortWith and stableSortWith then answer at once, before the slot check and without looking at the comparator, while sort and stableSort still make the slot check, so .array~of(, 5)~sort raises SYNTAX 98.975 and .array~of(, 5)~sortWith(.nil) does not. sort and stableSort take no argument: any raises SYNTAX 93.902. sortWith and stableSortWith take exactly one: none, or an omitted one, raises SYNTAX 93.903 and a second SYNTAX 93.902. An item or comparator that does not understand its message raises SYNTAX 97.1. The comparator's answer must be a whole number: another answer raises SYNTAX 26.903; the answer of an item's compareTo raises SYNTAX 26.902 in the same case.

[class.array.sort.sends]

sort and stableSort send compareTo to items, with another item of the array as the argument, and sortWith and stableSortWith send compare to the comparator, with two items as the arguments. Which items are compared, which of two is the receiver or the first argument, how many comparisons are made and in what order is not specified, except that an array of fewer than two items is not compared at all, and that nothing but compareTo and compare is sent to items or comparator; no argument is asked isA. The example checks what is specified, that every argument is an item of the array.

.local~calls = 0
.local~bad = 0
items~sort

.local~calls = 0
items~stableSortWith(.cmp~new)
say 'compare' (.local~calls > 0) .local~bad
.local~calls = 0
.array~of(.item~new(1))~sort
.array~of(.item~new(1))~sortWith(.cmp~new)
say 'single' .local~calls
out = ''
do it over items
  out = out it~n
end
say out~strip
::class item
::method init
  expose n
  use arg n
::method n
  expose n
  return n
::method compareTo
  expose n
  use arg other
  .local~calls = .local~calls + 1
  if \other~isA(.item) then .local~bad = .local~bad + 1
  return n - other~n
::class cmp
::method compare
  use arg x, y
  .local~calls = .local~calls + 1
  if \x~isA(.item) | \y~isA(.item) then .local~bad = .local~bad + 1
  return x~n - y~n

Copies and the methods of the mixins

[class.array.copy]

copy answers a new array of the same class as the receiver, with the same dimensions and size, the same items at the same indexes and the same empty slots, so that adding to or removing from one does not change the other. The items are the same objects: the copy is shallow. As the copy rule says of every object, the variables of a subclass instance are copied as they are and the name stays; init is not sent. The method takes no argument: one raises SYNTAX 93.902.

[class.array.inherited]

The methods union, difference, intersection, xor, subset, disjoint and equivalent and appendAll are not declared by Array. The methods union, difference, intersection, xor, subset and appendAll are those of OrderedCollection, and disjoint and equivalent those of Collection, as the pages of the mixins say, and an array is one of the collections they take as an argument, so that .array~of(1)~union(.list~of(2)) is an array of 1 and 2. union, difference and xor send the copy they work on isA with the class Array and answer its makeArray when that answers 1, as their rules say, so for an array, an instance of a subclass included, the answer is a new Array; intersection answers the collection that new of the receiver's class made, an instance of that class, and sends it neither message. appendAll answers the receiver.

Messages the methods send

[class.array.sends]

No method that Array declares sends a message to its receiver: an override of at, put, append or any other of the methods is never asked by another method, and [] and []= do not use at and put. The messages the methods do send are to other objects, and each has a rule of its own: new and init to the class and the new array by new, of and section (the new rule, the section rule); == to the argument by removeItem, hasItem and index (the search rule); objectName to the items by makeString and toString (the text rule); and compareTo to the items and compare to the comparator by the sorts (the sort rule). No argument is asked isA; a string value is read as the conversion rule says. The methods string and copy of an instance and the set operations send what the pages that own them say. In the example a subclass has every method of Array overridden to record its name, and each call records only its own.

  'empty fill first firstItem hasIndex hasItem index insert isEmpty items',
  'last lastItem makeArray makeString next previous put remove removeItem',
  'section',
  'size sort sortWith stableSort stableSortWith supplier toString copy'

do m over own~makeArray(' ')
  src = "if .local~on then .local~log~append('"m"'); forward class (super)"
  .spy~define(m, src)
end

[class.array.deviation.78]

A search for an item with the very object that is stored, by hasItem, index or removeItem, sends that object's == as for any other item, so an object whose == answers false is not found even at its own entry. ooRexx finds the very object without sending it ==, and sends == only for the items before it. Deviations: D78, D109, D118

A List is an ordered collection that grows and shrinks at any point. Its entries are addressed by indexes that the list chooses and hands back when an item is added: an index names an entry for as long as the entry is in the list, whatever is inserted or removed around it, so it is a handle on the entry, not a position. The order of the entries is a separate matter, and the list keeps it. The class inherits OrderedCollection, and through it Collection; the hierarchy rule lists what it inherits.

The page follows the order of the rexxref entry. Examples that show an error use a small routine try, as the builtin pages do. The page says nothing about an entry whose item was omitted in a put or an insert.

The class

[class.list.creation]

List declares twenty-six instance methods and two class methods, new and of. The instance methods are [], []=, allIndexes, allItems, append, at, delete, empty, first, firstItem, hasIndex, hasItem, index, insert, isEmpty, items, last, lastItem, makeArray, next, previous, put, remove, removeItem, section and supplier, and a copy that this page specifies (the copy rule). A list has no makeString, no toString, no size, no fill and no dimensions, and no method of its own that sorts: sort, sortWith, stableSort and stableSortWith are those of OrderedCollection, which sort a list through its makeArray, first, next and []= (the sort rule). The set operations and appendAll are those of the mixins, and one rule lists them.

l = .list~new
own = 'AT PUT APPEND INSERT SECTION SUPPLIER REMOVEITEM FIRSTITEM'
n = 0
do m over own~makearray(' ')
  if l~hasMethod(m) then n += 1
end
say l~class~id n .list~hasMethod('OF') l~hasMethod('OF')
say l~hasMethod('SORT') l~hasMethod('UNION') l~hasMethod('APPENDALL')
say l~hasMethod('MAKESTRING') l~hasMethod('TOSTRING') l~hasMethod('SIZE')
say l~hasMethod('FILL') l~hasMethod('DIMENSION')

Making a list

[class.list.new]

new makes an empty list. Its optional argument is a hint for how large the list will grow and changes nothing the program can see; it is read as the index rule reads an index and must be a whole number that is not negative, or SYNTAX 93.923 is raised. A second argument raises SYNTAX 93.902, and omitted arguments at the end count for nothing. new sends init to the new object with the arguments it received, so a subclass's init sees the hint, unlike the init of an array (the new rule).

l = .list~new
say l~items l~isEmpty l~first
say .list~new(0)~items .list~new(1000)~items .list~new(3, )~items
call try '.list~new(-1)'

[class.list.of]

of makes a list that holds its arguments in the order given: the first is the first entry. An argument left out at the end counts for nothing, so of(1, ) holds one item; an argument left out before a given one raises SYNTAX 93.903. .nil is an item like any other. The result is an instance of the class that received the message. of sends init to the new object with no argument and not new, and adds the items itself: the append, insert and put of a subclass are not sent for them. The indexes are those that a fresh list hands out, the index rule says which.

Indexes

[class.list.indexes]

An index of a list is a whole number of 0 or more, chosen by the list when an entry is created and kept until the entry is removed. A method that takes an index reads it from its string value (the conversion rule) as a whole-number argument of a builtin is (the form rule, the digits rule): "1", ' + 1 ' and 1.0 are as good as 1, NUMERIC DIGITS plays no part, and anything that is not a whole number of 0 or more, .nil included, or that those rules refuse, raises SYNTAX 93.918. A valid index that names no entry is not an error for the methods that look entries up: at, next, previous, delete and remove answer .nil and hasIndex answers 0; the methods that must have an entry, put, insert and section, raise SYNTAX 93.918. When an entry is removed its index becomes free. A new entry takes the index that was freed most recently, when one is free, and otherwise the lowest whole number that has not been used since the list was made or last emptied. A list that only grows therefore hands out 0, 1, 2 and so on; empty makes the list start again at 0. The number of an entry never changes, wherever it is inserted. A copy has the same indexes, and the same state, as the list it is made from.

l = .list~new
a = l~append('a'); b = l~append('b'); c = l~append('c')
say a b c
l~remove(a)
l~remove(c)
say l~append('x') l~append('y') l~append('z')
say l~allIndexes~makeString('L', ',')
say l~allItems~makeString('L', ',')
m = .list~of('p', 'q')
m~empty
say m~append('r') m~append('s')
say m~at('1') m~at(1.0) m~hasIndex(' 1 ') m~hasIndex(7) (m~at(7) == .nil)
call try 'm~at(-1)'
call try 'm~at("x")'
call try 'm~at(1.5)'
call try 'm~at(.nil)'
call try 'm~at(1000000000000000000)'
call try 'm~put("t", 9)'
call try 'm~insert("t", 9)'
call try 'm~section(9)'
exit

Taking part of a list

[class.list.section]

section(start, count) answers a new List that holds the entries from the one with index start on, in list order: count of them, or all of them up to the end when count is omitted or runs past the end. A count of 0 gives an empty list. The new list has its own indexes, handed out from 0 as for any list (the index rule), the items are the receiver's own objects, and the receiver is not changed. The start must name an entry, or SYNTAX 93.918 is raised, as for any index that is not a whole number of 0 or more; the count, read as the index rule reads an index, must be a whole number that is not negative, or SYNTAX 93.923. No start, or an omitted one, raises SYNTAX 93.903, and a third argument SYNTAX 93.902. The answer is an instance of List, whatever the class of the receiver is, and no new or init is sent for it.

Copies and the string value

[class.list.copy]

copy answers a new list of the same class as the receiver, with the same entries in the same order, the same indexes and the same state of free indexes, so that the next append to either hands out the same index and neither list sees the other's changes. The items are the same objects: the copy is shallow. As the copy rule says of every object, the variables of a subclass instance are copied as they are and the name stays; init is not sent. The method takes no argument: one raises SYNTAX 93.902.

Sorting

[class.list.sort]

sort, stableSort, sortWith(comparator) and stableSortWith(comparator) of a list are the methods of OrderedCollection, and they sort the list in place and answer the receiver. The entries keep their indexes and their places in the list, and the items change places among them: after a sort the first entry of the list holds the first item in the new order, and so on down the list. They are written in terms of other messages, as the sort rule says: the list's makeArray, first, next and []=, and the sort or sortWith, size and [] of the array that makeArray answers, which compares the items as the array rule says. If the answer holds fewer items than the list has entries the last entries are left as they were, and when it holds more the []= for the first item without an entry raises SYNTAX 93.918. The methods check their arguments as the sort rule says: sort and stableSort take none, and sortWith and stableSortWith take one, SYNTAX 93.901 being raised when it is missing; the comparator is not looked at, so the string "x" is accepted by a list of one item.

l = .list~of('c', 'a', 'b')
first = l~first
say (l~sort == l) l~allItems~makeString('L', ',')
say l~allIndexes~makeString('L', ',')
say l~at(first) l~sortWith(.desc~new)~allItems~makeString('L', ',')
say .list~new~sort~items .list~of('z')~sortWith('x')~items
call try 'l~sort(1)'
call try 'l~stableSort(1)'

The methods of the mixins

[class.list.inherited]

The methods union, difference, intersection, xor, subset, disjoint and equivalent and appendAll are not declared by List. The methods union, difference, intersection, xor, subset and appendAll are those of OrderedCollection, and disjoint and equivalent those of Collection, as the pages of the mixins say, and a list is one of the collections they take as an argument, so that .list~of(1)~union(.array~of(2)) is a list of 1 and 2. A list answers 0 to isA with Array, so union, difference and xor answer the copies they work on, and intersection the collection that new of the receiver's class made; all four are instances of the class of the receiver, and appendAll answers the receiver.

say i~class~id i~makeArray~makeString('L', ',')

say (a~appendAll(b) == a) a~makeArray~makeString('L', ',')

Messages the methods send

[class.list.sends]

No method that List declares sends a message to its receiver: an override of at, put, append or any other of the methods is never asked by another method, and [] and []= do not use at and put. The messages the methods do send go to other objects, and each has a rule of its own: init to the new object by new and of (the new rule, the of rule); == to the argument by removeItem, hasItem and index (the search rule). The sorts, which are not methods of the class, send messages to the receiver and to the array of makeArray, as their rule says. The methods string and copy of an instance and the set operations send what the pages that own them say. No argument is asked isA, and a string value is read as the conversion rule says. In the example a subclass has every method of List overridden to record its name, and each call records only its own.

own = '[] []= allIndexes allItems append at delete empty first firstItem',
  'hasIndex hasItem index insert isEmpty items last lastItem makeArray next',
  'previous put remove removeItem section supplier copy'
.local~log = .array~new
do m over own~makeArray(' ')
  src = "if .local~on then .local~log~append('"m"'); forward class (super)"
  .spy~define(m, src)
end
a = .spy~of('c', 'b', 'a')
calls = 'x = a[1]|a[1] = "x"|a~allIndexes|a~allItems|a~append("d")|a~at(1)',
  '|a~insert("e", 1)|a~hasIndex(1)|a~hasItem("q")|a~index("q")|a~isEmpty',
  '|a~items|a~first|a~last|a~firstItem|a~lastItem|a~makeArray|a~next(1)',
  '|a~previous(2)|a~put("y", 1)|a~section(0)|a~supplier|a~copy',
  '|a~removeItem("q")|a~remove(0)|a~delete(1)|a~empty'
n = 0
extra = 0
do c over calls~makeArray('|')
  .local~log~empty
  .local~on = 1
  interpret c
  .local~on = 0
  n += 1
  if .local~log~items <> 1 then do
    extra += 1
    say c '=>' .local~log~makeString('L', ' ')
  end
end

Deviations

[class.list.deviation.78]

A search for an item with the very object that is stored, by hasItem, index or removeItem, sends that object's == as for any other item, so an object whose == answers false is not found even at its own entry. ooRexx finds the very object without sending it ==, and sends == only for the items before it. See Deviation 78.

say (c~index(x) == .nil) .n
.local~n = 0
say (.nil == c~removeItem(x)) c~items .n

[class.list.deviation.109]

An index, a count or the size hint of new that is an instance of a subclass of String is read by its own characters, and REQUEST and MAKESTRING are not sent to it (Deviation 109). As an index, ooRexx sends such an instance request with STRING or MAKESTRING, so an override of either can change what is read. In the example MAKESTRING answers another index.

[class.list.deviation.118]

An instance of a subclass of List is read as any other collection is wherever an array is wanted. DO OVER sends it makeArray, as the loop rule says, and the methods that read an argument array with request('ARRAY') send it request, among them sendWith, so an override of either is used (Deviation 118). ooRexx sends such an instance neither message and uses the items it holds; it does send them to the subclasses of the other collection classes. The method makeArray itself is the one this page specifies, and a program that sends it gets the override. In the example the subclasses answer other items than they hold.

do x over l
  say x
end

Deviations: D78, D109

A Queue is an ordered collection that is addressed by position: the item at the head is at index 1, the next at index 2, and so on up to the number of items, so an index is where an item stands now, not a name for it. Adding an item at the head or in the middle, or taking one out, moves the items behind it to other indexes. The class inherits OrderedCollection, and through it Collection; the hierarchy rule lists what it inherits. CircularQueue is its subclass.

The page follows the order of the rexxref entry. Examples that show an error use a small routine try, as the builtin pages do. The page says nothing about an entry whose item was omitted in an insert.

The class

[class.queue.creation]

Queue declares the instance methods [], []=, allIndexes, allItems, append, at, delete, empty, first, firstItem, hasIndex, hasItem, index, insert, isEmpty, items, last, lastItem, makeArray, next, peek, previous, pull, push, put, queue, remove, removeItem, section, size and supplier, a copy that this page specifies (the copy rule), and the class methods new and of. A queue has no makeString, no toString, no fill and no dimensions, and no method of its own that sorts: sort, sortWith, stableSort and stableSortWith are those of OrderedCollection, which sort a queue through its makeArray, first, next and []= (the sort rule). The set operations and appendAll are those of the mixins, and one rule lists them.

own = 'AT PUT APPEND INSERT SECTION SUPPLIER REMOVEITEM FIRSTITEM PEEK PULL',
  'PUSH QUEUE SIZE'

  if q~hasMethod(m) then n += 1
end

say q~hasMethod('MAKESTRING') q~hasMethod('TOSTRING') q~hasMethod('FILL')
say q~hasMethod('DIMENSION') q~hasMethod('SIZE')

Making a queue

[class.queue.new]

new makes an empty queue. Its optional argument is a hint for how large the queue will grow; no method that this page specifies answers differently for it. It must be a whole number that is not negative, or SYNTAX 93.923 is raised. A second argument raises SYNTAX 93.902, and omitted arguments at the end count for nothing. new sends init to the new object with the arguments it received, so a subclass's init sees them (the new rule). The checks are those of the init that Queue supplies: they come after the init of a subclass has run, and a subclass whose init does not pass the arguments on is not refused for them.

say q~items q~isEmpty q~first
say .queue~new(0)~items .queue~new(1000)~items .queue~new(3, )~items

call try '.queue~new(.nil)'
call try '.queue~new(1.5)'
call try '.queue~new(1, 2)'
x = .watch~new(7)
y = .watch~new
call try '.watch~new("x")'
say .quiet~new("x", 2, 3)~items
exit

[class.queue.of]

of makes a queue that holds its arguments in the order given: the first is at the head. An argument left out at the end counts for nothing, so of(1, ) holds one item; an argument left out before a given one raises SYNTAX 93.903. .nil is an item like any other. The result is an instance of the class that received the message. of sends init to the new object with no argument and not new, and adds the items itself: the append, queue, push, insert and put of a subclass are not sent for them.

Indexes

[class.queue.indexes]

An index of a queue is a whole number of at least 1, the position of an item counted from the head. A method that takes an index reads it from its string value (the conversion rule) as a whole-number argument of a builtin is (the form rule, the digits rule): "2", ' 2 ' and 2.0 are as good as 2, NUMERIC DIGITS plays no part, and an argument that those rules refuse, a number below 1, or .nil raises SYNTAX 93.907. An object that is not a string is read by its string value, so an array is read through its makeString: an array of exactly one such index gives that index, and an array with none or with more than one gives a string that is not an index and raises SYNTAX 93.907, as does a list, whose string value is not an index either. An index above the number of items is not an error for the methods that look an item up: at answers .nil, hasIndex answers 0, delete and remove answer .nil, next answers .nil, previous answers the last index and section an empty queue; insert raises a condition (the insert rule). Where a method adds or removes an item in front of others, those others have other indexes afterwards, and the examples of the methods show it.

[class.queue.insert]

Taking part of a queue

[class.queue.section]

section(start, count) answers a new queue that holds the items from the index start on: count of them, or all of them up to the tail when count is omitted or runs past the tail. A count of 0, or a start above the number of items, gives an empty queue. The new queue has its own indexes from 1, the items are the receiver's own objects, and the receiver is not changed. The start is read as the index rule says; the count must be a whole number that is not negative, read as the hint of new is, or SYNTAX 93.923 is raised. No start, or an omitted one, raises SYNTAX 93.903, and a third argument SYNTAX 93.902. The answer is an instance of the class of the receiver, so that a subclass gets a queue of its own class back. The arguments are counted first, then start is read, then count.

Sorting

[class.queue.sort]

sort, stableSort, sortWith(comparator) and stableSortWith(comparator) of a queue are the methods of OrderedCollection, and they sort the queue in place and answer the receiver. The items change places among the indexes, which stay 1 to the number of items: after a sort the head holds the first item in the new order, and so on. They are written in terms of other messages, as the sort rule says: the queue's makeArray, first, next and []=, and the sort or sortWith, size and [] of the array that makeArray answers, which compares the items as the array rule says. The methods check their arguments as the sort rule says: sort and stableSort take none, and sortWith and stableSortWith take one, SYNTAX 93.901 being raised when it is missing; the comparator is not looked at, so the string "x" is accepted by a queue of one item.

The methods of the mixins

[class.queue.inherited]

The methods union, difference, intersection, xor, subset, disjoint and equivalent and appendAll are not declared by Queue. The methods union, difference, intersection, xor, subset and appendAll are those of OrderedCollection, and disjoint and equivalent those of Collection, as the pages of the mixins say, and a queue is one of the collections they take as an argument, so that .queue~of(1)~union(.list~of(2)) is a queue of 1 and 2. A queue answers 0 to isA with Array, so union, difference and xor answer the copies they work on, and intersection the collection that new of the receiver's class made; all four are instances of the class of the receiver, and appendAll answers the receiver.

Messages the methods send

[class.queue.sends]

No method that Queue declares sends a message to its receiver: an override of at, put, append, queue or any other of the methods is never asked by another method, and [] and []= do not use at and put. The messages the methods do send go to other objects, and each has a rule of its own: init to the new object by new and of (the new rule, the of rule), new and init by section (the section rule); == to the argument by removeItem, hasItem and index (the search rule). The sorts, which are not methods of the class, send messages to the receiver and to the array of makeArray, as their rule says. The methods string and copy of an instance and the set operations send what the pages that own them say. No argument is asked isA, and a string value is read as the conversion rule says. In the example a subclass has every method of Queue overridden to record its name, and each call records only its own.

own = '[] []= allIndexes allItems append at delete empty first firstItem',
  'hasIndex hasItem index insert isEmpty items last lastItem makeArray next',
  'previous put remove removeItem section supplier copy peek pull push queue',
  'size'
.local~log = .array~new
do m over own~makeArray(' ')
  src = "if .local~on then .local~log~append('"m"'); forward class (super)"
  .spy~define(m, src)
end

Deviations

[class.queue.deviation.78]

A search for an item with the very object that is stored, by hasItem, index or removeItem, sends that object's == as for any other item, so an object whose == answers false is not found even at its own entry. ooRexx finds the very object without sending it ==, and sends == only for the items before it. See Deviation 78.

c = .queue~new
c~append('a')
c~append(x)
c~append('b')
say c~hasItem(x) .n
.local~n = 0
say (c~index(x) == .nil) .n
.local~n = 0
say (.nil == c~removeItem(x)) c~items .n
::class liar
::method '=='
  .local~n += 1
  return 0

[class.queue.deviation.109]

An index or a count that is an instance of a subclass of String is read by its own characters, and REQUEST and MAKESTRING are not sent to it (Deviation 109). As an index, ooRexx sends such an instance request with STRING or MAKESTRING, so an override of either can change what is read. In the example MAKESTRING answers another index.

CircularQueue

rexxref: Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > CircularQueue Class; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > CircularQueue Class > of (Class Method); Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > CircularQueue Class > init; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > CircularQueue Class > append; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > CircularQueue Class > insert; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > CircularQueue Class > intersection; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > CircularQueue Class > makeArray; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > CircularQueue Class > makeString; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > CircularQueue Class > push; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > CircularQueue Class > queue; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > CircularQueue Class > resize; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > CircularQueue Class > section; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > CircularQueue Class > size; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > CircularQueue Class > string; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > CircularQueue Class > supplier; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > CircularQueue Class > union; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > CircularQueue Class > xor

Deviations: D78, D109

A CircularQueue is a Queue that has a size, fixed when it is made and changed by resize: it never holds more items than that. An item added to a full queue pushes another out at the opposite end, so a circular queue keeps the latest items, as a log of the last few commands does. Everything that this page does not specify is the behaviour of Queue: the indexes are positions from 1 at the head, and the methods that read, look up and remove items are those of the Queue page. The class inherits Queue, and through it OrderedCollection and Collection; the hierarchy rule lists what it inherits.

The page follows the order of the rexxref entry. Examples that show an error use a small routine try, as the builtin pages do.

The class

[class.circularqueue.creation]

CircularQueue declares the class method of and the instance methods init, append, insert, intersection, makeArray, makeString, push, queue, resize, section, size, string, supplier, union and xor, and a copy that this page specifies (the copy rule). All other methods are those of Queue (the Queue creation rule) and of the mixins; the rules below say where one of them behaves differently for a circular queue. A circular queue is a Queue: it has peek, pull and sort, and Queue has no resize and no makeString.

say q~class~id q~class~superclass~id q~isA(.queue) q~isA(.orderedcollection)
say q~hasMethod('RESIZE') q~hasMethod('MAKESTRING')
say .queue~new~hasMethod('RESIZE')
say .queue~new~hasMethod('MAKESTRING') .queue~new~hasMethod('SIZE')
say q~hasMethod('PEEK') q~hasMethod('PULL') q~hasMethod('SORT')

Making a circular queue

[class.circularqueue.new]

new needs the size of the queue: no argument raises SYNTAX 93.901 and a second one SYNTAX 93.902. The size must be a whole number from 0 to 999999999, read from its string value as a whole-number argument of a builtin is (the form rule, the digits rule): a negative number, a number that is not whole, text that is not a number and a number above that bound raise SYNTAX 93.906. A size of 0 makes a queue that holds nothing. A new queue is empty. new sends init to the new object with the arguments it received, so a subclass's init sees them (the new rule); the checks are those of the init that CircularQueue supplies.

q = .circularqueue~new(3)
say q~size q~items q~isEmpty
say .circularqueue~new(0)~size .circularqueue~new(999999999)~size
say .circularqueue~new(' 3 ')~size '|' .circularqueue~new(3.0)~size

call try '.circularqueue~new(.nil)'
call try '.circularqueue~new(.object~new)'

[class.circularqueue.new.sends]

init first reads the string value of the size, as the conversion rule says, and then sends it < with the argument 0, reading the answer as a logical value: an answer that is neither 0 nor 1 raises SYNTAX 34.901. SYNTAX 93.906 is raised when < answered 1 or when the string value is not a whole number or is above 999999999; only < decides whether the size is below 0, so a size whose string value is -1 and whose < answers 0 is not refused. An object that does not understand <, .nil included, raises SYNTAX 97.1. The queue then keeps the very object it was given as its size, size answers it (the size rule), and its string value is read again each time a method compares the number of items with the size.

[class.circularqueue.of]

of makes a circular queue that holds its arguments in the order given, with the size that is the number of arguments, an argument left out before a given one counting, one left out at the end not. An item that was left out is the null string. The result is an instance of the class that received the message. of sends new to that class with the size as the only argument, which sends init as the new rule says, and then sends queue once for each argument, in order, with that argument, the null string for an omitted one, as the only argument. of with no argument makes a queue of size 0.

[class.circularqueue.size]

size answers the size of the queue: the object that new was given, or that resize was given last, as it was given, so that the size ' 3 ' is answered as ' 3 ' and 3.0 as 3.0. Adding items

[class.circularqueue.queue]

queue(item, option) adds the item at the tail and push(item, option) at the head. When the queue already holds as many items as its size, the item at the opposite end is taken out first: queue takes out the item at the head and answers it, push takes out the item at the tail and answers it; when nothing was taken out, both answer .nil. A queue of size 0 holds nothing. The option is Normal by default; one whose first character is U, in either case, is Unique: before the item is added, every item that is equal to it by the strict == is taken out, and when that made room nothing else is. Any other option, a null string and one that begins with a blank included, is Normal, and option is read as the option rule says. No argument at all raises SYNTAX 93.901; an omitted item before an option raises SYNTAX 93.903; a third argument raises SYNTAX 93.902.

say (q~queue('a') == .nil) (q~queue('b') == .nil) (q~queue('c') == .nil)
say q~queue('d') q~allItems~makeString('L', ',') q~items
say q~push('z') q~allItems~makeString('L', ',') q~items
say q~queue('e') q~push('f') q~allItems~makeString('L', ',')
call try 'q~queue'
call try 'q~push'
call try 'q~queue(, "U")'
call try 'q~push(, "U")'
call try 'q~queue(1, "U", 3)'
call try 'q~push(1, "U", 3)'
say q~allItems~makeString('L', ',')
exit

[class.circularqueue.queue.sends]

queue and push send, to the receiver, items and then, when the answer is greater than the size, pull for queue or, for push, items again and remove with the answer as the index. With the option Unique they send hasItem with the item first and, for as long as it answers true, removeItem with the item and hasItem again, and only then the items. The strict == of that search is the one of the Queue search rule: the first example shows the order. For the very object that is stored, see the deviation rule. The option is sent caselessMatchChar with the arguments 1 and u, whose answer is read as a logical value: neither 0 nor 1 raises SYNTAX 34.1, and an option that does not understand the message raises SYNTAX 97.1, .nil included. The second example shows these.

q~resize(4)
q~queue(.thing~new('p'), 'U')
say q~items
q~push(.thing~new('q'), 'U')
say q~items
exit

[class.circularqueue.append]

append(item) adds the item at the tail and answers its index, which is the number of items afterwards; a queue of size 0 holds nothing, and append then answers .nil. A full queue takes out the item at its head first, so the index is the size then. It takes exactly one argument: none raises SYNTAX 93.901, and a second raises SYNTAX 93.902. After the item is added, append sends items to the receiver, and pull when the answer is greater than the size.

[class.circularqueue.insert]

insert(item, index) adds the item directly after the item at the index, as the Queue insert rule says of any queue, and answers the index of the new item, which is the index it had when it was added. When that makes the queue hold more items than its size, the item at the tail is taken out afterwards: so an item that was added after the last item, by the omitted index or by the index of the last item, is taken out at once from a full queue, and the answer is then the index above the size. The receiver is sent items after the item is added, and when its answer is greater than the size last and then remove with the answer of last.

say q~insert('u') q~allItems~makeString('L', ',') q~items
say q~insert('t', q~last) q~allItems~makeString('L', ',') q~items

Resizing

[class.circularqueue.resize]

resize(newSize, order) changes the size to newSize and answers newSize as it was given. When the queue holds more items than the new size, the surplus is taken out, from the head for the order Fifo, which is the default, and from the tail for Lifo, so that the other end is kept. The newSize is read as the size of the new rule is, with the message < and the errors that rule names; a missing newSize raises SYNTAX 93.901, an omitted one before an order raises SYNTAX 93.903, and a third argument SYNTAX 93.902; the arguments are counted first, then the newSize is read, then the order. The first character of the order, in either case, is F or L, and an order whose first character is another, the null string included, raises SYNTAX 93.914; the order is read by the order rule. A size 0 empties the queue.

[class.circularqueue.resize.sends]

resize sends items to the receiver. When the answer is greater than newSize it sends items again, and then remove once for each surplus item: with the index 1 for the order Fifo, and with the index newSize + 1 for Lifo, which is the index of the last item as the removals go on. The newSize and then the order, when given, are read first, the order as the order rule says.

Parts, arrays and strings

[class.circularqueue.section]

section(start, count) answers a new circular queue of the same class as the receiver, made by new with the size count, whose items are read from the receiver by position: the first at index start, the next ones at the indexes after it, wrapping from the size to the index 1, so that a section that runs past the tail goes on at the head. A position that holds no item gives .nil. count is at most the size of the receiver, and is the size of the receiver when it is omitted or larger; the new queue holds count items, .nil ones included. When start is above the size, the first entry is what [] answers for start, which is .nil, and the positions after it are 1, 2 and so on. The start is read as the Queue index rule says; count must be a whole number from 0 up, or SYNTAX 93.906 is raised, .nil raising SYNTAX 97.1. No start raises SYNTAX 93.901, and a third argument SYNTAX 93.902. The arguments are counted first. count is then checked with the messages and conditions of the new rule, after which its string value is read once more; that second value is the count, and one below 0 or not a whole number raises SYNTAX 93.906, so a count whose string value is -1 is refused even when its < answers 0. start is read last. The answer is not the receiver, and the receiver is not changed.

call show q~section(3, 2)
call show q~section(1, 2)

[class.circularqueue.order]

makeArray(order) answers a new Array of the items, from the head for the order Fifo, which is the default, and from the tail for Lifo; allItems answers the items from the head, and allIndexes the indexes 1 to the number of items, as for any queue (the Queue rule). supplier(order) answers a Supplier that goes over the same items, a snapshot as for any queue. The first character of the order, in either case, is F or L, the rest does not count, and anything else raises SYNTAX 93.914; an order that is a null string, a number, or a string with a leading blank is anything else. With Lifo the index of an item in the answer of supplier is its index in the queue, so that the supplier counts down. makeArray and supplier take at most one argument: a second raises SYNTAX 93.902.

[class.circularqueue.order.sends]

makeArray and supplier read the order by sending it upper with no argument, and use the first character of the answer. string and makeString send it caselessStartsWith with F and, when the answer is not true, with L, and raise SYNTAX 93.914 when neither is; they pass the order on to makeArray, which reads it as above. resize reads it as makeArray does. For the order Lifo, makeArray and supplier send copy to the receiver, then items to that copy, then at to the copy with each index from that number down to 1, and the answer holds what at answered, in that order; Fifo sends nothing to the receiver. string and makeString reach these through the makeArray they send. In the first example the order is an object that answers every message itself; the second shows the messages for Lifo.

call try 'q~makeArray(.ord~new)'
.local~up = 'L'

[class.circularqueue.string]

string(delimiter, order) answers a string that joins the items in the order, with the delimiter between one item and the next, and makeString answers what string answers for the same arguments. The delimiter is , when it is omitted, and may be the null string. The string value of a circular queue, which say and the joining operators use, is what its makeString answers with no argument, which is what string answers, so that say of a circular queue writes its items separated by commas. An item that is a string is used as it is and any other object, .nil included, gives the answer of its objectName: the Array rule says the same. A delimiter that is not a string and gives no string raises SYNTAX 88.909; the order is checked as the order rule says, and a third argument raises SYNTAX 93.902. A queue without items answers the null string.

say x~makeString('', 'F')

call try 'x~string("/", "X")'
call try 'x~string("/", "L", 1)'
call try 'x~string(.object~new)'
exit

makeString sends string to the receiver with its arguments, and string sends makeArray with the order, F when it was omitted. The order is read first, as the order rule says. A string item is sent nothing; each other item is sent objectName, from the one that the answer of makeArray holds first, as the Array rule says of makeString; the delimiter is sent its string value first. An item's own string and makeString are not used.

The set operations

[class.circularqueue.set]

union, intersection and xor answer a new circular queue of the same class as the receiver, and the receiver is not changed. union(other) holds the items of the receiver followed by every item of the argument, so an item that both have is there twice; the size of the answer is the size of the receiver, or, when the receiver's number of items plus the argument's is greater, that number. intersection(other) holds the items of the argument in its order that the receiver has, each counting as often as the receiver has it, as the OrderedCollection rule says, and has the size of the receiver. xor(other) holds what the OrderedCollection rule says of the items that only one of the two has, receiver items first, and has the size of the receiver, or, when it holds more items, their number. difference, subset, disjoint, equivalent and appendAll are those of the mixins; difference answers a circular queue of the receiver's class and size, and appendAll answers the receiver and adds through append, so that the items that do not fit push the first ones out. The argument is read as the operand rule says, and each takes exactly one: none raises SYNTAX 93.901 and a second raises SYNTAX 93.902.

a = .circularqueue~new(6)
a~queue(1); a~queue(2); a~queue(3)
call show a~union(.array~of(9))
call show a~union(.array~of(9, 8, 7, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1))
call show a~union(.list~of(9))
call show a~union(.array~new)
call show a~intersection(.array~of(2, 2, 3))
call show a~intersection(.array~of(5))
call show a~xor(.array~of(2, 9))
call show a~xor(.array~of(1, 1, 9))
call show a~xor(.array~of(7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13))
call show a~difference(.array~of(2))
say a~size a~items a~allItems~makeString('L', ',')
b = .circularqueue~new(3)
b~queue(1); b~queue(2); b~queue(3)
call show b~union(.array~of(9))
call show b~union(.array~of(1, 2))
call show b~xor(.array~of(5, 6, 7, 8))
call show b~appendAll(.array~of(7, 8))
call try 'a~union'
call try 'a~xor(.array~of(1), 2)'
call try 'a~intersection(.nil)'
exit

[class.circularqueue.set.sends]

The three operations send the messages shown. union sends copy to the receiver, which makes the answer, reads the argument as the operand rule says, and then sends items to the receiver and items to what the argument gave, the array that makeArray answered or the argument itself when it is a collection; when their sum is greater than the size it sends the two items again, and then resize with the sum to the answer. It then sends allItems to the argument's list, and append to the answer with each item in order. intersection and xor send the argument's list allItems; intersection sends copy to the receiver, which gives the working copy, hasItem to the working copy for each item of the list, and, when that answered true, append to the answer, a new circular queue, and then removeItem to the working copy. xor sends allItems to the receiver and copy, hasItem and, when true, removeItem to the working copy for each item, and then append to the answer for each item that is left, from the receiver's, and for those of the argument that found none. difference sends copy and then removeItem with each item of the list to the copy. The sizes the answers get are made by new, as the second example shows.

.local~log = .array~new
.local~on = 0
call run 'a~union(.parg~new)', 3
call run 'a~union(.parg~new)', 6
call run 'a~intersection(.parg~new)', 3
call run 'a~xor(.parg~new)', 3
call run 'a~difference(.parg~new)', 3
exit
run:
  use arg c, n
  a = .spy~new(n)
  do i = 1 to 3; a~queue(i); end
  .local~rh = a~identityHash~c2x
  .local~log~empty
  .local~on = 1
  interpret 'x =' c
  .local~on = 0
  out = ''
  do e over .local~log
    parse var e name '@' h
    if h = '' then out = out e
    else if h = .local~rh then out = out name'@R'
    else if h = x~identityHash~c2x then out = out name'@A'
    else out = out name'@C'
  end
  say c n
  do e over out~makeArray(' ')
    say '  'e
  end
  return

Copies

[class.circularqueue.copy]

copy answers a new circular queue of the same class as the receiver with the same size and the same items, so that neither sees the other's changes; the items are the same objects. As the Queue copy rule says, the variables of a subclass instance are copied as they are, and init is not sent. The method takes no argument: one raises SYNTAX 93.902.

q = .many~new(4)
q~queue('a'); q~queue('b'); q~queue('c')
q~tag = 'T'
c = q~copy
say c~class~id c~size c~items c~tag c~allItems~makeString('L', ',') (c == q)
c~queue('n'); c~queue('o')
say q~items c~items q~allItems~makeString('L', ',')
say c~allItems~makeString('L', ',')
call try 'q~copy(1)'
exit

The methods of Queue

[class.circularqueue.inherited]

The other methods are those of Queue, with the same arguments and answers for the items that are there: at and [] (the at rule), put and []=, hasIndex, hasItem, index, removeItem, delete and remove, first, firstItem, last, lastItem, peek, pull, next, previous, items, isEmpty, empty, allItems, allIndexes and the sorts, and the methods of the mixins that this page does not list. The differences are these. The size of the queue does not widen the indexes that put and insert accept: insert with an index above the number of items raises SYNTAX 93.966, whatever the size is. empty keeps the size. Each of the methods sends only the messages that the Queue rule lists. The example shows these.

q = .circularqueue~new(5)
q~queue('c'); q~queue('a'); q~queue('b')
say q~at(2) q[3] q~first q~last q~firstItem q~lastItem q~peek q~index('b')
say q~hasItem('a') q~hasIndex(4) q~next(1) q~previous(3) q~items q~isEmpty
say q~removeItem('a') q~delete(1) q~remove(9) q~allItems~makeString('L', ',')
q~put('z', 1)
say q~sort~allItems~makeString('L', ',') q~size
say q~pull q~pull (q~pull == .nil) q~items q~size
q~queue('p'); q~queue('q')
say (q~empty == q) q~items q~size
call try 'q~insert("x", 1)'
call try 'q~at(0)'
call try 'q~hasIndex'
call try 'q~items(1)'
call try 'q~peek(1)'
call try 'q~pull(1)'
say q~allItems~class~id q~class~id
exit

Messages the methods send

[class.circularqueue.sends]

The methods that CircularQueue declares send these messages to the receiver: items, pull, last, remove, hasItem, removeItem, copy, allItems, [], makeArray and string, and items and at to the copy that makeArray and supplier make for the order Lifo; the rules above say which each one sends, in which order and with which arguments, and the set rule those of the three set operations. append, insert, push and queue add the item themselves: none of them sends append, queue or push to the receiver. The example records, for each method, what it sends to a receiver whose methods are overridden to record themselves, with a queue that has room for one more item and with one that is full.

  'resize hasItem removeItem supplier string makeString insert'

  src = "if .local~on then .local~log~append('"m"('arg(1)')');",
    'forward class (super)'
  .spy~define(m, src)
end
.local~on = 0

call run 4, 'a~queue("d")'
call run 4, 'a~push("d")'
call run 4, 'a~insert("d", 1)'
say 'full'

call run 3, 'a~queue("d")'
call run 3, 'a~push("d")'
call run 3, 'a~insert("d", 1)'

call run 3, 'a~insert("d")'

call run 3, 'a~push("2", "U")'
call run 3, 'a~resize(5)'

call run 3, 'a~resize(2, "L")'
call run 3, 'a~resize(0)'
exit

  interpret 'x =' c
  .local~on = 0

    say '  'e
  end
  return

Deviations

[class.circularqueue.deviation.78]

A search for an item with the very object that is stored, by hasItem, index or removeItem, sends that object's == as for any other item, so an object whose == answers false is not found even at its own entry. ooRexx finds the very object without sending it ==, and sends == only for the items before it. See Deviation 78.

.local~n = 0
x = .liar~new
c = .circularqueue~new(5)
c~append('a')
c~append(x)
c~append('b')
say c~hasItem(x) .n
.local~n = 0
say (c~index(x) == .nil) .n
.local~n = 0
say (.nil == c~removeItem(x)) c~items .n
::class liar
::method '=='
  .local~n += 1
  return 0

[class.circularqueue.deviation.109]

An index, a count, a size given to new or resize, or a delimiter that is an instance of a subclass of String is read by its own characters, and REQUEST and MAKESTRING are not sent to it (Deviation 109). ooRexx sends such an instance request with STRING or MAKESTRING, so an override of either can change what is read. In the example MAKESTRING answers another index, count, size and delimiter.

say q~at(.num~new('1'))
say q~section(1, .num~new('1'))~items

r~queue('a'); r~queue('b')
say r~items
r~resize(.num~new('1'))
say r~items
say q~makeString(.sep~new('-'))

rexxref: Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Directory Class; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Directory Class > new (Class Method); Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Directory Class > []; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Directory Class > []=; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Directory Class > allIndexes; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Directory Class > allItems; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Directory Class > at; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Directory Class > empty; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Directory Class > entry; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Directory Class > hasEntry; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Directory Class > hasIndex; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Directory Class > hasItem; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Directory Class > index; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Directory Class > isEmpty; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Directory Class > items; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Directory Class > makeArray; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Directory Class > put; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Directory Class > remove; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Directory Class > removeEntry; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Directory Class > removeItem; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Directory Class > setEntry; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Directory Class > setMethod; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Directory Class > supplier; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Directory Class > unknown; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Directory Class > unsetMethod

Deviations: D29, D33, D78, D109

A Directory maps string indexes to items. An index is a string compared in full and by its exact characters, so ab and AB are two indexes, and an item is any object. A directory can also hold methods: a method that setMethod associates with a name runs when the name is read, and so makes a computed entry; a method named UNKNOWN answers every read of a name that has no entry. The class inherits MapCollection, and through it Collection; the hierarchy rule lists what it inherits. Properties is its subclass, and StringTable is a sibling that has the same entry methods without the methods of a directory.

A directory also gives its entries a second face: a message for which the method search finds no method, such as d~name, reaches the unknown method of the class, which reads or sets the entry of that name in upper case (the unknown rule). The page follows the order of the rexxref entry. Examples that show an error use a small routine try, as the builtin pages do. The page says nothing about the answer of isEmpty for a directory that holds only methods, and nothing about which of two items equal to the argument removeItem removes (the hash order rule).

The class

[class.directory.creation]

Directory declares the instance methods [], []=, allIndexes, allItems, at, empty, entry, hasEntry, hasIndex, hasItem, index, isEmpty, items, makeArray, put, remove, removeEntry, removeItem, setEntry, setMethod, supplier, unknown and unsetMethod, the init that new runs (the new rule) and the class method new; the copy of Object copies a directory as the copy rule says. The class method of and the instance methods putAll, union, difference, intersection, xor, subset, disjoint and equivalent are those of the mixins (one rule lists them). A directory has no makeString: the message reaches unknown, so it answers the entry MAKESTRING, .nil when there is none, and a directory is not a string (the string rule).

d = .directory~new
own = '[] []= ALLINDEXES ALLITEMS AT EMPTY ENTRY HASENTRY HASINDEX HASITEM',
  'INDEX ISEMPTY ITEMS MAKEARRAY PUT REMOVE REMOVEENTRY REMOVEITEM SETENTRY',
  'SETMETHOD SUPPLIER UNKNOWN UNSETMETHOD'
n = 0
do m over own~makearray(' ')
  if d~hasMethod(m) then n += 1
end
say d~class~id n .directory~hasMethod('OF') d~hasMethod('OF')
say d~hasMethod('UNION') d~hasMethod('PUTALL') d~hasMethod('APPENDALL')
say d~hasMethod('MAKESTRING') (d~makeString == .nil) d~hasMethod('FIRST')

Making a directory

[class.directory.new]

new makes an empty directory. Its optional argument is a hint for how large the directory will grow; no method that this page specifies answers differently for it. It must be a whole number that is not negative, or SYNTAX 93.923 is raised. A second argument raises SYNTAX 93.902, and omitted arguments at the end count for nothing. new sends init to the new object with the arguments it received, so a subclass's init sees them (the new rule). The checks are those of the init that Directory supplies: they come after the init of a subclass has run, and a subclass whose init does not pass the arguments on is not refused for them.

say .directory~new~items .directory~new(0)~items .directory~new(3, )~items
call try '.directory~new(-1)'
call try '.directory~new("x")'
call try '.directory~new(.nil)'
call try '.directory~new(1.5)'
call try '.directory~new(1, 2)'
x = .watch~new(7)
call try '.watch~new("x")'
say .quiet~new("x", 2, 3)~items
exit

Indexes

[class.directory.indexes]

An index is read as a string: a string is used as it is, and any other object by the string-value rule, which sends it request with the argument STRING, so an object whose makeString answers a string is used through that answer, and an object that has neither gives SYNTAX 88.909, as .nil does. The index is stored as that string, and two indexes are the same when their characters are the same: case counts, 5 and 5.0 are different, and the null string is an index. A method of this page that takes a name reads it this way, at, [], put, []=, hasIndex, remove and the methods whose name is changed to upper case by the entry rule. An instance of a subclass of String is read by its own characters (the deviation rule).

d~put('v1', 'Key')
d~put('v2', 5)
d~put('v3', .made~new)
d~put('v4', '')

call try 'd~put("x", .plain~new)'
call try 'd~at(.plain~new)'
exit

Reading and writing entries

[class.directory.at]

at(name) and [name] answer the item stored at the index, and .nil when there is none. When the name is the name of a method that setMethod associated, the method runs, with the directory as self and no argument, and the answer is what it returns, so it is run again for each read, and .nil when it returns nothing. When there is neither an item nor a method and the directory has an UNKNOWN method, that method runs with the name as its only argument, as the name was given, and its answer is the answer of at. The methods take exactly one argument: none, or an omitted one, raises SYNTAX 88.901, and a second raises SYNTAX 93.902; the number of arguments is checked before the name is read.

d = .directory~new
d~put('item', 'k')
d~setMethod('calc', .method~new('', 'return self~class~id arg()'))
say d~at('k') d['k'] d~at('K') d~at('CALC') d~at('calc')
d~setMethod('unknown', .method~new('', 'return "none:" arg(1)'))
say d~at('missing') d['MISSING'] d~at('k')
call try 'd~at'
call try 'd~at(, "x")'
call try 'd~at("a", "b")'
call try 'd[]'
exit

  return

[class.directory.put]

put(item, name) and [name] = item store the item at the index, replacing the item or the method that was there, and answer nothing. The item may be any object, .nil included. A method named UNKNOWN is not replaced by an item of that name: the two are kept apart. The methods take exactly two arguments: a missing or omitted one raises SYNTAX 88.901, and a third raises SYNTAX 93.902.
