Entries by upper-case name

[class.directory.entry]

entry(name), hasEntry(name), setEntry(name, item) and removeEntry(name) work like at, hasIndex, put and remove with the name changed to upper case first, so setEntry('abc', 1) stores the index ABC, and entry('abc') reads it, while at('abc') does not find it. entry falls back to a method and to the UNKNOWN method as at does, with the upper-case name as the argument of the latter. hasEntry is 1 when an item or a method has that name and does not count UNKNOWN; setEntry with the item omitted removes the entry, and with the item present stores it, replacing a method of that name. setEntry answers nothing and does not check the item. entry, hasEntry and removeEntry take exactly one argument, and setEntry one or two: a missing name raises SYNTAX 88.901, and one argument too many raises SYNTAX 93.902.

d~setEntry('abc', 1)

call try 'd~setEntry'

[class.directory.hasitem]

hasItem(item) answers 1 when some item is equal to the argument and 0 otherwise, and index(item) answers an index of such an item and .nil when there is none. The stored items are searched first. When none of them is equal, the methods are run one after the other, and the answer of each is compared before the next one runs, so a method runs only when nothing searched before it was equal, and at most once. The UNKNOWN method is not searched. Which index index answers when several items qualify is not specified (the hash order rule). Both take exactly one argument: none, or an omitted one, raises SYNTAX 93.903, and a second raises SYNTAX 93.902. .nil is an item like any other.

[class.directory.hasitem.sends]

hasItem, index and removeItem send == to the argument, once for each item that is searched, with that item as the argument, until one answers true, and send nothing else; the stored items are visited first, in an order that is not specified, and then the answers of the methods, in an order that is not specified either, so the number of messages is specified only when no item matches, as then every item is visited. The search with the very object that is stored is no exception: its == is sent as for any other item (the deviation rule).

say (d~index(q) == .nil) .local~n
.local~n = 0
say (d~removeItem(q) == .nil) .local~n d~items

::method '=='
  .local~n += 1
  return 0

Removing entries

[class.directory.remove]

remove(name) and removeEntry(name) remove the entry with that index (that name in upper case for removeEntry) and answer its item. When the entry is a method, the method is removed and the answer is what it returned when it ran. When there is no entry, the answer is .nil, or the answer of the UNKNOWN method run with the name as it was given (the upper-case name for removeEntry) when the directory has one; the UNKNOWN method itself is not removed by either. Each takes exactly one argument: none, or an omitted one, raises SYNTAX 88.901, and a second raises SYNTAX 93.902.

d = .directory~new
d~put('v', 'k')
d~setMethod('m', 'return "ran"')
say d~remove('k') d~remove('k') d~items
say d~remove('M') d~items d~hasEntry('m')
d~setMethod('m', 'return "ran"')
say d~removeEntry('m') d~items
d~setMethod('unknown', 'return "unk" arg(1)')
say d~remove('x') d~removeEntry('x') d~remove('UNKNOWN') d~at('y')
call try 'd~remove'
call try 'd~removeEntry'
call try 'd~remove("a", "b")'
call try 'd~removeEntry("a", "b")'
exit

Methods as entries

[class.directory.setmethod]

setMethod(name, method) associates the method with the name changed to upper case, replacing the item or the method that was there, and answers nothing. method is read as the setMethod of Object reads it (the setMethod rule): a Method, the source of a method as a string or an array of strings, or any other object, which is sent request with ARRAY and then with STRING. A source that does not translate raises its syntax error (the method rule), .nil and an object that answers neither raise SYNTAX 93.974. The items of a source array are read as the source rule reads them, so an item that gives no string raises SYNTAX 93.952. Without a method, or with it omitted, the entry of that name is removed. The method runs when the name is read (the read rule). setMethod('UNKNOWN', m) sets the method that answers the reads of names that have no entry; it replaces an item of that name and is not an entry of the directory. setMethod gives the directory no method of its own, unlike the setMethod of Object: hasMethod of the name answers what it answered before, and a message of that name runs the method of the directory that has the name when there is one, and otherwise reaches unknown, which runs the method with no arguments, whatever the message carried.

[class.directory.unknown]

unknown(name, args) runs when the method search finds no method for a message. When the name does not end in =, it answers what entry of the name answers, and the arguments of the message are ignored; when it ends in =, it stores the first of the arguments at the name without the = with what setEntry does and answers nothing, so d~title = 'x' and d~name('y') set and read the entries TITLE and NAME. The message name can be any string, so d~'two words' = 1 sets the entry TWO WORDS. Neither entry nor setEntry is sent to the directory by it. [class.directory.makearray]

allIndexes and makeArray answer a new Array of the indexes of the entries, and allItems a new Array of their items, with the answer of each method (run once for each call of allItems; makeArray and allIndexes do not run the methods). The methods of the mixins

[class.directory.inherited]

The class method of and the instance methods putAll, union, difference, intersection, xor, subset, disjoint and equivalent are not declared by Directory. of and putAll are those of MapCollection, and the others those of Collection; a directory is one of the collections they take as an argument, and the answers of the first four are instances of the class of the receiver. putAll stores with the put of the receiver. In the example the arguments are directories of pairs of an index and an item.

a = .many~of(.array~of('a', 'A1'), .array~of('b', 'B1'))
b = .directory~of(.array~of('b', 'B2'), .array~of('c', 'C2'))
do op over 'union difference intersection xor'~makeArray(' ')
  r = a~send(op, b)
  say op r~class~id r~items listed(r)
end
say a~subset(b) a~disjoint(b) a~equivalent(b) a~subset(a~copy)
c = .many~new
c~putAll(b)
say c~items listed(c)
exit

Messages the methods send

[class.directory.sends]

No method that Directory declares sends a message to its receiver: an override of at, put, entry, setEntry or any other of the methods is never asked by another method, [] and []= do not use at and put, and unknown does not use entry and setEntry. The messages the methods do send go to other objects and have a rule each: init to the new object by new (the new rule); == to the argument by hasItem, index and removeItem (the search rule); request with STRING to a name that is neither a string nor an instance of a subclass of String (the index rule); request with ARRAY and then STRING to a method argument of setMethod that is not a Method, a string or an array (the setMethod rule). The set operations send what the pages of the mixins say. In the example a subclass has every method overridden to record its name, and each call records only its own.

own = '[] []= allIndexes allItems at empty entry hasEntry hasIndex hasItem',
  'index isEmpty items makeArray put remove removeEntry removeItem setEntry',
  'setMethod supplier unknown unsetMethod copy string'
.local~log = .array~new
.local~on = 0
do m over own~makeArray(' ')
  src = "if .local~on then .local~log~append('"m"'); forward class (super)"
  .spy~define(m, src)
end

  interpret c
  .local~on = 0
  n += 1
  if .local~log~items <> 1 then do
    extra += 1
    say c '=>' .local~log~makeString('L', ' ')
  end
end

Deviations

[class.directory.deviation.29]

An assignment to a name that gives no value, d~"A="(), or the same through sendWith, is refused: interrexx ends the program with exit code 120. ooRexx stores an unrelated leftover object at the entry. A direct call of unknown with a name that ends in = and an argument array that holds no item, d~unknown('A=', .array~new(3)), is refused the same way; ooRexx removes the entry, as setEntry with the item omitted does. The assignment with a value is the unknown rule. See Deviation 29.

say 'before'
d = .directory~new
d~"A="()
say 'after'

before

say 'before'
d = .directory~new
d~unknown('A=', .array~new(3))
say 'after'

before
[class.directory.deviation.33]

The order of the answers of allIndexes, allItems, makeArray and supplier, and of the search of hasItem, index and removeItem, is not specified, and may differ from ooRexx's. Which entries are produced, and how often, is specified. In the example the answers are sorted.

d~put(1, 'one')
d~put(2, 'two')
d~put(3, 'three')
say d~allIndexes~sort~makeString('L', ',')
say d~allItems~sort~makeString('L', ',')
say d~items d~makeArray~items

[class.directory.deviation.78]

A search for an item with the very object that is stored, by hasItem, index or removeItem, sends that object's == as for any other item, so an object whose == answers false is not found even at its own entry. ooRexx compares identity first, finds it and sends nothing. See Deviation 78.

StringTable

rexxref: Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > StringTable Class; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > StringTable Class > new (Class Method); Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > StringTable Class > []; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > StringTable Class > []=; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > StringTable Class > allIndexes; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > StringTable Class > allItems; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > StringTable Class > at; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > StringTable Class > empty; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > StringTable Class > entry; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > StringTable Class > hasEntry; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > StringTable Class > hasIndex; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > StringTable Class > hasItem; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > StringTable Class > index; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > StringTable Class > isEmpty; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > StringTable Class > items; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > StringTable Class > makeArray; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > StringTable Class > put; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > StringTable Class > remove; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > StringTable Class > removeEntry; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > StringTable Class > removeItem; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > StringTable Class > setEntry; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > StringTable Class > supplier; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > StringTable Class > unknown

Deviations: D29, D33, D78, D84, D109

A StringTable maps string indexes to items, as a Directory does, and has the same entry methods, but it holds nothing else: no method can be associated with a name, and there is no UNKNOWN method. An index is a string compared in full and by its exact characters, and an item is any object. The class inherits MapCollection, and through it Collection; the hierarchy rule lists what it inherits.

A message for which the method search finds no method, such as t~name, reaches the unknown method of the class, which reads or sets the entry of that name in upper case (the unknown rule). The page follows the order of the rexxref entry. Examples that show an error use a small routine try, as the builtin pages do. The page says nothing about which of two items equal to the argument removeItem removes (the hash order rule).

The class

[class.stringtable.creation]

StringTable declares the instance methods [], []=, allIndexes, allItems, at, empty, entry, hasEntry, hasIndex, hasItem, index, isEmpty, items, makeArray, put, remove, removeEntry, removeItem, setEntry, supplier and unknown, the init that new runs (the new rule) and the class method new; the copy of Object copies a string table as the copy rule says. The class method of and the instance methods putAll, union, difference, intersection, xor, subset, disjoint and equivalent are those of the mixins (one rule lists them). It has no setMethod and no unsetMethod of the kind a directory has (the method rule), and no makeString, so a string table is not a string (the string rule).

own = '[] []= ALLINDEXES ALLITEMS AT EMPTY ENTRY HASENTRY HASINDEX HASITEM',
  'INDEX ISEMPTY ITEMS MAKEARRAY PUT REMOVE REMOVEENTRY REMOVEITEM SETENTRY',
  'SUPPLIER UNKNOWN'

do m over own~makearray(' ')
  if t~hasMethod(m) then n += 1
end

say t~hasMethod('UNION') t~hasMethod('PUTALL') t~hasMethod('APPENDALL')
say t~hasMethod('MAKESTRING') (t~makeString == .nil) t~hasMethod('FIRST')

Making a string table

[class.stringtable.new]

new makes an empty string table. Its optional argument is a hint for how large the table will grow; no method that this page specifies answers differently for it. It must be a whole number that is not negative, or SYNTAX 93.923 is raised. A second argument raises SYNTAX 93.902, and omitted arguments at the end count for nothing. new sends init to the new object with the arguments it received, so a subclass's init sees them (the new rule). The checks are those of the init that StringTable supplies: they come after the init of a subclass has run, and a subclass whose init does not pass the arguments on is not refused for them.

call try '.stringtable~new(.nil)'
call try '.stringtable~new(1.5)'
call try '.stringtable~new(1, 2)'

call try '.watch~new("x")'
say .quiet~new("x", 2, 3)~items
exit

Indexes

[class.stringtable.indexes]

An index is read as a string, exactly as a directory reads it: a string is used as it is, any other object by the string-value rule, so an object whose makeString answers a string is used through that answer, and an object that has neither, .nil included, gives SYNTAX 88.909. The index is stored as that string, case counts, 5 and 5.0 are different indexes, and the null string is an index. An instance of a subclass of String is read by its own characters (the deviation rule). Every method of this page that takes a name reads it this way, those that change it to upper case afterwards included (the entry rule).

t = .stringtable~new
t~put('v1', 'Key')
t~put('v2', 5)
t~put('v3', .made~new)
t~put('v4', '')
say t~at('Key') t~at('KEY') t~at(5) t~at('5') t~at(5.0)
say t~at('made') t~at(.made~new) t~hasIndex(.made~new) t~at('') t~items
call try 't~at(.nil)'
call try 't~put("x", .plain~new)'
exit

Reading and writing entries

[class.stringtable.at]

at(name) and [name] answer the item stored at the index, and .nil when there is none. The methods take exactly one argument: none, or an omitted one, raises SYNTAX 88.901, and a second raises SYNTAX 93.902; the number of arguments is checked before the name is read.

call try 't~at("a", "b")'
call try 't[]'
exit

Entries by upper-case name

[class.stringtable.entry]

entry(name), hasEntry(name), setEntry(name, item) and removeEntry(name) work like at, hasIndex, put and remove with the name changed to upper case first, so setEntry('abc', 1) stores the index ABC and entry('abc') reads it, while at('abc') does not find it. setEntry with the item omitted removes the entry, and answers nothing, and it does not check the item. entry, hasEntry and removeEntry take exactly one argument and setEntry one or two: a missing name raises SYNTAX 88.901, and one argument too many raises SYNTAX 93.902.

call try 't~setEntry'
call try 't~setEntry("a", 1, 2)'

[class.stringtable.unknown]

unknown(name, args) runs when the method search finds no method for a message. When the name does not end in =, it answers what entry of the name answers, and the arguments of the message are ignored; when it ends in =, it stores the first of the arguments at the name without the = with what setEntry does and answers nothing, so t~title = 'x' and t~name('y') set and read the entries TITLE and NAME. The message name can be any string. Neither entry nor setEntry is sent to the table by it. Called directly, it takes exactly two arguments: a missing name or a missing second argument raises SYNTAX 93.903, a third raises SYNTAX 93.902, a name that cannot be read as a string raises SYNTAX 88.909, and an arguments value that is .nil raises SYNTAX 98.913. The page says nothing about an assignment that has no value, which a deviation covers.

[class.stringtable.setmethod]

A string table has no setMethod and no unsetMethod of its own: the methods of those names that Object has are private (the private rule), and a message from outside the object does not reach them (the access rule). [class.stringtable.hasitem.sends]

hasItem, index and removeItem send == to the argument, once for each item that is searched, with that item as the argument, until one answers true, and send nothing else; the items are visited in an order that is not specified, so the number of messages is specified only when no item matches, as then every item is visited. Lists of the entries

[class.stringtable.makearray]

allIndexes and makeArray answer a new Array of the indexes of the entries, and allItems a new Array of their items. They are instances of Array for a subclass receiver too, never the receiver, and do not follow later changes. They take no argument: one raises SYNTAX 93.902. Copies and the string value

[class.stringtable.copy]

copy answers a new string table of the class of the receiver with the same entries. The items are the same objects, and the two tables do not see each other's changes. As the copy rule says of every object, the variables of a subclass instance are copied as they are, and init is not sent. It takes no argument: one raises SYNTAX 93.902.

c~remove('k1')
say t~items c~items t~at('k1') (c~at('k1') == .nil)
call try 't~copy(1)'

[class.stringtable.string]

A string table has no makeString method, so its string value is the one of Object: its name, a StringTable, as the string rule says, whatever the table holds, and request('STRING') answers .nil. Entries named STRING, MAKESTRING or OBJECTNAME do not change that: the methods of those names that every object has are found before unknown.

The methods of the mixins

[class.stringtable.inherited]

The class method of and the instance methods putAll, union, difference, intersection, xor, subset, disjoint and equivalent are not declared by StringTable. of and putAll are those of MapCollection, and the others those of Collection; a string table is one of the collections they take as an argument, and the answers of the first four are instances of the class of the receiver. putAll stores with the put of the receiver. In the example the arguments are string tables of pairs of an index and an item.

a = .many~of(.array~of('a', 'A1'), .array~of('b', 'B1'))
b = .stringtable~of(.array~of('b', 'B2'), .array~of('c', 'C2'))
do op over 'union difference intersection xor'~makeArray(' ')
  r = a~send(op, b)
  say op r~class~id r~items listed(r)
end
say a~subset(b) a~disjoint(b) a~equivalent(b) a~subset(a~copy)
c = .many~new
c~putAll(b)
say c~items listed(c)
exit
listed: procedure
  use arg r
  s = ''
  do i over r~allIndexes~sort
    s = s i'='r[i]
  end
  return s~strip

Messages the methods send

[class.stringtable.sends]

No method that StringTable declares sends a message to its receiver: an override of at, put, entry, setEntry or any other of the methods is never asked by another method, [] and []= do not use at and put, and unknown does not use entry and setEntry. The messages the methods do send go to other objects and have a rule each: init to the new object by new (the new rule); == to the argument by hasItem, index and removeItem (the search rule); request with STRING to a name that is neither a string nor an instance of a subclass of String (the index rule). The set operations send what the pages of the mixins say. In the example a subclass has every method overridden to record its name, and each call records only its own.

own = '[] []= allIndexes allItems at empty entry hasEntry hasIndex hasItem',
  'index isEmpty items makeArray put remove removeEntry removeItem setEntry',
  'supplier unknown copy string'
.local~log = .array~new
.local~on = 0
do m over own~makeArray(' ')
  src = "if .local~on then .local~log~append('"m"'); forward class (super)"
  .spy~define(m, src)
end
a = .spy~new
calls = 'x = a[1]|a["k1"] = "x"|a~allIndexes|a~allItems|a~at("k1")',
  '|a~entry("k1")|a~hasEntry("k1")|a~hasIndex("k1")|a~hasItem("q")',
  '|a~index("q")|a~isEmpty|a~items|a~makeArray|a~put(1, "k9")',
  '|a~remove("k9")|a~removeEntry("k9")|a~removeItem("q")|a~setEntry("k8", 1)',
  '|a~supplier|a~copy|a~string|a~unknown("fooz", .array~new)|a~fooz',
  '|a~fooz = 1|a~empty'
n = 0
extra = 0
do c over calls~makeArray('|')
  .local~log~empty
  .local~on = 1
  interpret c
  .local~on = 0
  n += 1
  if .local~log~items <> 1 then do
    extra += 1
    say c '=>' .local~log~makeString('L', ' ')
  end
end
say n 'calls,' extra 'sent more than one message to the receiver'

Deviations

[class.stringtable.deviation.29]

An assignment to a name that gives no value, t~"A="(), or the same through sendWith, is refused: interrexx ends the program with exit code 120. ooRexx stores an unrelated leftover object at the entry. A direct call of unknown with a name that ends in = and an argument array that holds no item, t~unknown('A=', .array~new(3)), is refused the same way; ooRexx removes the entry, as setEntry with the item omitted does. The assignment with a value is the unknown rule. See Deviation 29.

say 'before'
t = .stringtable~new
t~"A="()
say 'after'

before

say 'before'
t = .stringtable~new
t~unknown('A=', .array~new(3))
say 'after'

before
[class.stringtable.deviation.33]

The order of the answers of allIndexes, allItems, makeArray and supplier, and of the search of hasItem, index and removeItem, is not specified, and may differ from ooRexx's. Which entries are produced, and how often, is specified. In the example the answers are sorted.

t = .stringtable~new
t~put(1, 'one')
t~put(2, 'two')
t~put(3, 'three')
say t~allIndexes~sort~makeString('L', ',')
say t~allItems~sort~makeString('L', ',')
say t~items t~makeArray~items

1,2,3
3 3
[class.stringtable.deviation.78]

A search for an item with the very object that is stored, by hasItem, index or removeItem, sends that object's == as for any other item, so an object whose == answers false is not found even at its own entry. ooRexx compares identity first, finds it and sends nothing. See Deviation 78.

t = .stringtable~new
q = .thing~new
t~put(q, 'k')
say t~hasItem(q) .local~n
say (t~index(q) == .nil) .local~n
say (t~removeItem(q) == .nil) .local~n t~items

::method '=='
  .local~n += 1
  return 0

[class.stringtable.deviation.84]

When the == that removeItem sends to its argument empties the string table, items answers 0 afterwards and the method answers .nil. ooRexx's items answers -1. See Deviation 84.

.local~victim = c
c['a'] = .em~new

[class.stringtable.deviation.109]

A name, an index or the size argument of new that is an instance of a subclass of String is read by its own characters, and REQUEST and MAKESTRING are not sent to it (Deviation 109). ooRexx sends such an instance request with STRING or MAKESTRING, so an override of either changes the index that is stored or looked up and the size that new checks. In the example MAKESTRING answers another text.

Properties

rexxref: Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Properties Class; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Properties Class > load (Class method); Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Properties Class > new (Class method); Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Properties Class > []=; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Properties Class > getLogical; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Properties Class > getProperty; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Properties Class > getWhole; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Properties Class > load; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Properties Class > put; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Properties Class > save; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Properties Class > setLogical; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Properties Class > setProperty; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Properties Class > setWhole

Deviations: D29, D33, D78, D109

A Properties is a Directory whose items are strings, with methods to read and write them as text, as logical values and as whole numbers, and to load and save them as lines of a file. It inherits Directory, and through it MapCollection and Collection; the hierarchy rule lists what it inherits. Everything that the page of Directory says holds for a Properties, the entries read by upper-case name, the methods associated with names, unknown and the lists of the entries included; this page gives what differs and what is added.

The page follows the order of the rexxref entry. Examples that show an error use a small routine try, as the builtin pages do. Names and values of the examples are strings, and the examples that use files create them under a distinctive name and delete them. The page says nothing about what load does with a file that cannot be read, other than one that does not exist.

The class

[class.properties.creation]

Properties declares the instance methods []=, getLogical, getProperty, getWhole, load, put, save, setLogical, setProperty and setWhole, and the class method load; its new is that of Directory (the new rule). The class method of and the other instance methods are those of Directory and the mixins. A properties object answers the same of and set operations, hasEntry, setMethod and unsetMethod as a directory (the inheritance rule).

p = .properties~new
own = '[]= GETLOGICAL GETPROPERTY GETWHOLE LOAD PUT SAVE SETLOGICAL',
  'SETPROPERTY SETWHOLE'
n = 0
do m over own~makearray(' ')
  if p~hasMethod(m) then n += 1
end
say p~class~id n p~class~superclass~id .properties~hasMethod('LOAD')
say p~hasMethod('HASENTRY') p~hasMethod('SETMETHOD') p~hasMethod('UNION')

Making a properties object

[class.properties.new]

new makes an empty properties object and takes the optional size hint of the new of Directory: a whole number that is not negative, or SYNTAX 93.923; a second argument raises SYNTAX 93.902; init is sent with the arguments, and the checks come after the init of a subclass.

say .properties~new~items .properties~new(10)~items
call try '.properties~new(-1)'
call try '.properties~new("x")'
call try '.properties~new(1, 2)'
x = .watch~new(7)
exit

Writing values

[class.properties.put]

put(value, name), [name] = value and setProperty(name, value) store a string at the name. A value that is not a string is replaced by its string value as the string-value rule says, which sends it request with STRING, so a number is stored as its digits, an object whose makeString answers a string is stored as that answer, and an array as the text that its makeString gives; .nil and an object with no makeString raise SYNTAX 93.938. An instance of a subclass of String is stored as its own characters (the deviation rule). The name is read as a string as for a directory (the index rule), and .nil as the name raises SYNTAX 88.909. The three answer nothing, and none of them sends put, []= or setProperty to the receiver. put and setProperty take exactly two arguments and []= is the assignment [name] = value: fewer raises SYNTAX 93.901, an omitted place before the last argument given raises SYNTAX 93.903, and a third argument raises SYNTAX 93.902. The count is checked first, then the value, then the name.

p = .properties~new
p~put('v1', 'a')
p['b'] = 7
p~setProperty('c', .made~new)
p~put(.array~of(1, 2), 'd')
do i over p~allIndexes~sort
  say i p[i]~class~id '['p[i]~changeStr('0a'x, '/')']'
end
call try 'p~put(.nil, "k")'
call try 'p~put(.plain~new, "k")'
call try 'p["k"] = .nil'
call try 'p~setProperty("k", .plain~new)'
call try 'p~put("x", .nil)'
call try 'p~put("x")'
call try 'p~put(, "x")'
call try 'p~setProperty("x")'
call try 'p~setProperty(, "x")'
call try 'p~put("x", "y", "z")'
call try 'p~put(.nil, .nil)'
call try 'p~setProperty(.nil, .nil)'
exit

[class.properties.unchecked]

setEntry, the assignment through unknown (p~name = x) and the methods that setMethod associates do not check the value: an item stored by setEntry or through unknown keeps its class and may be .nil. putAll and of store with put, so they check.

call try '.properties~of(.array~of("k", .nil))'

Reading values

[class.properties.getproperty]

getProperty(name, default) answers the item at the name, read with at (the at rule), and when the directory has none the default, or .nil when the default is omitted. The default is any object and is not converted. It sends at to the receiver with the name. It takes one or two arguments: none raises SYNTAX 93.901, an omitted name before a default raises SYNTAX 93.903 and a third raises SYNTAX 93.902.

p~setProperty('a', 'x')

say (p~getProperty('zz') == .nil) (p~getProperty('zz', ) == .nil)
say p~getProperty('zz', 5)~class~id p~getProperty('zz', .array~new)~class~id
call try 'p~getProperty'
call try 'p~getProperty(, 1)'
call try 'p~getProperty("a", "b", "c")'
call try 'p~getProperty(.nil)'

[class.properties.getlogical]

getLogical(name, default) reads the value as getProperty does, with the same arguments, which it sends to the receiver, and answers 1 for the value 1 or true and 0 for 0 or false. Case counts, and no other text is accepted: SYNTAX 34.904 is raised. The default is used when the name has no value and is checked in the same way, so it must be one of those four strings (or a logical value), or the error is raised; when the name has a value, the default is not looked at. A missing name with no default raises SYNTAX 34.904 too. A value that is not a string is not converted and raises SYNTAX 34.904. The arguments are counted as for getProperty.

p = .properties~new
do v over .array~of('1', '0', 'true', 'false')
  p~setProperty('k', v)
  call charout , p~getLogical('k') ''
end
say
p~setProperty('k', 'true')
say p~getLogical('k', 'junk') p~getLogical('zz', 1)
say p~getLogical('zz', 'false')
say p~getLogical('zz', .true) p~getLogical('zz', .false)
do v over .array~of('TRUE', 'False', 'yes', '2', '-1', '00', '', ' 1')
  p~setProperty('k', v)
  call try 'p~getLogical("k")', '['v']'
end
p~setEntry('k', .text~new('true'))
call try 'p~getLogical("K")', 'object'
call try 'p~getLogical("zz")', 'missing'
call try 'p~getLogical("zz", "junk")', 'default junk'
call try 'p~getLogical("zz", .nil)', 'default nil'
call try 'p~getLogical', 'no name'
call try 'p~getLogical("a", 1, 2)', 'three'
exit

[class.properties.getwhole]

getWhole(name, default) reads the value as getProperty does, with the same arguments, which it sends to the receiver, and answers it as it is stored, not reformatted, when it is a whole number, and raises SYNTAX 26.901 when it is not. A whole number is judged at NUMERIC DIGITS 9 whatever the caller's setting: blanks around it are allowed, a sign, an exponent and a point followed by zeros are allowed, and a value that needs more than nine digits is not. The default is used when the name has no value and is checked in the same way, and is not looked at when the name has a value. A missing name with no default raises SYNTAX 26.901 too. A value that is not a string is read through the string-value rule.

p = .properties~new
do v over .array~of('0', '12', '-5', '+7', '007', '1.0', '1e2', '3.', ' 8 ')
  p~setProperty('k', v)
  say '['v']' '['p~getWhole('k')']'
end
do v over .array~of('1.5', 'abc', '1000000000', '99999999999', '0.5', '')
  p~setProperty('k', v)
  call try 'p~getWhole("k")', '['v']'
end
p~setProperty('w', '12')
say p~getWhole('w', 'junk') p~getWhole('zz', 5) p~getWhole('zz', '2.0')

call try 'p~getWhole("zz", .nil)', 'default nil'
call try 'p~getWhole', 'no name'
call try 'p~getWhole("a", 1, 2)', 'three'
exit

Setting logical and whole values

[class.properties.setlogical]

setLogical(name, value) sends datatype with the argument O to the value and, when that answers true, stores true for the value 1 and false for 0 with setProperty, which it sends to the receiver with the name and the new text. A string is accepted only as 0 or 1, and a logical value .true or .false too: true, 2, 00, a blank around the digit and the null string raise SYNTAX 34.901. A value that has no datatype method, .nil and an instance of a class that does not understand the message among them, raises SYNTAX 97.1; one whose datatype answers 1 but that is not a logical value raises SYNTAX 34.1, and one that answers 0 raises SYNTAX 34.901. The method answers nothing and takes exactly two arguments, counted as for put: fewer raises SYNTAX 93.901, an omitted name before the value SYNTAX 93.903 and a third SYNTAX 93.902; the value is checked before the name.

p = .properties~new
do v over .array~of('0', '1', .true, .false)
  p~setLogical('k', v)
  call charout , p['k'] ''
end
say
do v over .array~of('true', '2', '00', 'yes', '1.0', '', ' 1')
  call try 'p~setLogical("k", v)', '['v']'
end
call try 'p~setLogical("k", .nil)', 'nil'
call try 'p~setLogical("k", .object~new)', 'object'
call try 'p~setLogical("k", .answers~new(1))', 'answers 1'
call try 'p~setLogical("k", .answers~new(0))', 'answers 0'
call try 'p~setLogical("k")', 'one argument'
call try 'p~setLogical("k", 1, 2)', 'three'
call try 'p~setLogical(, 1)', 'omitted name'
call try 'p~setLogical(.nil, .nil)', 'both nil'
call try 'p~setLogical(.nil, 1)', 'name nil'
exit

Loading and saving

[class.properties.load.format]

load reads its source line by line as linein does (the line rule) and enters one property for each line that carries one. A line that is empty or holds only blanks and tab characters is skipped, and so is a line whose first characters after blanks and tab characters are --; a -- anywhere else is text. Any other line is split at its first =: the name is the text before it with the blanks and tab characters removed from both ends, and the value is all the text after it, blanks included. A line with no = is a name with the null string as its value, and a line that starts with = has the null string as its name. A later line with a name that an earlier line or the properties object already has replaces the value.

f = 'spec-properties-format.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
t = '09'x
n = '0a'x
text = 'alpha=1'||n||'  beta = two words  '||n||'-- comment'||n,
  || t||'  -- indented comment'||n||n||' '||t||' '||n||'gamma'||n,
  || 'delta=x=y=z'||n||'=nokey'||n||'empty='||n||'alpha=3'||n,
  || 'Mixed=Case'||n||'k -- c=v'||n||'-'||n,
  || t||t||'tab'||t||'='||t||'v'||t||n||'last=noeol'
call charout f, text
call stream f, 'c', 'close'
p = .properties~load(f)
say p~items
do i over p~allIndexes~sort
  say '['i']' '=' '['p[i]']'
end
call sysfiledelete f

[class.properties.load.class]

The class method load(source) answers a new Properties that holds what the source gives, an instance of Properties whatever class received the message, and new is not sent. source is the name of a file or a File object, which is read through a Stream made for it, or any other object, a Stream included, which is sent linein with no argument until it raises the NOTREADY condition, so a stream is read from its read position to its end, is opened by its first linein when it was not open, and is not closed (the instance rule). A file that does not exist gives an empty object and no error, and an object that does not understand linein raises SYNTAX 97.1. The method takes exactly one argument: none raises SYNTAX 93.901, a second raises SYNTAX 93.902.

f = 'spec-properties-load.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
call lineout f, 'a=1'
call lineout f, 'b=2'
call lineout f
p = .properties~load(f)
say p~class~id p~items p['a']
p = .properties~load(.file~new(f))
say p~items p['b']
s = .stream~new(f)
s~open('read')
say s~linein
p = .properties~load(s)
say p~items p['a'] p['b']
s~close
q = .sub~load(f)
s2 = .stream~new(f)
say .properties~load(s2)~items s2~state
s2~close
say q~class~id q~items
say .properties~load('spec-properties-nothing-here.tmp')~items
p = .properties~load(.lines~new)
say p~items p['x'] p['y']
.local~k = 0
.local~a = 0
s3 = .counting~new(f)
say .properties~load(s3)~items .local~k .local~a s3~state
s3~close
call try '.properties~load(.nil)'
call try '.properties~load'
call try '.properties~load(f, 1)'
call sysfiledelete f
exit

[class.properties.load]

The instance method load(source) reads the source as the class method does and adds what it reads to the receiver, replacing the values of names that it already has and leaving the others; it answers nothing. When the source is a name or a File, it first sends load to the receiver with a Stream made for it, and that message does the reading, so an override of load sees the message twice. For each line that carries a property it then sends put to the receiver with the value and the name, in the order of the lines, so an override of put sees them and its checks apply. It takes exactly one argument, as the class method does.

f = 'spec-properties-iload.tmp'
g = 'spec-properties-isave.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
call sysfiledelete g
call lineout f, 'n=1'
call lineout f, 'm=2'
call lineout f
.local~on = 0
p = .spy~new
p~put('keep', 'k')
p~put('old', 'n')
.local~on = 1
say 'by name'
p~load(f)
say p~items p['k'] p['n'] p['m']
say 'by stream'
p~load(.stream~new(f))
say 'save by name'
p~save(g)
.local~on = 0
call sysfiledelete f
call sysfiledelete g
call try 'p~load'
call try 'p~load(f, 1)'
exit

[class.properties.save]

save(target) writes one line name=value for each entry, each ended by a line feed, in an order that is not specified (the hash order rule); the name and the value are written as they are, a value that is not a string through the string-value rule, with no escaping, so a name that holds = or a value that holds a line feed does not load back as it was. target is the name of a file, whose old contents are replaced, a File object, treated the same, or an object that understands lineout, such as a Stream, which is written at its write position and is not closed. When the target is a name or a File, save first sends save to the receiver with a Stream made for it, and that message does the writing. The writing sends supplier to the receiver, and lineout with the line as the only argument to the target for each entry. The answer is nothing, and an object that does not understand lineout raises SYNTAX 97.1. It takes exactly one argument: none raises SYNTAX 93.901, a second raises SYNTAX 93.902.

f = 'spec-properties-save.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
p = .properties~new
p~put('a much longer value', 'k')
p~save(f)
say c2x(charin(f, 1, chars(f)))
call stream f, 'c', 'close'
p~put('x', 'k')
p~save(f)
say c2x(charin(f, 1, chars(f)))
call stream f, 'c', 'close'
p~save(.file~new(f))
say chars(f)
call stream f, 'c', 'close'
s = .stream~new(f)
s~open('write append')
p~save(s)
say s~state
s~close
say chars(f)
call stream f, 'c', 'close'
p~put('two', 'k2')
t = .recorder~new
p~save(t)
say t~lines~sort~makeString('L', '|')
q = .properties~new
q~put('', 'k=eq')
q~put('v', '')
q~save(f)
r = .properties~load(f)
say (r~at('k=eq') == .nil) r~at('k') r~items
call sysfiledelete f
call try 'p~save'
call try 'p~save(f, 1)'
call try 'p~save(.nil)'
exit

What a properties object inherits

[class.properties.inherited]

The methods that Properties does not declare are those of Directory: the entries read by upper-case name (entry, hasEntry, setEntry, removeEntry), at, remove, removeItem, hasIndex, hasItem, index, items, isEmpty, empty, copy, supplier, allIndexes, allItems, makeArray, unknown and setMethod and unsetMethod, and those of the mixins, of, putAll and the set operations, and each behaves as the page of Directory says, of a properties object and of an instance of a subclass of it. The copy is a Properties. The unknown that reads and sets the entries by message name does not check the value (the unchecked rule). A search for the very item stored sends its == as for any other item (the Properties rule). Its string value is a Properties.

p = .many~new
p~put('v', 'k')
p~setMethod('m', 'return "computed"')
p~title = 'x'
c = p~copy
say c~class~id c~items c~at('M') c~entry('TITLE') p~hasEntry('title')
say p p~string (p~request('STRING') == .nil)
say p~removeEntry('title') p~items p~union(c)~class~id
say .properties~new~isEmpty

Messages the methods send

[class.properties.sends]

The messages that Properties methods send to the receiver, to the values and to the source or target, are these. getProperty sends at with the name; getLogical and getWhole send getProperty with their own arguments; setLogical and setWhole send datatype to the value, and setProperty with the name and the text; setProperty, put and []= send nothing to the receiver; load and save send what the load rule and the save rule say, linein with no argument to a source that is not a name or a File and lineout with the line to a target that is not a name or a File. The methods put, setProperty, []= and the setters read a value that is not a string with request and the argument STRING (the put rule), and getWhole and save send request with STRING to a stored value that is not a string (the getWhole rule and the save rule). In the example each method of a subclass records its name, the number of its arguments and its first argument, and each call shows the records it caused.

f = 'spec-properties-sends.tmp'
own = '[]= put at getProperty setProperty getLogical getWhole setLogical',
  'setWhole unknown'
.local~log = .array~new
.local~on = 0
do m over own~makeArray(' ')
  src = "if .local~on then .local~log~append('"m"' arg()':'arg(1));",
    "forward class (super)"
  .spy~define(m, src)
end
a = .spy~new
a~put('1', 'n')
a~put('true', 't')
calls = 'a~setProperty("k", "v")|x = a~getProperty("k")',
  '|x = a~getProperty("zz", 1)',
  '|x = a~getLogical("t")|x = a~getLogical("zz", 1)|x = a~getWhole("n")',
  '|x = a~getWhole("zz", 5)|a~setLogical("k", 1)|a~setWhole("k", 3)',
  '|a["k"] = "v"|a~put("v", "k")|a~name = "v"|x = a~name'
do c over calls~makeArray('|')
  .local~log~empty
  .local~on = 1
  interpret c
  .local~on = 0
  say c '=>' .local~log~makeString('L', ' ')
end

Deviations

[class.properties.deviation.29]

An assignment through unknown that gives no value, by message or by a direct call, is refused as it is for a directory (the Directory rule): interrexx ends the program with exit code 120, and ooRexx stores an unrelated leftover object for the message and removes the entry for the direct call. See Deviation 29.

p = .properties~new
p~"A="()
say 'after'

before
[class.properties.deviation.33]

The order of the lines that save writes, and the order of the lists and searches that Properties inherits from Directory, is not specified, and may differ from ooRexx's (the Directory rule). Which lines are written, and how often, is specified. In the example the lines are sorted.

p~put('2', 'two')
p~put('3', 'three')
t = .recorder~new
p~save(t)

[class.properties.deviation.109]

A value that is an instance of a subclass of String is read by its own characters by put, []=, setProperty, setLogical and setWhole, and REQUEST and MAKESTRING are not sent to it (Deviation 109); a name is read as a directory reads it. ooRexx sends such a value request with STRING or MAKESTRING, so an override of either changes the text that is stored, and can make setLogical raise SYNTAX 34.1 and setWhole raise SYNTAX 93.905. rexxref: Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Table Class; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Table Class > new (Class Method); Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Table Class > []; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Table Class > []=; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Table Class > allIndexes; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Table Class > allItems; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Table Class > at; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Table Class > empty; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Table Class > hasIndex; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Table Class > hasItem; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Table Class > index; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Table Class > isEmpty; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Table Class > items; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Table Class > makeArray; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Table Class > put; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Table Class > remove; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Table Class > removeItem; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Table Class > supplier

Deviations: D33, D78, D84, D109

A Table maps indexes to items. Both are any objects: an index is found by the hashCode and the == that it answers to, so two indexes are one entry when they hash alike and compare equal, and a table holds at most one item for each index. The class inherits MapCollection, and through it Collection; the hierarchy rule lists what it inherits. Directory and StringTable are tables whose indexes are strings, IdentityTable is the table whose indexes are compared by identity, and Relation is the table that keeps several items for an index.

A table has no unknown method: a message that the method search does not resolve raises NOMETHOD, as the error rule of the chapter says. The page follows the order of the rexxref entry. Examples that show an error use a small routine try, as the builtin pages do. The page says nothing about which of two items equal to the argument removeItem removes (the hash order rule).

The class

[class.table.creation]

Table declares the instance methods [], []=, allIndexes, allItems, at, empty, hasIndex, hasItem, index, isEmpty, items, makeArray, put, remove, removeItem and supplier, the init that new runs (the new rule) and the class method new; the copy of Object copies a table as the copy rule says. The class method of and the instance methods putAll, union, difference, intersection, xor, subset, disjoint and equivalent are those of the mixins (one rule lists them). A table has no makeString, so it is not a string (the string rule), and no unknown and no allAt.

  'ITEMS MAKEARRAY PUT REMOVE REMOVEITEM SUPPLIER'
n = 0
do m over own~makearray(' ')
  if t~hasMethod(m) then n += 1
end

say t~hasMethod('UNION') t~hasMethod('PUTALL') t~hasMethod('APPENDALL')
say t~hasMethod('MAKESTRING') t~hasMethod('UNKNOWN') t~hasMethod('ALLAT')

Making a table

[class.table.new]

new makes an empty table. Its optional argument is a hint for how large the table will grow; no method that this page specifies answers differently for it. It must be a whole number that is not negative, or SYNTAX 93.923 is raised. A second argument raises SYNTAX 93.902, and omitted arguments at the end count for nothing. new sends init to the new object with the arguments it received, so a subclass's init sees them (the new rule). The checks are those of the init that Table supplies: they come after the init of a subclass has run, and a subclass whose init does not pass the arguments on is not refused for them.

call try '.table~new("x")'
call try '.table~new(.nil)'
call try '.table~new(1.5)'
call try '.table~new(1, 2)'
x = .watch~new(7)
call try '.watch~new("x")'
say .quiet~new("x", 2, 3)~items
exit

Indexes

[class.table.indexes]

An index is any object, .nil and the null string included, and is stored as it is: allIndexes answers the very objects that were stored. Two indexes are one entry when the lookup finds that hashCode answers the same string for both and that ==, sent to one with the other as argument, answers true. For an object that declares neither method that is the same object, and an Array is its own index only. A string is the index of its characters, compared by the strict comparison: case counts, a leading or trailing blank counts, and 5 and 5.0 are two indexes. An instance of a subclass of String that declares neither method is the index of its characters like any string. A class that declares == has to declare hashCode so that equal objects hash alike, as the hash code rule says. When a put finds the index already in the table, the entry keeps the index object it has and takes the new item.

t~put('v1', 'Key')
t~put('v2', 'KEY')
t~put('v3', 5)
t~put('v4', 5.0)
t~put('v5', ' a')
t~put('v6', '')
t~put('v7', .nil)

say t~at(.nil) t~at(a) (t~at(.array~of(1)) == .nil) t~at(.sub~new('Key'))
t~put('v8', .eq~new('x', 'first'))
t~put('v9', .eq~new('x', 'second'))
say t~items t~at(.eq~new('x', 'probe')) t~allIndexes~items
ix = t~allIndexes
do i over ix
  if i~isA(.eq) then say i~tag
end

[class.table.indexes.sends]

at, [], hasIndex, put, []= and remove look the index up by sending hashCode to the index argument, once, and then == to the index argument with a stored index as the argument, for stored indexes that have the same hash code, until one answers true; each of those is compared before the lookup gives up. Which further stored indexes are compared, by == or hashCode, and how often, is not specified (the hash order rule); when the table is empty, the only message is hashCode. The very object that is stored is no exception to the == (the deviation rule). In the example every index hashes to the same string, so each stored index is compared.

  '|t~put("v2", .k~new("p"))|t[.k~new("p")] = "v2"',
  '|t~put("v3", .k~new("s1"))|t~remove(.k~new("s1"))'
do c over calls~makeArray('|')
  t = .table~new
  t~put('v1', .k~new('s1'))
  .local~log~empty
  interpret c
  say c '=>' .local~log~makeString('L', ' | ')
end
exit

[class.table.hasitem.sends]

hasItem, index and removeItem send == to the argument with an item as the argument, item by item, until one answers true, and send nothing else, hashCode included. The items are visited in an order that is not specified; every item is compared at least once when none matches, and how often == is sent with the same item is not specified (the hash order rule). The search with the very object that is stored is no exception: its == is sent as for any other item (the deviation rule).

Lists of the entries

[class.table.makearray]

allIndexes and makeArray answer a new Array of the indexes of the entries, and allItems a new Array of their items. They are instances of Array for a subclass receiver too, never the receiver, and do not follow later changes. They take no argument: one raises SYNTAX 93.902. The order is not specified (the hash order rule), and is the same for the three answers and for the supplier of one unchanged table, so the item at a position belongs to the index at the same position. The methods of the mixins

[class.table.inherited]

The class method of and the instance methods putAll, union, difference, intersection, xor, subset, disjoint and equivalent are not declared by Table. of and putAll are those of MapCollection, and the others those of Collection; a table is one of the collections they take as an argument, and the answers of the first four are instances of the class of the receiver. putAll stores with the put of the receiver. In the example the arguments are tables of pairs of an index and an item.

a = .many~of(.array~of('a', 'A1'), .array~of('b', 'B1'))
b = .table~of(.array~of('b', 'B2'), .array~of('c', 'C2'))
do op over 'union difference intersection xor'~makeArray(' ')
  r = a~send(op, b)
  say op r~class~id r~items listed(r)
end
say a~subset(b) a~disjoint(b) a~equivalent(b) a~subset(a~copy)
c = .many~new
c~putAll(b)
say c~items listed(c)
exit
listed: procedure
  use arg r
  s = ''
  do i over r~allIndexes~sort
    s = s i'='r[i]
  end
  return s~strip

Messages the methods send

[class.table.sends]

No method that Table declares sends a message to its receiver: an override of at, put or any other of the methods is never asked by another method, and [] and []= do not use at and put. The messages the methods do send go to other objects and have a rule each: init to the new object by new (the new rule); hashCode and == to the index argument by at, [], hasIndex, put, []= and remove (the lookup rule); == to the argument by hasItem, index and removeItem (the search rule). makeArray, allIndexes, allItems, supplier, copy, items, isEmpty and empty send nothing to the indexes and the items. The set operations send what the pages of the mixins say. In the first example a subclass has every method overridden to record its name, and each call records only its own; in the second the indexes and items record every message a program is likely to override.

own = '[] []= allIndexes allItems at empty hasIndex hasItem index isEmpty',
  'items makeArray put remove removeItem supplier copy string'
.local~log = .array~new
.local~on = 0
do m over own~makeArray(' ')
  src = "if .local~on then .local~log~append('"m"'); forward class (super)"
  .spy~define(m, src)
end

calls = 'x = a[1]|a["k1"] = "x"|a~allIndexes|a~allItems|a~at("k1")',
  '|a~hasIndex("k1")|a~hasItem("q")|a~index("q")|a~isEmpty|a~items',
  '|a~makeArray|a~put(1, "k9")|a~remove("k9")|a~removeItem("q")',
  '|a~supplier|a~copy|a~string|a~empty'
n = 0
extra = 0
do c over calls~makeArray('|')
  .local~log~empty
  .local~on = 1
  interpret c
  .local~on = 0
  n += 1
  if .local~log~items <> 1 then do
    extra += 1
    say c '=>' .local~log~makeString('L', ' ')
  end
end

[class.table.deviation.33]

The order of the answers of allIndexes, allItems, makeArray and supplier, of the search of hasItem, index and removeItem, and which stored indexes or items a lookup or a search compares, by == or hashCode, beyond those it must compare, and how often, are not specified, and may differ from ooRexx's. Which entries are produced, and how often, is specified. In the example the answers are sorted.

say t~items t~makeArray~items

[class.table.deviation.78]

A lookup, a put or a remove with the very object that is stored as the index sends that object's == as for any other index, and a search for an item with the very object that is stored, by hasItem, index or removeItem, sends that object's == as for any other item, so an object whose == answers false is not found even at its own entry. ooRexx compares identity first, finds it and sends nothing but hashCode. IdentityTable

rexxref: Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > IdentityTable Class; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > IdentityTable Class > new (Class Method); Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > IdentityTable Class > []; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > IdentityTable Class > []=; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > IdentityTable Class > allIndexes; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > IdentityTable Class > allItems; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > IdentityTable Class > at; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > IdentityTable Class > empty; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > IdentityTable Class > hasIndex; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > IdentityTable Class > hasItem; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > IdentityTable Class > index; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > IdentityTable Class > isEmpty; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > IdentityTable Class > items; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > IdentityTable Class > makeArray; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > IdentityTable Class > put; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > IdentityTable Class > remove; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > IdentityTable Class > removeItem; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > IdentityTable Class > supplier

Deviations: D4, D33, D109

An IdentityTable maps indexes to items, as a Table does, but two indexes are one entry only when they are the very same object: the hashCode and the == of an index are never asked. Both indexes and items are any objects, and an item is found by its identity too. The table holds at most one item for each index. The class inherits MapCollection, and through it Collection; the hierarchy rule lists what it inherits.

An IdentityTable has no unknown method: a message that the method search does not resolve raises NOMETHOD, as the error rule of the chapter says. The page follows the order of the rexxref entry. Examples that show an error use a small routine try, as the builtin pages do. Whether two equal strings or numbers are one object is not specified (the identity rule), so the examples use other objects, or one variable read twice, for indexes and items. The page says nothing about which of two items found by the same object removeItem removes (the hash order rule).

The class

[class.identitytable.creation]

IdentityTable declares the instance methods [], []=, allIndexes, allItems, at, empty, hasIndex, hasItem, index, isEmpty, items, makeArray, put, remove, removeItem and supplier, the init that new runs (the new rule) and the class method new; the copy of Object copies a table as the copy rule says. The class method of and the instance methods putAll, union, difference, intersection, xor, subset, disjoint and equivalent are those of the mixins (one rule lists them). A table has no makeString, so it is not a string (the string rule), and no unknown and no allAt.

t = .identitytable~new
own = '[] []= ALLINDEXES ALLITEMS AT EMPTY HASINDEX HASITEM INDEX ISEMPTY',
  'ITEMS MAKEARRAY PUT REMOVE REMOVEITEM SUPPLIER'
n = 0
do m over own~makearray(' ')
  if t~hasMethod(m) then n += 1
end
say t~class~id n .identitytable~hasMethod('OF') t~hasMethod('OF')
say t~hasMethod('UNION') t~hasMethod('PUTALL') t~hasMethod('APPENDALL')
say t~hasMethod('MAKESTRING') t~hasMethod('UNKNOWN') t~hasMethod('ALLAT')

Making a table

[class.identitytable.new]

new makes an empty table. Its optional argument is a hint for how large the table will grow; no method that this page specifies answers differently for it. It must be a whole number that is not negative, or SYNTAX 93.923 is raised. A second argument raises SYNTAX 93.902, and omitted arguments at the end count for nothing. new sends init to the new object with the arguments it received, so a subclass's init sees them (the new rule). The checks are those of the init that IdentityTable supplies: they come after the init of a subclass has run, and a subclass whose init does not pass the arguments on is not refused for them.

say .identitytable~new~items .identitytable~new(0)~items,
  .identitytable~new(3, )~items

call try '.identitytable~new("x")'
call try '.identitytable~new(.nil)'
call try '.identitytable~new(1.5)'
call try '.identitytable~new(1, 2)'
x = .watch~new(7)
call try '.watch~new("x")'
say .quiet~new("x", 2, 3)~items
exit

Indexes

[class.identitytable.indexes]

An index is any object, .nil included, and is stored as it is: allIndexes answers the very objects that were stored. Two indexes are one entry when they are the same object, and in no other case: an object that declares == and hashCode to be equal to another is a different index from it, two arrays with the same items are two indexes, and a string read from the same variable twice is one index. Whether two strings or numbers with the same characters that were made separately are one object is not specified (the identity rule). When a put finds the index already in the table, the item is replaced. A lookup sends no message to the index, hashCode and == included (the lookup rule).

t = .identitytable~new
s = 'Key'
a = .array~of(1)
b = .array~of(1)
o1 = .eq~new('x')
o2 = .eq~new('x')
t~put('v1', s)
t~put('v2', a)
t~put('v3', b)
t~put('v4', .nil)
t~put('v5', o1)
t~put('v6', o2)
s2 = s
say t~items t~at(s) t~at(s2) t~at(a) t~at(b) t~at(.nil)
say (t~at(.array~of(1)) == .nil) t~at(o1) t~at(o2),
  (t~at(.eq~new('x')) == .nil)
t~put('v7', a)
say t~items t~at(a) t~hasIndex(b) t~hasIndex(.array~of(1))
say (o1 == o2) (o1~hashCode == o2~hashCode)

at, [], hasIndex, put, []= and remove send no message to the index argument and to the stored indexes: not hashCode, not ==, and nothing else. The same holds for hasItem, index and removeItem and the items (the search rule). In the example every object of the class records each message it is sent.

[class.identitytable.hasitem]

hasItem(item) answers 1 when some entry holds the argument itself as its item and 0 otherwise, and index(item) answers the index of such an entry and .nil when there is none. Which index index answers when several entries hold the item is not specified (the hash order rule). Lists of the entries

[class.identitytable.makearray]

allIndexes and makeArray answer a new Array of the indexes of the entries, and allItems a new Array of their items. They are instances of Array for a subclass receiver too, never the receiver, and do not follow later changes. They take no argument: one raises SYNTAX 93.902. The order is not specified (the hash order rule), and is the same for the three answers and for the supplier of one unchanged table, so the item at a position belongs to the index at the same position. The methods send no message to the table or to the indexes and items.

t = .many~new
do i = 1 to 40
  t~put('item'i, .array~of(i))
end
ix = t~allIndexes
it = t~allItems

[class.identitytable.copy]

copy answers a new table of the class of the receiver with the same entries. The indexes and the items are the same objects, and the two tables do not see each other's changes. The methods of the mixins

[class.identitytable.inherited]

The class method of and the instance methods putAll, union, difference, intersection, xor, subset, disjoint and equivalent are not declared by IdentityTable. of and putAll are those of MapCollection, and the others those of Collection; a table is one of the collections they take as an argument, and the answers of the first four are instances of the class of the receiver. They compare indexes as the table does, by identity, so the indexes that the arguments share are shared objects. putAll stores with the put of the receiver. In the example the arguments are tables of pairs of an index and an item.

ka = 'a'
kb = 'b'
kc = 'c'
a = .many~of(.array~of(ka, 'A1'), .array~of(kb, 'B1'))
b = .identitytable~of(.array~of(kb, 'B2'), .array~of(kc, 'C2'))
do op over 'union difference intersection xor'~makeArray(' ')
  r = a~send(op, b)
  say op r~class~id r~items listed(r)
end
say a~subset(b) a~disjoint(b) a~equivalent(b) a~subset(a~copy)
c = .many~new
c~putAll(b)
say c~items listed(c)
exit
listed: procedure
  use arg r
  s = ''
  do i over r~allIndexes~sort
    s = s i'='r[i]
  end
  return s~strip

Messages the methods send

[class.identitytable.sends]

No method that IdentityTable declares sends a message to its receiver: an override of at, put or any other of the methods is never asked by another method, and [] and []= do not use at and put. The messages the methods do send go to other objects and have a rule: init to the new object by new (the new rule). Neither the lookups by index nor the searches by item send anything to the indexes, the items or the arguments (the lookup rule), and makeArray, allIndexes, allItems, supplier, copy, items, isEmpty and empty send nothing to the indexes and the items. The set operations send what the pages of the mixins say. In the first example a subclass has every method overridden to record its name, and each call records only its own; in the second the indexes and items record every message a program is likely to override.

own = '[] []= allIndexes allItems at empty hasIndex hasItem index isEmpty',
  'items makeArray put remove removeItem supplier copy string'

do m over own~makeArray(' ')
  src = "if .local~on then .local~log~append('"m"'); forward class (super)"
  .spy~define(m, src)
end

  '|a~makeArray|a~put(1, "k9")|a~remove("k9")|a~removeItem("q")',
  '|a~supplier|a~copy|a~string|a~empty'
n = 0
extra = 0
do c over calls~makeArray('|')
  .local~log~empty
  .local~on = 1
  interpret c
  .local~on = 0
  n += 1
  if .local~log~items <> 1 then do
    extra += 1
    say c '=>' .local~log~makeString('L', ' ')
  end
end

Deviations

[class.identitytable.deviation.4]

Whether two strings or numbers with the same characters, produced separately, are one object is not specified, so whether a lookup of one finds the entry stored with the other is not specified either (Deviation 4). A value read from the same variable is one object. In the example the two literals are either one index or two.

t = .identitytable~new
t~put(1, 'abc')
t~put(2, 'abc')
say (t~items == 1) | (t~items == 2)
s = 'abc'
u = s
t~put(3, s)
say t~at(u)

[class.identitytable.deviation.33]

The order of the answers of allIndexes, allItems, makeArray and supplier, and which of two entries that hold the same item index and removeItem use, is not specified, and may differ from ooRexx's. Which entries are produced, and how often, is specified. In the example the answers are sorted.

t~put(1, .array~of('one'))
t~put(2, .array~of('two'))
t~put(3, .array~of('three'))
say t~allItems~sort~makeString('L', ',')
say t~allIndexes~items t~items t~makeArray~items

[class.identitytable.deviation.109]

The size argument of new that is an instance of a subclass of String is read by its own characters, and REQUEST and MAKESTRING are not sent to it (Deviation 109). ooRexx sends such an instance request with STRING or MAKESTRING, so an override of either changes the size that new checks. In the example MAKESTRING answers another text.

Relation

rexxref: Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Relation Class; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Relation Class > new (Class Method); Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Relation Class > []; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Relation Class > []=; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Relation Class > allAt; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Relation Class > allIndex; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Relation Class > allIndexes; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Relation Class > allItems; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Relation Class > at; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Relation Class > difference; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Relation Class > empty; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Relation Class > hasIndex; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Relation Class > hasItem; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Relation Class > index; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Relation Class > intersection; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Relation Class > isEmpty; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Relation Class > items; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Relation Class > makeArray; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Relation Class > put; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Relation Class > remove; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Relation Class > removeAll; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Relation Class > removeItem; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Relation Class > subset; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Relation Class > supplier; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Relation Class > union; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Relation Class > uniqueIndexes; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Relation Class > xor

Deviations: D33, D78, D84, D109, D118

A Relation is a Table that keeps every item put at an index: it holds entries, each a pair of an index and an item, and put always adds an entry, so one index, or one item, can occur in many entries, and the same pair can occur twice. Indexes are found as a table finds them, by the hashCode and the == that they answer to; items are found by ==. The class inherits MapCollection, and through it Collection; the hierarchy rule lists what it inherits.

A relation has no unknown method: a message that the method search does not resolve raises NOMETHOD, as the error rule of the chapter says. The page follows the order of the rexxref entry. Examples that show an error use a small routine try, as the builtin pages do. Where several entries qualify for a method that answers one, which entry it answers is not specified, and the examples then hold one entry or sort the answers (the hash order rule).

The class

[class.relation.creation]

Relation declares the instance methods [], []=, allAt, allIndex, allIndexes, allItems, at, difference, empty, hasIndex, hasItem, index, intersection, isEmpty, items, makeArray, put, remove, removeAll, removeItem, subset, supplier, union, uniqueIndexes and xor, the init that new runs (the new rule) and the class method new; the copy of Object copies a relation as the copy rule says. The class method of and the instance methods putAll, disjoint and equivalent are those of the mixins (one rule lists them). A relation has no makeString, so it is not a string (the string rule).

say r~hasMethod('UNION') r~hasMethod('PUTALL') r~hasMethod('APPENDALL')
say r~hasMethod('MAKESTRING') r~hasMethod('UNKNOWN') r~hasMethod('ENTRY')

Making a relation

[class.relation.new]

new makes an empty relation. Its optional argument is a hint for how large the relation will grow; no method that this page specifies answers differently for it. It must be a whole number that is not negative, or SYNTAX 93.923 is raised. A second argument raises SYNTAX 93.902, and omitted arguments at the end count for nothing. new sends init to the new object with the arguments it received, so a subclass's init sees them (the new rule). The checks are those of the init that Relation supplies: they come after the init of a subclass has run, and a subclass whose init does not pass the arguments on is not refused for them.

say .relation~new~items .relation~new(0)~items .relation~new(3, )~items

call try '.relation~new("x")'
call try '.relation~new(.nil)'
call try '.relation~new(1.5)'
call try '.relation~new(1, 2)'
x = .watch~new(7)
call try '.watch~new("x")'
say .quiet~new("x", 2, 3)~items
exit

Entries and indexes

[class.relation.indexes]

An index is any object, .nil and the null string included, and it is found as a table finds it: by hashCode and ==, so a string is the index of its characters, strictly compared, and an object that declares neither method is its own index only. A relation does not merge equal indexes: each entry keeps the index object that was put with it, so two entries can hold two distinct objects that are equal as indexes, and a method that takes an index considers every entry whose index is equal to the argument.

r = .relation~new
r~put('v1', 'Key')
r~put('v2', 'KEY')
r~put('v3', 5)
r~put('v4', 5.0)
r~put('v5', .nil)
r~put('v6', '')
a = .array~of(1)
r~put('arr', a)
say r~items r~at('Key') r~at('key') r~at(5) r~at('5.0') r~at('') r~at(.nil)
say r~at(a) (r~at(.array~of(1)) == .nil) r~hasIndex(.sub~new('Key'))
r~put('v7', .eq~new('x', 'first'))
r~put('v8', .eq~new('x', 'second'))
p = .eq~new('x', 'probe')
say r~items r~items(p) r~hasIndex(p) r~allAt(p)~sort~makeString('L', ',')
ix = r~allIndexes
n = 0
do i over ix
  if i~isA(.eq) then n += 1
end

[class.relation.indexes.sends]

at, [], hasIndex, remove and items with an index look the index up by sending hashCode to the index argument, once, and then == to the index argument with a stored index as the argument, for stored indexes that have the same hash code, until one answers true; each of those is compared before the lookup gives up. Which further stored indexes are compared, by == or hashCode, and how often, is not specified (the hash order rule); when the relation is empty, the only message is hashCode. put and []= send hashCode to the index and nothing else: no == is sent, as an entry is added whether or not an equal index is there. The very object that is stored is no exception to the == (the deviation rule). In the example every index hashes to the same string, so each stored index is compared.

  '|r~items(.k~new("p"))|r~remove(.k~new("p"))|r~remove(.k~new("s1"))',
  '|r~put("v2", .k~new("p"))|r[.k~new("p")] = "v2"',
  '|r~put("v3", .k~new("s1"))'
do c over calls~makeArray('|')
  r = .relation~new
  r~put('v1', .k~new('s1'))
  .local~log~empty
  interpret c
  say c '=>' .local~log~makeString('L', ' | ')
end
exit

Reading and writing entries

[class.relation.put]

put(item, index) and [index] = item add an entry for the item at the index and answer nothing. Entries already at the index, or already holding the item, stay, and the same pair put twice makes two entries. The item may be any object, .nil included. The methods take exactly two arguments: a missing or omitted one raises SYNTAX 88.901, and a third raises SYNTAX 93.902.

call try 'r~put("x", )'
call try 'r~put("x", "y", "z")'

[class.relation.allat]

allAt(index) answers a new Array of the items of all the entries whose index is equal to the argument, one for each entry, in an order that is not specified, and an empty Array when there is none. [class.relation.hasitem.sends]

hasItem(item), index and removeItem(item) send == to the item argument with the item of an entry as the argument, entry by entry, until one answers true, and send nothing else, hashCode included. allIndex sends == to the item argument with the item of every entry as the argument. The entries are visited in an order that is not specified, and how often == is sent with the same stored item is not specified (the hash order rule); every entry is compared at least once when none matches, and for allIndex always. hasItem(item, index) and removeItem(item, index) first look the index up as the lookup rule says, and then send == to the item argument with the item of each entry whose index matches, at least once for each, and no message when no index matches. The search with the very object that is stored is no exception: its == is sent as for any other item (the deviation rule).

.local~n = 0
.local~h = 0
r = .relation~new
r~put('s', 'k1')
r~put('t', 'k2')
r~put('u', 'k3')
q = .thing~new
calls = 'r~hasItem(q)|r~index(q)|r~allIndex(q)|r~removeItem(q)',
  '|r~hasItem(q, "none")',
  '|r~hasItem(q, "k1")|r~removeItem(q, "none")|r~removeItem(q, "k1")'
do c over calls~makeArray('|')
  .local~n = 0
  interpret 'x =' c
  if c~pos('none') > 0 then say c '=>' .local~n
  else if c~pos('k1') > 0 then say c '=>' (.local~n >= 1)
  else say c '=>' (.local~n >= 3)
end
say r~items .local~h
::class thing
::method '=='
  .local~n += 1
  return 0
::method hashCode
  .local~h += 1
  return 1

[class.relation.index]

index(item) answers the index of an entry whose item is equal to the argument, and .nil when there is none; when several entries qualify, which index is answered is not specified. allIndex(item) answers a new Array of the indexes of all such entries, one for each entry, in an order that is not specified, and an empty Array when there is none; the same index twice when two entries hold the item at it. The answer of allIndex is an instance of Array for a subclass receiver too, and does not follow later changes. Both take exactly one argument: none, or an omitted one, raises SYNTAX 93.903, and a second raises SYNTAX 93.902. The messages sent are those of the search rule.

r = .many~new
r~put('a', 'k')
r~put('a', 'k')
r~put('a', 'j')
r~put('b', 'm')
say r~index('b') (r~index('zz') == .nil) r~index('a')~length
x = r~allIndex('a')
say x~sort~makeString('L', ',') x~class~id r~allIndex('b')~items,
  r~allIndex('zz')~items
call try 'r~index'
call try 'r~allIndex'
call try 'r~index(, "x")'
call try 'r~allIndex(1, 2)'
exit

Removing entries

[class.relation.remove]

remove(index) removes one entry whose index is equal to the argument and answers its item, and answers .nil when there is none; when several entries qualify, which one is removed is not specified, and the others stay. The index stays in the relation while an entry has it. It takes exactly one argument: none, or an omitted one, raises SYNTAX 88.901, and a second raises SYNTAX 93.902.

r = .relation~new
r~put('v', 'k')
r~put('w', 'k')
r~put('z', 'j')
a = r~remove('k')
say (a == 'v' | a == 'w') r~items r~items('k') r~hasIndex('k')
b = r~remove('k')
say (b == 'v' | b == 'w') (a \== b) r~items r~hasIndex('k')
say (r~remove('k') == .nil) r~remove('j') r~isEmpty
call try 'r~remove'
call try 'r~remove("a", "b")'
exit

[class.relation.removeall]

removeAll(index) removes every entry whose index is equal to the argument and answers a new Array of their items, one for each entry, in an order that is not specified; the answer is an empty Array when there is none. It sends hashCode to the index once, and == to the index with every stored index of the same hash code as the argument; further sends, and how often each is sent, are not specified (the hash order rule). The answer is an instance of Array for a subclass receiver too. It takes exactly one argument: none, or an omitted one, raises SYNTAX 93.903, and a second raises SYNTAX 93.902.

[class.relation.removeitem]

removeItem(item) removes one entry whose item is equal to the argument, by the search of the search rule, and answers the item that was stored, or .nil when no entry matches; when several entries qualify, which one is removed is not specified. removeItem(item, index) removes one entry that has both an item equal to the first argument and an index equal to the second, and answers the item that was stored, or .nil when there is none. An omitted second argument is no argument. The index stays in the relation while an entry has it, and it is gone when the entry was the last one. The methods take one or two arguments: a missing or omitted item raises SYNTAX 93.903, and a third argument raises SYNTAX 93.902.

r = .relation~new
r~put('a', 'k')
r~put('a', 'k')
r~put('a', 'j')
r~put('b', 'k')

say (r~removeItem('a', 'k') == .nil) r~items
say (r~removeItem('b', 'j') == .nil) r~items
say r~removeItem('a') r~items r~hasIndex('j')
say (r~removeItem('a') == .nil) r~removeItem('b', ) r~items r~isEmpty
call try 'r~removeItem'
call try 'r~removeItem(, "k")'
call try 'r~removeItem("a", "k", 3)'
exit

Lists of the entries

[class.relation.makearray]

allIndexes and makeArray answer a new Array with the index of each entry, so an index that is in several entries appears several times, and allItems a new Array with the item of each entry. They are instances of Array for a subclass receiver too, never the receiver, and do not follow later changes. They take no argument: one raises SYNTAX 93.902. The order is not specified (the hash order rule), and is the same for the three answers and for the supplier of one unchanged relation, so the item at a position belongs to the index at the same position. The methods send no message to the relation, the indexes or the items.

r = .many~new
do i = 1 to 40
  r~put('item'i, 'key' || (i // 5))
end
ix = r~allIndexes
it = r~allItems
bad = 0
do i = 1 to ix~items
  if \r~allAt(ix[i])~hasItem(it[i]) then bad += 1
  if r~makeArray[i] \== ix[i] then bad += 1
end
say ix~class~id it~class~id r~makeArray~class~id ix~items it~items bad
a = r~allItems
r~put('x', 'extra')
say a~items r~items (ix == r~allIndexes)
call try 'r~allIndexes(1)'
call try 'r~allItems(1)'
call try 'r~makeArray(1)'
exit
