[class.relation.uniqueindexes]

uniqueIndexes answers a new Array with one index for each group of equal indexes in the relation, equal as the index rule says, so an index that is in several entries appears once, and two index objects with different hash codes are two indexes even when == answers true for them. Which of several equal index objects is answered is not specified, and so is the order (the hash order rule). An index object that is stored in more than one entry is compared as any other (the deviation rule). uniqueIndexes compares the stored indexes with each other by sending == to a stored index with another stored index as the argument; which stored indexes it sends == and hashCode to, and how often, is not specified (the hash order rule). The answer is an instance of Array for a subclass receiver too, and does not follow later changes. uniqueIndexes takes no argument: one raises SYNTAX 93.902.

r = .many~new
r~put('a', 'k')
r~put('b', 'k')
r~put('c', 'j')
r~put('d', 'm')
x = r~uniqueIndexes
r~put('e', 'zz')
say x~items x~class~id r~allIndexes~items r~uniqueIndexes~items
say x~sort~makeString('L', ',') .relation~new~uniqueIndexes~items
s = .relation~new
s~put('v1', .k~new('a', 'h1'))
s~put('v2', .k~new('a', 'h2'))
say s~uniqueIndexes~items
.local~log = .array~new

s~put('v1', .k~new('a', 'h'))
s~put('v2', .k~new('b', 'h'))
x = s~uniqueIndexes
say x~items (.local~log~items > 0)
call try 'r~uniqueIndexes(1)'
exit

[class.relation.supplier]

supplier answers a Supplier over the entries, the index and the item of each, and supplier(index) a Supplier over the entries whose index is equal to the argument. It is a snapshot: later changes do not reach it. Its order is that of allIndexes (the order rule). A relation with no entry, or none at the index, gives a supplier that is not available. It takes at most one argument, and an omitted argument is no argument: a second raises SYNTAX 93.902. With an index it sends hashCode to it once, and == to it with every stored index of the same hash code as the argument; further sends, and how often each is sent, are not specified (the hash order rule).

Combining relations

[class.relation.operand]

union, difference, intersection, xor and subset take exactly one argument, the other collection: none, or an omitted one, raises SYNTAX 93.901 and a second raises SYNTAX 93.902. The argument is read as a list of entries as the operand rule says: what its isA answers decides whether it is sent allItems, supplier or makeArray, and an answer that is neither 0 nor 1 raises SYNTAX 34.1. All five send supplier to a map, difference and subset included, and none of them sends items to the argument; in both the five differ from the operations of Collection. An element of a list is an index and an item at once, and an entry of a map is its own index with its own item. The answers of allItems and makeArray are read as the list rule says, an instance of a subclass of List included (Deviation 118); one with no makeArray method raises SYNTAX 98.913. A supplier is sent available, and while that answers true index and item, then next: union, difference and subset send item before index, intersection and xor index before item. An argument that isA does not report as ordered or as a map and that has no makeArray method, .nil included, raises SYNTAX 93.948, and so does a supplier that is .nil. The five work on the object that copy of the receiver answers, and intersection and xor also on the one that new of its class answers (their rule), so the answers are instances of the class of the receiver unless a subclass overrides those; any object that understands the messages sent to it will do. A message that the copy, the new object or the supplier does not understand raises SYNTAX 93.948 when it is sent; an UNKNOWN method counts as understanding it. The entries are compared as pairs: an index is equal by the index rule and an item by ==. In the example each kind of argument records the message it is sent, then a map argument records the order of the messages to its supplier, and the last cases show errors.

.local~log = .array~new
do op over 'union difference intersection xor subset'~makeArray(' ')
  line = op':'
  do k over .array~of(.ordered~new, .mapped~new, .plain~new, .both~new)
    .local~log~empty
    r = .relation~new~send(op, k)
    line = line .local~log~makeString('L', '+')
  end
  say line
end
say .relation~new~union(.array~of('x', 'y'))~items
do op over 'union difference intersection xor subset'~makeArray(' ')
  .local~log~empty
  r = .relation~new~send(op, .logmap~new)
  say op':' .local~log~makeString('L', ' ')
end
m = .many~new
say m~union(.array~new)~class~id m~difference(.array~new)~class~id,
  m~intersection(.array~new)~class~id m~xor(.array~new)~class~id
calls = 'r~union|r~union(,)|r~union(a, a)|r~union(.nil)|r~xor(.object~new)',
  '|r~subset(.liar~new)|r~difference(.mp~new(.nil))',
  '|r~intersection(.pk~new(.object~new))|r~union(.pk~new(.object~new))',
  '|r~xor(.ord~new)|.nocopy~new~union(.array~of(1))|r~union(.noitem~new)'
do c over calls~makeArray('|')
  call try c
end
exit

[class.relation.union]

union(other) answers the object that copy of the receiver answers, after put(item, index) has been sent to it for every entry of the argument, in the order the argument yields them (the operand rule). An entry is added even when the copy holds the same pair, so the answer has as many entries as the receiver and the argument have together. The receiver and the argument are not changed.

a = .relation~new
a~put("A1", "a"); a~put("B1", "b"); a~put("B1", "b"); a~put("X", "x")
b = .relation~new
b~put("B1", "b"); b~put("B2", "b"); b~put("C2", "c"); b~put("X", "x")
t = .table~new
t["b"] = "B1"; t["c"] = "C"
u = a~union(b)
say u~items listed(u)
say a~items b~items (u \== a) u~class~id
say listed(a~union(t))
say listed(a~union(.array~of("b", "q")))
say listed(.relation~new~union(a)) (listed(.relation~new~union(a)) == listed(a))
exit

[class.relation.difference]

difference(other) answers the object that copy of the receiver answers, after removeItem(item, index) has been sent to it for every entry of the argument, in the order the argument yields them (the operand rule). Each of those removes one entry with an equal index and an equal item, so a pair that the receiver holds twice and the argument once stays once, and a pair that the copy does not hold removes nothing, an equal index with another item included.

a = .relation~new
a~put("A1", "a"); a~put("B1", "b"); a~put("B1", "b"); a~put("X", "x")
b = .relation~new
b~put("B1", "b"); b~put("B2", "b"); b~put("C2", "c"); b~put("X", "x")
t = .table~new
t["b"] = "B1"; t["c"] = "C"
d = a~difference(b)
say d~items listed(d)
say listed(a~difference(t))
say listed(a~difference(.array~of("b", "q", "B1")))
say listed(a~difference(a~copy)) "|" a~items
exit

[class.relation.intersection]

intersection(other) answers a new relation of the class of the receiver, made by new without arguments, that holds a pair as often as the receiver and the argument both hold it. For every entry of the argument, in the order it yields them (the operand rule), it asks the copy of the receiver hasItem(item, index); when that answers true, the new relation is sent put(item, index) and the copy removeItem(item, index). The receiver and the argument are not changed, and the answer is not the copy.

a = .relation~new
a~put("A1", "a"); a~put("B1", "b"); a~put("B1", "b"); a~put("X", "x")
b = .relation~new
b~put("B1", "b"); b~put("B2", "b"); b~put("C2", "c"); b~put("X", "x")
t = .table~new
t["b"] = "B1"; t["c"] = "C"
i = a~intersection(b)
say i~items listed(i) (i \== a)
say listed(a~intersection(t))
say listed(b~intersection(a))
say listed(a~intersection(.array~of("b", "q")))
say listed(a~intersection(a)) a~items
exit

[class.relation.xor]

xor(other) answers the object that copy of the receiver answers, holding each pair as many times as the receiver and the argument differ in how often they hold it. For every entry of the argument, in the order it yields them (the operand rule), it asks the copy hasItem(item, index); when that answers true, the copy is sent removeItem(item, index), and otherwise a new relation of the class of the receiver, made by new without arguments, is sent put(item, index). Last, the copy is sent putAll with the new relation as the argument (the putAll rule), also when the new relation is empty, and its answer is not used; an override of putAll decides what is added. A pair that the argument holds more often than the receiver is therefore in the answer for the surplus, and one that the receiver holds more often for its surplus.

b = .relation~new

t["b"] = "B1"; t["c"] = "C"

say x~items listed(x)
say listed(a~xor(t))
say listed(a~xor(.array~of("b", "q")))
say listed(a~xor(a)) "|" listed(a~xor(.relation~new))
exit

[class.relation.subset]

subset(other) answers 1 when every pair of the receiver is held by the argument at least as often, and 0 otherwise, so an empty relation is a subset of every collection. It sends removeItem(item, index) to the copy of the receiver for every entry of the argument, in the order the argument yields them (the operand rule), and answers what isEmpty of the copy answers. The receiver and the argument are not changed.

[class.relation.copy]

copy answers a new relation of the class of the receiver with the same entries. The indexes and the items are the same objects, and the two relations do not see each other's changes. The methods of the mixins

[class.relation.inherited]

The class method of and the instance methods putAll, disjoint and equivalent are not declared by Relation. of and putAll are those of MapCollection, and disjoint and equivalent those of Collection; a relation is one of the collections they take as an argument. putAll stores with the put of the receiver, so an index that the receiver and the argument share is in two entries afterwards. disjoint sends intersection to the receiver and answers what isEmpty of that answer says (the disjoint rule), so what a relation and its argument have in common is what the intersection rule selects; equivalent sends items to the receiver and to the argument, then subset to the receiver (the equivalent rule), so it compares relations by the subset rule. In the example the arguments are relations of pairs of an index and an item.

c3 = .array~of('c', 'C3')
b = .relation~of(.array~of('b', 'B2'), .array~of('c', 'C2'), c3)

c~putAll(b)
say c~items c~items('b') listed(c)
exit

Messages the methods send

[class.relation.sends]

No method that Relation declares sends a message to its receiver, except union, difference, intersection, xor and subset, which send copy to it, and then put, hasItem, removeItem, putAll and isEmpty to that copy, an instance of the receiver's class, so the overrides of a subclass are used there (their rule). No other method asks an override of at, put or any other of the methods, and [] and []= do not use at and put. The messages the methods do send go to other objects and have a rule each: init to the new object by new (the new rule); hashCode, and == where the rule says so, to the index argument by at, [], put, []=, hasIndex, items, remove, allAt, removeAll, supplier, hasItem and removeItem with an index (the lookup rule); == to the item argument by hasItem, index, allIndex and removeItem (the search rule); == to a stored index, with another stored index as the argument, by uniqueIndexes (its rule). makeArray, allIndexes, allItems, copy, empty, isEmpty and items with no index send nothing to the indexes and the items. In the first example a subclass has every method overridden to record its name, and each call records only its own; in the second the indexes and items record every message a program is likely to override.

[class.relation.setops.sends]

The five set operations send these messages, in this order, to the receiver, to the argument, to the object that copy of the receiver answers (the copy) and to the new relation that new without arguments, sent to the class of the receiver, answers. The argument is read first by sending isA with OrderedCollection and, when that does not answer 1, isA with MapCollection, and then allItems, supplier or makeArray as the operand rule says; "reading" below stands for these, and "for each entry" means once for each entry the argument yields. union sends copy to the receiver, reads, and for each entry sends put(item, index) to the copy; it answers the copy. difference sends copy to the receiver, reads, and for each entry sends removeItem(item, index) to the copy; it answers the copy. intersection sends new to the class, copy to the receiver, reads, and for each entry sends hasItem(item, index) to the copy and, when that answers true, put(item, index) to the new relation and removeItem(item, index) to the copy; it answers the new relation. xor sends copy to the receiver, new to the class, reads, and for each entry sends hasItem(item, index) to the copy and then either removeItem(item, index) to the copy, when that answered true, or put(item, index) to the new relation; then it sends putAll to the copy with the new relation as the argument, whose answer it does not use, and answers the copy; the putAll of MapCollection then sends supplier to the new relation and put to the copy (its rule). subset sends copy to the receiver, reads, sends removeItem(item, index) to the copy for each entry and then isEmpty to the copy; it answers what isEmpty answered. Nothing else is sent to the receiver, the argument or either relation. In the example the receiver is R, the argument A, the copy C and the new relation W; the last field is the identity of the answer, - for none of them.

.local~log = .array~new
.local~on = 0
own = 'put hasItem removeItem putAll supplier isA isEmpty'
do m over own~makeArray(' ')
  src = "if .local~on then .local~log~append(who(self)'"m"');"
  src = src "forward class (super)"
  .spy~define(m, src)
end
cp = "r = self~copy:super; .local~cp = r;"
cp = cp "if .local~on then .local~log~append('copy'); return r"
.spy~define('copy', cp)
a = .spy~new
a~put('A1', 'a'); a~put('B1', 'b'); a~put('B1', 'b')
b = .spy~new
b~put('B1', 'b'); b~put('C', 'c')
.local~ra = a
.local~rb = b
do op over 'union difference intersection xor subset'~makeArray(' ')
  .local~log~empty
  .local~on = 1
  x = a~send(op, b)
  .local~on = 0
  line = op'=>'
  do msg over .local~log
    if line~length + msg~length > 66 then do
      say line
      line = ' '
    end
    line = line msg
  end
  say line '|' who(x)
end
::routine who public
  use arg o
  if o == .local~ra then return 'R.'
  if o == .local~rb then return 'A.'
  if o == .local~cp then return 'C.'
  if o == .local~nw then return 'W.'
  return '-'
::class spy subclass relation
::method new class
  r = self~new:super
  .local~nw = r
  if .local~on then .local~log~append('class.new')
  return r

difference=> copy A.isA A.isA A.supplier C.removeItem C.removeItem | C.
intersection=> class.new copy A.isA A.isA A.supplier C.hasItem
  W.put C.removeItem C.hasItem | W.

  C.hasItem W.put C.putAll W.supplier C.put | C.

  C.isEmpty | -

[class.relation.deviation.33]

The order of the answers of allIndexes, allItems, makeArray, uniqueIndexes, allAt, allIndex, removeAll and supplier, the entry that at, index, remove and removeItem choose among several, and which stored indexes or items a lookup, a search or uniqueIndexes compares, by == or hashCode, beyond those it must compare, and how often, are not specified, and may differ from ooRexx's. Which entries are produced, and how often, is specified. In the example the answers are sorted.

r~put(1, 'one')
r~put(2, 'two')
r~put(3, 'three')
r~put(4, 'three')
say r~allIndexes~sort~makeString('L', ',')
say r~allItems~sort~makeString('L', ',')
say r~uniqueIndexes~items r~items r~makeArray~items

[class.relation.deviation.78]

A lookup or a remove with the very object that is stored as an index sends that object's == as for any other index, and a search for an item with the very object that is stored, by hasItem, index, allIndex or removeItem, sends that object's == as for any other item, so an object whose == answers false is not found even at its own entry. uniqueIndexes does the same for an index object that is stored in more than one entry, so one whose == answers false counts once for each of those entries. ooRexx compares identity first, finds it and sends nothing but hashCode, and counts such an index object once. See Deviation 78.

[class.relation.deviation.84]

Deviations: D33, D45, D78, D84, D109

A Bag holds members, each an object that is its own index, and keeps every object that is put: put always adds, so one object can be a member many times, and items counts them all. Members are found as a relation finds its indexes, by the hashCode and the == that they answer to; the methods that take an item compare by == as well. The class inherits MapCollection and SetCollection, and through them Collection; the hierarchy rule lists what it inherits. Like Set it declares its own set operations, which read their argument as a list of members and not as a list of entries, and which count how often a member occurs.

A bag has no unknown method: a message that the method search does not resolve raises NOMETHOD, as the error rule of the chapter says. Examples that show an error use a small routine try, as the builtin pages do. Where several members qualify for a method that answers one, which one it answers is not specified, and the examples then hold one member or sort the answers (the hash order rule).

The class

[class.bag.creation]

Bag declares the instance methods [], []=, allAt, allIndex, allIndexes, allItems, at, difference, empty, hasIndex, hasItem, index, intersection, isEmpty, items, makeArray, put, putAll, remove, removeAll, removeItem, subset, supplier, union, uniqueIndexes and xor, the init that new runs (the new rule) and the class methods new and of; the copy of Object copies a bag as the copy rule says. The instance methods disjoint and equivalent are those of Collection (one rule covers them). A bag has no makeString, so it is not a string (the string rule), and no unknown. Its superclasses are Object, MapCollection and SetCollection, in that order.

Making a bag

[class.bag.new]

new makes an empty bag. Its optional argument is a hint for how large the bag will grow; no method that this page specifies answers differently for it. It must be a whole number that is not negative, or SYNTAX 93.923 is raised. A second argument raises SYNTAX 93.902, and omitted arguments at the end count for nothing. new sends init to the new object with the arguments it received, so a subclass's init sees them (the new rule). The checks are those of the init that Bag supplies: they come after the init of a subclass has run, and a subclass whose init does not pass the arguments on is not refused for them.

call try '.bag~new(1.5)'
call try '.bag~new(1, 2)'

say .quiet~new("x", 2, 3)~items
exit

[class.bag.of]

of(item, ...) answers a new bag of the class that received it that holds the arguments, each as often as it is given, and with no argument an empty bag. Members

[class.bag.members]

A member is any object, .nil and the null string included, and the bag stores every object that was put, whether or not an equal one is there. A member is found by the lookup: hashCode answers the same string for the argument and for the stored object, and ==, sent to the argument with the stored object as argument, answers true. For an object that declares neither method that is the same object, and an Array is its own member only. A string is a member of its characters, compared by the strict comparison: case counts, a leading or trailing blank counts, and 5 and 5.0 are two members. A class that declares == has to declare hashCode so that equal objects hash alike, as the hash code rule says. A method that takes an index considers every member that is equal to the argument, and the bag does not merge them: the objects stay distinct, and allItems answers each of them.

b = .bag~new
do x over .array~of('Key', 'KEY', 5, 5.0, ' a', '', .nil, 'Key')
  b~put(x)
end

b~put(a)
say b~items b~items('Key') b~items('key') b~items('5.0') b~items('a')
say b~items(a) b~items(.array~of(1)) b~items('') b~items(.nil)
b~put(.eq~new('x', 'first'))
b~put(.eq~new('x', 'second'))
say b~items b~items(.eq~new('x', 'probe')),
  b~allAt(.eq~new('x', 'probe'))~items
t = .array~new
do i over b~allAt(.eq~new('x', 'probe'))
  t~append(i~tag)

[class.bag.members.sends]

at, [], hasIndex, hasItem, index, remove, removeItem and items with an index look a member up by sending hashCode to the argument, once, and then == to the argument with a stored object as the argument, for stored objects that have the same hash code, until one answers true; each of those is compared before the lookup gives up. Which further stored objects are compared, by == or hashCode, and how often, is not specified (the hash order rule); when the bag is empty, the only message is hashCode. allAt, removeAll and supplier with an index send hashCode once and == to the stored objects of the same hash code, how often to each being left open by the hash order rule. put and []= send hashCode to the item and nothing else: no == is sent, as a member is added whether or not an equal one is there; with an index they send == to the item first (the put rule). The very object that is stored is no exception to the == (the deviation rule). In the example every member hashes to the same string, so each stored member is compared; index is shown by the item rule, and the messages of uniqueIndexes are left open by the hash order rule.

.local~log = .array~new
say 'empty:' .bag~new~at(.k~new('p')) .local~log~makeString('L', ' | ')
calls = 'b~at(.k~new("p"))|b[.k~new("p")]|b~hasIndex(.k~new("p"))',
  '|b~hasItem(.k~new("p"))|b~items(.k~new("p"))|b~remove(.k~new("p"))',
  '|b~removeItem(.k~new("p"))|b~put(.k~new("p"))',
  '|b[.k~new("p")] = .k~new("p")',
  '|b~remove(.k~new("s1"))|b~put(.k~new("s1"))|b~allAt(.k~new("p"))~items'
do c over calls~makeArray('|')
  b = .bag~new
  b~put(.k~new('s1'))
  .local~log~empty
  interpret c
  say c~strip '=>' .local~log~makeString('L', ' | ')
end
exit

Adding and reading members

[class.bag.put]

put(item) and put(item, index) add the item and answer nothing; [index] = item is the same as put(item, index), and [] = item the same as put(item). An index may be given only as another name for the item: when one is, and the item is not the very object, == is sent to the item with the index as argument first, and an answer that is not true raises SYNTAX 93.949 and leaves the bag unchanged. An index that is omitted counts for nothing. The methods take one or two arguments: none, or an omitted item, raises SYNTAX 88.901, and a third argument raises SYNTAX 93.902. The item may be any object, .nil included, and is added also when an equal member is held, so items grows by one.

b = .bag~new
b~put('a')
b~put('a', 'a')
b['b'] = 'b'
b[] = 'a'
b~put(.nil)
b~put('d', )
say b~items b~items('a') b~items('d') b~items(.nil)
call try 'b~put("a", "A")'
call try 'b~put(1, 2)'
call try 'b["x"] = "y"'
call try 'b~put'
call try 'b~put(, "a")'
call try 'b~put("a", "a", "a")'
say b~items
exit

[class.bag.allat]

allAt(index) answers a new Array of the stored objects that are equal to the argument, one for each member, in an order that is not specified (the hash order rule), and an empty Array when there is none. allIndex(item) is the same question asked with the item: it answers a new Array of the stored objects equal to it, and for a bag the two answers are alike. Both are instances of Array for a subclass receiver too, and do not follow later changes. Each takes exactly one argument: none, or an omitted one, raises SYNTAX 93.903, and a second raises SYNTAX 93.902. allAt looks the argument up as the lookup rule says; allIndex sends == to the argument with the stored objects as the argument, and no hashCode; how often is left open by the hash order rule.

remove(index) removes one member that is equal to the argument and answers the stored object, and .nil when there is none; the other equal members stay, and which of them is removed is not specified (the hash order rule). Lists of the members

[class.bag.makearray]

allIndexes and makeArray answer a new Array that holds each member as often as it occurs, and allItems does the same: for a bag index and item are the same object, so the three answers are alike. uniqueIndexes answers a new Array that holds one object for each group of equal members, and so as many objects as there are different members. All four are instances of Array for a subclass receiver too, never the receiver, and do not follow later changes. They take no argument: one raises SYNTAX 93.902. The order is not specified (the hash order rule), and is the same for allIndexes, makeArray, allItems and the supplier of one unchanged bag. allIndexes, allItems and makeArray send no message to the bag or to the members; the messages that uniqueIndexes sends to the members are left open by the hash order rule.

t = .many~new
do i = 1 to 20
  t~put('item'||(i // 5))
end
ix = t~allIndexes
it = t~allItems
say ix~class~id it~class~id t~makeArray~class~id t~uniqueIndexes~class~id
say ix~items it~items t~makeArray~items t~uniqueIndexes~items
say (ix~sort~makeString('L', ',') == it~sort~makeString('L', ','))
say t~uniqueIndexes~sort~makeString('L', ',')
a = t~allItems
t~put('x')
say a~items t~items
call try 't~allIndexes(1)'
call try 't~allItems(1)'
call try 't~makeArray(1)'
call try 't~uniqueIndexes(1)'
exit

[class.bag.supplier]

supplier answers a Supplier over the members, the index and the item of each being the same object, once for each time the member occurs. supplier(index) answers one over the members equal to the argument only. It takes at most one argument: a second raises SYNTAX 93.902.

    l~append(s~index'='s~item)
    s~next
  end
  return l~sort~makeString('L', ' ')

[class.bag.copy]

copy answers a new bag of the class of the receiver with the same members, each as often as before. The members are the same objects, and the two bags do not see each other's changes. As the copy rule says of every object, the variables of a subclass instance are copied as they are, and init is not sent. It takes no argument: one raises SYNTAX 93.902.

c~remove('v1')

call try 't~copy(1)'

Adding the members of a collection

[class.bag.putall]

putAll(collection) adds the members of the argument and answers the bag. It takes exactly one argument: none raises SYNTAX 93.901 and a second raises SYNTAX 93.902. The argument is read as a list of members (the operand rule), and each is added by sending put with it, as the only argument, to the bag, so an override of put in a subclass is used and every member counts, equal ones included. Unlike MapCollection, which stores the entries of a supplier, it reads items only: the indexes of a map argument are not added.

r = b~putAll(.array~of('a', 'b', 'a'))
say (r == b) b~items b~items('a')
b~putAll(.directory~new~~put('v', 'k'))
b~putAll(.bag~of('z', 'a'))
say b~items b~items('v') b~items('k') b~items('a') b~items('z')
call try 'b~putAll'
call try 'b~putAll(1, 2)'
call try 'b~putAll(.nil)'
exit

Combining bags

[class.bag.operand]

putAll, union, difference, intersection, xor and subset read their argument by sending it isA with the class Collection: an answer of 1 means the argument is sent allItems, an answer of 0 means it is sent makeArray, and any other answer, .nil among them, raises SYNTAX 34.1. An argument that does not understand the message it is sent, .nil among them, raises SYNTAX 93.948. The operations check the number of arguments first: none raises SYNTAX 93.901 and a second raises SYNTAX 93.902. What the argument answers is read as the list rule says. Every member of the argument counts, so an object that the argument holds twice is read twice. The example records the messages that each kind of argument is sent.

.local~log = .array~new
do op over 'putAll union difference intersection xor subset'~makeArray(' ')
  line = op':'
  do k over .array~of(.coll~new, .plain~new(0), .plain~new(2), .bare~new)
    call try op, k
    line = line result
  end
  say line
end
exit

[class.bag.operand.list]

The answer of allItems or makeArray is read by sending it items, with no argument, and then [] with each position from 1 up to the number that items answered, in that order; each answer of [] is a member of the argument. The answer need not be an Array: an object that understands the two messages will do, and an answer that lacks one raises SYNTAX 93.948. A subclass of Array is sent the two messages too, and no other. A position that holds nothing reads .nil, which is then a member, so an Array with a hole is read for as many positions as it has items, not as its size. The answer of items is read as a number: one that is not a number raises SYNTAX 41.1, and a negative one reads no position. An error that [] raises is the error of the operation, after the members before it have been handled.

a = .array~new(5)
a[2] = 'two'
b = .bag~new
b~putAll(.pk~new(a))
say b~items b~items('two') b~items(.nil)
b = .bag~new
b~putAll(.pk~new(.walk~new(3, 'e')))
say b~items b~allItems~sort~makeString('L', ',')
b = .bag~new
b~putAll(.pk~new(.logarr~of('p', 'q')))
say b~allItems~sort~makeString('L', ',')
call try 'b~putAll(.pk~new(.walk~new("x", "e")))'
b = .bag~new
call try 'b~putAll(.pk~new(.walk~new(2, "boom")))'
say b~items b~hasItem('boom1')
call try 'b~putAll(.pk~new(.object~new))'
say .bag~new~~putAll(.pk~new(.walk~new(-1, 'e')))~items
exit

[class.bag.union]

union(other) answers the object that copy of the receiver answers, after every member of the argument has been added to it: for each member, in the order of the list rule, put is sent to the copy with the member as the only argument. The answer holds as many members as the receiver and the argument have together, and is an instance of the class of the receiver. The receiver and the argument are not changed.

b = .bag~of('b', 'c', 'c')
u = a~union(b)
say u~class~id u~items (u \== a) a~items b~items sorted(u)
say sorted(a~union(.array~of('x', 'x', 'a')))
say sorted(a~union(.directory~new~~put('v', 'k'))),
  sorted(a~union(.set~of('b', 'z')))
say sorted(a~union('xy')) sorted(.bag~new~union(a)) sorted(a~union(a))
exit

[class.bag.difference]

difference(other) answers the object that copy of the receiver answers, after one member equal to each member of the argument has been removed from it: for each member, in the order of the list rule, remove is sent to the copy with the member. A member that the receiver holds twice and the argument once stays once, and a member the copy does not hold removes nothing. The receiver and the argument are not changed.

[class.bag.intersection]

intersection(other) answers a new bag of the class of the receiver, made by new with no argument, that holds each member as often as the receiver and the argument both hold it. For each member of the argument, in the order of the list rule, hasIndex is sent to the copy of the receiver with the member and, when that answers true, put with the member as the only argument is sent to the new bag and remove with the member to the copy. The receiver and the argument are not changed, and the answer is not the copy.

b = .bag~of('a', 'c', 'c', 'd', 'a', 'a')
i = a~intersection(b)
say i~class~id i~items (i \== a) a~items sorted(i)
say sorted(a~intersection(.array~of('a', 'q', 'b'))) sorted(a~intersection(a))

  '['sorted(.bag~new~intersection(a))']'

[class.bag.xor]

xor(other) answers the object that copy of the receiver answers, holding each member as many times as the receiver and the argument differ in how often they hold it. For each member of the argument, in the order of the list rule, hasIndex is sent to the copy with the member and then either remove with the member to the copy, when that answered true, or put with the member as the only argument to a new bag made by new with no argument. Last, the copy is sent putAll with the new bag as the argument, also when the new bag is empty. A member that the argument holds more often than the receiver is therefore in the answer for the surplus, and one that the receiver holds more often for its surplus. The receiver and the argument are not changed.

a = .bag~of('a', 'a', 'b', 'c')
b = .bag~of('a', 'c', 'c', 'd')
x = a~xor(b)
say x~class~id x~items (x \== a) a~items b~items sorted(x)
say sorted(a~xor(.array~of('a', 'z', 'z')))
say sorted(a~xor(a)) '|' sorted(a~xor(.bag~new)) '|' sorted(.bag~new~xor(a))
exit

[class.bag.subset]

subset(other) answers 1 when every member of the receiver is held by the argument at least as often, and 0 otherwise, so an empty bag is a subset of every collection. It sends remove with each member of the argument, in the order of the list rule, to the copy of the receiver, and answers what isEmpty of the copy answers. The receiver and the argument are not changed.

  a~subset(.array~of('b', 'a', 'a'))

The methods of the mixins

[class.bag.inherited]

The instance methods disjoint and equivalent are not declared by Bag; they are those of Collection. disjoint sends intersection to the receiver and answers what isEmpty of that answer says (the disjoint rule), so it asks what the intersection rule selects; equivalent sends items to the receiver and to the argument, then subset to the receiver (the equivalent rule), so it compares bags by the subset rule, and two bags are equivalent when they hold the same members equally often. The class method of is declared by Bag itself (the of rule), and putAll by its own rule.

a = .many~of('a', 'a', 'b')
say a~disjoint(.bag~of('x')) a~disjoint(.bag~of('x', 'b'))
say a~equivalent(.bag~of('b', 'a', 'a')) a~equivalent(.bag~of('a', 'b'))
say a~equivalent(.bag~of('a', 'b', 'b')),
  a~equivalent(.array~of('a', 'a', 'b'))

Messages the methods send

[class.bag.sends]

put and []= send == to the item with the index as argument when an index is given, hashCode to the item and nothing to the receiver. The other methods that look a member up, at, [], hasIndex, hasItem, index, remove, removeItem, allAt, removeAll, items and supplier with an index, send hashCode and == to the argument and nothing to the receiver (the lookup rule); allIndex sends == to the argument (the allAt rule). putAll sends put to the receiver for each member it reads (the putAll rule). The set operations send to the receiver, the argument, the copy and the new bag the messages that their rule lists. allIndexes, allItems, makeArray, supplier, copy, items, isEmpty and empty send nothing to the members. No other method asks an override of at, put or any of the methods, and [] and []= do not use at and put. In the first example a subclass has every method overridden to record its name, and each call records only its own; in the second the members record every message a program is likely to override.

  'uniqueIndexes copy string'

[class.bag.setops.sends]

The set operations send these messages, in this order, to the receiver, to the argument, to the object that copy of the receiver answers (the copy) and to the new bag that new with no argument, sent to the class of the receiver, answers. The argument is read first as the operand rule says: "reading" below stands for the isA and the allItems or makeArray that follows it, and "for each member" means once for each position that the list rule reads. union sends copy to the receiver, reads, and for each member sends put(member) to the copy; it answers the copy. difference sends copy to the receiver, reads, and for each member sends remove(member) to the copy; it answers the copy. intersection sends new to the class, copy to the receiver, reads, and for each member sends hasIndex(member) to the copy and, when that answers true, put(member) to the new bag and remove(member) to the copy; it answers the new bag. xor sends copy to the receiver, new to the class, reads, and for each member sends hasIndex(member) to the copy and then either remove(member) to the copy, when that answered true, or put(member) to the new bag; then it sends putAll to the copy with the new bag as the argument, whose answer it does not use, and answers the copy; the putAll of Bag then sends isA and allItems to the new bag and put to the copy for each member (its rule). subset sends copy to the receiver, reads, sends remove(member) to the copy for each member and then isEmpty to the copy; it answers what isEmpty answered. Nothing else is sent to the receiver, the argument or either bag. In the example the receiver is R, the argument A, the copy C and the new bag W; the last field is the identity of the answer, - for none of them.

.local~log = .array~new
.local~on = 0
own = 'put hasIndex remove isEmpty putAll allItems isA'
do m over own~makeArray(' ')
  src = "if .local~on then .local~log~append(who(self)'"m"');"
  src = src "forward class (super)"
  .spy~define(m, src)
end
cp = "r = self~copy:super; .local~cp = r;"
cp = cp "if .local~on then .local~log~append('copy'); return r"
.spy~define('copy', cp)
a = .spy~new
a~put('A1'); a~put('B1'); a~put('B1')
b = .spy~new
b~put('B1'); b~put('C')
.local~ra = a
.local~rb = b
do op over 'union difference intersection xor subset'~makeArray(' ')
  .local~log~empty
  .local~on = 1
  x = a~send(op, b)
  .local~on = 0
  line = op'=>'
  do msg over .local~log
    if line~length + msg~length > 66 then do
      say line
      line = ' '
    end
    line = line msg
  end
  say line '|' who(x)
end
::routine who public
  use arg o
  if o == .local~ra then return 'R.'
  if o == .local~rb then return 'A.'
  if o == .local~cp then return 'C.'
  if o == .local~nw then return 'W.'
  return '-'
::class spy subclass bag
::method new class
  r = self~new:super
  .local~nw = r
  if .local~on then .local~log~append('class.new' arg())
  return r

union=> copy A.isA A.allItems C.put C.put | C.
difference=> copy A.isA A.allItems C.remove C.remove | C.
intersection=> class.new 0 copy A.isA A.allItems C.hasIndex W.put
  C.remove C.hasIndex | W.
xor=> copy class.new 0 A.isA A.allItems C.hasIndex C.remove
  C.hasIndex W.put C.putAll W.isA W.allItems C.put | C.
subset=> copy A.isA A.allItems C.remove C.remove C.isEmpty | -

[class.bag.deviation.33]

The order of the answers of allIndexes, allItems, makeArray, allAt, allIndex, removeAll, uniqueIndexes and supplier, which of several equal members at, index, remove and removeItem choose, and which stored objects a lookup or a search compares, by == or hashCode, beyond those it must compare, and how often, and which members uniqueIndexes sends hashCode or ==, are not specified, and may differ from ooRexx's. Which members are produced, and how often, is specified. In the example the answers are sorted.

say b~allIndexes~sort~makeString('L', ',')

[class.bag.deviation.78]

A lookup, a put or a remove with the very object that is stored sends that object's == as for any other argument, and so does a search with the very object that is stored by hasItem, index, allIndex or removeItem, so an object whose == answers false is not found even at its own entry. A put or []= that names an index sends == to the item with the index as argument also when the two are the same object. ooRexx compares identity first, finds the object and sends nothing but hashCode for the lookup, and nothing for the index. See Deviation 78.

[class.bag.deviation.84]

When the == that remove or removeItem sends to its argument, or that removeAll or allAt sends, empties the bag, the search ends and items answers 0 afterwards; remove and removeItem answer .nil. ooRexx's items answers -1 after remove and removeItem, and its removeAll and allAt go on comparing with an object that is no stored member. rexxref: Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Set Class; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Set Class > new (Class Method); Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Set Class > of (Class Method); Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Set Class > []; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Set Class > []=; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Set Class > allIndexes; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Set Class > allItems; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Set Class > at; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Set Class > empty; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Set Class > hasIndex; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Set Class > hasItem; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Set Class > index; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Set Class > intersection; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Set Class > isEmpty; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Set Class > items; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Set Class > makeArray; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Set Class > put; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Set Class > putAll; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Set Class > remove; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Set Class > removeItem; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Set Class > subset; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Set Class > supplier; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Set Class > union; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Set Class > xor

Deviations: D33, D78, D84, D109

A Set holds members, each an object that is its own index: put stores an item and the item is the index it is found by, so a member occurs once however often it is put. Members are found as a table finds its indexes, by the hashCode and the == that they answer to. The class inherits MapCollection and SetCollection, and through them Collection; the hierarchy rule lists what it inherits. Unlike a table it declares its own set operations, which read their argument as a list of members and not as a list of entries.

A set has no unknown method: a message that the method search does not resolve raises NOMETHOD, as the error rule of the chapter says. Examples that show an error use a small routine try, as the builtin pages do. Where several members qualify for a method that answers one, which one it answers is not specified, and the examples then hold one member or sort the answers (the hash order rule).

The class

[class.set.creation]

Set declares the instance methods [], []=, allIndexes, allItems, at, empty, hasIndex, hasItem, index, intersection, isEmpty, items, makeArray, put, putAll, remove, removeItem, subset, supplier, union and xor, the init that new runs (the new rule) and the class methods new and of; the copy of Object copies a set as the copy rule says. The instance methods difference, disjoint and equivalent are those of Collection (one rule covers them). A set has no makeString, so it is not a string (the string rule), and no unknown, allAt, allIndex, removeAll or uniqueIndexes. Its superclasses are Object, MapCollection and SetCollection, in that order.

Making a set

[class.set.new]

new makes an empty set. Its optional argument is a hint for how large the set will grow; no method that this page specifies answers differently for it. It must be a whole number that is not negative, or SYNTAX 93.923 is raised. A second argument raises SYNTAX 93.902, and omitted arguments at the end count for nothing. new sends init to the new object with the arguments it received, so a subclass's init sees them (the new rule). The checks are those of the init that Set supplies: they come after the init of a subclass has run, and a subclass whose init does not pass the arguments on is not refused for them.

say .set~new~items .set~new(0)~items .set~new(3, )~items
call try '.set~new(-1)'
call try '.set~new("x")'
call try '.set~new(.nil)'
call try '.set~new(1.5)'
call try '.set~new(1, 2)'
x = .watch~new(7)
call try '.watch~new("x")'
say .quiet~new("x", 2, 3)~items
exit

[class.set.of]

of(item, ...) answers a new set of the class that received it that holds the arguments, each member once, and with no argument an empty set. An argument that is omitted before the last one raises SYNTAX 93.903, and a trailing omitted argument counts for nothing. The method does not send new to the class and does not send put to the set: it sends init with no argument to the new object and stores the arguments itself, so an override of new or put in a subclass is not used. Two arguments are one member when they are equal as members are, so 1 and 1.0 are two.

call try '.set~of(, 1)'
say .set~of(1, )~items

Members

[class.set.members]

A member is any object, .nil and the null string included, and the set stores the object that was put. A member is found by the lookup: hashCode answers the same string for the argument and for the stored object, and ==, sent to the argument with the stored object as argument, answers true. For an object that declares neither method that is the same object, and an Array is its own member only. A string is a member of its characters, compared by the strict comparison: case counts, a leading or trailing blank counts, and 5 and 5.0 are two members. A class that declares == has to declare hashCode so that equal objects hash alike, as the hash code rule says. When put finds an equal member, the set keeps the object it has as the index of the entry, and takes the new object as its item: at and allItems then answer the new object, and allIndexes and makeArray the old one.

s = .set~new
do x over .array~of('Key', 'KEY', 5, 5.0, ' a', '', .nil)
  s~put(x)
end
a = .array~of(1)
s~put(a)
say s~items s~hasItem('Key') s~hasItem('key') s~hasItem('5.0') s~hasItem('a')
say s~hasItem(a) s~hasItem(.array~of(1)) s~hasItem('') s~hasItem(.nil)
s~put(.eq~new('x', 'first'))
s~put(.eq~new('x', 'second'))
say s~items s~at(.eq~new('x', 'probe'))~tag
say s~allItems~items s~allIndexes~items
do i over s~allIndexes
  if i~isA(.eq) then say 'index' i~tag
end
do i over s~allItems
  if i~isA(.eq) then say 'item' i~tag
end

[class.set.members.sends]

at, [], hasIndex, hasItem, index, put, []=, remove and removeItem look a member up by sending hashCode to the argument, once, and then == to the argument with a stored object as the argument, for stored objects that have the same hash code, until one answers true; each of those is compared before the lookup gives up. Which further stored objects are compared, by == or hashCode, and how often, is not specified (the hash order rule); when the set is empty, the only message is hashCode. The very object that is stored is no exception to the == (the deviation rule). put and []= with an index first send == to the item with the index as argument (the put rule). In the example every member hashes to the same string, so each stored member is compared.

.local~log = .array~new
say 'empty:' .set~new~at(.k~new('p')) .local~log~makeString('L', ' | ')
calls = 's~at(.k~new("p"))|s[.k~new("p")]|s~hasIndex(.k~new("p"))',
  '|s~hasItem(.k~new("p"))|s~put(.k~new("p"))|s[.k~new("p")] = .k~new("p")',
  '|s~remove(.k~new("p"))|s~removeItem(.k~new("p"))',
  '|s~put(.k~new("s1"))|s~remove(.k~new("s1"))'
do c over calls~makeArray('|')
  s = .set~new
  s~put(.k~new('s1'))
  .local~log~empty
  interpret c
  say c~strip '=>' .local~log~makeString('L', ' | ')
end
exit

  .local~log~append('==' tag o~tag)
  return tag == o~tag
::method hashCode
  expose tag
  .local~log~append('hash' tag)
  return 'same'

Adding and reading members

[class.set.put]

put(item) and put(item, index) add the item and answer nothing; [index] = item is the same as put(item, index), and [] = item the same as put(item). An index may be given only as another name for the item: when one is, and the item is not the very object, == is sent to the item with the index as argument first, and an answer that is not true raises SYNTAX 93.949 and leaves the set unchanged. An index that is omitted counts for nothing. The methods take one or two arguments: none, or an omitted item, raises SYNTAX 88.901, and a third argument raises SYNTAX 93.902. The item may be any object, .nil included. The check of the index is made before the item is looked up (the lookup rule).

s~put('a')
s~put('a', 'a')
s['b'] = 'b'
s[] = 'c'
s~put(.nil)
s~put('d', )
say s~items s~hasItem('a') s~hasItem('d') s~hasItem(.nil) s~hasItem('e')
call try 's~put("a", "A")'
call try 's~put(1, 2)'
call try 's["x"] = "y"'
call try 's~put'
call try 's~put(, "a")'
call try 's~put("a", "a", "a")'
say s~items
exit

[class.set.hasitem]

hasItem(item) answers 1 when a member is equal to the item and 0 otherwise; for a set it is the same question as hasIndex. index(item) looks the item up as an index, as the lookup rule says, and answers the item of the entry it finds, which is the object put last for that member (the members rule), and .nil when there is none. Lists of the members

[class.set.makearray]

allIndexes and makeArray answer a new Array of the indexes of the entries, and allItems a new Array of their items. They are instances of Array for a subclass receiver too, never the receiver, and do not follow later changes. They take no argument: one raises SYNTAX 93.902. The order is not specified (the hash order rule), and is the same for the three answers and for the supplier of one unchanged set, so the item at a position belongs to the index at the same position. The methods send no message to the set or to the members.

t = .many~new
do i = 1 to 40
  t~put('item'i)
end
ix = t~allIndexes
it = t~allItems
bad = 0
do i = 1 to ix~items
  if t~at(ix[i]) \== it[i] then bad += 1
  if t~makeArray[i] \== ix[i] then bad += 1
end
say ix~class~id it~class~id t~makeArray~class~id ix~items it~items bad
a = t~allItems
t~put('extra')
say a~items t~items (ix == t~allIndexes)
call try 't~allIndexes(1)'
call try 't~allItems(1)'
call try 't~makeArray(1)'
exit

[class.set.copy]

copy answers a new set of the class of the receiver with the same entries. The indexes and the items are the same objects, and the two sets do not see each other's changes. As the copy rule says of every object, the variables of a subclass instance are copied as they are, and init is not sent. It takes no argument: one raises SYNTAX 93.902.

c~remove('v1')
say t~items c~items t~hasItem('v1') c~hasItem('v1')
call try 't~copy(1)'
exit

Adding the members of a collection

[class.set.putall]

putAll(collection) adds the members of the argument and answers the set. It takes exactly one argument: none raises SYNTAX 93.901 and a second raises SYNTAX 93.902. The argument is read as a list of members (the operand rule), and each is added by sending put with it, as the only argument, to the set, so an override of put in a subclass is used and members that are equal count once. Unlike MapCollection, which stores the entries of a supplier, it reads items only: the indexes of a map argument are not added.

s = .many~new
r = s~putAll(.array~of('a', 'b', 'a'))
say (r == s) s~items
s~putAll(.directory~new~~put('v', 'k'))
s~putAll(.set~of('z', 'a'))
say s~items s~hasItem('v') s~hasItem('k') s~hasItem('z')
call try 's~putAll'
call try 's~putAll(1, 2)'
call try 's~putAll(.nil)'
exit

Combining sets

[class.set.operand]

putAll, union, intersection and xor read their argument by sending it isA with the class Collection: an answer of 1 means the argument is sent allItems, an answer of 0 means it is sent makeArray, and any other answer, .nil among them, raises SYNTAX 34.1. An argument that does not understand the message it is sent, .nil among them, raises SYNTAX 93.948. subset sends no isA: it sends allItems to its argument whatever it is. difference is not declared by Set; the operand rule of Collection reads its argument. The operations check the number of arguments first: none raises SYNTAX 93.901 and a second raises SYNTAX 93.902. What the argument answers is read as the list rule says. The example records the messages that each kind of argument is sent.

.local~log = .array~new
do op over 'putAll union intersection xor subset'~makeArray(' ')
  line = op':'
  do k over .array~of(.coll~new, .plain~new(0), .plain~new(2), .bare~new)
    call try op, k
    line = line result
  end
  say line
end
exit

[class.set.operand.list]

The answer of allItems or makeArray is read by sending it items, with no argument, and then [] with each position from 1 up to the number that items answered, in that order; each answer of [] is a member of the argument. The answer need not be an Array: an object that understands the two messages will do, and an answer that lacks one raises SYNTAX 93.948. A subclass of Array is sent the two messages too, and no other. A position that holds nothing reads .nil, which is then a member, so an Array with a hole is read for as many positions as it has items, not as its size. The answer of items is read as a number: one that is not a number raises SYNTAX 41.1, and a negative one reads no position. An error that [] raises is the error of the operation, after the members before it have been handled.

[class.set.union]

union(other) answers the object that copy of the receiver answers, after each member of the argument has been added to it: for each member, in the order of the list rule, hasIndex is sent to the copy with the member and, when that answers false, put with the member as the only argument. The receiver and the argument are not changed, and the copy is an instance of the class of the receiver.

b = .set~of('b', 'c')
u = a~union(b)
say u~class~id u~items (u \== a) a~items b~items
say sorted(u) '|' sorted(a~union(.array~of('x', 'x', 'a')))
say sorted(a~union(.directory~new~~put('v', 'k'))),
  sorted(a~union(.bag~of('b', 'b', 'z')))
say sorted(a~union('xy')) sorted(.set~new~union(a))
exit

[class.set.intersection]

intersection(other) answers a new set of the class of the receiver, made by new with no argument, that holds each member that the receiver and the argument have in common. For each member of the argument, in the order of the list rule, hasIndex is sent to the receiver with the member and, when that answers true, put with the member as the only argument to the new set. No copy is made, and neither the receiver nor the argument is changed.

a = .set~of('a', 'b', 'c')
b = .set~of('b', 'c', 'd')
i = a~intersection(b)
say i~class~id i~items (i \== a) (i \== b) sorted(i)
say sorted(a~intersection(.array~of('c', 'c', 'q', 'a')))
say sorted(a~intersection(.set~new)) '|' a~items b~items
exit

[class.set.xor]

xor(other) answers the object that copy of the receiver answers, holding the members that only one of the receiver and the argument holds. For each member of the argument, in the order of the list rule, hasIndex is sent to the receiver with the member and then either remove with the member to the copy, when that answered true, or put with the member as the only argument to the copy. The receiver and the argument are not changed.

a = .set~of('a', 'b', 'c')

[class.set.subset]

subset(other) answers 1 when every member of the receiver is a member of the argument, and 0 otherwise, so an empty set is a subset of every collection. It sends copy to the receiver, then allItems to the argument, and sends remove with each member of the argument, in the order of the list rule, to the copy, and last isEmpty to the copy; the answer is what isEmpty answered. The receiver and the argument are not changed.

The methods of the mixins

[class.set.inherited]

The instance methods difference, disjoint and equivalent are not declared by Set; they are those of Collection. difference answers the object that copy of the receiver answers with the members removed that the argument lists, and is an instance of the class of the receiver, so what the difference rule says applies to a set. For a map argument it removes by the indexes of the argument, not its items. disjoint sends intersection to the receiver and answers what isEmpty of that answer says (the disjoint rule), so it asks what the intersection rule selects; equivalent sends items to the receiver and to the argument, then subset to the receiver (the equivalent rule), so it compares sets by the subset rule. The class method of is declared by Set itself (the of rule), and putAll by its own rule.

a = .many~of('a', 'b', 'c')
d = a~difference(.set~of('b', 'z'))
say d~class~id d~items sorted(d)
say sorted(a~difference(.array~of('a', 'a'))),
  sorted(a~difference(.bag~of('c')))
say sorted(a~difference(.table~new~~put('a', 'c'))) a~items
say a~disjoint(.set~of('x')) a~disjoint(.set~of('x', 'c'))
say a~equivalent(.set~of('c', 'a', 'b')) a~equivalent(.set~of('a', 'b'))
say a~equivalent(.array~of('a', 'b', 'c'))
exit

Messages the methods send

[class.set.sends]

put and []= send == to the item with the index as argument when an index is given, hashCode and == to the member that they look up, and nothing to the receiver. The other methods that look a member up, at, [], hasIndex, hasItem, index, remove and removeItem, send hashCode and == to the argument and nothing to the receiver (the lookup rule). putAll sends put to the receiver for each member it reads (the putAll rule). The set operations send to the receiver, the argument, the copy and the new set the messages that their rule lists. makeArray, allIndexes, allItems, supplier, copy, items, isEmpty and empty send nothing to the members. No other method asks an override of at, put or any of the methods, and [] and []= do not use at and put. In the first example a subclass has every method overridden to record its name, and each call records only its own; in the second the members record every message a program is likely to override.

[class.set.setops.sends]

The set operations send these messages, in this order, to the receiver, to the argument, to the object that copy of the receiver answers (the copy) and to the new set that new with no argument, sent to the class of the receiver, answers. The argument is read first as the operand rule says: "reading" below stands for the isA that union, intersection and xor send and for the allItems or makeArray that follows, and "for each member" means once for each position that the list rule reads. union sends copy to the receiver, reads, and for each member sends hasIndex(member) to the copy and, when that answers false, put(member) to the copy; it answers the copy. intersection sends new to the class, reads, and for each member sends hasIndex(member) to the receiver and, when that answers true, put(member) to the new set; it answers the new set, and no copy is made. xor sends copy to the receiver, reads, and for each member sends hasIndex(member) to the receiver and then either remove(member) to the copy, when that answered true, or put(member) to the copy; it answers the copy. subset sends copy to the receiver, sends allItems to the argument, sends remove(member) to the copy for each member and then isEmpty to the copy; it answers what isEmpty answered. Nothing else is sent to the receiver, the argument or either set. In the example the receiver is R, the argument A, the copy C and the new set W; the last field is the identity of the answer, - for none of them.

.local~log = .array~new
.local~on = 0
own = 'put hasIndex remove isEmpty allItems isA'
do m over own~makeArray(' ')
  src = "if .local~on then .local~log~append(who(self)'"m"');"
  src = src "forward class (super)"
  .spy~define(m, src)
end
cp = "r = self~copy:super; .local~cp = r;"
cp = cp "if .local~on then .local~log~append('copy'); return r"
.spy~define('copy', cp)
a = .spy~new
a~put('A1'); a~put('B1')
b = .spy~new
b~put('B1'); b~put('C')
.local~ra = a
.local~rb = b
do op over 'union intersection xor subset'~makeArray(' ')
  .local~log~empty
  .local~on = 1
  x = a~send(op, b)
  .local~on = 0
  line = op'=>'
  do msg over .local~log
    if line~length + msg~length > 66 then do
      say line
      line = ' '
    end
    line = line msg
  end
  say line '|' who(x)
end
::routine who public
  use arg o
  if o == .local~ra then return 'R.'
  if o == .local~rb then return 'A.'
  if o == .local~cp then return 'C.'
  if o == .local~nw then return 'W.'
  return '-'
::class spy subclass set
::method new class
  r = self~new:super
  .local~nw = r
  if .local~on then .local~log~append('class.new' arg())
  return r

union=> copy A.isA A.allItems C.hasIndex C.hasIndex C.put | C.
intersection=> class.new 0 A.isA A.allItems R.hasIndex W.put
  R.hasIndex | W.
xor=> copy A.isA A.allItems R.hasIndex C.remove R.hasIndex C.put | C.
subset=> copy A.allItems C.remove C.remove C.isEmpty | -

Deviations

[class.set.deviation.33]

The order of the answers of allIndexes, allItems, makeArray and supplier, and which stored objects a lookup compares, by == or hashCode, beyond those it must compare, and how often, are not specified, and may differ from ooRexx's. Which members are produced, and how often, is specified. In the example the answers are sorted.

[class.set.deviation.78]

A lookup, a put or a remove with the very object that is stored sends that object's == as for any other argument, and so does a search with the very object that is stored by hasItem, index or removeItem, so an object whose == answers false is not found even at its own entry. A put or []= that names an index sends == to the item with the index as argument also when the two are the same object. ooRexx compares identity first, finds the object and sends nothing but hashCode for the lookup, and nothing for the index. See Deviation 78.

Stem

rexxref: Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Stem Class; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Stem Class > new (Class Method); Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Stem Class > []; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Stem Class > []=; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Stem Class > allIndexes; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Stem Class > allItems; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Stem Class > at; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Stem Class > empty; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Stem Class > hasIndex; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Stem Class > hasItem; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Stem Class > index; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Stem Class > isEmpty; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Stem Class > items; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Stem Class > makeArray; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Stem Class > put; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Stem Class > remove; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Stem Class > removeItem; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Stem Class > request; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Stem Class > supplier; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Stem Class > toDirectory; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > Stem Class > unknown

Deviations: D1, D68, D78, D109, D118

A Stem is the collection that a stem symbol names: the value of a stem symbol is a Stem object, and the compound variables of the stem are its entries. An entry is a tail, a string, and the item stored at it; the stem also has a default, the value that every tail without an item has, and a name, which is the text that stands for the stem when it has no default. A Stem can be made without a variable, by new, and then behaves alike: the methods below read and write the same entries that s.tail reads and writes (the compound rule, the default rule). The class inherits MapCollection, and through it Collection; the hierarchy rule lists what it inherits.

A stem has an unknown method, and the page begins with what the other methods do; the unknown rule says what unknown does with the messages that no method answers. Examples that show an error use a small routine try, as the builtin pages do. The order in which the tails are listed is not specified, as the DO OVER rule says of a loop, and the examples then hold one tail or sort the answers (the order rule).

The class

[class.stem.creation]

Stem declares the instance methods [], []=, allIndexes, allItems, at, empty, hasIndex, hasItem, index, isEmpty, items, makeArray, put, remove, removeItem, request, supplier, toDirectory and unknown, and the class method new; the copy of Object copies a stem as the copy rule says. It has no init of its own: new makes the stem as the new rule says. The class method of and the instance methods putAll, union, difference, intersection, xor, subset, disjoint and equivalent are those of the mixins (one rule lists them). A stem has no makeString, and none of the comparison methods =, ==, \=, \==, <> and ><: a message with one of those names is passed on by the unknown rule. Its superclasses are Object and MapCollection, in that order.

  m~next

say s~hasMethod('=') s~hasMethod('==') s~hasMethod('\=') s~hasMethod('\==')
say s~hasMethod('<>') s~hasMethod('><')

Making a stem

[class.stem.new]

new makes an empty stem, with no default. Its first argument is the name: the text that the stem has as its value while it has no default, and the start of every tail that is read from it with no item. The name is the null string when it is omitted, and is not changed to end with a period. It must have a string value, found as the conversion rule says for a request that answers a string; an object whose request with STRING does not answer a string, .nil among them, raises SYNTAX 88.909 before init is sent. new then sends init to the new stem with the arguments that follow the name (the new rule). A stem has the init of Object, which takes no argument, so a second argument to new raises SYNTAX 93.902 when that init runs: after the init of a subclass has run, and not at all when the init of a subclass does not pass its arguments on.

s = .stem~new('abc.')
say s~string s['x'] s~items

say .stem~new('N', )~string .stem~new(.array~new)~string'|'
say .tracked~new('T.')~string

call try '.stem~new(.object~new)'
call try '.stem~new("a", "b")'
call try '.tracked~new(.nil)'
call try '.tracked~new("T.", "x")'
say .quiet~new('Q.', 'x', 'y')~string .quiet~new(, 'x')~string'|'
exit

Tails

[class.stem.tails]

The methods that take indexes take any number of them, and make one tail of them: each index argument is replaced by its string value, an omitted argument by the null string, and the strings are joined with a period between them, trailing omitted arguments being dropped. So s[1, 2] and s['1.2'] are the same tail, and s[1, , 3] is the tail 1..3. The tail is used as written: case counts, 01 and 1 are two tails, and blanks stay (the tail rule). An index that is not a string is replaced as the conversion rule says: the answer of its request with the argument STRING, and when that is not a string, of its string method; so .nil is the tail The NIL object. With no index at all the methods name the default of the stem and not a tail.

  s['1..3'] s['x', 'y']

Reading and writing items

[class.stem.at]

at(index, ...) and [index, ...] answer the item stored at the tail that the indexes make (the tails rule); when no item is stored there, the default of the stem; and when the stem has no default, the name of the stem followed by the tail, which is what the compound symbol would have as its value. With no index they answer the default, or the name when there is none. Reading stores nothing.

[class.stem.put]

put(item, index, ...) and [index, ...] = item store the item at the tail that the indexes make (the tails rule), replacing the item that was there, and answer nothing. The item may be any object, .nil included. With no index they store the item as the new default of the stem and remove every item from that same object, so the variable and every other reference to the stem see no entries. The item is required: none, or an omitted one, raises SYNTAX 93.903 for put.

Removing items

[class.stem.remove]

remove(index, ...) removes the item at the tail that the indexes make (the tails rule) and answers it, and answers .nil when no item is stored there; the tail then has the default again, or the derived name. With no index it removes the default and answers it, and answers the name of the stem when there is none, so that a second call answers the name. The other items stay.

Lists of the items

[class.stem.makearray]

allIndexes and makeArray answer a new Array of the tails that have an item, as strings, and allItems a new Array of the items. The default is in neither. They are instances of Array for a subclass receiver too, never the receiver, and do not follow later changes. They take no argument: one raises SYNTAX 93.902. The order is not specified (the order rule), and is the same for the three answers and for the supplier of one unchanged stem, so the item at a position belongs to the tail at the same position. The methods send no message to the stem, makeArray excepted when it is asked through request, or to the items.

t = .many~new('N.')
do i = 1 to 40
  t['item'i] = .array~of(i)
end
t[] = 'dflt'
t['x', 'y'] = 'xy'

it = t~allItems
bad = 0
do i = 1 to ix~items
  if t~at(ix[i]) \== it[i] then bad += 1
  if t~makeArray[i] \== ix[i] then bad += 1
end
say ix~class~id it~class~id t~makeArray~class~id ix~items it~items bad

t['extra'] = 'e'
say a~items t~items (ix == t~allIndexes)
call try 't~allIndexes(1)'
call try 't~allItems(1)'
call try 't~makeArray(1)'
exit

Conversions and unknown messages

[class.stem.request]

request(class) with the argument ARRAY, in any case, answers what makeArray answers, after sending makeArray to the stem, so an override of makeArray in a subclass answers. Any other class name is passed on: request is sent to the default of the stem with the same argument, or to the name when there is no default, and its answer is the answer. It takes exactly one argument: none raises SYNTAX 93.903 and a second raises SYNTAX 93.902. The argument must have a string value: .nil raises SYNTAX 88.909.

call try 's~request("a", "b")'
call try 's~request(.nil)'
exit

[class.stem.unknown]

A message that the stem does not understand, makeString and the comparison methods among them, is sent to the default of the stem with the same arguments, or to the name of the stem when there is no default, and what that answers is the answer. So a stem stands for its default in an expression: s~length, s + 1 and s = 'abc' are the messages length, + and = sent to the default (the extended assignment rule shows the operators); a default that does not understand the message is sent unknown by the method search, and one with no unknown method raises SYNTAX 97.1, as does .nil. The message unknown(name, arguments) does the same for the message name and the arguments that arguments holds: arguments is sent request with ARRAY, and an answer that is an instance of Array, or of a subclass of it, with one dimension is the array of arguments, while .nil and an object that is no collection raise SYNTAX 98.913; a position that holds nothing is an omitted argument. name must have a string value (.nil raises SYNTAX 88.909), and the message name is used as written: a name that is not in upper case names no method of the default, which handles it as a message it does not understand. An instance of a subclass of List given as arguments is sent request as any other object is (Deviation 118). It takes exactly two arguments: fewer raises SYNTAX 93.903 and more SYNTAX 93.902.

[class.stem.copy]

copy answers a new stem of the class of the receiver with the same name, the same default and the same items. The items are the same objects, and the two stems do not see each other's changes. [class.stem.string]

The string value of a stem is the string value of its default, and its name when it has no default (the stem rule); string and say use it, and a stem has no makeString of its own, so makeString is passed on by the unknown rule with the same answer. objectName is that of Object, a Stem, and is not the string value.

The stem variable and the object

[class.stem.variable]

The value of a stem symbol is a Stem object, so a. answers the object and the methods of this page work on the compound variables of the stem: an item put with put is the value of the compound variable, a compound variable that is assigned is an item, and a variable that is dropped has none. The name of such a stem is its symbol in upper case, with the period, and is the name that an unset compound variable has as its value. Assigning the stem symbol replaces the object (the stem rule), so an earlier value of the symbol is no longer the stem.

a.x = 'ex'

b.2 = 'jay'
drop b.1
say b.~items b.~allIndexes b.1 b.~at(1)
old = b.
b. = 'new'
say old~items old[2] b.~items b.~string
a.~put('d')
say a.2 a.~items a.1

The methods of the mixins

[class.stem.inherited]

The class method of and the instance methods putAll, union, difference, intersection, xor, subset, disjoint and equivalent are not declared by Stem. of and putAll are those of MapCollection, and the others those of Collection: a stem is one of the collections they take as an argument and as a receiver, and its tails are the indexes they work with. of and putAll store with put(item, index), and the answers of union, difference and xor are the object that copy of the stem answers, so they keep its name and default, and the answer of intersection is a new stem that new of the class makes, with no name and no default. union adds only the tails that the copy has no item at. In the example the arguments are stems.

a = .stem~new('A.')
a['p'] = 'P1'
a['q'] = 'Q1'
b = .stem~new('B.')
b['q'] = 'Q2'
b['r'] = 'R2'
do op over 'union difference intersection xor'~makeArray(' ')
  r = a~send(op, b)
  say op r~class~id r~items listed(r) '['r~string']'
end
say a~subset(b) b~subset(b) a~disjoint(b) a~equivalent(b) a~equivalent(a~copy)
s = .stem~of(.array~of('k1', 'x'), .array~of('k2', 'y'))
say s~items s['k1'] s['k2']
c = .stem~new('C.')
say (c~putAll(.array~of('m', 'n')) == c) c~items c[1] c[2]
exit
listed: procedure
  use arg r
  s = ''
  do i over r~allIndexes~sort
    s = s i'='r[i]
  end
  return s~strip

Messages the methods send

[class.stem.sends]

No method that Stem declares sends a message to its receiver, except request, which sends makeArray (the request rule). The set operations and putAll send what the pages of the mixins say, so union, difference, xor and subset send copy to the receiver, intersection sends hasIndex to it, disjoint sends intersection, equivalent sends items and putAll sends put. An index argument that is not a string is sent request with STRING (the tails rule), and hasItem, index and removeItem send == to the argument with the stored items as the argument (the item rule). The other methods send nothing to indexes or items. In the example a subclass has every method overridden to record its name, and each call records only its own.

own = '[] []= allIndexes allItems at empty hasIndex hasItem index isEmpty',
  'items makeArray put remove removeItem supplier toDirectory copy string'
.local~log = .array~new
.local~on = 0
do m over own~makeArray(' ')
  src = "if .local~on then .local~log~append('"m"'); forward class (super)"
  .spy~define(m, src)
end
a = .spy~new('N.')
calls = 'x = a[1]|a["k1"] = "x"|x = a~allIndexes|x = a~allItems',
  '|x = a~at("k1")',
  '|x = a~hasIndex("k1")|x = a~hasItem("q")|x = a~index("q")|x = a~isEmpty',
  '|x = a~items|x = a~makeArray|a~put(1, "k9")|x = a~remove("k9")',
  '|x = a~removeItem("q")|x = a~supplier|x = a~toDirectory|x = a~copy',
  '|x = a~string|a~empty'
n = 0
extra = 0
do c over calls~makeArray('|')
  .local~log~empty
  .local~on = 1
  interpret c
  .local~on = 0
  n += 1
  if .local~log~items <> 1 then do
    extra += 1
    say c '=>' .local~log~makeString('L', ' ')
  end
end
say n 'calls,' extra 'sent more than one message to the receiver'

[class.stem.hasitem.sends]

hasItem(item), index(item) and removeItem(item) send == to the argument with a stored item as the argument, once for each item, until one answers true, and send nothing else, hashCode included; when none matches, every item is compared. The order in which the items are compared is not specified (the order rule). The search with the very object that is stored is no exception: its == is sent as for any other item (the deviation rule). The messages sent to an index are those of the tails rule.

s['b'] = 't'

say (s~index(q) == .nil) .local~n
.local~n = 0
say (s~removeItem(q) == .nil) .local~n s~items

::method '=='
  .local~n += 1
  return 0
::method hashCode

  return 1

Deviations

[class.stem.deviation.1]

The order of the answers of allIndexes, allItems, makeArray and supplier, the order in which hasItem, index and removeItem compare the items, and so which tail index and removeItem choose among equal items, are not specified, and may differ from ooRexx's, which follows its storage. Which tails are produced, and how often, is specified. The DO OVER rule says the same of a loop. See Deviation 1. In the example the answers are sorted.

s = .stem~new
s['a'] = 3
s['b'] = 1
s['c'] = 2
say s~allIndexes~sort~makeString('L', ',')
say s~allItems~sort~makeString('L', ',')
say s~items s~makeArray~items

[class.stem.deviation.68]

The UNKNOWN method that a subclass of Stem declares runs for a message that the subclass does not understand, in place of the unknown rule of the class. ooRexx forwards such a message to the default of the stem and raises SYNTAX 97.1 when that does not understand it. See Deviation 68.

A search for an item with the very object that is stored, by hasItem, index or removeItem, sends that object's == as for any other item, so an object whose == answers false is not found even at its own tail. ooRexx compares identity first, finds it and sends nothing. See Deviation 78.

A name given to new and an index that are instances of a subclass of String are read by their own characters, and REQUEST and MAKESTRING are not sent to them (Deviation 109). ooRexx sends the name request with STRING, so an override of request changes the name; it reads an index by its characters. In the example MAKESTRING answers another text.

Built-in functions

ANSI: 9.2.1; rexxref: Functions > Built-in Functions

Deviations: D4, D98, D99, D101

This chapter has a page for each builtin function, and each page specifies the function call. The rules here hold for every builtin call, except that a builtin whose page links the native call rule follows that rule in place of the rules for the number of arguments, and also for the conversion of an object that is not a string, which has no fallback to STRING there. The pages link to these rules, and to the conventions, instead of restating them.

A page's syntax line names the arguments in order. A name in square brackets is an optional argument; every other argument is required. The number of names on the line is the most arguments the builtin takes, and the number of required ones is the fewest.

[bif.index.call.count]

The argument count of a call is the position of the last argument in it that is not omitted. Omitted places at the end of the list therefore add nothing to the count, and a call with only omitted places counts as a call with no arguments, a count of 0.

say substr('abc', 2, , ) word('a b', 2, , , )

bc b
[bif.index.call.too-few]

A call whose argument count is less than the number of required arguments raises SYNTAX 40.3.

signal on syntax name a
say substr('abc')
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say substr('abc', )
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say word(, , )
c: say condition('o')~code

[bif.index.call.too-many]

A call whose argument count is greater than the number of arguments on the syntax line raises SYNTAX 40.4, whatever the values of the arguments, and even when the arguments before the last are omitted.

say word('a b', 1, 2)
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b

b: say condition('o')~code

[bif.index.call.missing]

A required argument that is omitted, in a call whose argument count reaches past it, raises SYNTAX 40.5.

a: say condition('o')~code

b: say condition('o')~code
