[bif.index.call.order.count-before-missing]

A call whose argument count is wrong raises the too-few or too-many error even when it also omits a required argument.

signal on syntax name a
say word(, 1, 2)
a: say condition('o')~code

40.4
[bif.index.call.order.count-before-values]

A call whose argument count is wrong raises the too-few or too-many error even when an argument it does pass would fail its own check.

signal on syntax name a
say substr('abc', 'x', 1, '**', 5)
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say word('a b', 0, 2)
b: say condition('o')~code

[bif.index.call.order.missing-before-values]

A call whose argument count is right but that omits a required argument raises SYNTAX 40.5 even when an argument it passes after the omitted one would fail its own check, a form check or a range check.

signal on syntax name a
say substr(, 'x')
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say subword(, 0)
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say wordpos(, 'a', 0)
c: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name d
say verify('abc', , 'Y')
d: say condition('o')~code

Note. The ANSI draft (9.2.1) checks the arguments from left to right, raising 40.5 at an omitted required argument before it reaches the ones after it, and makes the range checks only once every argument is present.

[bif.index.call.native]

A builtin whose page links this rule does not follow the rules above for the number of arguments, from too few to the order of their errors; its errors for them are of the 88.9xx family. A required argument that is omitted, whether the call stops short of it or leaves its place empty, raises SYNTAX 88.901. An argument past the last one on the syntax line raises SYNTAX 88.922, even when the arguments before it are omitted. As for the other builtins, a trailing omitted place adds nothing to the count. An argument that such a page calls a string and that is an object other than a string is replaced by the string that request with the argument STRING answers, as for the other builtins, but there is no fallback to the STRING method: an object whose request answers no string, such as one with no MAKESTRING method, raises SYNTAX 88.909, whatever its STRING method answers. As for the other builtins, the count comes first: a call that has an argument past the last one on the syntax line raises 88.922 even when an argument before it is omitted or fails its own check (see Deviation 101).

b: say condition('o')~code

say directory(, 'x')
c: say condition('o')~code

d: say condition('o')~code
signal off syntax

[bif.index.call.native.deviation.101]

A builtin that follows the native call rule checks the count of its arguments before the arguments themselves, as the other builtins do: a call that has an argument past the last one on the syntax line raises SYNTAX 88.922 even when an argument before it is omitted, is an object whose request answers no string, or fails a check that its page gives. ooRexx reports an omitted argument, an object whose request answers no string and an argument that is not a whole number before the count, and the count before an argument's value: an option it does not allow or a number out of range.

c: say condition('o')~code

Words

[bif.index.words.split]

The builtins that count words split a string into words the same way. A word is a run of one or more characters, none of them whitespace, that has whitespace or an end of the string on each side. The words of a string are numbered from 1, left to right. Whitespace before the first word, between two words and after the last belongs to no word, so the null string and a string of only whitespace have no words. Every other character, line feed and '00'x among them, can be part of a word.

say words(' a'||'09'x||'b  c ') words('') words('  '||'09'x)
say word('one  two', 2) c2x(word('a'||'0a000c'x||'b c', 1))

3 0 0
two 610A000C62

Note. The ANSI draft (9.3.26 and the other word builtins) separates words by a set of blank characters that it leaves to the configuration: the blank and any others the configuration names. ooRexx fixes that set as the blank and the horizontal tab, and so does this book.

[bif.index.words.number]

Where a word builtin's page calls an argument a word number, that argument is a position that counts words: the word number n names word n of the string as the word rule numbers them. A word number greater than the number of words in the string is not an error, for every value that passes its check; it names no word, and the builtin's page says what the builtin answers then.

say '['word('a b', 3)']' wordindex('a b', 3) wordlength('a b', 999999999999999999),
    wordpos('a', 'a b', 3)
signal on syntax name e
say wordindex('a b', 0)
e: say condition('o')~code

[] 0 0 0
93.924

Answers that are counts

[bif.index.count.answer]

A builtin whose page links this rule answers a count: of characters, of words or of occurrences, or a position, which counts characters or words up to the one it names. Such a builtin writes it as a whole number in decimal digits only: no sign, no leading zero, no period and no exponent, and 0 for zero. The caller's NUMERIC DIGITS setting plays no part, so the answer is exact however many digits it has.

numeric digits 3
say wordindex(copies(' ', 1000) || 'a', 1) wordlength(copies('z', 1234), 1),
    wordpos('y', copies('x ', 1200) || 'y') wordpos('q', 'a b')
say compare(copies('a', 1500) || 'b', copies('a', 1500) || 'c') countstr('a', copies('a', 1500))
say verify(copies('a', 1200) || 'b', 'a') verify(copies('a', 1300), '', 'N', 1234),
    verify('ab', 'ab')

1001 1234 1201 0
1501 1500
1201 1234 0

Note. The reference manual does not say how these answers are written or whether NUMERIC DIGITS applies to them; this rule matches ooRexx.

[bif.index.count.answer.deviation.4]

interrexx does not specify whether the answer of a builtin that answers a count is the same object as another string of equal value: as an equal number the program already holds, such as the start argument of a call that answers it, or a literal such as '1201', or the equal answer of another call. Through identityHash, or as a key of an IdentityTable, the answer may be either, and a program can rely only on the value, which is equal under ==. ooRexx differs: it often answers a new object where interrexx answers the existing one.

w = copies('x ', 1200) || 'y'
n = 1200 + 1
say (wordpos('y', w, n) == n) (wordindex(copies(' ', 1200) || 'a', 1) == '1201'),
    (wordlength(copies('z', 1201), 1) == wordpos('y', w))
v = copies('a', 1300)
say (verify(v, '', 'N', n) == n) (verify(copies('a', 1200) || 'b', 'a') == '1201')

1 1

Bit-by-bit functions

[bif.index.bit.args]

BITAND, BITOR and BITXOR take the same arguments: string1, string2 and pad. Each runs as a String method, and string1, its first argument, is the receiver; string2 and pad become the message's arguments, in that order. string1 and string2 are strings and pad is a pad. Only string1 is required, string2 and pad are optional, and the argument count is checked by the builtin call rules: one is required and three is the most.

say c2x(bitor('a0'x)) c2x('a0'x~bitxor('01'x)) c2x('a0'x~bitand('f0'x, '00'x))
signal on syntax name a
say bitand()
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say bitor('a', 'b', 'c', 'd')
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say bitxor(, 'b')
c: say condition('o')~code

A0 A1 A0
40.3
40.4
40.5
[bif.index.bit.pad.check]

A pad that is present is checked as a pad whether or not the call needs it: a pad that is not one character long raises SYNTAX 40.23 even when the operands are equally long or both null, where no character of it would be used. The null string is not a pad, as an empty argument is not omitted.

signal on syntax name a
say bitand('a', 'b', '')
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say bitor('', '', '')
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say bitxor('ab', 'cd', 'xy')
c: say condition('o')~code
say c2x(bitor('ab', 'cd', 'x')) '['bitxor('', '', 'x')']'

40.23
40.23
40.23
6366 []
[bif.index.bit.bytes]

Each character of the result is made from the characters at the same position in the two operands: bit k of it is the function's operation on bit k of each, for each of the eight bits of a character, and nothing else about the operands matters. Every character code is an operand like any other. A string of digits is the characters of its digits, not a number, so NUMERIC DIGITS plays no part.

numeric digits 1
say c2x(bitxor(12, 5)) c2x(bitand('ff80'x, '80ff'x)) c2x(bitor('00ff'x, 'f00f'x))

0432 8080 F0FF
[bif.index.bit.nopad]

When pad is omitted, the answer is as long as the longer operand. The characters of the shorter one are combined with the characters at the same positions of the longer, and the characters of the longer beyond the end of the shorter are copied into the answer unchanged, whichever of the two is the longer.

say c2x(bitand('ff00ff'x, '0f'x)) c2x(bitand('0f'x, 'ff00ff'x))
say c2x(bitxor('ab', 'a')) c2x(bitor('a', 'ab'))

0F00FF 0F00FF
0062 6162
[bif.index.bit.pad]

When pad is present, copies of pad are appended to the shorter operand until the two are equally long, and the two are then combined character by character. The answer is as long as the longer operand, and each character of it beyond the end of the shorter operand is the operation applied to the longer's character and pad.

say c2x(bitand('ff00ff'x, '0f'x, 'f0'x)) c2x(bitand('0f'x, 'ff00ff'x, 'f0'x))
say c2x(bitxor('ab', 'a', ' ')) c2x(bitor('a', 'ab', ' '))

0F00F0 0F00F0
0042 6162
[bif.index.bit.string2-default]

An omitted string2 is the null string, and a string2 given as the null string behaves the same. The answer is then string1 itself when pad is omitted, and with a pad it is each character of string1 combined with pad.

say c2x(bitand('abc')) c2x(bitor('abc', '')) c2x(bitxor('abc', , 'ff'x))
say c2x(bitand('abc', , '0f'x)) c2x(bitor('abc', '', '0f'x))

616263 616263 9E9D9C
010203 6F6F6F
[bif.index.bit.commutative]

Exchanging the first two arguments does not change the answer, with a pad or without one.

say (bitand('abcd', 'ef') == bitand('ef', 'abcd')),
    (bitor('abcd', 'ef', 'x') == bitor('ef', 'abcd', 'x'))
say (bitxor('abc', 'z', 'q') == bitxor('z', 'abc', 'q')) (bitxor('', 'z') == bitxor('z', ''))

1 1
1 1
[bif.index.bit.deviation.4]

interrexx does not specify whether the answer of a bit-by-bit function is the same object as another string of equal value: as string1 itself when the answer equals it, as in bitor(s), or as an equal string produced some other way, such as a literal. Through identityHash, or as a key of an IdentityTable, the answer may be either, and a program can rely only on the value, which is equal under ==. ooRexx differs: it often answers a new object where interrexx answers the existing one.

s = 'ab' || 'cd'
say (bitor(s) == s) (bitand('', s) == 'abcd') (bitand('a', 'a') == 'a')

1 1 1

Conversion functions

Note. B2X, C2D, C2X, D2C, D2X, X2B, X2C and X2D convert between the characters of a string, a number written in decimal, and a string of hexadecimal or binary digits. The rules below are the ones that more than one of them follows; a function's page links the ones it uses and states the rest.

[bif.index.conv.digits]

In an argument that is a string of binary digits, the digits are 0 and 1. In an argument that is a string of hexadecimal digits, the digits are 0 to 9 and the letters A to F, each in either case, and the two cases may be mixed. Any character other than a digit that is not whitespace raises SYNTAX 93.934 in a binary string and SYNTAX 93.933 in a hexadecimal string. A sign, a period, a letter past F, a decimal digit above 1 in a binary string, line feed and '00'x are all such characters.

say b2x('0110') x2c('4a4B') x2b('aF')
signal on syntax name a
say b2x('102')
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say b2x('1' || '0a'x)
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say x2c('4G')
c: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name d
say x2c('-4')
d: say condition('o')~code

6 JK 10101111
93.934
93.934
93.933
93.933
[bif.index.conv.digits.null]

The null string is a valid digit string, binary or hexadecimal: it has no digits. B2X, X2B and X2C answer the null string for it, and X2D answers 0.

say '['b2x('')']' '['x2b('')']' '['x2c('')']' x2d('')

[] [] [] 0
[bif.index.conv.groups]

A digit string may have whitespace between its digits, which is not read as part of the number. A run of any number of blanks and tabs, in any mix, counts as one gap. A gap is allowed only where the digits that follow it, up to the end of the string, can be read in whole units: a multiple of 4 binary digits (the digits of one hexadecimal digit) in a binary string, and a multiple of 2 hexadecimal digits (the digits of one character) in a hexadecimal string. The first group of digits, before the first gap, may have any number of digits. A gap that does not fall at such a boundary raises SYNTAX 93.977 in a binary string and SYNTAX 93.976 in a hexadecimal string.

say b2x('10 0101 1100') b2x('1  1111') b2x('1111' || '09'x || ' 0000')
say x2c('4a 4B') c2x(x2c('4 4a4b')) x2d('1 23 45')
signal on syntax name a
say b2x('11 11')
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say b2x('1 111 1')
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say x2c('4A 4')
c: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name d
say x2c('1 2 3')
d: say condition('o')~code

25C 1F F0
JK 044A4B 74565
93.977
93.977

[bif.index.conv.groups.edge]

A digit string that starts or ends with whitespace raises SYNTAX 93.932 in a binary string and SYNTAX 93.931 in a hexadecimal string, as does a string that has only whitespace and so no digit. The null string is not such a string.

signal on syntax name a
say b2x(' 1111')
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say b2x('1111 ')
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say b2x('  ')
c: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name d
say x2c(' 41')
d: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name e
say x2b('41' || '09'x)
e: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name f
say x2d('  ')
f: say condition('o')~code

93.932
93.932
93.932
93.931
93.931
93.931

Note. The reference manual says whitespace may not lead or trail, and that groups are at 4-digit boundaries for binary strings and at byte boundaries for hexadecimal ones. When a string has more than one of the faults above (such as a non-digit and a misplaced gap), this book does not say which of the errors is raised; the examples above have one fault each.

[bif.index.conv.length]

Where a conversion function takes a length n, it is an optional whole-number argument whose value must not be negative (a length): a negative n raises SYNTAX 93.923, and an n of 0 is allowed. An omitted n is not the same as an n of 0, and the null string is not omitted. Its unit is the character in C2D and D2C and the hexadecimal digit in D2X and X2D.

signal on syntax name a
say c2d('a', -1)
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say d2x(65, -1)
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say c2d('a', '')
c: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name d
say d2c(65, 'x')
d: say condition('o')~code
say c2d('a') c2d('a', 0) c2d('a', '-0') '['d2c(65, 0)']' '['d2x(65, 0)']'

93.923
93.923
40.12
40.12
97 0 0 [] []
[bif.index.conv.signed.read]

When C2D or X2D is given an n, the string is read as a signed number of exactly n units. It is first made n units long: units are removed from its left when it is longer, and '00'x units (zero digits in X2D) are added there when it is shorter. The result is then read as a two's-complement number: when the leftmost bit of the leftmost unit is set, the number is negative, and its value is the unsigned value minus 256**n in C2D and 16**n in X2D. An n of 0 answers 0. Without an n, the string is read as a number with no sign, whatever its leftmost bit, and the answer is never negative.

say c2d('93'x) c2d('93'x, 1) c2d('93'x, 2) c2d('e3a1'x, 1) c2d('e3a1'x, 2)
say c2d('ff5a'x, 1) c2d('0107'x, 0) c2d('', 3)
say x2d('93') x2d('93', 2) x2d('93', 3)
say x2d('e3a1', 2) x2d('e3a1', 3) x2d('e3a1', 4)

147 -109 147 -95 -7263
90 0 0
147 -109 147
-95 929 -7263
[bif.index.conv.signed.write]

When D2C or D2X is given an n, the answer is exactly n units long. It is the number's remainder on division by 256**n in D2C and 16**n in D2X, a remainder that is never negative, written with '00'x units (0 digits in D2X) on its left to make n units. For a number that needs more than n units the leftmost ones are lost, so -257 with an n of 1 is 'FF'x. An n of 0 answers the null string. Without an n, a non-negative number is written in as few units as it takes, and at least one, so that no '00'x (or 0) stands on its left unless the number is 0; a negative number raises SYNTAX 93.927.

say c2x(d2c(72)) c2x(d2c(65, 3)) c2x(d2c(-65, 3)) c2x(d2c(321, 1))
say c2x(d2c(-129, 1))
say d2x(65) d2x(65, 4) d2x(-65, 4) d2x(321, 2) d2x(-129, 2)
say c2x(d2c(0)) d2x(0) c2x(d2c(256)) d2x(256) c2x(d2c(-256, 1)),
    c2x(d2c(-256, 2))
say c2x(d2c(-257, 1)) d2x(-4097, 2) c2x(d2c(-65537, 2))
signal on syntax name a
say d2c(-1)
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say d2x(-65)
b: say condition('o')~code

FF FF FFFF

[bif.index.conv.decimal]

The decimal argument of D2C and D2X is a string written as a Rexx number, with optional whitespace around it and after its sign, a period and an exponent, whose value is a whole number of at most NUMERIC DIGITS digits, the digits counted being those of the value written as a whole number with no leading zero: '1.0E9', '1E9' and '1000000000' all have ten, and '0001.000' has one. Each of these raises SYNTAX 93.929 in D2C and SYNTAX 93.928 in D2X: a string that is not a number, the null string among them; a number with a nonzero fractional part, when it is written with no more digits than NUMERIC DIGITS; and a whole number with more digits than NUMERIC DIGITS. The value is the number however it is written: 6.5E1 and 65.0 are 65. This book does not specify a number written with more digits than NUMERIC DIGITS and a nonzero fractional part.

say c2x(d2c(' 65 ')) c2x(d2c('+65')) c2x(d2c('6.5E1')) c2x(d2c('65.0')),
    d2x('0.65E2')

a: say condition('o')~code

[bif.index.conv.decimal.order]

The checks of a D2C or D2X call run in this order, and the first that fails is raised: the form of n (whole-number form, SYNTAX 40.12); whether the decimal argument is a number at all; the sign of n (SYNTAX 93.923); and last whether the decimal argument is a whole number with at most NUMERIC DIGITS digits. A decimal argument that is not a number is therefore raised even when n is negative, and a number that is not whole, or has too many digits, is raised only when n is not negative.

signal on syntax name a
say d2c('x', 'y')
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say d2c('x', -1)
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say d2c('1234567890', -1)
c: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name d
say d2x('1.5', -1)
d: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name e
say d2x('x', -1)
e: say condition('o')~code

[bif.index.conv.digits-limit]

The answer of C2D and X2D is a whole number written in decimal digits, with a leading - when it is negative, no leading zero, no period and no exponent, and 0 for zero. If the answer has more digits than NUMERIC DIGITS, the call raises SYNTAX 93.936 in C2D and SYNTAX 93.935 in X2D, instead of rounding it; the sign is not a digit. An answer with exactly NUMERIC DIGITS digits is allowed.

say c2d('3b9ac9ff'x) c2d(copies('00'x, 20) || '01'x) x2d('0' || 'ff'),
    x2d('f6', 2)
signal on syntax name a
say c2d('3b9aca00'x)
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say x2d('3b9aca00')
b: say condition('o')~code

c: say condition('o')~code

Note. The ANSI draft (9.6.1 to 9.6.11) differs from this book in the codes of the argument errors. It raises 40.24 for a binary string and 40.25 for a hexadecimal one that is not valid, where this book has the 93.9xx codes above; 40.12 for a decimal argument that is not a whole number, where D2C and D2X raise 93.929 and 93.928; and 40.13 for a negative n, or a negative decimal argument without an n, where this book raises 93.923 and 93.927. It raises 40.35 for an answer that does not fit NUMERIC DIGITS, where C2D raises 93.936 and X2D 93.935. The draft also checks the hexadecimal string of X2D when n is 0, which raises an error there for a string with a bad character; this book answers 0 without examining the string.

[bif.index.conv.deviation.4]

interrexx does not specify whether the answer of a conversion function is the same object as another string of equal value, such as a literal, the argument itself when the answer equals it, or the equal answer of another call. Through identityHash, or as a key of an IdentityTable, the answer may be either, and a program can rely only on the value, which is equal under ==. ooRexx differs: it often answers a new object where interrexx answers the existing one.

s = '6' || '1'
say (b2x('10000') == '10') (c2x('a') == s) (x2c(s) == 'a')
say (d2c(97) == 'a') (c2d('') == 0) (c2d(s) == 13873)

Numbers

Note. ABS, SIGN, TRUNC, FORMAT, MAX and MIN take a number as their first argument, which is the receiver when they run as String methods. The rules below say which strings are numbers, how a number is rounded to NUMERIC DIGITS, and how a result is written; the pages link to them instead of restating them.

[bif.index.num.arg]

The number argument must be a string of the whole-number form, which is also the form of a Rexx number, but its value need not be whole. Any other string raises SYNTAX 93.943, the null string and a string of only whitespace among them. An argument that is an object other than a string is first replaced by a string, as any string argument is, and that string must be a number.

say abs(' + 2.50E1 ') abs('.5') abs('5.') abs('-' || '09'x || ' 7')
say abs(.mutablebuffer~new('-7')) abs(.array~of('-4'))
signal on syntax name a
say abs('')
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say abs('1 E1')
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say sign('0x1')
c: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name d
say trunc('5' || '0a'x)
d: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name e
say format(.array~new)
e: say condition('o')~code

25.0 0.5 5 7
7 4
93.943
93.943
93.943
93.943
93.943

Note. The ANSI draft raises SYNTAX 40.11 for a string that does not have the form of a number, where ooRexx, which this book follows, raises 93.943.

[bif.index.num.limit]

A nonzero number is a number only within the exponent range of the language, which the next three conditions describe. Each failing number raises SYNTAX 93.943: one whose written exponent, the digits after E without the sign, has a value above 999999999; one whose first nonzero digit stands at a power of ten above 999999999; and one whose last written digit stands at a power of ten below -999999999. This book does not specify a zero written with an exponent above 999999999.

say abs('1e999999999') abs('12345e-999999999') abs('1e0000000001')
signal on syntax name a
say abs('1e1000000000')
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say abs('12.3e999999999')
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say abs('1.1e-999999999')
c: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name d
say abs('0.1e1000000000')
d: say condition('o')~code

1E+999999999 1.2345E-999999995 10
93.943
93.943
93.943
93.943
[bif.index.num.round]

Before it is used, the number is rounded to NUMERIC DIGITS significant digits, as the sum number + 0 would round it. Digits beyond the first NUMERIC DIGITS significant ones are dropped, and the last kept digit is raised by one when the first dropped digit is 5 or more, so the magnitude rounds up and a negative number rounds away from zero. Leading zeros are not significant, a number with fewer significant digits is not extended, and the zeros it ends in after the point are kept. A number whose value is zero is rounded to 0, with no sign and no decimal places, however it was written.

numeric digits 3
say abs('1.2349') abs('1.9996') abs('-0.0012350') abs(' 001.50 ')
say abs('-0.000') abs('0e5') abs('+0.00') abs('1234.5') abs('-125')
numeric digits 1
say abs('0.45') abs('0.55') abs('25') abs('-4.9')

1.23 2.00 0.00124 1.50
0 0 0 1.23E+3 125
0.5 0.6 3E+1 5
[bif.index.num.overflow]

The rounding of the rule above can carry into a new first digit, one power of ten higher than the first digit of the number. When that power is above 999999999, the call raises SYNTAX 42.901, although the number is within the limits before it is rounded. SIGN raises it too, for the same numbers, although its answer does not otherwise depend on NUMERIC DIGITS. In TRUNC and FORMAT the error comes after the checks of the arguments that their pages list, and in FORMAT before the checks of the fit of its result.

numeric digits 1
say abs('94e999999998') sign('94e999999998')
signal on syntax name a
say abs('99999e999999995')
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say sign('-95e999999998')
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say format('99999e999999995', 0)
c: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name d
say format('99999e999999995', -1)
d: say condition('o')~code
numeric digits 9
signal on syntax name e
say abs('9.999999995e999999999')

[bif.index.num.write]

A rounded number is written in plain or in scientific notation, depending on a trigger value T that is NUMERIC DIGITS unless a page gives another. In plain notation the digits are written in full, a point separates the integer part from the decimal part when the number has decimal places, and a number of magnitude below 1 starts 0.. Let W be the count of digits before the point in that notation and S the count of digits after it. A number of magnitude 1 or more, and zero, is written plain when W is at most T; a nonzero number of magnitude below 1 is written plain when S is at most twice T; any other number is written in scientific notation. A negative number has a - before its first character.

say abs(123456789) abs(1234567890) abs('-0.000000000000000001'),
    abs('0.0000000000000000001')
numeric digits 3
say abs(123) abs(1234) abs('0.000001') abs('0.0000012') abs('0.000012')
say abs('-1234.5') abs('0.000000') abs('12.30')
say '['format(0, , , 1, 0)']' '['format(0, , , 1, 1)']' '['format('0.5', , , 1, 1)']'

123456789 1.23456789E+9 0.000000000000000001 1E-19
123 1.23E+3 0.000001 1.2E-6 0.000012
1.23E+3 0 12.3
[0   ] [0] [0.5]
[bif.index.num.sci]

Scientific notation writes the digits of the rounded number, the first nonzero digit first, with a point after the first digit when there is a second, then E, the sign of the exponent (+ or -), and the exponent as a number without leading zeros. The exponent is the power of ten of the first digit. Under NUMERIC FORM SCIENTIFIC, which is the setting at the start of a program, that is all. Under NUMERIC FORM ENGINEERING the exponent is instead the multiple of 3 at or below the power of ten of the first digit, so that one to three digits stand before the point, and the digits are extended with zeros as far as the point needs.

say abs('-1234567890') abs('1e11') abs('0.0000000123') abs('1e-19')
numeric form engineering
say abs('-1234567890') abs('2e11') abs('1.5e-19') abs('12345678e10')

1.23456789E+9 1E+11 0.0000000123 1E-19
1.23456789E+9 200E+9 150E-21 123.45678E+15

Note. The reference manual gives the writing rule in its chapter on numbers, as the form of every arithmetic result. The ANSI draft keeps its test of the digits before the point but replaces the test of the digits after it: its arithmetic (7.4.10) writes a result in exponential form when more than five zeros follow the point before the first digit, whatever NUMERIC DIGITS is, and its FORMAT (9.4.2) decides again, with the same limit of five zeros, when expp or expt is given. So under the default NUMERIC DIGITS of 9 the ANSI draft writes '0.0000000123' + 0 as 1.23E-8, where ooRexx, which this book follows, writes 0.0000000123.

Note. MAX and MIN take a list of numbers instead of one, and the next two rules are theirs.

[bif.index.num.list]

The arguments of a call that takes a list of numbers are each a number that the call checks before it compares anything: first the receiver, which raises SYNTAX 93.943 when it is not a number, and then the other arguments in order, the first one that is not a number raising SYNTAX 93.904. This includes a number outside the exponent range, which for a later argument raises 93.904 where the receiver, and the other builtins, raise 93.943. The list has no upper limit on its length. Its argument count is checked by the builtin call rules, with one required argument and no most, so a call with no arguments raises SYNTAX 40.3 and no call raises SYNTAX 40.4; an omitted first argument raises SYNTAX 40.5. A function call that omits an argument after the first but passes one after it raises SYNTAX 40.5 too, as Deviation 53 says for MAX and MIN.

say max(31,7,-4,19,22,-8,0,13,5,26,-15,9,17,2,28,-1,11,24,6,3,20,14,-9,25,12),
    max(5,)

a: say condition('o')~code

b: say condition('o')~code

c: say condition('o')~code

signal on syntax name e

e: say condition('o')~code

f: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name g

g: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name h
say max(1, '1e1000000000')
h: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name i
say max('1e1000000000', 1)
i: say condition('o')~code

[bif.index.num.pick]

A call that picks one number from a list rounds every number to NUMERIC DIGITS digits first, then takes the first as the candidate and goes through the others in order, replacing the candidate by that number when the call's own test between the candidate and that number holds. The call answers the candidate, written as that rule says with NUMERIC DIGITS as the trigger. The test compares the two rounded numbers as the < and > operators do, so two numbers that NUMERIC FUZZ makes equal are equal here: the candidate stays, and the answer has its written form, the number of its decimal places included. So a call whose list has only one number answers that number rounded and written.

numeric digits 3
say max(1.0, 1.00) max(1.00, 1.0) min(1.0, 1.00) min(1.00, 1.0)
say max(1.0004, 1.0) min(1.0004, 1.0) min(1.0, 1.0004)
say max('+7') min(' 0.00 ') max(-1234567) min(12.3456)
numeric fuzz 1

say max(1.04, 1.09) min(1.04, 1.09)

1.00 1.00 1.0

Date and time

Note. DATE and TIME answer the current date or time, or convert a date or a time from one format to another. The rules here hold for both.

[bif.index.dt.letter]

Where an argument of DATE or TIME names an option or a format, only its first character counts, as a letter in either case; the rest of the argument is ignored, so Standard, s and s9 all name S. The argument is not trimmed: one that begins with a blank names nothing, and neither does the null string. A first character that is not one of the letters the page allows for that argument raises SYNTAX 40.904.

say date('Standard', '1 Jan 2000') date('s9', '1 Jan 2000') date('s', '20000101', 'Standard')
say time('Civil', '13:05:09') time('c', '13:05:09', 'N')
signal on syntax name a
say date(' S')
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say date('')
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say time('Q')
c: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name d
say time('N', '13:05:09', 'Q')
d: say condition('o')~code

20000101 20000101 20000101
1:05pm 1:05pm
40.904
40.904
40.904
40.904
[bif.index.dt.convert]

A call of DATE or TIME with a string is a conversion: it reads string in the format that informat names (N when informat is omitted) and answers it in the format that option names (N when option is omitted). A conversion does not ask the clock, except where a page says it does. A string that is not valid in informat raises SYNTAX 40.19, or the code that its page gives, as DATE does with an isep. An informat with no string raises SYNTAX 40.5, since a call that omits string asks for the current value and has nothing to read.

say date('E', '20000229', 'S') time('C', '13:05:09') date(, '29 Feb 2000') time(, '13:05:09')
signal on syntax name a
say date('S', , 'S')
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say time('N', , 'N')
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say time('N', 'noon')
c: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name d
say date('S', '2000-02-29')
d: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name e
say date('S', '2000-02-29', 'N', , '-')
e: say condition('o')~code

29/02/00 1:05pm 29 Feb 2000 13:05:09

40.44

Note. The ANSI draft (9.8.1, 9.8.5) raises SYNTAX 40.19 for an informat that has no string; ooRexx raises 40.5, and so does this book.

[bif.index.dt.stamp]

A clause has one moment, whatever DATE and TIME are asked in it: the clock is read at the first call of either, and every later call in the clause answers for that moment. The dates and times, the offset from UTC, and the elapsed time of the TIME clock all belong to it, however long the clause takes to run. A clause that continues over several lines is one clause. The next clause reads the clock again.

a = time('F') syssleep(0.1) time('F')
say word(a, 1) == word(a, 3)
b = time('F'),
    syssleep(0.1) time('F')
say word(b, 1) == word(b, 3)
c = time('F'); x = syssleep(0.1); d = time('F')
say c \== d
say (date('F') == time('F')) (date('T') == time('T')) (date('S') == date('S', time('T'), 'T'))

1
1 1 1
[bif.index.dt.stamp.scope]

A routine or a method that a clause calls reads the clock for itself, in each of its own clauses. Its readings are not seen by the clause that called it, and the reading of that clause is not seen by it, so a clause that calls a slow function still has one moment for its own calls.

a = time('F') slow() time('F')
say (word(a, 1) == word(a, 3)) (word(a, 1) == word(a, 2))
a = time('F') .o~new~m time('F')
say (word(a, 1) == word(a, 3)) (word(a, 1) == word(a, 2))
a = time('F') routine_slow() time('F')
say (word(a, 1) == word(a, 3)) (word(a, 1) == word(a, 2))
exit
slow:
call syssleep 0.1
return time('F')
::routine routine_slow
call syssleep 0.1
return time('F')
::class o
::method m
call syssleep 0.1
return time('F')

Streams

Note. The input and output builtins read and write streams. A stream is a source of characters, a destination for them, or both: a file, or one of the three standard streams. The rules here hold for every stream builtin; the pages link to them instead of restating them. The examples keep their files in the current directory under names of their own, and delete them.

[bif.index.stream.name]

A stream builtin names its stream with a string, its name argument. For a file the name is the file's name, taken from the current directory when it is not absolute (see Deviation 34). While the stream is open, a name denotes the same stream, whichever stream builtin it is given to, so what one builtin writes another reads. This holds in the main program and in one call of a method, and in the routines that either of them calls. Each call of a method has streams of its own, which a routine called from it shares, so a name that the method uses is not the stream that the main program, a routine called from the main program or another call of the method uses under that name.

f = 'spec-streams-name.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
call lineout f, 'first'
call charout f, 'second'
say linein(f) '/' charin(f, , 3)
call sysfiledelete f

first / sec

f = 'spec-streams-name2.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
call lineout f, 'one'
call lineout f, 'two'
call lineout f, 'three'
call stream f, 'C', 'CLOSE'
say 'main' linein(f)
o = .o~new
say 'call 1' o~two(f)
say 'call 2' o~two(f)
say 'main' linein(f)
call stream f, 'C', 'CLOSE'
call sysfiledelete f
::class o
::method two
  use arg f
  return linein(f) linein(f)

main one
call 1 one two
call 2 one two
main two
[bif.index.stream.std]

The names STDIN, STDOUT and STDERR denote the standard input, output and error streams, each with a colon after it or without one and with its letters in any case. A null string or an omitted name denotes the default stream of the builtin: the standard input for a builtin that reads, the standard output for a builtin that writes.

call charout 'stdout', 'one '
call charout 'Stdout:', 'two '
call charout , 'three '
call charout '', 'four'
say
say '['charin()']' '['charin('')']' '['charin('Stdin:')']' '['linein()']'

one two three four
[] [] [] []

Note. The examples run with an empty standard input, so every read of it ends at once.

[bif.index.stream.transient]

A standard stream that is connected to a pipe is transient: it has no positions. A start or line number given to a transient stream raises SYNTAX 93.958, whatever its value: after the checks of the argument rule on the argument count, the form of the arguments and the count, and in place of that rule's check that the start is 1 or more. CHAROUT given the name STDIN and a start is the exception: the start is not checked beyond its form, and the call fails as any write to the standard input does, with NOTREADY and the number of characters it did not write as its answer. The examples of this book run with a pipe as standard input and as standard output. What a standard stream that is connected to anything else does with a start is not specified either. Named transient streams, such as FIFOs and devices, are not specified in this chapter.

signal on syntax name a
say charin(, 1)
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say linein(, 0)
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say charout(, 'x', 5)
c: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name d
say charin(, 0, -1)
d: say condition('o')~code

93.958
93.958
93.958
88.907
[bif.index.stream.open]

A stream builtin opens its stream when it first uses it, and the program does no opening of its own. A file is opened for reading and for writing, each as far as the file allows; an operation that the file does not allow has the NOTREADY outcome that its page gives. A file that does not exist is created by a write, and a read of it creates nothing: it finds no characters and raises the NOTREADY condition. A stream just opened has its read position at the first character and its write position after the last, so a write adds to the data a file already holds.

f = 'spec-streams-open.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
say '['charin(f)']' (stream(f, 'c', 'query exists') == '')
call charout f, 'abc'
call charout f
call charout f, 'def'
say charin(f, 1, 6) (stream(f, 'c', 'query exists') \== '')
call sysfiledelete f

[] 1
abcdef 1
[bif.index.stream.positions]

A file that is open has two positions in it, counted in characters from 1: the read position, where the next read starts, and the write position, where the next write starts. A read moves the read position past what it read and leaves the write position where it was; a write moves the write position past what it wrote and leaves the read position where it was. A start (or line number) that a call gives sets the position that the call uses, before it reads or writes. A write at a position inside the data replaces the characters there.

f = 'spec-streams-pos.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
call charout f, 'abc'
say charin(f, , 1)
call charout f, 'd'
say charin(f, , 3)
call charout f, 'XY', 2
call charout f, 'Z'
say charin(f, 1, 4)
call sysfiledelete f

a
bcd
aXYZ
[bif.index.stream.lifetime]

A stream stays open, with its positions, until the program closes it or ends. The streams that a call of a method opened are closed when the call returns, so what the call wrote is in the file then. What it wrote to a name that the code which called it also has open is not specified. CHAROUT given only a name closes a stream; the pages of the other stream builtins name their forms. The next use of a closed name opens the stream again: the read position is at the start and the write position at the end of the data, and the characters written before the close are in the file. A standard stream is closed in the same way, by CLOSE and by CHAROUT or LINEOUT given neither a string nor a start or line: its state is then UNKNOWN, and the next stream builtin that reads from it, writes to it, counts what is left in it (CHARS or LINES) or opens it opens it again on the same input or output, so that later reads and writes carry on. ooRexx differs, as Deviation 98 says.

f = 'spec-streams-life.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
call charout f, 'abc'
say charin(f, , 2) charin(f)
call charout f
say charin(f)
call charout f, 'd'
call charout f
say charin(f, 1, 9)
call sysfiledelete f

ab c
a
abcd

f = 'spec-streams-method.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
.spec_writer~new~w(f)
say 'size after call' stream(f, 'C', 'QUERY SIZE')
call sysfiledelete f
::class spec_writer
::method w
  use arg f
  call lineout f, 'from method'

size after call 12
[bif.index.stream.lifetime.deviation.98]

A close of a standard stream is a logical one, as for a file: the lifetime rule holds for the standard input, output and error too. A call of CHAROUT or LINEOUT that gives neither a string nor a start or line, and either no stream name or the name of a standard stream, writes nothing, answers 0 and closes the stream, and the later output of the program is written as usual. In ooRexx, output written to the standard output or error after such a call, or after a CLOSE of it, does not appear at once: it appears when the program next closes, flushes or opens the stream, and what is written after the last of these is lost. Output written before the close can be lost too: when the stream is a file, the output written after the close can replace it. On the standard input, the same call of CHAROUT answers 0 and that of LINEOUT 1 in ooRexx, the state is then ERROR, and NOTREADY is raised. A CLOSE of the standard input has the same outcome on both until the program first reads from it; after a read, ooRexx can lose the input that the program had not read yet.

say 'one'
call charout
say charout('STDOUT') lineout('stdout:') charout('') lineout()
call lineout 'stdout'
call charout 'stderr'
say 'two'

one
0 0 0 0
two
[bif.index.stream.notready]

A call that cannot read, or write, as many characters as it was asked to raises the NOTREADY condition. That happens at the end of the data, when the stream cannot be opened, and when a write fails. condition('D') in a trap for it is the name of the stream, and condition('C') is NOTREADY. For a file the name is the spelling that the first call to name the stream gave. A later call that names the same file in another way, such as ./x for x or an absolute path, gets that spelling again, until a CLOSE ends the stream. For the standard input it is STDIN, whatever the spelling of the name in the call and also when the call gave none. The condition is not an error: when it is not trapped, or after a CALL ON trap returns, the call goes on and answers what its page says. A trap by SIGNAL ON NOTREADY abandons the clause that raised it, like any other condition. Reading the standard output or the standard error by name, with CHARIN or LINEIN and a count that is not 0, is a read the stream does not allow, whatever the stream is connected to, and raises NOTREADY too (see Deviation 99); condition('D') is STDOUT or STDERR, whatever the spelling of the name, with or without the colon. CHARS and LINES of them raise nothing and answer 0.

f = 'spec-streams-nr.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
call charout f, 'ab'
call charout f
x = charin(f, 1, 5)
say '[' || x || ']'
signal on notready name trapped
x = charin(f)
say 'not reached'
trapped: say condition('c') condition('d') x
call on notready name std
x = charin('Stdin:')
x = linein()
call sysfiledelete f
exit
std: say condition('d')
return

[ab]
NOTREADY spec-streams-nr.tmp ab
STDIN
STDIN

call on notready name h
f = 'spec-streams-nr2.tmp'
x = linein('./'f, 1, 1)
x = linein(f, 1, 1)
x = linein(directory()'/'f, 1, 1)
call stream f, 'C', 'CLOSE'
x = linein(f, 1, 1)
x = linein('./'f, 1, 1)
exit
h: say condition('d')
return

./spec-streams-nr2.tmp
./spec-streams-nr2.tmp
./spec-streams-nr2.tmp
spec-streams-nr2.tmp
spec-streams-nr2.tmp

call on notready name std
x = charin('stdout')
x = linein('Stderr:')
say chars('stdout') lines('stderr')
exit
std: say condition('c') condition('d')
return

NOTREADY STDOUT
NOTREADY STDERR

[bif.index.stream.notready.deviation.99]

A read of the standard output or the standard error reads nothing and raises NOTREADY whatever the stream is connected to, a file that is open for reading as well as for writing included. ooRexx reads from such a stream when it is open for reading, and answers the characters it finds there.

call on notready name std
say '[' || charin('Stdout', , 2) || ']'
say '[' || linein('stderr:') || ']'
exit
std: say condition('d')
return

[]
STDOUT

[bif.index.stream.line-end]

A line of a stream ends at the first line feed ('0a'x) after its start. When the character before that line feed is a carriage return ('0d'x), the carriage return belongs to the line end as well. The line end is not part of the line. Every other character is part of the line, a carriage return included when no line feed follows it directly. The last line of a stream may have no line end. Everything that counts the characters of a stream counts a line end as the one or two characters it is.

f = 'spec-streams-eol.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
call charout f, 'a' || '0a'x || 'b' || '0d0a'x || 'c' || '0d'x || 'd' || '0d0d0a'x || 'e'
call charout f
say chars(f)
do 4
  say c2x(linein(f))
end
say chars(f)
call sysfiledelete f

[bif.index.stream.args]

A start, a count and a line number are whole-number arguments with the value that the next rule gives; they are not checked as the position and length arguments of the String methods are. The call is checked in this order. The count of arguments comes first, by the call rules. Then the form and the value of every such argument, from left to right, raise SYNTAX 40.12. Then a count that is negative raises SYNTAX 88.907, and a count that the builtin's page does not allow raises the error that page names. Last, a start or line number that is below 1 raises SYNTAX 93.907.

f = 'spec-streams-args.tmp'
call charout f, 'abc'
signal on syntax name a
say charin(f, 0, 'x')
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say charin(f, 0, -1)
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say charin(f, 0, 1)
c: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name d
say charin(f, 1, -1)
d: say condition('o')~code
call charout f
call sysfiledelete f

[bif.index.stream.value]

The value of a start, a count or a line number is its number rounded to 20 significant digits; when the first digit dropped is 5 or more, the magnitude rounds up, otherwise down. The caller's NUMERIC DIGITS setting plays no part. If the rounded value has a fractional part other than zero, or is more than 2**63 - 1, which is 9223372036854775807, or is less than -2**63, which is -9223372036854775808, the argument raises SYNTAX 40.12; otherwise its value is that integer. This is not the rule of the conventions, which rounds to 18 digits and refuses 10**18 and more.

f = 'spec-streams-value.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
call charout f, 'abc'
call charout f
n = 0

x = charin(f, 1000000000000000000, 1)
say '[' || x || ']' n
x = charin(f, 9223372036854775807, 1)
say '[' || x || ']' n
numeric digits 3

signal on syntax name b
say charin(f, '2.0000000000000000001', 1)
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say charin(f, 1, '1.00000000000000000005')
c: say condition('o')~code
call sysfiledelete f
exit
nr: n = n + 1
return

[bif.index.stream.start]

A start, or line number, below 1 raises SYNTAX 93.907, and -0 is 0. A start is checked once the stream is open. For a stream that cannot be opened it is not checked: the call has the NOTREADY outcome that its page gives for such a stream.

f = 'spec-streams-start.tmp'

ABBREV

ABBREV(information, info [, length])

ANSI: 9.3.1; rexxref: Functions > Built-in Functions > ABBREV (Abbreviation)

ABBREV tests whether one string is an abbreviation of another: whether it is the beginning of that string and, when the call asks for it, long enough. The answer is 1 or 0.

Arguments

[bif.abbrev.method]

ABBREV is a builtin that runs as a String method, and information, its first argument, is the receiver; info and length become the message's arguments, in that order. information and info are strings, and length is a length. The arguments are checked in the order the conventions give, and the argument count by the builtin call rules: two are required and three is the most.

say abbrev('Stamp', 'Sta') 'Stamp'~abbrev('Sta') 'Stamp'~abbrev('Sta', 4)
signal on syntax name a
say abbrev('abc', 'ab', -1)
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say abbrev('abc', 'ab', 'x')
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say abbrev('abc', 'ab', )
say abbrev('abc')
c: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name d
say abbrev('abc', 'ab', 2, 1)
d: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name e
say abbrev(, 'ab')
e: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name f
say abbrev('abc', 'a', 'x', 1)
f: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name g
say abbrev('abc', , -1)
g: say condition('o')~code

1 1 0
93.923
40.12
1
40.3
40.4
40.5
40.4
40.5
[bif.abbrev.length.default]

When length is omitted, it is LENGTH(info): the whole of info takes part, and no info is too short.

say abbrev('STAMP', 'STA') abbrev('STAMP', 'STA', ) abbrev('STAMP', 'STA', 3),
    abbrev('STAMP', 'STA', 4)

1 1 1 0

The result

[bif.abbrev.result]

ABBREV returns 1 when all three of these hold, and 0 when any does not: info is no longer than information; the characters of info are equal to the first LENGTH(info) characters of information, in order; and LENGTH(info) is at least length. The answer is the single digit 1 or 0, for every call.

say abbrev('STAMP', 'STAMP') abbrev('STAMP', 'STAMP', 5) abbrev('STAMP', 'STA'),
    abbrev('STAMP', 'TAM') abbrev('STAMP', 'STAMPS') abbrev('STAMP', 'STX')

1 1 1 0 0 0
[bif.abbrev.length.minimum]

length is the least number of characters info may have. A length greater than LENGTH(info) therefore gives 0, for every length that passes its check, a very large one included, and even when info is the beginning of information. A length of 0, or any length up to LENGTH(info), leaves the answer to the comparison of the characters.

say abbrev('abc', 'ab', 0) abbrev('abc', 'ab', 2) abbrev('abc', 'ab', 3),
    abbrev('abc', 'ab', 999999999999999999) abbrev('abc', 'xy', 0)

1 1 0 0 0
[bif.abbrev.empty]

When info is the null string, it is the beginning of every information, the null string included, so the answer is 1 when length is omitted or 0, and 0 when length is 1 or more. When information is the null string, only a null info can be a beginning of it.

say abbrev('STAMP', '') abbrev('STAMP', '', 0) abbrev('STAMP', '', 1),
    abbrev('', '') abbrev('', '', 0) abbrev('', '', 1) abbrev('', 'a')

1 1 0 1 1 0 0
[bif.abbrev.exact]

The characters are compared for equality exactly, one by one. Case matters, no numeric comparison is made, and whitespace and every other character, '00'x among them, count like any other.

say abbrev('Stamp', 'sta') abbrev('1.50', '1.5') abbrev('1.50', '1.500'),
    abbrev('01', '1') abbrev('a b', 'a ') abbrev('a b', 'a') abbrev('a b', 'a  ')
say abbrev('a' || '00'x || 'b', 'a' || '00'x) abbrev('a' || '00'x, 'a' || '01'x)

0 1 0 0 1 1 0
1 0

ABS

ABS(number)

ANSI: 9.4.1; rexxref: Functions > Built-in Functions > ABS (Absolute Value)

Deviations: D4, D97

ABS answers the magnitude of a number: the number without its minus sign, rounded to NUMERIC DIGITS digits.

Arguments

[bif.abs.method]

ABS is a builtin that runs as a String method, and number, its only argument, is the receiver. number is a number. The argument count is checked by the builtin call rules: one is required and one is the most.

say abs(-3) (-3)~abs '-3'~abs
signal on syntax name a
say abs()
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say abs(,)
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say abs(1, 2)
c: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name d
say abs('three')
d: say condition('o')~code

3 3 3
40.3
40.3
40.4
93.943

The result

[bif.abs.result]

ABS returns the number rounded to NUMERIC DIGITS digits with its sign removed, and written in plain or scientific notation as that rule says, with NUMERIC DIGITS as the trigger. So the result has the value of the number when it is not negative, and the value of its negation when it is.

say abs('45.6') abs(' -0.809') abs('-1.500') abs('+4') abs('-1E2')
numeric digits 4
say abs('-123456') abs('123.456') abs('-0.00012345')
numeric form engineering
say abs('-123456')

45.6 0.809 1.500 4 100
1.235E+5 123.5 0.0001235
123.5E+3
[bif.abs.zero]

ABS of a number whose value is zero is 0, whatever its written form and sign.

say abs('-0') abs('0.00') abs('-0.0E5') abs(' +0 ')

0 0 0 0
[bif.abs.rounding]

The rounding is done before the sign is removed, and does not depend on the sign. It is the only change ABS makes to the magnitude.

numeric digits 3
say abs('-1.235') abs('1.235') abs('-1.2349') abs('9996') abs('-0.9995')

1.24 1.24 1.23 1.00E+4 1.00

Deviations

[bif.abs.deviation.4]

interrexx does not specify whether the answer of ABS is the same object as another string of equal value: as number itself, when the call leaves it unchanged, or as an equal string produced some other way. Through identityHash, or as a key of an IdentityTable, the answer may be either, and a program can rely only on the value, which is equal under ==. ooRexx differs: it answers the argument itself in a case where interrexx may answer an equal new string.

s = '12' || '5'
say (abs(s) == s) (abs('125') == '125') (abs(-s) == s)

1 1 1
[bif.abs.deviation.97]

ABS writes its answer in the NUMERIC FORM in force at the call, as the result rule says, also for a string that was converted to a number under the other form before. ooRexx may answer such a string as it was written.

numeric digits 3
say abs('0.0000001')
numeric form engineering
say abs('0.0000001')

1E-7
100E-9

ADDRESS

ADDRESS()

ANSI: 9.5.1; rexxref: Functions > Built-in Functions > ADDRESS

ADDRESS answers the name of the environment to which the program sends the commands it does not recognize as anything else: the name that the ADDRESS instruction last set, or the name the program started with.

Arguments

[bif.address.args]

ADDRESS takes no argument. The argument count is checked by the builtin call rules: none is required and none is the most, so a call with any argument, whatever it is, raises SYNTAX 40.4, and places that are only omitted add nothing. ADDRESS does not run as a String method: sending the message ADDRESS to a string raises SYNTAX 97.1.

d = address()
say address(,) == d
signal on syntax name a
say address('I')
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say address(, 'O')
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say 'x'~address
c: say condition('o')~code

1
40.4
40.4
97.1

Note. The ANSI draft (9.5.1) lets ADDRESS take an option that asks for the targets of command input and output as well. ooRexx does not, and neither does this book.

The result

[bif.address.initial]

Which environment a program starts with is not specified: it is the one that the platform and the way the program was started choose, and its name is different on different systems. What is fixed is that the ADDRESS instruction with no operand, given before any other ADDRESS instruction, leaves the environment as it was: the environment the program started with is also the one that the instruction would swap back to.

d = address()
address
say address() == d
address
say address() == d

1
1
[bif.address.name]

After ADDRESS name, the result is the name written in uppercase when it is a symbol, and exactly as written when it is a string, the case, leading and trailing blanks included. After ADDRESS VALUE expression, or an expression in parentheses, it is the value of the expression, also when that is the null string; a value that is not a string is replaced by a string, as a string argument says. The name is not checked and need not name any environment the program can use.

x = 'dyn Name '
address foo
say '['address()']'
address 'Mixed Case '
say '['address()']'
address value x
say '['address()']'
address (x)
say '['address()']'
address ''
say '['address()']' length(address())
address foo.bar
say '['address()']'

[FOO]
[Mixed Case ]
[dyn Name ]
[dyn Name ]
[] 0
[FOO.BAR]

Note. The reference manual says trailing whitespace is removed from the result. Neither interrexx nor ooRexx does so, and this rule matches them.

[bif.address.swap]

The ADDRESS instruction with no operand makes the previous environment the current one and the current one the previous one, so a second such instruction undoes the first. An instruction that sets a name makes the environment that was current the previous one, also when the name is the same as the current one, so after that the instruction with no operand changes nothing.

address first
address second
say address()
address
say address()
address
say address()
address second
address second
address
say address()

SECOND
FIRST
SECOND
SECOND
[bif.address.command]

ADDRESS name command sends one command to the named environment and changes neither the current environment nor the previous one, so the result and what the instruction with no operand swaps back to are as they were before it.

d = address()
address first
address system 'exit 0'
say address() rc
address
say address() == d

FIRST 0
1

Scope

[bif.address.scope.routine]

An internal routine, one that the program calls by its label, starts with the caller's current environment and its previous one, and when it returns, the caller has its own back: a setting made inside the routine, by ADDRESS instructions or in a routine it called, is lost on return. This holds for a routine with PROCEDURE and for one without it.

address outer
call plain
say address()
call hidden
say address()
call nested
say address()
exit
plain:
say 'plain' address()
address inner
say 'plain' address()
return
hidden: procedure
say 'hidden' address()
address deeper
say 'hidden' address()
return
nested:
call plain
say 'nested' address()
return

plain OUTER
plain INNER
OUTER
hidden OUTER
hidden DEEPER
OUTER
plain OUTER
plain INNER
nested OUTER
OUTER
[bif.address.scope.method]

A method, and a ::ROUTINE, starts with the environment the program started with, not the caller's, and as for an internal routine, a setting made in it is lost when it returns. Both have the start environment as the previous one too, so the instruction with no operand there swaps back to it.

d = address()
address outer
o = .o~new
say (o~start == d) (o~set == 'INNER') address()
say (o~start == d) address()
address one
say (word(rr(), 1) == d) (word(rr(), 2) == d) (word(rr(), 3) == d) address()
exit
::routine rr
a = address()
address
b = address()
address x
return a b address()
::class o
::method start
return address()
::method set
address inner
return address()

1 1 OUTER
1 OUTER
1 1 0 ONE
[bif.address.scope.interpret]

Code run by INTERPRET shares the environment of the code that runs it: a setting made there is still in effect after the INTERPRET ends.

address outer
interpret 'address inner'
say address()
interpret 'say address()'

INNER
INNER

ARG

ARG([n [, option]])

ANSI: 9.5.2; rexxref: Functions > Built-in Functions > ARG (Argument)

ARG reports on the arguments of the routine, method or program that is running: how many there were, what one of them was, whether one was passed at all, or all of them from a given one on.

Arguments

[bif.arg.args]

ARG takes at most two arguments, n and option, and both are optional. The argument count is checked by the builtin call rules: none is required and two is the most, so a call with three raises SYNTAX 40.4. ARG does not run as a String method: sending the message ARG to a string raises SYNTAX 97.1.

call show 'a'
exit
show:
say arg() arg(,) arg(1) arg(1, ) arg(1, 'E')
signal on syntax name a
say arg(1, 'E', 1)
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say 'a'~arg
b: say condition('o')~code

1 1 a a 1
40.4
97.1
[bif.arg.n.check]

n is a whole number that passes the whole-number rules and whose value is at least 1. A value of 0 or less raises SYNTAX 40.14; -0 is 0. A string that is not a whole number raises SYNTAX 40.12, the null string included, and so does a number whose magnitude is too large. The caller's NUMERIC DIGITS plays no part. These are not the range errors of the String-method builtins.

numeric digits 1
call show 'a', 'b'
exit
show:
say arg(2) arg(' 2 ') arg('2.0') arg(1e0)
signal on syntax name a
say arg(0)
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say arg('-0')
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say arg('')
c: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name d
say arg(1.5)
d: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name e
say arg(1e30)
e: say condition('o')~code

b b b a

40.14

[bif.arg.option.check]

option is a string; its first character, in either case, selects what ARG answers, and every character after the first is ignored. The letters are A, E, N and O. Any other first character, and the null string, raises SYNTAX 40.904. When option is given and n is omitted, the call raises SYNTAX 40.5. n is checked before option.

call show 'a'
exit
show:
say arg(1, 'E') arg(1, 'exists') arg(1, 'OMITTED') arg(1, 'n') arg(1, 'Array')~items
signal on syntax name a
say arg(1, 'x')
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say arg(1, '')
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say arg(1, ' e')
c: say condition('o')~code

say arg(, 'e')
d: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name e
say arg(0, 'x')
e: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name f
say arg(1, 1)
f: say condition('o')~code

The number of arguments

[bif.arg.count]

Without n, ARG answers the number of arguments of the call that started the running routine, method or program: the position of the last argument that was not omitted. Omitted places at the end of the list add nothing, and a call with only omitted places has no arguments. An omitted argument before a later one counts, and so does an argument that is the null string. The answer is written as a count, and whether it is a new object is not specified.

call show
call show 'a', 'b'
call show 'a', , 'c'
call show , 'b'
call show ''
x = show('a', , )
y = show(, )
exit
show:
say arg()
return 0

0
2
3
2
1
1
0

One argument

[bif.arg.n]

With n and no option, ARG answers argument n itself, the object the caller passed and not a string made from it. When argument n was omitted, or n is greater than the number of arguments, ARG answers the null string.

call show 'one', , .nil, .array~of(1, 2)
exit
show:
say '['arg(1)']' '['arg(2)']' '['arg(3)']' arg(4)~class arg(4)~items
say '['arg(5)']' '['arg(999999)']' '['arg(999999999999999999)']'

[one] [] [The NIL object] The Array class 2
[] [] []
[bif.arg.option.normal]

With the option N, ARG answers what it does for n alone.

call show 'x', , 'z'
exit
show:
say '['arg(1, 'N')']' '['arg(2, 'N')']' '['arg(3, 'N')']' '['arg(4, 'N')']'

[x] [] [z] []

Omitted and null arguments

[bif.arg.option.exists]

With the option E, ARG answers 1 when argument n was passed, and 0 when it was omitted or n is greater than the number of arguments. An argument whose expression is the null string was passed, so the answer for it is 1.

call show 'a', , '', , 'e'
exit
show:
say arg(1, 'E') arg(2, 'E') arg(3, 'E') arg(4, 'E') arg(5, 'E') arg(6, 'E')

1 0 1 0 1 0
[bif.arg.option.omitted]

With the option O, ARG answers the opposite of E: 0 when argument n was passed, 1 when it was omitted or n is greater than the number of arguments.

call show 'a', , '', , 'e'
call show
exit
show:
say arg(1, 'O') arg(2, 'O') arg(3, 'O') arg(4, 'O') arg(5, 'O') arg(6, 'O')
return

0 1 0 1 0 1
1 1 1 1 1 1
[bif.arg.null-versus-omitted]

Only the options E and O tell a null-string argument from an omitted one: ARG(n) and the option N answer the null string for both.

call show '', 'b'
call show , 'b'
exit
show:
say '['arg(1)']' arg(1, 'E') arg(1, 'O') (arg(1) == '')
return

[] 1 0 1
[] 0 1 1

All arguments from one on

[bif.arg.option.array]

With the option A, ARG answers an array of the arguments from argument n on. The item at index i is argument n + i - 1, for every i up to the number of arguments from n on, and an index whose argument was omitted has no item. The array has no places when n is greater than the number of arguments.

call show 'a', , 'c', , 'e'
exit
show:
do n = 1 to 6
  a = arg(n, 'A')
  s = ''
  do i = 1 to a~size
    if a~hasIndex(i) then s = s i':'a[i]
    else s = s i':-'
  end
  say 'n='n 'size' a~size 'items' a~items '|'s
end

n=1 size 5 items 3 | 1:a 2:- 3:c 4:- 5:e
n=2 size 4 items 2 | 1:- 2:c 3:- 4:e
n=3 size 3 items 2 | 1:c 2:- 3:e
n=4 size 2 items 1 | 1:- 2:e
n=5 size 1 items 1 | 1:e
n=6 size 0 items 0 |

Which arguments

[bif.arg.scope]

ARG answers for the routine, method or program whose code is running: for an internal or external routine, the arguments of the call that started it; for a method, the arguments of the message; for a program, those it was started with. When a routine returns, the caller's arguments are what ARG reports again. A routine does not see its caller's arguments, whether or not it is declared with PROCEDURE. INTERPRET runs in the routine that holds it, so ARG there reports that routine's arguments. A routine that a CALL ON trap starts as a handler has one argument, the condition object (see CONDITION); a SIGNAL ON handler continues in the routine that holds its label, and so sees that routine's arguments.

say 'program' arg() '['arg(1)']'
call outer 'o1', 'o2'
exit
outer:
say 'outer' arg() arg(1)
call inner 'i1'
call plain 'p1'
say 'outer again' arg() arg(1) arg(2)
interpret 'say "interpreted" arg() arg(2)'
call on user foo name hu
call raiser
signal on syntax name hs
x = 1 + 'a'
hs: say 'signal handler' arg() arg(1)
return
raiser: procedure
raise user foo return
hu: say 'call handler' arg() arg(1)~class arg(2, 'E')
return
inner: procedure
say 'inner' arg() arg(1) '['arg(2)']'
return
plain:
say 'plain' arg() arg(1) '['arg(2)']'
return

program 0 []
outer 2 o1
inner 1 i1 []
plain 1 p1 []
outer again 2 o1 o2
interpreted 2 o2
call handler 1 The Directory class 0
signal handler 2 o1
[bif.arg.method]

In a method, ARG reports the arguments of the message that ran it, counted as for a routine: omitted places at the end add nothing, and an omitted place before a later argument counts. A routine that the method calls has its own arguments. A ::ROUTINE directive gives a routine that is called like any other, and a routine and a method with the same arguments see the same ARG answers.

o = .box~new
say o~m('p', , 'q')
say o~m()
say o~m(,)
say rt('p', , 'q')
say rt()
::class box
::method m
return arg() arg(1, 'E') arg(2, 'E') arg(3, 'E') '['arg(1)']' '['arg(2)']' '['arg(3)']'
::routine rt
return arg() arg(1, 'E') arg(2, 'E') arg(3, 'E') '['arg(1)']' '['arg(2)']' '['arg(3)']'

3 1 0 1 [p] [] [q]
0 0 0 0 [] [] []
0 0 0 0 [] [] []
3 1 0 1 [p] [] [q]
0 0 0 0 [] [] []
[bif.arg.large]

The answer for the count is exact however many arguments there are, and however small the NUMERIC DIGITS setting of the code that asks.

src = .array~of('numeric digits 3', 'return arg() arg(1200, "E") arg(1200)')
r = .routine~new('big', src)
a = .array~new
do i = 1 to 1200; a~append(i); end
say r~callWith(a)

1200 1 1200

Note. The ANSI draft (9.5.2) defines ARG over the arguments of the current level, with the options E, N and O. ooRexx adds the option A, and interrexx follows ooRexx.

B2X

B2X(binary_string)

ANSI: 9.6.1; rexxref: Functions > Built-in Functions > B2X (Binary to Hexadecimal)

Deviations: D4

B2X answers the hexadecimal digits that stand for a string of binary digits: four binary digits for each hexadecimal digit, in capital letters.

Arguments

[bif.b2x.method]

B2X is a builtin that runs as a String method, and binary_string, its only argument, is the receiver. The argument count is checked by the builtin call rules: one is required and one is the most.

say b2x('1010') '1010'~b2x
signal on syntax name a
say b2x()
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say b2x('1', '1')
b: say condition('o')~code

A A
40.3
40.4
[bif.b2x.digits]

binary_string is a string of binary digits, which may have whitespace between its digits and not at its ends, and which may be null. The errors those rules give are those of a binary string: SYNTAX 93.934 for a character that is not a digit, SYNTAX 93.932 for whitespace at an end and SYNTAX 93.977 for a gap at a place that is not a multiple of 4 digits from the end.

say b2x('10 0101 1100') b2x('0001' || '09'x || '1111')
signal on syntax name a
say b2x('12')
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say b2x('1111 ')
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say b2x('1 11')
c: say condition('o')~code

25C 1F
93.934
93.932
93.977

The result

[bif.b2x.result]

The answer has one hexadecimal digit for each 4 binary digits of binary_string, taken from the right: the last 4 digits, ignoring whitespace, make the last hexadecimal digit, the 4 before them the one before that, and so on. A group of 4 digits is written as the hexadecimal digit of its value, 0 to 9 and A to F, with the letters in capitals. Leading zero digits are kept.

say b2x('10010110') b2x('00001010') b2x('0000') b2x('1111 0001 0010')
say b2x('0000000011111111')

96 0A 0 F12
00FF
[bif.b2x.partial]

The leftmost group may have 1, 2 or 3 digits; it is read as the 4-digit group that has 0 digits before it, so that 110 stands for 0110. The answer has ceil(n/4) hexadecimal digits for n digits.

say b2x('1') b2x('10') b2x('110') b2x('11001') b2x('1 0000 0000')
say length(b2x(copies('1', 9)))

1 2 6 19 100
3
[bif.b2x.null]

When binary_string is the null string, the answer is the null string.

say '['b2x('')']' length(b2x(''))

[] 0
[bif.b2x.not-number]

B2X reads the characters of its argument and not its value as a number, so an argument written as a number is treated as the digits it is written with and NUMERIC DIGITS plays no part.

numeric digits 2
say b2x(101) b2x(1111) b2x(0) b2x(0001)

5 F 0 1

Deviations

[bif.b2x.deviation.4]

interrexx does not specify whether the answer of B2X is the same object as another string of equal value, as the shared rule says for every conversion function. A program can rely only on the value, which is equal under ==.

say (b2x('0110') == '6') (b2x('') == '') (b2x('1' || '0000') == '10')

1 1 1

BEEP

BEEP(frequency, duration)

rexxref: Functions > Built-in Functions > BEEP

BEEP asks the system to sound a tone of a given pitch and length, and answers the null string. It is meant to be used as a subroutine, for its effect.

Whether a tone is heard depends on the system and on the terminal the program runs on, and this book does not specify it. It specifies what a program can check: the arguments that are accepted, the answer, and what is written to standard output when no tone can be sounded.

Note. The examples run with their output captured, where no tone can be sounded, so every accepted call in them writes the bell character, code 7. Their output blocks are marked escaped and show it as \a, as Reading an example describes.

Arguments

[bif.beep.args]

Both arguments are required. BEEP does not run as a String method: sending the message BEEP to a string raises SYNTAX 97.1. For the number of arguments it follows the native call rule, so BEEP(100, 0, ) is a call with two arguments. The null string is not an omitted argument; it is a value that fails the checks below.

signal on syntax name a
say beep()
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say beep(, 0)
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say beep(100, )
c: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name d
say beep(100, 0, 1)
d: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name e
say '100'~beep(0)
e: say condition('o')~code
signal off syntax
say 'done'

88.901
88.901
88.901
88.922
97.1
done
[bif.beep.range]

frequency and duration are whole numbers in the form that rule gives. The value of each is its number rounded to 20 significant digits, whatever the NUMERIC DIGITS setting; when the first digit dropped is 5 or more, the magnitude rounds up, otherwise down. This is not the rule of the conventions, which rounds to 18 digits and raises SYNTAX 40.12. The frequency must be from 37 to 32767 and the duration from 0 to 60000. An argument that is not in that form, whose rounded value has a fractional part other than zero, that is out of its range, or that is the null string raises SYNTAX 88.907, and so does an object whose string value fails these checks, such as .nil. A rounded value whose magnitude is 10**18 or more is not a whole number for this purpose, whichever sign it has: it fails the form check, which comes before the range checks, as the order rule shows.

signal on syntax name a
call beep 36, 0
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
call beep 32768, 0
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
call beep 100, 60001
c: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name d
call beep 100, -1
d: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name e
call beep 1.5, 0
e: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name f
call beep 100, ''
f: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name g
call beep .nil, 0
g: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name h
call beep 36, 'x'
h: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name i
call beep '37.000000000000000001', 0
i: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name j
call beep 100, '60000.000000000000001'
j: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name k
call beep '36.9999999999999999994', 0
k: say condition('o')~code
signal off syntax
numeric digits 3
call beep ' + 100 ', '-0'
call beep '1e+2', '0.0e1'
call beep 99.99999999999999999999, 60000.0000000000000000001
call beep '37.0000000000000000001', '60000.0000000000000001'
call beep '36.9999999999999999995', 0
call beep 37, 0
call beep 32767, 0
call beep .mutablebuffer~new('12345'), 0
say 'done'
