88.907
88.907
88.907
88.907
88.907
88.907
88.907
88.907
88.907
88.907
\a\a\a\a\a\a\a\adone
[bif.beep.order]

A call with no third argument checks the frequency first and the duration next, each for being present and a whole number, and only then checks the ranges: a frequency that is not a whole number is reported before a missing duration, and a missing duration before a frequency out of range. A frequency of magnitude 10**18 or more is not a whole number, so it is reported before a missing duration, while a frequency below that magnitude that is out of range is reported after it. A third argument is reported before any other error, as the native call rule says: before an argument that is missing, that is not a whole number or that is out of range.

signal on syntax name a
x = beep('x', )
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
x = beep(36, )
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
x = beep(, 'x')
c: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name d
x = beep(36, 0, 1)
d: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name e
x = beep(100, 60001, 1)
e: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name f
x = beep(1E18, )
f: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name g
x = beep(999999999999999999, )
g: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name h
x = beep('-1E18')
h: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name i
x = beep(36)
i: say condition('o')~code

88.907
88.901
88.901
88.922
88.922
88.907
88.901
88.907
88.901

The result

[bif.beep.answer]

BEEP answers the null string, which is a string of length 0, for every accepted pair of arguments. A call as a subroutine therefore sets RESULT to the null string rather than dropping it.

say '[' || beep(100, 0) || ']' length(beep(37, 0))
call beep 32767, 0
say symbol('RESULT') length(result)

\a\a[] 0
\aVAR 0
[bif.beep.bell]

When no tone can be sounded, as when the output of the program is not a console, an accepted call writes one bell character, code 7, to standard output, at the point of the call, and nothing else. It is not written through the .OUTPUT monitor: a program that has redirected .OUTPUT still has the bell written to standard output. A call that raises an error writes nothing. When a tone can be sounded the program cannot rely on anything being written.

call beep 100, 0
say 'after'
signal on syntax name a
call beep 100, 60001
a: say condition('o')~code
sink = .counter~new
.output~destination(sink)
say 'hidden'
call beep 100, 0
.output~destination
say 'shown' sink~count
exit
::class counter
::attribute count
::method init
  expose count
  count = 0
::method say
  expose count
  count += 1

\aafter
88.907
\ashown 1

BITAND

BITAND(string1 [, string2] [, pad])

ANSI: 9.6.2; rexxref: Functions > Built-in Functions > BITAND (Bit by Bit AND)

Deviations: D4

BITAND combines two strings bit by bit, keeping a bit set only where both strings have it set, and answers the string of the combined characters. How the two strings are lined up and what happens when their lengths differ are the rules of the bit-by-bit functions, shared with BITOR and BITXOR.

Arguments

[bif.bitand.method]

BITAND is a builtin that runs as a String method, and string1, its first argument, is the receiver; string2 and pad become the message's arguments, in that order. Its arguments, their checks and their defaults are those of the bit-by-bit functions: string1 is required, string2 defaults to the null string, and pad has its own check and no default.

say c2x(bitand('f0'x, '3c'x)) c2x('f0'x~bitand('3c'x)) c2x('f0'x~bitand('3c'x, '00'x))
signal on syntax name a
say bitand('a', 'b', 'xy')
a: say condition('o')~code

30 30 30
40.23

The result

[bif.bitand.result]

A bit of the answer is set when the corresponding bit of both operands is set, and clear otherwise, for every character of the answer that both operands have. The characters that only the longer operand has follow the rules for unequal lengths and for a pad.

say c2x(bitand('f0'x, '3c'x)) c2x(bitand('ff'x, '5a'x)) c2x(bitand('00'x, '5a'x))
say c2x(bitand('7f'x, 'c3'x)) c2x(bitand('12'x || '34'x, 'f0'x || '0f'x))

30 5A 00
43 1004
[bif.bitand.mask]

A character ANDed with 'FF'x is unchanged, and one ANDed with '00'x becomes '00'x. So a pad of 'FF'x keeps the characters of the longer operand that lie past the end of the shorter, and a pad of '00'x clears them.

say c2x(bitand('abc', 'a', 'ff'x)) c2x(bitand('abc', 'a', '00'x))
say bitand('abc', , 'ff'x) c2x(bitand('abc', , '00'x))

616263 610000
abc 000000

Deviations

[bif.bitand.deviation.4]

interrexx does not specify whether the answer of BITAND is the same object as another string of equal value, as the shared rule says for every bit-by-bit function. A program can rely only on the value, which is equal under ==.

say (bitand('ab', 'ab') == 'ab') (bitand('x', , 'ff'x) == 'x')

1 1

BITOR

BITOR(string1 [, string2] [, pad])

ANSI: 9.6.3; rexxref: Functions > Built-in Functions > BITOR (Bit by Bit OR)

Deviations: D4

BITOR combines two strings bit by bit, setting a bit wherever either string has it set, and answers the string of the combined characters. How the two strings are lined up and what happens when their lengths differ are the rules of the bit-by-bit functions, shared with BITAND and BITXOR.

Arguments

[bif.bitor.method]

BITOR is a builtin that runs as a String method, and string1, its first argument, is the receiver; string2 and pad become the message's arguments, in that order. Its arguments, their checks and their defaults are those of the bit-by-bit functions: string1 is required, string2 defaults to the null string, and pad has its own check and no default.

say c2x(bitor('f0'x, '3c'x)) c2x('f0'x~bitor('3c'x)) c2x('f0'x~bitor('3c'x, '00'x))
signal on syntax name a
say bitor('a', 'b', 'xy')
a: say condition('o')~code

FC FC FC
40.23

The result

[bif.bitor.result]

A bit of the answer is set when the corresponding bit of either operand, or of both, is set, and clear otherwise, for every character of the answer that both operands have. The characters that only the longer operand has follow the rules for unequal lengths and for a pad.

say c2x(bitor('f0'x, '3c'x)) c2x(bitor('00'x, '5a'x)) c2x(bitor('ff'x, '5a'x))
say c2x(bitor('12'x || '34'x, 'f0'x || '0f'x)) c2x(bitor('a1'x, '1a'x))

FC 5A FF
F23F BB
[bif.bitor.mask]

A character ORed with '00'x is unchanged, and one ORed with 'FF'x becomes 'FF'x. So a pad of '00'x keeps the characters of the longer operand that lie past the end of the shorter, and a pad of 'FF'x sets every bit of them.

say c2x(bitor('abc', 'a', '00'x)) c2x(bitor('abc', 'a', 'ff'x))
say bitor('abc', , '00'x) c2x(bitor('abc', , 'ff'x))

616263 61FFFF
abc FFFFFF

Deviations

[bif.bitor.deviation.4]

interrexx does not specify whether the answer of BITOR is the same object as another string of equal value, as the shared rule says for every bit-by-bit function. A program can rely only on the value, which is equal under ==.

say (bitor('ab', 'ab') == 'ab') (bitor('x', , '00'x) == 'x')

1 1

BITXOR

BITXOR(string1 [, string2] [, pad])

ANSI: 9.6.4; rexxref: Functions > Built-in Functions > BITXOR (Bit by Bit Exclusive OR)

Deviations: D4

BITXOR combines two strings bit by bit, setting a bit where exactly one of the two strings has it set, and answers the string of the combined characters. How the two strings are lined up and what happens when their lengths differ are the rules of the bit-by-bit functions, shared with BITAND and BITOR.

Arguments

[bif.bitxor.method]

BITXOR is a builtin that runs as a String method, and string1, its first argument, is the receiver; string2 and pad become the message's arguments, in that order. Its arguments, their checks and their defaults are those of the bit-by-bit functions: string1 is required, string2 defaults to the null string, and pad has its own check and no default.

say c2x(bitxor('f0'x, '3c'x)) c2x('f0'x~bitxor('3c'x)) c2x('f0'x~bitxor('3c'x, '00'x))
signal on syntax name a
say bitxor('a', 'b', 'xy')
a: say condition('o')~code

CC CC CC
40.23

The result

[bif.bitxor.result]

A bit of the answer is set when the corresponding bit of exactly one of the two operands is set, and clear otherwise, for every character of the answer that both operands have. The characters that only the longer operand has follow the rules for unequal lengths and for a pad.

say c2x(bitxor('f0'x, '3c'x)) c2x(bitxor('00'x, '5a'x)) c2x(bitxor('ff'x, '5a'x))
say c2x(bitxor('12'x || '34'x, 'f0'x || '0f'x)) c2x(bitxor('a1'x, '1a'x))

CC 5A A5
E23B BB
[bif.bitxor.inverse]

A string combined with itself gives '00'x for every character, and combining twice with the same operand, with a pad or without one, restores the string when the operand is not longer than the string. A character combined with 'FF'x has every bit flipped, so a pad of 'FF'x flips the characters of the longer operand that lie past the end of the shorter.

s = 'secret'
say c2x(bitxor(s, s)) (bitxor(bitxor(s, 'key'), 'key') == s),
    (bitxor(bitxor(s, 'key', 'k'), 'key', 'k') == s)
say c2x(bitxor('a0'x, , 'ff'x)) c2x(bitxor('abc', 'a', 'ff'x))

000000000000 1 1
5F 009D9C

Deviations

[bif.bitxor.deviation.4]

interrexx does not specify whether the answer of BITXOR is the same object as another string of equal value, as the shared rule says for every bit-by-bit function. A program can rely only on the value, which is equal under ==.

say (bitxor('ab', '') == 'ab') (bitxor('', 'x', ) == 'x')

1 1

C2D

C2D(string [, n])

ANSI: 9.6.5; rexxref: Functions > Built-in Functions > C2D (Character to Decimal)

Deviations: D4

C2D answers the number that the characters of a string stand for, when each character is a digit of base 256, the first one the most significant. With a length n it reads the string as a signed number of n characters.

Arguments

[bif.c2d.method]

C2D is a builtin that runs as a String method, and string, its first argument, is the receiver; n becomes the message's argument. string is a string, and n is a length. The argument count is checked by the builtin call rules: one is required and two is the most.

say c2d('ff'x) 'ff'x~c2d 'ff'x~c2d(1)
signal on syntax name a
say c2d()
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say c2d(, 1)
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say c2d('a', 1, 1)
c: say condition('o')~code

255 255 -1
40.3
40.5
40.4
[bif.c2d.n.default]

When n is omitted, the string is read as a number with no sign whatever its leftmost bit is, and the answer is never negative. An omitted n is not an n of the length of string: with that n a string whose leftmost bit is set is negative.

say c2d('80'x) c2d('80'x, ) c2d('ff'x) c2d('ff'x, , )
say c2d('80'x, 1) c2d('ff'x, 1)

128 128 255 255
-128 -1

The result

[bif.c2d.unsigned]

Without n, the answer is the sum, over the characters of string, of the character's code times 256 to the power of the number of characters after it. Leading '00'x characters therefore change nothing.

say c2d('0c'x) c2d('0100'x) c2d('e3a1'x) c2d('00000007'x) c2d('abc')

12 256 58273 7 6382179
[bif.c2d.signed]

With n, the string is read as a signed number of n characters: it is brought to n characters by adding '00'x characters on its left or removing characters from there, and the answer is negative when the leftmost bit of the result is set. Padding with '00'x means that a string shorter than n is never negative, and that only the last n characters of a longer string matter.

say c2d('93'x, 1) c2d('93'x, 2) c2d('ffa5'x, 2) c2d('ffa5'x, 1) c2d('ff5a'x, 1)
say c2d('e3a1'x, 2) c2d('0107'x, 0) c2d('ff'x, 5) c2d('80'x, 1) c2d('7f'x, 1)

-109 147 -91 -91 90
-7263 0 255 -128 127
[bif.c2d.null]

When string is the null string, the answer is 0, with an n or without one.

say c2d('') c2d('', 0) c2d('', 1) c2d('', 8)

0 0 0 0
[bif.c2d.characters]

C2D reads the characters of string, whatever they are, and not their value as a number: a string of digits is a number in base 256 of the codes of its digits.

say c2d('1') c2d('12') c2d(12) c2d(1.5)

49 12594 12594 3223093
[bif.c2d.digits]

The answer must fit in the caller's NUMERIC DIGITS setting, by the rule for the answer: when it has more digits than that, the call raises SYNTAX 93.936. The caller's setting decides, not the length of the string: a string can be longer than that when its leading characters are '00'x, or when n cuts it short.

say c2d('ffffffff'x, 4) c2d(copies('00'x, 30) || 'ff'x) c2d('ffffffffffffffffff'x, 1)
signal on syntax name a
say c2d('ffffffff'x)
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say c2d('8000000000'x, 5)
b: say condition('o')~code
numeric digits 20
say c2d('ffffffffffffffff'x) c2d('8000000000000000'x, 8)
signal on syntax name c
say c2d('ffffffffffffffffff'x)
c: say condition('o')~code

-1 255 -1
93.936
93.936
18446744073709551615 -9223372036854775808
93.936
[bif.c2d.errors]

The checks of the call run in this order: the form of n as a whole number, SYNTAX 40.12; then the sign of n, SYNTAX 93.923; and then the number of digits of the answer, SYNTAX 93.936. A negative n is therefore raised even when the answer would not fit either.

signal on syntax name a
say c2d('ffffffffffff'x, 'x')
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say c2d('ffffffffffff'x, -1)
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say c2d('ffffffffffff'x)
c: say condition('o')~code

40.12
93.923
93.936

Deviations

[bif.c2d.deviation.4]

interrexx does not specify whether the answer of C2D is the same object as another string of equal value, as the shared rule says for every conversion function. A program can rely only on the value, which is equal under ==.

say (c2d('') == 0) (c2d('a') == 97) (c2d('00'x) == '0')

1 1 1

C2X

C2X(string)

ANSI: 9.6.6; rexxref: Functions > Built-in Functions > C2X (Character to Hexadecimal)

Deviations: D4

C2X answers the hexadecimal digits that stand for the characters of a string: two for each character, in capital letters.

Arguments

[bif.c2x.method]

C2X is a builtin that runs as a String method, and string, its only argument, is the receiver. string is a string, so no value of it raises an error. The argument count is checked by the builtin call rules: one is required and one is the most.

say c2x('A') 'A'~c2x
signal on syntax name a
say c2x()
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say c2x('a', 'b')
b: say condition('o')~code

41 41
40.3
40.4

The result

[bif.c2x.result]

The answer has two hexadecimal digits for each character of string, in order. The digits of a character are those of its code, from '00'x to 'FF'x: the code's value divided by 16, then its remainder, each as 0 to 9 or A to F in capitals.

say c2x('4567'x) c2x('7f80ff'x) c2x('Qz9') length(c2x('abc'))

4567 7F80FF 517A39 6
[bif.c2x.any-character]

Every character is converted like any other: '00'x, whitespace, line feed and the characters above '7F'x included. A string of digits is converted as the characters it consists of, not as a number, so NUMERIC DIGITS plays no part and the answer for a number is that of the string it is written as.

numeric digits 3
say c2x('00'x) c2x(' ' || '09'x || '0a'x) c2x(12345) c2x(-1) c2x(1.50) c2x(1e5)

00 20090A 3132333435 2D31 312E3530 314535
[bif.c2x.null]

When string is the null string, the answer is the null string.

say '['c2x('')']' length(c2x(''))

[] 0
[bif.c2x.inverse]

X2C turns the answer back into string: converting the answer of C2X with X2C gives string itself, for every string.

s = 'Mixed' || '00ff'x || ' case'
say (x2c(c2x(s)) == s) (x2c(c2x('')) == '')

1 1

Deviations

[bif.c2x.deviation.4]

interrexx does not specify whether the answer of C2X is the same object as another string of equal value, as the shared rule says for every conversion function. A program can rely only on the value, which is equal under ==.

say (c2x('a') == '61') (c2x('') == '') (c2x('ab') == '6162')

1 1 1

CENTER

CENTER(string, length [, pad])

ANSI: 9.3.2; rexxref: Functions > Built-in Functions > CENTER (or CENTRE)

Deviations: D4

CENTER returns a string of a given length with a string placed in the middle of it: padded on both sides when the string is shorter than the length, and cut at both ends when it is longer. CENTRE is another spelling of the same builtin.

Arguments

[bif.center.method]

CENTER is a builtin that runs as a String method, and string, its first argument, is the receiver; length and pad become the message's arguments, in that order. string is a string, length is a length, and pad is a pad. The arguments are checked in the order the conventions give, and the argument count by the builtin call rules: two are required and three is the most.

say center('pqr', 9) '|' 'pqr'~center(9, '.')
signal on syntax name a
say center('abc')
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say center('abc', 5, '*', 1)
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say center('abc', , '*')
c: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name d
say center('abc', 'x')
d: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name e
say center('abc', -1)
e: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name f
say center('abc', 5, '**')
f: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name g
say center('abc', -1, '**')
g: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name h
say center('abc', 1000000000000000000)
h: say condition('o')~code

   pqr    | ...pqr...
40.3
40.4
40.5
40.12
93.923
40.23
40.23
40.12
[bif.center.centre]

CENTRE is the same builtin as CENTER: it takes the same arguments, runs as the String method of that name, and gives the same result and the same errors for the same arguments.

say centre('abc', 7, '.') 'abc'~centre(7, '.') center('abc', 7, '.')
signal on syntax name a
say centre('abc', -1)
a: say condition('o')~code

..abc.. ..abc.. ..abc..
93.923
[bif.center.pad.default]

When pad is omitted, it is the blank, '20'x.

say '['center('ab', 6)']' '['center('ab', 6, )']'

[  ab  ] [  ab  ]

The result

[bif.center.result]

CENTER returns a string of exactly length characters. Let d be length less LENGTH(string). When d is 0 the result is string. When d is positive, the result is string with d copies of pad added, d divided by 2 and rounded down on the left and the rest on the right, so that the right-hand end gains the extra one when d is odd. When d is negative, the result is string with its first -d divided by 2 (rounded down) characters and its last -d less that many characters removed, so the right-hand end loses the extra one when -d is odd.

say '['center('xyz', 9)']' '['center('xyz', 10, '-')']' '['center('a', 4, '*')']'
say '['center('xyz', 3)']' '['center('Red green blue', 10)']' '['center('Red green blue', 9)']'
say '['center('abcde', 2)']' '['center('abcdef', 1)']' '['center('abcd', 3)']'

[   xyz   ] [---xyz----] [*a**]
[xyz] [d green bl] [d green b]
[bc] [c] [abc]
[bif.center.length.zero]

When length is 0, the result is the null string, for every string. pad is still checked, as a pad always is.

say '['center('abc', 0)']' '['center('', 0)']' '['center('abc', '-0', '.')']'
signal on syntax name a
say center('abc', 0, '')
a: say condition('o')~code

[] [] []
40.23
[bif.center.empty]

When string is the null string, the result is length copies of pad.

say '['center('', 4)']' '['center('', 3, '*')']'

[    ] [***]
[bif.center.bytes]

CENTER pads and cuts by character, one byte each, and copies unchanged every byte of string that it keeps: whitespace, control characters and '00'x are characters like any other, in string and as pad.

say c2x(center('610062'x, 6, '00'x)) c2x(center(' a ', 1))

006100620000 61

Note. Whether, when and with which code CENTER fails for a length whose result cannot be held in memory is not specified.

Deviations

[bif.center.deviation.4]

interrexx does not specify whether the answer of CENTER is the same object as another string of equal value: as string itself, when the call returns all of it unchanged as center(s, length(s)) does, or as an equal string produced some other way, such as the literal 'abc'. Through identityHash, or as a key of an IdentityTable, the answer may be either, and a program can rely only on the value, which is equal under ==. ooRexx differs: it often answers a new object where interrexx answers the existing one.

s = 'ab' || 'c'
say (center(s, 3) == s) (center('xabcx', 3) == 'abc')

CHANGESTR

CHANGESTR(needle, haystack, newneedle [, count])

ANSI: 9.3.4; rexxref: Functions > Built-in Functions > CHANGESTR

Deviations: D4

CHANGESTR copies a string, replacing the occurrences of one string in it with another. Occurrences that overlap are not both replaced, and a count argument can limit how many are.

Arguments

[bif.changestr.method]

CHANGESTR is a builtin that runs as a String method, and haystack, its second argument, is the receiver; needle, newneedle and count become the message's arguments, in that order. needle, haystack and newneedle are strings, and the function form takes needle first. count is a whole number, described by its own rule. The argument count is checked by the builtin call rules: three arguments are required and four is the most.

say changestr('an', 'banana', '__') 'banana'~changestr('an', '__') 'banana'~changestr('an', '__', 1)
signal on syntax name a
say changestr('a', 'abc')
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say changestr('a', 'abc', 'x', 1, 1)
b: say condition('o')~code

[bif.changestr.count]

count is a whole-number argument, so it raises SYNTAX 40.12 when it does not have that form or has a value that is not a whole number. A whole number below 0 raises SYNTAX 93.906; -0 is 0. The null string is not a whole number, so an empty count raises 40.12 and does not stand for an omitted one. The form check comes first, so a count that fails it raises 40.12 whatever its sign.

say changestr('a', 'banana', 'x', ' + 2 ') changestr('a', 'banana', 'x', '-0'),
    changestr('a', 'banana', 'x', '2.000')
signal on syntax name a
say changestr('a', 'banana', 'x', -1)
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say changestr('a', 'banana', 'x', '')
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say changestr('a', 'banana', 'x', '-0.4')
c: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name d
say changestr('a', 'banana', 'x', '-1e5')
d: say condition('o')~code

[bif.changestr.count.default]

When count is omitted, every occurrence that the result rule selects is replaced. A count at least the number of such occurrences has the same effect, however large it is, up to the largest value the argument accepts.

say changestr('a', 'banana', 'x') changestr('a', 'banana', 'x', ),
    changestr('a', 'banana', 'x', 3) changestr('a', 'banana', 'x', 999999999999999999)

bxnxnx bxnxnx bxnxnx bxnxnx

The result

[bif.changestr.result]

CHANGESTR scans haystack from its first character to its last. At each position where needle occurs, it appends newneedle to the result and continues with the character after the occurrence; where needle does not occur, it appends the character at that position and continues with the next one. Every occurrence found this way is replaced, up to count of them when count is given: after the countth replacement the rest of haystack is appended unchanged. The match is exact, so case matters, and every character of the strings, whitespace and '00'x included, is an ordinary character.

say changestr('o', 'foolish', '') changestr('o', 'foolish', '0') changestr('o', 'foolish', '0', 1)
say changestr('A', 'banana', 'x') changestr(' ', 'a b  c', '_')
say c2x(changestr('00'x, 'a' || '00'x || 'b', '0000'x))

flish f00lish f0olish
banana a_b__c
61000062
[bif.changestr.overlap]

Occurrences that overlap are not all replaced: an occurrence is replaced only when it begins after the end of the one replaced before it, as COUNTSTR counts them. The text that newneedle brings in is never searched again, so a newneedle that holds needle does not make the call replace more.

say changestr('aa', 'aaaaa', 'b') changestr('aba', 'ababababa', 'X'),
    changestr('a', 'aaaa', 'aa') changestr('a', 'aaaa', 'aa', 2)

bba XbXba aaaaaaaa aaaaaa
[bif.changestr.count.zero]

When count is 0, nothing is replaced and the result is haystack unchanged. count is still checked, as it always is.

say changestr('a', 'banana', 'x', 0) changestr('a', 'banana', 'x', '0.0')
signal on syntax name a
say changestr('a', 'banana', 'x', 'zero')
a: say condition('o')~code

banana banana
40.12
[bif.changestr.empty-needle]

When needle is the null string, it is taken to occur nowhere, so nothing is replaced and the result is haystack unchanged, for every newneedle and every count that passes its check.

say '['changestr('', 'abc', 'x')']' '['changestr('', 'abc', 'x', 2)']'
say '['changestr('', '', 'x')']'

[abc] [abc]
[]
[bif.changestr.empty-haystack]

When haystack is the null string, needle occurs in it nowhere, and the result is the null string, for every count that passes its check.

say '['changestr('a', '', 'x')']' '['changestr('a', '', 'x', 3)']'
signal on syntax name a
say changestr('a', '', 'x', -1)
a: say condition('o')~code

[] []
93.906
[bif.changestr.empty-newneedle]

When newneedle is the null string, the occurrences replaced are deleted: the result is haystack without them. This is not the same as omitting newneedle, which is an error.

say changestr('a', 'banana', '') '['changestr('banana', 'banana', '')']'
say changestr('a', 'banana', '', 2)

bnn []
bnna

Note. The ANSI draft (9.3.4) has no count argument; it replaces every occurrence, searching from the end of the previous one, which gives the rules above for the call without count. The count argument and its checks follow ooRexx.

Deviations

[bif.changestr.deviation.4]

interrexx does not specify whether the answer of CHANGESTR is the same object as another string of equal value: as haystack itself, when the call replaces nothing, or as an equal string produced some other way, such as the literal 'banana'. Through identityHash, or as a key of an IdentityTable, the answer may be either, and a program can rely only on the value, which is equal under ==. ooRexx differs: it often answers a new object where interrexx answers the existing one.

s = 'ban' || 'ana'
say (changestr('x', s, 'y') == s) (changestr('', s, 'y') == 'banana')

1 1

CHARIN

CHARIN([name] [, [start] [, length]])

ANSI: 9.7.1; rexxref: Functions > Built-in Functions > CHARIN (Character Input)

Deviations: D62

CHARIN reads characters from a stream and answers them as a string. It reads from the stream's read position, which a start argument can set first, and it reads as many characters as length asks for, one when length is omitted.

Arguments

[bif.charin.args]

name is a string that names the stream; when it is omitted or null, the standard input is read. start and length are whole-number arguments whose value the stream rules give. CHARIN is not a String method. It takes three arguments at the most, by the call rules, and none is required. start is checked as the stream rules say, and length must not be negative.

f = 'spec-charin-args.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
call charout f, 'abcdef'
call charout f
say charin(f, 2, ) charin(f, , 2) charin(, , 0)'|'
signal on syntax name a
say charin(f, 1, 1, 1)
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say charin(f, 1, 'two')
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say charin(f, 1, -1)
c: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name d
say charin(f, 0)
d: say condition('o')~code
call sysfiledelete f

b cd |
40.4
40.12
88.907
93.907
[bif.charin.length.default]

When length is omitted, it is 1.

f = 'spec-charin-default.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
call charout f, 'xyz'
call charout f
say charin(f) charin(f, ) charin(f, 3)
call sysfiledelete f

x y z

The result

[bif.charin.result]

CHARIN returns the length characters that follow the read position, the characters in the order they are in the stream, and moves the read position past them. If fewer characters are left, it returns the ones that are left and raises the NOTREADY condition. Every character is data, a line end included, and so is '1a'x.

f = 'spec-charin-result.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
call charout f, 'ab' || '0d0a'x || 'c' || '1a'x || 'd'
call charout f
say c2x(charin(f, 1, 2)) c2x(charin(f, , 2)) c2x(charin(f, , 3))
say c2x(charin(f, 1, 100))
call sysfiledelete f

6162 0D0A 631A64
61620D0A631A64

Note. The second line shows the short read at the end of the data: 100 characters were asked for and the 7 that the stream has were returned.

[bif.charin.start]

When start is given, it is the read position for this call: CHARIN reads from the character at that position, the first of the stream being at 1, and leaves the read position after the last character read.

f = 'spec-charin-start.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
call charout f, '0123456789'
call charout f
say charin(f, 4, 3) charin(f, , 2) charin(f, 1, 2) charin(f)
say charin(f, 10, 1) charin(f, 9, 5)
call sysfiledelete f

345 67 01 2
9 89

The end of the data

[bif.charin.end]

When the read position is after the last character, CHARIN returns the null string and raises the NOTREADY condition. The same holds for a start that is after the last character, one past it or further, and the read position is then left where it was.

f = 'spec-charin-end.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
call charout f, 'abc'
call charout f
n = 0
call on notready name nr
x = charin(f, 4)
say 'one' '[' || x || ']' n chars(f)
x = charin(f, 9, 2)
say 'two' '[' || x || ']' n
x = charin(f, 3)
say 'three' '[' || x || ']' n
x = charin(f)
say 'four' '[' || x || ']' n
call sysfiledelete f
exit
nr: n = n + 1
return

one [] 1 3
two [] 2
three [c] 2
four [] 3

Note. A call that reads exactly the characters that are left raises nothing; only the next call, which finds none, does. The example shows the condition raised after the clause that made the call, which is when a CALL ON trap runs.

[bif.charin.zero]

When length is 0, CHARIN reads nothing and returns the null string. If start is given and names a character of the stream, it still sets the read position. A length of 0 raises NOTREADY only when start is after the last character, and that is the case of the end.

f = 'spec-charin-zero.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
call charout f, 'abcdef'
call charout f
n = 0
call on notready name nr
x = charin(f, 3, 0)
say '[' || x || ']' n charin(f, , 2)
x = charin(f, 7, 0)
say '[' || x || ']' n chars(f)
x = charin(f, 4, 0)
say '[' || x || ']' n chars(f)
call sysfiledelete f
exit
nr: n = n + 1
return

[] 0 cd
[] 1 2
[] 1 3
[bif.charin.missing]

A file that does not exist has no characters: CHARIN returns the null string and raises NOTREADY, whatever start is and whatever the valid length is, and creates no file. A name that cannot be opened for another reason, a directory for example, is answered the same way. The start of such a call is not checked (see the start rule), but a length that is not valid is.

n = 0
call on notready name nr
x = charin('spec-charin-nofile.tmp')
say '[' || x || ']' n
x = charin('spec-charin-nofile.tmp', 0, 5)
say '[' || x || ']' n
x = charin('.', 1, 1)
say '[' || x || ']' n
say stream('spec-charin-nofile.tmp', 'c', 'query exists') == ''
signal on syntax name a
say charin('spec-charin-nofile.tmp', 1, -1)
a: say condition('o')~code
exit
nr: n = n + 1
return

[] 2
[] 3

[bif.charin.stdin]

Without a name, CHARIN reads the standard input. It returns up to length characters of the input, and no more than the input holds. When there is no character left in the input, it returns the null string and raises NOTREADY.

call on notready name nr
x = charin()
y = charin(, , 7)
say '[' || x || ']' '[' || y || ']' '[' || charin(, , 0) || ']'
exit

notready STDIN
notready STDIN

[bif.charin.deviation.62]

A CHARIN that reads no character because the data is at its end leaves the stream in the state NOTREADY, with the description NOTREADY:EOF (STREAM answers them with its S and D options). ooRexx leaves the state ERROR, with the description ERROR:0.

f = 'spec-charin-dev62.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
call charout f, 'ab'
call charout f
say charin(f, 1, 2) '['charin(f)']' stream(f, 's') stream(f, 'd')
call sysfiledelete f

ab [] NOTREADY NOTREADY:EOF

CHAROUT

CHAROUT([name] [, [string] [, start]])

ANSI: 9.7.2; rexxref: Functions > Built-in Functions > CHAROUT (Character Output)

Deviations: D60

CHAROUT writes the characters of a string to a stream and answers how many of them it could not write, which is 0 when the write succeeded. Given a start it writes there; given no string it only sets the write position or, with a name alone, closes the stream.

Arguments

[bif.charout.args]

name is a string that names the stream; when it is omitted or null, the standard output is written. string is a string too. start is a whole-number argument whose value the stream rules give, and a valid start. CHAROUT is not a String method. It takes three arguments at the most, by the call rules, and none is required.

f = 'spec-charout-args.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
signal on syntax name a
say charout(f, 'abc', 1, 1)
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say charout(f, 'abc', 'two')
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say charout(f, 'abc', 0)
c: say condition('o')~code
say charout(f, 12, ) charout(f, 'x', 1.0)
call charout f
say charin(f, 1, 9)
call sysfiledelete f

40.4
40.12
93.907
0 0
x2

The result

[bif.charout.result]

CHAROUT writes the characters of string, in order, from the write position, and moves the write position past them. A character written at a position inside the data replaces the one there; written after the last character it extends the data. The answer is the number of characters of string not written, 0 when all were: it is written as a count, and whether it is a new object is not specified.

f = 'spec-charout-result.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
say charout(f, 'Jelly') charout(f, ' world') charout(f, 7 * 6)
call charout f, 'B', 1
say charin(f, 1, 20)
call sysfiledelete f

0 0 0
Belly world42
[bif.charout.start]

When start is given, it is the write position for this call: the first character of the stream is at 1. If it is more than one past the last character, the characters between the end of the data and start are '00'x.

f = 'spec-charout-start.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
call charout f, 'ab'
call charout f, 'Q', 5
call charout f, 'R', 3
say c2x(charin(f, 1, 20))
call sysfiledelete f

6162520051
[bif.charout.position-only]

When string is omitted or null and start is given, CHAROUT writes nothing, sets the write position to start and answers 0; the next write that gives no start begins there. If both are omitted, the call is a close. A null string with no start writes nothing and leaves the write position alone.

f = 'spec-charout-pos.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
call charout f, 'abcdef'
say charout(f, , 2) charout(f, '', 4)
call charout f, 'XY'
call charout f, ''
call charout f, 'Z'
say charin(f, 1, 20)
call sysfiledelete f

0 0
abcXYZ
[bif.charout.close]

When both string and start are omitted, CHAROUT closes the stream and answers 0. The characters written are in the stream afterwards, and its next use opens it afresh. CHAROUT opens a stream that is not open in order to close it, so on a file that does not exist this creates it; the same is true of every call of CHAROUT, even one that writes nothing. A standard stream is closed in the same way, and its next use opens it again, as the lifetime rule says; ooRexx differs (see Deviation 98).

f = 'spec-charout-close.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
say stream(f, 'c', 'query exists') == ''
say charout(f)
say (stream(f, 'c', 'query exists') \== '') chars(f)
call charout f, 'abc'
say charout(f) charin(f, , 1)
call sysfiledelete f

1
0
1 0
0 a

When the write fails

[bif.charout.fail]

When the stream cannot be written, CHAROUT writes nothing, answers the number of characters of string, and raises NOTREADY. That is the case when the name cannot be opened for writing, as a name in a directory that does not exist, or a directory, and when the name is STDIN. For a name that cannot be opened, a start is not checked (see the start rule). Nor is a start given with the name STDIN checked beyond its form, whatever its value (see the transient rule): the call fails in the same way, and without a string it answers 0.

n = 0
call on notready name nr
x = charout('spec-charout-nodir/x.tmp', 'abc')
say x n
x = charout('.', 'hello', 0)
say x n
x = charout('stdin', 'q')
say x n
exit
nr: n = n + 1
return

5 2
1 3

n = 0
call on notready name nr
say charout('stdin', 'a', 0) n
say charout('STDIN:', 'abc', -1) n
say charout('stdin', , 1) n
say n
exit
nr: n = n + 1
return

1 0
3 1
0 2
3

The standard streams

[bif.charout.std]

Without a name, CHAROUT writes to the standard output, and with the name STDERR to the standard error. A start for the standard output or the standard error, when it is transient, raises SYNTAX 93.958.

call charout , 'a'
call charout 'STDOUT:', 'b'
say charout(, 'c')
signal on syntax name a
call charout , 'd', 5
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
call charout 'STDERR', , 3
b: say condition('o')~code
signal off syntax
say charout('STDERR', 'x')

abc0

93.958
0

[bif.charout.deviation.60]

A '1a'x at the end of a stream is data like any other character: a write without a start goes after it, and a write at its position replaces it. ooRexx treats a final '1a'x as the end of the file, and a write there begins at its position.

f = 'spec-charout-dev60.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
call charout f, 'ab' || '1a'x
call charout f
call charout f, 'cd'
call charout f
say c2x(charin(f, 1, 20))
call sysfiledelete f

CHARS([name])

ANSI: 9.7.3; rexxref: Functions > Built-in Functions > CHARS (Characters Remaining)

CHARS answers how many characters a stream has left to read. It reads nothing and moves nothing.

Arguments

[bif.chars.args]

name is a string that names the stream; when it is omitted or null, the standard input is asked. CHARS is not a String method. It takes one argument at the most, by the call rules, and none is required.

f = 'spec-chars-args.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
call charout f, 'abc'
call charout f
say chars(f) chars(f, )
signal on syntax name a
say chars(f, 1)

signal on syntax name b
say chars(f, , 1)
b: say condition('o')~code
call sysfiledelete f

40.4
40.4

The result

[bif.chars.result]

For a file, CHARS answers the number of characters from the read position to the end of the data, the line ends among them. It is 0 when no character is left. The answer is written as a count, and whether it is a new object is not specified. Characters written to the stream are counted as soon as they are written, if the read position is not past them.

f = 'spec-chars-result.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
call charout f, 'ab' || '0d0a'x || 'cd'

say charin(f, , 2) chars(f)

say chars(f) '['charin(f, 7, 0)']' chars(f)

A name that cannot be opened for reading, a file that does not exist or a directory for example, has no characters: CHARS answers 0, raises NOTREADY and creates no file. CHARS raises no condition at the end of the data.

call on notready name nr
x = chars('spec-chars-nofile.tmp')
say x n (stream('spec-chars-nofile.tmp', 'c', 'query exists') == '')

Deviations

[bif.chars.deviation.54]

CHARS of the standard input, or of any other transient stream, answers whether characters wait to be read, 0 for none and a positive number otherwise, and consumes none. The positive number is not specified. When the input is empty, as it is for the examples of this book, the answer is 0. ooRexx answers 1 to some of these questions when the standard input is /dev/null, which holds no character. For an empty pipe, a pipe that holds data, and a file, it answers as this rule says.

say chars() chars('stdin')

COMPARE

COMPARE(string1, string2 [, pad])

ANSI: 9.3.5; rexxref: Functions > Built-in Functions > COMPARE

COMPARE tests two strings for equality and, when they differ, answers the position of the first character where they do. The shorter string is treated as if a pad character followed it.

Arguments

[bif.compare.method]

COMPARE is a builtin that runs as a String method, and string1, its first argument, is the receiver; string2 and pad become the message's arguments, in that order. string1 and string2 are strings, and pad is a pad. The arguments are checked in the order the conventions give, and the argument count by the builtin call rules: two are required and three is the most.

say compare('abc', 'abd') 'abc'~compare('abd') 'abc'~compare('ab', 'c')
signal on syntax name a
say compare('abc', 'ab', 'cc')
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say compare('abc', 'ab', '')
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say compare('abc')
c: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name d
say compare('abc', 'ab', 'c', 1)
d: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name e
say compare(, 'ab')
e: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name f
say compare('abc', , '')
f: say condition('o')~code

3 3 0
40.23
40.23
40.3
40.4
40.5
40.5
[bif.compare.pad.default]

When pad is omitted, it is the blank, '20'x.

say compare('xy ', 'xy') compare('xy ', 'xy', ) compare('xy  q', 'xy')

0 0 5
[bif.compare.pad.checked]

pad is checked as a pad always is, whatever the two strings are: it raises SYNTAX 40.23 when it is not one character even if the strings are equal or null and so no padding takes place.

signal on syntax name a
say compare('abc', 'abc', 'xy')
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say compare('', '', '')
b: say condition('o')~code

40.23
40.23

The result

[bif.compare.result]

Let p be pad, and let the two strings be made equally long by appending as many copies of p to the shorter one as are missing. COMPARE then returns 0 when the two lengthened strings are the same string, and otherwise the position of the first character at which they differ: the smallest i for which their characters at position i are not the same. The answer is written as a count, and whether it is a new object is not specified.

say compare('tuv', 'tuv') compare('tuv', 'tx') compare('abc', 'xbc'),
    compare('abc', 'abd') compare('abc', 'ab') compare('ab', 'abc')

0 2 1 3 3 3
[bif.compare.padding]

The padding makes a string equal to itself followed by any number of copies of pad, and only that. A string that is the other one followed by characters that are not all pad differs from it at the first such character; a longer string whose extra characters are all pad does not differ from the shorter one.

say compare('xy ', 'xy') compare('xy ', 'xy', ' ') compare('xy ', 'xy', 'z'),
    compare('xy== ', 'xy', '=') compare('xyzz', 'xy', 'z') compare('xyzzq', 'xy', 'z')

0 0 3 5 0 5
[bif.compare.empty]

The null string is a string of no characters, so it takes the padding alone: it is equal to the other string when that one is empty or all pad, and otherwise differs from it at the position of the first character of the other string that is not pad.

say compare('', '') compare('', 'a') compare('a', '') compare('', '  ') compare('', '  a')
say compare('', '  ', 'x') compare('', 'xx', 'x') compare('xx', '', 'x'),
    compare('xxy', '', 'x')

0 1 1 0 3
1 0 0 3
[bif.compare.exact]

Characters are compared for equality exactly, one by one. Case matters, no numeric comparison is made, and whitespace and every other character, '00'x among them, count like any other.

say compare('abc', 'ABC') compare('1', '1.0') compare(1, 1) compare('a b', 'a  b'),
    compare('a' || '00'x, 'a') compare('a' || '00'x, 'a', '00'x)

1 2 0 3 2 0

Note. The ANSI draft (9.3.5) pads the shorter string with LEFT and compares character by character. That gives the answers above.

CONDITION

CONDITION([option])

ANSI: 9.5.3; rexxref: Functions > Built-in Functions > CONDITION

Deviations: D106

CONDITION reports what the running routine knows about the condition that a trap caught most recently: its name, the instruction that handled it, the state of its trap, and the descriptive information it carried. The conditions themselves, and the traps that catch them, are not defined on this page; it specifies what CONDITION answers for each of its options, before any trap has caught a condition, after a SIGNAL ON trap or a CALL ON trap has caught one, and in the code that follows.

Arguments

[bif.condition.args]

CONDITION takes at most one argument, option, which is optional. The argument count is checked by the builtin call rules: none is required and one is the most, so a call with two arguments raises SYNTAX 40.4, whatever they are, and a call with only omitted places counts as a call with no arguments. CONDITION does not run as a String method: sending the message CONDITION to a string raises SYNTAX 97.1.

say 'x'~condition
b: say condition('o')~code

option is a string. Its first character, in either case, selects what CONDITION answers, and every character after the first is ignored, so Condition, cond and C select the same. When nothing has been caught

[bif.condition.none]

In a routine, method or program where no trap has caught a condition yet, CONDITION answers the null string for the options C, D, E, I and S and for R, and .nil for A and O.

say '['condition('C')']' '['condition('D')']' '['condition('E')']',

say (condition('A') == .nil) (condition('O') == .nil)

What a trapped condition answers

[bif.condition.name]

After a trap has caught a condition, the option C answers the name of the condition in capital letters: for a SYNTAX error SYNTAX, for an unset variable under NOVALUE NOVALUE. For a user condition raised by the RAISE instruction, it answers USER, a blank and the name of the condition in capital letters.

signal on syntax name s
x = 1 + 'a'
s: say condition('C')
signal on novalue name n
y = unset + 1
n: say condition('C')
call on user Foo name u
call raiser
exit
raiser: procedure
raise user fOo return
u: say condition('C')
return

[bif.condition.instruction]

After a trap has caught a condition, the option I answers SIGNAL when the trap is a SIGNAL ON trap and CALL when it is a CALL ON trap.

signal on syntax name s
x = 1 + 'a'
s: say condition('I')
call on user foo name u
call raiser
exit
raiser: procedure
raise user foo return
u: say condition('I')
return

[bif.condition.description]

After a trap has caught a condition, the option D answers the description that the condition carries, or the null string when it carries none. A user condition carries what the RAISE instruction's DESCRIPTION gave, and a NOVALUE condition the name of the variable, in capital letters. A SYNTAX condition that the interpreter raises because of an error carries no description string; one that the RAISE instruction raises carries what its DESCRIPTION gave, and none when it has no DESCRIPTION, whether or not it has an ADDITIONAL.

signal on syntax name s
x = 1 + 'a'
s: say '['condition('D')']'
signal on syntax name r
call rs
r: say '['condition('D')']'
signal on syntax name q
call rq
q: say '['condition('D')']'
signal on novalue name n
y = unset + 1
n: say '['condition('D')']'
call on user foo name u
call raiser
exit
raiser: procedure
raise user foo description 'a note' return
u: say '['condition('D')']'
return
rs: raise syntax 40.1 description 'dd' return
rq: raise syntax 40.1 additional ('ad') return

The answer of D is the object that the DESCRIPTION entry of the condition object holds, not a string made from it, so a RAISE whose DESCRIPTION is an array makes D answer that array, which is equal to the entry.

call on user u name h

After a trap has caught a SYNTAX condition, the option E answers the subcode of the error number: the part after the period, as 12 for 40.12. An error number raised without a subcode, as RAISE SYNTAX 40 does, has the subcode 0 and the code 40.0. After any other condition E answers the null string.

[bif.condition.additional]

After a trap has caught a condition, the option A answers the additional information object the condition carries, and .nil when it carries none. A user condition carries what the RAISE instruction's ADDITIONAL gave, as the object itself, and not a string made from it.

signal on novalue name n
y = unset + 1
n: say condition('A') == .nil
call on user foo name u
call raiser
exit

raise user foo additional (.array~of('p', 'q')) return
u: say condition('A')~class condition('A')~items condition('A')~at(2)

The Array class 2 q
[bif.condition.status]

After a trap has caught a condition, the option S answers the state of the trap for that condition as it is now: ON, OFF or DELAY. A SIGNAL ON trap that has caught a condition is OFF, and a CALL ON trap is DELAY while its handler runs. The state changes with the code that follows: a SIGNAL ON or CALL ON instruction for the condition makes it ON, and a SIGNAL OFF or CALL OFF instruction makes it OFF. A change that the routine of a CALL trap makes to the CONDITION entry of its argument does not change which trap that is, as a Deviation states.

signal on syntax name s
x = 1 + 'a'
s: say condition('S')
signal on syntax name s2
say condition('S')
s2: signal off syntax
say condition('S')
call on user foo name u
call raiser
exit
raiser: procedure
raise user foo return
u: say condition('S')
call on user foo name u
say condition('S')
call off user foo
say condition('S')
return

OFF
ON

[bif.condition.object]

After a trap has caught a condition, the option O answers a directory that holds the information of the condition, the same information as the other options answer, and more. Its entries CONDITION, DESCRIPTION and INSTRUCTION equal what C, D and I answer, and so does ADDITIONAL when the condition carries additional information. When it carries none, as with NOVALUE, the directory has no ADDITIONAL entry, and ~additional answers .nil as for any absent entry, which is also what A answers. The directory is a new copy of the condition's entries on each call, so two calls answer two objects. A copy holds the same objects as the condition: adding, removing or replacing an entry of a copy changes nothing that CONDITION answers, while a change to an object that an entry holds, such as the array of ADDITIONAL, shows wherever that object is held. The condition itself is the object that a CALL trap's routine gets as its argument, as the argument rule says.

signal on syntax name s
x = 1 + 'a'
s: o = condition('O')
say o~class (o~condition == condition('C')) (o~description == condition('D')),
    (o~instruction == condition('I')) (o~additional == condition('A'))
o~condition = 'changed'
say condition('C') condition('O')~condition
signal on novalue name n
y = unset + 1
n: o = condition('O')
say o~hasIndex('ADDITIONAL') (o~additional == .nil) (condition('A') == .nil)

  return

How long the information lasts

[bif.condition.persist]

The information stays until it is replaced. After a SIGNAL ON trap has caught a condition, the code from the handler's label on, running in the same routine, method or program, still gets it from CONDITION, until another trap catches a condition or the option R clears it. When the handler of a CALL ON trap returns, the information is what it was before the handler ran: that of an earlier trap, or none, in which case CONDITION answers as in the case of no condition.

call on user foo name u
call raiser
say '['condition('C')']' '['condition('I')']' '['condition('S')']'
signal on syntax name s
x = 1 + 'a'
s: say condition('C') '/' condition('C')
call raiser
say condition('C') condition('I') condition('S')
exit
raiser: procedure
raise user foo return
u: say 'handler' condition('C')
return

handler USER FOO

SYNTAX / SYNTAX
handler USER FOO
SYNTAX SIGNAL OFF
[bif.condition.reset]

The option R returns the null string and clears the information of the running routine, method or program, so that every option answers as in the case of no condition. A condition that a trap catches afterwards is recorded as usual.

signal on syntax name s
x = 1 + 'a'
s: say condition('C') '['condition('R')']' '['condition('C')']',
  (condition('A') == .nil) (condition('O') == .nil)
signal on syntax name t
y = 1 + 'b'
t: say condition('C') condition('S')

SYNTAX [] [] 1 1
SYNTAX OFF
[bif.condition.scope]

The information belongs to the code that holds it. An internal routine, a routine that CALL or a function call reaches by its label, starts with a copy of the information of the code that called it, and what it does to the copy, a trap that catches a condition in it or the option R, is not seen by the caller. A ::ROUTINE, a method and a routine made from other source text start with none. INTERPRET runs in the code that holds it, and shares its information.

call on user foo name u
call raiser
exit
raiser: procedure
raise user foo return
u: say 'handler' condition('C')
say 'internal' inner()
say 'directive' dir()
say 'method' .box~new~m
say 'made' .routine~new('x', 'return "["condition("C")"]"')~call
interpret 'say "interpreted" condition("C")'
say 'reset' inner2()
say 'trap' inner3()
say 'caller' condition('C')
return
inner: return condition('C')
inner2: procedure
r = condition('R')
return '['condition('C')']'
inner3: procedure
signal on syntax name z
x = 1 + 'a'
z: return '['condition('C')']'
::routine dir
return '['condition('C')']'
::class box
::method m
return '['condition('C')']'

handler USER FOO
internal USER FOO
directive []
method []
made []
interpreted USER FOO
reset []
trap [SYNTAX]
caller USER FOO

Note. The ANSI draft (9.5.3) has the options C, D, E, I and S only, and says every answer is null when no condition has been trapped. ooRexx adds A, O and R, and interrexx follows ooRexx. The conditions chapter lists every condition, the information each carries, and the traps that catch them.

Deviations

[bif.condition.deviation.106]

In the routine of a CALL trap, the option S of CONDITION answers the state of the trap that caught the condition, also after the routine has changed the CONDITION entry of its argument. ooRexx answers the state of the trap for the condition that the entry names at that moment, and OFF when no trap has that name as the entry spells it.

call on user foo name h
call on user bar name h2
call r
exit
r: raise user foo return
h: o = arg(1)
  say condition('s')
  o~condition = 'USER BAR'
  say condition('s')
  call on user foo name h
  say condition('s')
  call off user foo
  say condition('s')
  return
h2: return

COPIES(string, n)

ANSI: 9.3.6; rexxref: Functions > Built-in Functions > COPIES

COPIES repeats a string: it answers the string written one after another n times.

Arguments

[bif.copies.method]

COPIES is a builtin that runs as a String method, and string, its first argument, is the receiver; n becomes the message's argument. string is a string and n is a whole number of the kind the next rule describes. The argument count is checked by the builtin call rules: both arguments are required and two is the most.

say copies('abc', 2) 'abc'~copies(2)

say copies('abc')
a: say condition('o')~code

say copies('abc', 2, 1)
b: say condition('o')~code

say copies(, 2)
c: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name d
say copies('abc', )
d: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name e
say copies('abc', 'x', 1)
e: say condition('o')~code

[bif.copies.n.check]

n must be a whole number of the value the conventions describe, and not negative. An n that is not a whole number, including the null string, raises SYNTAX 40.12; an n that is a whole number and negative raises SYNTAX 93.906. An n of 0 is allowed, and so is -0, which is 0. The form check comes before the range check, as in the order of the checks.

say '['copies('rst', 0)']' '['copies('abc', '-0')']' copies('ab', ' + 2. ')

e: say condition('o')~code

The result

[bif.copies.result]

COPIES returns the characters of string written n times in a row: a string of n * LENGTH(string) characters whose characters at positions (j - 1) * LENGTH(string) + 1 through j * LENGTH(string), for each j from 1 to n, are the characters of string.

say copies('rst', 4) copies('ab', 1) copies('a', 5) copies(12, 2)
say length(copies('ab', 100000)) '['copies(' ', 2)']'

rstrstrstrst ab aaaaa 1212
200000 [  ]
[bif.copies.zero]

When n is 0, the result is the null string, for every string.

say '['copies('rst', 0)']' '['copies('', 0)']' '['copies(' ', 0)']'

[] [] []
[bif.copies.empty]

When string is the null string, the result is the null string, for every n that passes its check, a very large one included.

say '['copies('', 5)']' length(copies('', 999999999999999999))

[] 0
[bif.copies.bytes]

COPIES copies characters of string unchanged: whitespace, control characters and '00'x are characters like any other.

say c2x(copies('a' || '00'x, 3)) c2x(copies('09'x || 'c3a9'x, 2))

610061006100 09C3A909C3A9

Note. Whether, when and with which code COPIES fails for a count whose result cannot be held in memory is not specified.

Deviations

[bif.copies.deviation.4]

interrexx does not specify whether the answer of COPIES is the same object as another string of equal value: as string itself, when the call leaves it unchanged as copies(s, 1) does, or as an equal string produced some other way, such as the literal 'abab' beside copies('ab', 2), or the null string answered when n is 0 or string is null. Through identityHash, or as a key of an IdentityTable, the answer may be either, and a program can rely only on the value, which is equal under ==. ooRexx differs: it often answers a new object where interrexx answers the existing one.

s = 'ab' || 'cd'
say (copies(s, 1) == s) (copies('ab', 2) == 'abab') (copies(s, 0) == '')

COUNTSTR

COUNTSTR(needle, haystack)

ANSI: 9.3.7; rexxref: Functions > Built-in Functions > COUNTSTR

COUNTSTR counts the occurrences of one string in another, never counting two that share a character.

Arguments

[bif.countstr.method]

COUNTSTR is a builtin that runs as a String method, and haystack, its second argument, is the receiver; needle becomes the message's argument. Both are strings, and the function form takes needle first. The argument count is checked by the builtin call rules: both arguments are required and two is the most.

say countstr('an', 'banana') 'banana'~countstr('an')
signal on syntax name a
say countstr('a')
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say countstr('a', 'a', 1)
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say countstr(, 'a')
c: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name d
say countstr('a', )
d: say condition('o')~code

2 2
40.3
40.4
40.5
40.3

The result

[bif.countstr.result]

COUNTSTR scans haystack from its first character to its last. At each position where needle occurs, it counts one and continues with the character after the occurrence, so no character takes part in two counted occurrences; where it does not occur, it continues with the next character. The result is the number counted. It is written as a count, and whether it is a new object is not specified.

say countstr('7', '707707') countstr('QQ', 'R0QQQ0') countstr('ab', 'xabyabab'),
    countstr('a', 'bcd')

4 1 3 0
[bif.countstr.overlap]

Occurrences that overlap are not both counted: an occurrence is counted only when it begins after the end of the one counted before it. A run such as 'aaa' holds one 'aa', not two.

say countstr('aa', 'aaa') countstr('aa', 'aaaa') countstr('aba', 'ababababa'),
    countstr('aba', 'abababa')

1 2 2 2
[bif.countstr.empty]

When needle is the null string, the result is 0, for every haystack, the null string included: the null string occurs nowhere that counts. When haystack is the null string, the result is 0 for every needle.

say countstr('', 'abc') countstr('', '') countstr('a', '') countstr('abc', 'ab')

0 0 0 0
[bif.countstr.exact]

Characters are compared for equality exactly, one by one. Case matters, no numeric comparison is made, and whitespace and every other character, '00'x among them, count like any other.

say countstr('a', 'aA') countstr('1', '1.01 1') countstr(' ', 'a b  c'),
    countstr('a' || '00'x, 'a' || '00'x || 'a' || '00'x || 'a') countstr(1, 11211)

1 3 3 2 4

Note. The ANSI draft (9.3.7) defines COUNTSTR by repeated POS searches, each starting after the end of the previous match, and does not mention the case of a null needle, for which POS answers 0. The reference manual defines it only as the count of occurrences that do not overlap.

With n, the answer is exactly n characters, as the signed-writing rule says: the characters on the left of the number's own are '00'x for a non-negative number and 'FF'x for a negative one, and a number that needs more than n characters is cut to its last n.

[bif.d2c.n.negative]

A negative number with an n is written in two's complement: the answer is the number's remainder on division by 256 to the power of n, taken as a non-negative number and written in exactly n characters, with '00'x characters on its left. For n of 1, -257 leaves the remainder 255, so its answer is 'FF'x; a number that needs more than n characters is cut like a positive one.
