Deviations

[bif.stream.deviation.34]

In a stream's name, as in every name interrexx qualifies, each .. removes exactly the one component before it, however the component was written, so .b/../c names the file c beside the directory .b. ooRexx removes none after a doubled slash and two after a component that starts with a period, so its stream can be a different file.

address system 'mktemp -d' with output stem t.
base = t.1
call sysmkdir base || '/.b'
f = base || '/c'
call charout f, 'abc'
call charout f
g = base || '/.b/../c'
say (stream(g, 'c', 'query exists') == f) chars(g) charin(g, 1, 3)
call stream g, 'c', 'close'
call sysfiledelete f
call sysrmdir base || '/.b'
call sysrmdir base

1 3 abc
[bif.stream.deviation.35]

The names HANDLE:0, HANDLE:1 and HANDLE:2 denote the standard input, output and error streams, and read and write them; a HANDLE: stream with any other descriptor is refused when it is created. In ooRexx a HANDLE: stream never reaches its descriptor: reads see end of file, and writes crash.

call charout 'HANDLE:1', 'hello '
call charout 'handle:1', 'again'
say
say stream('HANDLE:1') '['charin('HANDLE:0')']'

hello again

[bif.stream.deviation.49]

On a stream open for reading and writing, a relative SEEK with READ moves from the read position, and one with WRITE from the write position, whatever operation came before. One with neither option moves from the read position. ooRexx counts from a position that it tracks, which can be the other one: with neither option, the position that the last read, write or SEEK used, and the write position when there has been none since the stream was opened.

call sysfiledelete f
call lineout f, 'ab'
call lineout f, 'cd'
call lineout f, 'ef'
call lineout f

say stream(f, 'c', 'seek +1 read') stream(f, 'c', 'query position read')
say stream(f, 'c', 'open')

say stream(f, 'c', 'open')
say stream(f, 'c', 'seek +2') stream(f, 'c', 'query position write')
x = charin(f, , 2)
call charout f, 'X'
say stream(f, 'c', 'seek -1') stream(f, 'c', 'query position write')
call stream f, 'c', 'close'
call sysfiledelete f

[bif.stream.deviation.74]

A stream opened APPEND on a file it can only write writes every line at the file's current end, after what another writer appended since the stream was opened. ooRexx writes at the end as it was when the stream was opened, overwriting what another writer appended meanwhile.

f = 'spec-stream-dev74.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
call lineout f, 'one'
call lineout f
address system 'chmod 200' f
call stream f, 'c', 'open write append'
address system 'printf "two\n" >>' f
call lineout f, 'three'
call lineout f
address system 'chmod 600' f
do while lines(f) > 0
  say linein(f)
end
call stream f, 'c', 'close'
call sysfiledelete f

two
three
[bif.stream.deviation.79]

On a stream opened APPEND, every write goes after the last character, wherever the write position has been set: a position past the end leaves no gap, and a position in data written since the stream was opened does not overwrite it. The write position cannot be moved into the data that the file held when it was opened: a SEEK of it there answers 0, and a CHAROUT or LINEOUT that names a position there writes nothing, all of them NOTREADY. After a write, the write position is just after the last character, wherever the write was asked to go. ooRexx differs there: it moves the position, and the write goes after the last character as any other does; the write position it reports afterwards is the one that a CHAROUT start named, or that a SEEK set, moved past the characters written.

call sysfiledelete f
call charout f, 'abcdefgh'
call charout f

say stream(f, 'c', 'open append')
say stream(f, 'c', 'seek 2 write')
say n stream(f, 'c', 'query position write')
say charout(f, 'Y', 1)
say n
say stream(f, 'c', 'seek 9 write') charout(f, 'Z', 9)
say stream(f, 'c', 'seek 20 write') charout(f, 'W') charout(f, 'V', 10) n
say stream(f, 'c', 'query position write') charout(f, 'U', 100),
    stream(f, 'c', 'query position write')
call stream f, 'c', 'close'
say charin(f, 1, 100)
call sysfiledelete f
exit
nr: n = n + 1
return

STRIP

STRIP(string [, option] [, chars])

ANSI: 9.3.20; rexxref: Functions > Built-in Functions > STRIP

Deviations: D4

STRIP removes characters from the start of a string, from its end, or from both, for as long as they belong to a set of unwanted characters. By default that set is the whitespace.

Arguments

[bif.strip.method]

STRIP is a builtin that runs as a String method, and string, its first argument, is the receiver; option and chars become the message's arguments, in that order. string and chars are strings, and option is an option. The argument count is checked by the builtin call rules: one is required and three is the most.

x = ' pq '~strip('t')
say '['strip('   mn   ')']' '[' || x || ']'
signal on syntax name a
say strip('ab', 'Q')
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say strip('ab', , 'a', 1)
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say strip(, 'L')
c: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name d
say strip()
d: say condition('o')~code

[bif.strip.option]

option selects the end or ends of string that are stripped, by its first character alone, in either case: L or l selects the leading end, T or t the trailing end, and B or b both. Only that character decides; option may go on with any characters, and they change nothing. When option is omitted, it is B.

say '['strip(' k  l ', 'l')']' '['strip(' k  l ', 'T')']' '['strip(' k  l ')']'
say '['strip('  a  ', 'Leading')']' '['strip('  a  ', 'trailing')']',
    '['strip('  a  ', 'Both')']'
say '['strip('  a  ', 'lx')']' '['strip('  a  ', , )']'

[bif.strip.option.check]

An option whose first character is not one of those six, and an option that is the null string, raise SYNTAX 93.915. No other argument has a check, so this is the only check STRIP makes of its own after the argument count, and it is made whatever string and chars are.

say strip('ab', 1, 'ab')
f: say condition('o')~code

Note. The reference manual names error 93.915 for a method option that is not one of those allowed. The ANSI draft (9.3.20) reads option the same way, by its first character in either case, but raises 40.21 for a null option and 40.28 for any other bad one, where ooRexx raises 93.915; and it makes chars one character, where ooRexx takes the characters of chars as a set, as the rule below says.

[bif.strip.chars]

chars is the set of unwanted characters: the characters it holds, in any order and whether or not one repeats. When chars is omitted, the set is the two whitespace characters, the blank and the tab. Case matters: a is not A. Any character may be in the set, '00'x and those from '80'x to 'FF'x included.

say '['strip('xyxaxyb', , 'xy')']' '['strip('A a A', , 'a')']'
say c2x(strip('00'x || 'a' || '00'x, , '00'x)) c2x(strip('80'x || 'a' || '81'x, , '81'x))
say c2x(strip('09'x || ' a' || '09'x)) c2x(strip('0a'x || 'a' || '0d'x))
say c2x(strip('0b'x || 'a' || '0c'x)) c2x(strip('09'x || ' a ' || '09'x, , ' '))

[axyb] [A a A]
61 8061
61 0A610D
0B610C 0920612009

The result

[bif.strip.result]

STRIP returns string with the run that option selects removed: the run at its start, the run at its end, or both. The leading characters removed are the longest run at the start of string made of characters in the set, and the trailing ones the longest such run at the end. Characters between them are not touched, whether or not they are in the set. A character of the set that is not in such a run, because a character outside the set stands between it and the end, stays.

say '['strip('xxaxbxx', 'L', 'x')']' '['strip('xxaxbxx', 'T', 'x')']',
    '['strip('xxaxbxx', 'B', 'x')']'
say '['strip('abcba', 'L', 'ba')']' '['strip('abcba', , 'ba')']' '['strip('  a b  ')']'
say c2x(strip(' ' || '09'x || 'a', , ' '))

[axbxx] [xxaxb] [axb]
[cba] [c] [a b]
0961
[bif.strip.all]

When every character of string is in the set, the result is the null string, whichever option is. The null string strips to the null string.

say '['strip('xxx', 'L', 'x')']' '['strip('xxx', 'T', 'x')']' '['strip('xxx', , 'x')']'
say '['strip('')']' '['strip('  ' || '09'x)']' '['strip('', , 'x')']'

[] [] []
[] [] []
[bif.strip.chars.null]

A null chars is an empty set, so STRIP removes nothing and returns string, for every option. A null chars is not omitted, so it does not give the default set.

say '['strip('  a  ', , '')']' '['strip('  a  ', 'L', '')']',
    '['strip('  a  ', 'T', '')']'

[  a  ] [  a  ] [  a  ]
[bif.strip.omitted-chars]

An omitted chars takes the default set, an omitted option takes B, and the two are independent of each other.

say '['strip('  a  ', 'L', )']' '['strip('  a  ', , )']' '['strip('xxaxx', , 'x')']'

[a  ] [a] [a]

Deviations

Note. An argument whose STRING method answers an object that is not a string falls under Deviation 30, as it does for every builtin.

[bif.strip.deviation.4]

interrexx does not specify whether the answer of STRIP is the same object as another string of equal value: as string itself, when nothing is stripped, as in strip(s) for an s with no whitespace at either end, or as an equal string produced some other way, such as the literal 'ab' beside strip(' ab'). Through identityHash, or as a key of an IdentityTable, the answer may be either, and a program can rely only on the value, which is equal under ==. ooRexx differs: it often answers a new object where interrexx answers the existing one.

s = 'p' || 'q'
say (strip(s) == s) (strip('  ab') == 'ab')

1 1

SUBSTR

SUBSTR(string, n [, length] [, pad])

ANSI: 9.3.21; rexxref: Functions > Built-in Functions > SUBSTR (Substring)

Deviations: D4

SUBSTR selects a run of characters from a string by position, and pads the run when it reaches past the end of the string.

Arguments

[bif.substr.method]

SUBSTR is a builtin that runs as a String method, and string, its first argument, is the receiver. string is a string, n is a position, length is a length, and pad is a pad. The arguments are checked in the order the conventions give, and the argument count by the builtin call rules: two are required and four is the most.

signal on syntax name a
say substr('abc', 0)
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say substr('abc', 2, -1)
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say substr('abc', 1, 2, '..')
c: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name d
say substr('abc', 1, 1, '.', 1)
d: say condition('o')~code

93.924
93.923
40.23
40.4
[bif.substr.length.default]

When length is omitted, it is the number of characters of string at position n and after it: LENGTH(string) - n + 1 when n is at most LENGTH(string), and 0 otherwise.

say '['substr('abcde', 2)']' '['substr('abcde', 5)']',
    '['substr('abcde', 6)']' '['substr('abcde', 100)']'

[bcde] [e] [] []

Note. The ANSI draft (9.3.21) computes the omitted length as LENGTH(string) + 1 - n and repeats that many times, so for n two or more past the end its count is negative and its definition raises SYNTAX 26.2 from inside the builtin. This page follows ooRexx, where the reference manual says the rest of the string is returned and positions past the end select nothing, so the result is the null string.

[bif.substr.pad.default]

When pad is omitted, it is the blank, '20'x.

say '['substr('xyz', 3, 3)']'

[z  ]

The result

[bif.substr.result]

SUBSTR returns a string of exactly length characters. Its character at position i, for each i from 1 to length, is the character of string at position n + i - 1 when string has a character there, and pad otherwise. So the result is the characters of string from position n on, at most length of them, followed by as many copies of pad as make up the length.

say '['substr('abcdef', 2, 3)']' '['substr('abcdef', 4, 5, '.')']',
    '['substr('abcdef', 1, 6)']'

[bcd] [def..] [abcdef]
[bif.substr.past-end]

When n is greater than LENGTH(string), no character of string is selected: the result is length copies of pad, and the null string when length is omitted. This holds for every n past the end that passes its check.

say '['substr('abc', 4, 2, '*')']' '['substr('abc', 999999999999999999, 3, '*')']',
    '['substr('abc', 4)']'

[**] [***] []
[bif.substr.length.zero]

When length is 0, the result is the null string, for every n that passes its check. pad is still checked, as a pad always is.

say '['substr('abc', 2, 0)']' '['substr('abc', 10, 0, '*')']'
signal on syntax name e
say substr('abc', 2, 0, '')
e: say condition('o')~code

[] []
40.23
[bif.substr.empty]

When string is the null string, every position is past its end, so the result is length copies of pad, or the null string when length is omitted.

say '['substr('', 1)']' '['substr('', 1, 3)']' '['substr('', 5, 2, '-')']'

[] [   ] [--]
[bif.substr.bytes]

SUBSTR selects and pads by character, one byte each, and copies every byte unchanged: whitespace, control characters and '00'x are characters like any other, in string and as pad.

say c2x(substr('61000962'x, 2, 4, '00'x))

00096200

Deviations

[bif.substr.deviation.4]

interrexx does not specify whether the answer of SUBSTR is the same object as another string of equal value: as string itself, when the call returns all of it unchanged as substr(s, 1) does, or as an equal string produced some other way, such as the literal 'abc' beside substr('abcdef', 1, 3). Through identityHash, or as a key of an IdentityTable, the answer may be either, and a program can rely only on the value, which is equal under ==. ooRexx differs: it often answers a new object where interrexx answers the existing one.

s = 'abc' || 'def'
say (substr(s, 1) == s) (substr('abcdef', 1, 3) == 'abc')

1 1

SUBWORD

SUBWORD(string, n [, length])

ANSI: 9.3.22; rexxref: Functions > Built-in Functions > SUBWORD

Deviations: D4

SUBWORD selects a run of consecutive words from a string, keeping the whitespace between them as it is. Words are those of the word rule.

Arguments

[bif.subword.method]

SUBWORD is a builtin that runs as a String method, and string, its first argument, is the receiver. string is a string, n is a word number, and length is a length that counts words. The arguments are checked in the order the conventions give, and the argument count by the builtin call rules: two are required and three is the most.

signal on syntax name a
say subword('a b', 0)
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say subword('a b', 1, -1)
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say subword('a b', 0, 'x')
c: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name d
say subword('a b', 1, 1, 1)
d: say condition('o')~code

93.924
93.923
40.12
40.4
[bif.subword.length.default]

When length is omitted, it selects every word from word n to the last word of string.

say '['subword('one two  three', 2)']' '['subword('one two  three', 3)']'

[two  three] [three]

The result

[bif.subword.result]

When string has a word n and length is not 0, SUBWORD returns the part of string that begins with the first character of word n and ends with the last character of word n + length - 1, or of the last word of string when it has fewer words than that. It is a slice of string and nothing is rewritten in it, so a run of blanks or tabs separating two selected words keeps its length and its characters. Since the slice starts and ends on word characters, whitespace before word n, and after the last selected word, falls outside it. The other cases have rules of their own: n past the last word, length 0 and a string with no words.

say '['subword('one two  three   four', 2, 2)']'
say '['subword('  one  two  ', 1)']' '['subword('a b c', 2, 100)']'
say c2x(subword('09'x||'a'||'0909'x||'b'||'09'x, 1))

[two  three]
[one  two] [b c]
61090962
[bif.subword.past-end]

When n is greater than the number of words in string, the result is the null string. This holds for every n past the last word that passes its check.

say '['subword('a b c', 4)']' '['subword('a b c', 999999999999999999, 2)']'

[] []
[bif.subword.length.zero]

When length is 0, the result is the null string, for every n that passes its check.

say '['subword('a b c', 2, 0)']' '['subword('a b c', 9, 0)']'

[] []
[bif.subword.empty]

When string has no words, the null string or a string of only whitespace among them, the result is the null string for every n and length that pass their checks.

say '['subword('', 1)']' '['subword(' '||'09'x||' ', 1, 2)']'

[] []
[bif.subword.nonblank]

A character that the word rule places inside a word, such as a line feed or a carriage return, is copied into the result as it stands, and SUBWORD ends the result after it when it is the last character of the last selected word.

say c2x(subword('a'||'0a'x||'b c', 1, 1)) c2x(subword('a'||'0d'x||' b', 1, 1))

610A62 610D

Deviations

[bif.subword.deviation.4]

interrexx does not specify whether the answer of SUBWORD is the same object as another string of equal value: as string itself, when the call returns all of it unchanged as subword(w, 1) does for a w with no whitespace around its words, or as an equal string produced some other way, such as the literal 'a b' beside subword('a b c', 1, 2). Through identityHash, or as a key of an IdentityTable, the answer may be either, and a program can rely only on the value, which is equal under ==. ooRexx differs: it often answers a new object where interrexx answers the existing one.

w = 'a' || ' b'
say (subword(w, 1) == w) (subword('a b c', 1, 2) == 'a b')

1 1

SYMBOL

SYMBOL(name)

ANSI: 9.8.4; rexxref: Functions > Built-in Functions > SYMBOL

SYMBOL tells whether a string is a symbol and, if so, whether a variable of that name holds a value where SYMBOL is called. The answer is one of the three strings BAD, VAR and LIT.

Arguments

[bif.symbol.args]

SYMBOL takes one argument, name, which is a string, and nothing else. The argument count is checked by the builtin call rules: one argument is required and one is the most. SYMBOL does not run as a String method: sending the message SYMBOL to a string raises SYNTAX 97.1.

signal on syntax name a
say symbol()
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say symbol('a', 'b')
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say symbol(, )
c: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name d
say 'a'~symbol
d: say condition('o')~code

40.3
40.4
40.3
97.1

The result

[bif.symbol.result]

The answer is BAD when name is not a symbol, VAR when it is a symbol that names a variable holding a value, and LIT for any other symbol. A string is a symbol when it has at least one character and each is a letter, a digit, or one of ., !, ? and _, as it is for the symbol type of DATATYPE, and it has at most 250 characters; the null string, a string with whitespace anywhere in it, even at an end, one with any other character, and one of more than 250 characters, whatever they are, is BAD. The string is read as it is, without trimming. A name that is an object other than a string is replaced by a string as any string argument says.

n = 7
say symbol('n') symbol('p') symbol('a_b') symbol('a!') symbol('a?') symbol('_')
say symbol('') symbol(' j') symbol('j ') symbol('a b') symbol('+5') symbol('a-b'),
    symbol('a$') symbol('"j"') symbol('é')
say symbol(.nil) symbol(.array~new) symbol(.mutablebuffer~new('n'))
say symbol(copies('a', 250)) symbol(copies('a', 251)) symbol(copies('1', 251)),
    symbol(copies('a', 100)'.'copies('b', 149)) symbol(copies('a', 100)'.'copies('b', 150))

VAR LIT LIT LIT LIT LIT
BAD BAD BAD BAD BAD BAD BAD BAD BAD
BAD BAD VAR
LIT BAD BAD LIT BAD

Note. The limit of 250 is on the whole string, stem and tail together.

[bif.symbol.case]

SYMBOL reads name in uppercase, as a program reads a symbol, so name names the same variable in either case.

n = 7
say symbol('n') symbol('N') symbol('p') symbol('P')

VAR VAR LIT LIT
[bif.symbol.constant]

A symbol that starts with a digit or a period is a constant symbol and is never a variable, so SYMBOL answers LIT for it. The name .nil and the other names that stand for environment objects are of this kind, whether or not the object exists.

say symbol('3') symbol('1.5') symbol('.5') symbol('1e5') symbol('.') symbol('..'),
    symbol('.nil') symbol('.zzz')

LIT LIT LIT LIT LIT LIT LIT LIT
[bif.symbol.simple]

For any other symbol without a period inside it, SYMBOL answers VAR when a variable of that name holds a value and LIT when it does not. A variable that has been dropped holds no value. SYMBOL looks at the name itself, not at the value: a variable whose value is the name of another variable makes the answer for the name VAR, and the answer for the value is a separate one that the call gets when it is given the value.

a = 'b'
b = 'c'
say symbol('a') symbol('b') symbol('c') symbol(a) symbol(b)
drop a
say symbol('a')

VAR VAR LIT VAR LIT
LIT
[bif.symbol.compound]

A symbol whose first period has at least one character after it, and that does not start with a period, is a compound symbol: the part before the first period is its stem, and the parts after it are its tail, so a.b. is a compound symbol with the tail b.. Every part of the tail that names a variable holding a value is replaced by that value, as in a program, and the answer is VAR when the compound variable so named holds a value, and LIT when it does not. The value of a tail part is used as it is, not translated to uppercase, and can be any string, whitespace included; it is not itself checked to be a symbol. An unset part of the tail stands for its own name in uppercase.

n = 7
t.7 = 'x'
say symbol('t.7') symbol('t.n') symbol('T.N') symbol('t.8') symbol('t.m')
drop n
say symbol('n') symbol('t.n') symbol('t.7')
w = 'x y'
c.w = 1
say symbol('c.w') symbol('c.x y')
v = 'k'
d.k = 1
say symbol('d.v') symbol('d.k') symbol('d.K')
e.f. = 1
say symbol('e.f.') symbol('e.f')

VAR VAR VAR LIT LIT
LIT LIT VAR
VAR BAD
LIT VAR VAR
VAR LIT
[bif.symbol.stem]

A symbol that ends at its first period is a stem. A stem is LIT until the program refers to the stem or to a compound variable of it, and VAR from then on, also after the stem is dropped. A reference is an assignment, a read, a DROP of the stem or of a compound variable of it, or a call of SYMBOL that names a compound variable of it; a call that names the stem itself is not a reference. After an assignment to the whole stem, a compound variable of it that was never assigned or dropped is VAR, because it has the value given to the stem. A compound variable that was dropped, and every compound variable of a dropped stem, holds no value and is LIT.

say symbol('a.')
say symbol('b.1') symbol('b.')
stem. = 0
say symbol('stem.') symbol('stem.zzz') symbol('other.')
h. = 0
drop h.1
say symbol('h.') symbol('h.1') symbol('h.2')
c.1 = 5
drop c.
say symbol('c.') symbol('c.1')
d = e.1
say symbol('e.')

LIT
LIT VAR
VAR VAR LIT
VAR LIT VAR
VAR LIT
VAR

Note. In the second line the call that names b.1 is a reference to b., which the call after it sees; the same two calls in the other order answer LIT LIT.

Scope

[bif.symbol.scope]

SYMBOL looks at the variables that the routine or method running it can see. A routine called with a PROCEDURE instruction sees none of its caller's variables, except the ones it EXPOSEs; a method sees an object variable only once it exposes it, and the variable is VAR only when it holds a value.

g = 1
call hide
call show
exit
hide: procedure
say symbol('g')
return
show: procedure expose g
say symbol('g')
return

LIT
VAR

o = .o~new
say o~plain '/' o~exposing '/' o~assigning '/' o~exposing
::class o
::attribute at
::method plain
return symbol('at') symbol('un')
::method exposing
expose at un
return symbol('at') symbol('un')
::method assigning
expose at
at = 1
return symbol('at')

LIT LIT / LIT LIT / VAR / VAR LIT
[bif.symbol.result-var]

The variable RESULT is VAR after a CALL of a routine that returned a value and LIT after a CALL of one that returned none, as the instruction sets or drops it.

call none
say symbol('result')
call one
say symbol('result')
call none
say symbol('result')
exit
none: return
one: return 1

LIT
VAR
LIT

TIME

TIME([option [, [string] [, informat]]])

ANSI: 9.8.5; rexxref: Functions > Built-in Functions > TIME

TIME answers a time of day. With no string it answers the current local time, or the reading of an elapsed-time clock that the program can start and reset; with a string it reads a time written in one format and writes it in another. The current time changes from moment to moment, so the examples of this page convert fixed times, or check only the form of the current time and how its formats agree with each other, and the elapsed-time clock is checked against pauses and not against figures.

Arguments

[bif.time.args]

TIME takes up to three arguments and requires none: option, string and informat. The argument count is checked by the builtin call rules: a call with more than three arguments raises SYNTAX 40.4, and a call with only omitted places counts as a call with no arguments. TIME does not run as a String method: sending the message TIME to a string raises SYNTAX 97.1. option and informat name formats by their first letter.

say time('C', '13:05:09') time(, '13:05:09') time('N', '13:05:09', 'N') time('N', '13:05:09', )
signal on syntax name a
say time('N', '13:05:09', 'N', 1)
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say '13:05:09'~time
b: say condition('o')~code

1:05pm 13:05:09 13:05:09 13:05:09
40.4
97.1
[bif.time.default]

An omitted option is N, and so is an omitted informat. A call with no string answers the current time, in the format option names; a call with a string is a conversion.

say time(, '07:08:09') time('N', '07:08:09') time(, '07:08:09', 'N')
say (time() == time('N')) (length(time()) == 8)

07:08:09 07:08:09 07:08:09
1 1

Formats written

[bif.time.out.clock]

Three options write the time of day as hours, minutes and seconds. N writes hh:mm:ss, with the hour from 00 to 23, and L writes hh:mm:ss.uuuuuu, which adds six digits for the microseconds. C writes h:mmam or h:mmpm, a civil time: the hour is from 1 to 12 with no leading zero, the minutes have two digits and the seconds are not written. The hour 0 is 12 with am, the hours 1 to 11 have am, the hour 12 is 12 with pm, and the hours 13 to 23 are 1 to 11 with pm.

say time('N', '00:00:00') time('N', '09:08:07') time('N', '23:59:59')
say time('L', '09:08:07') time('L', '09:08:07.5', 'L') time('L', '23:59:59.999999', 'L')
say time('C', '00:00:00') time('C', '00:59:59') time('C', '01:00:00') time('C', '11:59:59')
say time('C', '12:00:00') time('C', '12:59:59') time('C', '13:00:00') time('C', '23:59:59')

00:00:00 09:08:07 23:59:59
09:08:07.000000 09:08:07.500000 23:59:59.999999
12:00am 12:59am 1:00am 11:59am
12:00pm 12:59pm 1:00pm 11:59pm
[bif.time.out.counts]

Three options write the time of day as a count since midnight: H the whole hours, M the whole minutes and S the whole seconds. Each is written with no leading zero, point or exponent, as 0 for zero, and a part of a unit that is not complete is dropped, never rounded. NUMERIC DIGITS plays no part.

numeric digits 2
say time('H', '00:00:00') time('H', '09:59:59') time('H', '23:59:59')
say time('M', '00:00:59') time('M', '01:00:00') time('M', '23:59:59')
say time('S', '00:00:01') time('S', '01:00:00') time('S', '23:59:59')

0 9 23
0 60 1439
1 3600 86399
[bif.time.out.stamp]

Two options write a count that includes the date. F writes the number of microseconds since the start of 1 January 0001, and T the number of seconds since the start of 1 January 1970, which is negative before it. T is F divided by 1000000, rounded down, less 62135596800. A string read with the informat C, H, L, M, N or S has no date, so its date is 1 January 0001: F is then the time of day in microseconds, and T is that time of day in seconds less 62135596800, a negative number. NUMERIC DIGITS plays no part in how they are written.

say time('F', '00:00:00') time('F', '00:00:01') time('F', '23:59:59.999999', 'L')
say time('T', '00:00:00') time('T', '00:00:01') time('T', '23:59:59.999999', 'L')
numeric digits 3
say time('F', '13:05:09') time('T', '13:05:09')
say time('F', '13:05:09') + 0

0 1000000 86399999999
-62135596800 -62135596799 -62135510401
47109000000 -62135549691
4.71E+10

The current time

[bif.time.current]

A call with no string answers the current time in the local time zone, in the format option names, as of the moment the clause reads the clock. Every format of the current time is the same time: converting the current time in L form to N, C, H, M, S or L gives what that option gives for the current time. F and T include the date, and F with its whole days taken off is what the conversion of the L form gives for F.

numeric digits 20
say (time('N') == time('N', time('L'), 'L')) (time('C') == time('C', time('L'), 'L')),
    (time('H') == time('H', time('L'), 'L')) (time('M') == time('M', time('L'), 'L')),
    (time('S') == time('S', time('L'), 'L')) (time('L') == time('L', time('L'), 'L'))
say (time('F') // 86400000000 == time('F', time('L'), 'L')),
    (time('T') == date('T'))
say length(time('L')) length(time('N')) datatype(time('S'), 'W') datatype(time('F'), 'W') datatype(time('T'), 'W')

1 1 1 1 1 1
1 1
15 8 1 1 1

The time zone

[bif.time.zone]

The current time of every format is that of the local time zone, and the option O writes how far that zone is from UTC: a whole number of microseconds, positive east of UTC and negative to the west, and less than a day. F and T are local like the rest: the UTC reading of F is F - O. A call that gives O with a string reads the string as usual and answers the same offset, except with the informat O, whose answer is the offset that the string gives. This book does not specify which time zone a program runs in. The zone is read with the clock, at the clause's moment. A program that changes it, as by setting TZ with VALUE in the environment, has the new zone at the next reading of the clock: in the same clause when no DATE or TIME call came before the change there, and from the next clause otherwise.

numeric digits 20
o = time('O')
say datatype(o, 'W') (abs(o) < 86400000000) (time('O') == time('O', '12:00:00')),
    (time('T') == time('F') % 1000000 - 62135596800) (time('S') == time('T') // 86400)
say time('O', '00:00:00') == time('O', '23:59:59.5', 'L')
say time('O', '7200000000', 'O') time('O', '-7200000000', 'O') time('O', '0', 'O')
signal on syntax name a
say time('O', 'noon')

Reading a time

[bif.time.in.text]

The informats N, L and C read the formats that the options of the same letters write, and accept nothing else: no blank or other character before, after or inside the time, and no other number of digits in a field. N has two-digit hours from 00 to 23, minutes from 00 to 59 and seconds from 00 to 59. L has the same, followed by a point and from one to six digits, which are the microseconds when read as if completed on the right with zeros. C has an hour from 1 to 12 written with or without a leading zero, a colon, minutes of two digits from 00 to 59, and am or pm in lower case; 12 with am is midnight, 12 with pm is noon.

say time('N', '23:59:59') time('N', '12:00am', 'C') time('N', '12:30pm', 'C') time('N', '01:30pm', 'C'),
    time('N', '1:30pm', 'C') time('N', '11:59pm', 'C') time('N', '00:30:00')
say time('L', '01:02:03.4', 'L') time('L', '01:02:03.45', 'L') time('L', '01:02:03.000001', 'L')

[bif.time.in.number]

The informats H, M, S, F and T read a count: hours, minutes or seconds since midnight, or the number of microseconds or seconds that F and T write. The string may have any form of a number, such as 5, 5, +5, 5.0 and 5e0, and NUMERIC DIGITS does not apply. A string whose value is a whole number is read as that number, however many leading or trailing zeros it has, and the number must be in the range given below. A string whose value is not a whole number raises SYNTAX 40.19 when it has at most nine significant digits for H, M and S, or at most 18 for F and T, its significant digits being those from the first digit that is not 0 to the last digit that is not 0. This book does not specify whether a string with more significant digits, whose value is not a whole number, is accepted, nor what it then reads as. H must be from 0 to 23, M from 0 to 1439 and S from 0 to 86399. F must be from 0 to 315537897599999999 and T from -62135596800 to 253402300799, which are the instants from 1 January 0001 to 31 December 9999. An F or T names a date and a time, and a format other than F or T keeps only the time of day; F and T keep both.

say time('N', '5', 'H') time('N', ' 5 ', 'H') time('N', '+5', 'H') time('N', '5.0', 'H') time('N', '5e0', 'H')

say time('N', '0', 'T') time('N', '-1', 'T') time('N', '86400', 'T') time('N', '1709643909', 'T')

[bif.time.in.truncate]

A conversion answers the earliest time that fits the string. A part of the time that the string gives and the format of the answer has no place for is dropped, never rounded: N, C, H, M and S drop the microseconds, C, H and M drop the seconds as well, and H drops the minutes. A part that the answer needs and the string lacks is zero.

say time('N', '12:00:59.999999', 'L') time('C', '23:59:59.999999', 'L') time('M', '00:00:59.999999', 'L')
say time('S', '12:00:00.999999', 'L') time('H', '12:59:59', 'N') time('L', '12:34:56')

[bif.time.in.offset]

The informat O reads a whole number of microseconds, as the informats F and T read their counts, as an offset from UTC. The answer is the current time in a zone that far from UTC, as of the moment of the clause: with the offset of the local zone, the current local time. Every offset from -86400000000 to 86400000000, a day either way, is accepted; this book does not specify how much further the range of the offset goes.

numeric digits 20
say (time('F', time('O'), 'O') == time('F')) (time('N', time('O'), 'O') == time('N')),
    (time('F', 3600000000, 'O') - time('F', 0, 'O') == 3600000000),
    (time('T', -7200000000, 'O') - time('T', 0, 'O') == -7200)
say (time('F', 86400000000, 'O') - time('F', 0, 'O') == 86400000000),
    (time('F', -86400000000, 'O') - time('F', 0, 'O') == -86400000000)

The elapsed-time clock

[bif.time.elapsed.start]

The options E and R read an elapsed-time clock, which starts at the first call of E or R in the code that owns the clock. That call answers 0, and the clock then counts time from it. Other options do not start the clock and are not affected by it, and neither is DATE.

x = time('N') time('L') time('F') time('O') date('S')
call syssleep 0.3
say time('R')
call syssleep 0.3
say time('E') >= 0.25

0
1
[bif.time.elapsed.value]

After the clock has started, E answers the time since the start or the last reset in seconds with a fraction of six digits: whole seconds with no leading zeros, a point, and the six digits of the microseconds, 0.300268 and 12.000001 being examples. The figure is written whatever NUMERIC DIGITS is.

numeric digits 3
x = time('E')
call syssleep 0.3
e = time('E')
say datatype(e, 'N') (e >= 0.25) verify(e, '0123456789.') countstr('.', e) (pos('.', e) > 1),
    (length(e) - pos('.', e)) (left(e, 1) \== '0' | pos('.', e) == 2)
call syssleep 1.1
e = time('E')
say (e >= 1.35) verify(e, '0123456789.') countstr('.', e) (length(e) - pos('.', e)) (left(e, 1) \== '0')

1 1 0 1 1 6 1
1 0 1 6 1
[bif.time.elapsed.reset]

R answers what E would, and also resets the clock: the next call of E or R counts from the moment of this call.

x = time('R')
call syssleep 0.4
parse value resets() with a b
m = time('E')
/* m counts on through the label's reset; without the reset, b would include a */
say (a >= 0.35) (b >= 0.35) (a + b < m + 0.2)
exit
resets:
a = time('R')
call syssleep 0.4
return a time('E')

1 1 1
[bif.time.elapsed.clause]

All the calls of E and R in one clause answer the same figure, whichever they are, and a reset by R in the clause takes effect for the next clause and not for the calls after it in the same clause.

x = time('R')
call syssleep 0.3
parse value readings() with a '|' b
m = time('E')
say words(a) (word(a, 1) >= 0.25) (word(a, 1) == word(a, 2)) (word(a, 1) == word(a, 3)),
    (word(a, 1) == word(a, 4)) (word(a, 1) == word(a, 5))
/* m counts on through the label's reset; without the reset, b would include word(a, 1) */
say word(a, 1) + b < m + 0.2
exit
readings:
a = time('E') time('E') time('R') time('E') time('R')
return a '|' time('E')

5 1 1 1 1 1
1
[bif.time.elapsed.scope]

The clock belongs to the code that runs. A program shares its clock with the code that INTERPRET runs in it. A routine of the same program that CALL or a function call runs, a label of the program, begins with a copy of its caller's clock as it stands at the call, running if the caller's is and not started if not, and what it does to its copy is not seen by the caller. A ::ROUTINE, a method and a message sent with START each begin with no clock, which their first call of E or R starts.

call starter
call syssleep 0.3
say 'caller of a label that started a clock' kind(time('E'))
call syssleep 0.3
say 'label' kind(inside())
say 'main' kind(time('E'))
say 'routine' kind(outside())
say 'method' kind(.o~new~m)
say 'start' kind(.o~new~start('m')~result)
parse value interpreted() with y e
m = time('E')
/* m counts on through the label's reset; if INTERPRET had a clock of its own, e would include y */
say 'interpret' kind(y) (y + e < m + 0.2)
exit
starter: return time('R')
inside: v = time('E'); z = time('R'); return v
interpreted:
interpret 'y = time("R")'
return y time('E')
kind: procedure
parse arg v
if v >= 0.25 then return 'inherited'
return 'fresh'
::routine outside
return time('E')
::class o
::method m
return time('E')

caller of a label that started a clock fresh
label inherited
main inherited
routine fresh
method fresh
start fresh
interpret inherited 1

signal on syntax name a

b: say condition('o')~code

The order of the checks

[bif.time.order]

A call is checked in this order, and the first failure is the one raised: the argument count; a missing string that an informat needs (40.5); the options E and R with a string (40.29); the letter of informat; the string itself (40.19); and, last, the letter of option.

signal on syntax name a
say time('X', 'junk', 'Q', 1)
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say time('E', , 'N')
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say time('E', 'junk', 'Q')
c: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name d
say time('X', 'junk', 'Q')
d: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name e
say time('X', 'junk')
e: say condition('o')~code

say time('X', '13:05:09')
f: say condition('o')~code

Note. The ANSI draft (9.8.5) has neither the options F and T nor the informats F, O and T, and it raises SYNTAX 40.29 for O as well as E and R as option with a string, where ooRexx answers the offset. The reference manual describes an error when the system clock is set back below the start of the elapsed-time clock, and one for an elapsed time of more than nine digits of seconds; this book specifies neither.

TRACE

TRACE([option])

ANSI: 9.5.9; rexxref: Functions > Built-in Functions > TRACE

TRACE answers the trace setting in effect where it is called, and when it is given an option it changes the setting for the code that follows. The answer is the setting from before the call. This page specifies the setting and how a call changes it; what the interpreter writes while a setting is in effect is not part of it.

Arguments

[bif.trace.args]

TRACE takes one optional argument, option, a string. The argument count is checked by the builtin call rules: none is required and one is the most, so a call with two raises SYNTAX 40.4. A call with no argument, or with only an omitted one, changes nothing and only answers the setting. TRACE does not run as a String method: sending the message TRACE to a string raises SYNTAX 97.1.

call show
exit
show: procedure
say trace() trace(,) trace()
signal on syntax name a
say trace('N', 'O')
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say 'N'~trace
b: say condition('o')~code

N N N
40.4
97.1

The setting

[bif.trace.setting]

A setting is one of nine letters: A, C, E, F, I, L, N, O and R. The answer of a call is the setting in effect before the call, as one uppercase letter, with a question mark before it when interactive tracing is on, as its rule says. A program starts with N.

call show
exit
show: procedure
say trace()
say trace('R') trace('L')
say trace('C') trace()
call trace 'O'

N
N R
L C
[bif.trace.letter]

Of option after its prefix, only the first character matters. It selects the setting by the letter it is, in either case, and the characters after it play no part, a question mark among them, so the name of a setting, or a word that starts with its letter, does as well. When option is the null string, the setting is N; an option of only question marks is the case of the prefix rule.

call show
exit
show: procedure
say trace('Alpha') trace('c') trace('Ox') trace('r') trace('n5')
say trace('Results') trace('')
say trace('F') trace('?') trace('')
say trace()

N A C O R
N R
N F ?F
N

call show
exit
show: procedure
say trace('N?') trace('a?') trace('?N?') trace()
say trace('N??') trace('??N?') trace()

N N A ?N
?N N N
[bif.trace.prefix]

Interactive tracing is on or off beside the letter, and option can change it with question marks before the letter. When there is a letter, the tracing is on afterwards if the question marks are an odd number, and off if they are an even number, none included; a call that gives a letter without a question mark therefore turns it off. The letter O always turns it off. When option is only question marks, the letter stays and each question mark flips whether tracing is on. Where the setting is O, only question marks leave it O.

call show
exit
show: procedure
say trace('?N') trace('?N') trace('??N') trace('???N') trace('N') trace()
say trace('?') trace('?') trace('??') trace('???') trace('?O') trace('?')
say trace()

N ?N ?N N ?N N
N ?N N N ?N O
O
[bif.trace.instruction]

While interactive tracing is on, the TRACE instruction changes nothing; the TRACE function does, and a call that turns interactive tracing off lets the instruction work again. Without interactive tracing, the instruction and the function change the same setting.

call show
exit
show: procedure
trace results
say trace() trace('?A')
trace normal
say trace()
say trace('N') trace()
trace results
say trace()
trace off
say trace()

R R
?A
?A N
R
O

Scope

[bif.trace.scope]

The setting belongs to the code that is running, not to the program. An internal routine, one that the program calls by its label, starts with the caller's setting, and the caller has its own back when the routine returns, whatever the routine set. A method, and a ::ROUTINE, starts with N whatever the caller's setting is, and its setting is lost on return as well. Code run by INTERPRET shares the setting of the code that runs it.

call trace 'E'
call plain
say 'caller' trace()
call hidden
say 'caller' trace()
say .o~new~m 'caller' trace()
say rr() 'caller' trace()
interpret 'x = trace("F")'
say 'interpret' trace()
call trace 'O'
exit
plain:
say 'plain' trace()
call trace 'R'
say 'plain' trace()
return
hidden: procedure
say 'hidden' trace()
call trace 'I'
say 'hidden' trace()
call trace 'O'
return
::class o
::method m
x = trace()
call trace 'F'
return x trace()
::routine rr
x = trace()
call trace 'F'
return x trace()

plain R
caller E
hidden E
hidden I
caller E
N F caller E
N F caller E

Errors

[bif.trace.error]

When option is not valid, TRACE raises SYNTAX 24.1, and the setting is as it was. An option is valid when it is the null string, or when, after any question marks at its start, its first character is a letter of the setting in either case. Any other first character is invalid, among them a blank, a digit, a sign, another letter, a character that is not a letter in ASCII, a null character and a further question mark after a blank. An option that is only question marks is valid. An object other than a string is replaced by a string, as a string argument says.

call trace 'A'
call trace 'O'
call show
exit
show: procedure
call trace 'R'
say try(' n') try('x') try('5') try('-1') try('=') try('?x') try('? n')
say try('é') try('?' || '00'x) try(.nil) try('N' || '00'x) try(.array~new)
say trace()
call trace 'O'
exit
try: procedure
signal on syntax name e
x = trace(arg(1))
call trace 'R'
return 'ok'
e: return condition('o')~code

24.1 24.1 24.1 ok ok
R

Note. The ANSI draft (9.5.9) flips the interactive tracing once for each question mark in front of a letter, from whatever it was; ooRexx sets it from whether the count is odd, and the rule follows ooRexx. The reference manual allows a number in the TRACE instruction and not in the function, which matches the rule above.

TRANSLATE

TRANSLATE(string [, tableo] [, tablei] [, pad] [, pos] [, length])

ANSI: 9.3.23; rexxref: Functions > Built-in Functions > TRANSLATE

Deviations: D4, D94

TRANSLATE replaces characters of a string, or of a run of its characters, through a pair of tables: a character found in the input table tablei is replaced by the character at the same position in the output table tableo. Called with no table and no pad, it uppercases instead.

Arguments

[bif.translate.method]

TRANSLATE is a builtin that runs as a String method, and string, its first argument, is the receiver; the other five become the message's arguments, in their order. string, tableo and tablei are strings, pad is a pad, pos is a position, and length is a length. The arguments are checked in the order the conventions give, and the argument count by the builtin call rules: one is required and six is the most.

say translate('tab', 'TB', 'tb') 'tab'~translate('TB', 'tb', , 2)
signal on syntax name a
say translate('abc', , , , 0)
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say translate('abc', , , , 1, -3)
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say translate('abc', 'x', 'a', '--')
c: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name d
say translate('abc', , , , 'one')
d: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name f
say translate('abc', , , , 1, 1, 1)
f: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name g
say translate(, 'x')
g: say condition('o')~code

TaB taB
93.924
93.923
40.23
40.12
40.4
40.5
[bif.translate.tablei.default]

When tablei is omitted, it is the string of all 256 characters in order, from '00'x to 'FF'x. Each character is then found in it at the position one more than its byte value, C2D(c) + 1, so tableo is indexed by byte value.

say translate('0a0102'x, 'abc' || copies('-', 7) || 'k')

kbc
[bif.translate.tableo.default]

When tableo is omitted, it is the null string, so every character found in tablei is replaced by pad, unless the uppercasing rule applies.

say '['translate('abcabc', , 'ca')']' translate('abcabc', , 'ca', '#')

[ b  b ] #b##b#
[bif.translate.pad.default]

When pad is omitted, it is the blank, '20'x.

say '['translate('pq', 'x', 'pq')']'

[x ]
[bif.translate.pos.default]

When pos is omitted, it is 1: the run of characters translated starts at the first character of string.

say translate('aaa', 'b', 'a', , , 2) translate('aaa', 'b', 'a', , 1, 2)

bba bba
[bif.translate.length.default]

When length is omitted, the run is every character of string at position pos and after it, and no character when pos is greater than LENGTH(string).

say translate('aaaa', 'b', 'a', , 3) translate('aaaa', 'b', 'a', , 5)

aabb aaaa

The result

[bif.translate.upper]

When tableo, tablei and pad are all omitted, TRANSLATE returns string with each character of the run from pos for length characters uppercased as UPPER does, and every other character unchanged. The result is then UPPER(string, pos, length), with the same defaults for pos and length.

say translate('hello, world') translate('hello, world', , , , 8, 3)

HELLO, WORLD hello, WORld
[bif.translate.result]

When at least one of tableo, tablei and pad is given, TRANSLATE returns a string of LENGTH(string) characters. Each character c of string at a position from pos to pos + length - 1 is looked up in tablei. When c occurs in it, let k be the position of its first occurrence: the result has, in place of c, the character of tableo at position k when LENGTH(tableo) is at least k, and pad otherwise. When c does not occur in tablei, it is copied unchanged, and so is every character of string outside the run.

say translate('a1b2c3', 'xyz', 'abc') translate('a1b2c3', 'xyz', '123', , 3)

x1y2z3 a1bycz
[bif.translate.first]

When a character occurs more than once in tablei, its first occurrence alone decides what it becomes; the characters of tableo at the positions of the later occurrences are never used.

say translate('mom', 'abc', 'mmo') translate('mom', '123', 'omo')

aca 212
[bif.translate.tableo.length]

tableo need not be as long as tablei. When it is shorter, a character found in tablei at a position past the end of tableo is replaced by pad; when it is longer, its characters past the length of tablei are never used.

say translate('wxyz', 'WX', 'wxyz', '+') translate('wxyz', 'WXYZ123', 'wx')

WX++ WXyz
[bif.translate.pad-only]

When both tables are omitted and pad is given, every character of the run is replaced by pad, since every character is found in the default tablei and the default tableo has no characters.

say translate('secret', , , '*') translate('secret', , , '*', 3, 2)

****** se**et

Note. The ANSI draft (9.3.23) uppercases whenever both tables are omitted and ignores pad then. This page follows ooRexx, where the reference manual says a given pad replaces the whole string.

[bif.translate.tablei.empty]

When tablei is given as the null string, no character is found in it, and the result is string unchanged, for every tableo, pad, pos and length that pass their checks.

say translate('abc', 'xyz', '') translate('abc', , '', '*') translate('abc', '', '')

abc abc abc

Note. This holds however the null string was produced, which ooRexx does not do: see Deviation 94.

[bif.translate.past-end]

When pos is greater than LENGTH(string), no character is translated and the result is string, for every pos past the end that passes its check. When the run reaches past the end of string, it stops there, and nothing is added.

say translate('abc', , , '*', 4) translate('abc', , , , 999999999999999999),
    translate('abc', , , '*', 2, 50)

abc abc a**
[bif.translate.length.zero]

When length is 0, no character is translated and the result is string, for every pos that passes its check. pad is still checked, as a pad always is.

say translate('abc', , , '*', 2, 0) translate('abc', , , , 1, 0)
signal on syntax name e
say translate('abc', , , '', 1, 0)
e: say condition('o')~code

abc abc
40.23
[bif.translate.empty]

When string is the null string, the result is the null string, for every table, pad, pos and length that pass their checks.

say '['translate('')']' '['translate('', 'a', 'b', '*', 3, 4)']'

[] []
[bif.translate.bytes]

TRANSLATE looks characters up and replaces them by character, one byte each: whitespace, control characters and '00'x are found, replaced and used as replacements like any other character, in string, in both tables and as pad.

say c2x(translate('610009'x, '0920'x, '0009'x)) c2x(translate('ab', , 'b', '00'x))

610920 6100

Deviations

[bif.translate.deviation.4]

interrexx does not specify whether the answer of TRANSLATE is the same object as another string of equal value: as string itself, when no character of it changes, as in translate(s, '', ''), or as an equal string produced some other way, such as the literal 'MNOP' beside translate('mn' || 'op'). Through identityHash, or as a key of an IdentityTable, the answer may be either, and a program can rely only on the value, which is equal under ==. ooRexx differs: it often answers a new object where interrexx answers the existing one.

s = 'mn' || 'op'
say (translate(s, '', '') == s) (translate('mn' || 'op') == 'MNOP')

1 1
[bif.translate.deviation.94]

A tablei given as the null string is an empty table whether it was written as '' or answered by an expression, such as LEFT(s, 0), COPIES(s, 0) or STRIP of a string of blanks. ooRexx differs: a null string that some of its builtins answer counts as given, so it does not uppercase, but it is searched as if it were the default tablei, so every character of the run is translated. There translate('abc', , LEFT('abc', 0)) answers three blanks. The same holds for the String method's tablei. A null tableo produced the same way agrees on both.

z = left('abc', 0)
say '['translate('abc', , z)']' translate('abc', , z, '*') 'ab'~translate(z, z)

[abc] abc ab

TRUNC

TRUNC(number [, n])

ANSI: 9.4.6; rexxref: Functions > Built-in Functions > TRUNC (Truncate)

Deviations: D4

TRUNC cuts a number off after a given number of decimal places, without rounding at the cut, and writes the result in plain notation with exactly that many places.

Arguments

[bif.trunc.method]

TRUNC is a builtin that runs as a String method, and number, its first argument, is the receiver; n becomes the message's argument. number is a number and n is a whole-number argument that is the count of decimal places. The argument count is checked by the builtin call rules: one is required and two is the most.

say trunc(12.37) 12.37~trunc 12.37~trunc(1) trunc(12.37, 1)
signal on syntax name a
say trunc()
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say trunc(, 1)
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say trunc(1, 1, 1)
c: say condition('o')~code

12 12 12.3 12.3
40.3
40.5
40.4
[bif.trunc.n.default]

When n is omitted, it is 0.

say trunc(7.9) trunc(7.9, ) trunc(7.9, 0)

7 7 7
[bif.trunc.errors]

The checks run in this order, and the first that fails is raised: the form and value of n, which raise SYNTAX 40.12; that number is a number, SYNTAX 93.943; and last that n is not negative, SYNTAX 93.906. n is a whole-number argument, so the null string raises 40.12 and -0 is 0. A string that is not a number is therefore raised even when n is negative, and a negative n is raised only for a number that is valid.

say trunc(5, '-0') trunc(5, ' 2 ') trunc(5, '1e1')
signal on syntax name a
say trunc(5, '')
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say trunc('x', 'y')
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say trunc('x', -1)
c: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name d
say trunc(5, -1)
d: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name e
say trunc(5, 1.5)
e: say condition('o')~code

5 5.00 5.0000000000
40.12
40.12
93.943
93.906
40.12

The result

[bif.trunc.result]

TRUNC first rounds the number to NUMERIC DIGITS significant digits. It then keeps the digits of its integer part, and n digits after the point, and drops the rest, so the magnitude is cut, not rounded: a decimal place beyond n has no effect on the ones before it. When the number has fewer than n decimal places, zeros are added to make n. With n of 0 the result is the integer part alone, with no point.

say trunc(358.46913, 2) trunc(358.4, 3) trunc(358, 1) trunc(-12.79, 1),
    trunc(0.999, 0) trunc(-5.55, 1) trunc(5.55, 1)

358.46 358.400 358.0 -12.7 0 -5.5 5.5
[bif.trunc.plain]

The result is always written in plain notation, never with an exponent, however many digits that takes and whatever NUMERIC FORM is. A number that has an exponent is written out in full, and the digits dropped by the rounding to NUMERIC DIGITS are written as zeros, and a decimal place cut off after that rounding is not rounded again.

say trunc('1.5e3') trunc('1e20') trunc('1.5e-3', 5) trunc('1e-20', 3)
numeric form engineering
say trunc('1.2345E+11', 2) trunc('1e-7', 8)
numeric digits 5
say trunc('1234567.89', 1) trunc('99999.9') trunc('0.000012345678', 8)

1500 100000000000000000000 0.00150 0.000
123450000000.00 0.00000010
1234600.0 100000 0.00001234
[bif.trunc.sign]

A negative number keeps its - when the result has a nonzero digit, and loses it when every digit of the result is zero, so TRUNC never answers a negative zero.

say trunc(-0.5) trunc(-0.5, 2) trunc(-0.001, 2) trunc(-0.001, 3),
    trunc('-0') trunc('-0.0', 1) trunc(-1.2, 0)

0 -0.50 0.00 -0.001 0 0.0 -1

Note. The ANSI draft (9.4.6) checks number before an n that is not a whole number, where ooRexx, which this book follows, raises 40.12 for n first (for a negative n both check number first). It raises SYNTAX 40.13 for a negative n, where ooRexx raises 93.906.

Deviations

[bif.trunc.deviation.4]

interrexx does not specify whether the answer of TRUNC is the same object as another string of equal value: as number itself, when the call leaves it unchanged, or as an equal string produced some other way. Through identityHash, or as a key of an IdentityTable, the answer may be either, and a program can rely only on the value, which is equal under ==. ooRexx differs: it answers the argument itself in a case where interrexx may answer an equal new string.

s = '12' || '5'
say (trunc(s) == s) (trunc('125') == '125') (trunc(s, 1) == '125.0')

1 1 1

UPPER

UPPER(string [, n] [, length])

rexxref: Functions > Built-in Functions > UPPER

Deviations: D4

UPPER changes the lowercase letters of a string, or of a run of its characters, to uppercase, and leaves every other character as it is.

Arguments

[bif.upper.method]

UPPER is a builtin that runs as a String method, and string, its first argument, is the receiver; n and length become the message's arguments, in that order. string is a string, n is a position, and length is a length. The arguments are checked in the order the conventions give, and the argument count by the builtin call rules: one is required and three is the most.

say upper('mixed Case') 'mixed Case'~upper(7)
signal on syntax name a
say upper('abc', 0)
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say upper('abc', 1, -2)
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say upper('abc', 0, 'two')
c: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name d
say upper('abc', 1, 1, 1)
d: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name f
say upper(, 2)
f: say condition('o')~code

MIXED CASE mixed CASE
93.924
93.923
40.12
40.4
40.5
[bif.upper.n.default]

When n is omitted, it is 1: the run starts at the first character of string.

say upper('xyz', , 2) upper('xyz', 1, 2)

XYz XYz
[bif.upper.length.default]

When length is omitted, the run is every character of string at position n and after it, and no character when n is greater than LENGTH(string).

say upper('lower', 3) upper('lower', 5) upper('lower', 6)

loWER loweR lower

The result

[bif.upper.case]

Uppercasing changes exactly the 26 characters 'a' to 'z', '61'x to '7A'x, each to the letter 'A' to 'Z' with the same place in the alphabet, '41'x to '5A'x. Every other character is left as it is: the uppercase letters, the digits, whitespace, '00'x, and every character from '80'x to 'FF'x, including the bytes that an encoding such as Latin-1 or UTF-8 uses for a lowercase letter.

say upper('q-z 0?_') c2x(upper('e9c3a9ff'x)) c2x(upper('60617a7b'x))
all = xrange('00'x, 'ff'x)
say (upper(all) == translate(all, xrange('A', 'Z'), xrange('a', 'z')))

Q-Z 0?_ E9C3A9FF 60415A7B
1

Note. The reference manual's UPPER section does not name the characters it changes; its TRANSLATE section, which uppercases the same way, names the letters a to z, and this rule follows that. The ANSI draft has no UPPER builtin, and leaves the uppercase form of each character to the configuration (5.4.3).

[bif.upper.result]

UPPER returns a string of LENGTH(string) characters. The character at each position from n to n + length - 1 that string has is uppercased, and every other character of string is copied unchanged. A run that reaches past the end of string stops at the end, and nothing is added.

say '['upper('string', 2, 3)']' '['upper('string', 4, 100)']' '['upper('ab cd')']'

[sTRIng] [strING] [AB CD]
[bif.upper.past-end]

When n is greater than LENGTH(string), no character is changed and the result is string, for every n past the end that passes its check.

say upper('abc', 4) upper('abc', 999999999999999999, 2)

abc abc
[bif.upper.length.zero]

When length is 0, no character is changed and the result is string, for every n that passes its check.

say upper('abc', 2, 0) upper('abc', 50, 0)

abc abc
[bif.upper.empty]

When string is the null string, the result is the null string, for every n and length that pass their checks.

say '['upper('')']' '['upper('', 3, 2)']'

[] []

Deviations

Note. An argument whose STRING method answers an object that is not a string falls under Deviation 30, as it does for every builtin.

[bif.upper.deviation.4]

interrexx does not specify whether the answer of UPPER is the same object as another string of equal value: as string itself, when no character of it changes, as in upper(s) for an s with no lowercase letter, or as an equal string produced some other way, such as the literal 'GHIJ' beside upper('gh' || 'ij'). Through identityHash, or as a key of an IdentityTable, the answer may be either, and a program can rely only on the value, which is equal under ==. ooRexx differs: it often answers a new object where interrexx answers the existing one.

s = 'PQ' || 'RS'
say (upper(s) == s) (upper('gh' || 'ij') == 'GHIJ')

1 1

USERID

USERID()

rexxref: Functions > Built-in Functions > USERID

USERID answers the user name of the account that the program runs as. It takes no argument and changes nothing.

The name is the login name of the account, as the system's account database records it for the user the process runs as. On a Unix-like system that is the name the id -un command prints. Which name that is depends on whoever runs the program, so no rule fixes a value.

Note. The examples state the answer through a comparison with the name that the id command prints, and through its independence of the program's environment. They fix no name.

Arguments

[bif.userid.args]

USERID takes no argument. A call with an argument raises SYNTAX 40.4, by the call rules. A trailing omitted place adds nothing to the count, so USERID(,) is a call without an argument. USERID does not run as a String method: sending the message USERID to a string raises SYNTAX 97.1.

signal on syntax name a
say userid(1)
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say userid(, 'x')
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say 'x'~userid
c: say condition('o')~code
signal off syntax
say userid(,) == userid()

40.4
40.4
97.1
1

The result

[bif.userid.name]

The answer is the login name of the account the process runs as, which is what the id -un command prints. It has no blanks around it, and it is not the null string. For an account that the system's account database does not hold, such as one that only a network directory knows, the answer is not specified.

address system 'id -un' with output stem name.
say userid() == name.1
say (userid() == strip(userid())) (userid() \== '')

1
1 1
[bif.userid.environment]

For an account the system's account database holds, USERID does not read the environment: setting the USER or LOGNAME environment variable, or removing either of them, does not change the answer.

before = userid()
oldUser = value('USER', , 'ENVIRONMENT')
oldLog = value('LOGNAME', , 'ENVIRONMENT')
call value 'USER', 'spec_userid_other', 'ENVIRONMENT'
call value 'LOGNAME', 'spec_userid_other', 'ENVIRONMENT'
address system 'test -z "${USER+set}${LOGNAME+set}"'
say rc (userid() == before)
call value 'USER', .nil, 'ENVIRONMENT'
call value 'LOGNAME', .nil, 'ENVIRONMENT'
address system 'test -z "${USER+set}${LOGNAME+set}"'
say rc (userid() == before)
if oldUser == '' then call value 'USER', .nil, 'ENVIRONMENT'
else call value 'USER', oldUser, 'ENVIRONMENT'
if oldLog == '' then call value 'LOGNAME', .nil, 'ENVIRONMENT'
else call value 'LOGNAME', oldLog, 'ENVIRONMENT'
say (value('USER', , 'ENVIRONMENT') == oldUser) (value('LOGNAME', , 'ENVIRONMENT') == oldLog)

1 1
0 1
1 1

VALUE

VALUE(name [, newvalue [, selector]])

ANSI: 9.8.6; rexxref: Functions > Built-in Functions > VALUE

VALUE reads a variable whose name the program has as a string, and when it is given a new value, assigns that value to the variable. It answers the value the variable had before the call. Its third argument chooses where the variable is: among the variables of the running code, among the entries of the .environment directory, or among the environment variables of the operating system.

Arguments

[bif.value.args]

name and selector are strings and newvalue can be any object. The argument count is checked by the builtin call rules: one argument is required and three is the most. VALUE does not run as a String method: sending the message VALUE to a string raises SYNTAX 97.1.

x = 'a'
say value('x') value('x', ) value('x', , )
signal on syntax name a
say value()
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say value(, 1)
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say value('x', 1, , 2)
c: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name d
say 'x'~value
d: say condition('o')~code

a a a
40.3
40.5
40.4
97.1
[bif.value.selector]

selector chooses the variables name is looked up in. When it is omitted, they are the variables of the running code. When it is the null string, they are the entries of the .environment directory. When it is ENVIRONMENT, in any combination of cases and with nothing around it, they are the environment variables of the operating system. Any other selector raises SYNTAX 40.914, and it is checked before name is, so a call with an invalid selector raises it also when name is invalid.

signal on syntax name a
say value('x', , 'SYSTEM')
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say value('x y', , 'ENV')
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say value('x', , 'ENVIRONMENT ')
c: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name d
say value('x', , .nil)
d: say condition('o')~code
say value('x', , 'Environment') '/' value('x', , '')

40.914
40.914
40.914
40.914
 / .X

Variables of the running code

[bif.value.local]

When selector is omitted, VALUE works on the variables that the routine or method running it can see, as SYMBOL does: a routine with PROCEDURE sees none of its caller's variables except the ones it EXPOSEs, and a method sees an object variable once it exposes it. VALUE does not expose a variable: what it reads or assigns is not an object variable unless the method exposed it.

g = 'caller'
call plain
call hidden
say g
o = .o~new
say o~read o~exposed
exit
plain:
say value('g') value('g', 'changed') g
return
hidden: procedure
say value('g') value('g', 'private') g
return
::class o
::attribute at
::method read
return value('at') value('at', 'local') at
::method exposed
expose at
at = 'object'
return value('at') value('at', 'changed') at

caller caller changed
G G private
changed
AT AT local object object changed
[bif.value.name]

name must be a symbol: a string that SYMBOL does not call BAD. Any other, among them the null string, a string with a blank anywhere in it, one with a character that is not a symbol character and one of more than 250 characters, raises SYNTAX 40.26. It is read in uppercase, so it names the same variable in either case, and the name of a compound variable has the parts of its tail replaced by the values of the variables they name, as the compound rule of SYMBOL says. An object other than a string is replaced by a string, as a string argument says.

idx = 3
box.3 = 'three'
ab = 'plain'
say value('AB') value('ab') value('box.idx') value('BOX.IDXX') value('box.3')
signal on syntax name a
say value('')
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say value('a b')
b: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name c
say value('a-b')
c: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name d
say value(copies('a', 251))
d: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name e
say value(.nil)
e: say condition('o')~code
say length(value(copies('a', 250)))

plain plain three BOX.IDXX three

250
[bif.value.get]

The result is the value of the variable named by name, as the program sees it when it uses the symbol. A variable that holds no value, or has been dropped, answers the name as the program would then see it: in uppercase, with the parts of a compound name's tail that name a variable holding a value replaced by that value and the others left as they are. VALUE never raises the NOVALUE condition, so a trap for it does not see the call. A symbol that is a constant symbol, a number or one that starts with a period, is answered as it is, in uppercase, except that a name that stands for an object of the environment, such as .nil, answers that object. The value is the object the variable holds, not a copy of it, and a variable that holds a non-string object answers it, so the call can be used with ~.

signal on novalue name nv

o = .array~of(1, 2)

[bif.value.set]

When newvalue is given, even as the null string, the variable named by name is given it as its value, after the result has been found: the result is the value from before. An omitted newvalue is the only case where nothing is assigned. Any object can be the new value and is stored as it is, with no change by NUMERIC DIGITS. The name of a constant symbol, a number or a symbol that starts with a period, cannot be assigned to, and the call raises SYNTAX 40.26.

say value('v', 'first') value('v', 'second') value('v', ) value('v')

[bif.value.stem]

A name that ends at its first period is a stem. Read, it answers the stem object, which the program uses as it does the stem. Given a newvalue, it gives every compound variable of the stem that value, those assigned before included, as the assignment stem. = value does. Both are references to the stem, as for SYMBOL.

s.1 = 'own'
say value('s.', 'dflt') s.1 s.2 value('s.2') value('s.zz')
x = value('s.')

Stem dflt dflt 1

Entries of the .environment directory

[bif.value.directory]

When selector is the null string, VALUE works on the entries of the .environment directory, the one that the symbol .name finds its object in. The entry is the one whose index is name in uppercase, with no check that it is a symbol, no replacement in a compound name and no other change, so the name of a compound variable is the index of one entry. The result is the object in the entry, and for a name with no entry it is the string made of a period and the name in uppercase. A newvalue is stored in the entry as it is, and the null string and .nil are values like any other. Because the directory is the one that the symbol .name reads, the program sees an assigned object as .name.

k = 'tail'
say value('t14a', , '') value('T14A', 'one', '') value('t14a', 'two', '')
say value('T14A', , '') .t14a .environment~at('T14A')
say value('t14b.k', 'x', '') .environment~at('T14B.K') value('T14B.TAIL', , '')
say value('t14c', .array~of(1), '')~class~id value('t14c', .nil, '')~class~id,
    value('t14c', , '') '['value('t14d', '', '')']' '['value('t14d', , '')']'
say value('.t14e', 'dot', '') value('t14e', , '') value('.t14e', , '')

two two two
